Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AdjointDefectBou.text:
Fix any index j among the k certificate indices, a real field ψ(θ,y), center fields Wα⁰, fitted direction fields Wⁱ for i in a finite set I, and remaining fields Zαⁱ for i outside I; all fields are defined for real θ and y∈ℝ³. Membership j∈𝒥 is not required by this condition, although Lemma B.12 uses it for indices in 𝒥. The parameter set is 𝒦={α:|αi|≤ρi for i∈𝒥, ∑_{i∉𝒥}(diαi)²≤ρ*²}. The proposed coordinate bounds ρ̄i must satisfy ρi≤ρ̄i on 𝒥 and, off 𝒥, di≠0 and |ρ*|≤|di|ρ̄i.

For the center and each fitted direction s∈{0}∪I, supply potentials Gs,Us,Fs,qs and four nonnegative numbers nG,s,nU,s,nF,s,nR,s. Over [0,1]×ℝ³, require ‖Gs‖₂≤nG,s, ‖∇Us‖₂≤nU,s and ‖Fs‖₂≤nF,s, with Frobenius norms for matrices. Here this norm notation denotes bounds on the nonnegative extended integrals of the squares. The condition does not itself require measurability of these potential fields; that is needed for their usual L² interpretation. Put K=∇ψ−∑lYl[∇Φ̃l−(∇Φ̃l)ᵀ]. At the center, for every α∈𝒦, the residual Tα⁰−div K+∇q₀+∆G₀+w*∆U₀−div F₀ must have dual bound nR,0, where Tα⁰=−S₀⁻¹∂θψ−ψ−(y·∇)ψ/2+(DWα⁰)ᵀψ−(Wα⁰·∇)ψ. For each i∈I, the residual Ti+∇qi+∆Gi+w*∆Ui−div Fi must have dual bound nR,i, where Ti=(DWⁱ)ᵀψ−(Wⁱ·∇)ψ−ςi∂θψ. Matrix divergence means ∑a∂a(F ea), so the paper writes the flux divergence with a transpose under its matrix convention.

Here a dual bound n means a pointwise decomposition into two measurable summands with nonnegative allowances whose sum is at most n. One summand obeys 2‖|y|R′‖₂≤n′. Each of the three complex components R″₁+iR″₂, R″₁−iR″₂, R″₃ of the other is, at every time and almost everywhere in space, a finite sum e^{2πik′θ}g(y), with distinct integer frequency pairs per component and g(Rφy)=e^{ikφ}g(y). The sum of (|k|+1/2)⁻²∫|y|²|g|², counting each transverse component with weight 1/2, is at most n″². This is the condition before Lemma B.11 with the paper's separate periodicity requirement omitted.

For every i∉I require ϖi>0, and require nv,nd≥0. Uniformly for α∈𝒦, require ∫₀¹∫ℝ³(∑_{i∉I}ϖi|Zαⁱ|²)|ψ|²≤nv². There must be common bounds δi such that each (DZαⁱ)ᵀψ has dual bound δi for every α and ∑_{i∉I}ϖiδi²≤nd². The field ∂θψ must have dual bound nθ.

For the potential fields Φl, their replacements Φ̃l and the matrix-valued constraint fields Ξl, require nΦ,cΞ≥0, ‖∑lYl(Φl−Φ̃l)‖₂≤nΦ, and ‖∑lcl(Ξl−∇Φl)‖₂²≤cΞ²∑lcl² for every real vector c. Also require the Euclidean coefficient bound |Y|≤nY. Field norms and integrals are over [0,1]×ℝ³; the coefficient norms are finite-dimensional Euclidean norms.

Define Ds=[nG,s²+(w*nU,s+nF,s+nR,s)²/w*]¹ᐟ². The required total inequality is D₀+∑_{i∈I}ρ̄iDi+{[∑_{i∉I}ρ̄i²/ϖi]¹ᐟ²(nv+nd)+(∑_{i∉I}|ςi|ρ̄i)nθ}/√w*+nΦ+nYcΞ/√w*≤aj. This is the explicit generalization of (B.53) with selected directions treated by their own potentials; I empty gives the paper's collective treatment. The condition alone does not identify these supplied fields with the profile and adjoint of a certificate or impose their regularity, periodicity or w*>0. Those are separate linking and representation hypotheses. Division by zero and the square root of a negative number are defined to be zero in the raw formulas, so positive w* is needed for the stated energy interpretation.
Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AdjointDefectBou.summary: Collects the numerical assumptions for the linear adjoint estimate at index $j$: bounds on $|\alpha_i|$, potential and residual norms, dual bounds, $n_\Phi$, $c_\Xi$ and $n_Y$, with their total at most $a_j$. The paper's (B.53) is the case with no fitted directions.

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AdjointDefectBou.text: This field of the adjoint-defect assumptions requires, for every real coefficient vector x∈ℝⁿ, ∫₀¹∫_{ℝ³}|∑ᵢx_i(Ξ_i−∇Φ_i)|_F²≤c_Ξ²∑ᵢx_i². The matrix square is the sum of squared Euclidean norms of its columns, so the left side is the squared H norm in the paper. The integral is initially nonnegative and may be infinite; the finite right side bounds it. Nonnegativity of c_Ξ is required elsewhere in the same data condition. Consequently this squared inequality gives ‖∑ᵢx_i(Ξ_i−∇Φ_i)‖_H≤c_Ξ|x|. The hypothesis concerns all x, including combinations of distinct constraints; it is stronger than independent bounds for the individual tensors.
Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AdjointDefectBou.summary: Adjoint-defect assumption: for every $x\in\mathbb R^n$, $\int_0^1\int|\sum_ix_i(\Xi_i-\nabla\Phi_i)|_F^2\le c_\Xi^2\sum_ix_i^2$, giving $\|\sum_ix_i(\Xi_i-\nabla\Phi_i)\|_{\mathcal H}\le c_\Xi|x|$. It is stronger than separate bounds for each tensor.

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AdjointDefectEnt.text: The data provide an adjoint field ψ; k real constraint coefficients Yl and the two families of potential fields Φl,Φ̃l; a parameter-dependent center field Wα⁰; a base period S₀ and reciprocal-period rates ςi; a finite set I of parameter directions treated by separate potentials; fixed vector fields for those directions and parameter-dependent fields for the remaining directions. They also provide center and fitted potentials G,U,F,q and their four proposed norm bounds; coordinate bounds ρ̄i; weights ϖi for the remaining directions; bounds nv,nd,nθ; and constraint replacement errors nΦ,cΞ and a coefficient-norm bound nY. These are the data for (B.52)–(B.53), generalized to allow selected directions to be estimated by their own potentials. These data assert no field identity or error inequality.
Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AdjointDefectEnt.summary: Data for (B.52)–(B.53): an adjoint ψ, constraint coefficients and potential fields, a center field, periods and rates, fitted directions, residuals and potentials with proposed bounds, weights and constraint replacement errors. No identity or inequality is imposed.

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AdjointDefectEnt.text: For the chosen adjoint field ψ, center field Wα⁰, and base period S₀, this is −S₀⁻¹∂θψ−ψ−(y·∇)ψ/2+(DWα⁰)ᵀψ−(Wα⁰·∇)ψ. It is the center transport contribution in (B.52). The diffusion and constraint terms are supplied separately by the flux divergence, and the potentials are added separately. This definition applies to every parameter vector α, without requiring α∈𝒦 or S₀>0. At S₀=0 the reciprocal coefficient is zero by convention.
Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AdjointDefectEnt.summary: Defines −S₀⁻¹∂θψ−ψ−(y·∇)ψ/2+(DWα⁰)ᵀψ−(Wα⁰·∇)ψ, the center transport contribution in (B.52), for every α. Diffusion, constraint terms and potentials are added separately; at S₀=0 the reciprocal coefficient is zero by convention.

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AdjointDefectEnt.text: Let $w_*>0$. For potential bounds $n=(n_G,n_U,n_F,n_R)$ put $D(n)=\sqrt{n_G^2+(w_*n_U+n_F+n_R)^2/w_*}$. If a finite set $I$ of parameter directions has its own fitted potential bounds $n^{(i)}$, this definition is $D(n^{(0)})+\sum_{i\in I}\bar\varrho_iD(n^{(i)})+w_*^{-1/2}\{[\sum_{i\notin I}\bar\varrho_i^2/\varpi_i]^{1/2}(n_{\mathrm v}+n_{\mathrm d})+[\sum_{i\notin I}|\varsigma_i|\bar\varrho_i]n_\theta\}$. The paper-specific identification sets $I=\varnothing$, leaving the first two terms of (B.53). The constraint replacement charge is added separately. The definition itself accepts arbitrary real inputs and takes division by zero to be zero and the square root of a negative real number to be zero; its application requires $w_*>0$ and $\varpi_i>0$, and nonnegative norm bounds. It is a proposed numerical budget, with no assertion here that the fields satisfy it.
Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AdjointDefectEnt.summary: Defines $D(n^{(0)})+\sum_{i\in I}\bar\varrho_iD(n^{(i)})$ plus velocity, dual and $n_\theta$ terms over $i\notin I$, $D(n)=\sqrt{n_G^2+(w_*n_U+n_F+n_R)^2/w_*}$; $I=\varnothing$ gives the first two terms of (B.53). Division by zero and square roots of negatives are taken as zero.

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AdjointDefectEnt.text: For a fixed parameter direction i, vector field Wi, reciprocal-period rate ςi, and adjoint field ψ, the expression is (DWi)ᵀψ−(Wi·∇)ψ−ςi∂θψ. It is the coefficient of αi in the adjoint convection and period variation in the second line of (B.56). The formal construction permits selected directions to be treated by separate potential decompositions, whereas (B.53) presents a collective estimate for these directions. No potential, regularity, parameter bound, or error estimate is included in this definition.
Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AdjointDefectEnt.summary: Defines (DWi)ᵀψ−(Wi·∇)ψ−ςi∂θψ, the coefficient of αi in the adjoint convection and period variation in the second line of (B.56). The formal construction lets selected directions have their own potential decompositions, where (B.53) estimates them collectively.

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AdjointDefectEnt.text: This definition forms $n_\Phi+n_Yc_\Xi/\sqrt{w_*}$. Here $n_\Phi$ bounds $\|\sum_lY_{jl}(\Phi_l-\widetilde\Phi_l)\|_{\mathcal H}$, $n_Y$ bounds the Euclidean norm of the row $(Y_{jl})_l$, and $c_\Xi$ controls the $L^2$ matrix error in replacing $\Xi_l$ by $\nabla\Phi_l$. The two contributions pair with $\Delta v$ and $\nabla v$ respectively. For a positive constant weight they give the last part of (B.53) after division by the energy norm. This declaration defines the number; the assertions that it bounds those pairings, and that the indicated numbers bound the norms, are separate statements. Division by zero is defined to be zero, but the intended use has $w_*=39/50>0$.
Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AdjointDefectEnt.summary: Defines $n_\Phi+n_Yc_\Xi/\sqrt{w_*}$, the constraint replacement charge; for a positive constant weight it gives the last part of (B.53). That it bounds the pairings is a separate statement. Division by zero is taken as zero; the intended use has $w_*=39/50$.

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AdjointDefectEnt.text:
For the fixed adjoint $\psi_j$, compact generators $\widetilde\Phi_l$ and real coefficients $Y_{jl}$, this definition forms $K=
abla\psi_j-\sum_lY_{jl}(
abla\widetilde\Phi_l-(
abla\widetilde\Phi_l)^{\mathsf T})$. A gradient is represented by the map that sends a coordinate vector to the corresponding directional derivative. Thus the divergence of this matrix map is $\Delta\psi_j-\sum_lY_{jl}(\Delta\widetilde\Phi_l-
abla\operatorname{div}\widetilde\Phi_l)$. For the divergence-free generators of the paper, $-\operatorname{div}K=-\Delta\psi_j+\sum_lY_{jl}\Delta\widetilde\Phi_l$, which supplies precisely those terms in (B.52). The definition alone does not assert regularity or divergence-freeness. The skew part of the generator gradient is retained explicitly in the general formal construction. In this definition a pointwise derivative is zero wherever the corresponding function is not differentiable. Regularity is needed before these expressions can be read as distributional derivatives.
Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AdjointDefectEnt.summary:
Defines $K=
abla\psi_j-\sum_lY_{jl}(
abla\widetilde\Phi_l-(
abla\widetilde\Phi_l)^{\mathsf T})$. For divergence-free generators, $-\operatorname{div}K=-\Delta\psi_j+\sum_lY_{jl}\Delta\widetilde\Phi_l$, as in (B.52). Derivatives are zero where they do not exist; no regularity is asserted.

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AzimuthalBounded.text: Let $R$ be a measurable real vector field on $\mathbb R_\theta\times\mathbb R_y^3$, and let $n\ge0$. The condition represents each of $R_1+iR_2$, $R_1-iR_2$ and $R_3$, almost everywhere in $y$ for every $\theta$, as a finite sum $\sum e^{2\pi i k'\theta}g(y)$. Each amplitude is measurable and satisfies $g(R_\phi y)=e^{ik\phi}g(y)$ for every angle and point. The integers $k',k$ are distinct as pairs within each component. It requires $\sum c\,(|k|+1/2)^{-2}\int|y|^2|g|^2\le n^2$, with $c=1/2$ for each horizontal complex component and $c=1$ for the third. The denominator is positive for every integer $k$, including zero. The representation implies period one almost everywhere; exact pointwise periodicity is not a separate assumption. These are the harmonic terms called $R''$ in the paper's dual bound.
Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AzimuthalBounded.summary: A measurable field $R$ has each of $R_1\pm iR_2$, $R_3$ written as a finite sum $\sum e^{2\pi ik'\theta}g(y)$ with $g(R_\phi y)=e^{ik\phi}g(y)$ and distinct pairs $(k',k)$, and $\sum c(|k|+1/2)^{-2}\int|y|^2|g|^2\le n^2$, $c=1/2$ horizontal, $1$ vertical. These are the paper's $R''$ terms.

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AzimuthalParts.I.text: For real vectors $v,R\in\mathbb R^3$, define $v^+=v_1+iv_2$, $v^-=v_1-iv_2$ and $v^0=v_3$, and use the same convention for $R$. The formal statement proves $v\cdot R=\tfrac12\operatorname{Re}(\overline{v^+}R^+)+\tfrac12\operatorname{Re}(\overline{v^-}R^-)+v_3R_3$. This is an identity of real numbers, with no regularity or integrability hypotheses. It is the component decomposition used at the end of the proof of Lemma B.11. The two horizontal factors are $1/2$; the vertical factor is $1$. The formal component labels begin at zero and refer in order to $+$, $-$ and the vertical component.
Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AzimuthalParts.I.summary: For real $v,R\in\mathbb R^3$ with $v^\pm=v_1\pm iv_2$, $v\cdot R=\tfrac12\operatorname{Re}(\overline{v^+}R^+)+\tfrac12\operatorname{Re}(\overline{v^-}R^-)+v_3R_3$. It is the component decomposition at the end of the proof of Lemma B.11.

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AzimuthalParts.I.text: For any real matrix $M:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$, let $M^+$, $M^-$ and $M^0$ be the matrices obtained by taking the two horizontal rows as a complex pair, its conjugate, and the vertical row. The formal statement proves $\tfrac12|M^+|^2+\tfrac12|M^-|^2+|M^0|^2=|M|^2$, where each squared norm is the sum of the squared absolute values of its entries, and the complex pair is represented by its two real coordinates. Taking $M=\nabla v$ gives the weighted gradient identity in the proof of Lemma B.11. The formal theorem is purely algebraic for every matrix; applying it almost everywhere and integrating gives the same identity for any weakly differentiable field with finite gradient energy. No symmetry, periodicity or solenoidality is assumed.
Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AzimuthalParts.I.summary: For any real matrix $M$, with $M^\pm$ formed from the two horizontal rows as a complex pair and its conjugate and $M^0$ the vertical row, $\tfrac12|M^+|^2+\tfrac12|M^-|^2+|M^0|^2=|M|^2$. With $M=\nabla v$ it gives the gradient identity in Lemma B.11.

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AzimuthalParts.g.text: For a measurable matrix field $G:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^{3\times3}$, the formal statement proves that the sum over all integer azimuthal modes of its gradient energy in the rotating cylindrical frame is at most $\int_{\mathbb R^3}|G|^2$. The mode energy is integrated with cylindrical measure $2\pi r\,dr\,dz$ on $r>0$, $z\in\mathbb R$; the matrix norm on the right is the sum of squares of all entries. Both sides are nonnegative extended integrals. The statement applies to any measurable matrix field, without requiring that it be the derivative of a velocity. This is the spatial Fourier-energy estimate used to pass from single-mode inequalities to the total bound. Projection in the time variable is a separate operation.
Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AzimuthalParts.g.summary: For a measurable matrix field $G$ on $\mathbb R^3$, the sum over integer azimuthal modes of the gradient energy in the rotating cylindrical frame, with measure $2\pi r\,dr\,dz$, is at most $\int|G|^2$. $G$ need not be a derivative.

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AzimuthalParts.m.text: Let $v:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ and its weak gradient $G$ be measurable, with $v\in L^6$ and $G\in L^2$. Put $U=v_1+iv_2$, and let $U_k(r,z)$ be its normalized angular Fourier coefficient. Given the smooth azimuthal estimate, approximation by smooth compactly supported fields in gradient norm and local $L^2$, and the bound of the total Fourier gradient energy by $\int|G|^2$, the formal statement proves $\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}(|k|+1/2)^2\,2\pi\int_{r>0,z\in\mathbb R}r|U_k|^2/(r^2+z^2)\,dr\,dz\le\int|G|^2$. Thus it controls all angular projections together. The paper states (B.50) for a single complex field already having wave number $k$; representing that field by two real components yields its special case. The three analytic premises are supplied by separate proved declarations in the formalisation. No divergence or reflection assumption on $v$ occurs.
Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AzimuthalParts.m.summary: For $v\in L^6$ with weak gradient $G\in L^2$ and $U=v_1+iv_2$, $\sum_k(|k|+1/2)^2\,2\pi\int r|U_k|^2/(r^2+z^2)\le\int|G|^2$, over all angular modes together. The paper states (B.50) for a single field of wave number $k$, a special case.

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AzimuthalParts.m.text: Let $u,B:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb C$ be measurable, and assume $B(r\cos\phi,r\sin\phi,z)=e^{ik\phi}B(r,0,z)$ for an integer $k$. Let $u_k(r,z)$ be the angular coefficient normalized by $1/(2\pi)$. The formal statement gives $|\int\overline{u}B|^2\le[2\pi\int_{r>0,z\in\mathbb R}r|u_k|^2/(r^2+z^2)]\,[\int|y|^2|B|^2]$. This uses Cauchy–Schwarz after angular projection; combining it with the azimuthal Hardy estimate produces the factor $(|k|+1/2)^{-1}$ in the paper. The displayed conclusion uses the opposite complex conjugation from the paper's pairing, which has the same absolute value. There is no hypothesis that the ordinary complex integral on the left exists in the analytic sense. If its integrand is not integrable, that integral is assigned the value zero. The right-hand side uses nonnegative integrals, which may equal infinity. Thus this statement alone does not establish integrability of the pairing. In the application, finite weighted bounds and a separate integrability theorem justify its ordinary analytic interpretation.
Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AzimuthalParts.m.summary: If $B(r\cos\phi,r\sin\phi,z)=e^{ik\phi}B(r,0,z)$, then $|\int\overline uB|^2\le[2\pi\int r|u_k|^2/(r^2+z^2)][\int|y|^2|B|^2]$, with conjugation opposite to the paper's. A nonintegrable left integral is taken as zero, so integrability of the pairing is not established.

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AzimuthalParts.s.text: Let $u:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ be smooth with compact support, and let $U=u_1+iu_2$. For any integer $k$, form the angular coefficient $U_k(r,z)=(2\pi)^{-1}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}e^{-ik\phi}U(r\cos\phi,r\sin\phi,z)\,d\phi$. The formal statement bounds $(|k|+1/2)^2\,2\pi\int_{r>0}\int_{\mathbb R}r|U_k(r,z)|^2/(r^2+z^2)\,dz\,dr$ by the corresponding Fourier component of the full gradient energy, represented in the rotating cylindrical frame. It is a statement about an angular projection of a smooth real vector field. Taking $u=(\operatorname{Re}U,\operatorname{Im}U,0)$ when $U$ already has wave number $k$ gives the smooth scalar inequality in (B.50). Extending to an $L^6$ field with a weak $L^2$ gradient requires the separate approximation result. The denominator is nonzero on $r>0$.
Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AzimuthalParts.s.summary: For smooth compactly supported $u$, $U=u_1+iu_2$ and integer $k$, $(|k|+1/2)^2\,2\pi\int r|U_k|^2/(r^2+z^2)$ is at most the matching Fourier component of the gradient energy. With $u=(\operatorname{Re}U,\operatorname{Im}U,0)$ it gives the smooth inequality in (B.50).

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AzimuthalParts.t.text: Take a finite family of measurable complex amplitudes $a_p(y)$ and distinct integer temporal frequencies $k'_p$. The formal statement proves $\int_0^1\int|y|^2|\sum_p e^{2\pi i k'_p\theta}a_p(y)|^2\,dy\,d\theta\le\sum_p\int|y|^2|a_p(y)|^2\,dy$. Both sides are nonnegative extended integrals. The frequencies need be distinct only on the selected finite index set. In the adjoint proof this is applied separately to groups having the same azimuthal order, for which distinct pairs imply distinct temporal frequencies. Its conclusion is a weighted $L^2$ estimate for finite harmonic sums; the paper's displayed Bessel inequality concerns arbitrary space-time projections in gradient norm.
Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AzimuthalParts.t.summary: For finitely many measurable amplitudes $a_p$ and distinct integer frequencies $k'_p$, $\int_0^1\int|y|^2|\sum_pe^{2\pi ik'_p\theta}a_p|^2\le\sum_p\int|y|^2|a_p|^2$. The paper's Bessel inequality concerns arbitrary space-time projections in gradient norm.

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AzimuthalParts.w.text: Let a measurable vector field $v:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ have measurable weak gradient $G$, with $v\in L^6$ and $\int|G|^2<\infty$. There exists a sequence of smooth compactly supported real vector fields $u_n$ such that $\int|\nabla u_n-G|^2\to0$ and, for every real radius $R$, $\int_{B_R}|u_n-v|^2\to0$. The ball is centered at the origin; for negative $R$ it is empty. A specified azimuthal wave number is preserved by the subsequent angular projection, which is a separate step. The conclusion here is the approximation before that projection. Complex scalar functions are handled by their real and imaginary parts. No solenoidality condition is required.
Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AzimuthalParts.w.summary: If $v\in L^6$ has measurable weak gradient $G$ with $\int|G|^2<\infty$, there are smooth compactly supported $u_n$ with $\int|\nabla u_n-G|^2\to0$ and $\int_{B_R}|u_n-v|^2\to0$ for every $R$. No solenoidality is required.

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.DualBounded.text: A real field $R$ on $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3$ has this bound $n$ when it is the pointwise sum of two measurable fields $R_h+R_p$, with nonnegative bounds $n_h,n_p$ satisfying $n_h+n_p\le n$. The ordinary part obeys $2\||y|R_p\|_{L^2((0,1)\times\mathbb R^3)}\le n_p$. In each complex component $R_{h,1}\pm iR_{h,2}$ and $R_{h,3}$, the harmonic part is a finite sum $e^{2\pi i k'\theta}g(y)$ of measurable amplitudes with distinct integer pairs $(k',k)$ and $g(R_\phi y)=e^{ik\phi}g(y)$. The sum of $(|k|+1/2)^{-2}\int|y|^2|g|^2$, with weight $1/2$ on each horizontal component, is at most $n_h^2$. This is the paper's decomposition with its two terms listed in reverse order. Unlike the surrounding prose, the definition does not require exact periodicity of the ordinary part. The resulting estimate concerns the single normalized interval $(0,1)$.
Breakdown.AdjointDefect.DualBounded.summary: $R$ has dual bound $n$ when $R=R_h+R_p$ with $n_h+n_p\le n$, $2\||y|R_p\|_{L^2((0,1)\times\mathbb R^3)}\le n_p$, and $R_h$ a finite harmonic sum with weighted bound $n_h^2$. This is the paper's decomposition in reverse order, without exact periodicity of $R_p$.

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.Internal.Potenti.text: Let $v\in L^6(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$ have a measurable weak gradient $\nabla v\in L^2$. Suppose a locally integrable matrix field $A$ has the stated distributional divergence $d$, and for some $a>3/2$ and constant $B$ one has $|A(y)|_{\mathrm{op}}\le B(1+|y|)^{-a}$ everywhere and $|y||d(y)|\le B(1+|y|)^{-a}$ almost everywhere. Then $v\cdot d$ is integrable and $\int v\cdot d=-\int\nabla v:A$. The decay implies the $L^2$ conditions on $A$ and $|y|d$ used in the weak pairing theorem. This is the form needed for the potential fluxes. It has a narrower decay-based hypothesis than the printed general (B.55), while giving the same integration-by-parts identity in this application.
Breakdown.AdjointDefect.Internal.Potenti.summary: For $v\in L^6$ with $\nabla v\in L^2$ and a matrix field $A$ with divergence $d$, $|A|_{\mathrm{op}}\le B(1+|y|)^{-a}$ and $|y||d|\le B(1+|y|)^{-a}$, $a>3/2$, $\int v\cdot d=-\int\nabla v:A$. The decay hypothesis is narrower than the printed general (B.55).

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.Internal.Potenti.text:
Fix a time $	heta$, a real constant $w_*$ and a divergence-free $v\in L^6$ with weak gradient and Hessian, $
abla v,\Delta v\in L^2$. Let $T,K$ be residual and flux fields satisfying uniform decay $|T|\lesssim(1+|y|)^{-\gamma}$, $|K|\lesssim(1+|y|)^{-\gamma-1}$ and $|\operatorname{div}K|\lesssim(1+|y|)^{-\gamma}$ with $\gamma>5/2$, together with the distributional divergence identity. Let $G_j,U_j,F_j,q_j$ have the stated weak derivatives and potential decay. Define $R=T-\operatorname{div}K+
abla q_j+\Delta G_j+w_*\Delta U_j-\operatorname{div}F_j^{\mathsf T}$. The formal statement proves $\int v\cdot T+\int
abla v:K=\int v\cdot R-\int\Delta v\cdot G_j+\int
abla v:(w_*
abla U_j-F_j)$, and includes integrability of the first and the Laplacian pairings. The pressure term vanishes because $v$ is solenoidal. This is the potential part of (B.56) on one time slice; parameter changes and constraint replacement terms enter separately. The potential hypotheses mean that $G,U$ are jointly $C^1$, $F,q$ are measurable, and the indicated second derivatives, matrix divergence and pressure gradient are distributional derivatives on every time slice. Uniformly in time, $|G|\le C(1+r)^{-2}$, $|
abla G|\le C(1+r)^{-3}$, $|U|\le C(1+r)^{-1}$, and each of $|
abla U|,|F|_{\mathrm{op}},|q|$ is at most $C(1+r)^{-2}$. Almost everywhere in space, $|\Delta G|\le C(1+r)^{-4}$, $|\Delta U|\le C(1+r)^{-3}$, $r|\operatorname{div}F^{\mathsf T}|\le C(1+r)^{-2}$, and both $r|
abla q|$ and $r^3|
abla q|$ are at most $C$, where $r=|y|$. Pointwise matrix and derivative norms are operator norms; the period $L^2$ norms used in the energy and potential budgets are sums of squared entries. The residual on the selected time slice, $T(	heta,\cdot)$, is separately required to be measurable; joint almost-everywhere measurability alone would only give that property for almost every time.
Breakdown.AdjointDefect.Internal.Potenti.summary:
On one time slice, for solenoidal $v$ and decaying $T,K$ and potentials, $\int v\cdot T+\int
abla v:K=\int v\cdot R-\int\Delta v\cdot G_j+\int
abla v:(w_*
abla U_j-F_j)$, the pressure term vanishing. This is the potential part of (B.56).

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.Internal.Potenti.text: Let $v\in L^6(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$ have measurable weak gradient $G\in L^2$. Let measurable matrix columns $A_i\in L^2$ and a locally integrable vector field $d$ satisfy $d=\sum_i\partial_iA_i$ distributionally. Assume $|y|d\in L^2$. The formal statement proves $v\cdot d\in L^1$ and $\int v\cdot d=-\int\sum_iG e_i\cdot A_i$. Thus it gives (B.55) with a weighted $L^2$ condition on the divergence. The paper instead assumes $d\in L^{6/5}$; neither condition implies the other without further hypotheses, so the two displayed statements have different domains of validity. No divergence-free assumption on $v$ is needed here. The matrix columns describe the same contraction as the paper's $\nabla v:A$ once the transpose convention is taken into account.
Breakdown.AdjointDefect.Internal.Potenti.summary: For $v\in L^6$ with weak gradient $G\in L^2$, columns $A_i\in L^2$ and $d=\sum_i\partial_iA_i$ with $|y|d\in L^2$, $v\cdot d\in L^1$ and $\int v\cdot d=-\int\sum_iGe_i\cdot A_i$. This gives (B.55) under a weighted $L^2$ condition; the paper assumes $d\in L^{6/5}$.

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.Internal.transpo.text:
Suppose $W=W_c+\sum_{i\in I}\alpha_iW_i+E$ pointwise, with all coefficient fields differentiable in space, and $1/P=1/P_c+\sum_i\alpha_i\varsigma_i$. For $A_P(W,\psi)=-P^{-1}\partial_	heta\psi-\psi-	frac12(y\cdot
abla)\psi-(W\cdot
abla)\psi+(
abla W)^{\mathsf T}\psi$, the formal statement proves $A_P(W,\psi)=A_{P_c}(W_c,\psi)+\sum_{i\in I}\alpha_i[(
abla W_i)^{\mathsf T}\psi-(W_i\cdot
abla)\psi-\varsigma_i\partial_	heta\psi]+(
abla E)^{\mathsf T}\psi-(E\cdot
abla)\psi-(\sum_{i
otin I}\alpha_i\varsigma_i)\partial_	heta\psi$. This is a pointwise algebraic identity at every time and point. No integration or decay assumption enters it. With $I=\varnothing$ and $E=\sum_i\alpha_iW_\alpha^i$, it gives the parameter and inverse-period split used in (B.56). The adjoint field $\psi$ is arbitrary in this identity: its displayed time and spatial derivatives are assigned zero where they do not exist. The differentiability hypotheses concern the velocity pieces $W_c,W_i,E$. Division by a zero period is also assigned zero. The analytic application supplies a differentiable adjoint field and positive periods.
Breakdown.AdjointDefect.Internal.transpo.summary: When $W=W_c+\sum_{i\in I}\alpha_iW_i+E$ and $1/P=1/P_c+\sum_i\alpha_i\varsigma_i$, a pointwise algebraic identity splits $A_P(W,\psi)$ into $A_{P_c}(W_c,\psi)$, the fitted directions, the $E$ terms and the remaining inverse-period term. With $I=\varnothing$ it gives the split used in (B.56).

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.IsAdjointField.text: For real constants $C$ and $\gamma>5/2$, this condition requires a $C^1$ field $\psi:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ that is exactly one-periodic in time and divergence-free. Its spatial second derivatives must agree with weak derivatives, and the spatial Jacobian must be differentiable almost everywhere at every time. Uniformly in time, $|\psi|$ and $|\partial_\theta\psi|$ are bounded by $C(1+|y|)^{-\gamma}$ and $|\nabla\psi|$ by $C(1+|y|)^{-\gamma-1}$; its second derivative is bounded almost everywhere by $C(1+|y|)^{-\gamma}$. This is an analytic assumption, separate from the finite harmonic representation that produces an adjoint in the application. Its pointwise derivative bounds use operator norms. It allows every real $\gamma>5/2$. The paper's orders $3,4,5$ are more specific, and the second-derivative order 5 is stronger than the order 3 needed by this condition when $\gamma=3$.
Breakdown.AdjointDefect.IsAdjointField.summary: A $C^1$, divergence-free, one-periodic $\psi$ with $|\psi|,|\partial_\theta\psi|\le C(1+|y|)^{-\gamma}$, $|\nabla\psi|\le C(1+|y|)^{-\gamma-1}$ and weak second derivatives bounded a.e. by $C(1+|y|)^{-\gamma}$, for any real $\gamma>5/2$. The paper uses the more specific orders $3,4,5$.

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.IsPotentialData.text:
The four fields are $G_j,U_j:\mathbb R	imes\mathbb R^3	o\mathbb R^3$, a matrix field $F_j$, and a scalar $q_j$. This condition requires $G_j,U_j$ to be $C^1$, and $F_j,q_j$ to be measurable. Their indicated second derivatives, matrix divergence and scalar gradient must agree with distributional derivatives at every time. Uniformly in time, it requires $|G_j|\le C(1+r)^{-2}$, $|
abla G_j|\le C(1+r)^{-3}$, $|U_j|\le C(1+r)^{-1}$, and $|
abla U_j|+|F_j|+|q_j|\le3C(1+r)^{-2}$, where $r=|y|$ and the individual three terms are each bounded by $C(1+r)^{-2}$. Almost everywhere in space, $|\Delta G_j|\le C(1+r)^{-4}$, $|\Delta U_j|\le C(1+r)^{-3}$, $r|\operatorname{div}F_j^{\mathsf T}|\le C(1+r)^{-2}$, $r|
abla q_j|\le C$ and $r^3|
abla q_j|\le C$. The pointwise matrix and derivative norms are operator norms. These are sharper decay requirements than the common derivative estimate in (B.51), with almost-everywhere derivative bounds. The gradient $
abla q_j$ is an arbitrary pressure correction subject to these assumptions; no pressure equation is imposed by this condition.
Breakdown.AdjointDefect.IsPotentialData.summary: $C^1$ fields $G_j,U_j$ and measurable $F_j,q_j$ whose indicated derivatives agree with distributional ones, with $|G_j|\le C(1+r)^{-2}$, $|U_j|\le C(1+r)^{-1}$ and further decay and a.e. derivative bounds. These are sharper than the estimate in (B.51); no pressure equation is imposed.

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.PinData.text: For each of k constraints, the data supply real vector fields Φl and Φ̃l on ℝ×ℝ³. In the adjoint estimate, ∇Φl approximates the matrix-valued constraint field Ξl defining ℓl(v)=⟨Ξl,∇v⟩, and Φ̃l is a divergence-free replacement for Φl. These are the roles of the fields introduced after (B.10) and before (B.52). The formal data do not require compact support, one-periodicity, membership in a function space, div Φ̃l=0, or any approximation bound. Those properties and their numerical errors are independent conditions.
Breakdown.AdjointDefect.PinData.summary: For each of k constraints, supplies vector fields Φl and Φ̃l for the adjoint estimate before (B.52). The intended approximations Ξl≈∇Φl and Φl≈Φ̃l, support, periodicity, function spaces and div Φ̃l=0 are separate conditions.

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.PotentialData.text: The data consist of two real vector fields G,U on ℝ×ℝ³, a field F of linear maps ℝ³→ℝ³, and a real scalar field q. They are the auxiliary potentials in (B.51)–(B.52), used through ∆G+w*∆U−div Fᵀ+∇q. Their types impose no regularity, decay, one-periodicity, or relation to the adjoint field. The paper's hypotheses that these distributional derivatives are functions and obey the stated bounds are separate conditions on their representations.
Breakdown.AdjointDefect.PotentialData.summary: Supplies vector fields G,U, a matrix field F and a scalar q, the auxiliary potentials of (B.51)–(B.52) entering through ∆G+w*∆U−div Fᵀ+∇q. No regularity, decay, periodicity or relation to the adjoint field is imposed.

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.PotentialNorms.text: Let $G_j,U_j:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$, let $F_j$ be a matrix field and let $q_j$ be scalar. This condition requires $n_G,n_U,n_F,n_R\ge0$ and the three nonnegative-integral bounds $\int_0^1\int|G_j|^2\le n_G^2$, $\int_0^1\int|\nabla U_j|_{\mathrm F}^2\le n_U^2$, and $\int_0^1\int|F_j|_{\mathrm F}^2\le n_F^2$. Here $|A|_{\mathrm F}^2=\sum_{i,l}|A_{il}|^2$, and the integrals use Lebesgue measure. Measurability and the interpretation of the displayed derivative as a distributional derivative are separate assumptions. In particular the derivative is assigned zero where differentiability fails. When the potential regularity hypotheses are imposed, these become the three $L^2((0,1)\times\mathbb R^3)$ norm bounds preceding (B.53). The condition only requires $n_R\ge0$; a dual bound for the residual must be supplied separately. It imposes no bound on $q_j$.
Breakdown.AdjointDefect.PotentialNorms.summary: Requires $n_G,n_U,n_F,n_R\ge0$, $\int_0^1\!\int|G_j|^2\le n_G^2$, $\int_0^1\!\int|\nabla U_j|^2\le n_U^2$ and $\int_0^1\!\int|F_j|^2\le n_F^2$. With separate measurability and derivative assumptions these are the norm bounds before (B.53); no bound on $q_j$.

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.PotentialNumbers.text: Four real numbers are supplied: a proposed L²([0,1]×ℝ³) bound for G, a proposed L² bound for ∇U, a proposed L² bound for the matrix flux F, and a proposed dual bound for the residual R. These are nG,nU,nF,nR in (B.53). The matrix norm in the norm conditions is Frobenius. The data declaration contains no nonnegativity or validity assertion; those are imposed separately, and the residual dual bound is a separate condition from the three potential norm bounds.
Breakdown.AdjointDefect.PotentialNumbers.summary: Four real numbers nG,nU,nF,nR of (B.53): proposed L² bounds for G, ∇U and the matrix flux F (Frobenius norm), and a proposed dual bound for the residual. No nonnegativity or validity is asserted.

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.RemainderBounded.text: For a measurable vector field $R(\theta,y)$ on $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3$ and a nonnegative number $n$, this condition is $\int_0^1\int_{\mathbb R^3}|y|^2|R(\theta,y)|^2\,dy\,d\theta\le(n/2)^2$. Thus it is exactly $2\||y|R\|_{\mathcal H}\le n$. The condition is imposed by a finite upper bound for a nonnegative integral, so square integrability is part of it. No periodicity assumption on $R$ occurs in this definition. In the paper this is the condition on $R'$; the separate finite-harmonic part is $R''$. The factor 2 is the square root of the constant 4 in Hardy's inequality.
Breakdown.AdjointDefect.RemainderBounded.summary: For measurable $R$ and $n\ge0$, the condition $\int_0^1\int|y|^2|R|^2\le(n/2)^2$, that is $2\||y|R\|_{\mathcal H}\le n$, with square integrability included. In the paper it is the condition on $R'$; the factor 2 is the square root of Hardy's constant 4.

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.adjointDefectBri.text:
For positive constant weight, suppose each selected adjoint $\psi_j$ is $C^1$, divergence-free and one-periodic, decays with order $\gamma>5/2$, and has a $C^1$ curl potential of decay order $ eta>3/2$. Assume the profile has a decomposition into a central part, fitted directions and remaining directions, with each part $C^1$, divergence-free and one-periodic, bounded with gradient $O((1+|y|)^{-1})$. Require the affine inverse-period identity, constant constraint coefficients, regular potentials and compact constraint generators, and all norm and dual bounds in the adjoint error budget, whose total is at most $a_j$. Then for every parameter, every perturbation $v$ and every measurable one-periodic $F\in\mathcal H$ satisfying the linearized equation modulo a gradient, the conclusion is $|\langle F,\psi_jangle_{\mathcal H}-\sum_lY_{jl}\langle
abla v,\Xi_langle_{\mathcal H}|\le a_j\|v\|_w$. The theorem takes the adjoint representation, potential, dual, constraint replacement and free-direction estimates as explicit premises; each is proved separately and supplied in the final cell theorem. Setting the fitted set empty gives Lemma B.12. The precise adjoint assumptions are joint $C^1$ regularity, one-periodicity, solenoidality and a common constant $C$ such that $|\psi|,|\partial_	heta\psi|\le C(1+r)^{-\gamma}$ and $|
abla\psi|\le C(1+r)^{-\gamma-1}$. Its second spatial derivative agrees with the weak derivative, is bounded by $C(1+r)^{-\gamma}$ almost everywhere on every time slice, and its spatial Jacobian is differentiable almost everywhere. The pointwise derivative norms here are operator norms. Here $r=|y|$. The potential hypotheses mean that $G,U$ are jointly $C^1$, $F,q$ are measurable, and the indicated second derivatives, matrix divergence and pressure gradient are distributional derivatives on every time slice. Uniformly in time, $|G|\le C(1+r)^{-2}$, $|
abla G|\le C(1+r)^{-3}$, $|U|\le C(1+r)^{-1}$, and each of $|
abla U|,|F|_{\mathrm{op}},|q|$ is at most $C(1+r)^{-2}$. Almost everywhere in space, $|\Delta G|\le C(1+r)^{-4}$, $|\Delta U|\le C(1+r)^{-3}$, $r|\operatorname{div}F^{\mathsf T}|\le C(1+r)^{-2}$, and both $r|
abla q|$ and $r^3|
abla q|$ are at most $C$, where $r=|y|$. Pointwise matrix and derivative norms are operator norms; the period $L^2$ norms used in the energy and potential budgets are sums of squared entries. Here $y\in\mathbb R^3$, normalized time is $	heta\in\mathbb R$, and $\mathcal H=L^2((0,1)	imes\mathbb R^3)$. The squared energy is $\|v\|_w^2=\iint(|\Delta v|^2+w_*|
abla v|^2)$, with the Euclidean norm on vectors and the sum of squares of matrix entries on gradients. Integrating over $[0,1]$ in the formal statement gives the same integral as $(0,1)$. A perturbation is a measurable, divergence-free vector field on $\mathbb R	imes\mathbb R^3$, of period one in $	heta$, with spatial weak gradient and Hessian, $v(	heta)\in L^6$ for almost every $	heta$, and $
abla v$, $\Delta v$ and $(1/P)\partial_	heta v+v/2+(y\cdot
abla)v/2$ in $\mathcal H$. Any imposed spatial and temporal symmetries are included in this hypothesis; choosing no symmetries gives the unrestricted class.
Breakdown.AdjointDefect.adjointDefectBri.summary: With error budget at most $a_j$, any perturbation $v$ and $F\in\mathcal H$ solving the linearized equation modulo a gradient give $|\langle F,\psi_j\rangle-\sum_lY_{jl}\langle\nabla v,\Xi_l\rangle|\le a_j\|v\|_w$. An empty fitted set gives Lemma B.12.

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.adjointTransport.text:
For a real number $P$ and vector fields $W,\psi$ on $\mathbb R	imes\mathbb R^3$, this definition is $-P^{-1}\partial_	heta\psi-\psi-	frac12(y\cdot
abla)\psi-(W\cdot
abla)\psi+(
abla W)^{\mathsf T}\psi$. The final term has components $\sum_k\psi_k\partial_iW_k$. When $W$ is divergence-free and the fields have the regularity needed for integration by parts, this is the adjoint of the time, dilation and convection terms of the linearized operator. The term $-\Delta\psi$ is supplied through a separate matrix divergence when forming (B.52). Fields are represented as functions at every real time and every point of $\mathbb R^3$; the definition alone imposes no smoothness or period condition. Each pointwise derivative is assigned zero where the differentiated function is not differentiable, and $1/0=0$. In its analytic use, weak-derivative identifications and regularity are supplied, and the certificate has $P=S(\alpha)>0$.
Breakdown.AdjointDefect.adjointTransport.summary:
Defines $-P^{-1}\partial_	heta\psi-\psi-	frac12(y\cdot
abla)\psi-(W\cdot
abla)\psi+(
abla W)^{\mathsf T}\psi$. For divergence-free $W$ it is the formal adjoint of the time, dilation and convection terms in (B.52), without $-\Delta\psi$. Undefined derivatives and $1/0$ are set to zero.

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.advectionShift.text: For two real vector fields δ and ψ, the expression is (Dδ)ᵀψ−Dψ·δ, that is, ∑ₖψₖ∇δₖ−(δ·∇)ψ, at fixed normalized time and point. This is the convection part of the adjoint operator in (B.52). Identifying it as the formal adjoint of v↦(δ·∇)v+(v·∇)δ uses div δ=0 and the integration-by-parts hypotheses. The definition itself assumes neither condition. All derivatives are everywhere-defined expressions whose default value is zero when differentiability fails.
Breakdown.AdjointDefect.advectionShift.summary: Defines (Dδ)ᵀψ−Dψ·δ=∑ₖψₖ∇δₖ−(δ·∇)ψ, the convection part of the adjoint operator in (B.52). Its identification as the adjoint of v↦(δ·∇)v+(v·∇)δ uses div δ=0 and integration by parts, which are not assumed.

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.axisRotation.text: The map sends (y₁,y₂,y₃) to (cos α·y₁−sin α·y₂, sin α·y₁+cos α·y₂, y₃). It is the Euclidean rotation Rα about the y₃-axis used in the azimuthal wave-number condition before Lemma B.11. The angle α is any real number. The definition imposes no symmetry on a field; that symmetry is expressed by a separate transformation identity for its scalar amplitudes.
Breakdown.AdjointDefect.axisRotation.summary: Defines Rα(y₁,y₂,y₃)=(cos α·y₁−sin α·y₂, sin α·y₁+cos α·y₂, y₃) for any real α, the rotation about the y₃-axis used in the azimuthal wave-number condition before Lemma B.11.

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.complexComponent.text: From a real vector x=(x₁,x₂,x₃), the three choices are x₁+ix₂, x₁−ix₂, and x₃. These are exactly the components used in the dual-bound definition before Lemma B.11. They are not an orthonormal coordinate system without weights: the first two have to be counted with factor one half to recover |x|². The component selector has exactly three values; there is no additional component or arbitrary-dimensional extension.
Breakdown.AdjointDefect.complexComponent.summary: The three components x₁+ix₂, x₁−ix₂ and x₃ of a real vector, as in the dual-bound definition before Lemma B.11. The first two must be weighted by one half to recover |x|².

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.componentWeight.text: Assign weight 1/2 to each of x₁+ix₂ and x₁−ix₂, and weight one to x₃. Then the weighted sum of their squared complex moduli equals x₁²+x₂²+x₃². These are precisely the factors in the azimuthal dual bound before Lemma B.11. The declaration is an algebraic normalization, independent of any field, frequency, regularity, or integral.
Breakdown.AdjointDefect.componentWeight.summary: Assigns weight 1/2 to x₁+ix₂ and x₁−ix₂ and weight one to x₃, so the weighted sum of squared moduli is x₁²+x₂²+x₃². These are the factors in the azimuthal dual bound before Lemma B.11.

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.dualBoundedBound.text: Suppose a measurable field $R$ is a sum of a finite-harmonic part and an ordinary part whose respective nonnegative budgets are $n_h$ and $n_p$, with $n_h+n_p\le n$. The ordinary part has $2\||y|R_p\|_{\mathcal H}\le n_p$; the harmonic budget is the sum of $(|k|+1/2)^{-2}\int|y|^2|g|^2$ over distinct time and azimuthal modes, with horizontal component weights $1/2$, bounded by $n_h^2$. Assuming the ordinary and harmonic pairing estimates, the formal statement proves $|\int_0^1\int v\cdot R|\le n\|\nabla v\|_{\mathcal H}$ for the weak test class below. It also gives spatial integrability for almost every time and integrability in time of the resulting spatial integral. This conclusion does not itself state absolute integrability on the product space; that fact is obtained separately from the weighted-pairing theorem. The two pairing-estimate premises are proved separately in the formalisation. Here $\mathcal H=L^2((0,1)\times\mathbb R^3)$. The weak test class consists of measurable $v$ and a measurable weak spatial gradient $G=\nabla v$, with $v(\theta)\in L^6(\mathbb R^3)$ for almost every $\theta$ and $\iint|G|^2<\infty$ over $(0,1)\times\mathbb R^3$. Neither divergence-freeness nor time periodicity of $v$ is required.
Breakdown.AdjointDefect.dualBoundedBound.summary: If $R$ splits into a finite-harmonic part with budget $n_h$ and an ordinary part with $2\||y|R_p\|_{\mathcal H}\le n_p$, $n_h+n_p\le n$, then, given the two pairing estimates, $|\int_0^1\int v\cdot R|\le n\|\nabla v\|_{\mathcal H}$ for weak $L^6$ test fields $v$, periodic or not.

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.freeShiftBoundHo.text:
For finitely many directions $W_i$ that are $C^1$, divergence-free, one-periodic and bounded with $|
abla W_i|\lesssim(1+|y|)^{-1}$, let $\psi$ be an adjoint field with decay exponent $\gamma>5/2$. Choose positive weights $\varpi_i$ and nonnegative numbers $n_i,n_{\mathrm v},n_{\mathrm d}$. Assume $\|[\sum_i\varpi_i|W_i|^2]^{1/2}\psi\|_{\mathcal H}\le n_{\mathrm v}$, that $(
abla W_i)^{\mathsf T}\psi$ has dual pairing bound $n_i$, and that $\sum_i\varpi_i n_i^2\le n_{\mathrm d}^2$. For every real coefficient vector $\alpha$ and every perturbation $v$, the formal statement bounds the absolute pairing of $v$ with $(
abla\sum_i\alpha_iW_i)^{\mathsf T}\psi-(\sum_i\alpha_iW_i\cdot
abla)\psi$ by $(\sum_i\alpha_i^2/\varpi_i)^{1/2}(n_{\mathrm v}+n_{\mathrm d})\|
abla v\|_{\mathcal H}$. In (B.53), $|\alpha_i|\le ar\varrho_i$ supplies the uniform bound. The inverse-period term is estimated separately. The precise adjoint assumptions are joint $C^1$ regularity, one-periodicity, solenoidality and a common constant $C$ such that $|\psi|,|\partial_	heta\psi|\le C(1+r)^{-\gamma}$ and $|
abla\psi|\le C(1+r)^{-\gamma-1}$. Its second spatial derivative agrees with the weak derivative, is bounded by $C(1+r)^{-\gamma}$ almost everywhere on every time slice, and its spatial Jacobian is differentiable almost everywhere. The pointwise derivative norms here are operator norms. Here $r=|y|$. Here $y\in\mathbb R^3$, normalized time is $	heta\in\mathbb R$, and $\mathcal H=L^2((0,1)	imes\mathbb R^3)$. The squared energy is $\|v\|_w^2=\iint(|\Delta v|^2+w_*|
abla v|^2)$, with the Euclidean norm on vectors and the sum of squares of matrix entries on gradients. Integrating over $[0,1]$ in the formal statement gives the same integral as $(0,1)$. A perturbation is a measurable, divergence-free vector field on $\mathbb R	imes\mathbb R^3$, of period one in $	heta$, with spatial weak gradient and Hessian, $v(	heta)\in L^6$ for almost every $	heta$, and $
abla v$, $\Delta v$ and $(1/P)\partial_	heta v+v/2+(y\cdot
abla)v/2$ in $\mathcal H$. Any imposed spatial and temporal symmetries are included in this hypothesis; choosing no symmetries gives the unrestricted class.
Breakdown.AdjointDefect.freeShiftBoundHo.summary:
Given bounds $n_{\mathrm v}$, $n_i$ with $\sum_i\varpi_in_i^2\le n_{\mathrm d}^2$, $v$ paired with $(
abla\sum_i\alpha_iW_i)^{\mathsf T}\psi-(\sum_i\alpha_iW_i\cdot
abla)\psi$ is at most $(\sum_i\alpha_i^2/\varpi_i)^{1/2}(n_{\mathrm v}+n_{\mathrm d})\|
abla v\|_{\mathcal H}$ in absolute value.

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.matrixDivergence.text: For a field K of linear maps ℝ³→ℝ³, take ∑ᵢ∂ᵢ(K eᵢ), where eᵢ are the three coordinate vectors. Its jth component is ∑ᵢ∂ᵢ(K eᵢ)ⱼ. This fixes the matrix convention in the flux terms of (B.52) and the integration by parts (B.55): the map's input index is the differentiated index. In the paper's derivative-first matrix notation the corresponding expression is written div Fᵀ. The formula is defined even without differentiability, using zero as the default derivative; the distributional interpretation requires separate regularity.
Breakdown.AdjointDefect.matrixDivergence.summary: Defines div K=∑ᵢ∂ᵢ(K eᵢ), so the input index of the map is the differentiated one. This fixes the convention in (B.52) and (B.55); the paper's derivative-first notation writes it div Fᵀ. Nondifferentiable points get derivative zero.

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.periodInnerInteg.text: For real fields $v,R:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$, this definition is $\int_{[0,1]}(\int_{\mathbb R^3}v(\theta,y)\cdot R(\theta,y)\,dy)\,d\theta$. The inner integration is spatial, followed by time integration. Endpoints have measure zero, so this agrees with the paper's $\iint$ on $(0,1)\times\mathbb R^3$ whenever the product is integrable. The expression is defined for all fields, without a built-in integrability or periodicity condition. A nonintegrable signed integral is assigned zero in the formal convention; the pairing theorems supply the integrability hypotheses that give the expression its analytic meaning.
Breakdown.AdjointDefect.periodInnerInteg.summary: The iterated pairing $\int_{[0,1]}\int_{\mathbb R^3}v\cdot R\,dy\,d\theta$, which agrees with the paper's $\iint$ on $(0,1)\times\mathbb R^3$ whenever the product is integrable. A nonintegrable signed integral is assigned zero.

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.pinChargeHolds_p.text:
Let $w_*>0$, let $\Xi_l$ be square-integrable matrix fields, let $\Phi_l$ be compactly supported weakly differentiable vector fields with square-integrable gradients, and let $\widetilde\Phi_l$ be compactly supported $C^1$, one-periodic generators with bounded weak second derivatives. For coefficients $Y_l$, assume $\|(Y_l)_l\|_2\le n_Y$, $\|\sum_lY_l(\Phi_l-\widetilde\Phi_l)\|_{\mathcal H}\le n_\Phi$ and $\|\sum_lY_l(\Xi_l-
abla\Phi_l)\|_{\mathcal H}\le c_\Xi\|(Y_l)_l\|_2$, with $n_\Phi,c_\Xi\ge0$. The formal statement bounds the difference between $\sum_lY_l\langle
abla v,\Xi_langle$ and $\sum_lY_l\langle
abla v,
abla\widetilde\Phi_l-(
abla\widetilde\Phi_l)^{\mathsf T}angle$ by $(n_\Phi+n_Yc_\Xi/\sqrt{w_*})\|v\|_w$. It applies to every perturbation. The general statement uses skew generator gradients and does not require the generators themselves to be divergence-free; solenoidality of $v$ suffices for the cancellation used here. Here $y\in\mathbb R^3$, normalized time is $	heta\in\mathbb R$, and $\mathcal H=L^2((0,1)	imes\mathbb R^3)$. The squared energy is $\|v\|_w^2=\iint(|\Delta v|^2+w_*|
abla v|^2)$, with the Euclidean norm on vectors and the sum of squares of matrix entries on gradients. Integrating over $[0,1]$ in the formal statement gives the same integral as $(0,1)$. A perturbation is a measurable, divergence-free vector field on $\mathbb R	imes\mathbb R^3$, of period one in $	heta$, with spatial weak gradient and Hessian, $v(	heta)\in L^6$ for almost every $	heta$, and $
abla v$, $\Delta v$ and $(1/P)\partial_	heta v+v/2+(y\cdot

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.potentialBoundHo.text:
Let $w_*>0$ and let a perturbation $v$ be paired with a residual field $T$ and matrix flux $K$ having the weak divergence and uniform decay of orders $\gamma,\gamma+1$ for some $\gamma>5/2$. Choose potentials $G,U,F,q$ with the specified weak derivatives and decay, and let $R=T-\operatorname{div}K+
abla q+\Delta G+w_*\Delta U-\operatorname{div}F^{\mathsf T}$. Suppose $n_G,n_U,n_F,n_R\ge0$, $\|G\|_{\mathcal H}\le n_G$, $\|
abla U\|_{\mathcal H}\le n_U$, $\|F\|_{\mathcal H}\le n_F$, and $|\iint v'\cdot R|\le n_R\|
abla v'\|_{\mathcal H}$ for every weak $L^6$ test field with finite gradient energy, including the requisite iterated integrability. Then $|\iint v\cdot T+\iint
abla v:K|\le\sqrt{n_G^2+(w_*n_U+n_F+n_R)^2/w_*}\,\|v\|_w$. This is the first contribution to (B.53); the pressure correction disappears by solenoidality. The potential hypotheses mean that $G,U$ are jointly $C^1$, $F,q$ are measurable, and the indicated second derivatives, matrix divergence and pressure gradient are distributional derivatives on every time slice. Uniformly in time, $|G|\le C(1+r)^{-2}$, $|

abla U|,|F|_{\mathrm{op}},|q|$ is at most $C(1+r)^{-2}$. Almost everywhere in space, $|\Delta G|\le C(1+r)^{-4}$, $|\Delta U|\le C(1+r)^{-3}$, $r|\operatorname{div}F^{\mathsf T}|\le C(1+r)^{-2}$, and both $r|
abla q|$ and $r^3|
abla q|$ are at most $C$, where $r=|y|$. Pointwise matrix and derivative norms are operator norms; the period $L^2$ norms used in the energy and potential budgets are sums of squared entries. Here $y\in\mathbb R^3$, normalized time is $	heta\in\mathbb R$, and $\mathcal H=L^2((0,1)	imes\mathbb R^3)$. The squared energy is $\|v\|_w^2=\iint(|\Delta v|^2+w_*|
abla v|^2)$, with the Euclidean norm on vectors and the sum of squares of matrix entries on gradients. Integrating over $[0,1]$ in the formal statement gives the same integral as $(0,1)$. A perturbation is a measurable, divergence-free vector field on $\mathbb R	imes\mathbb R^3$, of period one in $	heta$, with spatial weak gradient and Hessian, $v(	heta)\in L^6$ for almost every $	heta$, and $
abla v$, $\Delta v$ and $(1/P)\partial_	heta v+v/2+(y\cdot

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.remainderAzimuth.text: Let the measurable real field $R$ have, in each of $R_1+iR_2$, $R_1-iR_2$ and $R_3$, a finite expansion $\sum e^{2\pi i k'\theta}g(y)$ with measurable amplitudes and distinct integer pairs $(k',k)$, where $g(R_\phi y)=e^{ik\phi}g(y)$. Let $W$ be a $C^1$, divergence-free, one-periodic field with $|W|\le D$ and $|

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.secondDeriv.text: For an arbitrary function f:ℝ³→ℝ³, this is the derivative of its spatial derivative, regarded as a bilinear map on two real spatial directions. Breakdown.AdjointDefect.testFieldDensity.text:
Let $\psi$ be a $C^1$, divergence-free, one-periodic adjoint field with decay order $\gamma>5/2$ and the weak second derivatives required of that class. Suppose $\psi=\operatorname{curl}A$ for a $C^1$, one-periodic potential $A$ with $|A|+|\partial_	heta A|=O((1+|y|)^{- eta})$, $|
abla A|=O((1+|y|)^{- eta-1})$ and $ eta>3/2$. For every smooth compactly supported time cutoff $\chi$, the formal statement gives smooth compactly supported solenoidal space-time fields $\varphi_n$ approximating $\chi\psi$. The fields and their spatial gradients converge in space-time $L^2$; the fields, their time derivatives and their dilation derivatives $y\cdot
abla\varphi_n$ converge in $L^2_	heta L^{6/5}_y$. All approximants have time support in one common compact interval. The hypothesis includes a curl potential, which the paper's brief cutoff discussion does not specify. The precise adjoint assumptions are joint $C^1$ regularity, one-periodicity, solenoidality and a common constant $C$ such that $|\psi|,|\partial_	heta\psi|\le C(1+r)^{-\gamma}$ and $|
abla\psi|\le C(1+r)^{-\gamma-1}$. Breakdown.AdjointDefect.timeDerivative.text: For a field f:ℝ×ℝ³→ℝ³ and fixed spatial point y, this is ∂θf(θ,y). Breakdown.AdjointDefect.timeDerivative.summary: Defines ∂θf(θ,y) for f:ℝ×ℝ³→ℝ³ over all real θ, the normalized-time derivative in the adjoint equation (B.52). It is zero where the ordinary derivative does not exist; regularity and period one are separate.

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.transposeApply.text: For a real linear map K on ℝ³ and vector z, the result is ∑ᵢ(K eᵢ·z)eᵢ, which is Kᵀz with respect to the Euclidean inner product. With K=DW and z=ψ, this is ∑ₖψₖ∇Wₖ, the adjoint convection term in (B.52). This declaration is a finite-dimensional algebraic operation. No symmetry of K is assumed, and it imposes no regularity condition on a field from which K might have been obtained.
Breakdown.AdjointDefect.transposeApply.summary: For a real linear map K on ℝ³, defines ∑ᵢ(K eᵢ·z)eᵢ=Kᵀz. With K=DW and z=ψ this is ∑ₖψₖ∇Wₖ, the adjoint convection term in (B.52). No symmetry of K is assumed.

Breakdown.AdjointDefect.weightedPairingI.text: Let $R$ be measurable and assume $\iint|y|^2|R|^2<\infty$ over $(0,1)\times\mathbb R^3$. For every field $v$ in the weak test class below, the formal statement proves $v\cdot R\in L^1((0,1)\times\mathbb R^3)$. This is product-space absolute integrability, so Fubini's theorem applies. The proof uses Hardy's inequality for $v/|y|$ and Cauchy–Schwarz with $|y|R$. The values assigned to $v/|y|$ at $y=0$ do not change any integral, since that point has measure zero. This result supplies the integrability clause of Lemma B.11 once the weighted $L^2$ finiteness of both parts of the dual decomposition is established. Here $\mathcal H=L^2((0,1)\times\mathbb R^3)$. The weak test class consists of measurable $v$ and a measurable weak spatial gradient $G=\nabla v$, with $v(\theta)\in L^6(\mathbb R^3)$ for almost every $\theta$ and $\iint|G|^2<\infty$ over $(0,1)\times\mathbb R^3$. Breakdown.AdjointDefect.weightedPairingI.summary: If $R$ is measurable with $\iint|y|^2|R|^2<\infty$, then $v\cdot R\in L^1((0,1)\times\mathbb R^3)$ for every weak $L^6$ test field with finite gradient energy, via Hardy's inequality and Cauchy–Schwarz. The formal statement only defines the following assertion. Separate theorems derive it from hypotheses, namely the existence of a periodic similarity profile with the stated decay, or the certificate conditions; no theorem proves it without such a hypothesis. For each viscosity $
u>0$ there is a smooth, compactly supported field $u_0:\mathbb R^3	o\mathbb R^3$ with $\operatorname{div}u_0=0$ for which no pair $u:\mathbb R	imes\mathbb R^3	o\mathbb R^3$, $p:\mathbb R	imes\mathbb R^3	o\mathbb R$ has all of the following properties: joint smoothness up to $t=0$ on $[0,\infty)	imes\mathbb R^3$; $u(0)=u_0$; $\partial_tu+(u\cdot

The single bound is uniform over the entire half-line, not a separate bound on each finite interval. The integral is the nonnegative integral, so an infinite energy cannot satisfy the inequality. Separate theorems derive it from a profile or certificate hypothesis; the definition gives no finite blow-up time, rate or profile estimate.

The formal statement only defines the following assertion. Separate theorems derive it from hypotheses, namely a smooth periodic similarity profile with the stated decay, or the cell conditions of Appendix B; no theorem proves it without such a hypothesis. For each viscosity $
u>0$ there is a smooth field $u_0:\mathbb R^3	o\mathbb R^3$ with $u_0(x+e_i)=u_0(x)$ for each coordinate vector $e_i$ and $\operatorname{div}u_0=0$, such that no pair of globally defined functions $u(t,x),p(t,x)$ is jointly smooth on $[0,\infty)	imes\mathbb R^3$, has $u(0)=u_0$, satisfies $\partial_tu+(u\cdot

Breakdown.BreakdownOnTorus.summary: Defines nonexistence of a global smooth solution with periodic velocity, for some smooth period-one solenoidal datum at every $\nu>0$. The pressure may be any smooth field; this target specifies no energy bound, finite blow-up time or rate.

Breakdown.CellCert.CellAnalysis.CellScal.text:
This declaration supplies three natural degree cutoffs, a finite set of resolved integer angular modes and a finite band of other modes. It also supplies functions of (r,z) intended to bound the strain, the mean vorticity gradient and its oscillatory part, and a real splitting length. For each integer mode there are an energy weight, a vorticity weight, a complex 12×12 matrix field acting on (G,v), separate curl, strain and velocity absorption coefficients, and a tail correction. Three real penalty coefficients and a real weight floor are recorded. Finally, three real weight arrays depend on a mode and two natural polynomial degrees, for the symmetric derivative, antisymmetric derivative and velocity contributions.

These are the ingredients of the polynomial and remainder estimates described around (B.25)–(B.27). The declaration is a more general data format: it does not require a valid cell, nonnegative constants, a Hermitian local matrix, disjoint mode sets or any of the intended upper and lower bounds. Its natural-number degrees are finite polynomial truncation orders; it contains no numerical validation.
Breakdown.CellCert.CellAnalysis.CellScal.summary: Supplies degree cutoffs, resolved and band modes, strain and vorticity-gradient bounds, a splitting length, per-mode weights, 12×12 matrix fields, absorption coefficients, tail corrections, penalties and weight arrays for the estimates around (B.25)–(B.27). No validity, sign or bound is required.

It converts between the radial orthogonal-polynomial measure and the cylindrical weight in the cell estimates behind (B.27). The value at the axis comes from the convention 0/0=0 and cannot be replaced pointwise by 1 without excluding that point.
