The two corrections differentiate the input and output cylindrical frames of a matrix. This is the component calculation behind the gradient angular bound in (B.35). It is an algebraic coefficient array for an arbitrary complex matrix G, so no harmonic transformation or differentiability property follows from the definition alone.
Breakdown.CellCert.CellEnergy.angularCom.summary: Gives coefficients of ikGₐᵦ−∑cJcbGₐc−∑cJcaGcb, with Jφr=1, Jrφ=−1 and other entries zero; the two corrections differentiate the input and output cylindrical frames. This is the component calculation behind the angular gradient bound in (B.35).

Breakdown.CellCert.CellEnergy.angularOff.text: For a retained mode and contraction C:G, let b_jl be its gradient coefficients and p their polynomial reconstruction. The form first contributes r₂⁻¹∑_{j,l=0}^Q|b_jl|². It then adds c*H⁻¹c with tests t_jl=r^(j+1)zˡ, 0≤j<Q and 0≤l≤Q, weight m=(r₂−r)/(rr₂), moments c_jl=∫_Qpm t_jldr dz and H_αβ=∫_Qmt_αt_βdr dz. This is the off-axis angular contribution in the cell energy near (B.26). The intended use needs 0<r₁<r₂ and a nondegenerate Gram matrix; all inverse or division operations are nevertheless defined with zero at singular inputs.
Breakdown.CellCert.CellEnergy.angularOff.summary: For C:G off the axis, adds r₂⁻¹∑|b_jl|² and c*H⁻¹c with tests r^(j+1)zˡ (0≤j<Q, 0≤l≤Q), weight m=(r₂−r)/(rr₂) and Gram matrix H: the off-axis angular contribution near (B.26). It needs 0<r₁<r₂ and nondegenerate H; singular inverses are zero.

Breakdown.CellCert.CellEnergy.angularOff.text: For p=(r,z) and outer radius r₂, this is (r₂−r)/(rr₂)=1/r−1/r₂ when r and r₂ are nonzero. On a valid cell with r₁>0 it is nonnegative. It measures the remainder beyond the constant lower bound 1/r₂ in the off-axis angular energy construction behind (B.26). At a vanishing denominator its formal value is zero; that extension does not justify using the reciprocal-radius identity on the axis.
Breakdown.CellCert.CellEnergy.angularOff.summary: Defines (r₂−r)/(rr₂), equal to 1/r−1/r₂ when rr₂≠0. It is nonnegative on a valid cell with r₁>0 and measures the excess over 1/r₂ in the angular energy near (B.26); a zero denominator gives zero.

Breakdown.CellCert.CellEnergy.angularTes.text: For natural j,l, this test is r^(j+1)zˡ, equivalently r times the monomial rʲzˡ. The extra radial factor is explicit and is used in the angular energy test forms behind (B.26) and (B.35). It is a polynomial on all of ℝ², with no assumption of positive radius.
Breakdown.CellCert.CellEnergy.angularTes.summary: Defines the test r^(j+1)zˡ, r times rʲzˡ, used in the angular energy test forms behind (B.26) and (B.35). It is a polynomial on all of ℝ².

Breakdown.CellCert.CellEnergy.basisFn.text: For radial polynomials P_j and vertical polynomials Q_l with natural indices j,l, this is the real function (r,z)↦P_j(r)Q_l(z). These tensor products are the polynomial basis for the retained velocity and gradient coefficients in Appendix B.3. No finite degree cutoff, orthonormality or cell-validity hypothesis is included in this definition.
Breakdown.CellCert.CellEnergy.basisFn.summary: Defines (r,z)↦P_j(r)Q_l(z), the tensor-product basis for the retained velocity and gradient coefficients in Appendix B.3. No cutoff, orthonormality or valid cell is assumed.

Breakdown.CellCert.CellEnergy.componentF.text: For a mode of frequency k=mn and a contraction C:G of the full gradient, this matrix adds the radial and vertical polynomial energies and their boundary test forms. On a cell with r₁≠0 it also adds the two interior test forms; on an axis cell those terms are omitted. The angular term uses the contraction obtained by differentiating both cylindrical tensor frames, then chooses the axis-cell or off-axis angular test form according to r₁=0. This gives one component of the finite energy E_Q described near (B.26). It is a definition of a matrix, with no assertion that it is a lower bound until cell validity, basis normalization and the analytic identities are supplied.
Breakdown.CellCert.CellEnergy.componentF.summary: For a mode k=mn and contraction C:G, sums radial and vertical polynomial energies with their boundary test forms, adds the interior test forms when r₁≠0, and adds the axis or off-axis angular form. It is one component of E_Q near (B.26), and no lower bound is asserted.

Breakdown.CellCert.CellEnergy.curlArray.text: For i∈{1,2,3}, the coefficient array is Cₐᵦ=εᵢᵦₐ. Its bilinear contraction ∑ₐᵦCₐᵦGₐᵦ equals the ith curl component when Gₐᵦ=∂ᵦvₐ. This supplies the curl parts of the cell energy in (B.26)–(B.27). The ordering of the alternating-symbol indices is explicit, and the array acts on the full gradient rather than its symmetric part.
Breakdown.CellCert.CellEnergy.curlArray.summary: Defines Cₐᵦ=εᵢᵦₐ, whose contraction ∑ₐᵦCₐᵦGₐᵦ is the ith curl component when Gₐᵦ=∂ᵦvₐ. It supplies the curl parts of the cell energy in (B.26)–(B.27) and acts on the full gradient.

Breakdown.CellCert.CellEnergy.energyForm.text: For a natural angular order m and each retained integer mode n, choose real weights a_n,b_n and a real highest-degree correction t_n. This matrix sums a_n times the nine component energies of the full gradient, plus b_n times the three component energies of its curl, and subtracts t_n times the specified highest-degree gradient form. The component energies include the radial, vertical and angular polynomial and side terms. It is the explicit finite energy used to construct the cell comparison (B.26), corresponding to the two derivative coefficients and their tail correction. The weights are arbitrary in this definition; positivity and the claimed lower bounds require separate hypotheses.
Breakdown.CellCert.CellEnergy.energyForm.summary: For each retained mode n, sums a_n times the nine component energies of the gradient and b_n times the three curl component energies, minus t_n times the highest-degree gradient form. This is the finite energy for the comparison (B.26); positivity of the weights is a separate hypothesis.

Breakdown.CellCert.CellEnergy.formOfRows.text: Let I be a finite test index set and D any coordinate set. For complex arrays R=(R_{id}) and G=(G_{ij}), the returned array on D×D has entries A_{dd′}=∑_{i,j∈I}conj(R_{id})G_{ij}R_{jd′}. Thus A=R*GR. When D is finite, its quadratic form on x∈ℂᴰ equals the form of G on Rx; the same finite-sum identity applies to finitely supported x when D is infinite. In Appendix B.3 the cell coordinates are finite, and this is the pullback used to assemble the forms in (B.26) and (B.38). No Hermitian symmetry or positivity is required.
Breakdown.CellCert.CellEnergy.formOfRows.summary: For a finite index set $I$, any coordinate set $D$, a complex $I\times D$ array $R$ and $I\times I$ array $G$, returns $R^*GR$; for finite $D$ or finitely supported $x$ its form on $x$ is that of $G$ on $Rx$. This is the pullback in (B.26) and (B.38). $G$ need not be Hermitian or positive.

Breakdown.CellCert.CellEnergy.frameTurn.text: In the ordered frame (eᵣ,eφ,e_z), this is the real matrix J with Jφr=1, Jrφ=−1 and all other entries zero. Thus d eᵣ/dφ=eφ and d eφ/dφ=−eᵣ. It supplies the frame terms when differentiating the gradient of a harmonic in Appendix B.3 and in the proof of (B.35). It is a constant 3×3 array, independent of any field or angular frequency.
Breakdown.CellCert.CellEnergy.frameTurn.summary: The constant matrix J in the frame (eᵣ,eφ,e_z) with Jφr=1, Jrφ=−1 and zeros elsewhere, so d eᵣ/dφ=eφ and d eφ/dφ=−eᵣ. It supplies the frame terms in Appendix B.3 and the proof of (B.35).

Breakdown.CellCert.CellEnergy.heightFace.text: For a mode, the lower or upper horizontal side, a degree 0≤j≤q and a complex array C, this row sums the supplied gradient-trace rows with coefficients Cₐᵦ. It is the horizontal-side moment of that tensor contraction in the construction behind (B.26). It assigns no field or derivative to the rows and assumes no trace regularity on its own.
Breakdown.CellCert.CellEnergy.heightFace.summary: For a mode, a horizontal side, a degree 0≤j≤q and a complex array C, sums the gradient-trace rows with coefficients Cₐᵦ: the horizontal-side moment of that contraction in the construction behind (B.26).

Breakdown.CellCert.CellEnergy.heightInne.text: For a mode and contraction C:G, reconstruct its polynomial p on the cell 𝒬=[r₁,r₂]×[z₁,z₂]. Put η(z)=(2z−z₁−z₂)/(z₂−z₁) and m=(r−r₁)(1−η(z)²), with division by zero assigned zero. For tests t_jl=rʲzˡ with 0≤j,l<Q, use moments b_jl=−∫_𝒬p∂z(m·t_jl)dr dz and Gram matrix H_αβ=∫_𝒬m·t_α·t_βdr dz. The matrix on cell unknowns is the pullback of H⁻¹ by these moment rows, so its form is b*H⁻¹b. This is a vertical interior term in the energy construction near (B.26). Validity of the cell and the test Gram matrix is separate; if Q=0 there are no tests, and a singular inverse is defined to be zero.
Breakdown.CellCert.CellEnergy.heightInne.summary: For $C:G$ with polynomial $p$, $\eta=(2z-z_1-z_2)/(z_2-z_1)$ (zero if the width is zero), weight $m=(r-r_1)(1-\eta^2)$, tests $r^jz^l$ with $0\le j,l<Q$, moments $b$ and weighted Gram matrix $H$, gives the form $b^*H^{-1}b$, a vertical interior term near (B.26). A singular inverse is zero.

Breakdown.CellCert.CellEnergy.heightInne.text: For a cell with lower radius r₁ and vertical reference coordinate η=(2z−z₁−z₂)/(z₂−z₁), this is (r−r₁)(1−η²). On a valid cell it is nonnegative and vanishes on the two horizontal sides. It is the weight for the vertical interior test optimization in the cell energy behind (B.26). Its nonnegativity is restricted to the cell and depends on the endpoint conditions.
Breakdown.CellCert.CellEnergy.heightInne.summary: Defines (r−r₁)(1−η²) with η=(2z−z₁−z₂)/(z₂−z₁). On a valid cell it is nonnegative and vanishes on both horizontal sides; it weights the vertical interior test optimization behind (B.26).

Breakdown.CellCert.CellEnergy.heightMome.text: For natural indices l,l′, this is ∫𝓏₁𝓏₂zˡQ_l′(z)dz, where Q_l′ is the supplied vertical basis polynomial. It converts a monomial test to basis coefficients in the cell boundary formulas of Appendix B.3. The integral is unweighted, both powers and degrees are natural numbers, and no orthonormality assumption is included in this definition.
Breakdown.CellCert.CellEnergy.heightMome.summary: Defines ∫𝓏₁𝓏₂zˡQ_l′(z)dz, the unweighted pairing converting a monomial test to basis coefficients in the cell boundary formulas of Appendix B.3.

Breakdown.CellCert.CellEnergy.heightOute.text: For a mode and contraction C:G, take the vertical boundary rows indexed by 0≤j≤q and 0≤l≤Q and let b be their values on a cell-coordinate vector. With monomial tests t_jl=rʲzˡ and H_αβ=∫_Qrt_αt_βdr dz, the returned form is b*H⁻¹b. It contributes the boundary-sensitive vertical energy in the construction of E_Q near (B.26). No positive-definiteness or trace assertion is part of the definition; a singular matrix inverse is assigned zero.
Breakdown.CellCert.CellEnergy.heightOute.summary: For C:G, takes the vertical boundary rows with 0≤j≤q, 0≤l≤Q as b and returns b*H⁻¹b with H_αβ=∫_Qrt_αt_β for t_jl=rʲzˡ: the boundary-sensitive vertical energy in E_Q near (B.26). A singular inverse is zero.

Breakdown.CellCert.CellEnergy.heightOute.text: For a mode, contraction C:G, 0≤j≤q and 0≤l≤Q, this row represents the integration-by-parts test rʲzˡ with the vertical reference factor. Its boundary part is the sum of upper and lower horizontal-side trace rows weighted by z₂ˡ and z₁ˡ, after expanding rʲ in the radial basis with weight ω. Its interior term is −∫_Qp∂z[rη(z)rʲzˡ]dr dz, where p is the retained contraction polynomial. Both boundary contributions have a plus sign because η takes values ±1. This is a cell-energy row underlying (B.26), and its analytic trace interpretation requires the separate layout hypotheses.
Breakdown.CellCert.CellEnergy.heightOute.summary: Integration by parts of C:G against rʲzˡ with the vertical reference factor: upper and lower trace rows weighted by z₂ˡ and z₁ˡ, both with plus signs, after expanding rʲ in the radial basis, plus −∫_Qp∂z[rη(z)rʲzˡ]dr dz. A cell-energy row for (B.26).

Breakdown.CellCert.CellEnergy.heightProj.text: Fix a mode and tensor contraction C:G, and let p be its polynomial reconstruction from coefficients of degrees 0,…,Q in each variable. The quadratic form is r_*∫_Qω(r)(1−η(z)²)|∂zp|²dr dz, with η the affine height coordinate in [−1,1], ω=r on an axis cell and 1 otherwise, and r_*=1 on an axis cell and r₁ otherwise. It contributes to the finite cell energy described near (B.26). This is a matrix formula for arbitrary supplied data; a valid cell and the normalized bases are needed for the stated energy interpretation.
Breakdown.CellCert.CellEnergy.heightProj.summary: Defines the form r_*∫_Qω(r)(1−η(z)²)|∂zp|²dr dz for the polynomial reconstruction p of C:G, with ω=r and r_*=1 on an axis cell and ω=1, r_*=r₁ otherwise. It contributes to the finite cell energy near (B.26).

Breakdown.CellCert.CellEnergy.heightSlop.text: For f:ℝ²→ℝ, this is the derivative of z↦f(r,z) with r fixed. It is the vertical derivative used in the test matrices underlying (B.26). The function is defined on all of ℝ², and the expression alone assumes no differentiability; where the ordinary derivative fails, its formal value is zero.
Breakdown.CellCert.CellEnergy.heightSlop.summary: Defines the derivative of z↦f(r,z) with r fixed for f:ℝ²→ℝ, used in the test matrices underlying (B.26). It is zero where the ordinary derivative fails to exist.

Breakdown.CellCert.CellEnergy.layoutInde.text: For a cell layout, this supplies the coordinate maps for gradient degrees 0,…,Q and velocity degrees 0,…,Q−1 directly from the corresponding coordinate families. The radial boundary rows are the layout's gradient-trace rows on sides 0 and 1; the horizontal rows are those on sides 2 and 3. This connects the abstract energy-matrix construction to the explicit cell unknowns described in Appendix B.3. It constructs the maps for every layout and does not assert its validity.
Breakdown.CellCert.CellEnergy.layoutInde.summary: Takes the coordinate maps for gradient degrees 0,…,Q and velocity degrees 0,…,Q−1 from a cell layout, with radial boundary rows from sides 0 and 1 and horizontal rows from sides 2 and 3, linking the energy matrices to the cell unknowns of Appendix B.3.

Breakdown.CellCert.CellEnergy.lowPairRow.text: For a mode, a coefficient array C and a real test φ(r,z), this row sums the retained gradient-coefficient rows over 0≤j,l≤Q, weighted by ∫_QP_j(r)Q_l(z)φ(r,z)dr dz. Applied to the coefficient vector, it is the unweighted planar pairing of the retained polynomial for ∑ₐᵦCₐᵦGₐᵦ with φ. This is used in the cell test optimizations of Appendix B.3. Neither the cylindrical factor r nor the orthogonality weight is implicit in the integral; either must be present in φ when required.
Breakdown.CellCert.CellEnergy.lowPairRow.summary: Sums the retained gradient-coefficient rows over 0≤j,l≤Q, weighted by ∫_QP_jQ_lφ dr dz, giving the unweighted planar pairing of the polynomial for ∑CₐᵦGₐᵦ with φ, as in Appendix B.3. Any factor r or orthogonality weight must be in φ.

Breakdown.CellCert.CellEnergy.lowRow.text: Fix a retained mode, degrees 0≤j,l≤Q and a complex array C. For a cell-coordinate vector x, this row evaluates ∑ₐᵦCₐᵦxₐᵦ,jl, where xₐᵦ,jl is the stored gradient coefficient at those indices. It is the linear combination used in the cell matrices behind (B.26). There is no conjugation on C. If different gradient labels were mapped to the same global coordinate, their contributions add; distinctness is not imposed by this row definition.
Breakdown.CellCert.CellEnergy.lowRow.summary: For a retained mode, degrees 0≤j,l≤Q and a complex array C, evaluates ∑ₐᵦCₐᵦxₐᵦ,jl from the stored gradient coefficients without conjugating C, as used in the cell matrices behind (B.26).

Breakdown.CellCert.CellEnergy.matrixSesq.text: For a complex 12×12 matrix A and U,V∈ℂ¹², this is U*AV=∑ᵢⱼconj(Uᵢ)AᵢⱼVⱼ. It is conjugate-linear in U and linear in V. The twelve entries represent the nine gradient entries followed by the three velocity components in the cell forms of Appendix B.3. The definition is complex-valued and does not assume A is Hermitian; the real quadratic form is obtained later by taking U=V and the real part.
Breakdown.CellCert.CellEnergy.matrixSesq.summary: Defines U*AV=∑ᵢⱼconj(Uᵢ)AᵢⱼVⱼ for a complex 12×12 matrix A, conjugate-linear in U and linear in V, with nine gradient entries then three velocity components, as in Appendix B.3. A need not be Hermitian.

Breakdown.CellCert.CellEnergy.monomial.text: For natural numbers j,l, this is (r,z)↦rʲzˡ on all of ℝ². It is the test monomial used to write the explicit cell matrices behind (B.26). Both exponents are natural numbers; the definition includes constants and uses 0⁰=1. It supplies no restriction to the quarter plane or to a particular cell.
Breakdown.CellCert.CellEnergy.monomial.summary: Defines (r,z)↦rʲzˡ on all of ℝ² for natural j,l, with 0⁰=1, the test monomial for the cell matrices behind (B.26).

Breakdown.CellCert.CellEnergy.radialFace.text: Fix a mode, an inner or outer radial side, a degree 0≤l≤q and a complex array C. This row is the sum ∑ₐᵦCₐᵦ times the supplied side-moment row for the gradient entry (a,b). It packages a tensor contraction of radial-side trace moments in the cell form construction of Appendix B.3. The formula is linear without conjugating C, and validity as a trace requires the supplied side rows to have that meaning.
Breakdown.CellCert.CellEnergy.radialFace.summary: For a mode, a radial side, 0≤l≤q and a complex array C, sums Cₐᵦ times the side-moment row of entry (a,b), giving a radial-side trace moment of the contraction in Appendix B.3. C is not conjugated.

Breakdown.CellCert.CellEnergy.radialInne.text: For a retained mode and contraction C:G, let p be the polynomial reconstructed from its gradient coefficients. The cell is 𝒬=[r₁,r₂]×[z₁,z₂]; put ξ(r)=(2r−r₁−r₂)/(r₂−r₁), and m(r,z)=(r−r₁)(1−ξ(r)²), with division by zero assigned zero. For monomials t_jl=rʲzˡ with 0≤j<Q−1 and 0≤l≤Q, form moments b_jl=−∫_𝒬p∂ᵣ(m·t_jl)dr dz and the Gram matrix H_αβ=∫_𝒬m·t_α·t_βdr dz. The returned matrix has quadratic form b*H⁻¹b. It is the interior radial contribution to the finite cell estimate described near (B.26). The subtraction Q−1 is a natural-number subtraction, so the test set is empty for Q≤1. A singular H has inverse assigned zero; positive definiteness is needed for the usual optimized-test interpretation.
Breakdown.CellCert.CellEnergy.radialInne.summary: For $C:G$ with $\xi=(2r-r_1-r_2)/(r_2-r_1)$ (zero if the width is zero), weight $m=(r-r_1)(1-\xi^2)$, tests $r^jz^l$ with $0\le j<Q-1$, $0\le l\le Q$, moments $b$ and Gram matrix $H$, gives $b^*H^{-1}b$, the radial interior term near (B.26). $Q-1$ truncates, so $Q\le1$ gives no tests.

Breakdown.CellCert.CellEnergy.radialInne.text: For a cell Q with lower radius r₁ and radial reference coordinate ξ=(2r−r₁−r₂)/(r₂−r₁), this is (r−r₁)(1−ξ²). On a valid cell it is nonnegative and vanishes on both radial sides. It supplies an interior integration-by-parts weight in the explicit energy matrices behind (B.26). The formula extends to every (r,z) and uses division by zero equal to zero if the cell width is zero.
Breakdown.CellCert.CellEnergy.radialInne.summary: Defines (r−r₁)(1−ξ²) with ξ=(2r−r₁−r₂)/(r₂−r₁). On a valid cell it is nonnegative and vanishes on both radial sides, giving an interior integration-by-parts weight behind (B.26).

Breakdown.CellCert.CellEnergy.radialMome.text: For natural j,j′, this is ∫ᵣ₁ʳ²ω(r)rʲP_j′(r)dr, with ω(r)=r on an axis cell and 1 otherwise. It is the weighted monomial-to-basis pairing used in the explicit side terms behind (B.26). It is distinct from an always-r-weighted cylindrical integral, since the basis weight changes between axis and nonaxis cells.
Breakdown.CellCert.CellEnergy.radialMome.summary: Defines ∫ᵣ₁ʳ²ω(r)rʲP_j′(r)dr with ω=r on an axis cell and 1 otherwise, the weighted monomial-to-basis pairing in the side terms behind (B.26).

Breakdown.CellCert.CellEnergy.radialOute.text: For a mode and contraction C:G, collect the radial boundary test rows indexed by 0≤j<Q and 0≤l≤q. Their tests are t_jl=ω(r)rʲzˡ, with ω=r on an axis cell and 1 otherwise. Let H_αβ=∫_Qrt_αt_βdr dz. The returned matrix has form b*H⁻¹b for the vector b of those rows, including their corner and side contributions. This is a boundary-sensitive part of E_Q in (B.26). It is a formal finite matrix expression until the cell, trace and Gram-matrix hypotheses are supplied; singular H is assigned inverse zero.
Breakdown.CellCert.CellEnergy.radialOute.summary: For C:G, collects radial boundary rows with 0≤j<Q, 0≤l≤q, for tests ω(r)rʲzˡ, and returns b*H⁻¹b with H_αβ=∫_Qrt_αt_β: a boundary-sensitive part of E_Q in (B.26). A singular inverse is zero.

Breakdown.CellCert.CellEnergy.radialOute.text: For a mode, contraction C:G, 0≤j<Q and 0≤l≤q, this forms the integration-by-parts moment for the test ω(r)rʲzˡ. Its boundary part uses the inner and outer radial trace rows, with coefficients r₁ω(r₁)r₁ʲ and r₂ω(r₂)r₂ʲ both with plus signs after the reference-coordinate signs have been inserted, and expands zˡ using its vertical moments. Its interior part is −∫_Qp∂ᵣ[rξ(r)ω(r)rʲzˡ]dr dz, where p is the retained polynomial for C:G. This is the explicit row used in the cell energy near (B.26); the formula's two positive boundary signs must be retained. Equality with an actual derivative pairing requires the trace and polynomial hypotheses.
Breakdown.CellCert.CellEnergy.radialOute.summary: Integration-by-parts moment of C:G against ω(r)rʲzˡ: inner and outer radial trace rows with coefficients r₁ω(r₁)r₁ʲ and r₂ω(r₂)r₂ʲ, both added, expanded in vertical moments, plus −∫_Qp∂ᵣ[rξ(r)ω(r)rʲzˡ]dr dz. A cell-energy row near (B.26).

Breakdown.CellCert.CellEnergy.radialOute.text: For natural j,l, the test is ω(r)rʲzˡ, where ω=r on an axis cell and 1 otherwise. It is used with the radial reference coordinate in the boundary-sensitive test optimization of the cell energy behind (B.26). The function is defined on all of ℝ²; it does not contain a cutoff to the cell or any boundary condition.
Breakdown.CellCert.CellEnergy.radialOute.summary: Defines the test ω(r)rʲzˡ, with ω=r on an axis cell and 1 otherwise, used with the radial reference coordinate in the boundary test optimization behind (B.26).

Breakdown.CellCert.CellEnergy.radialProj.text: Fix a mode and a tensor contraction C:G. Let b_jl be its retained coefficients and p(r,z)=∑_{j,l=0}^Q b_jlP_j(r)Q_l(z). This matrix has quadratic form r_*∫_Qω(r)(1−ξ(r)²)|∂ᵣp|²dr dz, where ξ maps the radial interval to [−1,1], ω=r on an axis cell and 1 otherwise, and r_*=1 on an axis cell and r₁ otherwise. It is a component of the polynomial energy entering E_Q near (B.26). The matrix is constructed by pulling this Gram form back to the full cell-coordinate vector; its interpretation as an energy lower bound requires the valid-cell and basis hypotheses.
Breakdown.CellCert.CellEnergy.radialProj.summary: Defines the form r_*∫_Qω(r)(1−ξ(r)²)|∂ᵣp|²dr dz for p=∑b_jlP_jQ_l (j,l≤Q), with ω=r and r_*=1 on an axis cell and ω=1, r_*=r₁ otherwise, pulled back to the cell unknowns. A component of the polynomial energy in E_Q near (B.26).

Breakdown.CellCert.CellEnergy.radialSlop.text: For a real function f on ℝ², this is the one-variable derivative of r↦f(r,z) at the supplied radius, with z held fixed. It is the radial derivative in the polynomial test and integration-by-parts matrices of Appendix B.3. If that ordinary derivative does not exist, the formal value is zero. Polynomial tests satisfy the required differentiability, but an arbitrary f need not.
Breakdown.CellCert.CellEnergy.radialSlop.summary: Defines the derivative of r↦f(r,z) with z fixed for real f on ℝ², used in the test and integration-by-parts matrices of Appendix B.3. It is zero where the ordinary derivative does not exist.

Breakdown.CellCert.CellEnergy.rectIntegr.text: For Q=[r₁,r₂]×[z₁,z₂] and a real function f(r,z), the value is ∫_Q f(r,z)dr dz. This is the planar integral used to define the cell matrices in Appendix B.3. It does not insert the cylindrical factor r or the radial polynomial weight; those must occur in f. Empty rectangles give zero, and the ordinary integral is also assigned zero for a nonintegrable integrand.
Breakdown.CellCert.CellEnergy.rectIntegr.summary: Defines ∫_Q f(r,z)dr dz over Q=[r₁,r₂]×[z₁,z₂], the planar integral for the cell matrices of Appendix B.3, with no factor r or polynomial weight inserted. A nonintegrable integrand gives zero.

Breakdown.CellCert.CellEnergy.slotIndex.text: For a retained mode and a gradient or velocity polynomial label, this selects the corresponding coordinate in a supplied coordinate set D, which need not be finite. Gradient labels use degrees at most Q in each variable; velocity labels use degrees less than Q. This identifies the polynomial subvector used by the 12-component forms in Appendix B.3. The assignment alone imposes no injectivity or analytic compatibility.
Breakdown.CellCert.CellEnergy.slotIndex.summary: For a retained mode and a gradient label (degrees at most $Q$) or velocity label (degrees below $Q$), selects a coordinate in a supplied, possibly infinite, coordinate set, giving the polynomial subvector of the 12-component forms in Appendix B.3. No injectivity is imposed.

Breakdown.CellCert.CellEnergy.slotRow.text: For a retained mode and a gradient or velocity polynomial label, this is the row equal to 1 at its assigned coordinate and 0 elsewhere in the full cell-unknown vector. It extracts a coefficient for the polynomial form in Appendix B.3. It carries no field or regularity assertion and can still be defined if the supplied coordinate assignment identifies two labels.
Breakdown.CellCert.CellEnergy.slotRow.summary: The row equal to 1 at the assigned coordinate of a retained gradient or velocity label and 0 elsewhere, extracting that coefficient for the polynomial form in Appendix B.3.

Breakdown.CellCert.CellFormula.CellDatum.text:

Breakdown.CellCert.CellFormula.CellLayou.text:
For one cell side, a gradient entry ∂ᵦvₐ and a natural test degree l, this forms a row from velocity moments, normal-gradient moments and corner values. On a horizontal side, a radial derivative is integrated by parts against rP_l(r); an angular derivative is the frame-turning row against P_l; a vertical derivative uses the gradient-trace data.

These are the boundary expressions in the cell relations of Appendix B.3. The displayed weights account for the cylindrical volume element. This assigns a complex row to every index of a linear relation among a cell's polynomial coefficients and boundary moments. The unknowns are the full gradient coefficients Gₐᵦ,jl, velocity coefficients vₐ,jl, segment and corner data and extra side moments; an actual admissible coordinate vector must annihilate the selected rows. In the first two families, a positive-degree velocity coefficient equals a sum of radial or vertical gradient coefficients weighted by the integration-by-parts entries divided by the corresponding eigenvalue in (B.27); the degree-zero row is explicitly zero. The third family expresses rGₐφ as ikvₐ plus the turning of the cylindrical frame, where k=mn. The fourth imposes Gᵣᵣ+Gφφ+Gzz=0. The fifth sets the angular derivative of the axial component in the zero mode to zero, if that mode is retained.

Two further families express radial and vertical integration by parts using extra side moments and monomial tests; one highest radial test on an axis cell is omitted. Two additional zero-mode axis identities use the radial vanishing of the transverse velocity components. The segment relation links the stream-function difference between its endpoints to the normal velocity flux, using the constant or affine segment test. The final family identifies selected extra side moments with sums of segment moments; it omits the inner side on the axis and respects the available side degree.

These are explicit sufficient relations for forming the maps of global unknowns described before (B.26), rather than a new PDE statement. If the zero mode is absent, each family requiring that mode is assigned the zero row. A missing corner contributes a zero coordinate selector to the stream relation; the other terms of that relation remain. Eigenvalue divisions occur only after a positive polynomial index is selected, and the segment normalization divisions require nonzero test coefficients; the standalone definition still assigns zero to any division by zero. It proves none of the analytic identities for a field by itself.

Breakdown.CellCert.CellFormula.CellLayou.summary: On a radial side, replaces the radial-normal diagonal entry by minus the angular and vertical diagonal entries; on a horizontal side, the vertical-normal entry by minus the radial and angular ones. Breakdown.CellCert.CellFormula.CellLayou.text: If a stored corner index is supplied, this row reads its zero-mode stream-function coordinate; if no corner index is supplied, it is the zero row. Breakdown.CellCert.CellFormula.CellLayou.summary: Reads the zero-mode stream-function coordinate at a stored corner, and is the zero row if no corner index is supplied: the convention for omitted axis corners in the side-flux relations of Appendix B.3.

Let F,Hᵣ,H_z:ℝ²→ℂ and ε=1 when o<c and ε=−1 otherwise. For a constant-radius segment the defined moment is ε∫_{[min(c,o),max(c,o)]×[a,b]}[F(r,z)/(c−o)+(r−o)Hᵣ(r,z)/(c−o)]t_d(z)dr dz. For a constant-height segment it is ε∫_{[a,b]×[min(c,o),max(c,o)]}[F(r,z)/(c−o)+(z−o)H_z(r,z)/(c−o)]w(r)t_d(r)dr dz, where the supplied choice sets w(r)=r or w(r)=1.

Breakdown.CellCert.CellFormula.IsCellLay.text:
This condition relates one layout to the prescribed symmetry order, cell, polynomial bases, resolved modes and degree cutoffs: all six must coincide with the corresponding supplied data. The cell must satisfy 0≤r₁<r₂ and 0≤z₁<z₂. Its polynomial bases must have positive leading coefficients and be orthonormal with radial weight r on axis cells and 1 otherwise. Every velocity/gradient segment and every pressure segment must have nonzero strip width, ordered endpoints and nonzero test leading coefficients. The pressure-gauge segment has the same properties, a nonzero constant test and nonnegative lower endpoint.

Each velocity/gradient segment lies on a specified side of the cell; radial segments have nonzero fixed radius. Its opposite level is the opposite cell side. Stored corners are actual nonaxis cell corners and their opposite points are the diagonally opposite corners. A supplied endpoint or cell-corner index must identify the corresponding geometric point. A missing segment endpoint is allowed only at the lower radial endpoint r=0 of a horizontal segment, and a missing cell corner only on the inner side of an axis cell. The constant radial test and the constant and linear horizontal tests have nonzero leading coefficients.

Writing q for the side degree and Q for the volume coefficient degree, the degrees obey 1≤q and q+1≤Q. Each side's assigned segments have the correct orientation and level, cover the entire side except the omitted inner axis side, and have pairwise disjoint interiors. Every segment is assigned to a side. On each segment the test polynomials of degrees 0,…,q+1 are orthonormal in ordinary one-dimensional measure. These are detailed hypotheses for the coordinate construction described in Appendix B.3. They do not assert any cell energy bound. The raw pressure-segment and gauge data have only the explicitly listed conditions here; further pressure compatibility is not inferred from the velocity-segment requirements.
Breakdown.CellCert.CellFormula.IsCellLay.summary: Requires the layout to match the supplied data, a valid cell with orthonormal bases, nondegenerate segments on the correct sides covering them with disjoint interiors, valid corners, orthonormal segment tests and degrees 1≤q, q+1≤Q. These are hypotheses for the coordinates of Appendix B.3.

This makes the linear elimination consistent with the relations described before (B.26). It is a sufficient algebraic hypothesis; it does not prove that a given fluid perturbation satisfies those rows, and it does not require every eligible boundary coordinate to be designated as shared.
Breakdown.CellCert.CellFormula.IsCellPar.summary: Requires an invertible square block of distinct selected variables, none in the designated shared-boundary set, with every relation row taken from the layout's ten families and each shared coordinate in a boundary family, consistent with the relations before (B.26).

Breakdown.CellCert.CellFormula.IsFaceSeg.text: A segment is required to have distinct transverse levels o≠c, ordered endpoints a<b in its varying coordinate, and a nonzero leading coefficient for every test polynomial t_d. They do not say that the segment lies on a cell, that its radii are nonnegative or that its tests are orthonormal.
Breakdown.CellCert.CellFormula.IsFaceSeg.summary: Requires o≠c, a<b and a nonzero leading coefficient for every test t_d, so the strip denominator is nonzero and t_d has degree exactly d, as needed for the side moments of Appendix B.3.

Breakdown.CellCert.CellFormula.IsParamDa.text: For s complex relations with selected coordinates d₁,…,dₛ and a chosen shared-boundary set, this requires three things: the selected coordinates are distinct; none belongs to the shared set; and the determinant of the selected s×s coefficient block is nonzero. Thus these coordinates can be uniquely solved in terms of the remaining ones without eliminating a designated shared variable. These are sufficient algebraic conditions for the relation construction described before (B.26); they do not impose any fluid equation or prove that the supplied relations hold for a perturbation.
Breakdown.CellCert.CellFormula.IsParamDa.summary: Requires the selected coordinates d₁,…,dₛ to be distinct and outside the shared set, and the selected s×s block to have nonzero determinant, so they can be solved uniquely from the rest, as in the construction before (B.26).

Breakdown.CellCert.CellFormula.ParamData.text: For a finite set D of complex cell unknowns, the data are a natural number s of linear relations, a complex s×D relation matrix R, a choice dⱼ∈D for each of the s variables to solve for, and a finite subset of D designated as shared boundary unknowns. This represents the elimination of cell relations before constructing the maps of global unknowns in Appendix B.3. No independence, invertibility or restriction on the chosen shared set is included at this stage; these are data, not a proof that elimination is possible.
Breakdown.CellCert.CellFormula.ParamData.summary: For a finite set D of cell unknowns, supplies s, an s×D complex relation matrix R, a coordinate dⱼ∈D to solve for in each relation and a set of shared boundary unknowns, representing elimination in Appendix B.3. No invertibility is included.

Breakdown.CellCert.CellFormula.ParamData.summary: Defines the square matrix Bᵢⱼ=Rᵢ,dⱼ of coefficients of the variables chosen for elimination, used for the global-to-cell maps of Appendix B.3. Invertibility is a separate condition.

Breakdown.CellCert.CellFormula.edgeSign.text: For two real numbers c and o, this complex-valued sign is +1 if o<c and −1 otherwise. Breakdown.CellCert.CellFormula.edgeSign.summary: Defines a sign equal to +1 if o<c and −1 otherwise, orienting the strip that recovers the trace at side c from side o in Appendix B.3. Equality c=o gives −1.

Breakdown.CellCert.CellFormula.presMode.summary: Defines (2π)⁻¹∫₀²πe^(−imnφ)P(r cos φ,r sin φ,z)dφ for a scalar pressure P on ℝ³, extracting angular frequency mn, as used for the cell pressure moments of Appendix B.3. A nonintegrable integrand gives zero.

Breakdown.CellCert.CellFormula.quadFormV.summary: Defines Re(u*Au)=Re∑ᵢⱼconj(uᵢ)Aᵢⱼuⱼ, the convention for cell forms in Appendix B.3, where the paper writes ⟨Au,u⟩ for the real part. Hermitian symmetry is not required.

Breakdown.CellCert.Exterior.rayLine.summary: For $a>0$ and real $g\in C_c^1(\mathbb R)$, $\int_a^\infty g(\rho)^2\,d\rho\le4\int_a^\infty\rho^2g'(\rho)^2\,d\rho$, the final inequality of (B.37). The input is real; the paper's complex case follows by adding real and imaginary parts.

Breakdown.CellCert.FracCellData.text:
This adds cell-estimate inputs to the steady fractional certificate data. It belongs to the package's fractional extension; the classical paper's cell data in Appendix B.1–B.3 are time-periodic and are specified separately. The inherited objects include a steady profile W(α,y), k forcing and constraint fields, N test fields and the proposed certificate constants.

The additional inputs are an interior energy weight and a curl weight; a set Ω⊂ℝ³ and a scalar weight on it; a centre field and a proposed second derivative; polynomial-model vector fields for velocity and vorticity, matrix fields for strain and vorticity gradient, and a model rotation rate. For each of k indices there are model forcing fields, proposed model forcing gradients, model constraint fields and proposed gradients of the original forcing fields. Separate real error allowances are supplied for the centre, rotation rate, strain, vorticity gradient, velocity, vorticity, forcing gradient, forcing and constraint field.

Each of the N test rows has a natural-number block index. A real-valued bound depending on a block index and a real argument, a base coefficient, a finite number of spectral levels with a coefficient and rate for each level, a cutoff, and a tail constant complete the data. These are supplied functions and numbers, without sign, measurability, derivative or approximation requirements in this declaration. Consequently their names do not yet assert the bounds needed for the cell inequalities, and this object is not the classical certificate of Proposition B.14.
Breakdown.CellCert.FracCellData.summary: Adds cell-estimate inputs (weights, model fields, error allowances, block indices, spectral levels, tail constants) to the steady fractional certificate data. It belongs to the fractional extension; the paper's time-periodic cell data of Appendix B.1–B.3 are separate.

Breakdown.CellCert.GivenFields.ChartPara.text: The data are three real numbers L,r_c,ε and a natural symmetry order m. In the shared coordinate construction L is the length in σ=|y|/(|y|+L), matching (B.3). The additional r_c and ε belong to the steady fractional construction, where they enter a logarithmic radial phase and an extra decay factor; the classical paper instead prescribes its radial phase separately in (B.5). This declaration imposes no positivity and permits m=0. It is therefore a data format broader than the paper's choices, not a condition that its coordinates are valid.
Breakdown.CellCert.GivenFields.ChartPara.summary: Three reals L,r_c,ε and a natural order m. L is the length in σ=|y|/(|y|+L) of (B.3); r_c and ε belong to the steady fractional construction, whereas the paper prescribes its radial phase in (B.5). No positivity is imposed and m=0 is allowed.

The restrictions on r_c and ε serve the separate fractional field construction and are not hypotheses of the classical paper's radial phase. The order requirement m≥1 is weaker than κ≥3 in Appendix B.1.
Breakdown.CellCert.GivenFields.IsChartPa.summary: Requires L>0, r_c>0, 0<ε<1/8 and m>0. L>0 puts σ=|y|/(|y|+L) in [0,1) as in (B.3); the conditions on r_c and ε serve the fractional construction, and m≥1 is weaker than the paper's κ≥3 in Appendix B.1.

No matching of adjacent polynomial pieces, reflection symmetry or differentiability is included in this condition.
Breakdown.CellCert.GivenFields.IsTensorM.summary: Requires both breakpoint lists to be strictly increasing from 0 to 1, giving finite partitions of [0,1] with positive widths: the compactified-radius and absolute-height partitions for the piecewise polynomials of Appendix B.1.

The array is supplied even outside the finite valid index ranges; no partition validity, degree bound, continuity, derivative matching or symmetry is built into this declaration.
Breakdown.CellCert.GivenFields.Spline.summary: Two breakpoint lists and a complex two-variable polynomial for every pair of natural indices, the polynomial on a mesh rectangle being the one at its interval indices: the piecewise polynomials of Appendix B.1. No validity, degree, continuity or symmetry is built in.

Breakdown.CellCert.GivenFields.Spline.Va.text: For piecewise-polynomial data and a real threshold t_b, the condition is that every piece whose radial left endpoint is at least t_b is the zero polynomial, for every natural height index. If the mesh is a valid partition of [0,1], the threshold t_b is one of its breakpoints with t_b<1, and the physical chart has length L>0, the evaluated polynomial vanishes for t≥t_b. Breakdown.CellCert.GivenFields.Spline.Va.summary: Requires zero polynomial pieces whenever their radial left endpoint is at least t_b; missing endpoints are taken as 1. Breakdown.CellCert.GivenFields.Spline.co.summary: Keeps the mesh and conjugates every polynomial coefficient, so evaluation at real chart coordinates gives the complex conjugate value. This implements the conjugate-pair requirement for harmonics in Appendix B.1.

Breakdown.CellCert.GivenFields.Spline.ev.text: For real coordinates t,x, this selects the polynomial whose indices count the internal breakpoints ≤t and ≤x, then evaluates it at (t,x). Outside the square it extrapolates the selected polynomial rather than vanishing; continuity across a knot requires the separate matching conditions.
Breakdown.CellCert.GivenFields.Spline.ev.summary: Selects the polynomial indexed by the numbers of internal breakpoints ≤t and ≤x and evaluates it at (t,x): the half-chart piecewise polynomial of Appendix B.1 on [0,1]². At a knot it uses the piece to the right; outside the square it extrapolates.

They specify the intended rectangular partition for a piecewise polynomial on the half chart. Appendix B.1 describes partitions in σ and signed η; the formal representation uses separate upper and lower half charts. This declaration does not order the lists or require their endpoints to be 0 and 1.
Breakdown.CellCert.GivenFields.TensorMes.summary: Two finite real lists, for the compactified radius σ and the height ratio |η|, specifying a rectangular half-chart partition. Appendix B.1 partitions σ and signed η; the formal version uses separate upper and lower half charts. Order and endpoints are not required.

Breakdown.CellCert.GivenFields.atFirst.text: For a complex polynomial P(t,x) and c∈ℂ, this substitutes c for t and leaves x unchanged. The result is still represented as a polynomial in two variables, now independent of the first. It is used to compare traces and derivatives of adjoining pieces at compactified-radius knots in Appendix B.1. This algebraic substitution imposes no equality between the pieces being compared.
Breakdown.CellCert.GivenFields.atFirst.summary: Substitutes c for t in a complex polynomial P(t,x), leaving a two-variable polynomial independent of t, used to compare traces and derivatives of adjoining pieces at radial knots in Appendix B.1.

Breakdown.CellCert.GivenFields.atSecond.text: For P(t,x) with complex coefficients and c∈ℂ, this substitutes c for x while leaving t unchanged. The result remains in the two-variable polynomial representation and is independent of the second variable. This supplies the polynomial boundary traces at height-ratio knots in Appendix B.1; matching such traces is a separate condition.
Breakdown.CellCert.GivenFields.atSecond.summary: Substitutes c for x in P(t,x), leaving a two-variable polynomial independent of x, giving the polynomial traces at height-ratio knots in Appendix B.1; matching them is a separate condition.

Breakdown.CellCert.GivenFields.azimVecQ.text: For y∈ℝ³, the defined vector is a=(−y₂/|y|,y₁/|y|,0). At y≠0 this equals e₃×y/|y| and has norm r/|y|=√(1−η²), where r=√(y₁²+y₂²) and η=y₃/|y|. It vanishes on the nonzero y₃ axis. Division by zero is zero, so the assigned value at the origin is also zero. This definition supplies one frame vector; differentiability of a field assembled from it requires the amplitude conditions.
Breakdown.CellCert.GivenFields.azimVecQ.summary: The vector $a=(-y_2/|y|,y_1/|y|,0)$, equal to $e_3\times y/|y|$ for $y\ne0$, with norm $\sqrt{1-\eta^2}$. It vanishes on the nonzero $y_3$ axis, and since division by zero is zero, also at the origin.

Breakdown.CellCert.GivenFields.cellCount.text: For a finite breakpoint list of length n, this is the natural number n−1, with subtraction truncated at zero. Thus empty and singleton lists both give zero intervals. For a valid partition of [0,1] it is the usual number of intervals used in the tensor-product polynomial mesh of Appendix B.1. No ordering or endpoint condition is asserted by this definition.
Breakdown.CellCert.GivenFields.cellCount.summary: For a breakpoint list of length n, gives n−1 with subtraction truncated at zero, the number of intervals of a valid partition of [0,1] in the mesh of Appendix B.1.

Breakdown.CellCert.GivenFields.cellIndex.text: For a real list of breakpoints and a real coordinate u, this counts the internal breakpoints b satisfying b≤u. On a valid strictly increasing partition of [0,1], it chooses the interval to the right of an internal knot, the first interval for u below the first knot, and the last for u beyond the final internal knot. This fixes the boundary convention for the piecewise polynomials of Appendix B.1. It is defined for malformed lists too and does not check that u lies in [0,1].
Breakdown.CellCert.GivenFields.cellIndex.summary: Counts the internal breakpoints b≤u. On a valid partition of [0,1] it selects the interval to the right of a knot, the first interval below the first knot and the last beyond the final one, fixing the boundary convention of Appendix B.1.

Breakdown.CellCert.GivenFields.chartT.text: For a supplied real length L, this is σ=|y|/(|y|+L). Under L>0 it maps ℝ³ to [0,1), equals 0 at the origin and tends to 1 as |y| tends to infinity, exactly as in (B.3). The definition itself permits other L, with division by zero set to zero if |y|+L=0. It does not impose a smooth chart at y=0.
Breakdown.CellCert.GivenFields.chartT.summary: Defines σ=|y|/(|y|+L). For L>0 it maps ℝ³ to [0,1), is 0 at the origin and tends to 1 at infinity, as in (B.3); other L are allowed, with division by zero set to zero.

Breakdown.CellCert.GivenFields.heightDer.text: For a complex function f(t,x) on ℝ², this is ∂xf(t,x) with t fixed. In a valid half chart x is the absolute height ratio |η|, used to construct the polynomial coefficients of (B.7)–(B.8). Reflection to negative η may introduce signs separately. The definition has no regularity hypothesis; where the ordinary one-variable derivative fails to exist its formal value is zero.
Breakdown.CellCert.GivenFields.heightDer.summary: Defines ∂xf(t,x) with t fixed for complex f on ℝ², where x is the absolute height ratio |η| in a half chart, used for the coefficients of (B.7)–(B.8). It is zero where the derivative does not exist.

Breakdown.CellCert.GivenFields.heightRat.text: For y∈ℝ³ this defines η=y₃/|y|. At a nonzero point it is the cosine of the polar angle and lies in [−1,1]. At the origin the formal formula gives η=0 because division by zero is taken to be zero. This assigned value does not give a polar direction at the origin. Regularity of a represented vector field there must follow from its vanishing factors and the separate origin estimates.
Breakdown.CellCert.GivenFields.heightRat.summary: $\eta=y_3/|y|$, the cosine of the polar angle at nonzero points. Division by zero is taken as zero, so $\eta=0$ at the origin, which gives no polar direction there.

Breakdown.CellCert.GivenFields.polarVecQ.text: For y≠0, let η=y₃/|y|. The defined vector is p=(ηy₁/|y|,ηy₂/|y|,−(1−η²)), equal to ηy/|y|−e₃. Its norm is √(1−η²), and it vanishes at nonzero points of the y₃ axis. The definition is also evaluated at y=0, where η=0 and every quotient with denominator |y| is zero; it therefore assigns p(0)=−e₃. The paper's spherical-coordinate description applies away from the origin. Vanishing of the complete represented field at the origin follows from the amplitude factors, rather than from p alone.
Breakdown.CellCert.GivenFields.polarVecQ.summary: For $y\ne0$, $p=(\eta y_1/|y|,\eta y_2/|y|,-(1-\eta^2))=\eta y/|y|-e_3$, of norm $\sqrt{1-\eta^2}$. Division by zero is zero, so $p(0)=-e_3$; vanishing of the full field at the origin comes from the amplitude factors.

Breakdown.CellCert.GivenFields.qOf.text: This is 1−η² with η=y₃/|y|. For y≠0 it equals (y₁²+y₂²)/|y|² and is the angular vanishing factor used in (B.4) and (B.7). At y=0 the formal η is zero, so this definition gives 1; the alternative ratio of squared norms would give 0 there. The two expressions therefore agree only away from the origin, and the smoothness of a complete field cannot be inferred from this factor alone.
Breakdown.CellCert.GivenFields.qOf.summary: Defines 1−η² with η=y₃/|y|, equal to (y₁²+y₂²)/|y|² for y≠0, the angular vanishing factor in (B.4) and (B.7). At y=0 it equals 1, since η is zero there by convention.

Breakdown.CellCert.GivenFields.radialSca.text: For a complex coefficient function u(t,x), this defines t(1−t)∂tu(t,x), with x held fixed. If ρ≥0, L>0, t=σ=ρ/(ρ+L), and u is differentiable in t, the chain rule identifies it with ρ∂ρ[u(ρ/(ρ+L),x)], as stated after (B.4). The radial phase f is a separate real function of squared radius. The full operator of (B.5) adds 2ilρ²f′(ρ²)u to the displayed derivative. If the ordinary derivative of u fails to exist, its formal value is zero; that default does not give a chain-rule identity.
Breakdown.CellCert.GivenFields.radialSca.summary: Defines $t(1-t)\partial_tu(t,x)$. With $t=\sigma=\rho/(\rho+L)$, $L>0$ and $u$ differentiable in $t$, it equals $\rho\partial_\rho$ of $u(\sigma,x)$, as stated after (B.4). It is the derivative part of (B.5); the radial-phase term $2il\rho^2f'(\rho^2)u$ is separate.

Breakdown.CellCert.GivenFields.radialVec.text: The ith component is y_i/|y|. Away from y=0 this gives the unit vector y/|y| used in (B.6); at the origin all components are defined to be zero. This is an everywhere-defined representative with an explicit exceptional value, not a continuous unit vector field at the origin. Regularity of a profile multiplying this vector must follow from its coefficient functions.
Breakdown.CellCert.GivenFields.radialVec.summary: Defines the field with components y_i/|y|, the unit vector y/|y| of (B.6) away from the origin, with all components zero at y=0. It is not a continuous unit field at the origin.

Breakdown.CellCert.GivenFields.tDeriv.text: For a complex polynomial P(t,x) and natural order o, this differentiates o times with respect to t, the compactified-radius variable. Order zero returns P itself. It represents the polynomial derivatives whose traces are matched across the radial partition in Appendix B.1. These are algebraic derivatives of a polynomial piece, not yet a proof that the assembled piecewise function has those derivatives at its knots.
Breakdown.CellCert.GivenFields.tDeriv.summary: Differentiates a complex polynomial P(t,x) o times in the compactified-radius variable t, order zero giving P, representing the derivatives matched across the radial partition in Appendix B.1.

Breakdown.CellCert.GivenFields.weightPol.text: For natural exponents h₀,h₁ and real t, this is t^h₀(1−t)^h₁, viewed as a complex number with zero imaginary part. With t=σ it is the polynomial radial factor used in (B.7)–(B.8). The definition accepts h₀=0 or h₁=0, whereas the particular profile formulas impose positive lower bounds. All powers are natural-number powers, so there is no choice of a complex branch; outside [0,1] the same polynomial formula is used.
Breakdown.CellCert.GivenFields.weightPol.summary: Defines t^h₀(1−t)^h₁ for natural exponents, as a complex number with zero imaginary part; with t=σ it is the radial factor in (B.7)–(B.8). It allows h₀=0 or h₁=0, whereas the profile formulas impose positive lower bounds.

Breakdown.CellCert.GivenFields.xDeriv.text: For a complex polynomial P(t,x) and a natural order o, this is its oth derivative with respect to x, the height-ratio variable. Order zero leaves P unchanged. It supplies the derivative traces used in the matching requirements of Appendix B.1. The operation is on each polynomial piece; smoothness of the entire piecewise polynomial still requires matching across partition lines.
Breakdown.CellCert.GivenFields.xDeriv.summary: For a complex polynomial P(t,x) and natural order o, this is its oth derivative in the height-ratio variable x; order zero leaves P unchanged. It acts on each polynomial piece and supplies the derivative traces for the matching requirements of Appendix B.1.

Breakdown.CellCert.permSign.text: For indices i,j,l∈{0,1,2}, this is the real alternating symbol εᵢⱼₗ: it equals 1 on cyclic permutations of (0,1,2), −1 on the other permutations, and 0 when an index repeats. It supplies the orientation in the curl expressions used in Appendix B.3, especially (B.25). This is a numerical definition for every triple, with no field or differentiability hypothesis; identifying its contraction with the curl of a vector field requires that the contracted matrix represent that field's spatial derivative.
Breakdown.CellCert.permSign.summary: The real alternating symbol εᵢⱼₗ on {0,1,2}: 1 on cyclic permutations, −1 on the others, 0 when an index repeats. It gives the orientation in the curl expressions of Appendix B.3, notably (B.25), and is defined for every triple with no field hypothesis.

Breakdown.CellLayerSystem.CellSystemCond.text: The formal statement is a condition on one consistent choice of seven collections of data: the certificate fields and mesh; their instance bounds; the cell forms and their expression in common coordinates; the matrix tree; the exterior, omitted-mode and error data; four coercive-estimate numbers; and the profile, pressure, adjoint and offset representations. It requires fifteen groups of assertions. These are: (1) the geometry, symmetries, row fields, reference field and matrix-tree hypotheses; (2) the identities and value bounds of the represented fields, including positive periods and constant weight $w_*=39/50$; (3) the conditions assembling the cell, exterior and error contributions; (4) admissibility of the multiplier bounds for every $\alpha\in\mathcal K$; (5) $c_1\ge\sqrt{50/3}\,c_{\mathsf M}$, where $c_{\mathsf M}^2=(50/3)(1+\mathsf n_\lambda+\mathsf n_{\nabla\lambda}/\sqrt{w_*})^2+\mathsf n_\mu/c_\mu$; (6) $c_2\ge\sqrt{1000\cdot50/3}$; (7) the remaining sign, norm, invertibility, smallness and parameter-inclusion inequalities of the certificate; (8) valid profile, pressure and adjoint representations with their identifications to the same certificate; (9) the affine inverse-period and forcing identities, offset coefficient enclosures and exterior bounds; (10) the four profile-change norms and their two scalar budgets; (11) the reference-strain and $L^3$ gradient bounds and their budget; (12) the $L^2$ or $L^3$ adjoint norms and quadratic budgets; (13) identification of central and directional profiles and a fixed adjoint, with no separately fitted directions; (14) valid finite potential and compact constraint-generator representations, identified with those in the adjoint estimate; and (15) the central residual, directional, time and constraint replacement bounds whose total is at most each $a_j$. In (5), $\mathsf n_\lambda$ and $\mathsf n_{\nabla\lambda}$ bound the multiplier error and its gradient, $\mathsf n_\mu$ is the velocity-piece ratio bound, and $c_\mu>0$ is its multiplier constant. The cell coercivity and constraint weight are fixed to $3/50$ and $1000$. The row bound also requires $c_0^2\ge(50/3)400(1+2^{-18})$. Fields live on $\mathbb R_\theta\times\mathbb R_y^3$ and all period integrals use $[0,1]$, equivalent to $(0,1)$. These conditions include functional identities, pointwise inequalities, weak derivatives, integrals and matrix inequalities. Finitely represented inputs do not make these assertions automatic, and this declaration gives no concrete data set satisfying them.
Breakdown.CellLayerSystem.CellSystemCond.summary: A condition on one choice of certificate, mesh, cell-form, tree, exterior, error and representation data, asserting fifteen groups of identities, bounds and inequalities, with $w_*=39/50$, cell coercivity $3/50$ and constraint weight $1000$. It gives no concrete data set satisfying them.

Breakdown.CellLayerSystem.CertificateCla.text:
This condition imposes the numerical and norm hypotheses that the cell estimates do not derive. There are finitely many parameters, nonzero slopes $d_i$, selected indices $\mathcal J$, nonnegative radii and an invertible real matrix $V$. Put $\vartheta=(c_1+c_0)c_{\mathrm r}$, $c_w=(4\pi\sqrt{w_*})^{-1/2}$, and $\mathcal H=L^2((0,1)	imes\mathbb R^3)$. It requires nonnegative bounds $c_0,c_1,c_2,c_{\mathrm r},c'_3,c''_3,b_*,\varepsilon$, positive $c_L,M,\omega$, $w_*\le w_{\max}$, $c'_3+c''_3\le c_3$, $\vartheta<1$, and $c_1+c_0\le(1-\vartheta)c_L$. Periods satisfy $S(\alpha)\le S_{\max}$. The integer $m$ is 1, or 2 with a half-period symmetry. The force fields satisfy $\sum_i\|b_i\|_{\mathcal H}^2\le b_*^2$; the residual has nonnegative bounds $\|F_\alpha^{\mathrm a}\|_{\mathcal H}\le\delta(\alpha)\le\delta_{\max}$ and $[F_\alpha^{\mathrm a}]\le\delta_0(\alpha)$, where $[F]^2=\sum_k	au_k\langle F,e_kangle^2$. For every parameter it requires $c_1\delta+\delta_0+c_2| ar\ell|\le(1-\vartheta)\varepsilon$, $2c_Lc_wM<1$, $4\varepsilon^2[w_*^{-1}+2(S_{\max}/m)(c_3+b_*/\omega+c_L^{-1})]\le M^2$, and $4\varepsilon^2[w_*^{-1}+2(S_{\max}/m)c_3]+4(S_{\max}/m)\varepsilon[\delta_{\max}+2c_w\varepsilon M+2b_*\varepsilon/\omega]\le M^2$. It also imposes finite nonnegative uniform $L^2$ bounds on selected adjoints, nonnegative $a_j,\widetilde a_j$, and $4\widetilde a_j\varepsilon^2+2\varepsilon\sqrt{a_j^2+|\langle b,\psi_jangle-V_j|^2/\omega^2}+o_j\le|d_j|\varrho_j$. On the complementary coordinates, $\sum_{j
otin\mathcal J}(V_j\cdot eta)^2\le a_*^2| eta|^2$, $a_*\ge0$, $[\sum_{j
otin\mathcal J}(V_j\cdot eta^{\mathrm a}(\alpha)-d_j\alpha_j)^2]^{1/2}\le o_*$, and $2\varepsilon a_*/\omega+o_*\le\varrho_*$. Finally $4\varepsilon^2/w_*<\|
abla W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}\|_{\mathcal H}^2$ ensures nontriviality. Positive weight and positive periods are supplied by other cell conditions. This declaration records assumptions on data and asserts no existence of a data set satisfying them.
Breakdown.CellLayerSystem.CertificateCla.summary: The numerical and norm hypotheses the cell estimates do not derive: nonnegative constants, $\vartheta=(c_1+c_0)c_{\mathrm r}<1$, residual, force and period bounds, smallness inequalities in $\varepsilon,M$, offset bounds and $4\varepsilon^2/w_*<\|\nabla W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}\|_{\mathcal H}^2$.

Breakdown.CellLayerSystem.CoerciveNumber.text: This supplies four real numbers: a bound for the sum of curl-multiplier weights, a bound for the sum of their spatial gradient magnitudes, the coefficient controlling the squared velocity-multiplier weight by its frequency-weighted sum, and a global forcing-error allowance. The first three determine the explicit a priori constant in Lemma B.2 and (B.22); the last is $\mathsf n_b$ in (B.34) and (B.43). The data definition does not require any of the bounds or signs. Their validity is imposed uniformly over the parameter set by the cell-system conditions.
Breakdown.CellLayerSystem.CoerciveNumber.summary: Four real numbers: bounds for the sum of curl-multiplier weights and of their gradients, the velocity-multiplier coefficient, and the forcing-error allowance $\mathsf n_b$ of (B.34) and (B.43). The first three give the a priori constant of Lemma B.2 and (B.22); no bounds or signs are required here.

Breakdown.CellLayerSystem.PotentialEntri.text: For every coefficient index, this supplies a finite series representing the four auxiliary fields $\mathsf G,\mathsf U,\mathsf F,q$, its shape parameters, and one common set of representations for the constraint tensors and the two compactly supported constraint-potential families. Only indices in the selected adjoint set are used by the adjoint-error estimate. These are the auxiliary choices in (B.51) to (B.53). The data definition imposes no regularity, matching with the adjoint-error data, or numerical norm bound.
Breakdown.CellLayerSystem.PotentialEntri.summary: For every coefficient index, a finite series representing the auxiliary fields $\mathsf G,\mathsf U,\mathsf F,q$, with shape parameters and common representations of the constraint tensors and potential families, as in (B.51) to (B.53). No regularity, matching or norm bound is imposed.

Breakdown.CellLayerSystem.PotentialEntri.text: For every selected adjoint index, its shape parameters and potential series must satisfy their regularity, origin, axis and decay conditions. The common constraint-potential representations must be valid. The central potential fields used in its adjoint-error entry must equal exactly the fields evaluated from that series, and its two constraint-potential families must equal the common represented families. Finally the represented constraint tensors must equal those used in the cell data. These are identification and representation requirements for (B.51) to (B.53). They do not alone establish the norms or dual bounds of the adjoint error; those are separate conditions. Indices outside the selected adjoint set impose no series conditions here.
Breakdown.CellLayerSystem.PotentialEntri.summary: For each selected adjoint index, the potential series is valid, the fields in its adjoint-error entry equal those evaluated from it, and the constraint data match the cell data. These are identification requirements for (B.51) to (B.53), not the adjoint-error norms.

Breakdown.CellLayerSystem.ReductionEntri.text: This supplies nine families of choices: the parameter-dependent approximate profile representation; its pressure representation; the adjoint field representations; the polynomial expansion and exterior bounds for the offset; the four numbers comparing the reference and approximate profiles; the strain and gradient numbers for the reference frozen form; the choice of $L^2$ or $L^3$ adjoint quadratic bounds and their sizes; an error decomposition for every adjoint index; and the represented potentials and constraint fields used in those decompositions. Together they provide the inputs to Lemmas B.9 to B.13. Their mere presence is data, not a proof that the corresponding estimates or equalities hold.
Breakdown.CellLayerSystem.ReductionEntri.summary: Nine families of data: profile, pressure and adjoint representations, the offset expansion, profile-change and frozen-form numbers, $L^2$ or $L^3$ adjoint bounds, adjoint error decompositions and potentials. They are the inputs to Lemmas B.9 to B.13, not proofs.

Breakdown.CellLayerSystem.ShiftNumbers.text:
The four supplied real numbers are intended to be $\mathsf n_0^\infty,\mathsf n_0^{(2)},\mathsf n_1^\infty,\mathsf n_1^{(3)}$ of (B.47). The first two bound the uniform norm of $W_0^{\mathrm a}-W^{\mathrm r}$ and the spatial $L^2$ norm of $|\nabla(W_0^{\mathrm a}-W^{\mathrm r})|_{\mathrm{op}}$, uniformly in time. The last two give the corresponding uniform and spatial $L^3$ bounds for $W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}-W_0^{\mathrm a}$, uniformly over time and $\alpha\in\mathcal K$. Here $W_0^{\mathrm a}$ is the approximate profile at parameter zero, and $|A|_{\mathrm{op}}=\sup_{|u|=1}|Au|$.

These are the two comparisons used in the transfer and frozen-form estimates of Lemma B.9. The definition supplies four real numbers only; it asserts neither their nonnegativity nor any estimate for the fields.
Breakdown.CellLayerSystem.ShiftNumbers.summary: Four proposed bounds from (B.47): uniform norms of $W_0^{\mathrm a}-W^{\mathrm r}$ and $W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}-W_0^{\mathrm a}$, and spatial $L^2$ and $L^3$ norms of their gradient operator norms. They enter Lemma B.9; this data definition imposes no bound or sign.

Breakdown.CellLayerSystem.ShiftNumbersBo.text:
Set $Z_0=W_0^{\mathrm a}-W^{\mathrm r}$ and $Z_1(\alpha)=W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}-W_0^{\mathrm a}$ on $\mathbb R_	heta	imes\mathbb R_y^3$. This condition requires nonnegative numbers $n_0^\infty,n_0^{(2)},n_1^\infty,n_1^{(3)}$ with $|Z_0|\le n_0^\infty$, $\|
abla Z_0(	heta)\|_{L^2(\mathrm{op})}\le n_0^{(2)}$, $|Z_1(\alpha)|\le n_1^\infty$ and $\|
abla Z_1(\alpha,	heta)\|_{L^3(\mathrm{op})}\le n_1^{(3)}$, for every $	heta$, every point in the pointwise bounds, and every $\alpha\in\mathcal K$. It also requires $c_w n_0^{(2)}+n_0^\infty/\sqrt{w_*}+2n_1^{(3)}/\sqrt{3w_*}+n_1^\infty/\sqrt{w_*}\le c_{\mathrm r}$ and $c_w n_0^{(2)}+n_0^\infty/(2\sqrt{w_*})+n_1^{(3)}/\sqrt{3w_*}+n_1^\infty/(2\sqrt{w_*})\le c''_3$, where $c_w=(4\pi\sqrt{w_*})^{-1/2}$. The norm inequalities are encoded by their squares or cubes, with nonnegativity imposed explicitly. This records the four difference estimates of (B.47) and the first and third budgets of (B.48); reference-strain and reference-gradient bounds are separate assumptions. The cell conditions identify $w_*=39/50$ and identify the represented fields with the certificate fields. Precisely, the recorded bounds are $\int^-|
abla Z_0|_{\mathrm{op}}^2\le(n_0^{(2)})^2$ and $\int^-|
abla Z_1|_{\mathrm{op}}^3\le(n_1^{(3)})^3$, using the nonnegative integral defined even for a nonmeasurable integrand. This condition alone supplies no measurability or weak-derivative identification. Under the separate regularity of the represented fields these are the stated $L^p$ bounds; without that regularity the bare condition is only an integral budget. Pointwise derivatives are zero where differentiability fails.
Breakdown.CellLayerSystem.ShiftNumbersBo.summary: Pointwise bounds for $Z_0=W_0^{\mathrm a}-W^{\mathrm r}$ and $Z_1(\alpha)=W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}-W_0^{\mathrm a}$, square and cube integral bounds for their gradients, and budgets at most $c_{\mathrm r}$ and $c''_3$: the estimates of (B.47) and two budgets of (B.48). Regularity is separate.

Breakdown.CellLayerSystem.breakdownOnSpa.summary: Assuming data meeting all fifteen groups of cell conditions, for every $\nu>0$ some smooth compactly supported divergence-free datum on $\mathbb R^3$ has no global smooth solution of bounded $L^2$ norm, and some unit-periodic datum has no global smooth periodic solution. No such cell data are built.

Breakdown.CellLayerSystem.breakdownOnSpa.text:
Assume that finite harmonic and piecewise-polynomial profile data, forcing and constraint fields, cell and exterior bounds, matrices and a finite global tree satisfy all the cell-system conditions of Proposition B.14. These include the pointwise and integral error estimates, the matrix enclosures and exact row relations, the fixed constants $w_*=39/50$, $c=3/50$ and constraint weight $1000$, the explicit lower bounds for the a priori constants, and all profile, residual, adjoint, offset and smallness conditions of Section 7.3.

The formal statement then asserts: for every viscosity $
u>0$, there exists a smooth compactly supported divergence-free $u_0:\mathbb R^3	o\mathbb R^3$ for which there are no globally defined real fields $u(t,x),p(t,x)$ smooth on $[0,\infty)	imes\mathbb R^3$, with $u(0)=u_0$, satisfying $\partial_tu+(u\cdot
abla)u=
u\Delta u-
abla p$ and $\operatorname{div}u=0$ at every positive time, and having $\sup_{t\ge0}\int_{\mathbb R^3}|u(t,x)|^2\,dx<\infty$. The datum may depend on $
u$. The fields are represented for all real times, but only nonnegative times are constrained.

This is the whole-space nonexistence consequence of Proposition B.14, Theorem 7.1 and Corollary 7.2. It states less than Theorem 1.1: it does not assert in its conclusion a solution up to time one, the two-sided blow-up rate (1.6), or convergence to the profile. Its hypothesis is conditional on a valid cell certificate; the statement does not certify the numerical data announced in Section 1.1.
Breakdown.CellLayerSystem.breakdownOnSpa.summary: Under the conditions of Proposition B.14, for every $\nu>0$ some smooth compactly supported divergence-free $u_0$ on $\mathbb R^3$ has no global smooth solution with $\sup_{t\ge0}\int|u|^2<\infty$. This is less than Theorem 1.1: no rate (1.6) or profile convergence.

Breakdown.CellLayerSystem.breakdownOnTor.text:
Assume that the finite profile, forcing, constraint, cell, tree and adjoint data satisfy the complete conditions of Proposition B.14: exact representation and row identities, pointwise and integral bounds, matrix enclosures, the fixed weight $39/50$, coercivity coefficient $3/50$ and constraint weight $1000$, and the residual, transfer, smallness, offset and parameter-inclusion conditions of Section 7.3.

For every viscosity $\nu>0$, the formal statement asserts the existence of a smooth divergence-free $u_0:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ with period one in every coordinate for which no globally smooth solution of the unforced incompressible Navier–Stokes equations exists on $[0,\infty)\times\mathbb R^3$ with that initial datum and with velocity periodic in each spatial coordinate at every nonnegative time. The pressure is any smooth real scalar field; it is not required to be periodic. The torus is represented by these periodic functions on $\mathbb R^3$, and the fields are formally defined also at negative times, without conditions there.

This excludes a larger class of global candidates than the paper's periodic-pressure convention in Section 1.1. At the same time its stated conclusion contains less quantitative information than (1.7): it does not give a finite terminal time, a solution up to that time, the blow-up rate or local profile approximation. It is the conditional torus consequence of Proposition B.14 and Corollary 7.2, with validity of the numerical certificate assumed.
Breakdown.CellLayerSystem.breakdownOnTor.summary: Under the conditions of Proposition B.14, for every $\nu>0$ some smooth period-one divergence-free datum has no global smooth solution with periodic velocity; the pressure need not be periodic, a larger excluded class than Section 1.1. The data of (1.7) are omitted.

Breakdown.CellLayerSystem.isExtendedCert.text:
Assume one choice of certificate fields, cell mesh, row bounds, multiplier data, cell forms, matrix tree, exterior estimates, profile and pressure representations, adjoint potentials and offset enclosures satisfies all fifteen groups of cell conditions. The formal statement proves that there exists a common decay constant $C$ for which these same certificate data, with that decay constant supplied, satisfy the full certificate assumptions: regularity and symmetries, the coercive estimate, profile-change and quadratic-form bounds, all adjoint and offset estimates, and the remaining numerical and nontriviality conditions. It takes ten analytic implications as explicit premises: interpretation of the represented fields, the offset estimate, the profile-change estimate, the change in the quadratic form, the reference-form bound, the quadratic adjoint bound, the linear adjoint bound, identification of the adjoint decomposition, differentiation of the profile decomposition, and regularity of the represented potentials. The packet supplies these premises in the final cell theorem with those premises supplied. The conclusion is the certificate of Proposition B.14, with an existential decay constant; it does not assert that any concrete collection of numerical data meets the cell conditions.

The complete grouping of the conditions assumed here is as follows. The hypothesis is a condition on one consistent choice of seven collections of data: the certificate fields and mesh; their concrete bounds; the cell forms and their expression in common coordinates; the matrix tree; the exterior, omitted-mode and error data; four coercive-estimate numbers; and the profile, pressure, adjoint and offset representations. It requires fifteen groups of assertions. These are: (1) the geometry, symmetries, row fields, reference field and matrix-tree hypotheses; (2) the identities and value bounds of the represented fields, including positive periods and constant weight $w_*=39/50$; (3) the conditions assembling the cell, exterior and error contributions; (4) admissibility of the multiplier bounds for every $\alpha\in\mathcal K$; (5) $c_1\ge\sqrt{50/3}\,c_{\mathsf M}$, where $c_{\mathsf M}^2=(50/3)(1+\mathsf n_\lambda+\mathsf n_{\nabla\lambda}/\sqrt{w_*})^2+\mathsf n_\mu/c_\mu$; (6) $c_2\ge\sqrt{1000\cdot50/3}$; (7) the remaining sign, norm, invertibility, smallness and parameter-inclusion inequalities of the certificate; (8) valid profile, pressure and adjoint representations with their identifications to the same certificate; (9) the affine inverse-period and forcing identities, offset coefficient enclosures and exterior bounds; (10) the four profile-change norms and their two scalar budgets; (11) the reference-strain and $L^3$ gradient bounds and their budget; (12) the $L^2$ or $L^3$ adjoint norms and quadratic budgets; (13) identification of central and directional profiles and a fixed adjoint, with no separately fitted directions; (14) valid finite potential and compact constraint-generator representations, identified with those in the adjoint estimate; and (15) the central residual, directional, time and constraint replacement bounds whose total is at most each $a_j$. In (5), $\mathsf n_\lambda$ and $\mathsf n_{\nabla\lambda}$ bound the multiplier error and its gradient, $\mathsf n_\mu$ is the velocity-piece ratio bound, and $c_\mu>0$ is its multiplier constant. The cell coercivity and constraint weight are fixed to $3/50$ and $1000$. The row bound also requires $c_0^2\ge(50/3)400(1+2^{-18})$. Fields live on $\mathbb R_\theta\times\mathbb R_y^3$ and all period integrals use $[0,1]$, equivalent to $(0,1)$. These conditions include functional identities, pointwise inequalities, weak derivatives, integrals and matrix inequalities. Finitely represented inputs do not make these assertions automatic, and this theorem gives no concrete data set satisfying them.
Breakdown.CellLayerSystem.isExtendedCert.summary: Given data meeting the fifteen groups of cell conditions, and ten analytic implications as premises, there is a common decay constant $C$ with which the same data satisfy the full certificate of Proposition B.14. No concrete numerical data are shown to meet the conditions.

Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.Ad.text: For every $j\in\mathcal J$, this condition identifies the adjoint field with the fixed finite-harmonic field $\psi_j$ and the constraint coefficients with $Y_{jl}$, independent of $\alpha\in\mathcal K$. It sets the separately fitted parameter directions to the empty set, identifies the central profile with $W_\alpha^0$, and identifies each remaining direction with $W_\alpha^i$. It also equates the central inverse period with the constant coefficient of $1/S(\alpha)$ and the period rates with the affine coefficients $\varsigma_i$. Hence the general decomposition specializes to $W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}=W_\alpha^0+\sum_i\alpha_iW_\alpha^i$ and $1/S(\alpha)=1/S(0)+\sum_i\varsigma_i\alpha_i$, once the separate profile and period conditions are supplied. These are identifications between given data. They supply no norm estimate and do not verify (B.53). Their role is to ensure that the adjoint estimate applies to the same profile and period as the certificate.
Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.Ad.summary: For each $j\in\mathcal J$, it identifies the adjoint with the fixed $\psi_j$, the coefficients with $Y_{jl}$ independent of $\alpha$, the fitted set with $\varnothing$ and the profiles with $W_\alpha^0,W_\alpha^i$. These are identifications only; they give no norm estimate and do not verify (B.53).

Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.Ad.text: For each selected adjoint index j∈J, every α∈K and every constraint index l, this identification requires Y_{jl}(α) to equal a fixed real coefficient Y_{jl} stored with that adjoint. Hence only the rows indexed by J are required to be parameter independent. The statement imposes no condition on rows outside J and no bound on the Euclidean norm of the fixed row. The latter is supplied separately in the numerical adjoint-defect conditions.
Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.Ad.summary: For each $j\in\mathcal J$, every $\alpha\in\mathcal K$ and every $l$, $Y_{jl}(\alpha)$ equals a fixed real coefficient $Y_{jl}$, so only the rows indexed by $\mathcal J$ must be parameter independent. No bound on the fixed row's Euclidean norm is imposed here.

Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.Ad.text: The data provide one common length, symmetry order, radial phase, and origin correction, together with one finite harmonic vector-field expansion for each of k indices. These are the representations of ψj in Appendix B.1. The shared parameters express the paper's use of one length, phase, and origin correction for all adjoints. The declaration itself imposes neither validity nor decay exponent h≥3, and it does not identify these fields with the certificate's adjoint fields.
Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.Ad.summary: One common length, symmetry order, radial phase and origin correction, with a finite harmonic vector-field expansion for each of k indices: the representations of ψj in Appendix B.1. It imposes neither validity nor decay h≥3 and does not identify them with the certificate's adjoints.

Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.In.text: The condition identifies three families of fields from Appendix B.1. For every parameter α, the approximate profile and its supplied Hessian equal the represented family (B.9) and its second-derivative field. The stored constraint target is ℓ(Wαᵃ), so the perturbation target is zero. The supplied pressure-gradient field equals ∇(qα−|Wαᵃ|²/2), with valid pressure expansions. For j∈𝒥, the adjoint equals a valid parameter-independent harmonic field with decay exponent at least three. The stated representation and regularity conditions are required; numerical residual, coercivity and adjoint-error estimates are separate conditions.
Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.In.summary: Requires the approximate profile and Hessian to match (B.9), with zero perturbation constraint target; the pressure gradient to equal ∇(qα−|Wαᵃ|²/2); and adjoints on 𝒥 to match valid harmonic fields with decay at least three. No residual or coercivity estimate is included.
