Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.In.summary: Under the representation, joining and phase hypotheses, at $|y|<r_\chi$ where the pressure coefficients are differentiable, $F_\alpha^{\mathrm a}=F^{(0)}+\sum_i\alpha_iF^{(i)}+\sum_{i,i'}\alpha_i\alpha_{i'}Q_{ii'}$; pairing off-diagonal terms gives the paper's sum over $i\le i'$, a.e.

Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.In.text: Let $d_i\ne0$ for every one of the finitely many parameter coordinates, and suppose $\alpha\in\mathcal K$, where $|\alpha_i|\le\varrho_i$ for $i\in\mathcal J$ and $\sum_{i\notin\mathcal J}(d_i\alpha_i)^2\le\varrho_*^2$. The formal statement proves $|\alpha_i|\le\varrho_i$ on $\mathcal J$ and $|\alpha_i|\le|\varrho_*|/|d_i|$ elsewhere. In the latter case it uses that one nonnegative summand is bounded by the sum, then takes square roots and divides by $|d_i|>0$. The statement does not require $\varrho_*\ge0$; imposing that certificate condition recovers the paper's radius exactly. The nonzero-slope premise prevents division by zero from weakening the conclusion.
Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.In.summary: If $d_i\ne0$ for every coordinate and $\alpha\in\mathcal K$, then $|\alpha_i|\le\varrho_i$ on $\mathcal J$ and $|\alpha_i|\le|\varrho_*|/|d_i|$ elsewhere. With the certificate condition $\varrho_*\ge0$ this is exactly the paper's radius.

Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.In.text: This is a finite-dimensional estimate. Suppose $|\alpha_i|\le r_i$, an interior pairing is exactly $B_0+\sum_i\alpha_iB_i+\sum_{i\le i'}\alpha_i\alpha_{i'}B_{ii'}$, and the full pairing differs from it by at most $ab$. Suppose the constant, linear and quadratic coefficients obey $|C_0-(V_j\cdot\beta^0-B_0)|\le e_0$, $|C_i-(V_j\cdot\beta^i-B_i)|\le e_i$ and $|C_{ii'}+B_{ii'}|\le e_{ii'}$. The formal statement proves that $|V_j\cdot(\beta^0+\sum_i\alpha_i\beta^i)-\text{full pairing}-d_j\alpha_j|$ is at most $|C_0|+e_0+\sum_i(|C_i-\mathbf1_{i=j}d_j|+e_i)r_i+\sum_{i\le i'}(|C_{ii'}|+e_{ii'})r_ir_{i'}+ab$. All quantities here are real numbers and finite sums. The analytic work of proving the pairing identity and its enclosures is an explicit hypothesis of this estimate.
Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.In.summary: A finite-dimensional estimate: from $|\alpha_i|\le r_i$, an exact quadratic interior pairing, exterior error at most $ab$ and enclosures $e_0,e_i,e_{ii'}$, it bounds $|V_j\cdot(\beta^0+\sum_i\alpha_i\beta^i)-\text{full pairing}-d_j\alpha_j|$ by enclosed coefficients times radii plus $ab$.

Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.In.text: Let $F,G$ be measurable real vector fields in $L^2((0,1)\times\mathbb R^3)$. For a real radius $r$ and nonnegative numbers $a,b$, suppose $\|F\mathbf1_{|y|>r}\|_{L^2}\le a$ and $\|G\mathbf1_{|y|>r}\|_{L^2}\le b$. The formal statement proves $|\langle F,G\rangle_{\mathcal H}-\langle F,G\rangle_{\chi,r}|\le ab$, where the second pairing is over $[0,1]\times\{|y|\le r\}$. This is Cauchy–Schwarz on the exterior. Taking $F=F_\alpha^{\mathrm a}$ and $G=\psi_j$ gives the last term of (B.59). The conclusion includes no residual expansion or coefficient approximation; those are separate inputs for the interior part.
Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.In.summary: For measurable $F,G\in L^2((0,1)\times\mathbb R^3)$ with $\|F\mathbf1_{|y|>r}\|\le a$ and $\|G\mathbf1_{|y|>r}\|\le b$, the full pairing and the pairing over $[0,1]\times\{|y|\le r\}$ differ by at most $ab$ (Cauchy–Schwarz). With $F=F_\alpha^{\mathrm a}$, $G=\psi_j$ this is the last term of (B.59).

Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.In.text: Let L>0 and let χ be a C² piecewise polynomial on a finite strictly increasing partition of [0,1], zero up to a breakpoint σ_χ∈(0,1) and equal to 1 near 1. For f_*(s)=∫₀^{√s}χ(ρ/(ρ+L))dρ/ρ, there exist R>0 and C∈ℝ such that f_*(s)=C+(log s)/2 whenever s>R². In particular f_*(|y|²)=C+log|y| for |y|>R. The theorem gives existence of a threshold and constant; it supplies no numerical values for them. The all-real definition of f_* uses √s=0 for negative s and zero division at ρ=0, neither of which enters the positive tail.
Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.In.summary: For $L>0$ and a $C^2$ piecewise polynomial cutoff $\chi$, $f_*(s)=\int_0^{\sqrt s}\chi(\rho/(\rho+L))\,d\rho/\rho$ equals $C+(\log s)/2$ for $s>R^2$, for some $R>0$ and real $C$, so $f_*(|y|^2)=C+\log|y|$ for $|y|>R$. No numerical values of $R$ or $C$ are given.

Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.Is.text:
For each j in the selected adjoint index set J, the condition prescribes ψ_{α,j}(θ,y)=ψ_j(θ,y) for all α, where ψ_j is represented by (B.6)–(B.8). All these fields share one positive length, one positive azimuthal order, one admissible radial phase and one origin function g. Each has its own admissible finite amplitude data, and every term has natural-number decay exponent h≥3. Hence parameter independence is an equality required by the condition. The order-three decay theorem and the adjoint estimates are separate consequences; this condition alone imposes no bounds on the matrix Y or on a linear adjoint defect.

The finite vector representation and its hypotheses in this statement are as follows. Let L>0 and κ∈ℕ with κ>0. Let f:ℝ→ℝ be C³ on (−δ,∞) for some δ>0, with |sf′(s)|, |s²f″(s)| and |s³f‴(s)| bounded for s≥0. Let g(σ) be a real polynomial up to 0<σ_g≤1 and a constant afterward, with g(0)=1; when σ_g<1 the values and the first two derivatives join at σ_g. No join beyond σ=1 is required. Take finitely many modes (ι,l)∈ℤ²×ℤ, closed under (ι,l)↦(−ι,−l) and (ι,l)↦(ι^♭,l), where ι^♭=(−ι₁,ι₂−ι₁). Each active complex amplitude is polynomial on a finite rectangular partition of [0,1]×[−1,1]. The joins in (σ,η) have orders (2,1) for A, (1,2) for B, (2,2) for S and (1,1) for T. Here A,B are used when ι₁≠0 and S,T,γ when ι₁=0. In the latter branch S(0,η)=T(0,η)=0. Negated modes have conjugate active data and equal exponents. Reflected nonzero modes have A(σ,−η), −B(σ,−η) and equal exponents; S,T of a zero azimuthal mode are odd in η. All h are natural numbers ≥1, and h₀≥2 in the nonzero branch. For y≠0 put σ=|y|/(|y|+L), η=y₃/|y|, φ=arg(y₁+iy₂), p=ηy/|y|−e₃ and a=e₃×y/|y|. Put V_l=σ(1−σ)∂_σ+2ilρ²f′(ρ²), with ρ=Lσ/(1−σ). If ι₁≠0, set u₀=σ^{h₀}(1−σ)^h(1−η²)²A, u₁=σ^{h₀}(1−σ)^h(1−η²)²B and u₂=i[(V_l+2)u₀−∂_η((1−η²)u₁)]/(κι₁). If ι₁=0, set Ψ=γg(σ)η+S and p₀=σ(1−σ)^h, and put (u₀,u₁,u₂)=(−p₀∂_η((1−η²)Ψ),−(V_l+2)(p₀Ψ),p₀T). Write U_{ι,l}=exp(i[2π(2ι₂−ι₁)θ+κι₁φ+lf(|y|²)])[u₀y/|y|+u₁p+u₂a] and W=Re∑U_{ι,l}. Time θ ranges over ℝ. At the origin all quotients by |y| and the axis angle are assigned zero, so p(0)=−e₃ and the full amplitude factors give U_{ι,l}(θ,0)=0.
Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.Is.summary: For each $j\in\mathcal J$, $\psi_{\alpha,j}=\psi_j$ for all $\alpha$, with $\psi_j$ given by (B.6)–(B.8), all sharing one length, azimuthal order, radial phase and origin function, and every term having decay exponent $h\ge3$. It imposes no bound on $Y$ or on a linear adjoint defect.

Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.Is.text: For all $\alpha\in\mathcal K$, this condition requires the exact affine identities $1/S(\alpha)=\nu_0+\sum_i\alpha_i\varsigma_i$ and $\beta^{\mathrm a}(\alpha)=\beta^0+\sum_i\alpha_i\beta^i$. For every selected adjoint $j$, it requires the absolute enclosures $|C_j^0-V_j\cdot\beta^0+\langle F^{(0)},\psi_j\rangle_\chi|\le\widetilde C_j^0$, $|C_{ji}^1-V_j\cdot\beta^i+\langle F^{(i)},\psi_j\rangle_\chi|\le\widetilde C_{ji}^1$, and $|C_{jii'}^2+\langle F^{(ii')},\psi_j\rangle_\chi|\le\widetilde C_{jii'}^2$ for $i\le i'$. It also requires nonnegative exterior bounds $n_F^{\mathrm{out}},n_j^{\mathrm{out}}$ for the residual and adjoint in $L^2$ on $(0,1)\times\{|y|>r_\chi\}$ and requires $o_j$ to equal the complete constant, linear, upper-triangular quadratic and exterior sum in (B.59). The ball pairing uses a closed ball and the time interval $[0,1]$, with no change to the integral at their null boundaries. All these are assumptions on given coefficients and fields. The condition does not compute or certify numerical enclosures on its own. Explicitly, $o_j=|C_j^0|+\widetilde C_j^0+\sum_i(|C_{ji}^1-\mathbf1_{i=j}d_j|+\widetilde C_{ji}^1)\hat\varrho_i+\sum_{i\le l}(|C_{jil}^2|+\widetilde C_{jil}^2)\hat\varrho_i\hat\varrho_l+n_F^{\mathrm{out}}n_j^{\mathrm{out}}$. Here $\hat\varrho_i=\varrho_i$ for $i\in\mathcal J$ and $\hat\varrho_i=|\varrho_*|/|d_i|$ otherwise; this is the paper's $\varrho_*/|d_i|$ when $\varrho_*\ge0$. The exterior budgets are inequalities for nonnegative integrals of squared magnitudes; measurability of the represented fields comes from separate representation hypotheses. Ordinary ball pairings are assigned zero if nonintegrable, so this numerical condition alone does not justify the subsequent integral manipulations.
Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.Is.summary: For all $\alpha\in\mathcal K$: affine identities for $1/S(\alpha)$ and $\beta^{\mathrm a}(\alpha)$, enclosures of the constant, linear and quadratic offset coefficients against ball pairings with $\psi_j$, nonnegative exterior $L^2$ bounds beyond $r_\chi$, and $o_j$ equal to the sum in (B.59).

Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.Is.text: Among the offset-data conditions, this field requires β_l^a(α)=β_l^0+∑ᵢαᵢβ_l^i for every α in the parameter set K and every forcing index l=1,…,n. All central and tangent coefficients are real and supplied with the offset data. The conclusion is a coordinate identity for the prescribed forcing coefficients; it does not estimate the residual of the approximate velocity or assert that β^a vanishes. Those questions require the profile equation and the separate interval bounds.
Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.Is.summary: $\beta_l^{\mathrm a}(\alpha)=\beta_l^0+\sum_i\alpha_i\beta_l^i$ for every $\alpha\in\mathcal K$ and every forcing index $l$, with supplied real coefficients. It is a coordinate identity; it does not estimate the residual or assert that $\beta^{\mathrm a}$ vanishes.

Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.Is.text: Among the offset-data conditions, this field requires 1/S(α)=s₀+∑ᵢαᵢς_i for every α∈K, where s₀ and the real coefficients ς_i are supplied as data. Thus it prescribes an affine reciprocal period. The paper writes s₀=1/S(0), which follows when 0∈K. Positivity of S throughout K is required by the certificate conditions and is not contained in this identity alone. Reciprocal division is defined to be zero at S=0, so that positivity condition is needed for the intended interpretation as a period.
Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.Is.summary: $1/S(\alpha)=s_0+\sum_i\alpha_i\varsigma_i$ for every $\alpha\in\mathcal K$, with supplied $s_0,\varsigma_i$; the paper's $s_0=1/S(0)$ follows when $0\in\mathcal K$. Division by zero is zero, so positivity of $S$, imposed elsewhere, is needed to read it as a period.

Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.Is.text: The scalar q is the real part of a finite sum of E_{ι,l}σ^{h₀}(1−σ)^h(1−η²)^{h′}P(σ,η). This condition imposes natural-number exponents, h≥2, and continuous complex polynomial pieces on rectangular meshes. It requires h′≥1 when ι₁≠0 and h′=0 when ι₁=0. For h₀=0 the value of P at σ=0 is zero in nonzero azimuthal modes and is constant in η in zero modes. The set of modes is closed under conjugation and reflection; their exponents agree, their coefficients are conjugated for (−ι,−l), and P(σ,−η) is used for (ι^♭,l). The condition is on the coefficients, with phase and length conditions supplied separately. It neither fixes a pressure gauge nor solves a Poisson equation. Here σ=|y|/(|y|+L), η=y₃/|y| and E_{ι,l}=exp(i[2π(2ι₂−ι₁)θ+κι₁φ+lf(|y|²)]), with φ=arg(y₁+iy₂) and ι^♭=(−ι₁,ι₂−ι₁). The partitions have domains [0,1] and [−1,1]. At y=0 the quotients by |y| and the angle are assigned zero. Positivity of L and κ and the regularity of f are separate shape assumptions.
Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.Is.summary: $q$ is the real part of a finite sum of $E_{\iota,l}\sigma^{h_0}(1-\sigma)^h(1-\eta^2)^{h'}P(\sigma,\eta)$ with $h\ge2$, continuous polynomial pieces, $h'\ge1$ exactly in nonzero azimuthal modes, origin conditions and conjugation and reflection symmetry. No gauge or Poisson equation is imposed.

Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.Is.text:
For the represented approximate velocity W_α^a and scalar q_α=q_α^0+∑ᵢαᵢq_α^i, this condition requires the scalar data for qα⁰ and qαⁱ to satisfy the finite pressure representation conditions of B.1. For every selected $j\in\mathcal J$, the formal statement specifies $|V_j\cdot eta+\langle F_\alpha^{\mathrm a},\psi_{\alpha,j}angle_{\mathcal H}+(Y(\alpha) ar\ell(\alpha))_j|\le\widetilde a_j(2\varepsilon)^2+2\varepsilon\sqrt{a_j^2+|\langle b,\psi_{\alpha,j}angle_{\mathcal H}-V_j|^2/\omega^2}$. The pairings are over $[0,1]	imes\mathbb R^3$. The discrepancy vector has components $\langle b_l,\psi_{\alpha,j}angle-V_{lj}$ and its norm is Euclidean; $V_j$ is the $j$th column of $V$, so $V_j\cdot eta=\sum_lV_{lj} eta_l$. The certificate constants $a_j$ and $\widetilde a_j$ bound, respectively, the error in the linear adjoint relation by $a_j\|v\|_w$ and the quadratic pairing by $\widetilde a_j\|v\|_w^2$ on its weak perturbation class. The formula retains $\omega$, although the premise makes it one. This declaration specifies the enclosure; a separate theorem proves it from the analytic identities and the combined energy bound.
Breakdown.Cert.ExtendedAdjointEnclosureH.summary: Specifies, for normalized certificates and a bounded nonlinear correction, $|V_j\cdot\beta+\langle F_\alpha^{\mathrm a},\psi_{\alpha,j}\rangle+(Y\bar\ell)_j|\le\widetilde a_j(2\varepsilon)^2+2\varepsilon\sqrt{a_j^2+|\langle b,\psi_{\alpha,j}\rangle-V_j|^2/\omega^2}$ for each $j\in\mathcal J$.

Breakdown.Cert.ExtendedStiffEnclosureHol.text: For a certificate normalized to $\omega=1$, reference profile equal to the approximate profile and zero reference gap and form shift, every bounded nonlinear perturbation satisfies $(\sum_{j\notin\mathcal J}(V_j\cdot\beta)^2)^{1/2}\le2\varepsilon a_*/\omega$. This proposition specifies the consequence of the matrix estimate (7.36) and $\|(v,\beta)\|_{w,1}\le2\varepsilon$. It concerns the additional coefficients $\beta$, before adding the approximate coefficients and offset. With an empty complementary set, the sum is zero. The declaration gives the proposition, and a separate theorem proves it.
Breakdown.Cert.ExtendedStiffEnclosureHol.summary: Specifies that, for normalized certificates, every bounded nonlinear perturbation satisfies $(\sum_{j\notin\mathcal J}(V_j\cdot\beta)^2)^{1/2}\le2\varepsilon a_*/\omega$, the consequence of (7.36) and $\|(v,\beta)\|_{w,1}\le2\varepsilon$.

Breakdown.Cert.ExtendedSupBoundHolds.text:
For a certificate and $\alpha\in\mathcal K$, put $S=S(\alpha)>0$. Let $f\in\mathcal H_{\mathrm{div}}^\Gamma$, where $\mathcal H_{\mathrm{div}}=L^2(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z;L^2_{\mathrm{div}}(\mathbb R^3))$, let $ eta\in\mathbb R^n$, and take the constructed velocity $v=\mathcal T_S^{-1}f$. Its weak gradient and Laplacian are square integrable over a period, and its spatial velocity has an $L^6$ representative for almost every time. Invariance means $v(	heta+	heta_0,Ry)=Rv(	heta,y)$ almost everywhere for each $(R,	heta_0)\in\Gamma$. Here $\mathcal H=L^2([0,1]	imes\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$ and $\|v\|_w^2=\int_0^1\int_{\mathbb R^3}(|\Delta v|^2+w|
abla v|_{m F}^2)$, where $w$ is measurable and $0<w_*\le w\le w^*<\infty$. Set $\mathcal T_S=S^{-1}\partial_	heta+	frac12+	frac12y\cdot
abla-\Delta$, $\mathcal C_\alpha v=(W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}\cdot
abla)v+(v\cdot
abla)W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}$ and $F=\mathbb P(\mathcal T_Sv+\mathcal C_\alpha v+\sum_i eta_i b_i)$. The formal statement specifies finiteness of $U=\operatorname*{ess\,sup}_	heta\|
abla v(	heta)\|_2$ and $U^2\le[w_*^{-1}+2Sc_3/m]\|v\|_w^2+(2S/m)(\|F\|_{\mathcal H}+b_*| eta|)\|v\|_w$. Here $| eta|$ is Euclidean and $\sum_i\|b_i\|_{\mathcal H}^2\le b_*^2$. The number $c_3$ is the lower-bound constant for the frozen form $\int(|\Delta u|^2+	frac14|
abla u|_{m F}^2)-\int(\mathcal C_\alpha(	heta)u)\cdot\Delta u\ge-c_3\int(|\Delta u|^2+w|
abla u|_{m F}^2)$, assumed for every real time and every solenoidal $u\in L^6$ with weak $
abla u\in L^2$, weak Hessian, $\Delta u\in L^2$, and invariance under every $(R,0)\in\Gamma$. The positive integer factor permits $m=1$ in all cases and $m=2$ only when $(R,1/2)\in\Gamma$ for some orthogonal $R$. It is converted to a real divisor. This declaration specifies the estimate for constructed inverse solutions, using the norm of the projected right side. It is not itself a proof of the estimate or a statement for every physical member of the transport domain.
Breakdown.Cert.ExtendedSupBoundHolds.summary: Specifies, for the constructed $v=\mathcal T_S^{-1}f$, that $U=\operatorname*{ess\,sup}_\theta\|\nabla v(\theta)\|_2$ is finite and $U^2\le[w_*^{-1}+2Sc_3/m]\|v\|_w^2+(2S/m)(\|F\|_{\mathcal H}+b_*|\beta|)\|v\|_w$, with $m=2$ only under a half-period symmetry.

Breakdown.Cert.HH.text: The space represents $L^2(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z;L^2_{\rm div}(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3))$. Spatial fields are stored through their Fourier transforms, as complex $L^2$ fields satisfying the reality relation $\widehat F(-\xi)=\overline{\widehat F(\xi)}$ and $\xi\cdot\widehat F(\xi)=0$ almost everywhere. The scalar field of the Hilbert space is real. The time variable is the circle of circumference one; its measure agrees with Lebesgue measure on a fundamental interval. Both time and space functions are identified up to equality almost everywhere. This encodes $\mathcal H_{\mathrm{div}}$, rather than the unrestricted space $\mathcal H$.
Breakdown.Cert.HH.summary: Represents $L^2(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z;L^2_{\rm div}(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3))$ as a real Hilbert space of Fourier transforms with $\widehat F(-\xi)=\overline{\widehat F(\xi)}$ and $\xi\cdot\widehat F(\xi)=0$ almost everywhere. It encodes $\mathcal H_{\mathrm{div}}$, not the unrestricted $\mathcal H$.

Breakdown.Cert.Internal.AtProfile.coerci.text:
Assume a certificate with measurable bounded $w\ge w_*>0$, coefficient weight $\omega>0$, the reference coercive bound $\|(v, eta)\|_{w,\omega}\le c_1\|F\|_{\mathcal H}+[F]+c_2|\ell(v)|$, the seminorm bound $[F]\le c_0\|F\|_{\mathcal H}$, and convection difference at most $c_{\mathrm r}\|v\|_w$. Put $\vartheta=(c_1+c_0)c_{\mathrm r}<1$, fix $\alpha\in\mathcal K$, and set $S=S(\alpha)>0$. The quantified class consists of measurable period-one representatives $v,G,H,g$ on $\mathbb R	imes\mathbb R^3$: for almost every time, $v\in L^6$, $G=
abla v$ and $H=
abla^2v$ in the weak spatial sense, and $\operatorname{div}v=0$; the period integrals of $|G|_{m F}^2$, $|\operatorname{tr}H|^2$ and $|g|^2$ are finite. Here $g=S^{-1}\partial_	heta v+	frac12v+	frac12(y\cdot
abla)v$ in distributions, and $v(	heta+	heta_0,Ry)=Rv(	heta,y)$ almost everywhere for each $(R,	heta_0)\in\Gamma$. The time derivative and dilation term are controlled through their sum, without separate square-integrability assumptions. Here $\mathcal H=L^2([0,1]	imes\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$ and $\|v\|_w^2=\int_0^1\int_{\mathbb R^3}(|\Delta v|^2+w|
abla v|_{m F}^2)$, where $w$ is measurable and $0<w_*\le w\le w^*<\infty$. The seminorm is $[F]=(\sum_{a=1}^N	au_a\langle F,e_aangle_{\mathcal H}^2)^{1/2}$, with period-one orthonormal $e_a\in\mathcal H$ and $0\le	au_a\le c_0^2$. The constraint functional is $\ell_i(v)=\int_0^1\int
abla v:\Xi_i$, with the Frobenius matrix pairing and square-integrable $\Xi_i$ on the displayed period. For every such $v$, every $ eta\in\mathbb R^n$, and every period-one $F\in\mathcal H$ satisfying $F\simeq\mathcal T_Sv+\mathcal C_\alpha v+\sum_i eta_i b_i$, the formal statement proves $\|(v, eta)\|_{w,\omega}\le[c_1\|F\|_{\mathcal H}+[F]+c_2|\ell(v)|]/(1-\vartheta)$. Here $\|(v, eta)\|_{w,\omega}=(\|v\|_w^2+\omega^2\sum_i eta_i^2)^{1/2}$, $\mathcal T_Sv=g-\Delta v$, and $\mathcal C_\alpha v=(W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}\cdot
abla)v+(v\cdot
abla)W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}$. The relation $\simeq$ means equality after pairing against every smooth compactly supported solenoidal space-time test; $F$ itself is not projected before its norm or seminorm is taken. The full certificate is a premise of the formal statement. Its returned seminorm uses weights rescaled by $(1-\vartheta)^{-2}$, exactly giving $[F]/(1-\vartheta)$ because the denominator is positive. With $\ell(v)=0$ and $c_1+c_0\le(1-\vartheta)c_L$, the estimate implies $\|(v, eta)\|_{w,\omega}\le c_L\|F\|_{\mathcal H}$.
Breakdown.Cert.Internal.AtProfile.coerci.summary: Under the certificate, for every weak perturbation $v$, every $\beta$ and every period-one $F\simeq\mathcal T_Sv+\mathcal C_\alpha v+\sum_i\beta_ib_i$, $\|(v,\beta)\|_{w,\omega}\le[c_1\|F\|_{\mathcal H}+[F]+c_2|\ell(v)|]/(1-\vartheta)$, with $F$ unprojected.

Breakdown.Cert.Internal.Convection.weigh.text: On $\mathbb R^3$ with Lebesgue measure, the function $y\mapsto(1+|y|)^{-2}$ belongs to $L^3$. The formal statement includes measurability and finiteness of its $L^3$ norm. The exponent $-2$ is a real exponent; since $1+|y|>0$, it has its ordinary reciprocal-square meaning at every point. No vector field, time variable, coefficient constant or certificate is assumed. This is the scalar integrability used with $v\in L^6$ and Hölder's inequality to show $(v\cdot\nabla)W\in L^2$ under $|\nabla W|\le C_a(1+|y|)^{-2}$.
Breakdown.Cert.Internal.Convection.weigh.summary: On $\mathbb R^3$, $y\mapsto(1+|y|)^{-2}$ is measurable and belongs to $L^3$. With Hölder and $v\in L^6$ this shows $(v\cdot\nabla)W\in L^2$ when $|\nabla W|\le C_a(1+|y|)^{-2}$.

Breakdown.Cert.Internal.ConvectionFirstO.text:
Let $W:\mathbb R	imes\mathbb R^3	o\mathbb R^3$ be jointly $C^1$ and one-periodic in time, and suppose $|W(	heta,y)|\le D/(1+|y|)$ and $\|
abla W(	heta,y)\|_{m op}\le D/(1+|y|)^2$ for all $(	heta,y)$. These bounds imply $D\ge0$. For every real $	heta$, every $v\in X=\dot H^1_{m div}(\mathbb R^3)$ and each coordinate $j\in\{1,2,3\}$, the formal statement proves $W_j(	heta,\cdot)\partial_jv\in L^2$ with norm at most $D\|
abla v\|_2$. The derivative of $v$ is weak and represented by an $L^2$ equivalence class. The derivative bound on $W$ is part of the common coefficient hypothesis, although the proof of this summand only uses the velocity bound. This is a global spatial $L^2$ estimate for a single summand of $(W\cdot
abla)v$. Equation (7.50) gives a pointwise estimate for the sum of both convection terms with their spatial decay factors.
Breakdown.Cert.Internal.ConvectionFirstO.summary: For jointly $C^1$ one-periodic $W$ with $|W|\le D/(1+|y|)$ and $\|\nabla W\|_{\rm op}\le D/(1+|y|)^2$, every $\theta$, $v\in\dot H^1_{\rm div}$ and $j$, $\|W_j(\theta,\cdot)\partial_jv\|_2\le D\|\nabla v\|_2$. Equation (7.50) instead gives a pointwise estimate for both convection terms.

Breakdown.Cert.Internal.ConvectionFirstO.text:
Let $W$ be a jointly $C^1$, one-periodic field with $|W(	heta,y)|\le D/(1+|y|)$ and $\|
abla W(	heta,y)\|_{m op}\le D/(1+|y|)^2$. For every real time $	heta$ and every $v\in\dot H^1_{m div}(\mathbb R^3)$, the formal statement proves $(v\cdot
abla)W(	heta)\in L^2$ and $\|(v\cdot
abla)W(	heta)\|_2\le D\|(1+|y|)^{-2}\|_{L^3}C_S\|
abla v\|_2$. Here $C_S$ is the operator norm of the physical velocity map from the homogeneous gradient space to $L^6$, so it is a Sobolev embedding constant. The matrix norm of $
abla W$ is the operator norm, and its application to $v$ has the usual meaning. The $L^3$ decay norm and the $L^6$ velocity norm combine by Hölder with $1/2=1/3+1/6$. This conclusion estimates the second convection term in the whole-space $L^2$ norm; it does not state the combined pointwise inequality (7.50).
Breakdown.Cert.Internal.ConvectionFirstO.summary:
For jointly $C^1$ periodic $W$ with $|W|\le D(1+|y|)^{-1}$ and $\|
abla W\|_{m op}\le D(1+|y|)^{-2}$, $\|(v\cdot
abla)W(	heta)\|_2\le D\|(1+|y|)^{-2}\|_3C_S\|
abla v\|_2$ for $v\in\dot H^1_{m div}$, where $C_S$ is a Sobolev constant. This estimates one term of (7.50).

Breakdown.Cert.Internal.DenseEnergyBand..text: For every $s\ge0$, the bounded linear map $u\mapsto D_{e^{-s}}e^{(1-e^{-s})\Delta}u$ on the solenoidal homogeneous Sobolev space $X$ has operator norm at most $e^{-s/4}$. Thus $\|\nabla U(s)\|_2\le e^{-s/4}\|\nabla u\|_2$ for every $u\in X$. Here $D_\mu u(y)=\sqrt\mu\,u(\sqrt\mu\,y)$; the $1/4$ is a real exponent determined by this three-dimensional gradient scaling. The norm of an element is computed from the Fourier representative $2\pi|\xi|\widehat u$, which has exactly the physical gradient norm. The assumptions $s\ge0$ ensure $1-e^{-s}\ge0$ and $e^{-s}>0$, so the forward heat operator and positive dilation are used. The formal statement proves the first estimate in (7.47), also for nonsmooth elements of $X$. It gives no separate estimate with $e^{-3s/4}$ for $\Delta U$.
Breakdown.Cert.Internal.DenseEnergyBand..summary: For every $s\ge0$, $u\mapsto D_{e^{-s}}e^{(1-e^{-s})\Delta}u$ on the solenoidal homogeneous Sobolev space has norm at most $e^{-s/4}$, so $\|\nabla U(s)\|_2\le e^{-s/4}\|\nabla u\|_2$. This is the first estimate in (7.47); no $e^{-3s/4}$ bound for $\Delta U$ is given.

Breakdown.Cert.Internal.ExtendedBordered.text: Fix a parameter in a certificate reduced to unit multiplier weight, coincident reference and approximate fields, zero convection gap and zero form-transfer error. Assume the coercive estimate for the constrained equation. Let $f\in\mathcal H_{\rm div}^{\Gamma}$ and $\beta\in\mathbb R^n$, and set $v$ equal to the constructed free inverse of $f$. If $f+\mathbb P\mathcal C_\alpha v+\mathbb P\sum_i\beta_i b_i=0$ and $\ell(v)=0$, then the formal statement concludes $f=0$ and $\beta=0$. The argument first makes the combined nonnegative energy and coefficient sum vanish. The spatial derivative graph has no nonzero element with zero Laplacian, since its Fourier multiplier $2\pi|\xi|$ vanishes only on the measure-zero set $\{0\}$. The linear equation then gives $f=0$. The theorem uses the forcing variable $f$ and the reduced certificate; the paper's paragraph proves injectivity for the original variables $(v,\beta)$ using (7.52) and the Sobolev inequality.
Breakdown.Cert.Internal.ExtendedBordered.summary: For a reduced certificate, if $f\in\mathcal H_{\rm div}^\Gamma$, $v=\mathcal T_S^{-1}f$, $f+\mathbb P\mathcal C_\alpha v+\mathbb P\sum_i\beta_ib_i=0$ and $\ell(v)=0$, then $f=0$ and $\beta=0$. The paper proves injectivity in the variables $(v,\beta)$ using (7.52).

Breakdown.Cert.Internal.ExtendedConvecti.text:
Let $W$ be jointly $C^1$, one-periodic, and satisfy $|W|\le D/(1+|y|)$ and $\|
abla W\|_{m op}\le D/(1+|y|)^2$. For every $R\ge0$, every real time $	heta$ and every $v\in\dot H^1_{m div}(\mathbb R^3)$, the formal statement proves $\int_{|y|>R}|(W\cdot
abla)v+(v\cdot
abla)W|^2dy\le C(D)(1+R)^{-1}\|
abla v\|_2^2$, where $C(D)=6D^2+2(D C_S\|(1+|y|)^{-3/2}\|_{L^3})^2$ and $C_S$ is the operator norm of the Sobolev velocity map from $X$ to $L^6$. The integral is a nonnegative extended integral; this finite upper bound also proves square integrability on the exterior. No division by zero occurs, because $1+R>0$. Equation (7.51) gives a sharper coefficient: its $L^3$ tail is of order $R^{-1}$ in three dimensions, so its squared estimate decays as $R^{-2}$ for large $R$. The formal estimate has squared decay $R^{-1}$. Both give a tail tending to zero uniformly on a bounded gradient set, which is the property used for compactness.
Breakdown.Cert.Internal.ExtendedConvecti.summary:
Under the decay bounds on $W$, $\int_{|y|>R}|(W\cdot
abla)v+(v\cdot
abla)W|^2\le C(D)(1+R)^{-1}\|
abla v\|_2^2$ for $R\ge0$. Equation (7.51) gives squared decay $R^{-2}$; both give tails uniformly small on bounded gradient sets.

Breakdown.Cert.Internal.ExtendedDataCont.text:
Fix certificate data, $\alpha\in\mathcal K$ and a smooth compactly supported divergence-free $\varphi$ on $\mathbb R	imes\mathbb R^3$. Put $A=W_\alpha^{m a}$ and $S=S(\alpha)>0$. The formal statement identifies $\int F_\alpha^{m a}\cdot\varphi$ with $\int[(S^{-1}\partial_	heta A+ rac12A+ rac12(y\cdot
abla)A+(A\cdot
abla)A)\cdot\varphi+
abla A:
abla\varphi]+\sum_i eta_i^{m a}(\alpha)\int b_i\cdot\varphi$. All these integrals run over $\mathbb R	imes\mathbb R^3$. It uses the supplied Hessian as a weak spatial derivative, integration by parts, square-integrability of the residual and forcing, and the hypothesis that the supplied pressure contribution annihilates all such tests. The Laplacian therefore disappears in favor of first spatial derivatives. No norm continuity of $F_\alpha^{m a}$ is needed, and no pressure value is identified. The denominator is nonzero by $S>0$.
Breakdown.Cert.Internal.ExtendedDataCont.summary:
For $\alpha\in\mathcal K$, $A=W_\alpha^{m a}$ and divergence-free test $\varphi$, $\int F_\alpha^{m a}\cdot\varphi=\int[(S^{-1}\partial_	heta A+ rac12A+ rac12(y\cdot
abla)A+(A\cdot
abla)A)\cdot\varphi+
abla A:
abla\varphi]+\sum_i eta_i^{m a}\int b_i\cdot\varphi$.

Breakdown.Cert.Internal.ExtendedExistsZe.text: For $n\geq0$, let $\mathcal J\subset\{1,\ldots,n\}$, let $\varrho_j\geq0$ for $j\in\mathcal J$, let $\varrho_*\geq0$, and let every $d_j\ne0$. Set $\mathcal K=\{\alpha:|\alpha_j|\leq\varrho_j\ (j\in\mathcal J),\ \sum_{j\notin\mathcal J}(d_j\alpha_j)^2\leq\varrho_*^2\}$. Empty sums, including the case $n=0$, are zero. The data are assumed to satisfy the formal certificate conditions: the period is continuous and positive on the parameter set; the approximate field is divergence-free, periodic and invariant under the prescribed orthogonal space-time symmetries; its velocity, spatial derivative and supplied weak Hessian have bounds proportional to $(1+|y|)^{-1}$, $(1+|y|)^{-2}$ and $(1+|y|)^{-3}$; the forcing fields and the matrix fields defining the constraints are square integrable over a period; and the coercivity, residual, smallness, nonzero and parameter enclosure inequalities hold. The approximate field is required to be jointly $C^1$ in the parameter, time and space, on the full finite-dimensional parameter space. The derivative bounds just mentioned use operator norms. The data are further normalized by taking $\omega=1$, taking the reference field to equal the approximate profile, and setting the comparison gap and form shift equal to zero. These are extra hypotheses of this particular formal statement. For original data the weight normalization replaces $b_i$ by $b_i/\omega$, $\beta_i$ by $\omega\beta_i$, $\beta_i^{\rm a}$ by $\omega\beta_i^{\rm a}$, $V$ by $V/\omega$, $b_*$ by $b_*/\omega$ and $a_*$ by $a_*/\omega$. The physical force, the joint weighted bound and the column pairings in the parameter update are then preserved. The formulas in this card refer to the resulting normalized data. Assume the unique bounded nonlinear correction exists at every $\alpha\in\mathcal K$ and satisfies the adjoint error enclosure. Write $\Phi(\alpha)=\beta^{\rm a}(\alpha)+\beta(\alpha)$, and let $V_j$ be the $j$th column of the supplied matrix $V$. For every $\alpha\in\mathcal K$ and every $j\in\mathcal J$, the formal statement proves $|V_j\cdot\Phi(\alpha)-d_j\alpha_j|\leq|d_j|\varrho_j$. Its inputs include the offset bound $o_j$ and $\tilde a_j(2\varepsilon)^2+2\varepsilon\sqrt{a_j^2+|\langle b,\psi_{\alpha,j}\rangle-V_j|^2}+o_j\leq|d_j|\varrho_j$, in normalized variables. The matrix is transposed in the coordinate computation because the vectors $V_j$ are columns. This is exactly the coordinate part of the parameter enclosure after normalization; the complementary sum of squares is a separate result.
Breakdown.Cert.Internal.ExtendedExistsZe.summary: For normalized certificate data with a unique bounded correction satisfying the adjoint enclosure, $|V_j\cdot\Phi(\alpha)-d_j\alpha_j|\le|d_j|\varrho_j$ for every $\alpha\in\mathcal K$ and $j\in\mathcal J$, with $\Phi=\beta^{\rm a}+\beta$. The complementary part is separate.

Breakdown.Cert.Internal.ExtendedExistsZe.text: For any finite real vectors $V,M,K$ and real scalars $x,P,G,O,B,R$, assume $|V\cdot M-P-G-x|\leq O$, $|V\cdot K+P+G|\leq B$ and $B+O\leq R$. The formal statement concludes $|V\cdot(M+K)-x|\leq R$. It is the triangle inequality after the two terms $P+G$ cancel. In the paper's application $V=V_j$, $M=\beta^{\rm a}(\alpha)$, $K=\beta$, $x=d_j\alpha_j$, $P=\langle F_\alpha^{\rm a},\psi_{\alpha,j}\rangle$, $G=(Y(\alpha)\bar\ell(\alpha))_j$, and $R=|d_j|\varrho_j$. No PDE, positivity or integrability assumptions are built into this algebraic statement; those belong to the separate bounds being combined.
Breakdown.Cert.Internal.ExtendedExistsZe.summary: For finite real vectors $V,M,K$ and scalars, $|V\cdot M-P-G-x|\le O$, $|V\cdot K+P+G|\le B$ and $B+O\le R$ give $|V\cdot(M+K)-x|\le R$, the triangle inequality after $P+G$ cancels.

Breakdown.Cert.Internal.ExtendedExistsZe.text:
For $n\geq0$, let $\mathcal J\subset\{1,\ldots,n\}$, let $\varrho_j\geq0$ for $j\in\mathcal J$, let $\varrho_*\geq0$, and let every $d_j
e0$. Set $\mathcal K=\{\alpha:|\alpha_j|\leq\varrho_j\ (j\in\mathcal J),\ \sum_{j
otin\mathcal J}(d_j\alpha_j)^2\leq\varrho_*^2\}$. Empty sums, including the case $n=0$, are zero. The data are assumed to satisfy the formal certificate conditions: the period is continuous and positive on the parameter set; the approximate field is divergence-free, periodic and invariant under the prescribed orthogonal space-time symmetries; its velocity, spatial derivative and supplied weak Hessian have bounds proportional to $(1+|y|)^{-1}$, $(1+|y|)^{-2}$ and $(1+|y|)^{-3}$; the forcing fields and the matrix fields defining the constraints are square integrable over a period; and the coercivity, residual, smallness, nonzero and parameter enclosure inequalities hold. The approximate field is required to be jointly $C^1$ in the parameter, time and space, on the full finite-dimensional parameter space. The derivative bounds just mentioned use operator norms. The data are further normalized by taking $\omega=1$, taking the reference field to equal the approximate profile, and setting the comparison gap and form shift equal to zero. These are extra hypotheses of this particular formal statement. For original data the weight normalization replaces $b_i$ by $b_i/\omega$, $ eta_i$ by $\omega eta_i$, $ eta_i^{m a}$ by $\omega eta_i^{m a}$, $V$ by $V/\omega$, $b_*$ by $b_*/\omega$ and $a_*$ by $a_*/\omega$. The physical force, the joint weighted bound and the column pairings in the parameter update are then preserved. The formulas in this card refer to the resulting normalized data. Assume a bounded correction exists uniquely for each parameter and that its complementary force satisfies $ igl(\sum_{j
otin\mathcal J}(V_j\cdot eta)^2 igr)^{1/2}\leq2\varepsilon a_*$ in normalized variables. The data also impose $ igl(\sum_{j
otin\mathcal J}(V_j\cdot eta^{m a}(\alpha)-d_j\alpha_j)^2 igr)^{1/2}\leq o_*$ and $o_*+2\varepsilon a_*\leq\varrho_*$. The formal statement proves, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal K$, $\sum_{j
otin\mathcal J}(V_j\cdot( eta^{m a}(\alpha)+ eta(\alpha))-d_j\alpha_j)^2\leq\varrho_*^2$. It is the squared Euclidean enclosure, including the case of an empty complement. The inequalities on $\mathcal J$ itself are supplied separately.
Breakdown.Cert.Internal.ExtendedExistsZe.summary: For normalized data, the complementary force bound, the offset bound $o_*$ and $o_*+2\varepsilon a_*\le\varrho_*$ give $\sum_{j\notin\mathcal J}(V_j\cdot(\beta^{\rm a}(\alpha)+\beta(\alpha))-d_j\alpha_j)^2\le\varrho_*^2$ for every $\alpha\in\mathcal K$, including an empty complement.

Breakdown.Cert.Internal.ExtendedExistsZe.text: For any three vectors $V,M,K$ indexed by the same finite set and any real $x$, the formal statement is the identity $V\cdot(M+K)-x=(V\cdot M-x)+V\cdot K$. All coordinates and sums are real. Taking $V=V_j$, $M=\beta^{\rm a}(\alpha)$, $K=\beta$ and $x=d_j\alpha_j$ gives exactly the decomposition used outside $\mathcal J$. The result is valid without sign, norm, symmetry or invertibility hypotheses and includes an empty index set.
Breakdown.Cert.Internal.ExtendedExistsZe.summary: For vectors $V,M,K$ on a common finite index set and real $x$, $V\cdot(M+K)-x=(V\cdot M-x)+V\cdot K$. With $V=V_j$, $M=\beta^{\rm a}(\alpha)$, $K=\beta$, $x=d_j\alpha_j$ it is the decomposition used outside $\mathcal J$.

Breakdown.Cert.Internal.ExtendedExistsZe.text: Let $J$ be any finite index set and let $a_j,b_j$ be real numbers. Assume $(\sum_{j\in J}a_j^2)^{1/2}\leq o$, $(\sum_{j\in J}b_j^2)^{1/2}\leq t$ and $o+t\leq r$. The formal statement concludes $\sum_{j\in J}(a_j+b_j)^2\leq r^2$. The displayed assumptions imply the nonnegativity needed when squaring. For the parameter enclosure use $J=\{1,\ldots,n\}\setminus\mathcal J$, $a_j=V_j\cdot\beta^{\rm a}(\alpha)-d_j\alpha_j$, $b_j=V_j\cdot\beta$, $o=o_*$, $t=2\varepsilon a_*/\omega$ and $r=\varrho_*$. This is the Euclidean triangle inequality in squared form; it does not establish either input bound.
Breakdown.Cert.Internal.ExtendedExistsZe.summary: For real $a_j,b_j$ on a finite set $J$, $(\sum a_j^2)^{1/2}\le o$, $(\sum b_j^2)^{1/2}\le t$ and $o+t\le r$ give $\sum_{j\in J}(a_j+b_j)^2\le r^2$, the squared Euclidean triangle inequality.

Breakdown.Cert.Internal.ExtendedFrozenBr.text:
Let certificate data satisfy the reference form bound $\mathfrak q_{W_\alpha^{\mathrm r}(	heta)}(u)\ge-c_{3,\mathrm r}|u|_w^2$, the form-shift bound $\mathfrak q_{W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}(	heta)}(u)-\mathfrak q_{W_\alpha^{\mathrm r}(	heta)}(u)\ge-c_{3,\mathrm{shift}}|u|_w^2$, and $c_{3,\mathrm r}+c_{3,\mathrm{shift}}\le c_3$, with bounded measurable $w\ge w_*>0$. For every $\alpha\in\mathcal K$, every real $	heta$, and every solenoidal $u\in L^6$ with weak $
abla u\in L^2$, weak Hessian and $\Delta u\in L^2$, invariant under all $(R,0)\in\Gamma$, the theorem proves $\int(|\Delta u|^2+	frac14|
abla u|^2)-\int[(W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}(	heta)\cdot
abla)u+(u\cdot
abla)W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}(	heta)]\cdot\Delta u\ge-c_3\int(|\Delta u|^2+w|
abla u|^2)$. The gradient norm is Frobenius. The actual formal premise is the full certificate assumption, which supplies those three bounds and the positivity used in their addition. Its time quantifier is every real time, not merely almost every time of a constructed solution.
Breakdown.Cert.Internal.ExtendedFrozenBr.summary: From the reference form bound, the form-shift bound and $c_{3,\mathrm r}+c_{3,\mathrm{shift}}\le c_3$, the frozen form at $W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}(\theta)$ is at least $-c_3\int(|\Delta u|^2+w|\nabla u|^2)$ for every $\alpha\in\mathcal K$, every real $\theta$ and every invariant solenoidal $u$.

Breakdown.Cert.Internal.ExtendedHeldMaps.text: Let $e_a\in\mathcal H$ be a finite orthonormal family, let $0\leq\tau_a\leq c_0^2$ and $c_0\geq0$, and set $[F]=(\sum_a\tau_a\langle F,e_a\rangle_{\mathcal H}^2)^{1/2}$. For periodic square-integrable fields $D$ and $G$, the formal statement proves $[-D-G]\leq[D]+c_0\|G\|_{\mathcal H}$. It takes the triangle inequality, invariance under sign and domination of this row seminorm by $c_0\|\cdot\|_{\mathcal H}$ as a supplied analytic result, together with certificate data guaranteeing the stated row hypotheses. The application has $D=F_\alpha^{\rm a}$ and $G=(u\cdot\nabla)u$. The definition also allows no rows, when the seminorm is zero. This conclusion supplies the second forcing estimate in the paper; the ordinary $L^2$ triangle estimate is separate.
Breakdown.Cert.Internal.ExtendedHeldMaps.summary: For orthonormal $e_a$, $0\le\tau_a\le c_0^2$ and the row seminorm $[F]$, periodic square-integrable $D,G$ satisfy $[-D-G]\le[D]+c_0\|G\|_{\mathcal H}$. In the application $D=F_\alpha^{\rm a}$ and $G=(u\cdot\nabla)u$.

Breakdown.Cert.Internal.ExtendedHeldMaps.text: This is an elementary real inequality. Assume $Z\leq c_1N+R+c_2p$, $N\leq\delta+A$, $R\leq\delta_0+c_0A$, $c_1\geq0$, $c_1\delta+\delta_0+c_2p\leq\varepsilon$, $c_1+c_0\leq c_L$, $c_L>0$, $0\leq A\leq2c_w\varepsilon M$, $2c_Lc_wM<1$ and $\varepsilon\geq0$. Then $Z\leq2\varepsilon$. In the application $Z=(E_w(v)+|\beta|^2)^{1/2}$, $N$ is the forcing norm, $R$ is its finite-row seminorm and $p=|\bar\ell(\alpha)|$. The statement itself is quantified over arbitrary real numbers and does not require that these numbers be norms. It is the normalized arithmetic step, with the factor $1-\vartheta$ already absorbed into the coefficients; no division occurs in this statement.
Breakdown.Cert.Internal.ExtendedHeldMaps.summary: Elementary real inequality: from $Z\le c_1N+R+c_2p$, $N\le\delta+A$, $R\le\delta_0+c_0A$, $c_1\delta+\delta_0+c_2p\le\varepsilon$, $c_1+c_0\le c_L$, $0\le A\le2c_w\varepsilon M$, $2c_Lc_wM<1$ and the sign conditions, $Z\le2\varepsilon$.

Breakdown.Cert.Internal.ExtendedInvarian.text: For certificate data, an admissible parameter $\alpha\in\mathcal K$ and a specified symmetry $(R,\theta_0)\in\Gamma$, the formal statement rewrites the assumed pointwise symmetry of the approximate field as $W_\alpha^{\rm a}(\theta+\theta_0,y)=R W_\alpha^{\rm a}(\theta,R^{-1}y)$ for every real $\theta$ and every $y\in\mathbb R^3$. The alternative input form uses $Ry$ on the left; invertibility of the orthogonal map gives the displayed form. The field is defined on all time and space, and the equality is pointwise. The result concerns the prescribed approximation only and says nothing about the correction or the exact smooth output.
Breakdown.Cert.Internal.ExtendedInvarian.summary: For $\alpha\in\mathcal K$ and $(R,\theta_0)\in\Gamma$, the assumed symmetry of the approximate field is rewritten as $W_\alpha^{\rm a}(\theta+\theta_0,y)=RW_\alpha^{\rm a}(\theta,R^{-1}y)$ at every point, using invertibility of $R$. It says nothing about the correction.

Breakdown.Cert.Internal.FreeEnergyLocal..text: Fix $S>0$ and a one-periodic solenoidal $L^2$ forcing $f$. Assume the free propagator bound $e^{-s/4}[2e(1-e^{-s})]^{-1/2}$, convergence of the inverse integral, closedness of the spatial derivative graph and the averaged inverse estimate. There is a continuous curve $c:\mathbb R\to X$, with $c(\theta+1)=c(\theta)$ for every $\theta$, agreeing almost everywhere in time with the gradient-space component of the constructed free inverse. Here $X$ represents solenoidal fields on $\mathbb R^3$ with norm $\|\nabla v\|_2$; in Fourier variables its element is $2\pi|\xi|\widehat v(\xi)$. For every $a\le b$, the curve satisfies $\frac{\|c(b)\|_X^2-\|c(a)\|_X^2}{2S}=\int_a^b[-\langle f,\Delta v\rangle-\|\Delta v\|_2^2-\frac14\|c\|_X^2]\,d\theta$, where the second stored component has physical value $-\Delta v$. Thus the conclusion includes a continuous Sobolev-valued representative, rather than just continuity of its norm. It is proved for the constructed free inverse. The quantification over every member of the physical domain $\mathcal D_S$ in Lemma 7.4 is a further identification.
Breakdown.Cert.Internal.FreeEnergyLocal..summary: For $S>0$ and one-periodic solenoidal $L^2$ forcing $f$, under the stated propagator and inverse assumptions, a continuous periodic curve $c$ in $X$ agrees a.e. with the free inverse and satisfies the energy identity on every $[a,b]$. Lemma 7.4 for all of $\mathcal D_S$ needs a further step.

Breakdown.Cert.Internal.FreeInv.period_i.text: Let $f,k,v$ be square-integrable functions on the unit time circle with values in a real Hilbert space. Let $c:\mathbb R\to E$ agree almost everywhere with $v$, and assume $c(1)=c(0)$. If, for some real $r$, $r(\|c(1)\|^2-\|c(0)\|^2)=\int_0^1(\langle f,k\rangle-\|k\|^2-\frac14\|c\|^2)\,d\theta$, then $\langle f,k\rangle_{L^2}=\|k\|_{L^2}^2+\frac14\|v\|_{L^2}^2$. The theorem needs neither a time derivative nor positivity of $r$: periodicity cancels the endpoint term. To use it in (7.43), take $r=(2S)^{-1}$, let the first stored component represent $(-\Delta)^{1/2}v$, and the second represent $-\Delta v$. The conclusion becomes $-\langle\mathcal T_Sv,\Delta v\rangle_{\mathcal H}=\|\Delta v\|_{\mathcal H}^2+\frac14\|\nabla v\|_{\mathcal H}^2$. The integrated identity is a hypothesis of this lemma; the local energy theorem supplies it for the constructed free solution.
Breakdown.Cert.Internal.FreeInv.period_i.summary: For square-integrable $f,k,v$ on the unit time circle and $c$ equal to $v$ a.e. with $c(1)=c(0)$, the integrated identity $r(\|c(1)\|^2-\|c(0)\|^2)=\int_0^1(\langle f,k\rangle-\|k\|^2-\frac14\|c\|^2)$ gives $\langle f,k\rangle=\|k\|^2+\frac14\|v\|^2$. No time derivative or sign of $r$ is needed.

Breakdown.Cert.Internal.FreePerturbation.text:
Let $f\in L^2_{m div}(\mathbb R^3)$ and let $U(s)=D_{e^{-s}}e^{(1-e^{-s})\Delta}f$ for $s>0$. For every smooth compactly supported vector test $\chi(s,y)$, the formal statement differentiates its physical pairing at every $s>0$ and gives $ rac d{ds}\int U(s,y)\cdot\chi(s,y)dy=\int U(s,y)\cdot(\partial_s\chi+\Delta\chi+\chi+ rac12y\cdot
abla\chi)dy$. The test is not required to be divergence-free. The $+\chi$ coefficient results from integration by parts in three dimensions: the adjoint of $- rac12U- rac12y\cdot
abla U+\Delta U$ is $\Delta+1+ rac12y\cdot
abla$. The forcing is stored in its solenoidal Fourier $L^2$ representation; the velocity of the evolved gradient-space element is the physical field $U$. The theorem takes the free propagator bound as a premise. This is the weak form of (7.46) for positive time and permits general solenoidal $L^2$ initial data. It does not include the initial value at $s=0$ or a pointwise smooth equation there.
Breakdown.Cert.Internal.FreePerturbation.summary: For $f\in L^2_{\rm div}$ and $U(s)=D_{e^{-s}}e^{(1-e^{-s})\Delta}f$, $\frac d{ds}\int U\cdot\chi=\int U\cdot(\partial_s\chi+\Delta\chi+\chi+\frac12y\cdot\nabla\chi)$ at every $s>0$ for smooth compact tests $\chi$, not necessarily divergence-free. This is the weak form of (7.46) for positive time.

Breakdown.Cert.Internal.HeldLimit.inner_.text: In any real inner-product space, let $a_k,b_k,c_k,r_k,e_k$ have sum zero for every $k$. Fix $z$ and suppose the five real pairings with $z$ converge respectively to those of $a,b,c,r,e$. The formal statement concludes $\langle a+b+c+r+e,z\rangle=0$. It uses only these five scalar limits; it does not require norm convergence or weak convergence against other vectors. In the application the five terms are the free operator, linear convection, the finite-dimensional force, quadratic convection and the approximate residual, and $z$ is the periodic solenoidal test field. A separate density result is required to turn the collection of test identities into equality of the Hilbert-space elements.
Breakdown.Cert.Internal.HeldLimit.inner_.summary: In a real inner-product space, if $a_k+b_k+c_k+r_k+e_k=0$ for every $k$ and the five pairings with a fixed $z$ converge to those of $a,b,c,r,e$, then $\langle a+b+c+r+e,z\rangle=0$. A density result is needed to conclude equality of elements.

Breakdown.Cert.Internal.HeldLimit.isClos.text: For any set $\Gamma$ of pairs $(R,\theta_0)$, $R\in O(3)$ and $\theta_0\in\mathbb R$, the formal statement says that $\mathcal H_{\rm div}^{\Gamma}$ is closed in the norm of $\mathcal H_{\rm div}=L^2(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z;L^2_{\rm div}(\mathbb R^3))$. The subspace is the intersection of the kernels of the continuous operators $F\mapsto F(\theta+\theta_0)-R F(\theta,R^{-1}\cdot)$, one for each pair in $\Gamma$. These are identities of equivalence classes, hence almost-everywhere identities. The result permits an empty or infinite symmetry set. It establishes closedness for solenoidal fields; it does not state weak compactness or metrizability of the paper's ball of unprojected fields.
Breakdown.Cert.Internal.HeldLimit.isClos.summary: For any set $\Gamma$ of pairs $(R,\theta_0)$, $\mathcal H_{\rm div}^\Gamma$ is closed in $\mathcal H_{\rm div}$, as an intersection of kernels of continuous operators. Weak compactness of the paper's ball of unprojected fields is not stated.

Breakdown.Cert.Internal.HeldLimit.readin.text: Here $X$ is the divergence-free homogeneous Sobolev space on $\mathbb R^3$, represented by its $L^6$ velocity, with $\|v\|_X=\|\nabla v\|_{L^2}$. The periodic forcing space is $\mathcal H_{\rm div}=L^2(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z;L^2_{\rm div}(\mathbb R^3))$. Its elements, and the periodic perturbations, are identified when equal almost everywhere. Fix real numbers $0<a\leq b$, positive periods $S_k\in[a,b]$ with $S_k\to S$, and solenoidal periodic forcings $f_k$ uniformly bounded in $\mathcal H_{\rm div}$ and weakly converging to $f$. Assuming weak continuity of the free inverse, its local compactness, its boundedness and existence of physical representatives, the formal statement supplies a subsequence along which $v_k=\mathcal T_{S_k}^{-1}f_k$ and every column of $\nabla v_k$ converge in $L^2((0,1)\times B_R)$ to $v=\mathcal T_S^{-1}f$ and the corresponding column, for every $R>0$. The conclusion is written as convergence to zero of the squared local integrals. The open unit interval can be replaced by its closed counterpart since its endpoints have measure zero. This includes strong local convergence of the gradient, in addition to the velocity convergence used in the printed argument; the lower bound $a>0$ is explicit.
Breakdown.Cert.Internal.HeldLimit.readin.summary: For periods $S_k\in[a,b]$, $a>0$, $S_k\to S$, and bounded $f_k\rightharpoonup f$, a subsequence of $v_k=\mathcal T_{S_k}^{-1}f_k$ and of each gradient column converges in $L^2((0,1)\times B_R)$ to $v=\mathcal T_S^{-1}f$ for every $R>0$. This adds gradient convergence to the printed argument.

Breakdown.Cert.Internal.HeldLimit.tendst.text: Let $E$ be a real Hilbert space, let $L:E\to\mathbb R^n$ be a bounded linear map and let $u_k\rightharpoonup u$ in $E$, meaning convergence of the inner products against every fixed vector of $E$. The formal statement concludes $L(u_k)\to L(u)$ in the finite-dimensional space $\mathbb R^n$. Applied to the vector of constraint functionals on the periodic perturbation space, it gives $\ell(v_k)\to\ell(v)$. The matrix fields defining the constraints define bounded functionals because they are square integrable and pair with the square-integrable gradient over a period. The theorem itself is more general than this application and imposes no equation, symmetry or period assumptions.
Breakdown.Cert.Internal.HeldLimit.tendst.summary: In a real Hilbert space, a bounded linear $L:E\to\mathbb R^n$ and $u_k\rightharpoonup u$ give $L(u_k)\to L(u)$. Applied to the constraint functionals it gives $\ell(v_k)\to\ell(v)$.

Breakdown.Cert.Internal.HeldLimit.tendst.text: Let $E,F$ be real Hilbert spaces, let $T_k:E\to F$ be bounded linear operators tending to $T$ in operator norm, and let $u_k\rightharpoonup u$ in $E$ with $\|u_k\|\leq B$. For every $z\in F$, the formal statement proves $\langle T_ku_k,z\rangle\to\langle Tu,z\rangle$. It controls the operator error by $\|T_k-T\|B\|z\|$ and handles the remaining term by the adjoint of $T$. In the formal certificate proof it is applied to the parameter-dependent convection operator. The printed proof instead isolates the two physical convection terms and uses convergence of their coefficients on the compact support of a test field. The hypotheses and the conclusion of this declaration are abstract Hilbert-space statements.
Breakdown.Cert.Internal.HeldLimit.tendst.summary: If bounded $T_k\to T$ in operator norm and $u_k\rightharpoonup u$ with $\|u_k\|\le B$, then $\langle T_ku_k,z\rangle\to\langle Tu,z\rangle$ for every $z$. The printed proof instead treats the two convection terms on the compact support of a test field.

Breakdown.Cert.Internal.HeldLimit.tendst.text:
Here $X$ is the divergence-free homogeneous Sobolev space on $\mathbb R^3$, represented by its $L^6$ velocity, with $\|v\|_X=\|
abla v\|_{L^2}$. The periodic forcing space is $\mathcal H_{m div}=L^2(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z;L^2_{m div}(\mathbb R^3))$. Its elements, and the periodic perturbations, are identified when equal almost everywhere. Let $0<a\leq b$, $S_k\in[a,b]$, $S_k	o S$, and $f_kightharpoonup f$ in $\mathcal H_{m div}$, with $\sup_k\|f_k\|_{\mathcal H}<\infty$. Put $v_k=\mathcal T_{S_k}^{-1}f_k$ and assume their essential time suprema $\mathop{m ess\,sup}_	heta\|
abla v_k(	heta)\|_2$ are bounded by one finite real constant. Given weak continuity and local compactness of the free inverse and the physical product pairing identity, the formal statement gives a subsequence for which $\int (v_k\cdot
abla)v_k\cdot\varphi	o\int(v\cdot
abla)v\cdot\varphi$ for every smooth compactly supported divergence-free $\varphi$ on space-time, where $v=\mathcal T_S^{-1}f$. The integrals are equivalently pairings of the projected convection with periodized solenoidal tests. The conclusion is quantified over solenoidal tests only. It does not state convergence against every vector test or weak convergence of the full, unprojected convection in $\mathcal H$.
Breakdown.Cert.Internal.HeldLimit.tendst.summary:
For $S_k\in[a,b]$, $S_k	o S$, bounded $f_kightharpoonup f$ and bounded $\operatorname*{ess\,sup}_	heta\|
abla v_k(	heta)\|_2$, a subsequence has $\int(v_k\cdot
abla)v_k\cdot\varphi	o\int(v\cdot

Breakdown.Cert.Internal.SupBound.core_bo.text: Let $S,w_*>0$, let $w$ be measurable with $w_*\le w\le W$, and let $m\in\{1,2\}$. Consider a periodic derivative-graph field $v$ and periodic solenoidal $L^2$ fields $f,B,A,C$ with $B=f+C+A$ and $\|A\|_{\mathcal H}\le A_*b$. Assume a continuous one-periodic function $E(\theta)=\|\nabla v(\theta)\|_2^2$ almost everywhere, satisfying $[E(b_1)-E(a_1)]/(2S)=\int_{a_1}^{b_1}[-\langle f,\Delta v\rangle-\|\Delta v\|_2^2-E/4]$ for every $a_1\le b_1$. If $m=2$, assume $E$ has period $1/2$. Assume $c_3\ge0$ and $\|\Delta v\|_2^2+E/4-\langle C,\Delta v\rangle\ge-c_3|v|_w^2$ almost everywhere, where the time slices used for $C$ agree with its $L^2$ representative. The formal statement proves, at every real $\theta$, $E(\theta)\le(w_*^{-1}+2Sc_3/m)\|v\|_w^2+(2S/m)(\|B\|_{\mathcal H}+A_*b)\|v\|_w$. Its stored second component represents $-\Delta v$, accounting for the sign of the pairings. The averaged growth estimate corresponding to (7.56) occurs inside the proof; the declared conclusion is this pointwise energy estimate.
Breakdown.Cert.Internal.SupBound.core_bo.summary: For a continuous periodic $E=\|\nabla v(\theta)\|_2^2$ a.e. satisfying the integrated energy identity, with the frozen-form bound and $m\in\{1,2\}$, at every real $\theta$, $E(\theta)\le(w_*^{-1}+2Sc_3/m)\|v\|_w^2+(2S/m)(\|B\|_{\mathcal H}+A_*b)\|v\|_w$.

Breakdown.Cert.Internal.SupBound.half_pe.text: Let $v$ be a periodic derivative-graph field whose homogeneous-gradient component is invariant under a set $\Gamma\subset O(3)\times\mathbb R$. Suppose $(R,1/2)\in\Gamma$ for some orthogonal map $R$. Let $E:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be continuous and equal almost everywhere to $\|\nabla v(\theta)\|_2^2$. The formal statement proves $E(\theta+1/2)=E(\theta)$ for every real $\theta$. Invariance is initially equality of $L^2$ equivalence classes under time shift and rotation. Orthogonal action preserves the homogeneous gradient norm, giving the energy equality almost everywhere; continuity extends it to all times. The statement needs no time equation, no forcing bound and no coefficient estimate. It establishes half-periodicity of the scalar energy, without asserting a pointwise-in-space symmetry for a selected physical velocity representative.
Breakdown.Cert.Internal.SupBound.half_pe.summary: If the gradient component of $v$ is invariant under $\Gamma$ with some $(R,1/2)\in\Gamma$, and $E$ is continuous and equal a.e. to $\|\nabla v(\theta)\|_2^2$, then $E(\theta+1/2)=E(\theta)$ for every real $\theta$. No pointwise spatial symmetry is asserted.

Breakdown.Cert.Internal.SupBound.le_of_i.text: Let $E,h,\Lambda:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ and $c\ge0$. Assume $E$ is continuous and one-periodic, $\Lambda\ge0$ is one-periodic and Lebesgue integrable on $[0,1]$, and $E(b)-E(a)=c\int_a^b h$ for every $a\le b$, with $h\le\Lambda$ almost everywhere. Let the natural number $m$ be one or two, and assume $E$ also has period $1/2$ when $m=2$. The formal statement proves $E(\theta)\le\int_0^1E+(c/m)\int_0^1\Lambda$ for every real $\theta$. It does not require $\Lambda$ to have period $1/2$. No separate integrability hypothesis is imposed on $h$: the real interval integral is assigned zero if the function is not integrable, and the assumed identity is required with that convention on every interval. The proof compares $E$ with a minimum on a full period and, when $m=2$, adds the inequalities on two translated half-period intervals. In Proposition 7.9, set $c=2S$ and $E=\|\nabla v\|_2^2$; the weighted mean bound and (7.56) then yield (7.55). Positivity of $m$ follows from its two allowed values.
Breakdown.Cert.Internal.SupBound.le_of_i.summary: If $c\ge0$, $m\in\{1,2\}$, $E$ is continuous with periods $1$ and $1/m$, $E(b)-E(a)=c\int_a^bh$, $h\le\Lambda$ a.e., $\Lambda\ge0$ one-periodic and integrable, then $E(\theta)\le\int_0^1E+(c/m)\int_0^1\Lambda$. With $c=2S$ and the weighted mean bound this gives (7.55).

Breakdown.Cert.IsAdmissibleWeight.text: For $w:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$ and a real number $w_*$, this condition means $w_*>0$, $w$ is measurable, $w(y)\ge w_*$ for every $y$, and $w$ has a finite constant upper bound. These are the weight assumptions in (7.14). They make the weighted gradient integral finite whenever the gradient is square integrable. This definition imposes no symmetry on $w$; the complete formal certificate adds $w(Ry)=w(y)$ for its prescribed orthogonal symmetries.
Breakdown.Cert.IsAdmissibleWeight.summary: A weight $w$ is admissible when $w_*>0$, $w$ is measurable, $w\ge w_*$ everywhere and $w$ is bounded above. These are the assumptions in (7.14); symmetry of $w$ is added separately in the full certificate.

Breakdown.Cert.IsPeriodicField.text: For $F:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$, the condition requires joint measurability up to a null set, the identity $F(\theta+1,y)=F(\theta,y)$ at every point, and $\int_0^1\int_{\mathbb R^3}|F|^2<\infty$. These are physical representatives of the paper’s $\mathcal H$. Divergence freedom is an additional condition. The integral is written over $[0,1]$; endpoints have zero Lebesgue measure, so it agrees with the paper’s integral over $(0,1)$.
Breakdown.Cert.IsPeriodicField.summary: A field $F:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ qualifies when it is measurable, satisfies $F(\theta+1,y)=F(\theta,y)$ at every point, and has $\int_0^1\int|F|^2<\infty$. These represent elements of the paper's $\mathcal H$; divergence freedom is a separate condition.

Breakdown.Cert.ProductBoundHolds.text:
Let $w$ be measurable and bounded, with $w\ge w_*>0$, and let $v,v'$ be solenoidal period-one graph fields on $\mathbb R	imes\mathbb R^3$. This means their $L^6(\mathbb R^3)$ velocity representatives exist for almost every time, their first and second spatial derivatives are weak derivatives, and $
abla v,\Delta v,
abla v',\Delta v'$ are square integrable over $[0,1]	imes\mathbb R^3$. Assume $\operatorname*{ess\,sup}_	heta\|
abla v'(	heta)\|_2<\infty$. Put $\mathcal H=L^2([0,1]	imes\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$ and $\|v\|_w^2=\int_0^1\int(|\Delta v|^2+w|
abla v|_{m F}^2)$. The formal statement specifies that the reconstructed field $(v\cdot
abla)v'$ is measurable, period one and in $\mathcal H$, with $\|(v\cdot
abla)v'\|_{\mathcal H}\le c_w\|v\|_w\operatorname*{ess\,sup}_	heta\|
abla v'(	heta)\|_2$, and the same upper bound for its Leray projection, where $c_w=(4\pi\sqrt{w_*})^{-1/2}$. The derivatives are represented by Fourier variables and interpreted as weak physical derivatives; the gradient norm is Frobenius. Only the second argument has a finite essential-gradient-supremum hypothesis. No transport equation or separate time derivative is imposed on either argument. This declaration specifies the property; its proof is a separate theorem.
Breakdown.Cert.ProductBoundHolds.summary:
Specifies that for solenoidal period-one graph fields $v,v'$ with $\operatorname*{ess\,sup}_	heta\|
abla v'(	heta)\|_2<\infty$, $(v\cdot
abla)v'\in\mathcal H$ and it and its Leray projection have norm at most $c_w\|v\|_w\operatorname*{ess\,sup}_	heta\|
abla v'(	heta)\|_2$.

Breakdown.Cert.bordered.text: Here $X$ is the divergence-free homogeneous Sobolev space on $\mathbb R^3$, represented by its $L^6$ velocity, with $\|v\|_X=\|\nabla v\|_{L^2}$. The periodic forcing space is $\mathcal H_{\rm div}=L^2(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z;L^2_{\rm div}(\mathbb R^3))$. Its elements, and the periodic perturbations, are identified when equal almost everywhere. For supplied parameter data and $\alpha$, write $S=S(\alpha)$. On a pair $(f,\beta)$ with $f\in\mathcal H_{\rm div}$ and $\beta\in\mathbb R^n$, the defined bounded linear operator has first component $f+\mathbb P\mathcal C_\alpha(\mathcal T_S^{-1}f)+\mathbb P\sum_i\beta_i b_i$ and second component $\ell(\mathcal T_S^{-1}f)$. Thus its unknown $f$ represents $\mathcal T_Sv$, and the second component adds the finite constraints to the PDE. Assigning right side $(-\mathbb PF_\alpha^{\rm a}-\mathbb Pg,\bar\ell(\alpha))$ gives the projected version of (7.57). This definition itself neither solves the equation nor requires an invariant forcing. The inverse and the operators are selected from their defining specifications and assigned zero if those specifications have no solution; positivity of the period and the certificate theorems are required to identify them with the intended mathematical operators.
Breakdown.Cert.bordered.summary: Defines the bounded operator $(f,\beta)\mapsto(f+\mathbb P\mathcal C_\alpha\mathcal T_S^{-1}f+\mathbb P\sum_i\beta_ib_i,\ \ell(\mathcal T_S^{-1}f))$; with right side $(-\mathbb PF_\alpha^{\rm a}-\mathbb Pg,\bar\ell(\alpha))$ it is the projected (7.57). It solves nothing by itself.

Breakdown.Cert.exists_gradInvSpec.text: For every real $S$ the formal statement constructs a bounded linear operator on the one-periodic solenoidal $L^2$ forcing space, represented on $\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$, whose value is the Bochner integral over $s>0$ of the rescaled heat propagator applied to $f(\theta-s/S)$. In physical notation, for $S>0$ its gradient-space value represents $v(\theta)=\int_0^\infty D_{e^{-s}}e^{(1-e^{-s})\Delta}f(\theta-s/S)\,ds$. The input Fourier vector represents the forcing in $L^2$; the output Fourier vector represents $(-\Delta)^{1/2}v$, with norm $\|\nabla v\|_{\mathcal H}$. The time shift has no effect on an $L^2$ norm, and the propagator bound is integrable at both zero and infinity. The theorem itself has no assumption $S>0$: at $S=0$, the quotient $s/S$ is defined to be zero. Consequently its extension to $S\le0$ is an operator construction only; the interpretation as the inverse of the paper's operator requires $S>0$. It gives the first derivative component, without asserting the physical free equation, a Laplacian bound or bijectivity.
Breakdown.Cert.exists_gradInvSpec.summary: For every real $S$, a bounded operator on one-periodic solenoidal $L^2$ forcing whose value for $S>0$ represents $v(\theta)=\int_0^\infty D_{e^{-s}}e^{(1-e^{-s})\Delta}f(\theta-s/S)\,ds$. In that transformation $c_1$ and $c_2$ are divided by $1-\vartheta$, each row weight $\tau_a$ is divided by $(1-\vartheta)^2$, the convection gap is set to zero, and the frozen-form reference bound is replaced by the already allowed total bound. The formal statement proves that $f\mapsto\mathbb P\mathcal C_\alpha\mathcal T_S^{-1}f$ is a compact bounded linear operator on $\mathcal H_{\rm div}$. Its input and output are one-periodic solenoidal $L^2$ equivalence classes; the intermediate inverse is represented by its homogeneous gradient and Laplacian. Compactness here means relative compactness of the image of bounded sets in the norm topology. The proof combines local compactness of both velocity and gradient with an exterior estimate uniform on bounded forcing sets. Lemma 7.7 asserts compactness of the unprojected map into $\mathcal H$; the formal conclusion retains the Leray projection. The latter follows from the former, while compactness after projection alone would not recover the unprojected statement.

Let $v,G,H$ be physical representatives of the constructed free inverse and its weak first and second spatial derivatives. Under the free inverse, symmetry, projection, test-pairing, propagator, integral and closed-graph results, the formal statement produces a one-periodic square-integrable field $g$ equal in distributions to $S^{-1}\partial_	heta v+ rac12v+ rac12(y\cdot
abla)v$. The field $v$ is solenoidal, belongs to $L^6$ in space for almost every time, has square-integrable gradient and Laplacian over a period, and is $\Gamma$-invariant almost everywhere. For every smooth compactly supported solenoidal test field $\varphi$, $\int(g\cdot\varphi+G:
abla\varphi)=\langle f,\mathbb P\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}\varphi(	heta+k,\cdot)angle_{\mathcal H}$. Thus $\mathcal T_Sv=f$ modulo gradients. Separate square-integrability of $\partial_	heta v$ and $y\cdot
abla v$ is never required. This produces admissible physical perturbations from the inverse; it does not quantify over arbitrary elements already given in $\mathcal D_S$.
Breakdown.Cert.freePerturbationHolds_of.summary: For $S>0$ and $\Gamma$-invariant one-periodic solenoidal $L^2$ forcing $f$, the constructed free inverse $v$ is an admissible perturbation with $\mathcal T_Sv=f$ modulo gradients. It does not quantify over arbitrary given elements of $\mathcal D_S$.

Breakdown.Cert.invariantHH.text: For any set $\Gamma$ of orthogonal maps and time shifts, this is the subspace of $\mathcal H_{\mathrm{div}}$ satisfying $F(\theta+\theta_0)=\rho_RF(\theta)$ in $L^2$ for every $(R,\theta_0)\in\Gamma$. It is defined as the intersection of the kernels of the bounded linear differences between time translation and spatial rotation. Consequently each constraint is an almost-everywhere equality and the subspace is closed. With no prescribed symmetries it is the whole solenoidal space. The definition specifies no invariance of a non-solenoidal field before projection.
Breakdown.Cert.invariantHH.summary: Defines the subspace of $\mathcal H_{\mathrm{div}}$ with $F(\theta+\theta_0)=\rho_RF(\theta)$ in $L^2$ for every $(R,\theta_0)\in\Gamma$, as an intersection of kernels of bounded maps, so it is closed. With no symmetries it is the whole solenoidal space.

Breakdown.Cert.localCompactnessHolds_of.text: Fix $0<a\le b<\infty$, a sequence of periods $S_k\in[a,b]$ and a sequence of one-periodic solenoidal forcings with $\sup_k\|f_k\|_{\mathcal H}<\infty$. Assume the time-translation and space-translation estimates for the free inverse, the local $L^2$ translation compactness criterion, the inverse energy bound and physical reconstruction. The formal statement finds one strictly increasing subsequence $k_j$ such that, for every $R>0$, the reconstructed velocities and each of their three gradient columns are Cauchy in $L^2([0,1]\times\overline B_R)$. Explicitly, for every $\varepsilon>0$ both differences are smaller than $\varepsilon$ once both subsequence indices are sufficiently large. Closed balls and the closed time interval give the same integrals as their open counterparts because their boundaries have measure zero. This supplies subsequential local compactness simultaneously for velocity and gradient. Proposition 7.5 instead identifies the limit of the entire sequence when $S_k\to S$ and $f_k\rightharpoonup f$; those convergence hypotheses and that identification are absent from this statement.
Breakdown.Cert.localCompactnessHolds_of.summary: For periods $S_k\in[a,b]$, $0<a$, and bounded forcings, one subsequence makes the reconstructed free velocities and their gradients Cauchy in $L^2([0,1]\times\overline B_R)$ for every $R>0$. Unlike Proposition 7.5 it does not identify the limit of the whole sequence.

Breakdown.Cert.periodContinuityHolds_of.text: Here $X$ is the divergence-free homogeneous Sobolev space on $\mathbb R^3$, represented by its $L^6$ velocity, with $\|v\|_X=\|\nabla v\|_{L^2}$. The periodic forcing space is $\mathcal H_{\rm div}=L^2(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z;L^2_{\rm div}(\mathbb R^3))$. Its elements, and the periodic perturbations, are identified when equal almost everywhere. Let $S_k>0$ converge to $S>0$, and let $f_k\in\mathcal H_{\rm div}$ be uniformly bounded and weakly converge to $f$. Assuming the free inverse and its propagator construction have the stated properties, the formal statement proves weak convergence $\mathcal T_{S_k}^{-1}f_k\rightharpoonup\mathcal T_S^{-1}f$ in the periodic graph space whose norm controls both the gradient and the Laplacian in $L^2$ over a period. Convergence is expressed by pairing with every fixed vector of that graph Hilbert space. Hence the gradients also converge weakly in the periodic $L^2$ space. This theorem supplies no local strong convergence; that comes from compactness. The positive limit period and positivity of every period are explicit, so the time shifts involving division by $S_k$ are used away from zero.
Breakdown.Cert.periodContinuityHolds_of.summary: If $S_k\to S$ with all $S_k,S>0$ and bounded $f_k\rightharpoonup f$ in $\mathcal H_{\rm div}$, then $\mathcal T_{S_k}^{-1}f_k\rightharpoonup\mathcal T_S^{-1}f$ weakly in the periodic graph space controlling gradient and Laplacian. No local strong convergence is supplied.

Breakdown.Cert.periodize.text: For a field $\varphi$ on $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3$, the expression is $\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}\varphi(\theta+k,y)$. For a smooth compactly supported space-time field only finitely many terms can contribute near each point, and it gives a smooth field of period one. Spatial divergence freedom is preserved. The definition is also assigned a value for arbitrary inputs; an unsummable series has value zero. Compact support excludes this default in the application. The displayed products $a(\theta)\psi(y)$ in (7.3) are a further description of a dense class, not the defining formula here.
Breakdown.Cert.periodize.summary: Defines $\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}\varphi(\theta+k,y)$; for a smooth compactly supported field this is locally finite, smooth, period one and preserves divergence freedom. An unsummable series is assigned zero, which compact support excludes.

Breakdown.Cert.physToHH.text: For $F:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$, this map takes the spatial Leray projection at each time, represents the result in Fourier variables, and passes from the real time axis to $\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$. Under period-one measurability and finite $\mathcal H$ norm it represents $\mathbb PF$. The formal map chooses the representative time in $[0,1)$, uses zero for a spatial slice outside $L^2$, and uses zero if the resulting circle-valued field is outside $L^2$. These defaults are excluded almost everywhere by the stated hypotheses. The output has already lost the gradient component of $F$; norms of the original residual in (7.23) are imposed before this map.
Breakdown.Cert.physToHH.summary: Applies the spatial Leray projection at each time and passes to $\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$; under period-one measurability and finite $\mathcal H$ norm it represents $\mathbb PF$. Defaults of zero for non-$L^2$ slices are excluded almost everywhere by the hypotheses.

Breakdown.Cert.productBoundHolds_of.text:
Here $X$ is the divergence-free homogeneous Sobolev space on $\mathbb R^3$, represented by its $L^6$ velocity, with $\|v\|_X=\|
abla v\|_{L^2}$. The periodic forcing space is $\mathcal H_{m div}=L^2(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z;L^2_{m div}(\mathbb R^3))$. Its elements, and the periodic perturbations, are identified when equal almost everywhere. Write $E_w(v)=\int_0^1\int_{\mathbb R^3}(|\Delta v|^2+w(y)|
abla v|_F^2)\,dy\,d	heta$, where $|
abla v|_F^2=\sum_{j=1}^3|\partial_jv|^2$, and $U(v)=\mathop{m ess\,sup}_{	heta\in(0,1)}\|
abla v(	heta)\|_2$. Let $w$ be measurable with $0<w_*\leq w\leq w^*<\infty$, and let $u,v$ be periodic graph-space fields with square-integrable gradient and Laplacian over a period. Assume $U(v)<\infty$. From the slice pointwise estimate and the physical interpretation of this graph space, the formal statement proves that $(u\cdot
abla)v$ is measurable, periodic and square integrable, and that both its $\mathcal H$ norm and the norm of its Leray projection are at most $c_w E_w(u)^{1/2}U(v)$, where $c_w=(4\pi\sqrt{w_*})^{-1/2}$. Thus $E_w(v)^{1/2}\leq2\varepsilon$ and $U(v)\leq M$ give $\|(v\cdot
abla)v\|_{\mathcal H}\leq2c_w\varepsilon M$. The finiteness assumption makes conversion of the essential supremum from an extended nonnegative number to a real number legitimate. This result contains no symmetry assertion.
Breakdown.Cert.productBoundHolds_of.summary: For a weight $0<w_*\le w\le w^*$ and periodic graph-space fields $u,v$ with $U(v)<\infty$, $(u\cdot\nabla)v$ is square integrable and it and its Leray projection have $\mathcal H$ norm at most $c_wE_w(u)^{1/2}U(v)$, $c_w=(4\pi\sqrt{w_*})^{-1/2}$. No symmetry is asserted.

Breakdown.Cert.rowNormHolds.text: Let $e_1,\ldots,e_N$ be measurable period-one fields in $\mathcal H$ with $\langle e_j,e_k\rangle=\delta_{jk}$, let $0\le\tau_k\le c_0^2$, and assume $c_0\ge0$. For $F,F′\in\mathcal H$ define $[F]=(\sum_k\tau_k\langle F,e_k\rangle^2)^{1/2}$. The theorem proves $[F+F′]\le[F]+[F′]$, $[-F]=[F]$, and $[F]\le c_0\|F\|_{\mathcal H}$. The last is Bessel’s inequality. Replacing $e_k$ by $\sqrt{\tau_k}e_k$ gives the paper’s orthogonal fields of norm at most $c_0$. All integrals here are finite, so the zero defaults in the unrestricted pairing and norm definitions are irrelevant.
Breakdown.Cert.rowNormHolds.summary: For $c_0\ge0$, orthonormal period-one $e_k\in\mathcal H$, $0\le\tau_k\le c_0^2$ and $F,F′\in\mathcal H$, the seminorm $[F]$ satisfies $[F+F′]\le[F]+[F′]$, $[-F]=[F]$ and $[F]\le c_0\|F\|_{\mathcal H}$, as in (7.17).

Breakdown.Cert.sizeZ.text: For a periodic perturbation represented in the Hilbert space of its first and second derivatives, a real spatial weight $w$, and $\beta\in\mathbb R^n$, this expression is $(E_w(v)+\sum_i\beta_i^2)^{1/2}$. Under the physical energy identification and an admissible weight, $E_w(v)=\int_0^1\int(|\Delta v|^2+w|\nabla v|^2)$, so it equals $\|(v,\beta)\|_{w,1}$. The coefficient weight is one. A general positive $\omega$ in (7.14) is handled by rescaling the forcing fields and coefficients before this quantity is used. With no force coefficients the sum is zero.
Breakdown.Cert.sizeZ.summary: Defines $(E_w(v)+\sum_i\beta_i^2)^{1/2}$, which for an admissible weight equals $\|(v,\beta)\|_{w,1}$. The coefficient weight is one; a general $\omega$ in (7.14) is handled by rescaling the forcing fields and coefficients first.

Breakdown.Cert.sliceConvection.text: For a spatial field $W$ and a solenoidal velocity $v\in\dot H^1(\mathbb R^3)\cap L^6$, this definition forms $\sum_jW_j\partial_jv+(DW)v$. The velocity and its weak first derivatives are recovered as measurable representatives from the Fourier variable $|D|v$. At a point where $W$ is differentiable, $DW$ is its usual spatial derivative. At any other point the formal derivative is zero. The definition itself imposes no regularity, decay or integrability on $W$. For a differentiable approximate or reference profile it is exactly $(W\cdot\nabla)v+(v\cdot\nabla)W$, as in (7.13) and (7.16).
Breakdown.Cert.sliceConvection.summary: Defines $\sum_jW_j\partial_jv+(DW)v$ for solenoidal $v\in\dot H^1\cap L^6$, with $DW$ taken as zero where $W$ is not differentiable. For a differentiable profile it is exactly $(W\cdot\nabla)v+(v\cdot\nabla)W$, as in (7.13) and (7.16).

Breakdown.Cert.sliceSupBoundHolds_of.text: Let $u\in\dot H^1_{\rm div}(\mathbb R^3)$ with $\Delta u\in L^2(\mathbb R^3)$. The formal statement, expressed for an element of the closed spatial derivative graph, proves $|u(y)|^2\le(2\pi)^{-1}\|\nabla u\|_2\|\Delta u\|_2$ for almost every $y$. The first graph component is $2\pi|\xi|\widehat u$ and the second is $(2\pi|\xi|)^2\widehat u$, so their Hilbert norms are respectively the gradient and Laplacian norms. The hypothesis is that the closed graph still satisfies this Fourier multiplier relation. The chosen physical velocity is an $L^6$ equivalence class; the conclusion is an essential supremum estimate and imposes no value on exceptional spatial points. For any $w_*>0$, the arithmetic–geometric mean inequality gives $(2\pi)^{-1}ab\le(4\pi\sqrt{w_*})^{-1}(b^2+w_*a^2)$, yielding (7.48). This result states the sharper product bound before the choice of $w_*$. It contains no time-periodic convection estimate.
Breakdown.Cert.sliceSupBoundHolds_of.summary: For $u\in\dot H^1_{\rm div}(\mathbb R^3)$ with $\Delta u\in L^2$, $|u(y)|^2\le(2\pi)^{-1}\|\nabla u\|_2\|\Delta u\|_2$ for almost every $y$. This is the sharper product bound before choosing $w_*$; the arithmetic-geometric mean inequality then gives (7.48).

Breakdown.Cert.testDenseHolds_proof.text: For a field $f\in\mathcal H_{\mathrm{div}}$, if its $\mathcal H$ pairing with the periodization of every smooth compactly supported solenoidal space-time test is zero, then $f=0$ in the Hilbert space, hence almost everywhere. The conclusion is a separation statement for the periodic test family. Together with the physical pairing identity, it implies $F\simeq G$ if and only if $\mathbb PF=\mathbb PG$ for $F,G\in\mathcal H$. It does not state the intermediate density of separated products $a(\theta)\psi(y)$ as a separate conclusion.
Breakdown.Cert.testDenseHolds_proof.summary: If $f\in\mathcal H_{\mathrm{div}}$ has zero pairing with the periodization of every smooth compactly supported solenoidal test, then $f=0$. With the pairing identity this gives $F\simeq G$ if and only if $\mathbb PF=\mathbb PG$ for $F,G\in\mathcal H$.

Breakdown.Cert.testPairingHolds_proof.text: For every measurable period-one field $F$ with finite $\mathcal H$ norm and every smooth compactly supported solenoidal test $\varphi$, the theorem identifies $\langle\mathbb PF,\mathbb P\sum_k\varphi(\theta+k,\cdot)\rangle_{\mathcal H}$ with $\int_{\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3}F\cdot\varphi$. The periodic solenoidal fields on the left are represented in Fourier variables and are identified almost everywhere. For the test field, periodization is locally a finite sum and preserves divergence freedom. This identity transfers tests on the real time axis into the periodic Hilbert space. It does not alone prove that these tests are dense.
Breakdown.Cert.testPairingHolds_proof.summary: For a measurable period-one $F$ with finite $\mathcal H$ norm and a smooth compactly supported solenoidal test $\varphi$, $\langle\mathbb PF,\mathbb P\sum_k\varphi(\theta+k,\cdot)\rangle_{\mathcal H}=\int_{\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3}F\cdot\varphi$. It does not alone prove density of the tests.

Breakdown.CertCell.AdmissibleTuple.text:
For cell data, a parameter $\alpha$ and a real density coefficient $c$, this packages a real velocity $v$, its proposed gradient $G$, Hessian $H$, transport derivative $g$, forcing coefficients $ eta\in\mathbb R^n$ and a right-hand side $F$, all fields defined on $\mathbb R	imes\mathbb R^3$. The four perturbation fields are measurable and one-periodic; $G,H$ are weak derivatives almost every time, $v$ is solenoidal and lies in $L^6$ almost every time, and $G,\operatorname{tr}H,g$ have finite squared integrals over one period and space. In distributions, $g=S(\alpha)^{-1}\partial_	heta v+v/2+(y\cdot
abla)v/2$, and $v$ has the certificate symmetries almost everywhere. The field $F$ is measurable, one-periodic and square integrable; against all compactly supported solenoidal tests it equals $g-\Delta v+(W_\alpha^{\mathrm r}\cdot
abla)v+(v\cdot
abla)W_\alpha^{\mathrm r}+\sum_i eta_i b_i$. Finally the positive part of the reduced multiplier density with coefficient $c$ has finite integral.
