Its gradient entry $(a,b)$ is the conjugate of $\sum_{i,j,l}\epsilon_{iba}\epsilon_{ijl}W_j\overline{\varphi_l}$; its velocity entry $a$ is the conjugate of $\sum_{j,l}\epsilon_{ajl}\overline{\varphi_j}\Omega_l$. This conjugation matches the convention that the test is conjugated in the cell integral. It is the algebraic coupling used in Proposition B.4. No derivative relation between $W$ and $\Omega$ is assumed by the definition.
Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.crossTest.summary: For velocity $W$, vorticity $\Omega$ and test $\varphi$, twelve convection coefficients: conjugates of $\sum\epsilon_{iba}\epsilon_{ijl}W_j\overline{\varphi_l}$ (gradient entries) and of $\sum\epsilon_{ajl}\overline{\varphi_j}\Omega_l$ (velocity entries). No link between $W$ and $\Omega$ is assumed.

Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.deactSources.text: This forms every difference $\iota-\alpha$ of a tested perturbation harmonic and a reference harmonic in the prescribed finite list, then removes all labels resolved or eliminated in the cell. The result is finite. These are the remaining perturbation harmonics that can contribute to an equation row through the reference field in Proposition B.4. The list is a possible-coupling list, so it can contain labels whose coefficient happens to vanish. Error conditions ensure that all of it is covered by the further mode allowances.
Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.deactSources.summary: Every difference $\iota-\alpha$ of a tested harmonic and a listed reference harmonic, with labels resolved or eliminated in the cell removed. This finite list contains the remaining harmonics that can reach an equation row through the reference field in Proposition B.4.

Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.epsOwnCharge.text: Write $c_*=3/(2\sqrt2)$, let $\varepsilon_S,\varepsilon_V$ be the proposed strain and vorticity-gradient errors, and let $h_\varepsilon,h$ be the two balancing lengths. For a gradient-velocity pair $(G,u)$ this defines $2\varepsilon_S|\operatorname{curl}G|^2+c_*\varepsilon_V(h_\varepsilon+h)|G|_{\mathrm F}^2+2c_*\varepsilon_V|u|^2/h_\varepsilon$. It is the model-error form subtracted in the cell stretching estimate of Proposition B.4. The sign and positive-length conditions are separate hypotheses. A zero denominator is interpreted as zero by the raw formula, but the intended estimate requires $h_\varepsilon>0$.
Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.epsOwnCharge.summary: With $c_*=3/(2\sqrt2)$, the form $2\varepsilon_S|\operatorname{curl}G|^2+c_*\varepsilon_V(h_\varepsilon+h)|G|_{\mathrm F}^2+2c_*\varepsilon_V|u|^2/h_\varepsilon$, subtracted in the stretching estimate of Proposition B.4. A zero denominator gives zero; the estimate needs $h_\varepsilon>0$.

For every allowed parameter and weak perturbation, the formal statement proves $ ar J\ge-\sum_\iota\mathcal L(

Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.gradOf.text: For a twelve-component complex vector, this returns its first nine entries as a $3\times3$ array: position $3a+b$ is component $a$ differentiated in cylindrical direction $b$. The last three entries are ignored. This implements the gradient coordinate of the pair $(\mathbf G,\mathbf v)$ in Appendix B.3. The operation extracts a matrix and does not assert that it is symmetric, trace-free, or the derivative of the velocity entries.
Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.gradOf.summary: The first nine entries of a twelve-component complex vector as a $3\times3$ array, position $3a+b$ being component $a$ differentiated in direction $b$; the last three are ignored. This is the gradient coordinate of $(\mathbf G,\mathbf v)$ in Appendix B.3.

Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.gradSlot.text: This embeds the nine gradient-component positions into the first nine positions of a twelve-component vector, leaving its last three positions for velocity. The ordering is row-major for a $3\times3$ gradient: position $3a+b$ has vector component $a$ and derivative direction $b$. This is the coordinate convention for the pairs $(\mathbf G,\mathbf v)$ acted on by the $12\times12$ matrices of Appendix B.3. The operation concerns indices only and adds no mathematical hypothesis.
Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.gradSlot.summary: Embeds the nine gradient positions into the first nine positions of a twelve-component vector in row-major order, position $3a+b$ for component $a$ and direction $b$, leaving the last three for velocity. This is the convention for the $12\times12$ matrices of Appendix B.3.

Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.groupCharge.text: For one group of reference harmonics, let $s,v$ be its proposed strain and vorticity-gradient bounds, $c$ its stretching constant and $h$ the common cell balancing length. This defines $s|\operatorname{curl}G|^2+(cvh/2)|G|_{\mathrm F}^2+(cv/(2h))|u|^2$ on a gradient-velocity pair. It is the Young-inequality form used to bound group couplings in the proof of Proposition B.4. The later conditions choose $c=\sqrt{7/2}$ or $\sqrt{9/2}$, according to the trace information available for the model, and require $h>0$. The separately supplied balance of the group does not enter this formula. The definition itself allows other values.
Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.groupCharge.summary: For a group with bounds $s,v$, stretching constant $c$ and the common cell balancing length $h$, the form $s|\operatorname{curl}G|^2+(cvh/2)|G|_{\mathrm F}^2+(cv/(2h))|u|^2$, the Young bound for group couplings in Proposition B.4. The group's own balance does not enter.

Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.headUnit.text: For a chosen harmonic in a cell, this inserts the constant-pressure vector of that harmonic's layout into the corresponding resolved coordinates and sets every other harmonic, auxiliary coordinate, forcing coefficient and constraint multiplier to zero. It represents adding a spatially constant pressure in that harmonic. This is the freedom that the cell matrices and equation rows must ignore, as mentioned after Proposition B.14. An arbitrary chosen label need not be resolved, in which case all entries are zero. Invariance of any matrix is a separate condition.
Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.headUnit.summary: For a chosen harmonic in a cell, the constant-pressure vector of its layout in the resolved coordinates, with all other entries zero: adding a spatially constant pressure in that harmonic. Cell matrices and rows must ignore this freedom; for an unresolved label all entries are zero.

Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.highOwnAmoun.text:
Let $\mathcal S\subset\mathbb Z^2$ be finite and let $U_\iota(r,z)$ be a twelve-component complex field on a closed meridian cell $\mathsf Q$. Write its first nine entries as a matrix $G_\iota$ and its last three as a vector $u_\iota$, entered row by row. Supply real bounds $S_H,V_H$ and real balancing numbers $a_c,a_g,a_v$. The formal definition is
$\displaystyle \sum_{\iota\in\mathcal S}\int_{\mathsf Q}r\left[a_cS_H|\operatorname{curl}G_\iota|^2+\frac{3V_H}{2\sqrt2}\left(a_g|G_\iota|_{\mathrm F}^2+a_v|u_\iota|^2\right)\right]\,dr\,dz.$
Here $|G|_{\mathrm F}^2$ is the sum of squared moduli of the nine matrix entries. This is the cost assigned to the retained polynomial modes for the part of the reference strain and vorticity gradient orthogonal to the cell polynomials, in the stretching estimate behind (B.26). Positivity of the balances and validity of the error bounds are separate hypotheses. Each ordinary integral is assigned zero if its integrand is not integrable; the definition alone asserts neither integrability nor an error estimate.
Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.highOwnAmoun.summary: For finite $\mathcal S$ and twelve-component $U_\iota=(G_\iota,u_\iota)$, $\sum_\iota\int_{\mathsf Q}r[a_cS_H|\operatorname{curl}G_\iota|^2+\tfrac{3V_H}{2\sqrt2}(a_g|G_\iota|_{\mathrm F}^2+a_v|u_\iota|^2)]\,dr\,dz$, the cost charged to retained modes in the stretching estimate of (B.26).

Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.highOwnCharg.text: Let $S_H,V_H$ bound the strain and vorticity-gradient parts omitted orthogonally from the polynomial model, and let $a_c,a_g,a_v$ be the three positive balancing candidates. For a gradient-velocity pair $(G,u)$ this defines $a_cS_H|\operatorname{curl}G|^2+\frac3{2\sqrt2}V_H(a_g|G|_{\mathrm F}^2+a_v|u|^2)$. It is one side of the Young-inequality allocation for the omitted parts in Proposition B.4. The reciprocal balancing costs on the other side are imposed separately. Positivity of the balances and adequacy of $S_H,V_H$ are hypotheses, not part of this formula.
Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.highOwnCharg.summary: With bounds $S_H,V_H$ on the orthogonally omitted parts and balances $a_c,a_g,a_v$, the form $a_cS_H|\operatorname{curl}G|^2+\frac3{2\sqrt2}V_H(a_g|G|_{\mathrm F}^2+a_v|u|^2)$, one side of the Young allocation in Proposition B.4. The reciprocal costs are imposed separately.

Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.isPressureDa.text: For a coordinate in one harmonic's cell layout, this returns true exactly for the pressure-side-moment alternative and false for gradient coefficients, velocity coefficients, other side moments, corner values and auxiliary coordinates. It is used to forbid the polynomial splitting matrix from mixing pressure with the other cell variables. This supports the pressure-normalization and global-coordinate conditions named after Proposition B.14. The classification does not inspect the numerical value of the coordinate or determine whether its segment is valid.
Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.isPressureDa.summary: True exactly for pressure side-moment coordinates and false for gradient, velocity, other side moments, corners and auxiliary coordinates. It forbids the splitting matrix from mixing pressure with other variables, supporting the pressure-normalization conditions after Proposition B.14.

Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.keyFlipSign.text: The assigned sign is $+1$ for a radial velocity or corner component and $-1$ for angular or axial components. A normal-gradient moment has the opposite sign; a pressure moment has sign $+1$; a stream value has sign $-1$; and an auxiliary label has value zero. These are the component signs of $R_*$ in (B.24), with the derivative direction accounted for. Unlike the plane-specific test, this definition returns a sign for geometrically labeled coordinates even away from $z=0$. It is used for a reflection identity only when the separate on-plane condition holds.
Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.keyFlipSign.summary: The reflection sign of a trace: $+1$ for radial velocity or corner components, $-1$ for angular or axial ones, opposite for normal-gradient moments, $+1$ for pressure, $-1$ for stream values, zero for auxiliary labels. These are the signs of $R_*$ in (B.24), used only on $z=0$.

Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.keyOnPlane.text: This holds for velocity, gradient or pressure side coordinates precisely when the side is axial and has height zero, and for corner or stream-function coordinates precisely when their point has $z=0$. It is false for an auxiliary label with no geometric meaning. This identifies where the relation (B.24) may identify a harmonic with its reflected harmonic in the global unknowns. The condition alone does not require nonnegative radius, a nondegenerate segment or a valid trace.
Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.keyOnPlane.summary: Holds for velocity, gradient or pressure side coordinates exactly when the side is axial at height zero, and for corner or stream coordinates exactly when $z=0$; false for auxiliary labels. It marks where (B.24) may identify a harmonic with its reflection.

Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.keyVelNormal.text: This identifies a velocity-side coordinate whose angular integer is zero and whose vector component is normal to the side: radial on a radial side, axial on an axial side. All other labels fail the condition. Such moments can be expressed through stream-function differences because the zero-angular divergence equation has a stream representation. This is one of the divergence relations for global unknowns in Appendix B.3. The condition itself imposes neither solenoidality of a field nor a valid side geometry.
Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.keyVelNormal.summary: Identifies a velocity side coordinate with angular integer zero and component normal to the side: radial on a radial side, axial on an axial side. Such moments are expressible by stream-function differences, one of the divergence relations of Appendix B.3.

Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.keyWithMode.text: This replaces the stored angular integer in a velocity, gradient, pressure or corner trace label by a supplied integer, retaining its geometry, component and polynomial-test index. A stream-function label and an auxiliary label are unchanged. It is the index operation used when complex conjugation or plane reflection relates harmonics in (B.2) and (B.24). It does not alter a numerical trace value or assert that the two harmonics satisfy a symmetry; the row conditions supply those relations.
Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.keyWithMode.summary: Replaces the angular integer in a velocity, gradient, pressure or corner trace label, keeping its geometry, component and test index; stream and auxiliary labels are unchanged. This is the index operation for conjugation or reflection in (B.2) and (B.24).

Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.leakGram.text: This divides the cell test Gram matrix in each harmonic block by the positive error weight assigned to that harmonic. It measures the row cost allowed for the portion of the test pairing left after the retained polynomial terms. It enters the matrix dominance condition used in Proposition B.4. This is a definition from supplied weights; positivity of each weight and positive definiteness of the unweighted Gram matrix are separate hypotheses. A zero denominator would give zero by the formal convention and is excluded in the intended use.
Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.leakGram.summary: Divides the cell test Gram matrix in each harmonic block by that harmonic's positive error weight, measuring the row cost for the unretained test pairing in Proposition B.4. A zero denominator would give zero by convention and is excluded in the intended use.

Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.linearField.text: For a finite family of twelve-component complex functions $S_d(r,z)$ and a complex vector $x$ of coefficients, this defines $U(r,z)=\sum_d x_dS_d(r,z)$. The twelve components represent nine gradient entries followed by three velocity entries when used in the cell estimates. This is the linear dependence of the source terms on the cell unknowns in the assembly of (B.26). The sum is finite, but measurability, boundedness or a derivative relation for its components requires corresponding hypotheses on the supplied functions.
Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.linearField.summary: For finitely many twelve-component complex functions $S_d(r,z)$ and coefficients $x$, the field $U=\sum_dx_dS_d$, nine gradient entries then three velocity entries. This is the linear dependence of the sources on the cell unknowns in (B.26).

Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.longFactor.text: For a harmonic $\iota$, a natural-number cutoff $N$ and a real balance $b$, this returns $b$ when $|\iota_1|\le N$ and $1+1/b$ otherwise. It distinguishes the two sides of the angular separation used to estimate the omitted reference harmonics in Proposition B.4. The time index is unrestricted. The formal definition accepts any real $b$, with $1/0=0$; the associated conditions require $b>0$, which is needed for the Young-inequality interpretation.
Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.longFactor.summary: For harmonic $\iota$, cutoff $N$ and real balance $b$, the value $b$ when $|\iota_1|\le N$ and $1+1/b$ otherwise, separating the two sides of the angular cutoff for omitted reference harmonics in Proposition B.4. Here $1/0=0$; the conditions require $b>0$.

Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.longOwnCharg.text: For a harmonic and a gradient-velocity pair, this multiplies the ordinary three-term error form by its angular balance factor. In that form the error coefficients are the proposed bounds $S_L,V_L$ on the remote angular strain and vorticity gradient: $2S_L|\operatorname{curl}G|^2+\frac3{2\sqrt2}V_L(h_\varepsilon+h)|G|^2+\frac3{\sqrt2}V_L|u|^2/h_\varepsilon$. The factor is $b$ below the angular cutoff and $1+1/b$ above it. This allocates the omitted-harmonic errors of Proposition B.4. Nonnegative error coefficients and positive $b,h_\varepsilon,h$ are required elsewhere.
Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.longOwnCharg.summary: The remote angular error form $2S_L|\operatorname{curl}G|^2+\frac3{2\sqrt2}V_L(h_\varepsilon+h)|G|^2+\frac3{\sqrt2}V_L|u|^2/h_\varepsilon$, multiplied by $b$ below the angular cutoff and $1+1/b$ above. This allocates omitted-harmonic errors in Proposition B.4.

Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.longRowCost.text: For a harmonic $\iota$ and the natural-number cutoff $N$ of the remote angular remainder, this selects the cell's low-angular row cost when $|\iota_1|\le N$, and its high-angular row cost otherwise. The time index is unrestricted. These are the two positive weights used to absorb the remote angular contribution to the equation rows in Proposition B.4. The choice itself does not require either weight to be positive.
Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.longRowCost.summary: For harmonic $\iota$ and cutoff $N$, the cell's low-angular row cost when $|\iota_1|\le N$ and its high-angular row cost otherwise. These weights absorb the remote angular row contribution in Proposition B.4; positivity is not required here.

Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.longRowTerm.text: If both the remote angular velocity and vorticity bounds are exactly zero, this contribution to a row budget is zero. Otherwise it is the reciprocal of the low- or high-angular row cost selected by that row's harmonic. This is the corresponding Young-inequality term in the row-error budget of Proposition B.4. The zero-error branch uses exact equality of the supplied real bounds, not a numerical tolerance. Division by zero is taken to be zero in the definition; the conditions used in the estimate require the selected costs to be strictly positive.
Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.longRowTerm.summary: Zero if both remote angular velocity and vorticity bounds are exactly zero; otherwise the reciprocal of the low- or high-angular row cost for that harmonic. This is a Young term in the row budget of Proposition B.4; division by zero is taken to be zero.

Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.longSourceCo.text: For a source harmonic with $|\iota_1|\le N$, this chooses the high-angular row cost. For a harmonic above the cutoff it chooses the sum of the low- and high-angular costs. The reversed assignment reflects that the remote reference field has no small angular harmonics and couples separated groups of perturbation modes. This is the source-side error allocation used in Proposition B.4. The cutoff is an integer label cutoff; the physical frequency is multiplied by $\varkappa$. Positivity and the spectral-gap hypothesis are separate requirements.
Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.longSourceCo.summary: For a source harmonic with $|\iota_1|\le N$, the high-angular row cost; above the cutoff, the sum of the low- and high-angular costs. This source-side allocation in Proposition B.4 reflects that the remote reference field has no small angular harmonics.

Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.lowAt.text: For any integer harmonic label, this returns its reconstructed twelve-component polynomial gradient and velocity if the label is resolved in the chosen cell, and the zero vector otherwise. It therefore defines a family on all of $\mathbb Z^2$ with finite harmonic support. This is the resolved-mode polynomial family in the decomposition of Proposition B.4. Zero outside the resolved set is a convention for this family; it does not say that the actual perturbation has no unresolved harmonics.
Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.lowAt.summary: For any integer harmonic label, its reconstructed twelve-component polynomial gradient and velocity if resolved in the cell, and zero otherwise, giving a finitely supported family on $\mathbb Z^2$. The zero is a convention, not a claim that unresolved harmonics vanish.

Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.lowGrad.text: For a resolved harmonic, this reconstructs its gradient polynomials from the corresponding cell coefficients and sums over the angular indices in that harmonic's layout. Every component is a product-basis polynomial of separate degree at most the coefficient degree $d$. It is the polynomial part of $\nabla\hat v_\iota$ in the proof of Proposition B.4. The definition does not require the layout to contain only the intended angular index or the coefficients to be the actual projection of a perturbation; those are supplied by layout and evaluation conditions.
Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.lowGrad.summary: For a resolved harmonic, its gradient polynomials reconstructed from the cell coefficients and summed over the layout's angular indices, each of separate degree at most $d$. It is the polynomial part of $\nabla\hat v_\iota$ in Proposition B.4.

Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.lowProfile.text: For a resolved harmonic and a vector of cell coefficients, this concatenates the nine entries of its reconstructed gradient matrix, in row-major order, with the three entries of its reconstructed velocity. It is the pair $(\mathbf G,\mathbf v)\in\mathbb C^{3\times3}\times\mathbb C^3$ on which the $12\times12$ matrices in Appendix B.3 act. All entries are polynomials in the meridian variables. This definition only arranges them in one vector; the claim that they are the polynomial projections of an actual mode is separate.
Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.lowProfile.summary: For a resolved harmonic and cell coefficients, the nine entries of its reconstructed gradient in row-major order followed by the three of its velocity: the pair $(\mathbf G,\mathbf v)$ on which the $12\times12$ matrices of Appendix B.3 act. All entries are polynomials.

Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.lowVel.text: For a resolved harmonic, this reconstructs the velocity components from the selected cell coefficients, summing their product-basis polynomials over the angular indices of the layout. Each variable has degree at most $d-1$ when the coefficient degree is $d\ge1$. The result is the polynomial part of $\hat v_\iota$ used in Proposition B.4. With $d=0$ the reconstruction is zero because the sums are empty. Solenoidality and consistency with the separately reconstructed gradient require the cell relations.
Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.lowVel.summary: For a resolved harmonic, its velocity components reconstructed from the cell coefficients, each of degree at most $d-1$ in each variable when $d\ge1$, and zero when $d=0$. It is the polynomial part of $\hat v_\iota$ in Proposition B.4.

Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.meanStretchT.text:
Assume a periodic divergence-free reference field with the specified decay, a symmetric weak Hessian, a finite harmonic expansion, admissible weights, and the axial and half-turn symmetries. For any weak perturbation the formal statement expresses $ ar J(r,z)$, almost everywhere on the quarter plane, as a sum over perturbation labels $\iota$ and a finite sum over reference-field labels $\alpha$. Each term is the real part of the complex sesquilinear pairing of $(
abla\hat v_\iota,\hat v_\iota)$ with $(
abla\hat v_{\iota-\alpha},\hat v_{\iota-\alpha})$, through the matrix made from the $\alpha$ modes of $
abla W^{\mathrm r}$ and $
abla^2W^{\mathrm r}$. The velocity and the separately supplied fields $G,H,g$ are measurable on $\mathbb R	imes\mathbb R^3$ and exactly period one in $	heta$. The velocity has divergence zero, $v(	heta)\in L^6(\mathbb R^3)$ for almost every $	heta$, and weak spatial derivatives $G=
abla v$, $H=
abla^2v$. Over $[0,1]	imes\mathbb R^3$, $G$, $\operatorname{tr}H=\Delta v$ and $g=S^{-1}\partial_	heta v+ rac12v+ rac12y\cdot
abla v$ are in $L^2$; the last identity is distributional. For every supplied symmetry $(R,	au)\in\Gamma$, $v(	heta+	au,Ry)=Rv(	heta,y)$ almost everywhere. The difference of labels is the precise rule for harmonic coupling. The identity contains no lower bound for those couplings; the majorant and trace-free estimate supply that next step.
Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.meanStretchT.summary: For a periodic divergence-free reference with finite harmonic expansion and both symmetries, $\bar J(r,z)$ is a.e. a sum over $\iota$ and finitely many $\alpha$ of real pairings of $(\nabla\hat v_\iota,\hat v_\iota)$ with $(\nabla\hat v_{\iota-\alpha},\hat v_{\iota-\alpha})$, with no lower bound.

Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.modelBilin.text: For complex matrices $S,V$, two velocity vectors $a,a'$ and two gradient arrays $g,g'$, this defines $-(\operatorname{curl}g)^{\mathsf T}S\operatorname{curl}g'+(Va)\cdot\operatorname{curl}g'+\tfrac12\sum_{i,l,n,j}\epsilon_{iln}V_{jl}g_{ij}a'_n$. The curl is formed from antisymmetric entries of the gradient. This is the algebraic stretching expression obtained from the polynomial models of $\mathbb S$ and $\mathbb V$ in the proof of Proposition B.4. All products here are complex bilinear, with no conjugation in this definition. Conjugation is inserted when a Hermitian mode coupling is formed. Neither symmetry of $S$ nor zero trace of $V$ is assumed here.
Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.modelBilin.summary: The complex bilinear expression $-(\operatorname{curl}g)^{\mathsf T}S\operatorname{curl}g'+(Va)\cdot\operatorname{curl}g'+\tfrac12\sum\epsilon_{iln}V_{jl}g_{ij}a'_n$, the stretching expression from the models of $\mathbb S,\mathbb V$ in Proposition B.4, without conjugation.

Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.modelLabels.text: This takes the union of the finite harmonic sets supplied for the polynomial models of velocity, vorticity, strain and vorticity gradient, and retains a label only if at least one corresponding component is nonzero at some point of the closed cell. It therefore removes identically zero model harmonics without testing a numerical tolerance. This is the exact harmonic support used to determine which modes couple in Proposition B.4. The definition is mathematical and may require deciding an existential statement over real points; it does not describe a finite numerical zero test.
Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.modelLabels.summary: The union of the harmonic sets of the cell's velocity, vorticity, strain and vorticity-gradient models, keeping a label only if some component is nonzero at some point of the closed cell. This exact support decides which modes couple in Proposition B.4; it is not a numerical zero test.

Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.modelTriple.text: This takes one half of the sum of the bilinear stretching expression with its two gradient-velocity arguments interchanged. The reference strain matrix $S$ and vorticity-gradient matrix $V$ remain fixed. It is symmetric and complex bilinear in the two pairs; conjugating one argument produces a sesquilinear form. Hermitian symmetry requires additional reality or harmonic-conjugacy relations on the reference matrices. This is the polarization used to represent the model stretching couplings by the $12\times12$ harmonic matrices in Proposition B.4. No analytic hypothesis or sign conclusion is imposed by the symmetrization itself.
Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.modelTriple.summary: One half of the sum of the bilinear stretching expression with its two gradient-velocity arguments interchanged, with $S$ and $V$ fixed. It is symmetric and complex bilinear, the polarization representing the model couplings by $12\times12$ matrices in Proposition B.4.

Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.modelVelocit.text: For a cell, an integer time-angle harmonic and a point of the meridian plane, this evaluates the three cylindrical components of the supplied polynomial model of the reference velocity. The harmonic factors of (B.2) are absent here; this is their coefficient. It enters the coupling of two perturbation modes in the proof of Proposition B.4. The model is a supplied approximation. The model-decomposition hypotheses control its difference from $W^{\mathrm r}$ through an orthogonal remainder, a remote-angular remainder and a final bounded error; they permit all three to be nonzero. This definition asserts no equality with the exact harmonic.
Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.modelVelocit.summary: For a cell, harmonic and meridian point, the three cylindrical coefficients of the supplied polynomial velocity model, before multiplication by (B.2). The decomposition conditions bound its difference from the reference field and allow nonzero remainders.

Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.modelVortici.text: For a cell and harmonic label, this evaluates the three cylindrical polynomial coefficients supplied for the reference vorticity model. It is used alongside the velocity model to construct the convection row in Proposition B.4. The definition does not differentiate the velocity model and therefore does not assert that these polynomials equal its curl. Both models approximate their respective reference quantities under independently stated error bounds.
Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.modelVortici.summary: For a cell and harmonic, the three cylindrical polynomial coefficients of the reference vorticity model, used to build the convection row in Proposition B.4. They are not asserted to be the curl of the velocity model; both carry separate error bounds.

Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.offModeCondi.text:
Fix a parameter $\alpha\in\mathcal K$. The multiplier hypotheses are the following. There are finitely many frequency classes and finitely many $\lambda$ and $\mu$ pieces, with $0<c,c_\mu<1$, $S(\alpha)>0$, and a measurable axisymmetric energy weight $w\ge w_0>0$. A finite set of reference harmonics, invariant under sign change and containing zero, represents $W^{\mathrm r}$. Its amplitude functions bound the modes of $W^{\mathrm r}$, $
abla W^{\mathrm r}$, $\operatorname{curl}W^{\mathrm r}$ and $
abla\operatorname{curl}W^{\mathrm r}$; two further functions bound the vorticity and its gradient along all rotations. No measurability hypothesis on these reference and transport bound functions is included in this regional implication. For each piece $p$, the transport bound dominates $|W^{\mathrm r}+y/2-
u_p\mathbf e_3	imes y|$ and $\Omega_p$ has a strictly positive lower bound on $\mathcal N_p$. The weights $\lambda_p,\mu_p$ are nonnegative, globally Lipschitz and axisymmetric, with uniform bounds on $|y|\lambda_p$, $\mu_p$, $|y|^2\mu_p$ and $|y||
abla\mu_p|$. For some finite $n_\lambda,n_{
abla\lambda},n_\mu$ with $n_\mu\ge0$, $\sum_p\lambda_p\le n_\lambda$, $\sum_p|
abla\lambda_p|\le n_{
abla\lambda}$, and $(\sum_p|\operatorname{sgn}_p(\xi)|\mu_p)^2\le n_\mu\sum_p|\operatorname{sgn}_p(\xi)||\Omega_p(\xi)|\mu_p$ at every point and frequency. Here $\operatorname{sgn}_p$ is $1$ on $\mathcal N_p$, $-1$ on $-\mathcal N_p$ and zero elsewhere. All balancing lengths, allocation factors and other auxiliary functions used in the coefficient formulas are positive, measurable and axisymmetric, and the $\mu$ auxiliary scalars are positive. The convection weights $D_\xi,Z_\xi$ are $C^2$, axisymmetric and equal at opposite frequencies; $D_\xi\ge0$, their derivatives through order two have the bounds $|y|^j|
abla^jD_\xi|\le B$ and $(1+|y|)^j|
abla^jZ_\xi|\le B$, and the convection allocation leaves $I'_{2,\xi}\ge0$. At points where a Lipschitz weight is not differentiable, its formal pointwise derivative is assigned zero; the pointwise inequalities involving $|
abla\lambda_p|$ or $|
abla\mu_p|$ use that convention. On a measurable region $Z\subset\{r>0,z>0\}$, supply a harmonic set with $|\varkappa\iota_1|\ge k_0$ and uniform coefficient bounds after subtracting the stretching and other charges: lower bounds $f_2,f'_2,f'_1,f_1,f_0$ for the five square coefficients and an upper bound $f_{01}$ for the coefficient of the negative mixed product. The formal input provides these bounds through common multiplier-class, membership and harmonic-interaction data; the regional stretching bounds dominate the actual mode bounds and have the same positive balancing length. Set $f_1^*=f_1+2\min(f'_1+f'_2(k_0-1)_+^2/r^2,0)+f_2(k_0-2)_+^2/r^2$ and $f_0^*=f_0+t(k_0-1)_+^2/r^2$. At every point require $f_2\ge0$, $0\le t\le f_1^*$, $f_0^*\ge0$ and $f_{01}^2\le4(f_1^*-t)f_0^*$. Then, for every weak perturbation and every harmonic in the set, $\mathcal I_\iota^\circ\ge0$ almost everywhere on $Z$. The velocity and the separately supplied fields $G,H,g$ are measurable on $\mathbb R	imes\mathbb R^3$ and exactly period one in $	heta$. The velocity has divergence zero, $v(	heta)\in L^6(\mathbb R^3)$ for almost every $	heta$, and weak spatial derivatives $G=
abla v$, $H=
abla^2v$. Over $[0,1]	imes\mathbb R^3$, $G$, $\operatorname{tr}H=\Delta v$ and $g=S^{-1}\partial_	heta v+ rac12v+ rac12y\cdot
abla v$ are in $L^2$; the last identity is distributional. For every supplied symmetry $(R,	au)\in\Gamma$, $v(	heta+	au,Ry)=Rv(	heta,y)$ almost everywhere. The mode labelled $\iota\in\mathbb Z^2$ has frequencies $(2\iota_2-\iota_1,\varkappa\iota_1)$ and is evaluated after averaging over time and angle, at $	heta=0$, $y=(r,0,z)$. The quarter plane is $r>0,z>0$ with measure $r\,dr\,dz$; its excluded boundary has zero measure. Matrix norms in the densities are Frobenius norms. The density $\mathcal I_\iota^\circ$ is the modal quadratic density minus the majorant (B.25), with $c^*$ replacing $\sqrt{7/2}$, and minus the specified curl, gradient and velocity charges. The theorem treats one region; nonnegativity on a whole cell also requires that the regions cover that cell for the harmonic concerned.
Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.offModeCondi.summary: Under the multiplier hypotheses, on a measurable region $Z$ with $|\varkappa\iota_1|\ge k_0$ and coefficient bounds satisfying $f_2\ge0$, $0\le t\le f_1^*$, $f_0^*\ge0$, $f_{01}^2\le4(f_1^*-t)f_0^*$, each weak perturbation has $\mathcal I_\iota^\circ\ge0$ a.e. on $Z$; cells also need coverage.

Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.pairArray.text: This rewrites a complex matrix with separate component and direction indices as an array indexed by the ordered pair of those indices. Every entry is unchanged. It allows the cylindrical gradient matrix to be used in the curl and stretching formulas of Appendix B.3, whose indices are ordered pairs. The definition is purely an indexing convention and imposes no symmetry, derivative relation or norm estimate.
Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.pairArray.summary: Rewrites a complex matrix with component and direction indices as an array indexed by the ordered pair, with entries unchanged, so the gradient can be used in the curl and stretching formulas of Appendix B.3. It is an indexing convention only.

Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.pairWeightOf.text: From a vector containing local coordinates and the two coefficient families, this extracts the forcing entries $\beta_i$ unchanged and twice the constraint entries $\zeta_i$. The resulting complex vector is indexed by the disjoint union of the two families. It is the coefficient vector of $\sum_i\beta_i\nabla b_i+2\sum_i\zeta_i\Xi_i$ in the term $\mathsf B_{\mathsf Q}$ of (B.26) and in (B.34). Reality of these entries in the intended application is a separate condition on the allowed cell vectors.
Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.pairWeightOf.summary: From a vector of local coordinates and the two coefficient families, the forcing entries $\beta_i$ unchanged and twice the constraint entries $\zeta_i$: the coefficients of $\sum_i\beta_i\nabla b_i+2\sum_i\zeta_i\Xi_i$ in $\mathsf B_{\mathsf Q}$ of (B.26) and in (B.34).

Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.pairingExact.text: This sums, over resolved harmonics in the common pairing list, the integrals $\int_{\mathsf Q}r\operatorname{Re}(G_\iota:\overline{P_\iota(\beta,2\zeta)})\,dr\,dz$, where $G_\iota$ is the reconstructed polynomial gradient. It then subtracts, for each listed error harmonic, the quadratic form of its supplied coefficient matrix on $(\beta,2\zeta)$ divided by four times its error weight. This is the explicit candidate $\mathsf B_{\mathsf Q}$ in (B.26). The subtraction accounts for unresolved or orthogonal parts by Young's inequality. Positive weights and valid norm bounds are separate conditions; a quotient by zero is assigned zero and cannot justify the intended error estimate.
Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.pairingExact.summary: The candidate $\mathsf B_{\mathsf Q}$ of (B.26): over resolved harmonics, $\int_{\mathsf Q}r\operatorname{Re}(G_\iota:\overline{P_\iota(\beta,2\zeta)})$, minus each error harmonic's matrix form on $(\beta,2\zeta)$ over four times its weight, by Young's inequality. A quotient by zero is zero.

Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.pairingProfi.text: For one cell, a harmonic and a complex coefficient vector $w$ on the forcing and constraint families, this defines the matrix field $\sum_gw_gP_{g,\iota}(r,z)$ from the supplied pairing profiles. In application $w=(\beta,2\zeta)$, and the profiles represent harmonics of $\nabla b_i$ and $\Xi_i$, with permitted approximations for the former. This is the matrix paired with the mode gradient in $\mathsf B_{\mathsf Q}$ of (B.26). The formula alone does not assert that the supplied profiles equal those derivatives or that their error bounds hold.
Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.pairingProfi.summary: For a cell, harmonic and coefficient vector $w$, the matrix field $\sum_gw_gP_{g,\iota}(r,z)$ from the supplied pairing profiles; with $w=(\beta,2\zeta)$ it is the matrix paired with the mode gradient in $\mathsf B_{\mathsf Q}$ of (B.26).

Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.partVec.text: Given optional real and imaginary global-coordinate indices, this forms the coefficient row with weight $1$ at the real index and $i$ at the imaginary index, or $-i$ there if conjugation is requested. An absent index contributes zero; if the two indices coincide their coefficients add. Evaluation on a real global vector gives the corresponding complex number or its conjugate. This is the real-coordinate representation of complex cell traces in Appendix B.3. Whether either part may be absent is checked separately.
Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.partVec.summary: From optional real and imaginary global indices, the coefficient row with $1$ at the real index and $i$ (or $-i$ under conjugation) at the imaginary one; absent indices contribute zero and coinciding ones add. This represents complex cell traces by real coordinates in Appendix B.3.

Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.potentialExa.text: Split a cell vector as $x=x^++x^b$, using the supplied matrix $P$, so $x^b=Px$ and $x^+=x-Px$. The expression is the integrated model coupling of $(x^+,x^+)$ plus twice that of $(x^+,x^b)$. It subtracts the local $12\times12$ lower form on $x^b$, the allocated curl-gradient-velocity absorption form on $x^b$, and the supplied matrix bound for projection remainders. It also subtracts, on the resolved harmonics in each group, that group's three-term cost multiplied by its positive balance, and subtracts the ordinary-model and remote-angular error forms on each resolved polynomial reconstructed from $x^+$. The lower-matrix integrals use $r\,dr\,dz$; the absorption integral uses the radial basis weight, $r$ on axis cells and $1$ otherwise. This is the fully specified candidate lower form for $\mathsf P_{\mathsf Q}$ in (B.26). Its relation to the true stretching integral is conditional on the model, grouping and error inequalities; the definition does not prove that comparison.
Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.potentialExa.summary: With $x^b=Px$ and $x^+=x-Px$, the model coupling of $(x^+,x^+)$ plus twice that of $(x^+,x^b)$, minus lower, absorption, remainder, group, ordinary and remote-angular error forms: the candidate for $\mathsf P_{\mathsf Q}$ in (B.26). Its comparison with the true stretching is conditional.

Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.presUnitMome.text: For each pressure-side coordinate in a layout, this takes the weighted side moment of the angular mode of the constant scalar field $1$, using zero radial and axial derivatives. Every nonpressure coordinate receives zero. It is the direction of a uniform pressure change within one harmonic layout in the normalization after Proposition B.14. The angular averaging makes it nonzero only in the zero-angular mode under the valid harmonic conventions. The definition uses the strip representation of a side moment; its agreement with the usual trace relies on the valid-segment conditions.
Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.presUnitMome.summary: For each pressure side coordinate in a layout, the weighted side moment of the angular mode of the constant field $1$, and zero for other coordinates. It is the direction of a uniform pressure change in one layout, in the normalization after Proposition B.14.

Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.rHatMax.text: For a cell with outer radius $r_2$, this defines $r_2/w(r_2)$, where the radial basis weight is $w(r)=r$ on an axis cell and $w(r)=1$ otherwise. Thus for valid cells it equals $1$ on an axis cell and $r_2$ on a cell separated from the axis. It bounds the factor converting the basis measure to cylindrical measure in the error estimates of Proposition B.4. If a degenerate cell had $r_2=0$, division by zero would give zero; the valid-cell hypotheses exclude that case.
Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.rHatMax.summary: For a cell with outer radius $r_2$, the value $r_2/w(r_2)$, which is $1$ on an axis cell and $r_2$ away from the axis. It bounds the measure conversion factor in the error estimates of Proposition B.4; a degenerate $r_2=0$ would give zero.

Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.restrictData.text: Given a complex vector of all unknowns in a cell and a harmonic resolved there, this selects exactly the entries belonging to that harmonic's layout. The auxiliary coordinates and the families representing $\beta$ and $\zeta$ are discarded. This is the restriction used to reconstruct the resolved-mode polynomial in the proof of Proposition B.4. It is a coordinate operation, with no condition that the selected values actually arise as moments or traces of a field.
Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.restrictData.summary: From a complex vector of all cell unknowns and a resolved harmonic, the entries of that harmonic's layout, discarding auxiliary coordinates and the $\beta$, $\zeta$ families. It is the restriction used to reconstruct the resolved-mode polynomial in Proposition B.4.

Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.retileKey.text: For a velocity, gradient or pressure side label, this retains its harmonic, side orientation, level and component, while replacing the interval endpoints, polynomial-test coefficients and test index by supplied ones. All other kinds of labels remain unchanged. It represents a subsegment moment used to express one side trace through a partition, among the global-coordinate conditions named after Proposition B.14. The definition itself requires neither that the new interval lies inside the old one nor that the old test polynomial expands in the new tests.
Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.retileKey.summary: For a velocity, gradient or pressure side label, keeps its harmonic, orientation, level and component and replaces the endpoints, test coefficients and test index; other labels are unchanged. It represents a subsegment moment; containment and test expansion are not required here.

Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.rowBaseWeigh.text:
Let $G$ be the Gram matrix of the polynomial equation tests in one cell, with entries $\int_{\mathsf Q}r\sum_a\varphi_{i',a}\overline{\varphi_{i,a}}\,dr\,dz$ when rows $i,i'$ have the same harmonic and zero otherwise. For a stored real cell weight $t_{\mathsf Q,\iota}$, the formal definition sets the corresponding block of the base row matrix equal to $G/t_{\mathsf Q,\iota}$.

The stored cell weight differs from the weight in (B.11). The row-identification condition gives the certificate weight $\tau=t_{\mathsf Q,\iota}/c$, where $c$ is the coercivity coefficient. The paper’s scaled field has squared norm $\tau$, whereas the formal certificate records a normalized row field and this weight separately. Thus the denominator here is $c\tau$, and is $(3/50)\tau$ in the final cell system. Every row in one harmonic block uses the same denominator. The definition alone permits arbitrary real weights and assigns zero to division by zero; the row hypotheses require positive weights.
Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.rowBaseWeigh.summary: Divides each harmonic block of the cell test Gram matrix by its stored cell weight $t_{\mathsf Q,\iota}$. The certificate weight corresponding to (B.11) is $\tau=t/c$, so the denominator is $c\tau$, with $c=3/50$ in the final system.

Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.rowCrossTest.text: For a row with harmonic $\iota$ and a perturbation harmonic $\iota'$, this forms the twelve-component convection test from the velocity and vorticity model at the difference $\iota-\iota'$ and from that row's polynomial test triple. Thus only reference harmonics that bridge the two labels contribute. This is the harmonic-selection rule described in the proof of Proposition B.4. The expression is evaluated at a meridian point; no time or angle integration is performed here, and model validity remains a separate hypothesis.
Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.rowCrossTest.summary: For a row with harmonic $\iota$ and perturbation harmonic $\iota'$, the convection test built from the velocity and vorticity model at $\iota-\iota'$ and the row's test triple, so only bridging reference harmonics contribute, as in Proposition B.4. It is evaluated at a meridian point.

Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.rowGram.text: For two equation rows in one cell, this is zero if their harmonic labels differ. If the labels agree, it is the integral $\int_{\mathsf Q}r\sum_{a}\varphi_{i',a}\overline{\varphi_{i,a}}\,dr\,dz$ of their complex cylindrical test triples. Thus the matrix is block diagonal by harmonic and uses the cylindrical Jacobian $r$. It is the cell Gram matrix underlying the orthogonalization in (B.11) and the row forms of Proposition B.4. Positive definiteness is required separately and does not follow merely from having a finite list of polynomials.
Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.rowGram.summary: For two equation rows of a cell, zero if their harmonics differ and otherwise $\int_{\mathsf Q}r\sum_a\varphi_{i',a}\overline{\varphi_{i,a}}\,dr\,dz$. This block-diagonal Gram matrix underlies (B.11) and the row forms of Proposition B.4; positive definiteness is required separately.

Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.rowTestPoly.text: For a numbered equation row, this selects the triple of complex cell polynomials given by its harmonic label and its natural-number test index. These are the cylindrical components $\varphi$ whose pairing with $F$ enters (B.11) and (B.34). The selection itself supplies no bounds or regularity beyond the polynomial representation. The row hypotheses check that the label is tested, the index is in its finite range, the triple is solenoidal and axis-regular, and its degrees fit the cell layout.
Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.rowTestPoly.summary: For a numbered equation row, the triple of complex cell polynomials given by its harmonic label and test index: the components $\varphi$ whose pairing with $F$ enters (B.11) and (B.34). Range, solenoidality, axis regularity and degrees are checked by the row hypotheses.

Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.rowsEliminat.text: For a cell vector $x$, subtract from its vector of local equation rows the integrals, over all eliminated harmonics, of the supplied gradient approximation paired with each converted row source, with weight $r$. This definition takes the inverse-matrix quadratic form of that adjusted vector using the supplied full row matrix. It is the equation-row contribution $\mathsf e_{\mathsf Q}$ in (B.26), after eliminating those harmonics. The matrix need not be invertible by definition; the conditions comparing it to a positive definite row matrix and a nonnegative Gram contribution give the required invertibility. A singular inverse has the formal default zero value.
Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.rowsEliminat.summary: The inverse-matrix quadratic form, with the full row matrix, of the local equation rows minus their pairings with the eliminated-harmonic gradient approximations: the row contribution $\mathsf e_{\mathsf Q}$ in (B.26). Invertibility comes from other conditions; a singular inverse defaults to zero.

Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.scaledRowGra.text: Given a real weight $c_\iota$ for each harmonic, this divides every entry of the cell test Gram matrix in a harmonic block by that block's weight. Entries between different harmonics remain zero. It is a weighted quadratic form for the row estimates in (B.26). For a positive-definite interpretation the relevant weights must be positive, imposed by the hypotheses in which it is used. Division by zero is taken to be zero, so this definition alone cannot justify a positive or inverse-weighted estimate.
Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.scaledRowGra.summary: Divides each harmonic block of the cell test Gram matrix by a real weight $c_\iota$, leaving cross-harmonic entries zero; a weighted form for the row estimates in (B.26). Division by zero is taken to be zero, so positive weights must be supplied where it is used.

Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.sesq12.text: For a complex $12\times12$ matrix $M$ and complex vectors $U,U'$, this is $U^*MU'=\sum_{i,j}\overline{U_i}M_{ij}U'_j$. It is conjugate-linear in the first vector and linear in the second. Its real part is the pairing used for the cell forms in Appendix B.3, where $U$ contains a gradient and a velocity. The definition does not require $M$ to be Hermitian; consequently $U^*MU$ need not be real until a Hermitian condition or an explicit real part is supplied.
Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.sesq12.summary: For a complex $12\times12$ matrix $M$ and vectors $U,U'$, the form $U^*MU'=\sum\overline{U_i}M_{ij}U'_j$, conjugate-linear in the first argument. Its real part gives the cell pairings of Appendix B.3; $M$ need not be Hermitian, so $U^*MU$ need not be real.

Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.sideKeyGeom.text: For a velocity, gradient or pressure side label, this returns the radial-or-axial choice, fixed level, two endpoints, real test-polynomial coefficients and moment index. It drops the harmonic and vector-component information. A corner, stream or auxiliary label has no side geometry and returns no value. This extraction is used when a side is subdivided in the global-unknown relations of Appendix B.3. It supplies the recorded data without checking endpoint order, radial placement or coverage.
Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.sideKeyGeom.summary: For a velocity, gradient or pressure side label, its radial-or-axial choice, level, endpoints, test coefficients and moment index, dropping harmonic and component; corner, stream and auxiliary labels return no value. Used when subdividing sides in Appendix B.3.

Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.sourceSum.text: For one harmonic, a complex vector $x$ of cell unknowns and a point $(r,z)$, this adds the twelve-component linear source from the stretching estimate to the source from the forcing-and-constraint pairing. Each is a finite sum $\sum_dx_dS_d(r,z)$. The first nine components correspond to gradient variables and the last three to velocity variables. This is the combined source that is eliminated in the completion-of-squares part of the proof of Proposition B.4. It is a definition; the error bounds for the two sources remain separate hypotheses.
Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.sourceSum.summary: For one harmonic, cell vector $x$ and point $(r,z)$, the sum of the twelve-component linear sources from the stretching and forcing-and-constraint estimates, each of the form $\sum_dx_dS_d(r,z)$. This is the source eliminated by completing squares in Proposition B.4.

Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.splitCharge.text: For real coefficients $a_c,a_g,a_v$, a complex velocity $u$ and gradient array $G$, this is $a_c|\operatorname{curl}G|^2+a_g|G|_{\mathrm F}^2+a_v|u|^2$. The squared Frobenius norm $|G|_{\mathrm F}^2$ is the sum of squared moduli of all nine entries. It is the diagonal error form used to allocate cell losses among the three lower-order terms of (B.16). The definition permits arbitrary signs of the three coefficients; nonnegativity is imposed by the error estimates that use the form.
Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.splitCharge.summary: For real $a_c,a_g,a_v$, velocity $u$ and gradient $G$, the form $a_c|\operatorname{curl}G|^2+a_g|G|_{\mathrm F}^2+a_v|u|^2$, with the sum of squared moduli of all nine entries. It allocates cell losses among the lower-order terms of (B.16); signs are unrestricted here.

Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.strainOfVec.text: For a twelve-component complex gradient-velocity pair, this returns the full $3\times3$ gradient matrix from its first nine entries. In particular it does not take the symmetric part of that matrix. This distinction matters in the curl, Frobenius norm and stretching costs used in Proposition B.4. The paper's $\mathbf G$ denotes the full gradient of a mode, while $\mathbb S$ denotes the symmetric gradient of the reference field. This operation extracts the former type of object and imposes no derivative or trace condition.
Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.strainOfVec.summary: The full $3\times3$ gradient matrix from the first nine entries of a twelve-component pair, without taking its symmetric part. This is the paper's full mode gradient $\mathbf G$, distinct from the symmetric reference gradient $\mathbb S$, as used in Proposition B.4.

Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.streamEnds.text: For a radial segment at radius $c$ with coordinate interval $[a,b]$, the two points are $(c,a)$ and $(c,b)$. For an axial segment at height $c$, they are $(a,c)$ and $(b,c)$. This merely returns the stored endpoints, with index zero for the first and one for the second. They are used in the stream-function and divergence identities for cell traces in Appendix B.3. Ordering of the interval and compatibility with cell corners are separate hypotheses.
Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.streamEnds.summary: For a radial segment at radius $c$ over $[a,b]$ the points $(c,a)$, $(c,b)$; for an axial segment at height $c$ the points $(a,c)$, $(b,c)$. These are the endpoints used in the stream-function and divergence identities of Appendix B.3; ordering is a separate hypothesis.

Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.tailGramPart.text: For one resolved harmonic this integrates the products of the supplied twelve-component row-remainder tests over the cell. A selector retains either the first nine gradient components or the last three velocity components. The weight is $r$ on an axis cell and $1$ on a cell separated from the axis, matching the orthogonal polynomial basis convention. This produces the Gram matrix used to allocate the row error between gradient and velocity remainder costs in Proposition B.4. Measurability and boundedness of the tests, and positive denominators in the subsequent cost comparison, are separate conditions.
Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.tailGramPart.summary: For one resolved harmonic, the cell integral of products of the row-remainder tests, keeping either the nine gradient or the three velocity components, with weight $r$ on an axis cell and $1$ otherwise. This Gram matrix allocates the row error between remainder costs in Proposition B.4.

Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.testAt.text: For a cell, a harmonic label, a natural-number test index and a cylindrical component, this evaluates the corresponding supplied test polynomial at $(r,z)$ in that cell's coordinates. It is the triple $\varphi$ used to pair the local equation with the right-hand side in Proposition B.4 and to form the Gram matrix in (B.11). The definition allows every natural-number index; the row conditions restrict it to the finite list of tests actually supplied. Solenoidality, polynomial degree and axis conditions are additional hypotheses.
Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.testAt.summary: For a cell, harmonic, test index and cylindrical component, the supplied test polynomial evaluated at $(r,z)$: the triple $\varphi$ pairing the local equation with the right-hand side in Proposition B.4 and forming the Gram matrix in (B.11). Every natural index is allowed here.

Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.topValue.text: For a resolved harmonic with coefficient degree $d$, this sums squares of selected polynomial gradient coefficients. Radial derivative entries with radial degree $j$ satisfying $d\le j+1$ receive weight $1/\Lambda_d^r$. Axial derivative entries receive weight $1/\Lambda_d^z$ when $j+1\le d$ and $d\le l+1$, where $l$ is the axial degree. The sums also range over all components and the layout's angular indices. This is the explicit highest-degree contribution $\mathsf T_{\mathsf Q}$ described after (B.26). At degenerate degrees or cells the reciprocals are defined to be zero if an eigenvalue vanishes; valid layouts and degree bounds provide the positive eigenvalues needed in the estimate.
Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.topValue.summary: For a resolved harmonic of degree $d$, the sum of squared selected gradient coefficients weighted by $1/\Lambda_d^r$ or $1/\Lambda_d^z$ by the stated degree rules: the highest-degree contribution $\mathsf T_{\mathsf Q}$ after (B.26). A vanishing eigenvalue gives reciprocal zero.

Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.totalStrainC.text: For one cell and one harmonic, this adds the three proposed costs assigned to the gradient square by the stretching-form estimate, the forcing-and-constraint pairing estimate and the equation-row estimate. The result is a real number. It is the total gradient loss that the spectral tail budget must absorb in the proof of Proposition B.4 and in (B.27). This sum alone imposes no sign condition or bound; the tail conditions compare it with the available allowances.
Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.totalStrainC.summary: For one cell and harmonic, the sum of the gradient-square costs from the stretching, forcing-and-constraint pairing and equation-row estimates. It is the gradient loss the tail budget must absorb in Proposition B.4 and (B.27); no bound is imposed here.

Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.totalVelCost.text: For one cell and one harmonic, this adds the velocity-square cost from the stretching-form estimate to the corresponding cost from the equation rows. It is the velocity loss to be absorbed by the tail estimate associated with (B.27). The forcing-and-constraint pairing contributes through its separate gradient cost and is absent from this sum. The definition merely adds two supplied real numbers; their validity and the comparison with a nonnegative tail allowance are separate conditions.
Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.totalVelCost.summary: For one cell and harmonic, the sum of the velocity-square costs from the stretching estimate and the equation rows; the pairing estimate is absent. It is the velocity loss absorbed by the tail estimate of (B.27); validity is separate.

Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.turnMatrix.text:
For an integer $k$, this is the complex matrix $T_k= egin{pmatrix}ik&-1&0\1&ik&0\0&0&ik\end{pmatrix}$. On cylindrical components it gives $r(\mathbf e_\phi\cdot
abla)u=T_ku$ for a harmonic of angular frequency $k$, as in the proof of Lemma B.5. It is used to eliminate velocity in terms of an angular gradient. The matrix is invertible precisely when $k
e0$ and $k^2
e1$; these exclusions are required later for eliminated harmonics. The definition itself accepts all integers.
Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.turnMatrix.summary:
For integer $k$, the matrix $T_k$ with rows $(ik,-1,0)$, $(1,ik,0)$, $(0,0,ik)$, giving $r(\mathbf e_\phi\cdot
abla)u=T_ku$ for angular frequency $k$, as in Lemma B.5. It is invertible exactly when $k
e0$ and $k^2
e1$.

Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.turnedRowBan.text: For one equation row and one eliminated harmonic, this converts the row's twelve-component source into nine gradient components using the same angular identity $r(\mathbf e_\phi\cdot\nabla)u=T_{\varkappa\iota_1}u$. Only the angular-gradient column receives the contribution from velocity, with the conjugate transpose of the inverse angular matrix. This is the row source used in the eliminated-mode part of (B.26). The formula is defined even for singular angular matrices, whose inverse is set to zero; the cell elimination hypotheses exclude those frequencies.
Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.turnedRowBan.summary: For one equation row and eliminated harmonic, converts the twelve-component row source to nine gradient components via $T_{\varkappa\iota_1}$, adding the velocity part to the angular-gradient column. This is the row source in the eliminated part of (B.26); a singular inverse is set to zero.

Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.turnedSource.text: For a harmonic $\iota$, a cell vector $x$ and a point $(r,z)$, this first sums the stretching and forcing-pairing sources, then converts their three velocity entries into angular-gradient entries using $T_{\varkappa\iota_1}^{-1}$. The result has nine complex components. It is the source for completing squares in the eliminated modes in Proposition B.4. The inverse is mathematically meaningful under $\varkappa\iota_1\ne0$ and $(\varkappa\iota_1)^2\ne1$, required by the elimination conditions. Its default zero value at a singular matrix makes the raw definition total but does not supply that elimination identity.
Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.turnedSource.summary: For harmonic $\iota$, vector $x$ and point $(r,z)$, sums the stretching and pairing sources and converts the velocity entries to angular-gradient entries with $T_{\varkappa\iota_1}^{-1}$, giving nine components for completing squares in Proposition B.4. A singular matrix gives inverse zero.

Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.turnedVec.text:
Let $U$ be a twelve-component complex source, with gradient entries $U_{ab}$ and velocity entries $U_b^{\mathrm v}$. For angular frequency $k$ and radius $r$, this returns nine entries: it retains $U_{ab}$ if $b
e\phi$, and replaces the angular column by $U_{a\phi}+r\sum_b\overline{(T_k^{-1})_{ba}}U_b^{\mathrm v}$, where $T_ku=(ik u_r-u_\phi,ik u_\phi+u_r,ik u_z)$. This transfers the velocity source to angular derivatives in the eliminated harmonics of Proposition B.4. The matrix inverse is defined to be zero when the matrix is singular; the intended elimination is used only under $k
e0$ and $k^2
e1$.
Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.turnedVec.summary:
For a twelve-component source $U$, frequency $k$ and radius $r$, keeps $U_{ab}$ for $b
e\phi$ and replaces the angular column by $U_{a\phi}+r\sum_b\overline{(T_k^{-1})_{ba}}U_b^{\mathrm v}$. A singular inverse is zero; the elimination is used only for $k
e0$, $k^2
e1$.

Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.upperPart.text: Given the supplied splitting matrix $P$ and a complex cell vector $x$, this defines $x-Px$. It is the complementary polynomial part used to compute the stretching form $\mathsf P_{\mathsf Q}$ in (B.26). The formal definition does not require $P^2=P$ or $P=P^*$, so this expression should not by itself be interpreted as an orthogonal projection. The exact matrix identity and bounds needed by the decomposition are asserted separately.
Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.upperPart.summary: For the splitting matrix $P$ and a cell vector $x$, the vector $x-Px$, the complementary part used for $\mathsf P_{\mathsf Q}$ in (B.26). Neither $P^2=P$ nor $P=P^*$ is required, so it is not by itself an orthogonal projection.

Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.upperProfile.text: Apply the complementary matrix $I-P$ to a cell vector, reconstruct its gradient and velocity polynomials for each resolved harmonic, and assign zero to every other harmonic. This defines the twelve-component family used in the retained stretching and projection-error estimates in (B.26). Its support is finite because the resolved harmonic set is finite. The definition asserts neither that $P$ is an orthogonal projection nor that the actual field is zero outside the resolved harmonics.
Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.upperProfile.summary: Applies $I-P$ to a cell vector, reconstructs gradient and velocity polynomials for each resolved harmonic, and assigns zero elsewhere: the finitely supported family used in the retained stretching and projection-error estimates of (B.26).

Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.velOf.text: For a twelve-component complex vector representing a gradient-velocity pair, this returns entries ten through twelve, the three cylindrical velocity components. The first nine entries are reserved for the gradient matrix. This is the component convention for the matrices acting on $(\mathbf G,\mathbf v)$ in Appendix B.3. It is only a projection of a finite vector and does not assert that the extracted components are the values of a field or satisfy the divergence equation.
Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.velOf.summary: Entries ten through twelve of a twelve-component gradient-velocity vector, the three cylindrical velocity components. This is the component convention for matrices acting on $(\mathbf G,\mathbf v)$ in Appendix B.3.

Breakdown.CertCell.Bridge.ClassSupportHo.text: Let κ∈ℕ with κ≥1 and let Γ contain (R_{π/κ},1/2) and (R_*,0). Let v be a measurable 1-periodic Γ-invariant solenoidal field, with supplied periodic weak gradient G, weak Hessian H and transport g=S^{−1}∂_θv+(v+y·∇v)/2. Require v(θ,·)∈L⁶ for almost every θ, and G, tr H and g square integrable over [0,1]×ℝ³. For every physical integer frequency (j,j′) outside the set {(2ι₂−ι₁,κι₁):ι∈ℤ²}, the formal assertion says that the projected velocity, gradient and Hessian all vanish almost everywhere in time and space. These projections use the inverse-rotation Fourier averages, with the corresponding action on every tensor index. Thus only the paper's symmetry lattice contributes to the integrals. The assertion specifies almost-everywhere vanishing; it does not give pointwise vanishing for an arbitrary measurable representative. Its proof is obtained from the mode transformation and the arithmetic of the two integer frequencies. The parameter S is any real number in this support assertion; the assigned value of 1/S at S=0 is zero. Its use in the multiplier theorem is restricted to S>0.
Breakdown.CertCell.Bridge.ClassSupportHo.summary: For $\kappa\ge1$ and $\Gamma\ni(R_{\pi/\kappa},1/2),(R_*,0)$, a $\Gamma$-invariant weak perturbation has projected velocity, gradient and Hessian vanishing almost everywhere at each frequency $(j,j')$ outside $\{(2\iota_2-\iota_1,\kappa\iota_1)\}$, so only the paper's symmetry lattice contributes.

Breakdown.CertCell.Bridge.CreditPatch.text: The data specify an integer frequency pair; radial endpoints r₁,r₂ and height h; a real spatial charge with proposed lower and upper bounds; finitely many real test functions with a common nonnegative Lipschitz constant; and a real matrix proposed to bound their weighted Dirichlet energies. They also provide finitely many segments on z=0 with scalar trace tests, a finite selection of those trace data, a real matrix expressing the rectangle tests through them, and a complex matrix for the resulting quadratic contribution. This is the trace-rectangle construction described before (B.29). The second frequency component is the angular integer used in the Dirichlet integrand. Positivity, boundary vanishing, coverage, and matrix inequalities are separate conditions.
Breakdown.CertCell.Bridge.CreditPatch.summary: Data for a trace rectangle before (B.29): a frequency pair, endpoints r₁,r₂ and height h, a charge with bounds, test functions with a Lipschitz constant and energy matrix, bottom segments with trace tests, and matrices expressing and bounding the contribution. Validity is separate.

Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.CellCalc.summary: For every cell: axis cells resolve only $\iota_1=0$, layouts are valid, matrix bounds and allowances hold on $\mathcal K$, stretching bounds and model decompositions hold with $1/S(\alpha)$ approximated uniformly, profiles are bounded, and pressure and plane trace conditions hold.

Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.CellCalc.text: For every mesh cell this specifies the layouts of its harmonics, the lower matrix fields and error allowances, the constants used to absorb errors, two families of omitted reference fields, and the harmonic-dependent charges. It also gives a finite common set of harmonics for the forcing and constraint pairings, their matrix-valued profiles on each cell, finitely many auxiliary cell coordinates with integer labels, and a complex matrix on all cell unknowns. A second finite set of pairing harmonics in each cell has positive weights to be checked later, and a proposed forcing-error cost is supplied for each cell. Finally it specifies finitely many rectangles at the plane $z=0$, their moment matrices, and for every rectangle moment the owning cell and the matching resolved-mode coordinate. These are data for (B.26), (B.33) and (B.34). Their definitions impose no validity, positivity or error bound; those are separate hypotheses. The paper describes these objects collectively and names the remaining data conditions after Proposition B.14.
Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.CellCalc.summary: For every mesh cell: harmonic layouts, lower matrices and allowances, error constants, omitted reference fields, charges, pairing harmonics and profiles, auxiliary coordinates, a cell matrix, forcing-error costs, and plane rectangles with moment data. Data for (B.26), (B.33), (B.34).

Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.CellInde.text: This is the disjoint collection of the unknowns of all resolved harmonics in one cell, $N$ auxiliary coordinates, and two real-coordinate families of size $n$ that will represent the forcing coefficients $\beta$ and the free multipliers $\zeta$. In a cell matrix every one of these coordinates is allowed a complex value; the global assembly later relates it to real global unknowns. It implements the enlarged vector of cell unknowns in Appendix B.3. The auxiliary count $N$ and the parameter count $n$ are nonnegative integers, so either family can be empty.
Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.CellInde.summary: The disjoint union of all resolved-harmonic unknowns of a cell, $N$ auxiliary coordinates, and two families of size $n$ for $\beta$ and $\zeta$, each allowed a complex value in a cell matrix. It is the enlarged vector of cell unknowns in Appendix B.3; either family may be empty.

Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.CellMode.text: For one cell, the data provide a common family of radial and vertical polynomial bases; a layout of volume, side, pressure, and corner unknowns for every harmonic label; a finite matrix of relations, selected solved coordinates, and retained boundary coordinates for each layout; and a selector identifying every relation with one of the layout's prescribed rows. These are the local unknown and relation data described before (B.26). The declaration asserts no invertibility or validity of the relations. It assigns layouts to all integer pairs, although the cell conditions use only the finitely many resolved labels.
Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.CellMode.summary: For one cell, common polynomial bases, a layout of volume, side, pressure and corner unknowns for every harmonic, a relation matrix with solved and retained coordinates, and a selector matching relations to prescribed rows. These are the local data before (B.26); no validity is asserted.

Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.CellMode.text: This specifies four real fields on $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3$: a velocity remainder, a vorticity remainder, a matrix remainder for the symmetric gradient, and a matrix remainder for the gradient of vorticity. These are the portions of the reference fields omitted by the cell polynomials in the description following Proposition B.4. The four fields are independent data here. Measurability, symmetry of the strain remainder, bounds, and orthogonality of every harmonic to the specified cell polynomials are imposed separately. The paper names the omitted portions after Proposition B.14 but does not give this four-field representation.
Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.CellMode.summary: Four real fields on $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3$: remainders for velocity, vorticity, the symmetric gradient and the vorticity gradient, omitted by the cell polynomials. Measurability, symmetry, bounds and orthogonality are imposed separately. The paper does not give this four-field representation.

Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.CellMode.text: This specifies four real fields on time and $\mathbb R^3$, for velocity, vorticity, symmetric gradient and gradient of vorticity, together with a nonnegative integer cutoff $N$ and four proposed real bounds. In the cell decomposition of Appendix B.3 these fields account for omitted harmonics separated in angular frequency from the retained modes. The definition places no sign condition on the four bounds and no spectral or regularity condition on the fields. Later conditions require nonnegative bounds and vanishing harmonics whenever $|\iota_1|\le2N$. The paper names these omitted parts after Proposition B.14 without specifying this representation.
Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.CellMode.summary: Four real fields for velocity, vorticity, symmetric gradient and vorticity gradient, with a cutoff $N$ and four real bounds, accounting for omitted harmonics beyond an angular cutoff. No sign or spectral condition is imposed here. The paper names these parts without this representation.

Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.CellMode.text: For an integer harmonic label $\iota=(\iota_1,\iota_2)$ and the nonnegative integer cutoff $N$ supplied with the omitted reference fields, this condition is $|\iota_1|\le N$. Only the angular index is tested; the time index $2\iota_2-\iota_1$ is unrestricted. The corresponding physical angular frequency is $\varkappa\iota_1$ in (B.2), so $N$ is a cutoff in harmonic labels, rather than in physical angular frequency. This is a precise choice used in the cell decomposition of Appendix B.3, among the harmonic-group conditions named after Proposition B.14.
Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.CellMode.summary: For a harmonic label $\iota=(\iota_1,\iota_2)$ and cutoff $N$, the condition is $|\iota_1|\le N$. Only the angular index is tested, so $N$ is a cutoff in harmonic labels; the physical angular frequency is $\varkappa\iota_1$.

Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.CellVar.text: For a fixed cell and its mode-dependent layouts, this is the finite collection of pairs consisting of a harmonic resolved in that cell and one unknown from that harmonic's layout. The unknowns include polynomial coefficients, side moments, pressure moments and corner values, as described in Appendix B.3. A pair remembers which harmonic its coordinate belongs to, even when different layouts use the same local label. This is an indexing set, not a field or an assertion that any assigned numbers are the values of a perturbation.
Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.CellVar.summary: For a fixed cell, the finite set of pairs of a resolved harmonic and one unknown of its layout: polynomial coefficients, side moments, pressure moments and corner values, as in Appendix B.3. It is an indexing set only.

Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.IsAxisRe.text:
Let $\mathsf Q$ be a closed meridian cell, let $\varphi=(\varphi_r,\varphi_\phi,\varphi_z)$ be a triple of complex polynomials on it, and let $k\in\mathbb R$. The condition is that some real constant $C$ satisfies
$\displaystyle |ik\varphi_r-\varphi_\phi|\le Cr,\qquad |ik\varphi_\phi+\varphi_r|\le Cr,\qquad |ik\varphi_z|\le Cr$
at every $(r,z)\in\mathsf Q$. Thus the angular column of the cylindrical gradient is bounded for $r>0$ and its numerator vanishes where the cell meets $r=0$.

The paper requires $\varphi_r=\varphi_\phi=0$ on the axis before (B.11), and in Appendix B.3 it resolves only harmonics with $\iota_1=0$ on an axis cell. For that application $k=0$, and, on a nondegenerate axis cell, the polynomial bound above is equivalent to the stated vanishing of the two transverse components. The present definition permits all real $k$. For $k=1$, for example, the constant triple $(1,i,0)$ satisfies the bound with $C=0$ although its transverse components do not vanish. Hence there is no unconditional claim here that the formal condition is stronger than the paper’s axis condition.
Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.IsAxisRe.summary: For polynomial components $\varphi$ and real frequency $k$, a constant $C$ bounds each component of $(ik\varphi_r-\varphi_\phi,ik\varphi_\phi+\varphi_r,ik\varphi_z)$ by $Cr$ on the cell. Its relation to the paper’s axis condition depends on $k$.

Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.IsCellFo.text:
Fix a cell $Q$ and its supplied complex matrix, polynomial data and error allocations. For every $\alpha\in\mathcal K$, weak perturbation, real $ eta,\zeta$ and finite complex auxiliary vector, form the local coordinate vector $x$ from its modal coefficients, traces, pressure data and these coefficient vectors. The forcing $F$ is measurable, period one and square integrable over a period. The supplied pressure-gradient field $P_g$ is measurable, period one and locally square integrable over a period; each sine and cosine time Fourier coefficient is a spatial gradient, and $P_g(	heta,R_*y)=R_*P_g(	heta,y)$ almost everywhere. The velocity and the separately supplied fields $G,H,g$ are measurable on $\mathbb R	imes\mathbb R^3$ and exactly period one in $	heta$. The velocity has divergence zero, $v(	heta)\in L^6(\mathbb R^3)$ for almost every $	heta$, and weak spatial derivatives $G=
abla v$, $H=

abla v$ are in $L^2$; the last identity is distributional. For every supplied symmetry $(R,	au)\in\Gamma$, $v(	heta+	au,Ry)=Rv(	heta,y)$ almost everywhere. To state the precise conclusion, let $a=\langle A_Qx,xangle$, let $b$ be the sum of the cell's forcing-row and actuator/constraint pairings, let $s$ be its allocated gradient error, let $c_Q(v)$ be its rectangle contribution, and let $k_Q$ be its coefficient cost. All five are fixed by the supplied data. With $a^+=\max(a,0)$, the required inequality is $a^++(-b)^++s^++c_Q(v)^++D_Q^-+U_Q^+\le D_Q^++U_Q^-+b^++(-a)^++(k_Q| eta|^2)^+$. It is meaningful for infinite nonnegative integrals.
