Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.IsTestOf.text: For a cell and a natural number $q$, this condition says that the three complex polynomial components of $\varphi$ have degree bounds $(q,q-1)$, $(q,q)$ and $(q-1,q)$ in $(r,z)$, respectively. More precisely, it requires an everywhere-valid expansion of each component as a finite sum of $c_{ij}r^iz^j$ within those bounds. The components are ordered as radial, azimuthal and vertical. Setting $q=d_0$ gives the three bounds in B.3. Natural-number subtraction is truncated: if $q=0$, the expression $q-1$ is zero. The application has $d_0\ge2$ for tested harmonics, so the subtraction has its usual meaning. Solenoidality and regularity at the axis are separate conditions.
Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.IsTestOf.summary: The radial, azimuthal and vertical polynomial components of $\varphi$ have degree bounds $(q,q-1)$, $(q,q)$, $(q-1,q)$ in $(r,z)$; $q=d_0$ gives the bounds in B.3. Natural-number subtraction is truncated, so $q-1=0$ when $q=0$; the application has $d_0\ge2$.

Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.IsTestSo.text: On a cell $\mathsf Q$, a triple of complex polynomials $\varphi$ with angular frequency $k$ must satisfy $\partial_r(r\varphi_r)+ik\varphi_\phi+r\partial_z\varphi_z=0$ at every point of the closed rectangle. This is the divergence equation multiplied by $r$. It is exactly the equation required for the triples before (B.11), with $k=\varkappa\iota_1$ in the paper's application. The formal definition permits an arbitrary real $k$ and does not itself impose the separate boundary conditions on the axis, degree restrictions or positive definiteness of their Gram matrix.
Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.IsTestSo.summary: On the closed cell, $\partial_r(r\varphi_r)+ik\varphi_\phi+r\partial_z\varphi_z=0$, the divergence equation multiplied by $r$. It is exactly the equation required before (B.11), there with $k=\varkappa\iota_1$; here $k$ is any real number.

Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.IsVecOrt.text: For every harmonic label ι, component a, and natural exponents i,j≤d, require ∫_Q (v̂ι)a(r,z) rⁱzʲ dr dz=0, where the mode uses raw frequency (2ι₂−ι₁,κι₁), is evaluated at time zero, and is expressed in the rotating frame. The cell Q is the meridian rectangle. This is a finite-degree moment-vanishing condition used for omitted parts in the cell estimates of Appendix B.3. The integral is unweighted planar measure: there is no additional cylindrical factor r. The condition quantifies over all integer labels and does not itself assert integrability; that hypothesis is necessary to interpret it as ordinary polynomial orthogonality.
Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.IsVecOrt.summary: For every label ι, component a and natural exponents i,j≤d, ∫_Q (v̂ι)a(r,z) rⁱzʲ dr dz=0 in the rotating frame at time zero. The measure is unweighted planar measure, without a factor r, and integrability is not asserted.

Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.LeafValu.text: For each harmonic label, the data supply lower Hessian and curl-gradient coefficients, a complex 12×12 matrix depending on the meridian point, and three groups of three real coefficients. Each group weights |curl G|², |G|F², and |v|²: one supplies absorption terms, one supplies the error subtraction in the matrix upper bound, and one supplies the additional subtraction in the matrix lower bound. These are the local matrix and error data described before (B.26). No positivity, Hermitian symmetry, boundedness, measurability, or validity inequality is imposed by this declaration.
Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.LeafValu.summary: For each harmonic label: lower Hessian and curl-gradient coefficients, a complex 12×12 matrix on the meridian, and three groups of three coefficients for absorption, matrix error and pairing cost, as before (B.26). No positivity or validity is imposed.

Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.LeafValu.text: For a label ι and arbitrary complex pair (G,v), form a′ι|curl G|²+aι|G|F²+bι|v|² from the three absorption constants. These terms are added to the weighted local matrix-minus-stretching comparison before (B.26), and ultimately enter the tail budget (B.27). The definition supplies no sign condition or estimate on an actual mode. Its role as a permitted cost is established only by the associated pointwise and tail inequalities.
Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.LeafValu.summary: For a label ι and complex pair (G,v), the expression a′ι|curl G|²+aι|G|F²+bι|v|² from the three absorption constants. It enters the local comparison before (B.26) and the tail budget (B.27); no sign condition is supplied.

Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.LeafValu.text: For a label ι, complex gradient array G, and complex vector v, use the second set of three supplied constants to form a′ι|curl G|²+aι|G|F²+bι|v|². This is the additional constant-coefficient cost subtracted in the lower comparison of the local matrix with the stretching form, described before (B.26). The declaration merely evaluates that quadratic expression. It does not identify it with the error of a specific pairing or require its coefficients to be nonnegative.
Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.LeafValu.summary: For a label ι and complex (G,v), the expression a′ι|curl G|²+aι|G|F²+bι|v|² from the second set of constants: the additional pairing cost subtracted in the lower comparison before (B.26). Coefficients need not be nonnegative.

Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.LeafValu.text: For a label ι and arbitrary complex gradient array G and vector v, form a′ι|curl G|²+aι|G|F²+bι|v|² using the three coefficients assigned to the matrix upper-bound error. This is the constant-coefficient subtraction from the three lower-order terms of (B.16) described before (B.26). The expression is defined for arbitrary real coefficients, so it need not be nonnegative. Whether it bounds a polynomial-model error is a separate cell condition.
Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.LeafValu.summary: For a label ι and complex (G,v), the expression a′ι|curl G|²+aι|G|F²+bι|v|² from the matrix upper-bound error coefficients: the subtraction from the lower-order terms of (B.16) described before (B.26). It need not be nonnegative.

Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.basisVal.text: For natural-number indices $j,l$ and a meridian point $(r,z)$, this is $P_j(r)Q_l(z)$, where $P_j$ and $Q_l$ are the real radial and axial polynomials supplied with the cell basis, regarded as a complex number. It is the product polynomial basis used for the cell unknowns in Appendix B.3. Orthonormality and the choice of Legendre or Jacobi weights are conditions on the supplied basis, not consequences of this product definition. Both indices range over all nonnegative integers here; finite degree cutoffs are imposed by the expressions that sum these products.
Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.basisVal.summary: For natural indices $j,l$ and a meridian point $(r,z)$, the value $P_j(r)Q_l(z)$ of the supplied radial and axial basis polynomials, regarded as complex. It is the product basis for the cell unknowns in Appendix B.3.

Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.coefPair.text: For a complex 3×3 array G and vector v∈ℂ³, form I′₁|curl G|²+I₁|G|F²+I₀|v|², where the three supplied real coefficients are those of curl, gradient, and velocity, and curl G is the antisymmetric combination of its entries. This is the lower-order part of (B.16), omitting the Hessian and curl-gradient squares. The definition does not require G to be the gradient of v, nor impose any sign on the coefficients. It is therefore a quadratic expression on an arbitrary twelve-component pair.
Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.coefPair.summary: For a complex 3×3 array G and v∈ℂ³, the expression I′₁|curl G|²+I₁|G|F²+I₀|v|², the lower-order part of (B.16). G need not be the gradient of v, and no sign is imposed on the coefficients.

Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.coupling.text: Given vector fields $W(\theta,y),v(\theta,y)$ and a matrix field $G(\theta,y)$ on $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3$, the formal expression is $c(G)\times W+c(D_yW)\times v$. The convention is $G_{ij}=(G e_j)_i$ and $c(G)=(G_{32}-G_{23},G_{13}-G_{31},G_{21}-G_{12})$. The derivative $D_yW$ is the ordinary spatial derivative where it exists and is assigned zero elsewhere. If $W$ is spatially differentiable and $G$ represents the weak gradient of $v$, then $c(D_yW)=\operatorname{curl}W$ and $c(G)=\operatorname{curl}v$ in the weak sense, so this is the pair of linearized curl-cross terms in (C.2), almost everywhere when the gradient identification is almost everywhere. The definition accepts all three fields independently and imposes no derivative or regularity hypothesis. Time derivative, drift, diffusion and computation of a discrete derivative matrix are outside this definition.
Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.coupling.summary: Defines $c(G)\times W+c(D_yW)\times v$, where $c(G)=(G_{32}-G_{23},G_{13}-G_{31},G_{21}-G_{12})$. For spatially differentiable $W$ and $G=\nabla v$, these are the two curl-cross terms in (C.2); those derivative hypotheses are not part of the definition.

Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.coupling.text: Given a cell layout, supplied reference velocity and vorticity harmonics, and a polynomial test triple, this forms a row on all cell unknowns. Its gradient entries are the integrals with two alternating symbols from the velocity harmonic, and its velocity entries are the cross-product integrals from the vorticity harmonic. Every side, corner, pressure and other auxiliary entry is zero. This is the harmonic-coupling part of the local row in the proof of Proposition B.4. It is a definition of coefficients; the mode-selection rule, period factor, model error and validity of the row equation are not asserted by it.
Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.coupling.summary: A row on all cell unknowns built from reference velocity and vorticity harmonics and a test triple: gradient entries from the velocity harmonic, velocity entries from the vorticity harmonic, all other entries zero. It is the harmonic-coupling part of the row in Proposition B.4.

Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.coupling.text: For a cell, a reference velocity harmonic $W_\alpha(r,z)\in\mathbb C^3$, a polynomial test triple $\varphi$, and a gradient basis entry $(a,b,j,l)$, this defines $\int_{\mathsf Q}rP_jQ_l\sum_{i,p,q}\epsilon_{iba}\epsilon_{ipq}(W_\alpha)_p\overline{\varphi_q}\,dr\,dz$. Here $\epsilon$ is the usual alternating symbol with the fixed orientation of $\mathbb R^3$. It is the coefficient arising from the vorticity form of convection in the cell row, among the harmonic couplings described in the proof of Proposition B.4. The reference harmonic is an arbitrary supplied function in this definition; its connection with the model of $W^{\mathrm r}$ and its approximation error are separate conditions.
Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.coupling.summary: For a gradient basis entry $(a,b,j,l)$, the coefficient $\int_{\mathsf Q}rP_jQ_l\sum_{i,p,q}\epsilon_{iba}\epsilon_{ipq}(W_\alpha)_p\overline{\varphi_q}\,dr\,dz$, arising from convection in vorticity form in the cell row of Proposition B.4.

Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.coupling.text: For a reference vorticity harmonic $\Omega_\alpha(r,z)$, a test triple $\varphi$ and a velocity basis entry $(a,j,l)$, this defines $\int_{\mathsf Q}rP_jQ_l\sum_{p,q}\epsilon_{apq}\overline{\varphi_p}(\Omega_\alpha)_q\,dr\,dz$. It supplies the velocity part of the local convection row in the cell argument of Proposition B.4. Complex conjugation is applied to the test; the vorticity harmonic is supplied independently. No statement that it equals the curl of a reference velocity is included here. That consistency and the errors of the polynomial model belong to the cell hypotheses.
Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.coupling.summary: For a velocity basis entry $(a,j,l)$, the coefficient $\int_{\mathsf Q}rP_jQ_l\sum_{p,q}\epsilon_{apq}\overline{\varphi_p}(\Omega_\alpha)_q\,dr\,dz$, the velocity part of the convection row in Proposition B.4. The vorticity harmonic is supplied independently.

Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.energyLe.text: This places the lower matrix of each resolved harmonic on a diagonal block of one complex matrix indexed by all cell unknowns. Every coefficient involving an auxiliary coordinate, a forcing coefficient or a free constraint multiplier is zero, as are cross terms between distinct resolved harmonics. It is the assembled derivative and polynomial contribution $\mathsf E_{\mathsf Q}$ of (B.26). The formula defines this matrix even before the cell lower bounds have been checked; it does not itself prove a comparison with the true integral or with the final matrix $\mathsf A_{\mathsf Q}$.
Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.energyLe.summary: One complex matrix on all cell unknowns with each resolved harmonic's lower matrix on a diagonal block and zeros elsewhere. It is the assembled contribution $\mathsf E_{\mathsf Q}$ of (B.26), defined before any cell lower bound is checked.

Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.frameWei.text: At a meridian point $(r,z)$ this returns $r$, $0$ or $z$ according as the selected cylindrical direction is radial, angular or axial, with the real value regarded as complex. These are the components of $y$ in the cylindrical frame. They insert the term $\tfrac12(y\cdot\nabla)v$ of the similarity equation into the cell integration-by-parts rows of Proposition B.4. No angular drift is present in this coordinate vector. This is a coordinate definition underlying the paper's equation, with no extra analytic hypothesis.
Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.frameWei.summary: At $(r,z)$, returns $r$, $0$ or $z$ for the radial, angular or axial direction: the cylindrical components of $y$. They insert the term $\tfrac12(y\cdot\nabla)v$ of the similarity equation into the cell rows of Proposition B.4.

Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.gradAt.text: For label ι=(ι₁,ι₂), symmetry order κ, and supplied matrix field G(θ,y), take its Fourier coefficient with raw frequency (2ι₂−ι₁,κι₁) in the rotating spatial frame, evaluate it at θ=0 and y=(r,0,z), and return entry (a,b). This is the meridian gradient coefficient used in Appendix B.3 after (B.23). The first matrix index is the output component and the second the input spatial direction. The definition does not require G to equal ∇v, nor require differentiability or symmetry of an underlying velocity.
Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.gradAt.summary: For label ι and matrix field G(θ,y), the Fourier coefficient with raw frequency (2ι₂−ι₁,κι₁) in the rotating frame, at θ=0 and y=(r,0,z), entry (a,b). This is the meridian gradient coefficient after (B.23); G need not equal ∇v.

Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.lowSlotF.text: Given a cell layout and a complex $12\times12$ matrix field $A(r,z)$, this forms the matrix of its integral on the polynomial gradient and velocity coefficients. The twelve entries at a point are the nine components of the gradient and the three velocity components. It integrates each pair of product-basis functions with the prescribed radial basis weight times the complementary radial factor, and sets cross terms between distinct angular modes to zero. The coefficient-to-polynomial map is then applied on both sides of the matrix. This is the polynomial integral of $A^{\mathsf Q,\iota}$ contributing to $\mathsf E_{\mathsf Q}$ in (B.26). Measurability, boundedness and Hermitian symmetry are separate hypotheses; the definition itself supplies no lower bound.
Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.lowSlotF.summary: For a cell layout and a $12\times12$ matrix field $A(r,z)$, the matrix of its weighted integral on the polynomial gradient and velocity coefficients, with no cross terms between distinct angular modes. It is the integral of $A^{\mathsf Q,\iota}$ contributing to $\mathsf E_{\mathsf Q}$ in (B.26).

Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.lowStrai.text: For a cell layout of coefficient degree $d$, a complex vector of its unknowns, an angular mode and indices $a,b$, this reconstructs $G_{ab}(r,z)=\sum_{j,l=0}^{d}g_{abjl}P_j(r)Q_l(z)$ from the gradient coefficients. These are the polynomial components of the gradient used in the resolved-mode decomposition of Proposition B.4. The reconstruction is defined on the entire meridian plane. No velocity field, derivative relation or projection identity is part of this definition; those are supplied by the conditions identifying a vector of unknowns with a perturbation.
Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.lowStrai.summary: From the gradient coefficients of a layout of degree $d$, reconstructs $G_{ab}(r,z)=\sum_{j,l=0}^{d}g_{abjl}P_j(r)Q_l(z)$ on the whole meridian plane, the polynomial gradient of the resolved-mode decomposition in Proposition B.4.

Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.lowVeloc.text: For a cell layout of coefficient degree $d$, a complex vector of its unknowns and an angular mode, this reconstructs each velocity component by $u_a(r,z)=\sum_{j,l<d}u_{ajl}P_j(r)Q_l(z)$. This matches the degree at most $d-1$ for velocity coefficients in Appendix B.3. If $d=0$, both finite sums are empty and the reconstructed field is zero; the degree assumptions used in the cell estimates exclude that case. The polynomial is defined for every real $(r,z)$ and need not be divergence-free unless the additional cell relations hold.
Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.lowVeloc.summary: From the velocity coefficients, reconstructs $u_a(r,z)=\sum_{j,l<d}u_{ajl}P_j(r)Q_l(z)$, matching degree at most $d-1$ in Appendix B.3. If $d=0$ the field is zero; the cell estimates exclude that case.

Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.modeBloc.text: For a resolved harmonic in a cell, this forms a complex matrix by adding two contributions: the derivative-energy matrix with the specified lower bounds for $|\nabla^2u|^2$ and $|\nabla\operatorname{curl}u|^2$, and the integral of the supplied $12\times12$ lower matrix on the reconstructed gradient and velocity polynomials. The third coefficient in the derivative-energy construction is set to zero. This is the contribution of that harmonic to $\mathsf E_{\mathsf Q}$ in (B.26). The formula alone does not establish positivity or the comparison with the full mode density; those conclusions require the cell layout and lower-bound conditions.
Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.modeBloc.summary: For a resolved harmonic, the sum of the derivative-energy matrix with lower bounds for $|\nabla^2u|^2$ and $|\nabla\operatorname{curl}u|^2$ and the integral of the $12\times12$ lower matrix on the reconstructed polynomials: that harmonic's part of $\mathsf E_{\mathsf Q}$ in (B.26).

Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.opBound.text: For a complex $3\times3$ matrix $A$ and a real number $c$, the formal statement requires $\sum_a|\sum_bA_{ab}u_b|^2\le c^2\sum_b|u_b|^2$ for every $u\in\mathbb C^3$. Equivalently, the Euclidean operator norm of $A$ is at most $|c|$. This encodes the operator bounds used for the vorticity gradient in (B.25). Because the number appears squared, this condition alone does not require $c\ge0$; that sign condition must accompany an interpretation of $c$ as the nonnegative bound used in the paper.
Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.opBound.summary: Requires $\sum_a|\sum_bA_{ab}u_b|^2\le c^2\sum_b|u_b|^2$ for all $u\in\mathbb C^3$, so the operator norm of $A$ is at most $|c|$, as used in (B.25). Since $c$ appears squared, the condition alone does not require $c\ge0$.

Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.ownRowVe.text: For a cell layout, angular frequency $k$, temporal frequency $\omega$ and polynomial test triple $\varphi$, this constructs one complex coefficient for each cell unknown. On gradient coefficients it uses the integral of $rP_jQ_l(\overline{\nabla_k\varphi}+y\overline\varphi/2)$; on velocity coefficients it uses $(i\omega+1/2)\int rP_jQ_l\overline\varphi$; on normal-gradient and pressure moments it uses the respective integration-by-parts boundary coefficients. All other types of cell unknown receive coefficient zero. It is the uncoupled part of the row paired with the right-hand side in Proposition B.4. It does not include convection by the reference profile or assert that a supplied vector of unknowns satisfies the row equation.
Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.ownRowVe.summary: For a layout, frequencies $k,\omega$ and test triple $\varphi$, one coefficient per cell unknown from gradient, velocity, normal-gradient and pressure terms, zero for others. It is the uncoupled part of the row in Proposition B.4, without convection by the reference profile.

Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.ownSolid.text: For one cell, take spatial points in its solid of revolution, with positive cylindrical radius, that belong to no other cell's solid. The solid already includes reflection across y₃=0. This selects an unambiguous region on which to use that cell's polynomial model, as in Appendix B.3. Shared boundaries are excluded because they belong to more than one closed solid. The definition itself does not require disjoint interiors or assert that the excluded set has measure zero; those facts use a valid cell mesh.
Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.ownSolid.summary: Points of a cell's solid of revolution, including its reflection across y₃=0, with positive radius and belonging to no other cell's solid. Shared boundaries are excluded; disjointness and null boundaries come from a valid mesh.

Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.ownStrai.text: For a cell $\mathsf Q$, a test triple $\varphi$, angular frequency $k$, a vector component $a$, derivative direction $b$ and basis indices $j,l$, this defines $\int_{\mathsf Q}rP_j(r)Q_l(z)[\overline{(\nabla_k\varphi)_{ab}}+\tfrac12y_b\overline{\varphi_a}]\,dr\,dz$, where $(y_r,y_\phi,y_z)=(r,0,z)$ and $\nabla_k$ includes the cylindrical angular derivative. It is the coefficient of a gradient unknown in the local equation paired with a test triple, as described in the proof of Proposition B.4. The polynomial weights and test field are supplied data. The expression itself asserts neither validity of the equation nor regularity at the axis; those enter the row conditions.
Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.ownStrai.summary: The coefficient $\int_{\mathsf Q}rP_j(r)Q_l(z)[\overline{(\nabla_k\varphi)_{ab}}+\tfrac12y_b\overline{\varphi_a}]\,dr\,dz$ of a gradient unknown in the test row of Proposition B.4, with $(y_r,y_\phi,y_z)=(r,0,z)$.

Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.ownVeloc.text: For a cell $\mathsf Q$, real temporal frequency $\omega$, a complex test triple $\varphi$ and basis indices $j,l$, this defines the coefficient $(i\omega+\tfrac12)\int_{\mathsf Q}rP_j(r)Q_l(z)\overline{\varphi_a}\,dr\,dz$ of the $a$th velocity component. It represents the time derivative and the $\tfrac12v$ term in the normalized similarity equation paired with a cell test, as used in Proposition B.4. In applications $\omega$ includes the inverse period and the temporal index of (B.2); this definition accepts any real frequency and does not impose that relation.
Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.ownVeloc.summary: The coefficient $(i\omega+\tfrac12)\int_{\mathsf Q}rP_j(r)Q_l(z)\overline{\varphi_a}\,dr\,dz$ of the $a$th velocity component, representing the time derivative and $\tfrac12v$ term in Proposition B.4. Any real $\omega$ is accepted.

Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.sideGrad.text: For a side segment of a cell, a component $\varphi_a$ of a complex polynomial test, and a moment index $d$, this is the negative outward sign times the conjugate test moment, with an additional factor equal to the fixed radius on a radial side. On an axial side that additional factor is one. It supplies the boundary coefficient of the normal derivative in the integration by parts for $-\Delta v$ in Proposition B.4. The sign is determined from the side's level and its opposite level; valid placement of those levels is a separate geometric condition. The paper describes this integration by parts without writing these coefficients.
Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.sideGrad.summary: For a side segment, the negative outward sign times the conjugate test moment, multiplied by the fixed radius on a radial side: the normal-derivative boundary coefficient for $-\Delta v$ in Proposition B.4. The paper does not write these coefficients.

Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.sidePres.text: For a pressure segment on a cell side and a natural-number moment index, this is the outward sign times the conjugate moment of the test's normal component, multiplied by the side's fixed radius on radial sides and by one on axial sides. The normal component is $\varphi_r$ on a radial side and $\varphi_z$ on an axial side. This is the pressure boundary term from pairing $\nabla p$ with a divergence-free polynomial test in Proposition B.4. Boundary placement, orientation and coverage of the pressure segments are separate hypotheses. The paper does not list this individual row coefficient.
Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.sidePres.summary: The outward sign times the conjugate moment of the test's normal component ($\varphi_r$ radial, $\varphi_z$ axial), times the fixed radius on radial sides: the pressure boundary term in Proposition B.4. The paper does not list this coefficient.

Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.sideTest.text: Let the directed side have level $c$, opposite level $o$, endpoints $a,b$ and real test polynomial $t_d$, of degree at most the natural number $d$. For a complex function $f(r,z)$, the radial-side moment is $\epsilon\int_{\min(c,o)}^{\max(c,o)}\int_a^b [f+(r-o)\partial_rf]t_d(z)/(c-o)\,dz\,dr$, where $\epsilon=1$ if $o<c$ and $\epsilon=-1$ otherwise. The axial-side formula interchanges $r,z$, using $[f+(z-o)\partial_zf]t_d(r)/(c-o)$ on $[a,b]\times[\min(c,o),\max(c,o)]$. There is no radial weight in this definition. For a regular function and $c\ne o$, integration in the normal direction gives the ordinary side integral $\int_a^b f(c,z)t_d(z)\,dz$ or $\int_a^b f(r,c)t_d(r)\,dr$. The strip formula also defines moments when only weak regularity is later available. As a bare definition it uses zero for derivatives where differentiability fails and for an integral whose integrand is not integrable; division by zero is zero, so $c=o$ gives zero. The subsequent geometric and regularity hypotheses supply the intended trace interpretation. This is the explicit side-pairing convention behind the integration-by-parts rows of Proposition B.4; the paper does not print this strip definition.
Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.sideTest.summary: A strip-integral definition of the moment of $f$ against a side test $t_d$, without radial weight, which for regular $f$ and $c\ne o$ equals the ordinary side integral. Division by zero is zero, so $c=o$ gives zero. The paper does not print this definition.

Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.strainOf.text: For a real vector field $W(\theta,y)$ on $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3$, this defines $\mathbb S=(\nabla W+(\nabla W)^{\mathsf T})/2$ at each time and point. The transpose uses the Euclidean inner product on $\mathbb R^3$. This is the strain matrix of the reference profile in Appendix B.2 and B.3. The definition alone imposes neither differentiability nor zero divergence; under the regularity of the reference profile its derivative has the usual meaning, and zero divergence then makes the trace of $\mathbb S$ zero. The formal derivative is defined even where a classical derivative fails, with value zero there.
Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.strainOf.summary: For a real field $W(\theta,y)$, defines $\mathbb S=(\nabla W+(\nabla W)^{\mathsf T})/2$, the strain of the reference profile in Appendix B.2 and B.3. The derivative is taken as zero where a classical derivative fails.

Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.testGrad.text: For a triple of complex cell polynomials $\varphi=(\varphi_r,\varphi_\phi,\varphi_z)$ and angular frequency $k$, this defines the cylindrical gradient matrix: its radial column is $\partial_r\varphi$, its axial column is $\partial_z\varphi$, and its angular column is $r^{-1}(ik\varphi_r-\varphi_\phi,ik\varphi_\phi+\varphi_r,ik\varphi_z)$. The first matrix index is the vector component, the second the direction of differentiation. This is the gradient used for the test triples in Appendix B.1 and the cell integration by parts in Proposition B.4. Division by zero is taken to be zero at $r=0$; the axis estimates and identities used later are separate hypotheses, and the formula agrees with the classical gradient for $r>0$.
Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.testGrad.summary: The cylindrical gradient of a test triple: columns $\partial_r\varphi$, $\partial_z\varphi$ and $r^{-1}(ik\varphi_r-\varphi_\phi,ik\varphi_\phi+\varphi_r,ik\varphi_z)$. Division by zero is taken to be zero at $r=0$; the formula is classical for $r>0$.

Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.testValu.text: For a cell $\mathsf Q$ and three complex polynomials $\varphi_r,\varphi_\phi,\varphi_z$ represented in its cell coordinates, this returns their three values at a meridian point $(r,z)$. They are the cylindrical components of the test harmonic in Appendix B.1, immediately before (B.11). No time or angular factor is inserted here; multiplication by $E_\iota(\theta,\phi)$ and conversion to Cartesian vectors occur elsewhere. Evaluation is defined at every real pair $(r,z)$, including outside the cell. This definition imposes no solenoidal or axis condition.
Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.testValu.summary: The values at a meridian point $(r,z)$ of three complex polynomials $\varphi_r,\varphi_\phi,\varphi_z$, the cylindrical components of the test harmonic before (B.11). No time or angular factor is included, and no solenoidal or axis condition.

Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.turnVect.text: For $k\in\mathbb R$ and $x=(x_r,x_\phi,x_z)\in\mathbb C^3$, this defines $(ikx_r-x_\phi,ikx_\phi+x_r,ikx_z)$. For a vector harmonic $e^{ik\phi}$ written in the cylindrical frame, it is its angular derivative with the rotation of that frame included. This is the coordinate expression behind the identity $r(\mathbf e_\phi\cdot\nabla)u=iku+\mathbf e_z\times u$ in the proof of Lemma B.5. The definition permits any real $k$; the paper's harmonics use the integer $k=\varkappa\iota_1$.
Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.turnVect.summary: For $k\in\mathbb R$ and $x\in\mathbb C^3$, defines $(ikx_r-x_\phi,ikx_\phi+x_r,ikx_z)$, the angular derivative of a cylindrical vector harmonic including frame rotation, behind the identity in the proof of Lemma B.5. Any real $k$ is allowed.

Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.velAt.text: For label ι=(ι₁,ι₂) and symmetry order κ, take the velocity's rotating-frame Fourier mode with raw frequency (2ι₂−ι₁,κι₁), and evaluate component a at normalized time zero and point (r,0,z). This is the meridian representation of v̂ι used after (B.23). The mode is defined by averaging over one time period and one angular revolution. The expression alone asserts neither periodicity nor integrability of v; ordinary integrals have default zero where their integrability requirements fail, so the intended Fourier interpretation uses the surrounding analytic hypotheses.
Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.velAt.summary: For label ι, component a of the velocity's rotating-frame Fourier mode with raw frequency (2ι₂−ι₁,κι₁), at time zero and point (r,0,z): the meridian representation of v̂ι after (B.23). Periodicity and integrability are not asserted.

Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.vorticit.text: Given a field $H(\theta,y)$ of real bilinear maps on $\mathbb R^3$ with values in $\mathbb R^3$, this contracts its indices with the alternating symbol to define the matrix representing $\nabla\operatorname{curl}W$ when $H$ is the spatial Hessian of $W$. It is the matrix $\mathbb V$ used in (B.25) and the polynomial models of Appendix B.3. No field $W$ or derivative identity is required by this definition itself: the identification of $H$ with the Hessian is a separate hypothesis. Thus this is an algebraic construction from the supplied second derivative, rather than an additional regularity assertion.
Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.vorticit.summary: From a field $H$ of bilinear maps, contracts indices with the alternating symbol to give the matrix representing $\nabla\operatorname{curl}W$ when $H$ is the Hessian of $W$: the matrix $\mathbb V$ of (B.25). That identification is a separate hypothesis.

Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.vorticit.text: For a real vector field W(θ,y), take its spatial derivative at fixed θ and form the three antisymmetric component differences, yielding curl W. This is the vorticity of the reference profile used in the stretching form (B.18) and in the polynomial models of Appendix B.3. The expression is defined for all fields and points, with a default zero derivative wherever spatial differentiability fails. The declaration does not itself impose C¹ regularity, divergence-freeness, symmetry, or any bound on the resulting vorticity.
Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.vorticit.summary: For a real field W(θ,y), forms curl W from the spatial derivative at fixed θ, the reference vorticity in (B.18) and Appendix B.3. The derivative is taken as zero where differentiability fails; no regularity or bound is imposed.

Breakdown.CertCell.CellHypothesis.text: For one fixed set of certificate fields, cells, local calculations and matrix tree, this condition requires the row, weight, forcing and constraint representations, the local cell inequalities, tree bounds, and global error budget. It also requires the continuum conditions, pointwise bounds on represented fields, and a finite Hermite representation of the reference field with compact forcing support. The mesh is valid, the data have the prescribed common parameter dependence, and Γ contains the twisted half-period rotation and spatial half-turn with κ≥3. The constants are fixed by w(y)=39/50, c=3/50, t=1000 and maximum cell test weight 400(1+2^{−18}). These are simultaneous hypotheses. The statement is neither a numerical evaluation of any field nor a proof that such cell data exist; the subsequent assembly theorem derives the density lower bound from them together with the required assembly data.
Breakdown.CertCell.CellHypothesis.summary: For one set of certificate fields, cells, local calculations and matrix tree: the representations, cell inequalities, tree bounds, error budget, continuum conditions and symmetries with $\kappa\ge3$, at $w=39/50$, $c=3/50$, $t=1000$, test weight $400(1+2^{-18})$. Existence of such data is not shown.

Breakdown.CertCell.CellLayerData.text:
For k parameter coordinates, a set of mode classes and finite numbers of the two multiplier-piece families, these data supply a proposed time-periodic certificate as in §7.3, parameter-dependent multiplier weights and harmonic bounds, a reference field Wʳ(θ,y), a separately supplied reference Hessian, and a finite set of its ordinary Fourier indices. A natural angular order m specifies the lattice map (ι₁,ι₂)↦(2ι₂−ι₁,mι₁).

The remaining inputs are a finite cell mesh; row-generator data with the certificate's row count; polynomial models of velocity, vorticity, strain and vorticity gradient and of the reciprocal period; an error-allowance record for each cell; stretching-loss coefficient functions for every cell and a separate choice for the exterior; k cell-polynomial constraint matrices and k cell-polynomial forcing vectors; and three real constants for coercivity, the form comparison and the constraint penalty.

This organizes the objects of Appendix B.1–B.4, but every item is supplied as data. It does not establish that the reference Hessian is a derivative, that the field lies in the indicated harmonic span, that the mesh and generators are valid, or that any bound, certificate inequality or numerical enclosure holds. The forcing polynomials here are the supplied cell representations used in the estimates; equality with or approximation to the certificate's forcing fields is a separate requirement.
Breakdown.CertCell.CellLayerData.summary: Data organizing Appendix B.1 to B.4: a proposed time-periodic certificate, multiplier weights, reference field Wʳ and Hessian, a cell mesh, polynomial models, error allowances, constraint and forcing polynomials and three constants. Every item is supplied as data; no bound is established.

Breakdown.CertCell.CellLayerData.formPos.text: For supplied v,G,H and parameter α, this is ∑_{ι∈ℤ²}∫_{r>0,z>0}r max(I_ι(r,z),0)dr dz plus ∫_{r>0,z>0}r times the time-angle mean of max(J,0)dr dz. Each I_ι is the complete five-term density in (B.16), evaluated at normalized time and angle zero. All summands are nonnegative extended-real integrals, so the value may be +∞ and no cancellation is used. This is the quarter-plane positive contribution in the reduction (B.23), without the factor 4π needed for the full-space quantity. It does not assert finiteness or the symmetry and derivative hypotheses that justify equality with the full-space integral.
Breakdown.CertCell.CellLayerData.formPos.summary: Sums ∫r max(I_ι,0) over all labels on r,z>0 and adds ∫r mean(max(J,0)). It may be +∞ and corresponds to the separate positive contributions in (B.23), before multiplication by 4π; it is not the positive part of the combined signed form.

Breakdown.CertCell.CellLayerData.labelDe.text:
Fix a parameter α, a natural angular order m, a label ι=(ι₁,ι₂) and p=(r,z). Use the ordinary Fourier pair (2ι₂−ι₁,mι₁). Let V, A and B be the rotating-frame Fourier coefficients of the supplied vector field v, matrix field G and three-index field H, evaluated at normalized time 0 and y=(r,0,z). The tensor indices of A and B are output component first, followed by input directions. Define c_i=∑_{j,l}ε_{ijl}A_{lj} and D_{il}=∑_{j,a}ε_{ija}B_{a,l,j}, with ε the usual alternating symbol.

The defined real number is I₂|B|²+I′₂|D|²+I′₁|c|²+I₁|A|²+I₀|V|². Tensor squares are sums of squared complex component moduli. The five real coefficients are evaluated at y=(r,0,z) from the supplied multiplier weights, harmonic bounds, spatial energy weight and period S(α). This is the five-term structure of (B.16). It becomes the expression written there with actual derivatives when G=∇v and H=∇²v and differentiation commutes with the Fourier averages under the required regularity.

The definition includes no derivative identification, symmetry, admissibility or numerical choice of the coefficients. It accepts all real r,z; the paper’s quarter-plane reduction uses r,z>0. The value is signed and contains no cylindrical factor r. Ordinary Fourier integrals receive zero when not integrable, so their use as actual modes requires the corresponding integrability hypotheses.
Breakdown.CertCell.CellLayerData.labelDe.summary: $I_2|B|^2+I'_2|D|^2+I'_1|c|^2+I_1|A|^2+I_0|V|^2$, with $V,A,B$ the rotating-frame Fourier coefficients of supplied $v,G,H$ at time 0 and $y=(r,0,z)$ and $c,D$ their curl contractions: the five terms of (B.16). No factor $r$; $G=\nabla v$, $H=\nabla^2v$ are not imposed.

Breakdown.CertCell.CellLayerData.meanStr.text: For a reference field $W^{\mathrm r}$ with a supplied Hessian and fields $v,G$, this defines $\bar J(r,z)=(2\pi)^{-1}\int_0^1\int_0^{2\pi}J(\theta,R_\phi(r,0,z))\,d\phi\,d\theta$. The time interval already has length one; only the angular integral needs the factor $(2\pi)^{-1}$. The density $J$ is formed from the supplied velocity, gradient and reference derivatives by the three stretching terms of (B.18). The definition itself does not assert that $G$ and the supplied Hessian are derivatives, or that the integral is finite. An ordinary integral is assigned the value zero when its integrand is not integrable, so the surrounding integrability hypotheses are essential for interpreting this as the analytic mean in B.3.
Breakdown.CertCell.CellLayerData.meanStr.summary: $\bar J(r,z)=(2\pi)^{-1}\int_0^1\int_0^{2\pi}J(\theta,R_\phi(r,0,z))\,d\phi\,d\theta$, with $J$ the three stretching terms of (B.18). A nonintegrable integrand gives the value zero, so the integrability hypotheses are needed to read it as the analytic mean in B.3.

Breakdown.CertCell.CellLayerData.pinFiel.text: For a chosen constraint index i, this evaluates its cell-polynomial matrix data at normalized time θ and y∈ℝ³ using the prescribed angular order and the mesh. It gives the proposed tensor Ξ_i of (B.10), with value zero outside the sets {(r,|z|)∈𝒬}. Below z=0, label ι is replaced by ι♭=(−ι₁,ι₂−ι₁) and entry (a,b) is multiplied by s_as_b, where (s_r,s_φ,s_z)=(1,−1,−1). Its first index is the output component, so the entry corresponding to the paper’s Ξ_{i,ab} in (B.10) is stored in position (b,a). Contributions on overlapping closed boundaries are summed. This definition does not establish equality with the certificate's separately supplied constraint tensor, its approximation by a gradient, or any bound for the constraint functional.
Breakdown.CertCell.CellLayerData.pinFiel.summary: Evaluates the cell-polynomial data for constraint $i$ at $(\theta,y)$, giving $\Xi_i$ of (B.10) with $\Xi_{i,ab}$ stored at $(b,a)$; below $z=0$ label $\iota^\flat=(-\iota_1,\iota_2-\iota_1)$, signs $s_as_b$, $(s_r,s_\phi,s_z)=(1,-1,-1)$; zero off the cells. Equality with the given tensor is open.

Breakdown.CertCell.CellLayerData.stretch.text: For a perturbation v and a supplied gradient G, this takes the positive part max(J,0) of the stretching expression, then averages it over normalized time θ∈[0,1] and angle φ∈[0,2π] at R_φ(r,0,z), with factor 1/(2π). The reference field and its supplied Hessian determine the strain and vorticity-gradient terms of J in (B.18). The result lies in [0,∞] and may be infinite. As in the positive-part discussion after (B.24), this is the mean of the positive part, which can exceed max(mean J,0); interchanging those operations changes the quantity.
Breakdown.CertCell.CellLayerData.stretch.summary: The positive part max(J,0) of the stretching expression (B.18), averaged over θ∈[0,1] and φ∈[0,2π] with factor 1/(2π). The value lies in [0,∞]; this mean of the positive part can exceed max(mean J,0).

Breakdown.CertCell.CellLayerData.withFor.text: For given cell-certificate data and a real number $c$, this retains every datum except the coefficient of the energy term in each parameter-dependent multiplier family, which it replaces by $c$. This permits comparison of the positive part of the density at different coercivity coefficients in the cell estimates of Appendix B.3. It is a definition of modified data. It asserts no positivity of $c$ and no preservation of the multiplier inequalities; those must be supplied when the modified density is used. The paper fixes the final value $3/50$ in (B.21).
Breakdown.CertCell.CellLayerData.withFor.summary: The same cell data with the coefficient of the energy term in each multiplier family replaced by a real number $c$, for comparisons in Appendix B.3. No positivity of $c$ is asserted; the paper fixes $3/50$ in (B.21).

Breakdown.CertCell.CellLayerEntries.text: For the cell data and a proposed global tree, this supplies six items: the cell assembly matrices and row-error data; the stretching and pairing coupling data; a finite pointwise cover for unresolved cell modes; a finite exterior cover with pointwise and integrated tests; represented majorants for the exterior reference field; and the rows expressing cell unknowns through real global unknowns. These are the remaining choices used to prove Proposition B.8 from the analytic estimates and the tree. Their existence as data does not require any of their inequalities to be valid.
Breakdown.CertCell.CellLayerEntries.summary: For the cell data and a proposed tree, six items: cell assembly and row-error data, stretching and pairing coupling data, a cover for unresolved modes, an exterior cover, exterior majorants, and rows expressing cell unknowns through global unknowns. No inequality is required to hold.

Breakdown.CertCell.CellLayerEntryConditi.text:
The cell charges must be measurable and uniformly bounded, and every entry of every local lower matrix must be measurable and bounded on its cell. The conditional stretching requirements, the forcing-and-constraint pairing estimates, the equation-row matrix bounds, the exact equation-row formulas and all polynomial tail budgets must hold on the allowed vectors. Each highest-degree block must evaluate exactly to the selected top-degree gradient sum, and the elimination inequalities must hold there too.

Every equation-row matrix must annihilate both the pressure-normalization directions and every constant-pressure direction. All pressure coordinates must have zero row and column in the retained stretching, retained pairing, highest-degree and projection-error matrices, and in each highest-degree block; their coefficients in both eliminated-mode sources and the eliminated-mode approximation must also vanish. These are exact independence-of-pressure requirements, rather than numerical smallness bounds.

The unresolved-cell cover and the exterior cover must be valid, the exterior stretching constant at least $\sqrt{7/2}$, and the represented exterior majorants must bound the reference field at all points. The global rows must satisfy their exact trace, divergence and evaluation conditions and the global negative-form inequality. The pressure-normalization matrices and kernel conditions, the radial and harmonic consistency of real trace labels, and the transport of every retained pressure direction through the global rows must hold. These are the detailed hypotheses completing (B.26), (B.33), (B.34) and hence Proposition B.8. The paper explicitly says after Proposition B.14 that several of these polynomial, geometric, matrix and pointwise conditions are not written out. The formal statement requires them; it does not establish them for any numerical data merely from the choice of those data.
Breakdown.CertCell.CellLayerEntryConditi.summary: Detailed hypotheses completing (B.26), (B.33), (B.34) and Proposition B.8: measurability, pairing and tail bounds, exact pressure independence, valid covers, exterior stretching constant at least $\sqrt{7/2}$, and global row conditions. The paper says several are not written out.

Breakdown.CertCell.CellMatField.text: For each cell there is a finite harmonic set and, for every label and pair of cylindrical component indices, one complex polynomial. The first matrix index is the output component and the second the input direction: A_{ab} multiplies eₐ⊗eᵦ. In (B.10) the paper puts the derivative direction first, so, when the array represents a constraint field, this entry corresponds to the paper’s coefficient Ξ_{i,ba}. This is the matrix-field representation of the constraints Ξ_i in (B.10) and of the strain and vorticity-gradient models in Appendix B.3. These raw polynomial arrays need not be symmetric, conjugate paired, derivatives of a vector field or valid approximations.
Breakdown.CertCell.CellMatField.summary: For each cell, a finite harmonic set and one complex polynomial per label and pair of cylindrical indices, with first index the output, so for a constraint $A_{ab}=\Xi_{i,ba}$ in (B.10). It represents the constraints and the strain and vorticity-gradient models. No symmetry or validity is required.

Breakdown.CertCell.CellMatField.IsConjug.text: For each cell, its harmonic set is closed under ι↦−ι and ι↦ι♭. At every meridian point, for every label and matrix entry, the polynomial with label −ι evaluates to the conjugate of the polynomial with label ι. This is the matrix version of the conjugacy condition in Appendix B.1. It holds for all labels and all points, beyond the active cell and label ranges. It does not imply that the matrix is symmetric or is a derivative of another supplied field.
Breakdown.CertCell.CellMatField.IsConjug.summary: Each cell's harmonic set is closed under ι↦−ι and ι↦ι♭, and at every point the polynomial for −ι is the conjugate of that for ι: the matrix conjugacy condition of Appendix B.1, required for all labels and points.

Breakdown.CertCell.CellMatField.field.text: For finitely many rectangles Q in the (r,z) quarter plane and complex tensor polynomials attached to integer labels, the defined real tensor is zero outside their reflected spatial cells. Inside a cell it sums the real parts of E_ι times those polynomials in the cylindrical frame. At z<0 it evaluates the polynomial with reflected label ι^♭ at (r,−z) and multiplies by −1 exactly when one matrix index is radial and the other is azimuthal or vertical. Its matrix indices are output component followed by input direction. Therefore the coefficient of e_b·(e_a·∇)v is entry (b,a). Closed cells may overlap on their boundaries, where their contributions add; disjoint interiors make these overlaps negligible in the constraint integral. Boundedness and compact support use finite valid cells and polynomial data.
Breakdown.CertCell.CellMatField.field.summary: A real tensor, zero outside the reflected cells and inside equal to real parts of $E_\iota$ times complex polynomials in the cylindrical frame; at $z<0$ it uses $\iota^\flat$ at $(r,-z)$ with sign $-1$ on radial-against-other entries. Entry $(b,a)$ is the coefficient of $e_b\cdot(e_a\cdot\nabla)v$.

Breakdown.CertCell.CellMatField.frameMap.text: For a real array Aₐᵦ and angle φ, this is the linear map v↦∑ₐᵦAₐᵦ(eᵦ(φ)·v)eₐ(φ). Thus the bth frame vector is mapped to ∑ₐAₐᵦeₐ. The first index is therefore the output component. To represent (B.10), whose first index is the derivative direction, set A_{ab}=Ξ_{i,ba}; this transposition is part of the dictionary between the two formulas. The definition imposes neither symmetry nor that the matrix be a gradient; the frame is supplied even at the axis.
Breakdown.CertCell.CellMatField.frameMap.summary: For a real array $A_{ab}$ and angle $\phi$, the map $v\mapsto\sum_{ab}A_{ab}(e_b(\phi)\cdot v)e_a(\phi)$, first index the output; representing (B.10) requires the transpose $A_{ab}=\Xi_{i,ba}$. Neither symmetry nor gradient structure is imposed.

Breakdown.CertCell.CellMatField.planeVal.text: For matrix entry (a,b), the value above z=0 is its polynomial with label ι. Below z=0 it is s_as_b times the polynomial with label ι♭ at (r,−z), where (s_r,s_φ,s_z)=(1,−1,−1). The product s_as_b is −1 exactly when precisely one of the two indices is radial, and is +1 otherwise. This is the sign rule stated after (B.10). The upper branch is used on z=0, and no matching or derivative interpretation follows from the definition.
Breakdown.CertCell.CellMatField.planeVal.summary: Entry (a,b) is its label-ι polynomial for z≥0, and s_as_b times the label-ι♭ polynomial at (r,−z) for z<0, with (s_r,s_φ,s_z)=(1,−1,−1). The sign is negative exactly when precisely one index is radial, as stated after (B.10).

Breakdown.CertCell.CellMesh.text: The data comprise a natural number of cells and their meridian rectangles. For each cell there are three finite sets of lattice labels in ℤ²: the resolved harmonics, those used by the test fields, and an additional band intended for elimination. For every cell and every label there are an integer side degree d₀ and a natural volume degree d. This is the mesh information described in Appendix B.3. Raw data may include negative d₀, overlapping cells or inconsistent mode sets; the validity conditions are separate. The integer side degree allows the value −1 to represent absence of some side data.
Breakdown.CertCell.CellMesh.summary: A number of cells with meridian rectangles and, for each, three finite label sets in ℤ² (resolved, test, elimination band), with an integer side degree d₀ and natural volume degree d per label, as in Appendix B.3. Validity conditions are separate.

Breakdown.CertCell.CellMesh.closedHalfPl.text: This is {(r,z)∈ℝ²:r≥0 and z≥0}. It is the closed quarter plane used for the meridian reduction in Appendix B.3. The axis r=0 and the symmetry plane z=0 are included here; the integral reduction (B.23) is written on the open quarter plane.
Breakdown.CertCell.CellMesh.closedHalfPl.summary: The set {(r,z)∈ℝ²:r≥0 and z≥0}, the closed quarter plane of the meridian reduction in Appendix B.3. The axis and the plane z=0 are included; (B.23) is written on the open quarter plane.

Breakdown.CertCell.CellMesh.exterior.text: This is {(r,z):r≥0,z≥0} minus the union of all closed cell rectangles. It is the complement on which the exterior estimates of Appendix B.3 are imposed. Thus cell boundaries belong to the cell region and are excluded from this complement; parts of the coordinate axes can still lie in it. The construction does not assert that the complement is connected, bounded or a single region.
Breakdown.CertCell.CellMesh.exterior.summary: The closed quarter plane minus the union of all closed cell rectangles, where the exterior estimates of Appendix B.3 are imposed. Cell boundaries are excluded; connectedness or boundedness is not asserted.

Breakdown.CertCell.CellMesh.maxVolumeDeg.text: For a specified cell, this is the maximum of its natural volume degrees over its finite set of resolved harmonics. If that set is empty the value is 0. It provides one common degree bound for polynomial constructions in Appendix B.3; it does not assert that all harmonics have this degree or that the associated side-degree inequalities hold.
Breakdown.CertCell.CellMesh.maxVolumeDeg.summary: For a cell, the maximum of its volume degrees over its resolved harmonics, or 0 if there are none. It gives one common degree bound for the polynomial constructions of Appendix B.3.

Breakdown.CertCell.CellMesh.region.text: For a finite family of meridian rectangles Q_K, this is their union ⋃_KQ_K in ℝ². It is the region whose cell integrals occur in Appendix B.3. The rectangles are closed, so the union includes their boundaries. The definition itself neither places them in the quarter plane nor prevents overlap; these facts require the separate mesh conditions.
Breakdown.CertCell.CellMesh.region.summary: The union ⋃_KQ_K of the closed meridian rectangles, including their boundaries: the region of the cell integrals in Appendix B.3. Placement in the quarter plane and non-overlap need separate mesh conditions.

Breakdown.CertCell.CellPoly.text: The data are a natural degree d and a finite array of complex coefficients cᵢⱼ for 0≤i,j≤d. On a cell they will define a polynomial in its affine reference radius and height. This represents the finite cell polynomials used for constraints and test fields in (B.10)–(B.11). The separate bound d in each variable does not mean total degree d, and the declaration imposes no reality, solenoidality or matching across cells.
Breakdown.CertCell.CellPoly.summary: A natural degree d and complex coefficients cᵢⱼ for 0≤i,j≤d, defining a polynomial in a cell's affine reference radius and height, as in (B.10) and (B.11). The bound d applies in each variable separately, and no reality or solenoidality is imposed.

Breakdown.CertCell.CellPoly.eval.text: For cell Q=[r₁,r₂]×[z₁,z₂] and coefficients cᵢⱼ, this is ∑ᵢⱼcᵢⱼξ(r)ⁱη(z)ʲ, with ξ=(2r−r₁−r₂)/(r₂−r₁) and η=(2z−z₁−z₂)/(z₂−z₁). It is the polynomial component in (B.10), expressed on reference coordinates. It is evaluated for every (r,z), including points outside Q; support is imposed separately. The exponents are natural, and degenerate widths use division by zero equal to zero.
Breakdown.CertCell.CellPoly.eval.summary: For Q=[r₁,r₂]×[z₁,z₂], the value ∑ᵢⱼcᵢⱼξ(r)ⁱη(z)ʲ with ξ=(2r−r₁−r₂)/(r₂−r₁), η=(2z−z₁−z₂)/(z₂−z₁), the polynomial component in (B.10). It is defined at every (r,z); degenerate widths use division by zero equal to zero.

Breakdown.CertCell.CellPoly.scale.text: For c∈ℂ and a cell polynomial P, this multiplies every complex coefficient of P by c and keeps the same declared degree. Hence evaluation gives cP at every point. It is the scalar multiplication used to form the real and imaginary generator fields in Appendix B.1. The stored degree need not become smaller when c=0.
Breakdown.CertCell.CellPoly.scale.summary: For c∈ℂ, multiplies every coefficient of a cell polynomial by c with the same declared degree, so its value is cP everywhere. It is the scalar multiplication used for the real and imaginary generator fields in Appendix B.1.

Breakdown.CertCell.CellPoly.zero.text: This is the degree-zero complex polynomial whose only coefficient is zero. Its value is zero on every cell and at every point, regardless of the reference-coordinate convention. It supplies absent components in the finite cell fields of (B.10)–(B.11); it asserts no cancellation or approximation property for other supplied polynomials.
Breakdown.CertCell.CellPoly.zero.summary: The degree-zero polynomial with only coefficient zero, vanishing everywhere. It supplies absent components in the cell fields of (B.10) and (B.11).

Breakdown.CertCell.CellVecField.text: For each of a finite number of cells, the data specify a finite set of lattice harmonics and three complex cell polynomials for every label. The three components are in the cylindrical frame (eᵣ,eφ,e_z). This is the representation of vector test and model fields used in (B.10)–(B.11) and Appendix B.3. Coefficients are supplied even for labels outside the finite summation set. The declaration imposes no conjugacy, symmetry, divergence condition, support or error bound by itself.
Breakdown.CertCell.CellVecField.summary: For each cell, a finite set of lattice harmonics and three complex cell polynomials per label in the frame (eᵣ,eφ,e_z): the representation of vector test and model fields in (B.10), (B.11) and Appendix B.3. No conjugacy, divergence or error condition is imposed.

Breakdown.CertCell.CellVecField.IsConjug.text: In each cell the finite label set must contain both −ι and ι♭ whenever it contains ι. For every label, every component and every meridian point, the evaluated polynomial at −ι must be the complex conjugate of the one at ι. This is the conjugate-pair condition for the real harmonic sum in Appendix B.1. The polynomial identity is required for all labels, including those outside the summation set, and for all points, including outside the cell. The condition alone does not impose matching on z=0, divergence-freeness or continuity across cell boundaries.
Breakdown.CertCell.CellVecField.IsConjug.summary: Each cell's label set contains −ι and ι♭ with ι, and at every point the polynomial at −ι is the conjugate of that at ι, for every label and component: the conjugate-pair condition for the real harmonic sum in Appendix B.1.

Breakdown.CertCell.CellVecField.field.text: For normalized time θ and y∈ℝ³, this sums over all cells containing (r,|z|), all their supplied lattice labels ι, and the three cylindrical components the vectors Re(E_ι(θ,φ)fᵢ(r,z))eᵢ(φ). Here r=(y₁²+y₂²)¹ᐟ², z=y₃, φ is the chosen argument, and fᵢ below z=0 is obtained by the reflected-label rule with signs (1,−1,−1). This is the real cell-polynomial construction of Appendix B.1. It is zero outside the union of cell solids. The closed-cell indicators are summed, so shared boundaries can receive contributions from more than one cell; a valid mesh makes these overlaps negligible for volume integrals. No smoothness, solenoidality or conjugacy is built into this definition.
Breakdown.CertCell.CellVecField.field.summary: At (θ,y), sums Re(E_ι(θ,φ)fᵢ(r,z))eᵢ(φ) over cells containing (r,|z|), their labels and components, with the reflected-label rule and signs (1,−1,−1) below z=0: the real cell-polynomial field of Appendix B.1. It is zero outside the cell solids.

Breakdown.CertCell.CellVecField.planeVal.text: For component a in the order (r,φ,z), use sign s_a=1,−1,−1 respectively. The value at (r,z) is the cell polynomial with label ι when z≥0 and s_a times the polynomial with label ι♭ at (r,−z) when z<0. This implements the vector reflection rule in Appendix B.1. It is an everywhere-defined component formula without a cell cutoff; equatorial matching and other symmetry conditions are separate.
Breakdown.CertCell.CellVecField.planeVal.summary: For component a in order (r,φ,z) with sign s_a=1,−1,−1, the value is the polynomial with label ι for z≥0 and s_a times that with label ι♭ at (r,−z) for z<0, implementing the reflection rule of Appendix B.1.

Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.ComplexNo.text:
These data specify a finite set of complex coordinates and finite families of positive and negative complex columns. A map z=Ex from the real global unknowns is given by optional real and imaginary coordinate indices and real imaginary multipliers. The remaining inputs are a real scale t, complex square matrices H,K, a finite pivot set U, real arrays p,w,m on the complex coordinates, and the positive and negative column matrices Y₊,Y₋. They are exactly the kinds of objects used for the complex-node alternative after (B.40).

No condition here makes t nonnegative, H or K Hermitian, the w_j positive, or the pivot coordinate multipliers ±1. It also does not identify the real and imaginary parts of √t E*Y₋ with the tree's global columns. All these are hypotheses of the subsequent enclosure condition, so these raw data alone establish no matrix lower bound.
Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.ComplexNo.summary: A finite set of complex coordinates, a map z=Ex from real unknowns, a scale t, complex matrices H,K, a pivot set, real arrays p,w,m and columns Y₊,Y₋, as for the complex-node alternative after (B.40). No sign or Hermitian condition is imposed.

Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.Coordinat.text: For each complex coordinate j, the data specify either a real-coordinate index a(j) or no real part, either an index b(j) or no imaginary part, and a real multiplier s_j. They represent z_j=x_a(j)+is_jx_b(j), omitting absent terms. This is the coordinate form allowed in the complex-node tests after (B.40). No restriction on s_j, distinctness of the two indices, independence of different coordinates or injectivity of the resulting map is imposed at this stage.
Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.Coordinat.summary: For each complex coordinate j, optional real indices a(j), b(j) and a real multiplier s_j, representing z_j=x_a(j)+is_jx_b(j) as allowed after (B.40). No restriction on s_j or distinctness of indices is imposed here.

Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.Coordinat.text: For a complex coordinate j and real-coordinate index k, this condition says that k occurs as either the real or the imaginary index in z_j=x_a(j)+is_jx_b(j). It is the incidence relation used to transfer pivot slacks to global unknowns after (B.40). It records the selected index even if its numerical multiplier happens to vanish, so incidence alone is not a nonzero-coefficient assertion outside the pivot conditions.
Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.Coordinat.summary: Says that a real index k occurs as the real or imaginary index in z_j=x_a(j)+is_jx_b(j), the incidence used to transfer pivot slacks after (B.40). It holds even if the multiplier vanishes.

Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.Coordinat.text: For each complex coordinate j and real coordinate k, the matrix entry is 1 when k is its selected real index, plus is_j when k is its selected imaginary index, with absent terms omitted. Hence Ex has entries x_a(j)+is_jx_b(j) for real x. This is the map X_ξ used after (B.40). If the same real index appears in both parts, both contributions are added; the separate pivot condition forbids this only on pivot coordinates.
Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.Coordinat.summary: Entry 1 where k is the real index of coordinate j, plus is_j where k is its imaginary index, so Ex has entries x_a(j)+is_jx_b(j): the map X_ξ after (B.40). If one index appears in both parts, both contributions add.

Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.Coordinat.text: For a finite set U of complex pivot coordinates, this is the set of real-coordinate indices that occur in at least one of their real or imaginary parts. It is the global pivot set U_ξ prescribed in the complex-coordinate version after (B.40). Each real index is included only once in the set, even if several complex pivots contain it; the associated slack is summed separately.
Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.Coordinat.summary: For a finite set U of complex pivots, the set of real indices occurring in at least one of their real or imaginary parts: the global pivot set U_ξ after (B.40). Each real index is included once.

Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.Coordinat.text: For a real-coordinate index k, this sums p_j over the selected complex pivots j whose real or imaginary part uses k, where p_j is the supplied real value for that pivot. Each pivot contributes at most once to this sum. With p_j equal to the margin after error subtraction, multiplication by the node factor gives the global slack bound following (B.40). No positivity or coordinate-sign condition is asserted by this definition.
Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.Coordinat.summary: For a real index k, the sum of p_j over the complex pivots j whose real or imaginary part uses k, each pivot counted once. Multiplied by the node factor this gives the global slack bound after (B.40).

Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.IsCoordin.text: On each chosen complex pivot coordinate j, require s_j²=1 and, if both real and imaginary indices are present, require them to be different. Thus a pivot is an optional real unknown plus ±i times a different optional real unknown, exactly as required after (B.40). The sign condition is imposed even if the imaginary term is absent. There is no restriction here on nonpivot coordinates or on sharing a real unknown between different complex pivots.
Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.IsCoordin.summary: On each complex pivot coordinate j, requires s_j²=1 and distinct real and imaginary indices when both exist, so a pivot is an optional real unknown plus ±i times a different one, as required after (B.40).

Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.PassesCom.text: At one node the complex coordinates are $z_l=x_{j(l)}+i\varepsilon_lx_{j'(l)}$, with either term possibly absent. On pivot coordinates $\varepsilon_l^2=1$ and the two real indices, when both present, are distinct. Let $A=N_\xi+\sum_{\xi'}V_{\xi'}$, the sum being over children. The condition requires $t\ge0$, Hermitian $H,K$, symmetric entrywise nonnegative real $H',K'$, and $w_l>0$. For every real global $x$, it requires $t\langle Hz,z\rangle\le\langle Ax,x\rangle+t\langle H'|z|,|z|\rangle$ and $\langle V_\xi x,x\rangle\le t(\langle Kz,z\rangle-\sum_{l\text{ not pivot}}m_l|z_l|^2+\langle K'|z|,|z|\rangle)$. The global pivots are precisely the real variables occurring in pivot coordinates, with lower bounds at most $t\sum_l(p_l-m_l)$ over the coordinates containing them. For every column $y$ of $Y$, the real and imaginary parts of $\sqrt tX^*y$ must occur as distinct indexed global columns at this node. Complex forms mean their real Hermitian quadratic values; $|z|$ is componentwise modulus. The statement allows $t=0$, while strict positivity of global pivot bounds is imposed separately.
Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.PassesCom.summary: At one node, with complex coordinates $z_l$ and $A=N_\xi+\sum_{\xi'}V_{\xi'}$: $t\ge0$, Hermitian $H,K$, nonnegative $H',K'$, $w_l>0$, two quadratic inequalities for all real $x$, a weighted row bound on the residual $B$ by $m_l$, pivot lower bounds and column conditions. $t=0$ is allowed.

Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.PassesNod.text: At a fixed matrix-tree node, this condition says that there exist either real enclosure data and real error matrices satisfying the real comparisons and weighted row bounds (B.39)–(B.40), or complex-coordinate enclosure data and real error matrices satisfying the complex alternative described immediately afterwards. Only one of the two alternatives is required. The statement is existential and supplies no particular numerical matrices. It is a local hypothesis for Lemma B.7; valid tree bookkeeping, positive pivot slacks, the nonnegative root form and the global column-count bound are still required separately.
Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.PassesNod.summary: At a tree node, there exist either real enclosure data satisfying (B.39) and (B.40) or complex-coordinate data satisfying the alternative after them. It is a local hypothesis for Lemma B.7; the tree, slack, root and column conditions are separate.

Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.PassesPiv.text: For finite determined and free coordinate sets, this condition requires every real global coordinate to be a pivot at some node, every assigned pivot lower bound to be strictly positive, the quadratic form of the matrix passed by the root to be nonnegative on every real vector, and the total number of negative columns to be at most the number of free coordinates. A repeated occurrence of a coordinate as a pivot is allowed. The number of columns counts their indices, even if some column vectors coincide. The condition alone does not assert the node inequalities; together they yield the positive subspace needed at the end of B.3.
Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.PassesPiv.summary: Every real global coordinate is a pivot at some node, every pivot lower bound is strictly positive, the root's passed form is nonnegative on real vectors, and there are at most as many negative columns as free coordinates. With the node inequalities this gives the positive subspace of B.3.

Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.PassesRea.text: At one node, let $A=N_\xi+\sum_{\xi'}V_{\xi'}$, with the sum over its children, and let $V_\xi$ be the matrix passed to its parent. Given pivots $\mathcal U_\xi$ and columns $Y_\xi$, the condition supplies symmetric $H,K$, symmetric entrywise nonnegative $H',K'$, positive weights $w_j$, real $p_j,m_j$, and a rectangular real matrix $Y'$. For every real $x$ it requires $\langle Hx,x\rangle\le\langle Ax,x\rangle+\langle H'|x|,|x|\rangle$ and $\langle V_\xi x,x\rangle\le\langle Kx,x\rangle-\sum_{j\notin\mathcal U_\xi}m_jx_j^2+\langle K'|x|,|x|\rangle$. On each pivot $\underline p_{\xi,j}\le p_j-m_j$. Here $|x|$ means componentwise absolute value. All spaces are finite-dimensional and the forms are real. The positive weights exclude zero denominators. These are assumptions on the supplied node matrices and bounds; they perform no numerical verification themselves.
Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.PassesRea.summary: At a node with $A=N_\xi+\sum_{\xi'}V_{\xi'}$: symmetric $H,K$, nonnegative $H',K'$, $w_j>0$, $\langle Hx,x\rangle\le\langle Ax,x\rangle+\langle H'|x|,|x|\rangle$ and the $\langle V_\xi x,x\rangle$ bound for real $x$, weighted row bounds $m_i$ on $B$, and $\underline p_{\xi,j}\le p_j-m_j$ on pivots.

Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.RealNodeD.text: For the global coordinate sets A,B, these data specify a finite family of positive correction columns and two real square matrices H,K. A real pivot value p_j, positive-weight candidate w_j and error-radius candidate m_j are supplied for every global coordinate, together with the column matrix Y₊. These are the real-node quantities in (B.39)–(B.40). The negative-column matrix is supplied by the tree's assigned columns. This data declaration requires no symmetry, w_j>0, row-bound inequality or comparison with the actual node input and outgoing matrix.
Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.RealNodeD.summary: Positive correction columns Y₊, real square matrices H,K, and a pivot value p_j, weight w_j and radius m_j for every global coordinate: the real-node quantities in (B.39) and (B.40). No symmetry or inequality is required.

Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.SignedTre.text:
Given two coordinate sets A and B, intended as the determined and free global unknowns, the data specify finite sets of leaves, nodes and column indices. Each leaf carries a real square matrix on A⊔B and is assigned to a node. Each node has an optional parent; one node is designated as the root. A real matrix V_ξ is supplied at every node, together with a finite pivot set and a real slack value for every coordinate. Each column index is assigned to a node and carries a real vector on A⊔B.

These are the matrices and columns described in Appendix B.3 around (B.38)–(B.41). The finite-coordinate hypotheses are supplied when the matrix sums and quadratic forms are used. The data declaration by itself does not make the parent relation an acyclic rooted tree, make the slacks positive, require matrix symmetry or certify any node enclosure. It is therefore substantially less than the conditions of Lemma B.7.
Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.SignedTre.summary: Leaves with matrices assigned to nodes, nodes with optional parents and a root, a matrix V_ξ, pivot set and slacks at each node, and columns assigned to nodes, as around (B.38) to (B.41). It is substantially less than the conditions of Lemma B.7.

Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.SignedTre.text: For a node ξ, this matrix contains every recorded global column in its own index position if that column is assigned to ξ, and a zero column otherwise. No linear independence or sign assumption is imposed on those columns.
Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.SignedTre.summary: For a node ξ, the matrix holding every recorded column assigned to ξ in its own index position and zero columns otherwise, implementing Y_ξ in (B.40) to (B.42). No independence or sign is assumed.

Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.complexDi.summary: For a pivot set U and real values p_j, the complex diagonal matrix with entry p_j on U and zero elsewhere: the complex version of diag_U(p) in (B.40). Positivity of the entries is not required.

With complex column matrices $Y',Y$, the residual $B=H-\operatorname{diag}_{\text{pivots}}(p)-Y'Y'^*+YY^*-K$ satisfies $w_l\sum_j(|B_{lj}|+H'_{lj}+K'_{lj})/w_j\le m_l$. The global pivots are precisely the real variables occurring in pivot coordinates, with lower bounds at most $t\sum_l(p_l-m_l)$ over the coordinates containing them. For every column $y$ of $Y$, the real and imaginary parts of $\sqrt tX^*y$ must occur as distinct indexed global columns at this node. Complex forms mean their real Hermitian quadratic values; $|z|$ is componentwise modulus. The statement allows $t=0$, while strict positivity of global pivot bounds is imposed separately. The conclusion is $\langle V_\xi x,x\rangle+\sum_{j\in\mathcal U_\xi}\underline p_{\xi,j}x_j^2-|Y_\xi^{\mathsf T}x|^2\le\langle N_\xi x,x\rangle+\sum_{\xi^{\prime}}\langle V_{\xi^{\prime}}x,x\rangle$ for every real global vector $x$, with the sum over children. Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.ofRealVec.summary: Sends a real vector x to the complex vector with the same entries and zero imaginary parts, before applying z=X_ξx in the node tests after (B.40).

The lower bound comparing the root expression with $N$ is a separate theorem.
Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.pivotCoun.summary: If every coordinate is a pivot somewhere, every assigned pivot bound is positive, the root's passed matrix is nonnegative and negative columns number at most the free coordinates, the root expression is strictly positive on a subspace of dimension at least the number of determined coordinates.

It is diag_U(p) in (B.40). Values outside U are ignored. No positivity of the retained p_j, and no relation to the certified slack, is required by the definition.
Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.pivotDiag.summary: For a pivot set U and real values p_j, the real diagonal matrix with p_j on U and zero off U: diag_U(p) in (B.40). Positivity and relation to the slack are not required.

Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.realColum.text: For a complex coordinate map E, real t and a complex column matrix Y, this produces two real columns for each column y of Y: Re(√t E*y) and Im(√t E*y). These are the columns used in the complex-node alternative after (B.40), because t|y*Ex|² is the sum of their two squared pairings with real x when t≥0. Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.realNodeE.text: Assume the weighted symmetric-matrix error inequality: for a symmetric real matrix $B$ and positive weights $w_i$, the row bounds $w_i\sum_j|B_{ij}|/w_j\le m_i$ imply $|\langle Bx,x\rangle|\le\sum_i m_i x_i^2$ for all real $x$. For each row, $w_i\sum_j(|B_{ij}|+H'_{ij}+K'_{ij})/w_j\le m_i$, where $B=H-\operatorname{diag}_{\mathcal U_\xi}(p)-Y'Y'^T+Y_\xi Y_\xi^T-K$ and the diagonal is zero off the pivots. On each pivot $\underline p_{\xi,j}\le p_j-m_j$. Here $|x|$ means componentwise absolute value. All spaces are finite-dimensional and the forms are real. The positive weights exclude zero denominators. These are assumptions on the supplied node matrices and bounds; they perform no numerical verification themselves. The conclusion is $\langle V_\xi x,x\rangle+\sum_{j\in\mathcal U_\xi}\underline p_{\xi,j}x_j^2-|Y_\xi^{\mathsf T}x|^2\le\langle N_\xi x,x\rangle+\sum_{\xi^{\prime}}\langle V_{\xi^{\prime}}x,x\rangle$ for every real global vector $x$, with the sum over children. Here $Y_\xi$ is the matrix of the global real negative columns at this node. This is (B.42).
