Breakdown.CertReduction.frozenFormBridge.summary: Given the transport identity, a decaying periodic solenoidal $C^1$ reference with $\mathbb S\ge-s_-I$, $L^3$ gradient bound $n$, $s_-/w_*+n/\sqrt{3w_*}\le c'_3$ and standing profile and adjoint assumptions, $Q_{W^{\mathrm r}}(u)\ge-c'_3|u|_w^2$ for symmetric test fields: reference part of Lemma B.9.

Breakdown.CertReduction.gapGradCoeff.text: For positive w*, choose 2/(√3√w*) when a gradient difference is bounded in L³, or cw=(4π√w*)⁻¹ᐟ² when it is bounded in L². These are the two gradient coefficients in the first inequality of (B.48), obtained respectively from the L⁶ Sobolev bound and the L∞ bound in (B.46). The formal function selects one of the two cases by a yes-or-no argument. It does not supply the required norm bound. For nonpositive w*, its square-root and division conventions no longer give the stated analytic constants.
Breakdown.CertReduction.gapGradCoeff.summary: For positive $w^*$, $2/(\sqrt3\sqrt{w^*})$ for an $L^3$-bounded gradient difference or $c_w=(4\pi\sqrt{w^*})^{-1/2}$ for an $L^2$ one, the coefficients in the first inequality of (B.48), from the $L^6$ and $L^\infty$ bounds in (B.46). No norm bound is supplied.

Breakdown.CertReduction.gapGradTermHolds.text:
Let $w_*>0$, $n\ge0$, and let $A(	heta,y)$ be a measurable matrix field. Suppose either $\|A(	heta)\|_{L^2(\mathrm{op})}\le n$ at every time or $\|A(	heta)\|_{L^3(\mathrm{op})}\le n$ at every time. For a perturbation $v$, the formal statement proves $\iint|Av|^2\le c_w^2n^2\|v\|_w^2$ in the first case and $\iint|Av|^2\le4n^2/(3w_*)\,\|v\|_w^2$ in the second, where $c_w=(4\pi\sqrt{w_*})^{-1/2}$. For (B.49), take $A=
abla Z_0$ or $
abla Z_1$. The coefficient is allowed to be a measurable matrix field without an independent assumption that it is the gradient of a function. These are period-integrated estimates; the printed inequalities are first obtained on one time slice. Here $y\in\mathbb R^3$, normalized time is $	heta\in\mathbb R$, and $\mathcal H=L^2((0,1)	imes\mathbb R^3)$. The squared energy is $\|v\|_w^2=\iint(|\Delta v|^2+w_*|
abla v|^2)$, with the Euclidean norm on vectors and the sum of squares of matrix entries on gradients. Integrating over $[0,1]$ in the formal statement gives the same integral as $(0,1)$. A perturbation is a measurable, divergence-free vector field on $\mathbb R	imes\mathbb R^3$, of period one in $	heta$, with spatial weak gradient and Hessian, $v(	heta)\in L^6$ for almost every $	heta$, and $
abla v$, $\Delta v$ and $(1/P)\partial_	heta v+v/2+(y\cdot
abla)v/2$ in $\mathcal H$. Any imposed spatial and temporal symmetries are included in this hypothesis; choosing no symmetries gives the unrestricted class.
Breakdown.CertReduction.gapGradTermHolds.summary: For $w_*>0$, $n\ge0$ and measurable $A$ whose operator norm has $L^2$ norm, or $L^3$ norm, at most $n$ at all times, each perturbation has $\iint|Av|^2\le c_w^2n^2\|v\|_w^2$, or $\le4n^2\|v\|_w^2/(3w_*)$, $c_w=(4\pi\sqrt{w_*})^{-1/2}$. (B.49) uses $A=\nabla Z_0,\nabla Z_1$.

Breakdown.CertReduction.gapSupTermHolds_.text:
Let $w_*>0$ and $s\ge0$. For a perturbation $v$ and any coefficient field $Z$ satisfying $|Z(	heta,y)|\le s$ at every time and point, the formal statement proves $\iint|(Z\cdot
abla)v|^2\le(s^2/w_*)\|v\|_w^2$. No derivative of $Z$ enters this statement. Taking $Z=Z_0+Z_1$ and $s=n_0^\infty+n_1^\infty$ gives the period-integrated transport estimate used after (B.49). Its conclusion includes the conversion from gradient energy to the weighted energy; the paper's first line of (B.49) is a spatial inequality before this conversion. Here $y\in\mathbb R^3$, normalized time is $	heta\in\mathbb R$, and $\mathcal H=L^2((0,1)	imes\mathbb R^3)$. The squared energy is $\|v\|_w^2=\iint(|\Delta v|^2+w_*|
abla v|^2)$, with the Euclidean norm on vectors and the sum of squares of matrix entries on gradients. Integrating over $[0,1]$ in the formal statement gives the same integral as $(0,1)$. A perturbation is a measurable, divergence-free vector field on $\mathbb R	imes\mathbb R^3$, of period one in $	heta$, with spatial weak gradient and Hessian, $v(	heta)\in L^6$ for almost every $	heta$, and $
abla v$, $\Delta v$ and $(1/P)\partial_	heta v+v/2+(y\cdot
abla)v/2$ in $\mathcal H$. Any imposed spatial and temporal symmetries are included in this hypothesis; choosing no symmetries gives the unrestricted class. There is no measurability hypothesis on $Z$ in this statement. Accordingly the displayed left-hand side denotes the nonnegative integral defined also for nonmeasurable inputs; the theorem by itself does not assert Lebesgue integrability of the corresponding transport term. When $Z$ is measurable, as for the profile differences in the application, the finite bound gives the usual integral estimate.
Breakdown.CertReduction.gapSupTermHolds_.summary: For $w_*>0$, $s\ge0$ and any $Z$ with $|Z|\le s$ everywhere, with no measurability assumed, every perturbation has $\iint|(Z\cdot\nabla)v|^2\le(s^2/w_*)\|v\|_w^2$ as a nonnegative integral; for measurable $Z$ this is the usual bound. With $Z=Z_0+Z_1$ it gives the estimate after (B.49).

Breakdown.CertReduction.gapTransferBridg.text:
Let $w_*>0$ be constant. Assume finite decompositions $W^{\mathrm a}_\alpha-W^{\mathrm r}_\alpha=\sum_a Z_a$ and $
abla W^{\mathrm a}_\alpha-
abla W^{\mathrm r}_\alpha=\sum_a A_a$, with separately supplied measurable vector fields $Z_a$ and matrix fields $A_a$. Require $|Z_a|\le s_a$ and an $L^2$ or $L^3$ operator-norm bound $n_a$ for each $A_a$, uniformly in time and in $\alpha\in\mathcal K$. There is no hypothesis $A_a=
abla Z_a$ for each summand; the paper makes this additional identification in its application. Assume the reference is $C^1$, periodic and divergence-free, with weak second derivatives and decay of orders $1,2,3$, and the actual profile is $C^1$ with decay of orders $1,2$. For an $L^2$ term put $b_a=c_w n_a+s_a/\sqrt{w_*}$; for an $L^3$ term put $b_a=2n_a/\sqrt{3w_*}+s_a/\sqrt{w_*}$, where $c_w=(4\pi\sqrt{w_*})^{-1/2}$. If the nonnegative bounds satisfy $\sum_a b_a\le c_{\mathrm r}$, then every perturbation satisfies $\|((W^{\mathrm a}_\alpha-W^{\mathrm r}_\alpha)\cdot
abla)v+(v\cdot
abla)(W^{\mathrm a}_\alpha-W^{\mathrm r}_\alpha)\|_{\mathcal H}^2\le c_{\mathrm r}^2\|v\|_w^2$. The paper uses two terms, with exponents 2 and 3. The formal statement proves this estimate; it does not provide numerical values of the bounds. Here $y\in\mathbb R^3$, normalized time is $	heta\in\mathbb R$, and $\mathcal H=L^2((0,1)	imes\mathbb R^3)$. The squared energy is $\|v\|_w^2=\iint(|\Delta v|^2+w_*|
abla v|^2)$, with the Euclidean norm on vectors and the sum of squares of matrix entries on gradients. Integrating over $[0,1]$ in the formal statement gives the same integral as $(0,1)$. A perturbation is a measurable, divergence-free vector field on $\mathbb R	imes\mathbb R^3$, of period one in $	heta$, with spatial weak gradient and Hessian, $v(	heta)\in L^6$ for almost every $	heta$, and $
abla v$, $\Delta v$ and $(1/P)\partial_	heta v+v/2+(y\cdot
abla)v/2$ in $\mathcal H$. Any imposed spatial and temporal symmetries are included in this hypothesis; choosing no symmetries gives the unrestricted class. The standing certificate assumptions also require every selected adjoint to be jointly almost-everywhere measurable for each $\alpha\in\mathcal K$, although no adjoint occurs in this conclusion.

If $Z=W^{\mathrm a}-W^{\mathrm r}=\sum_aZ_a$, $

Breakdown.CertReduction.shiftGradCoeff.text: For positive w*, the L³ choice is 1/(√3√w*), and the L² choice is cw=(4π√w*)⁻¹ᐟ². These are the gradient coefficients in the last inequality of (B.48). The L³ coefficient is half the one used to bound the linearized-operator difference, because 2√w*‖∇u‖₂‖∆u‖₂≤|u|w². This declaration only chooses the coefficient; it does not assert a bound on a profile difference. Square roots of negative numbers and division by zero are assigned zero, so the intended interpretation requires w*>0.
Breakdown.CertReduction.shiftGradCoeff.summary: For positive $w^*$, $1/(\sqrt3\sqrt{w^*})$ for $L^3$ and $c_w=(4\pi\sqrt{w^*})^{-1/2}$ for $L^2$, the coefficients in the last inequality of (B.48); the $L^3$ one is half that for the operator difference. Negative square roots and division by zero are taken as zero, so $w^*>0$ is needed.

Breakdown.CertReduction.shiftGradTermHol.text:
For $w_*>0$ and $n\ge0$, let $A(y)$ be a measurable matrix field whose operator norm has $L^2$ norm at most $n$, or whose operator norm has $L^3$ norm at most $n$. For every spatial test field $u$, the formal statement proves $\int|Au|\,|\Delta u|\le c_w n|u|_w^2$ in the first case and $\int|Au|\,|\Delta u|\le n|u|_w^2/\sqrt{3w_*}$ in the second, with $c_w=(4\pi\sqrt{w_*})^{-1/2}$. These two alternatives give the contributions of $
abla Z_0$ and $
abla Z_1$ to $c''_3$ in (B.48). The estimate controls the integral of the absolute value, so it also controls the absolute value of the signed integral. The spatial test field is $u\in L^6(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$, divergence-free, with weak gradient in $L^2$, weak second derivatives and $\Delta u\in L^2$. Its squared energy is $|u|_w^2=\int_{\mathbb R^3}(|\Delta u|^2+w_*|
abla u|^2)$. The gradient energy uses the sum of squares of the matrix entries; norms of coefficient matrices below are operator norms. For a fixed symmetry set $\Gamma$, this spatial class also requires $u(Ry)=Ru(y)$ almost everywhere whenever $(R,0)\in\Gamma$. Taking $\Gamma=\varnothing$ removes this restriction.
Breakdown.CertReduction.shiftGradTermHol.summary: For $w_*>0$, $n\ge0$ and measurable $A$ whose operator norm has $L^2$, or $L^3$, norm at most $n$, each spatial test field invariant under the zero-time-shift symmetries has $\int|Au||\Delta u|\le c_wn|u|_w^2$, or $\le n|u|_w^2/\sqrt{3w_*}$: the $\nabla Z_0$, $\nabla Z_1$ parts of $c''_3$ in (B.48).

Breakdown.CertReduction.shiftSupTermHold.text:
For $w_*>0$, $s\ge0$, a spatial test field $u$ and a vector field $Z$ with $|Z(y)|\le s$, the formal statement proves $\int|(Z\cdot
abla)u|\,|\Delta u|\le s|u|_w^2/(2\sqrt{w_*})$. For measurable $Z$, this absolute-integral estimate bounds either sign of the corresponding pairing. It uses $2\sqrt{w_*}\|
abla u\|_2\|\Delta u\|_2\le|u|_w^2$. No smoothness of $Z$ is assumed. In Lemma B.9 it is applied to the change in the advecting profile. The spatial test field is $u\in L^6(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$, divergence-free, with weak gradient in $L^2$, weak second derivatives and $\Delta u\in L^2$. Its squared energy is $|u|_w^2=\int_{\mathbb R^3}(|\Delta u|^2+w_*|
abla u|^2)$. The gradient energy uses the sum of squares of the matrix entries; norms of coefficient matrices below are operator norms. For a fixed symmetry set $\Gamma$, this spatial class also requires $u(Ry)=Ru(y)$ almost everywhere whenever $(R,0)\in\Gamma$. Taking $\Gamma=\varnothing$ removes this restriction. There is no measurability hypothesis on $Z$ in this statement. Accordingly the displayed left-hand side denotes the nonnegative integral defined also for nonmeasurable inputs; the theorem by itself does not assert Lebesgue integrability of the corresponding transport term. When $Z$ is measurable, as for the profile differences in the application, the finite bound gives the usual integral estimate.
Breakdown.CertReduction.shiftSupTermHold.summary: For $w_*>0$, $s\ge0$, a spatial test field $u$ invariant under the zero-time-shift symmetries and any $Z$ with $|Z|\le s$, $\int|(Z\cdot\nabla)u||\Delta u|\le s|u|_w^2/(2\sqrt{w_*})$ as a nonnegative integral; for measurable $Z$ it bounds the pairing. Lemma B.9 applies it to the profile change.

Breakdown.CertificateData.text: These are inputs to an earlier sufficient certificate, with k≥0 real parameters. The fields specify: a set Γ of orthogonal transformations with time shifts; the center and coordinate radii of a parameter box; parameter-dependent periods S, approximate velocities Wᵃ, scalar pressures q, force coefficients βᵃ and target constraint values; k forcing fields bᵢ and k matrix constraint fields Ξᵢ; a real slope matrix, a proposed left inverse and coordinate error bounds; global and ball-restricted residual bounds. Scalar data give a lower weight w*, a spatial weight w(y) and its proposed upper bound, constants c₁,c_B,c₂,c_L for the inverse estimate, a ball radius, a common spatial-decay constant, an upper period, an integer m for a possible half-period symmetry, forcing and frozen-form bounds b*,c₃, a maximum residual δmax, a correction size ε and an upper bound M for the homogeneous H¹ norm. Supplying these fields asserts none of their sign, regularity or inequality conditions. Relative to §§7.2–7.3 of this paper, this is a different, earlier certificate: its parameter set is a translated box, it uses a ball norm instead of the finite directional seminorm (7.17), has force weight ω=1, and has no separate reference profile or adjoint-coordinate conditions (7.32)–(7.37).
Breakdown.CertificateData.summary: Inputs to an earlier sufficient certificate with $k\ge0$ parameters: symmetries, a box, periods, profiles, forcing and constraint fields, slope data, residual bounds and constants. It differs from §§7.2-7.3: a translated box, a ball norm instead of (7.17), $\omega=1$, and no (7.32)-(7.37).

Breakdown.CertificateData.box.text: For real vectors α₀ and ρ in ℝᵏ, the parameter set consists of all α with α₀,ᵢ−ρᵢ≤αᵢ≤α₀,ᵢ+ρᵢ in every coordinate. It is a closed coordinate box. If any radius is negative it is empty; the earlier certificate requires all radii nonnegative. If k=0 it is the single empty vector. This is different from the centered product of intervals and a scaled Euclidean ball in (7.29); it belongs to the earlier certificate version.
Breakdown.CertificateData.box.summary: For $\alpha_0,\rho\in\mathbb R^k$, the closed box of $\alpha$ with $\alpha_{0,i}-\rho_i\le\alpha_i\le\alpha_{0,i}+\rho_i$; it is empty if a radius is negative and a single point if $k=0$. It differs from the product of intervals and scaled ball in (7.29) and belongs to the earlier certificate.

Breakdown.CertificateHypothesis.text:
The formal statement asserts that there exist an integer k≥0 and data satisfying every condition below. It is an existence hypothesis and supplies no numerical values.

This formal statement is a sufficient certificate in an earlier format, different from the certificate now defined in §§7.2–7.3. Its parameter set K is the coordinate box α₀−ρ≤α≤α₀+ρ in ℝᵏ, for an integer k≥0. The set Γ consists of pairs (R,θ₀)∈O(3)×ℝ; Γ-invariance means v(θ+θ₀,Ry)=Rv(θ,y), pointwise for approximate profiles and almost everywhere for perturbations. Conditions involving α hold for every α∈K unless all parameters are explicitly specified. The conditions are the following.

Every radius is nonnegative. The scalar lower weight w* is positive; w(y) is measurable, Γ-invariant, and lies between w* and a finite upper bound. The constants c₁,c_B,c₂,b*,c₃,ε are nonnegative; M and c_L are positive; c₁+c_B≤c_L. The period is continuous on K and 0<S(α)≤Smax. The integer m is 1, or 2 with an orthogonal half-period symmetry in Γ. The maps βᵃ and the target constraint are continuous on K.

Wᵃ is jointly C² in all parameters, normalized time and space, is period one for every parameter, and for α∈K is solenoidal, Γ-invariant, and satisfies |DʲWᵃ|≤C/(1+|y|)ʲ⁺¹ for j=0,1,2. These spatial derivative norms are operator norms and C is one common constant. The chosen pressure is C¹ and period one. Each forcing field bᵢ is measurable, period one, Γ-invariant almost everywhere, and ∑ᵢ‖bᵢ‖²𝓗≤b*². Each Ξᵢ is jointly measurable up to null sets and square integrable over [0,1]×ℝ³. No periodicity of Ξᵢ is required outside this interval, whose restriction suffices to define the constraint. Here 𝓗=L²((0,1)×ℝ³), ℓᵢ(v)=⟨∇v,Ξᵢ⟩𝓗 and E=∫₀¹∫(|Δv|²+w|∇v|²).

A weak perturbation is represented by v,g:ℝ×ℝ³→ℝ³, a linear-map field G and a bilinear-map field H, all jointly measurable up to null sets and pointwise period one in θ. For almost every θ, v,G,H are locally integrable in space, G=∇v and H(a,eⱼ)=∂ₐ(Geⱼ) distributionally, div v=tr G=0 almost everywhere, and v(θ)∈L⁶(ℝ³). Require G, tr H and g in 𝓗, with the Frobenius norm for G and tr H=∑ⱼH(eⱼ,eⱼ). Against every compactly supported smooth vector test on ℝ×ℝ³, g represents S⁻¹∂θv+½v+½(y·∇)v. For each (R,θ₀)∈Γ require v(θ+θ₀,Ry)=Rv(θ,y) almost everywhere in space and time. This specifies representatives and their distributional identities; it does not require the chosen v to be continuous in time. In these certificate conditions S>0. Put 𝓣ˢv=g−tr H. For a reference P, the equation F≃𝓣ˢv+(P·∇)v+(v·∇)P+∑ᵢβᵢbᵢ means that, for every compactly supported smooth solenoidal test φ, ∫F·φ=∫[(g+GP+(DP)v+∑ᵢβᵢbᵢ)·φ+G:∇φ], integrated over ℝ×ℝ³. Here F is jointly measurable up to a null set, pointwise period one and in 𝓗; F is not required to be solenoidal or Γ-invariant.

For every such perturbation, every β∈ℝᵏ and every such right-hand side F with P=Wᵃ, √(E+|β|²)≤c₁‖F‖𝓗+c_B‖F‖L²((0,1)×B_R)+c₂|ℓ(v)|. For the frozen-time estimates, a spatial test field is represented by u,Gᵤ,Hᵤ with locally integrable weak derivatives Gᵤ=∇u and Hᵤ(a,eⱼ)=∂ₐ(Gᵤeⱼ), div u=0, u∈L⁶(ℝ³), and Gᵤ,tr Hᵤ∈L²(ℝ³). It obeys u(Ry)=Ru(y) almost everywhere for each (R,0)∈Γ. Write |u|²w=∫ℝ³(|tr Hᵤ|²+w|Gᵤ|²), with the Frobenius norm for Gᵤ. All unlabelled space integrals use Lebesgue measure. The formal ball is {y∈ℝ³:|y|≤R}, with the supplied real radius R. It is empty when R<0 and is {0} when R=0; its Lebesgue L² norm equals that over the corresponding open ball. At every normalized time θ, the frozen-time form ∫(|Δu|²+¼|∇u|²)−∫[(Wᵃ·∇)u+(u·∇)Wᵃ]·Δu is bounded below by −c₃|u|²w for every admissible spatial solenoidal u and the zero-time-shift symmetries.

The residual Fᵃ=S⁻¹∂θWᵃ+½Wᵃ+½y·∇Wᵃ−ΔWᵃ+(Wᵃ·∇)Wᵃ+∑βᵢᵃbᵢ+∇q has nonnegative bounds δ,δB on its global and ball norms, with δ≤δmax. These obey c₁δ+c_BδB+c₂|target−ℓ(Wᵃ)|≤ε. With c_w=(4π√w*)⁻¹ᐟ² and L=Smax/m, the three size conditions are 2c_Lc_wM<1, 4ε²(1/w*+2Lc₃+2Lb*+2L/c_L)≤M², and 4(1/w*+2Lc₃)ε²+4Lε(δmax+2c_wεM+2b*ε)≤M².

A matrix B and a proposed inverse A obey AB=I. The coordinate bounds |βⱼᵃ(α)−(B(α−α₀))ⱼ|≤oⱼ and ∑ⱼ|Aᵢⱼ|(2ε+oⱼ)≤ρᵢ keep the parameter correction in the box. Finally 4ε²/w*<‖∇Wᵃ‖²𝓗 for every α∈K prevents a zero corrected profile. Compared with the printed certificate, there are stronger C² and Hessian-decay hypotheses, the force weight is one, and the ball norm and slope-inverse conditions replace the row and adjoint construction. The formal choice m=1 remains allowed even if Γ contains a half-period symmetry; (7.6) instead assigns m=2 in that case. Using m=1 doubles the factor Smax/m in the two corresponding size conditions. These conditions do not assert that any numerical data satisfying them have been supplied.
Breakdown.CertificateHypothesis.summary: There exist $k\ge0$ and data satisfying all conditions of the earlier certificate; no values are supplied. Unlike §§7.2–7.3 it uses a coordinate box, a $C^2$ profile with Hessian decay, force weight one, a ball-restricted forcing norm and a slope-inverse inclusion in place of rows and adjoints.

Breakdown.Coercive.Internal.TestDensityP.text: For every smooth field $\varphi:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ and every $y\in\mathbb R^3$, the formal statement proves $-\Delta\varphi(y)=\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}\varphi(y)-\nabla\operatorname{div}\varphi(y)$. No decay, support, periodicity or solenoidality is required. For a divergence-free field the last term vanishes, giving the diffusion term in (C.1) and (C.2). The smoothness hypothesis makes each differential operation a classical derivative. The theorem is a pointwise vector-calculus identity and does not assert that any candidate solves the equation.
Breakdown.Coercive.Internal.TestDensityP.summary: For every smooth $\varphi:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$, $-\Delta\varphi=\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}\varphi-\nabla\operatorname{div}\varphi$ pointwise, with no decay, support or solenoidality assumption. For divergence-free fields this gives the diffusion term in (C.1) and (C.2).

Breakdown.Coercive.IsSmoothApproximation.text: Fix supplied fields v,g:ℝ×ℝ³→ℝ³, a linear-map field G and a bilinear-map field H, a real period S, and a sequence uₙ indexed by n=0,1,2,… . The approximation condition requires every uₙ to be jointly C∞, pointwise period one and solenoidal, with every time slice in L⁶; uₙ/(1+|y|), ∂θuₙ/(1+|y|), every positive integer spatial derivative of uₙ and of ∂θuₙ, and every nonnegative integer spatial derivative of S⁻¹∂θuₙ+½uₙ+½(y·∇)uₙ must be in L²([0,1]×ℝ³). As n→∞, the period integrals of |∇uₙ−G|², |∇²uₙ−H|², |uₙ−v|²/(1+|y|)² and |S⁻¹∂θuₙ+½uₙ+½(y·∇)uₙ−g|² must tend to zero. Matrix and Hessian differences use Frobenius norms; the higher derivative finiteness conditions use multilinear operator norms. This is the approximation required in the proof of Proposition B.1. The formal definition tests a supplied sequence; it does not assert that such a sequence exists, or that the limit fields are derivatives. Convergence is stated for nonnegative extended integrals and therefore also requires eventual smallness and finiteness. The approximants are not required to retain Γ symmetry. At S=0 its reciprocal is assigned zero.
Breakdown.Coercive.IsSmoothApproximation.summary:
Each $u_n$ is in the smooth periodic solenoidal class, and the period integrals of $|
abla u_n-G|^2$, $|
abla^2u_n-H|^2$, $|u_n-v|^2/(1+|y|)^2$ and $|S^{-1}\partial_	heta u_n+	frac12u_n+	frac12(y\cdot
abla)u_n-g|^2$ tend to zero, as in the proof of Proposition B.1. Existence is not asserted.

Breakdown.Coercive.IsSmoothPerturbation.text: The field u(θ,y) is jointly C∞ on ℝ×ℝ³, has period one, is pointwise solenoidal, and u(θ)∈L⁶(ℝ³) for every θ. Over [0,1]×ℝ³, both u/(1+|y|) and ∂θu/(1+|y|) are square integrable. Every positive integer spatial derivative of u and of ∂θu is square integrable. Every nonnegative integer spatial derivative, including order zero, of gᵤ=S⁻¹∂θu+½u+½(y·∇)u is square integrable. This is the class used to justify integrations by parts and passage to the perturbation domain in the proof of Proposition B.1. The derivative norms in the higher-order conditions are operator norms of multilinear derivatives. No spatial symmetry Γ is required here, and neither u nor ∂θu is required to be in unweighted L². The period S is arbitrary in this definition; S>0 is imposed in applications, and S⁻¹ has value zero if S=0. The formal condition is an auxiliary approximation class, rather than the assertion that every perturbation already has this regularity.
Breakdown.Coercive.IsSmoothPerturbation.summary: $u$ is $C^\infty$, period one, solenoidal and $L^6$ per slice, with $u/(1+|y|)$, $\partial_\theta u/(1+|y|)$, positive-order derivatives of $u,\partial_\theta u$ and all derivatives of $S^{-1}\partial_\theta u+\tfrac12u+\tfrac12(y\cdot\nabla)u$ in $L^2$: the approximation class of Proposition B.1.

Breakdown.Coercive.IsSplitLowerBound.text: Let X be real; let Pι(θ,y), Rι(θ,y), B(θ,y) and J(θ,y) be real densities, with ι∈ℤ². Write a⁺=max(a,0) and integrate over [0,1]×ℝ³. The formal condition is ∫(∑ι(−Rι)⁺+(−B)⁺)<∞ together with ∫(∑ιPι⁺+∑ιRι⁺+B⁺+J⁺)+(−X)⁺≤X⁺+∫(∑ι(−Rι)⁺+(−B)⁺+(−J)⁺). The sums and integrals are nonnegative extended real quantities. This records the intermediate splitting used in the proof of Proposition B.1 before the losses are absorbed into (B.16). If the densities are measurable, both displayed positive and negative integrals are finite, and Pι≥0, it says ∫(∑ιPι+∑ιRι+B+J)≤X. The formal condition alone does not require ∫(−J)⁺ finite, so that signed-integral reformulation cannot be made unconditionally. This is a definition of a hypothesis, not a proved estimate.
Breakdown.Coercive.IsSplitLowerBound.summary: With $a^+=\max(a,0)$, finiteness of $\int(\sum_\iota(-R_\iota)^++(-B)^+)$ and a bound of positive parts by $X^+$ plus negative parts, the splitting used in Proposition B.1 before absorption into (B.16). It gives $\int(\sum P+\sum R+B+J)\le X$ only if $\int(-J)^+$ is also finite.

Breakdown.Coercive.SmoothApproximationHo.text: The formal statement defines the following assertion for every symmetry set Γ, real S and perturbation in 𝓓ˢΓ. Here a perturbation is given by v,g:ℝ×ℝ³→ℝ³, a field G of linear maps and a field H of bilinear maps. All four are jointly measurable up to null sets and pointwise period one. For almost every θ, v(θ),G(θ),H(θ) are locally integrable in space, G=∇v and H(a,eⱼ)=∂ₐ(Geⱼ) distributionally, div v=tr G=0 almost everywhere, and v(θ)∈L⁶(ℝ³). Require G, tr H and g in L²([0,1]×ℝ³), where tr H=∑ⱼH(eⱼ,eⱼ) and the size of G is Frobenius. The identity g=S⁻¹∂θv+½v+½(y·∇)v is tested against every compactly supported C∞ vector field on ℝ×ℝ³. For the supplied set Γ of pairs (R,θ₀), with R orthogonal and θ₀ real, require v(θ+θ₀,Ry)=Rv(θ,y) almost everywhere for each pair. These conditions represent 𝓓ˢΓ when S>0; the formal conditions themselves admit every real S, with S⁻¹=0 at S=0, and do not select the continuous-in-time representative chosen in §7.1. Fix supplied fields v,g:ℝ×ℝ³→ℝ³, a linear-map field G and a bilinear-map field H, a real period S, and a sequence uₙ indexed by n=0,1,2,… . The approximation condition requires every uₙ to be jointly C∞, pointwise period one and solenoidal, with every time slice in L⁶; uₙ/(1+|y|), ∂θuₙ/(1+|y|), every positive integer spatial derivative of uₙ and of ∂θuₙ, and every nonnegative integer spatial derivative of S⁻¹∂θuₙ+½uₙ+½(y·∇)uₙ must be in L²([0,1]×ℝ³). As n→∞, the period integrals of |∇uₙ−G|², |∇²uₙ−H|², |uₙ−v|²/(1+|y|)² and |S⁻¹∂θuₙ+½uₙ+½(y·∇)uₙ−g|² must tend to zero. Matrix and Hessian differences use Frobenius norms; the higher derivative finiteness conditions use multilinear operator norms. The assertion is that such a sequence exists for each perturbation. It is the approximation step used in the proof of Proposition B.1; this declaration names the proposition and is not itself its proof. The hypotheses require only the trace of H in L², while the conclusion approximates the entire Hessian in L². That is a substantive elliptic consequence in the approximation argument. No Γ symmetry is required of the approximating sequence; S>0 is not a hypothesis of this general assertion.
Breakdown.Coercive.SmoothApproximationHo.summary: The assertion that every perturbation in $\mathcal D^S_\Gamma$ has a sequence of smooth approximants converging in the stated norms, the approximation step in the proof of Proposition B.1; it is named, not proved. Only $\mathrm{tr}\,H\in L^2$ is assumed while the whole Hessian is approximated.

Breakdown.Coercive.baseDensity.text: For a class of modes, let D(y),Z(y) be its two conversion weights on ℝ³, w(y) the energy weight, and c a real constant. On five real arguments x₂,x_c,x₁,x_ω,x₀ the expression is (D−c)x₂²+(1−D)x_c²+(¼−Z)x_ω²+(Z−‖∇²D‖op−cw)x₁²−‖∇²Z‖op x₀². The intended arguments are |∇²v̂|, |∇curl v̂|, |∇v̂|, |curl v̂| and |v̂| for a Fourier mode v̂ of the perturbation. This is the part of (B.16) before adding the contributions of the curl and velocity pieces, which include positive frequency terms as well as subtracted shares and losses, with c replacing 3/50. The Hessian sizes of D and Z are operator norms. The definition requires neither C² weights nor nonnegative arguments. The Hessian is formed by differentiating the ordinary derivative; each derivative operation has value zero where its own differentiability condition fails. The definition asserts no lower bound.
Breakdown.Coercive.baseDensity.summary: For a class with weights $D,Z$, energy weight $w$ and constant $c$, $(D-c)x_2^2+(1-D)x_c^2+(\tfrac14-Z)x_\omega^2+(Z-\|\nabla^2D\|_{\mathrm{op}}-cw)x_1^2-\|\nabla^2Z\|_{\mathrm{op}}x_0^2$, the part of (B.16) before all piece contributions, with $c$ replacing $3/50$. No lower bound is asserted.

Breakdown.Coercive.curlWeightIdentityDec.text: Let φ:ℝ³→ℝ be C², with (1+|y|)^j|∇^jφ(y)| uniformly bounded for j=0,1,2. Let u:ℝ³→ℝ³ be C² and divergence-free, with ∇u∈L² and u/(1+|y|)∈L². The theorem proves ∫φ|curl u|²=∫φ|∇u|²−∫∑_{i,j}(∂_{ij}φ)u_i u_j. Thus ∫φ(|∇u|²−|curl u|²)=∫∇²φ[u,u], with the sign used in B.2. The assumptions justify the whole-space integrations by parts. Applying this identity to complex modes requires its real and imaginary parts; the tensor-derivative application for D is another use of the same spatial identity.
Breakdown.Coercive.curlWeightIdentityDec.summary:
For $C^2$ scalar $\varphi$ with $(1+|y|)^j|
abla^j\varphi|$ bounded for $j\le2$, and $C^2$ divergence-free $u$ with $
abla u\in L^2$, $u/(1+|y|)\in L^2$: $\int\varphi|\operatorname{curl}u|^2=\int\varphi|
abla u|^2-\int\sum_{i,j}(\partial_{ij}\varphi)u_iu_j$, with the sign used in B.2.

Breakdown.Coercive.edgeSum.text: For a finite reference harmonic set H and a one-sided mode set T, define E_T(A,b;ι) as follows. If ι∈T, it is ∑_{α∈H, ι−α∉T}Aα b_{ι−α}. Otherwise, if −ι∈T, it is ∑_{α∈H, −ι−α∉T}Aα b_{ι+α}; otherwise it is zero. The first branch takes precedence if T meets −T. This is the finite coupling sum used when estimating the commutators in the proof of Proposition B.1. It retains only translations that leave the selected one-sided piece. In applications the strictly positive frequency condition makes T and −T disjoint. The definition itself requires neither this disjointness nor nonnegative A,b, and it does not assert any bound. Its indices are raw time and angular frequencies; the paper's ι corresponds to (2ι₂−ι₁,ϰι₁).
Breakdown.Coercive.edgeSum.summary: The coupling sum $E_T(A,b;\iota)$: $\sum_{\alpha\in H,\,\iota-\alpha\notin T}A_\alpha b_{\iota-\alpha}$ if $\iota\in T$, the reflected sum if $-\iota\in T$, else zero, keeping translations that leave the piece, as in the commutator estimates of Proposition B.1. $T,-T$ need not be disjoint.

Breakdown.Coercive.frameSpeedSup.text: For a reference field W, a real angular rate a, and y∈ℝ³, the expression takes the real supremum of |W(θ,Rφy)+½Rφy−a e₃×Rφy| over every real time θ and angle φ. It is the quantity bounded by the corresponding supplied function in the piece estimates of Appendix B.2. There is no periodicity or boundedness assumption in this definition. A real supremum is assigned zero when the set is unbounded above; it cannot then be read as a finite bound. Regularity of W and the pointwise estimates used in Proposition B.1 are separate requirements.
Breakdown.Coercive.frameSpeedSup.summary: The real supremum over $\theta,\varphi$ of $|W(\theta,R_\varphi y)+\tfrac12R_\varphi y-a\,e_3\times R_\varphi y|$, the quantity bounded in the piece estimates of Appendix B.2. An unbounded supremum is assigned zero, so it is then no finite bound.

Breakdown.Coercive.gradAmp.text: For a supplied field G of real linear maps ℝ³→ℝ³, this expression is the square root of the sum of the squared absolute values of the nine complex components of Ĝ. Here θ∈ℝ is normalized time, y∈ℝ³, and Rφ is rotation through φ about the third axis. The raw mode (n,k) averages the tensor at (θ+τ,Rφy) against exp(−i(2πnτ+kφ))/(2π) over 0≤τ≤1 and 0≤φ≤2π. Vector outputs are rotated back by R₋φ; each derivative input is the rotated standard basis vector Rφeⱼ. Thus v gives three complex components, a supplied linear map G gives nine, and a supplied bilinear map H gives 27. This is (B.12) with raw frequencies (n,k)=(2ι₂−ι₁,ϰι₁) for the paper's label ι. Each component integral is assigned zero if it is not integrable. When G=∇v and differentiation commutes with the Fourier projection, this is |∇v̂| in (B.16). The definition imposes no derivative identity or integrability. It returns a nonnegative real number. The tensor sizes are Euclidean component norms; they are Frobenius norms for the arrays with two or three indices.
Breakdown.Coercive.gradAmp.summary: For a field $G$ of linear maps, the Frobenius norm of the nine complex components of its rotating-frame Fourier mode $\hat G$ from (B.12); for $G=\nabla v$, when differentiation commutes with the projection, it is $|\nabla\hat v|$ in (B.16). Nonintegrable integrals are taken as zero.

Breakdown.Coercive.modeVals.text: Here θ∈ℝ is normalized time, y∈ℝ³, and Rφ is rotation through φ about the third axis. The raw mode (n,k) averages the tensor at (θ+τ,Rφy) against exp(−i(2πnτ+kφ))/(2π) over 0≤τ≤1 and 0≤φ≤2π. Vector outputs are rotated back by R₋φ; each derivative input is the rotated standard basis vector Rφeⱼ. Thus v gives three complex components, a supplied linear map G gives nine, and a supplied bilinear map H gives 27. This is (B.12) with raw frequencies (n,k)=(2ι₂−ι₁,ϰι₁) for the paper's label ι. Each component integral is assigned zero if it is not integrable. Given v and proposed derivatives G,H, a real function f of five real variables is evaluated at (|Ĥ|,|curl Ĥ|,|Ĝ|,|curl Ĝ|,|v̂|), where the first curl contraction gives the gradient of vorticity if H=∇²v. Thus the derivative orders are Hessian, gradient of vorticity, gradient, vorticity, velocity. These are the five amplitudes in (B.16). In this argument list the gradient precedes vorticity, whereas (B.16) prints the vorticity term before the gradient term. Substituting the quadratic density uses the corresponding coefficients in their assigned argument positions. The formal statement is an evaluation rule for arbitrary f; it does not prove the derivative identifications, convergence of the Fourier integrals or positivity of the result.
Breakdown.Coercive.modeVals.summary: Evaluates a real function at (|Ĥ|,|curl Ĥ|,|Ĝ|,|curl Ĝ|,|v̂|). These are the five amplitudes in (B.16), with gradient preceding vorticity in the argument list; the paper prints those two terms in the opposite order.

Breakdown.Coercive.pieceBlock.text: At (θ,y), write Vι=|v̂ι|, Aι=|Ĝι|, Oι=|curl Ĝι| and Cι=|curl Ĥι| for the Euclidean component amplitudes in the rotating-frame Fourier expansion. For a mode set T put N(b)=(∑_{ι∈T∪(−T)}bι²)¹ᐟ². This uses a real sum, assigned zero if nonsummable. Let U be the real supremum of |W(τ,Rφy)+½Rφy−νe₃×Rφy|, let Q be the real supremum of |curl W(τ,Rφy)|, and let Q₁ be the real supremum of ‖∇curl W(τ,Rφy)‖op, over τ,φ∈ℝ. An unbounded real supremum has default value zero. Sum −(λU+|∇λ|)N(C)N(O)−λ(½Q+|ν|)N(O)²−λQ₁N(V)N(O)−λQN(A)N(O) over the finite curl pieces, and −(μU+|∇μ|)N(A)N(V)−μ|ν|N(V)² over the finite velocity pieces. Each N and U uses that piece's mode set and angular rate. The expression is the sum of whole-piece losses in the derivation of Proposition B.1. Unlike (B.16), it still contains products of norms over several modes. No estimate or summability conclusion is asserted; the admissibility hypotheses are needed before these formulas have their intended analytic meaning.
Breakdown.Coercive.pieceBlock.summary: The sum of whole-piece losses in the derivation of Proposition B.1 over the curl and velocity pieces, built from piece norms $N(\cdot)$ and real suprema $U,Q,Q_1$, unbounded suprema and nonsummable sums being zero. Unlike (B.16) it still has products of norms over several modes.

Breakdown.Coercive.pieceEpsBlock.text: At (θ,y), write Vι=|v̂ι|, Aι=|Ĝι|, Oι=|curl Ĝι| and Cι=|curl Ĥι| for the Euclidean component amplitudes in the rotating-frame Fourier expansion. For a mode set T put N(b)=(∑_{ι∈T∪(−T)}bι²)¹ᐟ². This uses a real sum, assigned zero if nonsummable. Let U be the real supremum of |W(τ,Rφy)+½Rφy−νe₃×Rφy|, let Q be the real supremum of |curl W(τ,Rφy)|, and let Q₁ be the real supremum of ‖∇curl W(τ,Rφy)‖op, over τ,φ∈ℝ. An unbounded real supremum has default value zero. For one curl piece (T,λ,ν), the expression is −(λU+|∇λ|)N(C)N(O)−λ(½Q+|ν|)N(O)²−λQ₁N(V)N(O)−λQN(A)N(O). It collects the terms on a whole mode piece before Young's inequalities distribute them among the coefficients in (B.16). All weights and bounds are evaluated at y. With λ≥0 the displayed algebraic expression is nonpositive, including its default-value cases. Interpreting it as an analytic loss requires convergence of the Fourier square sums and finite suprema. Admissibility bounds the reference suprema; it alone places no summability condition on the arbitrary perturbation fields in this definition. The identities G=∇v,H=∇²v are also separate. The raw mode of the formal expansion is (2ι₂−ι₁,ϰι₁) in the paper's notation.
Breakdown.Coercive.pieceEpsBlock.summary: For one curl piece, $-(\lambda U+|\nabla\lambda|)N(C)N(O)-\lambda(\tfrac12Q+|\nu|)N(O)^2-\lambda Q_1N(V)N(O)-\lambda QN(A)N(O)$, the whole-piece terms before Young's inequalities in (B.16). With $\lambda\ge0$ it is nonpositive; the analytic reading needs convergent sums and finite suprema.

Breakdown.Coercive.pieceEpsPos.text: Here θ∈ℝ is normalized time, y∈ℝ³, and Rφ is rotation through φ about the third axis. The raw mode (n,k) averages the tensor at (θ+τ,Rφy) against exp(−i(2πnτ+kφ))/(2π) over 0≤τ≤1 and 0≤φ≤2π. Vector outputs are rotated back by R₋φ; each derivative input is the rotated standard basis vector Rφeⱼ. Thus v gives three complex components, a supplied linear map G gives nine, and a supplied bilinear map H gives 27. This is (B.12) with raw frequencies (n,k)=(2ι₂−ι₁,ϰι₁) for the paper's label ι. Each component integral is assigned zero if it is not integrable. For one curl piece p with weight λₚ(y), angular rate νₚ and mode set Tₚ, define χₚ(ι)=1 if ι∈Tₚ∪(−Tₚ), and zero otherwise. The contribution is χₚ λₚ |Ωₚ| |curl Ĝι|², where Ωₚ=2πn/S+νₚk. This is the positive curl term obtained from (B.14)–(B.15) before estimating commutators. It is nonnegative when λₚ≥0, an admissibility hypothesis absent from this bare definition. No identification G=∇v or positivity of S is imposed here; at S=0 its reciprocal is zero.
Breakdown.Coercive.pieceEpsPos.summary: For a curl piece, $\chi_p\lambda_p|\Omega_p||\mathrm{curl}\,\hat G_\iota|^2$ with $\Omega_p=2\pi n/S+\nu_pk$, the positive curl term from (B.14)-(B.15) before the commutator estimates. It is nonnegative when $\lambda_p\ge0$, which is not imposed; at $S=0$ the reciprocal is zero.

Breakdown.Coercive.pieceEpsRestMode.text: For a finite reference harmonic set H and a one-sided mode set T, define E_T(A,b;ι) as follows. If ι∈T, it is ∑_{α∈H, ι−α∉T}Aα b_{ι−α}. Otherwise, if −ι∈T, it is ∑_{α∈H, −ι−α∉T}Aα b_{ι+α}; otherwise it is zero. The first branch takes precedence if T meets −T. Here θ∈ℝ is normalized time, y∈ℝ³, and Rφ is rotation through φ about the third axis. The raw mode (n,k) averages the tensor at (θ+τ,Rφy) against exp(−i(2πnτ+kφ))/(2π) over 0≤τ≤1 and 0≤φ≤2π. Vector outputs are rotated back by R₋φ; each derivative input is the rotated standard basis vector Rφeⱼ. Thus v gives three complex components, a supplied linear map G gives nine, and a supplied bilinear map H gives 27. This is (B.12) with raw frequencies (n,k)=(2ι₂−ι₁,ϰι₁) for the paper's label ι. Each component integral is assigned zero if it is not integrable. For a curl piece with weight λ and mode set T, write Vι=|v̂ι|, Aι=|Ĝι|, Oι=|curl Ĝι| and Cι=|curl Ĥι|. For the reference W use superscript W and its ordinary spatial derivatives. The loss is −λ Oι[E_T(Vᵂ,C;ι)+E_T(Aᵂ,O;ι)+E_T(Cᵂ,V;ι)+E_T(Oᵂ,A;ι)]. It is the cross-boundary curl coupling in the proof of Proposition B.1, before the pointwise bounds in (B.16) are applied. The definition alone supplies no regularity for W, no weak derivative identities for v,G,H and no sign of λ. Under the intended nonnegative weights and amplitudes, this term is nonpositive.
Breakdown.Coercive.pieceEpsRestMode.summary: For a curl piece, $-\lambda O_\iota[E_T(V^W,C;\iota)+E_T(A^W,O;\iota)+E_T(C^W,V;\iota)+E_T(O^W,A;\iota)]$, the cross-boundary curl coupling in Proposition B.1 before (B.16). No regularity, derivative identity or sign of $\lambda$ is supplied; with nonnegative weights it is nonpositive.

Breakdown.Coercive.pieceMuBlock.text: At (θ,y), write Vι=|v̂ι|, Aι=|Ĝι|, Oι=|curl Ĝι| and Cι=|curl Ĥι| for the Euclidean component amplitudes in the rotating-frame Fourier expansion. For a mode set T put N(b)=(∑_{ι∈T∪(−T)}bι²)¹ᐟ². This uses a real sum, assigned zero if nonsummable. For a velocity piece (T,μ,ν), let U(y)=sup_{τ,φ}|W(τ,Rφy)+½Rφy−νe₃×Rφy|. The scalar is −(μU+|∇μ|)N(A)N(V)−μ|ν|N(V)². It is the whole-piece velocity loss before the coefficient estimates of (B.16). Nonnegativity of μ makes it nonpositive once the Fourier sums converge and the speed is bounded. These are assumptions of the surrounding analytic argument, absent from the definition. The real supremum is assigned zero if unbounded, and the derivative of μ is assigned zero where differentiability fails. The raw frequencies are related to the paper by (n,k)=(2ι₂−ι₁,ϰι₁).
Breakdown.Coercive.pieceMuBlock.summary:
For a velocity piece $(T,\mu,
u)$, $-(\mu U+|
abla\mu|)N(A)N(V)-\mu|
u|N(V)^2$ with $U$ the rotating-frame speed supremum, the whole-piece loss before (B.16). It is nonpositive for $\mu\ge0$ once sums converge and $U$ is finite; unbounded suprema are taken as zero.

Breakdown.Coercive.pieceMuPos.text: Here θ∈ℝ is normalized time, y∈ℝ³, and Rφ is rotation through φ about the third axis. The raw mode (n,k) averages the tensor at (θ+τ,Rφy) against exp(−i(2πnτ+kφ))/(2π) over 0≤τ≤1 and 0≤φ≤2π. Vector outputs are rotated back by R₋φ; each derivative input is the rotated standard basis vector Rφeⱼ. Thus v gives three complex components, a supplied linear map G gives nine, and a supplied bilinear map H gives 27. This is (B.12) with raw frequencies (n,k)=(2ι₂−ι₁,ϰι₁) for the paper's label ι. Each component integral is assigned zero if it is not integrable. For a velocity piece p with weight μₚ(y), mode set Tₚ and angular rate νₚ, put χₚ(ι)=1_{ι∈Tₚ∪(−Tₚ)} and Ωₚ=2πn/S+νₚk. The expression is χₚ(1−cμ)μₚ|Ωₚ||v̂ι|². The fraction cμ is retained for the multiplier seminorm; this is the remaining positive velocity term in the derivation of (B.16). Nonnegativity uses μₚ≥0 and cμ≤1, neither imposed by the definition. Period positivity and convergence of the Fourier integrals are also separate. Division by S=0 has value zero.
Breakdown.Coercive.pieceMuPos.summary: For a velocity piece, $\chi_p(1-c_\mu)\mu_p|\Omega_p||\hat v_\iota|^2$ with $\Omega_p=2\pi n/S+\nu_pk$, the remaining positive velocity term in the derivation of (B.16). Nonnegativity needs $\mu_p\ge0$ and $c_\mu\le1$, which are not imposed; division by $S=0$ gives zero.

Breakdown.Coercive.pieceMuRestMode.text: For a finite reference harmonic set H and a one-sided mode set T, define E_T(A,b;ι) as follows. If ι∈T, it is ∑_{α∈H, ι−α∉T}Aα b_{ι−α}. Otherwise, if −ι∈T, it is ∑_{α∈H, −ι−α∉T}Aα b_{ι+α}; otherwise it is zero. The first branch takes precedence if T meets −T. Here θ∈ℝ is normalized time, y∈ℝ³, and Rφ is rotation through φ about the third axis. The raw mode (n,k) averages the tensor at (θ+τ,Rφy) against exp(−i(2πnτ+kφ))/(2π) over 0≤τ≤1 and 0≤φ≤2π. Vector outputs are rotated back by R₋φ; each derivative input is the rotated standard basis vector Rφeⱼ. Thus v gives three complex components, a supplied linear map G gives nine, and a supplied bilinear map H gives 27. This is (B.12) with raw frequencies (n,k)=(2ι₂−ι₁,ϰι₁) for the paper's label ι. Each component integral is assigned zero if it is not integrable. For one velocity piece with weight μ, mode set T and balancing constant η, write Vι=|v̂ι|, Aι=|Ĝι|, Vᵂα=|Ŵα| and Aᵂα=|∇Ŵα|. With χι=1_{ι∈T∪(−T)}, the expression is −μVιE_T(Vᵂ,A;ι)−χι[(∑_{α∈H}AᵂαV_{ι−α})²/(2η)+ημ²Vι²/2]. These are the velocity commutator and stretching losses estimated in the proof of Proposition B.1. This definition imposes no derivative identities or sign assumptions. The applications require η>0 and μ≥0; without η>0 the displayed Young-inequality interpretation fails, and at η=0 the division term is defined to be zero.
Breakdown.Coercive.pieceMuRestMode.summary: For a velocity piece, $-\mu V_\iota E_T(V^W,A;\iota)-\chi_\iota[(\sum_{\alpha\in H}A^W_\alpha V_{\iota-\alpha})^2/(2\eta)+\eta\mu^2V_\iota^2/2]$, the velocity commutator and stretching losses in Proposition B.1. Applications need $\eta>0$, $\mu\ge0$; at $\eta=0$ the division term is zero.

Breakdown.Coercive.pieceNorm.text: For T⊂ℤ² and a real amplitude sequence bι, the expression is N_T(b)=(∑ι1_{ι∈T or −ι∈T}bι²)¹ᐟ². Modes in T∩(−T) are counted once. This is the ℓ² amplitude on the symmetric piece used in the estimates leading to (B.16). The sum is a real infinite sum: if the sequence is not summable, its formal value is zero, and so is N_T. It is therefore an actual ℓ² norm only after square summability has been established. The definition imposes no finiteness, sign or symmetry condition on T or b.
Breakdown.Coercive.pieceNorm.summary: For $T\subset\mathbb Z^2$, $N_T(b)=(\sum_\iota1_{\iota\in T\text{ or }-\iota\in T}b_\iota^2)^{1/2}$, the $\ell^2$ amplitude on the symmetric piece in the estimates for (B.16), counting $T\cap(-T)$ once. A nonsummable sum is taken as zero, so it is an $\ell^2$ norm only after summability.

Breakdown.Coercive.piecePos.text: Here θ∈ℝ is normalized time, y∈ℝ³, and Rφ is rotation through φ about the third axis. The raw mode (n,k) averages the tensor at (θ+τ,Rφy) against exp(−i(2πnτ+kφ))/(2π) over 0≤τ≤1 and 0≤φ≤2π. Vector outputs are rotated back by R₋φ; each derivative input is the rotated standard basis vector Rφeⱼ. Thus v gives three complex components, a supplied linear map G gives nine, and a supplied bilinear map H gives 27. This is (B.12) with raw frequencies (n,k)=(2ι₂−ι₁,ϰι₁) for the paper's label ι. Each component integral is assigned zero if it is not integrable. For finitely many curl and velocity pieces, let χₚ(ι)=1_{ι∈Tₚ∪(−Tₚ)} and Ωₚ=2πn/S+νₚk. The expression is ∑_{curl p}χₚλₚ|Ωₚ||curl Ĝι|²+∑_{velocity p}χₚ(1−cμ)μₚ|Ωₚ||v̂ι|². It collects the positive terms in the proof of Proposition B.1 before the other piece contributions are subtracted. It is nonnegative under λₚ,μₚ≥0 and cμ≤1. Those assumptions, the weak derivative identity G=∇v and S>0 are supplied elsewhere; the definition alone proves none of them. Empty piece families contribute zero.
Breakdown.Coercive.piecePos.summary: $\sum_{\text{curl}}\chi_p\lambda_p|\Omega_p||\mathrm{curl}\,\hat G_\iota|^2+\sum_{\text{vel}}\chi_p(1-c_\mu)\mu_p|\Omega_p||\hat v_\iota|^2$, the positive terms in Proposition B.1 before other piece terms. Breakdown.Coercive.pieceRest.text: For one raw mode ι at (θ,y), evaluate (D−c)x₂²+(1−D)x_c²+(¼−Z)x_ω²+(Z−‖D²D‖op−cw)x₁²−‖D²Z‖op x₀² at the amplitudes |Ĥι|,|curl Ĥι|,|Ĝι|,|curl Ĝι|,|v̂ι|. Add, over the finite curl pieces, the four cross-boundary products between reference amplitudes and perturbation amplitudes, each with factor −λₚ|curl Ĝι|. Add, over velocity pieces, the cross-boundary product −μₚ|v̂ι| times the coupling of reference velocity to Ĝ, and the two negative Young-inequality terms with balancing constant ηₚ. In each coupling only translates leaving the chosen one-sided piece are retained. This is the modewise remainder in the proof of Proposition B.1 before the whole-piece losses are absorbed into the five coefficients of (B.16). The conversion weights are those of the class assigned to ι, and c becomes 3/50 in the paper. This definition supplies no lower bound, integrability or derivative identity; in particular it is not yet the final Iι of (B.16).
Breakdown.Coercive.pieceRest.summary: For one mode, the base density at the five amplitudes plus cross-boundary curl and velocity couplings and two Young-inequality terms: the modewise remainder in Proposition B.1 before whole-piece losses enter (B.16). In the paper $c=3/50$. It is not yet the final $I_\iota$.

Breakdown.Coercive.secondDerivAmp.text: For a supplied field H of real bilinear maps ℝ³×ℝ³→ℝ³, this expression is the square root of the sum of the squared absolute values of the 27 complex components of Ĥ. Here θ∈ℝ is normalized time, y∈ℝ³, and Rφ is rotation through φ about the third axis. The raw mode (n,k) averages the tensor at (θ+τ,Rφy) against exp(−i(2πnτ+kφ))/(2π) over 0≤τ≤1 and 0≤φ≤2π. Vector outputs are rotated back by R₋φ; each derivative input is the rotated standard basis vector Rφeⱼ. Thus v gives three complex components, a supplied linear map G gives nine, and a supplied bilinear map H gives 27. This is (B.12) with raw frequencies (n,k)=(2ι₂−ι₁,ϰι₁) for the paper's label ι. Each component integral is assigned zero if it is not integrable. When H=∇²v and differentiation commutes with the Fourier projection, this is |∇²v̂| in (B.16). The definition imposes no derivative identity or integrability. It returns a nonnegative real number. The tensor sizes are Euclidean component norms; they are Frobenius norms for the arrays with two or three indices.
Breakdown.Coercive.secondDerivAmp.summary: For a field $H$ of bilinear maps, the Frobenius norm of the 27 complex components of its rotating-frame Fourier mode $\hat H$ from (B.12); for $H=\nabla^2v$, when differentiation commutes with the projection, it is $|\nabla^2\hat v|$ in (B.16). Breakdown.Coercive.secondDerivSq.text: For a bilinear vector map H on ℝ³, the formal expression is ∑ⱼ,ₗ|H(eⱼ,eₗ)|², with both sums over the three standard unit vectors. When H=∇²v this is the squared Frobenius norm |∇²v|² used in (B.16). It differs from |Δv|²=|∑ⱼH(eⱼ,eⱼ)|² and from the squared operator norm of the bilinear map. Equality of the integrals of the first two quantities requires additional analytic hypotheses; it is not asserted here. No regularity or derivative interpretation is imposed on H by this definition.
Breakdown.Coercive.secondDerivSq.summary: For a bilinear map $H$, $\sum_{j,l}|H(e_j,e_l)|^2$; for $H=\nabla^2v$ it is the squared Frobenius norm $|\nabla^2v|^2$ of (B.16). It differs from $|\Delta v|^2$ and from the squared operator norm, and equality of integrals with $|\Delta v|^2$ is not asserted.

Breakdown.Coercive.smoothApproximationHo.text: Let v be a measurable 1-periodic divergence-free field on ℝ×ℝ³, with weak gradient G and Hessian H, L⁶ spatial slices almost everywhere, ∇v,Δv∈H and transport g=S^{−1}∂_θv+(v+y·∇v)/2∈H. Assume its stated almost-everywhere Γ invariance. The theorem supplies smooth divergence-free 1-periodic fields v_n such that ∇v_n→G, ∇²v_n→H and the corresponding transports converge to g in L²((0,1)×ℝ³), while (v_n−v)/(1+|y|)→0 in the same L² space. Every v_n has the higher derivative and weighted integrability required for the smooth multiplier argument. The conclusion does not require v_n to retain the Γ symmetries. The theorem supplies the approximation; passing the signed density inequality through the limit is a separate estimate. Here S is allowed to be any real number in the approximation assertion; if S=0, the factor 1/S in the transport is assigned zero. The multiplier application separately imposes S>0.
Breakdown.Coercive.smoothApproximationHo.summary: A weak perturbation has smooth divergence-free 1-periodic approximants $v_n$ with $\nabla v_n\to G$, $\nabla^2v_n\to H$, transports converging to $g$ and $(v_n-v)/(1+|y|)\to0$ in $L^2((0,1)\times\mathbb R^3)$. Breakdown.Coercive.transportPart.text: For a real period S and v(θ,y)∈ℝ³, define g=S⁻¹∂θv+½v+½(y·∇)v. The derivatives are evaluated pointwise. Thus 𝓣ˢv=g−Δv in (7.4); the diffusion term is kept separate in the formal weak formulation. This definition is made for every function v and every real S, without smoothness or S>0. A derivative is assigned zero where the relevant differentiability condition fails, and S⁻¹ is zero at S=0. The intended operator on 𝓓ˢΓ therefore requires the positive period and weak derivative hypotheses stated in the analytic results.
Breakdown.Coercive.transportPart.summary: For real $S$, $g=S^{-1}\partial_\theta v+\tfrac12v+\tfrac12(y\cdot\nabla)v$, so $\mathcal T^Sv=g-\Delta v$ in (7.4), with diffusion kept separate. It is defined for every $v$ and $S$: failed derivatives are zero and $S^{-1}=0$ at $S=0$.

Breakdown.Coercive.velAmp.text: For a supplied vector field v:ℝ×ℝ³→ℝ³, this expression is the square root of the sum of the squared absolute values of the three complex components of v̂. Here θ∈ℝ is normalized time, y∈ℝ³, and Rφ is rotation through φ about the third axis. The raw mode (n,k) averages the tensor at (θ+τ,Rφy) against exp(−i(2πnτ+kφ))/(2π) over 0≤τ≤1 and 0≤φ≤2π. Vector outputs are rotated back by R₋φ; each derivative input is the rotated standard basis vector Rφeⱼ. Thus v gives three complex components, a supplied linear map G gives nine, and a supplied bilinear map H gives 27. This is (B.12) with raw frequencies (n,k)=(2ι₂−ι₁,ϰι₁) for the paper's label ι. Each component integral is assigned zero if it is not integrable. For an integrable velocity projection, this is |v̂| in (B.16). The definition imposes no derivative identity or integrability. It returns a nonnegative real number. The tensor sizes are Euclidean component norms; they are Frobenius norms for the arrays with two or three indices.
Breakdown.Coercive.velAmp.summary: For a vector field $v$, the Euclidean norm of the three complex components of its rotating-frame Fourier mode $\hat v$ from (B.12), which for an integrable projection is $|\hat v|$ in (B.16). Nonintegrable component integrals are taken as zero; the result is a nonnegative real.

Breakdown.Coercive.vortAmp.text: For a supplied field G of real linear maps ℝ³→ℝ³, this expression is the Euclidean norm of the curl contraction of Ĝ. Here θ∈ℝ is normalized time, y∈ℝ³, and Rφ is rotation through φ about the third axis. The raw mode (n,k) averages the tensor at (θ+τ,Rφy) against exp(−i(2πnτ+kφ))/(2π) over 0≤τ≤1 and 0≤φ≤2π. Vector outputs are rotated back by R₋φ; each derivative input is the rotated standard basis vector Rφeⱼ. Thus v gives three complex components, a supplied linear map G gives nine, and a supplied bilinear map H gives 27. This is (B.12) with raw frequencies (n,k)=(2ι₂−ι₁,ϰι₁) for the paper's label ι. Each component integral is assigned zero if it is not integrable. When G=∇v and differentiation commutes with the Fourier projection, this is |curl v̂| in (B.16). The definition imposes no derivative identity or integrability. It returns a nonnegative real number. The tensor sizes are Euclidean component norms; they are Frobenius norms for the arrays with two or three indices.
Breakdown.Coercive.vortAmp.summary: For a field $G$ of linear maps, the Euclidean norm of the curl contraction of its rotating-frame Fourier mode $\hat G$ from (B.12); for $G=\nabla v$, when differentiation commutes with the projection, it is $|\mathrm{curl}\,\hat v|$ in (B.16). Nonintegrable component integrals are taken as zero.

Breakdown.Coercive.vortGradAmp.text: For a supplied field H of real bilinear maps ℝ³×ℝ³→ℝ³, this expression is the Frobenius norm of the curl-gradient contraction of Ĥ. Here θ∈ℝ is normalized time, y∈ℝ³, and Rφ is rotation through φ about the third axis. The raw mode (n,k) averages the tensor at (θ+τ,Rφy) against exp(−i(2πnτ+kφ))/(2π) over 0≤τ≤1 and 0≤φ≤2π. Vector outputs are rotated back by R₋φ; each derivative input is the rotated standard basis vector Rφeⱼ. Thus v gives three complex components, a supplied linear map G gives nine, and a supplied bilinear map H gives 27. This is (B.12) with raw frequencies (n,k)=(2ι₂−ι₁,ϰι₁) for the paper's label ι. Each component integral is assigned zero if it is not integrable. When H=∇²v and differentiation commutes with the Fourier projection, this is |∇curl v̂| in (B.16). The definition imposes no derivative identity or integrability. It returns a nonnegative real number. The tensor sizes are Euclidean component norms; they are Frobenius norms for the arrays with two or three indices.
Breakdown.Coercive.vortGradAmp.summary: For a field $H$ of bilinear maps, the Frobenius norm of the curl-gradient contraction of its rotating-frame Fourier mode $\hat H$ from (B.12); for $H=\nabla^2v$, when differentiation commutes with the projection, it is $|\nabla\mathrm{curl}\,\hat v|$ in (B.16).

Breakdown.Coercive.vortGradSup.text: For a reference field W, and y∈ℝ³, the expression takes the real supremum of ‖∇curl W(θ,Rφy)‖op over every real time θ and angle φ. It is the quantity bounded by the corresponding supplied function in the piece estimates of Appendix B.2. There is no periodicity or boundedness assumption in this definition. A real supremum is assigned zero when the set is unbounded above; it cannot then be read as a finite bound. Regularity of the first two spatial derivatives of W and the pointwise estimates used in Proposition B.1 are separate requirements.
Breakdown.Coercive.vortGradSup.summary: For a reference field $W$ and $y\in\mathbb R^3$, the real supremum over all $\theta,\varphi$ of $\|\nabla\mathrm{curl}\,W(\theta,R_\varphi y)\|_{\mathrm{op}}$, the quantity bounded in the piece estimates of Appendix B.2. An unbounded supremum is assigned zero, so it is then no finite bound.

Breakdown.Coercive.vortSup.text: For a reference field W, and y∈ℝ³, the expression takes the real supremum of |curl W(θ,Rφy)| over every real time θ and angle φ. Breakdown.Coercive.vortSup.summary: For a reference field $W$ and $y\in\mathbb R^3$, the real supremum over all $\theta,\varphi$ of $|\mathrm{curl}\,W(\theta,R_\varphi y)|$, the quantity bounded in the piece estimates of Appendix B.2. An unbounded supremum is assigned zero, so it is then no finite bound.

Breakdown.CoerciveClause.text:
For every parameter in the box and every period-one Γ-invariant solenoidal weak perturbation v with v(θ)∈L⁶, ∇v, Δv and S⁻¹∂θv+½v+½y·∇v in L² over the period, require the following. If F is measurable, period one and in L² and F≃𝓣ˢv+(Wᵃ·∇)v+(v·∇)Wᵃ+∑βᵢbᵢ, then (‖v‖²w+|β|²)¹ᐟ²≤c₁‖F‖𝓗+c_B‖F‖L²((0,1)×B_R)+c₂|ℓ(v)|. Here 𝓣ˢv=S⁻¹∂θv+½v+½y·∇v−Δv, ‖v‖²w is the formal squared energy, and ℓᵢ(v)=∫₀¹∫∇v:Ξᵢ. This extracts one condition of the earlier certificate. Compared with (7.18), the force weight is one, Wᵃ is used directly, and a local L² norm replaces the finite directional seminorm.

For arbitrary supplied data, put I=∫₀¹∫ℝ³ max(|tr H|²+w|G|²,0), with values in [0,∞] and the Frobenius norm for G. The formal squared energy equals I when I is finite and equals zero when I is infinite. With G=∇v, H=∇²v and a bounded measurable weight w≥w*>0, the perturbation hypotheses make this the usual energy ∫₀¹∫ℝ³(|Δv|²+w|∇v|²). The isolated condition does not impose those assumptions on w.
Breakdown.CoerciveClause.summary: For every box parameter and admissible $\Gamma$-invariant weak $v$, if $F\simeq\mathcal T^Sv+(W^a\cdot\nabla)v+(v\cdot\nabla)W^a+\sum\beta_ib_i$ then $(\|v\|_w^2+|\beta|^2)^{1/2}\le c_1\|F\|_{\mathcal H}+c_B\|F\|_{L^2(B_R)}+c_2|\ell(v)|$. Unlike (7.18): force weight one and a local norm.

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.EnergyIdentitySmo.text: The formal assertion fixes S>0 and a C¹ divergence-free, 1-periodic reference W with a supplied weak Hessian and decay |W|≲(1+|y|)^{−1}, |∇W|≲(1+|y|)^{−2}, |∇²W|≲(1+|y|)^{−3}. It assumes a smooth periodic divergence-free perturbation v with L⁶ spatial slices, finite weighted L² norm of v and ∂_θv, all positive-order spatial derivatives of v and ∂_θv in H, and all spatial derivatives of S^{−1}∂_θv+(v+y·∇v)/2 in H. Then ⟨T_Sv+C_Wv,−Δv⟩_H=∫(|∇curl v|²+|curl v|²/4+J), with J formed using the supplied weak Hessian of W. The integration is over one period and ℝ³. This states the smooth-stage identity used in the proof; extension to every weak perturbation is separate. The additional integrability assumptions make precise the paper's phrase “for smooth perturbations”.
Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.EnergyIdentitySmo.summary: For $S>0$, a decaying periodic divergence-free $C^1$ reference $W$ and a smooth periodic divergence-free $v$ with the stated integrability, $\langle T_Sv+C_Wv,-\Delta v\rangle_H=\int(|\nabla\operatorname{curl}v|^2+|\operatorname{curl}v|^2/4+J)$. Weak perturbations are treated separately.

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.ExtendedCoerciveC.text: Let J⊂{1,…,k} be the selected parameter indices, let ρⱼ,ρ*,dⱼ be supplied real numbers, and put K={q∈ℝᵏ: |qⱼ|≤ρⱼ for j∈J, ∑ⱼ∉J(dⱼqⱼ)²≤ρ*²}, the parameter set (7.29). For every q∈K, use S=S(q), reference Wʳ(q), force fields bᵢ and the symmetry set Γ. Here a perturbation is given by v,g:ℝ×ℝ³→ℝ³, a field G of linear maps and a field H of bilinear maps. All four are jointly measurable up to null sets and pointwise period one. For almost every θ, v(θ),G(θ),H(θ) are locally integrable in space, G=∇v and H(a,eⱼ)=∂ₐ(Geⱼ) distributionally, div v=tr G=0 almost everywhere, and v(θ)∈L⁶(ℝ³). Require G, tr H and g in L²([0,1]×ℝ³), where tr H=∑ⱼH(eⱼ,eⱼ) and the size of G is Frobenius. The identity g=S⁻¹∂θv+½v+½(y·∇)v is tested against every compactly supported C∞ vector field on ℝ×ℝ³. For the supplied set Γ of pairs (R,θ₀), with R orthogonal and θ₀ real, require v(θ+θ₀,Ry)=Rv(θ,y) almost everywhere for each pair. These conditions represent 𝓓ˢΓ when S>0; the formal conditions themselves admit every real S, with S⁻¹=0 at S=0, and do not select the continuous-in-time representative chosen in §7.1. For any such perturbation, any β∈ℝᵏ and any F jointly measurable up to a null set, pointwise period one and satisfying ∫₀¹∫ℝ³|F|²<∞, require F≃𝓣ˢv+(Wʳ·∇)v+(v·∇)Wʳ+∑βᵢbᵢ. Here 𝓣ˢv=g−tr H. Precisely, every compactly supported C∞ solenoidal vector test φ on ℝ×ℝ³ satisfies ∫F·φ=∫[(g+G Wʳ+(DWʳ)v+∑βᵢbᵢ)·φ+G:∇φ]. These test integrals are over all space and time; F need not be solenoidal or Γ-invariant. The estimate is √(E+ω²∑ᵢβᵢ²)≤c₁‖F‖𝓗+[F]+c₂|ℓ(v)|, with the supplied real force weight ω and constants c₁,c₂. For arbitrary supplied w define E as the real value of ∫₀¹∫ℝ³max(|tr H|²+w|G|²,0), with the value infinity converted to zero. When w is bounded, measurable and positive, the perturbation conditions make E=∫₀¹∫ℝ³(|Δv|²+w|∇v|²) finite. Let eₐ:ℝ×ℝ³→ℝ³ be the supplied finite row family, τₐ its real weights, and Ξᵢ the supplied linear-map fields in the constraints. Set [F]=√(∑ₐτₐ⟨F,eₐ⟩²), ℓᵢ(v)=∫₀¹∫ℝ³G:Ξᵢ and |ℓ(v)|=√(∑ᵢℓᵢ(v)²). Pairings use the iterated ordinary integrals over [0,1]×ℝ³; a nonintegrable ordinary integral has default value zero. A real square root of a negative number is zero, so [F]²=max(∑ₐτₐ⟨F,eₐ⟩²,0) for unrestricted row weights. Under the certificate hypotheses eₐ are orthonormal and τₐ≥0; the corresponding paper rows in (7.17) are √τₐeₐ. Under the certificate's positivity, integrability and row hypotheses this is the a priori estimate (7.18) about Wʳ. The declaration itself defines a condition on supplied data and imposes none of the other certificate clauses: K may be empty, S and w need not be positive, and the rows need not be orthonormal or nonnegatively weighted. Thus its unrestricted scope is wider than the paper's setting, although its inequality has the same form. It supplies no solution of the nonlinear profile equation.
Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.ExtendedCoerciveC.summary: For every $q\in\mathcal K$ of (7.29), weak perturbation $v$, $\beta$ and $F\simeq\mathcal T^Sv+(W^{\mathrm r}\cdot\nabla)v+(v\cdot\nabla)W^{\mathrm r}+\sum\beta_ib_i$: $\sqrt{E+\omega^2|\beta|^2}\le c_1\|F\|_{\mathcal H}+[F]+c_2|\ell(v)|$, the form of (7.18), with wider unrestricted scope.

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.IsAdmissibleWeak.text: Fix a positive period S, a reference field W with a supplied second derivative, finitely many classes of physical integer frequencies, and finitely many λ and μ indices. This condition requires 0<c,c_μ<1 and a measurable axisymmetric weight w≥w₀>0. A finite sign-symmetric harmonic set containing zero must represent W. Its four amplitude bounds control the modes of W, ∇W, curl W and ∇curl W, and its two further bounds control |curl W| and the operator norm of ∇curl W along axial rotations. Each transport bound dominates |W+y/2−ν_pe₃×y|, and Ω_p has a positive lower bound on its selected set. The nonnegative λ,μ weights are globally Lipschitz and axisymmetric; |y|λ, μ, |y|²μ and |y||∇μ| have uniform bounds. For all y, ∑_pλ_p(y)≤n_λ and ∑_p|∇λ_p(y)|≤n_{∇λ}; for all frequencies ξ, (∑_p|sgn_p(ξ)|μ_p(y))²≤n_μ∑_p|sgn_p(ξ)||Ω_p(ξ)|μ_p(y), with n_μ≥0. Here Ω_p(j,j′)=2πj/S+ν_pj′ and sgn_p is 1 on the selected set, −1 on its negative and 0 elsewhere. The positive lower frequency bound makes those two sets disjoint. All auxiliary functions are positive, measurable and axisymmetric, and the μ auxiliary numbers are positive. The functions D,Z are C², axisymmetric, equal at opposite frequencies, and D≥0; |y|^j|∇^jD| and (1+|y|)^j|∇^jZ| are uniformly bounded for j=0,1,2. Finally I′₂≥0. The condition permits a variable w and c other than 3/50. It does not itself assume the field regularity and decay of W, a bound above on w, or the perturbation equation; these are separate premises of the multiplier theorem.
Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.IsAdmissibleWeak.summary: Admissibility at $S>0$: $0<c,c_\mu<1$, axisymmetric $w\ge w_0>0$, a harmonic representation of $W$ with amplitude and transport bounds, positive $\Omega_p$ on selected sets, Lipschitz $\lambda,\mu$ weights with sum bounds, $C^2$ even $D\ge0$ and $Z$, and $I'_2\ge0$; $w$ may vary.

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.IsWeakSecondDeriv.text: Let W:ℝ×ℝ³→ℝ³ be jointly C¹, pointwise period one in θ and pointwise solenoidal. Let Hᵂ(θ,y):ℝ³×ℝ³→ℝ³ be a supplied bilinear map at every point, jointly measurable up to a null set and pointwise period one. For every θ and each standard basis vector eⱼ, require ∂ⱼW and the map a↦Hᵂ(θ,·)(a,eⱼ) to be locally integrable and to satisfy ∇(∂ⱼW)=Hᵂ(·,eⱼ) distributionally. With one real decay constant C_W, require at every θ,y the bounds |W|≤C_W/(1+|y|), ‖DW‖op≤C_W/(1+|y|)² and ‖Hᵂ‖op≤C_W/(1+|y|)³. These are the exact requirements on the reference in the weak version of Proposition B.1. The distributional identities are required at every fixed time; the representative Hᵂ satisfies its decay bound at every point, including any interfaces where a classical Hessian need not exist. This permits the C¹, piecewise smooth reference fields of Appendix B.1. It imposes more than the C¹, periodic reference assumption in §7.3, through solenoidality, weak second derivatives and global pointwise decay of orders zero through two. The formal condition neither assumes C² regularity nor asserts that W solves the profile equation. Each requirement is a hypothesis; this declaration constructs no reference field.
Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.IsWeakSecondDeriv.summary: $W$ is $C^1$, period one and solenoidal, $\nabla(\partial_jW)=H^W(\cdot,e_j)$ distributionally, and $W$, $DW$, $H^W$ decay like $(1+|y|)^{-1},(1+|y|)^{-2},(1+|y|)^{-3}$: the reference hypotheses of the weak Proposition B.1, more than the $C^1$ assumption of §7.3.

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.IsWeakSecondDeriv.text: Let W:ℝ×ℝ³→ℝ³ be jointly C¹, pointwise period one in θ and pointwise solenoidal. Let Hᵂ(θ,y):ℝ³×ℝ³→ℝ³ be a supplied bilinear map at every point, jointly measurable up to a null set and pointwise period one. For every θ and each standard basis vector eⱼ, require ∂ⱼW and the map a↦Hᵂ(θ,·)(a,eⱼ) to be locally integrable and to satisfy ∇(∂ⱼW)=Hᵂ(·,eⱼ) distributionally. With one real decay constant C_W, require at every θ,y the bounds |W|≤C_W/(1+|y|), ‖DW‖op≤C_W/(1+|y|)² and ‖Hᵂ‖op≤C_W/(1+|y|)³. Each piece has a mode set Nₚ, angular rate νₚ, transport bound uₚ(y), and weight λₚ(y) or μₚ(y). Put Ωₚ(ξ)=2πn/S+νₚk, χₚ(ξ)=1_{ξ∈Nₚ or −ξ∈Nₚ}, and sgnₚ(ξ)=1 on Nₚ, −1 on −Nₚ and zero elsewhere.

A finite harmonic set A⊂ℤ² contains zero, is closed under negation, and reconstructs W pointwise as ∑_{α∈A}Re Ŵα. The four prescribed real functions b⁰α,b¹α,bωα,b∇ωα must bound respectively |Ŵα|, |(DW)̂α|, |curl (DW)̂α| and |curl Ĥᵂα| at every time and point, for each α∈A. These Fourier modes are the rotating-frame averages (B.12) with raw pair (n,k)=(2ι₂−ι₁,ϰι₁). The sizes are Euclidean component norms. Two supplied functions Q,Q₁ must bound |curl W(θ,Rφy)| and ‖L_{Hᵂ(θ,Rφy)}‖op at every θ,φ,y; here (L_A eₘ)ⱼ=∑_{a,b}εⱼₐᵦA(eₘ,eₐ)ᵦ. Each uₚ(y) must dominate |W(θ,Rφy)+½Rφy−νₚe₃×Rφy| for all θ,φ,y. For each piece there is a positive constant Ω*ₚ such that Ωₚ(ξ)≥Ω*ₚ for every ξ∈Nₚ. This makes Nₚ and −Nₚ disjoint.

Every λₚ and μₚ is nonnegative, globally Lipschitz and axisymmetric. At every y, require ∑ₚ∈𝓟λ λₚ≤E* and ∑ₚ∈𝓟λ |∇λₚ|≤E′*. One constant bounds |y|λₚ uniformly over all curl pieces and points; another bounds μₚ, |y|²μₚ and |y||∇μₚ| uniformly over velocity pieces and points. With R≥0 require, for every ξ,y, (∑ₚ∈𝓟μ |sgnₚ(ξ)|μₚ)²≤R∑ₚ∈𝓟μ |sgnₚ(ξ)||Ωₚ(ξ)|μₚ. Each curl piece has eight functions a₁,ₚ,a₂,ₚ,Lₚ,t₀,ₚ,t₁,ₚ,t₂,ₚ,t₃,ₚ,sₚ; each is everywhere positive, measurable and axisymmetric. Each velocity piece has two functions a₄,ₚ,t₄,ₚ with the same three properties and a positive real number ηₚ.

The conversion functions D and Z for every class are C² and axisymmetric; D is nonnegative. The functions assigned to ξ and −ξ must agree. There is a uniform bound for |y|ʲ‖∇ʲD‖op for all classes, y and integer j=0,1,2, and a possibly different uniform bound for (1+|y|)ʲ‖∇ʲZ‖op. To state the final share condition, define Oₚ(ξ)=1_{ξ∉Nₚ}∑_{α∈A,ξ+α∈Nₚ}b⁰α+1_{−ξ∉Nₚ}∑_{α∈A,−ξ+α∈Nₚ}b⁰α, with all functions evaluated at y. Require Dξ(y)≤1−∑ₚ∈𝓟λ[a₁,ₚχₚ1_{λₚ+|∇λₚ|>0}+a₂,ₚ1_{λₚ>0}Oₚ(ξ)/sₚ] at every ξ,y. This makes the coefficient of |∇curl v̂ξ|² nonnegative. Derivatives of a merely Lipschitz weight are assigned zero at its nondifferentiability points, so these are bounds on the chosen everywhere-defined derivative expressions. These are requirements on supplied functions, not estimates proved merely by specifying them. Assume also w is bounded above. Every forcing field bᵢ:ℝ×ℝ³→ℝ³, 1≤i≤k, is jointly measurable up to a null set, pointwise period one and square integrable over [0,1]×ℝ³. No symmetry or restriction on the harmonics of these forcing fields is imposed in this statement. Here a perturbation is given by v,g:ℝ×ℝ³→ℝ³, a field G of linear maps and a field H of bilinear maps. All four are jointly measurable up to null sets and pointwise period one. For almost every θ, v(θ),G(θ),H(θ) are locally integrable in space, G=∇v and H(a,eⱼ)=∂ₐ(Geⱼ) distributionally, div v=tr G=0 almost everywhere, and v(θ)∈L⁶(ℝ³). Require G, tr H and g in L²([0,1]×ℝ³), where tr H=∑ⱼH(eⱼ,eⱼ) and the size of G is Frobenius. The identity g=S⁻¹∂θv+½v+½(y·∇)v is tested against every compactly supported C∞ vector field on ℝ×ℝ³. For the supplied set Γ of pairs (R,θ₀), with R orthogonal and θ₀ real, require v(θ+θ₀,Ry)=Rv(θ,y) almost everywhere for each pair. These conditions represent 𝓓ˢΓ when S>0; the formal conditions themselves admit every real S, with S⁻¹=0 at S=0, and do not select the continuous-in-time representative chosen in §7.1. For any such perturbation, any β∈ℝᵏ and any F jointly measurable up to a null set, pointwise period one and satisfying ∫₀¹∫ℝ³|F|²<∞, require F≃𝓣ˢv+(W·∇)v+(v·∇)W+∑βᵢbᵢ. Here 𝓣ˢv=g−tr H. Precisely, every compactly supported C∞ solenoidal vector test φ on ℝ×ℝ³ satisfies ∫F·φ=∫[(g+G W+(DW)v+∑βᵢbᵢ)·φ+G:∇φ]. These test integrals are over all space and time; F need not be solenoidal or Γ-invariant. The conclusion is existence of such a multiplier M. The multiplier requirement means that M is jointly measurable up to a null set, pointwise period one and square integrable over [0,1]×ℝ³; ∫M·∇q=0 for every smooth periodic scalar q of uniformly compact spatial support; and, for every smooth periodic solenoidal vector ψ of uniformly compact spatial support, ⟨M,ψ⟩=⟨−tr H,ψ⟩+∑ξ∫Re[i∑ₚ∈𝓟λ sgnₚ(ξ)λₚ curl Ĝξ·overline(curl (∇ψ)̂ξ)+i∑ₚ∈𝓟μ sgnₚ(ξ)μₚv̂ξ·overline(ψ̂ξ)]. The integrals and pairings in this identity are over [0,1]×ℝ³. It is (B.14) after the weak derivative identifications. The real infinite series in the identity has default value zero if nonsummable. Its frequency energy N=∑ₚ∈𝓟μ∑ξ∫|sgnₚ(ξ)||Ωₚ(ξ)|μₚ|v̂ξ|² is finite and ‖M‖𝓗≤a√(cE+cμN), where E=∫(|tr H|²+w|G|²) and a=√((1+E*+E′*/√w*)²/c+R/cμ). All these integrals are over one normalized period and ℝ³, and the derivative energy is finite under the stated assumptions. With X=⟨F,M⟩−cE−cμN−∑βᵢ⟨bᵢ,M⟩, the density integrals satisfy I⁺+max(−X,0)≤max(X,0)+I⁻. Here I± integrate the separate positive and negative parts of the modal density (B.16) and stretching expression (B.18), using Hᵂ and c in place of 3/50. This inequality is between nonnegative extended real numbers. If I⁻<∞, it implies I⁺<∞ and I⁺−I⁻≤X, exactly the conclusion of (B.20) after c=3/50. This declaration defines that universally quantified assertion. It does not itself establish it. It is the weak-Hessian version of Proposition B.1, adapted to the C¹ reference fields and arbitrary c∈(0,1); the formal hypothesis includes the stated global pointwise derivative decay.
Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.PieceMultiplierDe.summary: The assertion that, for a weak-Hessian reference and admissible pieces, each weak perturbation has a multiplier $M$ satisfying (B.14) with $N<\infty$, $\|M\|_{\mathcal H}\le a\sqrt{cE+c_\mu N}$ and $I^++(-X)^+\le X^++I^-$: the weak Proposition B.1, named, not proved.

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.RowMultiplierIneq.text: Let J⊂{1,…,k} be the selected parameter indices, let ρⱼ,ρ*,dⱼ be supplied real numbers, and put K={q∈ℝᵏ: |qⱼ|≤ρⱼ for j∈J, ∑ⱼ∉J(dⱼqⱼ)²≤ρ*²}, the parameter set (7.29).
