For any such perturbation, any β∈ℝᵏ and any F jointly measurable up to a null set, pointwise period one and satisfying ∫₀¹∫ℝ³|F|²<∞, require F≃𝓣ˢv+(Wʳ·∇)v+(v·∇)Wʳ+∑βᵢbᵢ. Here 𝓣ˢv=g−tr H. Precisely, every compactly supported C∞ solenoidal vector test φ on ℝ×ℝ³ satisfies ∫F·φ=∫[(g+G Wʳ+(DWʳ)v+∑βᵢbᵢ)·φ+G:∇φ]. These test integrals are over all space and time; F need not be solenoidal or Γ-invariant. There must exist a field M measurable up to a null set, with ∫₀¹∫ℝ³|M|²<∞, and a real n≥0 such that ‖M‖𝓗≤a√(cE+cμn²) and c(E+ω²∑ᵢβᵢ²)+cμn²≤⟨F,M⟩𝓗+c[F]²+t|ℓ(v)|². The norm of M here is the L² norm of its restriction to one period. For arbitrary supplied w define E as the real value of ∫₀¹∫ℝ³max(|tr H|²+w|G|²,0), with the value infinity converted to zero. When w is bounded, measurable and positive, the perturbation conditions make E=∫₀¹∫ℝ³(|Δv|²+w|∇v|²) finite. Let eₐ:ℝ×ℝ³→ℝ³ be the supplied finite row family, τₐ its real weights, and Ξᵢ the supplied linear-map fields in the constraints. Set [F]=√(∑ₐτₐ⟨F,eₐ⟩²), ℓᵢ(v)=∫₀¹∫ℝ³G:Ξᵢ and |ℓ(v)|=√(∑ᵢℓᵢ(v)²). Pairings use the iterated ordinary integrals over [0,1]×ℝ³; a nonintegrable ordinary integral has default value zero. A real square root of a negative number is zero, so [F]²=max(∑ₐτₐ⟨F,eₐ⟩²,0) for unrestricted row weights. Under the certificate hypotheses eₐ are orthonormal and τₐ≥0; the corresponding paper rows in (7.17) are √τₐeₐ. These are the fields of the formal condition. They express the intermediate estimate in Lemma B.2, with arbitrary c,cμ,t,a and the force weight ω. The quantified field M is not required here to be periodic, solenoidal or to satisfy the testing identity (B.14); a later construction supplies those additional properties. The auxiliary n is a nonnegative real number, not an integer or a mode index. This definition does not prove the inequalities or impose the remaining certificate assumptions. Norm expressions for arbitrary data retain their default-value conventions.
Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.RowMultiplierIneq.summary: For every $q\in\mathcal K$ and weak perturbation, some $M\in L^2$ and $n\ge0$ satisfy $\|M\|_{\mathcal H}\le a\sqrt{cE+c_\mu n^2}$ and $c(E+\omega^2|\beta|^2)+c_\mu n^2\le\langle F,M\rangle_{\mathcal H}+c[F]^2+t|\ell(v)|^2$: the intermediate estimate of Lemma B.2.

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.RowRestClause.text: For every α in the prescribed parameter set K, every measurable 1-periodic divergence-free perturbation v with weak ∇v,Δv∈H, L⁶ spatial slices and distributional transport g∈H, and every measurable 1-periodic F∈H satisfying the reference linearized equation modulo gradients with coefficients β, this condition requires the following for every multiplier M satisfying (B.14). The negative density integral I⁻ is finite, and I⁺+max(−Y,0)≥max(Y,0)+I⁻, where Y=cω²|β|²−∑β_i⟨b_i,M⟩−c[F]²−t|ℓ(v)|². All integrals are on [0,1]×ℝ³; [F] is the nonnegative row quantity defined below, and ℓ is the tensor-gradient constraint. Once I⁺ is also finite, this says I⁺−I⁻≥Y. With c=3/50 and t=1000 it is (B.21), accompanied by the required finiteness of I⁻. It is a condition on data, whose derivation from cells is a separate theorem. For the row term, put R_F=∑_kτ_k(∫₀¹∫F·u_k)². The formal quantity is [F]=√max(R_F,0). The row fields u_k and real weights τ_k are supplied data; this statement does not assume that the rows are normalized, square integrable or mutually orthogonal, or that τ_k≥0. Under the separate certificate row conditions, the u_k are orthonormal and τ_k≥0, so [F]²=R_F; rescaling e_k=√τ_k u_k gives the paper’s convention. The ordinary integrals defining the row pairings and the constraint pairings have value zero if the corresponding integrand is not integrable. Square-integrable row fields and constraint tensors remove that possibility in the certificate application. The constraint is ℓ_i(v)=∫₀¹∫Ξ_i:∇v, with the tensor indices identified as output and differentiation direction. The admitted perturbations have Γ invariance almost everywhere. Their right-hand-side equation is understood against smooth solenoidal tests compactly supported in time and space, so equality modulo a pressure gradient suffices. Here H=L²((0,1)×ℝ³). The perturbation consists of measurable 1-periodic v, a weak gradient G, a weak Hessian H_v and g, with v(θ,·)∈L⁶ for almost every θ, zero divergence and Γ invariance almost everywhere, and G, tr H_v and g in H. The transport identity is g=S(α)^{−1}∂_θv+(v+y·∇v)/2 in distributions. The right-hand-side equation is F=g−tr H_v+(W_α·∇)v+(v·∇)W_α+∑β_i b_i modulo gradients, tested against all smooth solenoidal functions compactly supported in time and space. This auxiliary statement imposes no sign condition on the real parameter S. Normalized time still has period one; when S=0 the coefficient 1/S in the transport identity is assigned zero. The paper’s physical period is positive. The reference and forcing fields in this condition are arbitrary supplied data. Derivatives used in their test equation are defined everywhere, with value zero where differentiability fails; ordinary test integrals have the nonintegrability convention stated above.
Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.RowRestClause.summary: For $\alpha\in\mathcal K$, admissible $v$, $F$ solving the equation modulo gradients and $M$ with (B.14): $I^-<\infty$, $I^++\max(-Y,0)\ge\max(Y,0)+I^-$, $Y=c\omega^2|\beta|^2-\sum_i\beta_i\langle b_i,M\rangle-c[F]^2-t|\ell(v)|^2$, $[F]=\sqrt{\max(R_F,0)}$ for bare rows; $c=3/50$, $t=1000$: (B.21).

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.actuator_finite.text: Let b₁,…,bₖ be the finite family of forcing fields and let b* be any real constant. If ∑ᵢ∫₀¹∫ℝ³|bᵢ|²≤b*², then for every index i the nonnegative period integral ∫₀¹∫ℝ³|bᵢ|² is finite. This is the componentwise consequence of (7.9) needed in the multiplier theorem. The source assumption is an inequality of nonnegative extended integrals, so it does not require the individual bᵢ to be measurable. Measurability must be supplied separately before describing bᵢ as elements of 𝓗. The statement does not require b*≥0 because its square is used.
Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.actuator_finite.summary: If $\sum_i\int_0^1\int_{\mathbb R^3}|b_i|^2\le b^{*2}$, then each $\int_0^1\int_{\mathbb R^3}|b_i|^2$ is finite, the componentwise consequence of (7.9). The integrals are nonnegative extended integrals, so measurability of $b_i$ is not required, nor is $b^*\ge0$.

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.densityNegWith.text: For a velocity v, supplied spatial derivative arrays and a reference field W with its supplied weak second derivative, this defines ∑_{ξ∈ℤ²}max(−I_ξ(θ,y),0)+max(−J(θ,y),0). The whole five-term mode expression I_ξ is grouped before taking its negative part, and J is grouped separately. Integration over [0,1]×ℝ³ gives I⁻∈[0,∞]. Finiteness is a separate hypothesis in the signed multiplier inequality and a conclusion of the cell estimate. Keeping this quantity in the extended nonnegative reals prevents a divergent negative integral from being silently treated as an ordinary real number.
Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.densityNegWith.summary: $\sum_{\xi\in\mathbb Z^2}\max(-I_\xi,0)+\max(-J,0)$, with each five-term $I_\xi$ grouped before its negative part is taken. Its integral over $[0,1]\times\mathbb R^3$ is $I^-\in[0,\infty]$; finiteness is a separate hypothesis or conclusion.

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.densityNegWith_se.text: For each raw Fourier mode ι, let Iι be the explicit five-term quadratic density of the formal statement, evaluated on |Ĥι|, |curl Ĥι|, |Ĝι|, |curl Ĝι|, |v̂ι|. It has the five squared quantities of (B.16), with the gradient amplitude supplied before the vorticity amplitude. When both multiplier families are empty and c=3/50, the coefficients agree with the five formulas printed immediately below (B.16). The paper describes the multiplier contributions but omits their full error formulas, so it supplies no second full formula for a term-by-term comparison with these coefficients. The sum here runs over every raw pair ι∈ℤ²; identifying it with the paper’s sum also requires the symmetries that make modes outside the paper’s frequency lattice vanish. The paper's mode label corresponds to the raw pair (2ι₂−ι₁,ϰι₁). Put ω=curl G, let 𝕊=(DW+(DW)ᵀ)/2, and put L=L_{Hᵂ}, where (L eₘ)ⱼ=∑_{a,b}εⱼₐᵦHᵂ(eₘ,eₐ)ᵦ. At (θ,y) define J=−ω·𝕊ω+(Lv)·ω+½∑ⱼ,m(L eₘ)ⱼ(v×G eⱼ)ₘ. For every reference W and every v,G,H,θ,y, setting Hᵂ to the ordinary second spatial derivative of W makes ∑ιmax(−Iι,0)+max(−J,0) exactly equal to the corresponding density formed directly with the ordinary Hessian. No smoothness or finiteness assumption is required, and the equality includes the value infinity. This is an identity between the two versions of the signed-part convention after (B.18); it does not identify a default-valued ordinary derivative with a weak derivative of a nonsmooth W.
Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.densityNegWith_se.summary: For every $W,v,G,H,\theta,y$, taking $H^W$ to be the ordinary second spatial derivative of $W$ makes $\sum_\iota\max(-I_\iota,0)+\max(-J,0)$ equal to the density formed with the ordinary Hessian, including the value infinity, with no smoothness or finiteness assumption.

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.densityPosWith.text: For a velocity v, supplied gradient and Hessian, and reference field W with a supplied weak Hessian, this defines at each real time θ and y∈ℝ³ the nonnegative extended value ∑_{ξ∈ℤ²}max(I_ξ(θ,y),0)+max(J(θ,y),0). Here I_ξ is the entire five-term mode density of (B.16), and J is the three-term stretching density (B.18), using the supplied derivative arrays. The positive part is taken after summing the five terms within each I_ξ. Its integral over one time period and space is I⁺. Infinite values are allowed. This definition does not require I⁻ to be finite and does not define an ∞−∞ subtraction.
Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.densityPosWith.summary: $\sum_{\xi\in\mathbb Z^2}\max(I_\xi,0)+\max(J,0)$, with $I_\xi$ the five-term mode density (B.16) and $J$ the stretching density (B.18), positive parts taken after summing within each $I_\xi$. Its integral is $I^+$, possibly infinite; no $\infty-\infty$ subtraction is defined.

When both multiplier families are empty and c=3/50, the coefficients agree with the five formulas printed immediately below (B.16). The paper's mode label corresponds to the raw pair (2ι₂−ι₁,ϰι₁). Put ω=curl G, let 𝕊=(DW+(DW)ᵀ)/2, and put L=L_{Hᵂ}, where (L eₘ)ⱼ=∑_{a,b}εⱼₐᵦHᵂ(eₘ,eₐ)ᵦ. At (θ,y) define J=−ω·𝕊ω+(Lv)·ω+½∑ⱼ,m(L eₘ)ⱼ(v×G eⱼ)ₘ. No smoothness or finiteness assumption is required, and the equality includes the value infinity. This is an identity between the two versions of the signed-part convention after (B.18); it does not identify a default-valued ordinary derivative with a weak derivative of a nonsmooth W.

These test integrals are over all space and time; F need not be solenoidal or Γ-invariant. The estimate is √(E+ω²∑ᵢβᵢ²)≤c₁‖F‖𝓗+[F]+c₂|ℓ(v)|, with the supplied real force weight ω and constants c₁,c₂. A real square root of a negative number is zero, so [F]²=max(∑ₐτₐ⟨F,eₐ⟩²,0) for unrestricted row weights. Under the certificate hypotheses eₐ are orthonormal and τₐ≥0; the corresponding paper rows in (7.17) are √τₐeₐ. The formal statement returns this assumed inequality. Its mathematical content is extraction of the coercive hypothesis, rather than a derivation of (7.18) from the other certificate conditions. Those other conditions, including the formalization's stronger global parameter regularity and pointwise Hessian decay for the approximate profile, are unused by this extraction. The theorem neither checks a concrete certificate nor supplies the later nonlinear solution.
Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.extendedCoerciveC.summary: From the formal certificate condition of §§7.2-7.3, the formal statement returns its assumed coercive estimate $\sqrt{E+\omega^2|\beta|^2}\le c_1\|F\|_{\mathcal H}+[F]+c_2|\ell(v)|$. It extracts this hypothesis; it does not derive (7.18) from the other certificate conditions.

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.extendedCoerciveC.text:
Let J⊂{1,…,k} be the selected parameter indices, let ρⱼ,ρ*,dⱼ be supplied real numbers, and put K={q∈ℝᵏ: |qⱼ|≤ρⱼ for j∈J, ∑ⱼ∉J(dⱼqⱼ)²≤ρ*²}, the parameter set (7.29). Suppose ρⱼ≥0 for j∈J and w(y)≤wmax everywhere. Every forcing field bᵢ is jointly measurable up to a null set and pointwise period one, and ∑ᵢ∫₀¹∫ℝ³|bᵢ|²≤b*² for a supplied real b*. For every q∈K, set S=S(q) and W=Wʳ(q), and impose the following reference conditions with decay constant C_W=C_W(q). Let W:ℝ×ℝ³→ℝ³ be jointly C¹, pointwise period one in θ and pointwise solenoidal. Let Hᵂ(θ,y):ℝ³×ℝ³→ℝ³ be a supplied bilinear map at every point, jointly measurable up to a null set and pointwise period one. For every θ and each standard basis vector eⱼ, require ∂ⱼW and the map a↦Hᵂ(θ,·)(a,eⱼ) to be locally integrable and to satisfy ∇(∂ⱼW)=Hᵂ(·,eⱼ) distributionally. With one real decay constant C_W, require at every θ,y the bounds |W|≤C_W/(1+|y|), ‖DW‖op≤C_W/(1+|y|)² and ‖Hᵂ‖op≤C_W/(1+|y|)³. At each such q impose all the following piece conditions. Fix finitely many classes of raw modes ξ=(n,k)∈ℤ², finitely many curl pieces p∈𝓟λ and velocity pieces p∈𝓟μ, a real field W and a supplied bilinear field Hᵂ. Require 0<c<1, 0<cμ<1, S>0, and a measurable axisymmetric weight w with w(y)≥w*>0 everywhere. Here axisymmetric means unchanged by every rotation Rφ about the third axis. Each piece has a mode set Nₚ, angular rate νₚ, transport bound uₚ(y), and weight λₚ(y) or μₚ(y). Put Ωₚ(ξ)=2πn/S+νₚk, χₚ(ξ)=1_{ξ∈Nₚ or −ξ∈Nₚ}, and sgnₚ(ξ)=1 on Nₚ, −1 on −Nₚ and zero elsewhere.

A finite harmonic set A⊂ℤ² contains zero, is closed under negation, and reconstructs W pointwise as ∑_{α∈A}Re Ŵα. The four prescribed real functions b⁰α,b¹α,bωα,b∇ωα must bound respectively |Ŵα|, |(DW)̂α|, |curl (DW)̂α| and |curl Ĥᵂα| at every time and point, for each α∈A. These Fourier modes are the rotating-frame averages (B.12) with raw pair (n,k)=(2ι₂−ι₁,ϰι₁). The sizes are Euclidean component norms. Two supplied functions Q,Q₁ must bound |curl W(θ,Rφy)| and ‖L_{Hᵂ(θ,Rφy)}‖op at every θ,φ,y; here (L_A eₘ)ⱼ=∑_{a,b}εⱼₐᵦA(eₘ,eₐ)ᵦ. Each uₚ(y) must dominate |W(θ,Rφy)+½Rφy−νₚe₃×Rφy| for all θ,φ,y. For each piece there is a positive constant Ω*ₚ such that Ωₚ(ξ)≥Ω*ₚ for every ξ∈Nₚ. This makes Nₚ and −Nₚ disjoint.

Every λₚ and μₚ is nonnegative, globally Lipschitz and axisymmetric. At every y, require ∑ₚ∈𝓟λ λₚ≤E* and ∑ₚ∈𝓟λ |∇λₚ|≤E′*. One constant bounds |y|λₚ uniformly over all curl pieces and points; another bounds μₚ, |y|²μₚ and |y||∇μₚ| uniformly over velocity pieces and points. With R≥0 require, for every ξ,y, (∑ₚ∈𝓟μ |sgnₚ(ξ)|μₚ)²≤R∑ₚ∈𝓟μ |sgnₚ(ξ)||Ωₚ(ξ)|μₚ. Each curl piece has eight functions a₁,ₚ,a₂,ₚ,Lₚ,t₀,ₚ,t₁,ₚ,t₂,ₚ,t₃,ₚ,sₚ; each is everywhere positive, measurable and axisymmetric. Each velocity piece has two functions a₄,ₚ,t₄,ₚ with the same three properties and a positive real number ηₚ.

The conversion functions D and Z for every class are C² and axisymmetric; D is nonnegative. The functions assigned to ξ and −ξ must agree. There is a uniform bound for |y|ʲ‖∇ʲD‖op for all classes, y and integer j=0,1,2, and a possibly different uniform bound for (1+|y|)ʲ‖∇ʲZ‖op. To state the final share condition, define Oₚ(ξ)=1_{ξ∉Nₚ}∑_{α∈A,ξ+α∈Nₚ}b⁰α+1_{−ξ∉Nₚ}∑_{α∈A,−ξ+α∈Nₚ}b⁰α, with all functions evaluated at y. Require Dξ(y)≤1−∑ₚ∈𝓟λ[a₁,ₚχₚ1_{λₚ+|∇λₚ|>0}+a₂,ₚ1_{λₚ>0}Oₚ(ξ)/sₚ] at every ξ,y. This makes the coefficient of |∇curl v̂ξ|² nonnegative. Derivatives of a merely Lipschitz weight are assigned zero at its nondifferentiability points, so these are bounds on the chosen everywhere-defined derivative expressions. These are requirements on supplied functions, not estimates proved merely by specifying them. The finite families have fixed sizes and the classes have the same index set for all q. The values c,cμ,w*,E*,E′*,R are common to all q; the retained fractions in the piece data equal these c,cμ. Every other piece function, harmonic bound and the reference Hessian may depend on q. The paper's B.2 restricts parameter dependence among its weights to the angular rates; this formal theorem allows the larger family just described. Take t≥0. The multiplier requirement means that M is jointly measurable up to a null set, pointwise period one and square integrable over [0,1]×ℝ³; ∫M·∇q=0 for every smooth periodic scalar q of uniformly compact spatial support; and, for every smooth periodic solenoidal vector ψ of uniformly compact spatial support, ⟨M,ψ⟩=⟨−tr H,ψ⟩+∑ξ∫Re[i∑ₚ∈𝓟λ sgnₚ(ξ)λₚ curl Ĝξ·overline(curl (∇ψ)̂ξ)+i∑ₚ∈𝓟μ sgnₚ(ξ)μₚv̂ξ·overline(ψ̂ξ)]. The integrals and pairings in this identity are over [0,1]×ℝ³. It is (B.14) after the weak derivative identifications. The real infinite series in the identity has default value zero if nonsummable. Assume additionally, for every q∈K, perturbation and right-hand side satisfying the conditions below, and every multiplier satisfying that identity, that I⁻<∞ and max(Y,0)+I⁻≤I⁺+max(−Y,0), with Y=cω²|β|²−∑βᵢ⟨bᵢ,M⟩−c[F]²−t|ℓ(v)|². Here I± integrate the separate positive and negative parts of (B.16) and (B.18), with this Hᵂ and retained constant c. Let eₐ:ℝ×ℝ³→ℝ³ be the supplied finite row family, τₐ its real weights, and Ξᵢ the supplied linear-map fields in the constraints. Set [F]=√(∑ₐτₐ⟨F,eₐ⟩²), ℓᵢ(v)=∫₀¹∫ℝ³G:Ξᵢ and |ℓ(v)|=√(∑ᵢℓᵢ(v)²). Pairings use the iterated ordinary integrals over [0,1]×ℝ³; a nonintegrable ordinary integral has default value zero. A real square root of a negative number is zero, so [F]²=max(∑ₐτₐ⟨F,eₐ⟩²,0) for unrestricted row weights. Under the certificate hypotheses eₐ are orthonormal and τₐ≥0; the corresponding paper rows in (7.17) are √τₐeₐ. Put a=√((1+E*+E′*/√w*)²/c+R/cμ), and assume a/√c≤c₁ and √(t/c)≤c₂. For every q∈K, use S=S(q), reference Wʳ(q), force fields bᵢ and the symmetry set Γ. Here a perturbation is given by v,g:ℝ×ℝ³→ℝ³, a field G of linear maps and a field H of bilinear maps. All four are jointly measurable up to null sets and pointwise period one. For almost every θ, v(θ),G(θ),H(θ) are locally integrable in space, G=∇v and H(a,eⱼ)=∂ₐ(Geⱼ) distributionally, div v=tr G=0 almost everywhere, and v(θ)∈L⁶(ℝ³). Require G, tr H and g in L²([0,1]×ℝ³), where tr H=∑ⱼH(eⱼ,eⱼ) and the size of G is Frobenius. The identity g=S⁻¹∂θv+½v+½(y·∇)v is tested against every compactly supported C∞ vector field on ℝ×ℝ³. For the supplied set Γ of pairs (R,θ₀), with R orthogonal and θ₀ real, require v(θ+θ₀,Ry)=Rv(θ,y) almost everywhere for each pair. These conditions represent 𝓓ˢΓ when S>0; the formal conditions themselves admit every real S, with S⁻¹=0 at S=0, and do not select the continuous-in-time representative chosen in §7.1. For any such perturbation, any β∈ℝᵏ and any F jointly measurable up to a null set, pointwise period one and satisfying ∫₀¹∫ℝ³|F|²<∞, require F≃𝓣ˢv+(Wʳ·∇)v+(v·∇)Wʳ+∑βᵢbᵢ. Here 𝓣ˢv=g−tr H. Precisely, every compactly supported C∞ solenoidal vector test φ on ℝ×ℝ³ satisfies ∫F·φ=∫[(g+G Wʳ+(DWʳ)v+∑βᵢbᵢ)·φ+G:∇φ]. These test integrals are over all space and time; F need not be solenoidal or Γ-invariant. The formal conclusion is √(∫₀¹∫ℝ³(|Δv|²+w|∇v|²)+ω²|β|²)≤c₁‖F‖𝓗+[F]+c₂|ℓ(v)|. This gives the inequality in (7.18) by Proposition B.1 and Lemma B.2 with general c,t, specialized in the paper to 3/50 and 1000. The supplied source invokes the universal multiplier-density theorem directly; it is no extra hypothesis of this statement. The all-perturbation lower bound (B.21) is still assumed. No row positivity or orthogonality is imposed by this theorem; the conclusion becomes the paper's row seminorm estimate when those additional row conditions hold. The theorem checks no numerical cells and constructs no Navier–Stokes solution.
Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.extendedCoerciveC.summary: From weak-Hessian references, admissible pieces, the lower bound (B.21), $a/\sqrt c\le c_1$ and $\sqrt{t/c}\le c_2$, the formal statement derives (7.18) by Proposition B.1 and Lemma B.2 with general $c,t$ (paper: $3/50$, $1000$). It allows more parameter dependence than B.2; (B.21) is still assumed.

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.extendedCoerciveC.text: Assume the reference linearized problem is given over a parameter set K whose adjoint coordinate radii are nonnegative. The energy weight has a positive lower bound w₀ and finite upper bound; the forcing fields are measurable, 1-periodic and have a finite common sum of squared H norms. At every α∈K, the reference W_α is C¹, periodic and divergence-free, with a measurable weak Hessian and decay of orders 1,2,3. Assume admissible multiplier data at every α with common 0<c,c_μ<1 and common numerical bounds n_λ,n_{∇λ},n_μ. Assume t≥0 and the remaining density condition (B.21), including I⁻<∞, with c and t in place of 3/50 and 1000. If c_M/√c≤c₁ and √(t/c)≤c₂, where c_M²=(1+n_λ+n_{∇λ}/√w₀)²/c+n_μ/c_μ, the theorem proves ‖(v,β)‖_{w,ω}≤c₁‖F‖_H+[F]+c₂|ℓ(v)| for every admitted periodic weak perturbation solving the reference equation modulo gradients. Here H=L²((0,1)×ℝ³), ‖(v,β)‖²=∫(|Δv|²+w|∇v|²)+ω²|β|², and [F] is the nonnegative row quantity defined below. The paper's choice c=3/50,t=1000 gives Lemma B.2. The theorem is uniform over K; it includes explicit hypotheses beyond the two scalar inequalities alone. For the row term, put R_F=∑_kτ_k(∫₀¹∫F·u_k)². The formal quantity is [F]=√max(R_F,0). The row fields u_k and real weights τ_k are supplied data; this statement does not assume that the rows are normalized, square integrable or mutually orthogonal, or that τ_k≥0. Under the separate certificate row conditions, the u_k are orthonormal and τ_k≥0, so [F]²=R_F; rescaling e_k=√τ_k u_k gives the paper’s convention. The ordinary integrals defining the row pairings and the constraint pairings have value zero if the corresponding integrand is not integrable. Square-integrable row fields and constraint tensors remove that possibility in the certificate application. The constraint is ℓ_i(v)=∫₀¹∫Ξ_i:∇v, with the tensor indices identified as output and differentiation direction. The admitted perturbations have Γ invariance almost everywhere. Their right-hand-side equation is understood against smooth solenoidal tests compactly supported in time and space, so equality modulo a pressure gradient suffices. Here H=L²((0,1)×ℝ³). The perturbation consists of measurable 1-periodic v, a weak gradient G, a weak Hessian H_v and g, with v(θ,·)∈L⁶ for almost every θ, zero divergence and Γ invariance almost everywhere, and G, tr H_v and g in H. The transport identity is g=S(α)^{−1}∂_θv+(v+y·∇v)/2 in distributions. The right-hand-side equation is F=g−tr H_v+(W_α·∇)v+(v·∇)W_α+∑β_i b_i modulo gradients, tested against all smooth solenoidal functions compactly supported in time and space.
Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.extendedCoerciveC.summary: With admissible multiplier data uniform on $\mathcal K$, decaying references, $t\ge0$ and (B.21) with $I^-<\infty$, if $c_M/\sqrt c\le c_1$, $\sqrt{t/c}\le c_2$ then $\|(v,\beta)\|_{w,\omega}\le c_1\|F\|_H+[F]+c_2|\ell(v)|$, $[F]=\sqrt{\max(R_F,0)}$ for bare rows. At $c=3/50$, $t=1000$: Lemma B.2.

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.extendedCoerciveC.text: Assume c>0, c_μ≥0, t≥0 and a≥0. Suppose that, for every α∈K and every admitted weak solution of the reference linearized equation with right-hand side F∈H and forcing coefficients β, there exist M∈H and n≥0 such that ‖M‖_H≤a(c‖v‖_w²+c_μn²)^{1/2} and c(‖v‖_w²+ω²|β|²)+c_μn²≤⟨F,M⟩+c[F]²+t|ℓ(v)|². Assume a/√c≤c₁ and √(t/c)≤c₂. Then the theorem proves ‖(v,β)‖_{w,ω}≤c₁‖F‖_H+[F]+c₂|ℓ(v)| for every such α,v,β,F. Here H=L²((0,1)×ℝ³), the quantity written ‖v‖_w² is defined by first integrating max(|tr H_v|²+w|G|_F²,0) over space and then over θ∈[0,1], and taking its real value when finite or zero when infinite, and ‖(v,β)‖_{w,ω}²=‖v‖_w²+ω²|β|². The perturbation is specified by periodic weak derivatives, L⁶ spatial slices, Γ invariance and square-integrable transport; the equation holds against solenoidal tests. Cauchy–Schwarz and the scalar quadratic inequality give the conclusion. Positivity of c excludes zero in the two displayed scalar denominators. The statement imposes no sign assumption on S(α); in the transport identity, 1/S(α) is assigned zero when S(α)=0. For the row term, put R_F=∑_kτ_k(∫₀¹∫F·u_k)². The formal quantity is [F]=√max(R_F,0). The row fields u_k and real weights τ_k are supplied data; this statement does not assume that the rows are normalized, square integrable or mutually orthogonal, or that τ_k≥0. Under the separate certificate row conditions, the u_k are orthonormal and τ_k≥0, so [F]²=R_F; rescaling e_k=√τ_k u_k gives the paper’s convention. The ordinary integrals defining the row pairings and the constraint pairings have value zero if the corresponding integrand is not integrable. Square-integrable row fields and constraint tensors remove that possibility in the certificate application. The constraint is ℓ_i(v)=∫₀¹∫Ξ_i:∇v, with the tensor indices identified as output and differentiation direction. The admitted perturbations have Γ invariance almost everywhere. Their right-hand-side equation is understood against smooth solenoidal tests compactly supported in time and space, so equality modulo a pressure gradient suffices. Here H=L²((0,1)×ℝ³). The perturbation consists of measurable 1-periodic v, a weak gradient G, a weak Hessian H_v and g, with v(θ,·)∈L⁶ for almost every θ, zero divergence and Γ invariance almost everywhere, and G, tr H_v and g in H. The transport identity is g=S(α)^{−1}∂_θv+(v+y·∇v)/2 in distributions. The right-hand-side equation is F=g−tr H_v+(W_α·∇)v+(v·∇)W_α+∑β_i b_i modulo gradients, tested against all smooth solenoidal functions compactly supported in time and space. The nonnegative integrals here are lower Lebesgue integrals, defined as suprema of integrals of measurable nonnegative simple functions lying below the integrand. No positivity, measurability or boundedness hypothesis on w is present in this scalar implication. For a measurable positive bounded energy weight, the weak perturbation assumptions make the energy finite and it is the usual integral of |Δv|²+w|∇v|_F². The supplied coefficient ω need not be positive in this implication; it appears only through ω². The reference field and forcing fields are also unrestricted data here: their test equation uses everywhere-defined spatial derivatives, assigned zero where differentiability fails, and ordinary integrals with the convention already stated.
Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.extendedCoerciveC.summary: For $c>0$ and $c_\mu,t,a\ge0$, the multiplier norm bound and the quadratic inequality give (7.18) whenever $a/\sqrt c\le c_1$ and $\sqrt{t/c}\le c_2$. The formal statement allows an arbitrary energy weight and arbitrary row data.

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.isWeakSecondDeriv.text: Let K={q∈ℝᵏ: |qⱼ|≤ρⱼ for j∈J, ∑ⱼ∉J(dⱼqⱼ)²≤ρ*²}, with a selected index set J, radii ρⱼ,ρ* and scales dⱼ, as in (7.29). Let W(q,θ,y) be a supplied profile family and Hᵂ(q,θ,y) a bilinear vector map. Assume W is jointly C¹ on all of ℝᵏ×ℝ×ℝ³, has period one for every q∈ℝᵏ, and is solenoidal for q∈K. For each q∈K require Hᵂ(q) jointly measurable up to a null set and pointwise period one; require ∇(∂ⱼW(q))=Hᵂ(q)(·,eⱼ) distributionally at every time, including local integrability of both fields. With one constant D independent of q, require |W|≤D/(1+|y|), ‖DW‖op≤D/(1+|y|)² and ‖Hᵂ‖op≤D/(1+|y|)³ at every q∈K,θ,y. For any fixed q∈K, the formal conclusion is precisely these C¹ reference-field conditions for W(q),Hᵂ(q). It extracts the hypotheses needed in Proposition B.1 from a family; it supplies no numerical certificate or profile solution. Compared with §7.2, global C¹ dependence on the parameters requires derivatives that the paper does not assume, and (7.8) bounds only the field and first spatial derivative. The formal hypothesis adds the pointwise second-derivative bound.
Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.isWeakSecondDeriv.summary: For a profile family $C^1$ in $(q,\theta,y)$, periodic, solenoidal on $\mathcal K$, with weak Hessian and uniform decay of orders zero to two, each fixed $q\in\mathcal K$ gives the reference conditions of Proposition B.1. This assumes more than §7.2, including a second-derivative bound.

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.pieceBlockWith.text: At (θ,y), write Vι=|v̂ι|, Aι=|Ĝι|, Oι=|curl Ĝι| and Cι=|curl Ĥι| for the Euclidean component amplitudes in the rotating-frame Fourier expansion. For a mode set T put N(b)=(∑_{ι∈T∪(−T)}bι²)¹ᐟ². This uses a real sum, assigned zero if nonsummable. For a curl piece (T,λ,ν), let U(y) be the real supremum of |W(τ,Rφy)+½Rφy−νe₃×Rφy|, Q(y) that of |curl W(τ,Rφy)|, and Q₁(y) that of ‖L_{Hᵂ(τ,Rφy)}‖op. Here (L_A eₘ)ⱼ=∑_{a,b}εⱼₐᵦA(eₘ,eₐ)ᵦ. Each supremum is over τ,φ∈ℝ and is assigned zero when unbounded. The scalar is −(λU+|∇λ|)N(C)N(O)−λ(½Q+|ν|)N(O)²−λQ₁N(V)N(O)−λQN(A)N(O). Sum this expression over the finite curl pieces. Add over the finite velocity pieces the terms −(μU+|∇μ|)N(A)N(V)−μ|ν|N(V)², using each piece's own mode set and angular rate. The resulting sum is the whole-piece remainder used in the weak-Hessian proof of Proposition B.1. It precedes the modewise estimates of (B.16). The definition neither verifies the derivative interpretation of Hᵂ nor establishes convergence, nonpositivity or an analytic bound; these require the stated reference and admissibility conditions in the surrounding theorem.
Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.pieceBlockWith.summary: Defines the whole-piece remainder in the weak-Hessian proof of Proposition B.1: the sum over curl pieces of the norm-product losses built from U, Q and Q₁ (with Q₁ from the supplied Hessian Hᵂ), plus the velocity-piece terms. It proves no convergence, sign or bound.

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.pieceEpsBlockWith.text: At (θ,y), write Vι=|v̂ι|, Aι=|Ĝι|, Oι=|curl Ĝι| and Cι=|curl Ĥι| for the Euclidean component amplitudes in the rotating-frame Fourier expansion. For a mode set T put N(b)=(∑_{ι∈T∪(−T)}bι²)¹ᐟ². This uses a real sum, assigned zero if nonsummable. For a curl piece (T,λ,ν), let U(y) be the real supremum of |W(τ,Rφy)+½Rφy−νe₃×Rφy|, Q(y) that of |curl W(τ,Rφy)|, and Q₁(y) that of ‖L_{Hᵂ(τ,Rφy)}‖op. Here (L_A eₘ)ⱼ=∑_{a,b}εⱼₐᵦA(eₘ,eₐ)ᵦ. Each supremum is over τ,φ∈ℝ and is assigned zero when unbounded. The scalar is −(λU+|∇λ|)N(C)N(O)−λ(½Q+|ν|)N(O)²−λQ₁N(V)N(O)−λQN(A)N(O). This is the whole-piece curl loss in the proof of Proposition B.1, with the reference Hessian supplied separately. Nonnegativity of λ, convergence of the sums, boundedness of the suprema and all derivative identifications are separate hypotheses. The expression is not yet the scalar mode density (B.16), since it contains products of norms over the entire piece.
Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.pieceEpsBlockWith.summary: Defines the whole-piece curl loss of one curl piece (T,λ,ν) in the proof of Proposition B.1, −(λU+|∇λ|)N(C)N(O)−λ(½Q+|ν|)N(O)²−λQ₁N(V)N(O)−λQN(A)N(O), with Q₁ from a supplied Hessian. It is not yet the modewise density (B.16).

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.pieceEpsRestModeW.text: For a finite reference harmonic set H and a one-sided mode set T, define E_T(A,b;ι) as follows. If ι∈T, it is ∑_{α∈H, ι−α∉T}Aα b_{ι−α}. Otherwise, if −ι∈T, it is ∑_{α∈H, −ι−α∉T}Aα b_{ι+α}; otherwise it is zero. The first branch takes precedence if T meets −T. Here θ∈ℝ is normalized time, y∈ℝ³, and Rφ is rotation through φ about the third axis. The raw mode (n,k) averages the tensor at (θ+τ,Rφy) against exp(−i(2πnτ+kφ))/(2π) over 0≤τ≤1 and 0≤φ≤2π. Vector outputs are rotated back by R₋φ; each derivative input is the rotated standard basis vector Rφeⱼ. Thus v gives three complex components, a supplied linear map G gives nine, and a supplied bilinear map H gives 27. This is (B.12) with raw frequencies (n,k)=(2ι₂−ι₁,ϰι₁) for the paper's label ι. Each component integral is assigned zero if it is not integrable. For one curl piece with weight λ and mode set T, use amplitudes Vι=|v̂ι|, Aι=|Ĝι|, Oι=|curl Ĝι| and Cι=|curl Ĥι|. For W use Vᵂ,Aᵂ,Oᵂ from W,DW, and Cᵂ=|curl Ĥᵂ| from the supplied reference Hessian. The expression is −λOι[E_T(Vᵂ,C;ι)+E_T(Aᵂ,O;ι)+E_T(Cᵂ,V;ι)+E_T(Oᵂ,A;ι)]. It is the cross-boundary curl loss in the proof of Proposition B.1. Only the reference vorticity-gradient amplitude uses Hᵂ. The definition does not identify Hᵂ as ∇²W, G as ∇v or H as ∇²v, or impose λ≥0. With those identities and nonnegative weights it is the corresponding nonpositive analytic loss before the estimates of (B.16).
Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.pieceEpsRestModeW.summary: Defines the cross-boundary curl loss −λOι[E_T(Vᵂ,C;ι)+E_T(Aᵂ,O;ι)+E_T(Cᵂ,V;ι)+E_T(Oᵂ,A;ι)] of one curl piece in the proof of Proposition B.1, with only Cᵂ taken from the supplied Hessian. No derivative identity or λ≥0 is imposed.

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.pieceEpsRestModeW.text: For a finite reference harmonic set H and a one-sided mode set T, define E_T(A,b;ι) as follows. If ι∈T, it is ∑_{α∈H, ι−α∉T}Aα b_{ι−α}. Otherwise, if −ι∈T, it is ∑_{α∈H, −ι−α∉T}Aα b_{ι+α}; otherwise it is zero. The first branch takes precedence if T meets −T. Here θ∈ℝ is normalized time, y∈ℝ³, and Rφ is rotation through φ about the third axis. The raw mode (n,k) averages the tensor at (θ+τ,Rφy) against exp(−i(2πnτ+kφ))/(2π) over 0≤τ≤1 and 0≤φ≤2π. Vector outputs are rotated back by R₋φ; each derivative input is the rotated standard basis vector Rφeⱼ. Thus v gives three complex components, a supplied linear map G gives nine, and a supplied bilinear map H gives 27. This is (B.12) with raw frequencies (n,k)=(2ι₂−ι₁,ϰι₁) for the paper's label ι. Each component integral is assigned zero if it is not integrable. For one curl piece with weight λ and mode set T, use amplitudes Vι=|v̂ι|, Aι=|Ĝι|, Oι=|curl Ĝι| and Cι=|curl Ĥι|. For W use Vᵂ,Aᵂ,Oᵂ from W,DW, and Cᵂ=|curl Ĥᵂ| from the supplied reference Hessian. The expression is −λOι[E_T(Vᵂ,C;ι)+E_T(Aᵂ,O;ι)+E_T(Cᵂ,V;ι)+E_T(Oᵂ,A;ι)]. For every W, substituting its ordinary second spatial derivative for Hᵂ yields exactly the classical curl-coupling expression, as a function of all v,G,H, piece indices, modes, times and points. This is an algebraic equality in the derivation of Proposition B.1. It needs no C² hypothesis, since both formulas use the identical formal derivative values. It does not assert that those values are weak derivatives, or that the Fourier integrals have the intended analytic interpretation.

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.pieceMultiplierDe.text:
Let W:ℝ×ℝ³→ℝ³ be jointly C¹, pointwise period one in θ and pointwise solenoidal. Let Hᵂ(θ,y):ℝ³×ℝ³→ℝ³ be a supplied bilinear map at every point, jointly measurable up to a null set and pointwise period one. For every θ and each standard basis vector eⱼ, require ∂ⱼW and the map a↦Hᵂ(θ,·)(a,eⱼ) to be locally integrable and to satisfy ∇(∂ⱼW)=Hᵂ(·,eⱼ) distributionally. With one real decay constant C_W, require at every θ,y the bounds |W|≤C_W/(1+|y|), ‖DW‖op≤C_W/(1+|y|)² and ‖Hᵂ‖op≤C_W/(1+|y|)³. Fix finitely many classes of raw modes ξ=(n,k)∈ℤ², finitely many curl pieces p∈𝓟λ and velocity pieces p∈𝓟μ, a real field W and a supplied bilinear field Hᵂ. Require 0<c<1, 0<cμ<1, S>0, and a measurable axisymmetric weight w with w(y)≥w*>0 everywhere. Here axisymmetric means unchanged by every rotation Rφ about the third axis. Each piece has a mode set Nₚ, angular rate νₚ, transport bound uₚ(y), and weight λₚ(y) or μₚ(y). Put Ωₚ(ξ)=2πn/S+νₚk, χₚ(ξ)=1_{ξ∈Nₚ or −ξ∈Nₚ}, and sgnₚ(ξ)=1 on Nₚ, −1 on −Nₚ and zero elsewhere.

A finite harmonic set A⊂ℤ² contains zero, is closed under negation, and reconstructs W pointwise as ∑_{α∈A}Re Ŵα. The four prescribed real functions b⁰α,b¹α,bωα,b∇ωα must bound respectively |Ŵα|, |(DW)̂α|, |curl (DW)̂α| and |curl Ĥᵂα| at every time and point, for each α∈A. These Fourier modes are the rotating-frame averages (B.12) with raw pair (n,k)=(2ι₂−ι₁,ϰι₁). The sizes are Euclidean component norms. Two supplied functions Q,Q₁ must bound |curl W(θ,Rφy)| and ‖L_{Hᵂ(θ,Rφy)}‖op at every θ,φ,y; here (L_A eₘ)ⱼ=∑_{a,b}εⱼₐᵦA(eₘ,eₐ)ᵦ. Each uₚ(y) must dominate |W(θ,Rφy)+½Rφy−νₚe₃×Rφy| for all θ,φ,y. For each piece there is a positive constant Ω*ₚ such that Ωₚ(ξ)≥Ω*ₚ for every ξ∈Nₚ. This makes Nₚ and −Nₚ disjoint.

Every λₚ and μₚ is nonnegative, globally Lipschitz and axisymmetric. At every y, require ∑ₚ∈𝓟λ λₚ≤E* and ∑ₚ∈𝓟λ |∇λₚ|≤E′*. One constant bounds |y|λₚ uniformly over all curl pieces and points; another bounds μₚ, |y|²μₚ and |y||∇μₚ| uniformly over velocity pieces and points. With R≥0 require, for every ξ,y, (∑ₚ∈𝓟μ |sgnₚ(ξ)|μₚ)²≤R∑ₚ∈𝓟μ |sgnₚ(ξ)||Ωₚ(ξ)|μₚ. Each curl piece has eight functions a₁,ₚ,a₂,ₚ,Lₚ,t₀,ₚ,t₁,ₚ,t₂,ₚ,t₃,ₚ,sₚ; each is everywhere positive, measurable and axisymmetric. Each velocity piece has two functions a₄,ₚ,t₄,ₚ with the same three properties and a positive real number ηₚ.

The conversion functions D and Z for every class are C² and axisymmetric; D is nonnegative. The functions assigned to ξ and −ξ must agree. There is a uniform bound for |y|ʲ‖∇ʲD‖op for all classes, y and integer j=0,1,2, and a possibly different uniform bound for (1+|y|)ʲ‖∇ʲZ‖op. To state the final share condition, define Oₚ(ξ)=1_{ξ∉Nₚ}∑_{α∈A,ξ+α∈Nₚ}b⁰α+1_{−ξ∉Nₚ}∑_{α∈A,−ξ+α∈Nₚ}b⁰α, with all functions evaluated at y. Require Dξ(y)≤1−∑ₚ∈𝓟λ[a₁,ₚχₚ1_{λₚ+|∇λₚ|>0}+a₂,ₚ1_{λₚ>0}Oₚ(ξ)/sₚ] at every ξ,y. This makes the coefficient of |∇curl v̂ξ|² nonnegative. Derivatives of a merely Lipschitz weight are assigned zero at its nondifferentiability points, so these are bounds on the chosen everywhere-defined derivative expressions. These are requirements on supplied functions, not estimates proved merely by specifying them. Assume also w is bounded above. Every forcing field bᵢ:ℝ×ℝ³→ℝ³, 1≤i≤k, is jointly measurable up to a null set, pointwise period one and square integrable over [0,1]×ℝ³. No symmetry or restriction on the harmonics of these forcing fields is imposed in this statement. Here a perturbation is given by v,g:ℝ×ℝ³→ℝ³, a field G of linear maps and a field H of bilinear maps. All four are jointly measurable up to null sets and pointwise period one. For almost every θ, v(θ),G(θ),H(θ) are locally integrable in space, G=∇v and H(a,eⱼ)=∂ₐ(Geⱼ) distributionally, div v=tr G=0 almost everywhere, and v(θ)∈L⁶(ℝ³). Require G, tr H and g in L²([0,1]×ℝ³), where tr H=∑ⱼH(eⱼ,eⱼ) and the size of G is Frobenius. The identity g=S⁻¹∂θv+½v+½(y·∇)v is tested against every compactly supported C∞ vector field on ℝ×ℝ³. For the supplied set Γ of pairs (R,θ₀), with R orthogonal and θ₀ real, require v(θ+θ₀,Ry)=Rv(θ,y) almost everywhere for each pair. These conditions represent 𝓓ˢΓ when S>0; the formal conditions themselves admit every real S, with S⁻¹=0 at S=0, and do not select the continuous-in-time representative chosen in §7.1. For any such perturbation, any β∈ℝᵏ and any F jointly measurable up to a null set, pointwise period one and satisfying ∫₀¹∫ℝ³|F|²<∞, require F≃𝓣ˢv+(W·∇)v+(v·∇)W+∑βᵢbᵢ. Here 𝓣ˢv=g−tr H. Precisely, every compactly supported C∞ solenoidal vector test φ on ℝ×ℝ³ satisfies ∫F·φ=∫[(g+G W+(DW)v+∑βᵢbᵢ)·φ+G:∇φ]. These test integrals are over all space and time; F need not be solenoidal or Γ-invariant. The conclusion is existence of such a multiplier M. The multiplier requirement means that M is jointly measurable up to a null set, pointwise period one and square integrable over [0,1]×ℝ³; ∫M·∇q=0 for every smooth periodic scalar q of uniformly compact spatial support; and, for every smooth periodic solenoidal vector ψ of uniformly compact spatial support, ⟨M,ψ⟩=⟨−tr H,ψ⟩+∑ξ∫Re[i∑ₚ∈𝓟λ sgnₚ(ξ)λₚ curl Ĝξ·overline(curl (∇ψ)̂ξ)+i∑ₚ∈𝓟μ sgnₚ(ξ)μₚv̂ξ·overline(ψ̂ξ)]. The integrals and pairings in this identity are over [0,1]×ℝ³. It is (B.14) after the weak derivative identifications. The real infinite series in the identity has default value zero if nonsummable. Its frequency energy N=∑ₚ∈𝓟μ∑ξ∫|sgnₚ(ξ)||Ωₚ(ξ)|μₚ|v̂ξ|² is finite and ‖M‖𝓗≤a√(cE+cμN), where E=∫(|tr H|²+w|G|²) and a=√((1+E*+E′*/√w*)²/c+R/cμ). All these integrals are over one normalized period and ℝ³, and the derivative energy is finite under the stated assumptions. With X=⟨F,M⟩−cE−cμN−∑βᵢ⟨bᵢ,M⟩, the density integrals satisfy I⁺+max(−X,0)≤max(X,0)+I⁻. Here I± integrate the separate positive and negative parts of the modal density (B.16) and stretching expression (B.18), using Hᵂ and c in place of 3/50. This inequality is between nonnegative extended real numbers. If I⁻<∞, it implies I⁺<∞ and I⁺−I⁻≤X, exactly the conclusion of (B.20) after c=3/50. The formal statement asserts this implication for every choice of the data, without an additional certificate or numerical lower-bound assumption. It corresponds to Proposition B.1, with a supplied weak Hessian and c∈(0,1) rather than the fixed 3/50. The conclusion does not yet supply (B.21) or the complete coercive estimate (7.18). This card describes the theorem's statement; it is not a report of a new proof-checking run.
Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.pieceMultiplierDe.summary: For a jointly C¹ periodic solenoidal W with a supplied weak Hessian, decay bounds and admissible finite pieces, a multiplier M satisfying (B.14) exists with ‖M‖𝓗≤a√(cE+cμN), and I⁺−I⁻≤X when I⁻<∞. This is Proposition B.1 with c∈(0,1) in place of 3/50.

The admissibility assumptions in this theorem are the following. Fix a positive period S, a reference field W with a supplied second derivative, finitely many classes of physical integer frequencies, and finitely many λ and μ indices. This condition requires 0<c,c_μ<1 and a measurable axisymmetric weight w≥w₀>0. A finite sign-symmetric harmonic set containing zero must represent W. Its four amplitude bounds control the modes of W, ∇W, curl W and ∇curl W, and its two further bounds control |curl W| and the operator norm of ∇curl W along axial rotations. Each transport bound dominates |W+y/2−ν_pe₃×y|, and Ω_p has a positive lower bound on its selected set. The nonnegative λ,μ weights are globally Lipschitz and axisymmetric; |y|λ, μ, |y|²μ and |y||∇μ| have uniform bounds. For all y, ∑_pλ_p(y)≤n_λ and ∑_p|∇λ_p(y)|≤n_{∇λ}; for all ξ, (∑_p|sgn_p(ξ)|μ_p(y))²≤n_μ∑_p|sgn_p(ξ)||Ω_p(ξ)|μ_p(y), with n_μ≥0. Here Ω_p(j,j′)=2πj/S+ν_pj′ and sgn_p is 1 on the selected set, −1 on its negative and 0 elsewhere; the positive lower frequency bound makes the two sets disjoint. All auxiliary functions are positive, measurable and axisymmetric, and the μ auxiliary numbers are positive. The functions D,Z are C², axisymmetric, equal at opposite frequencies, and D≥0; |y|^j|∇^jD| and (1+|y|)^j|∇^jZ| are uniformly bounded for j=0,1,2. Finally I′₂≥0. The condition permits a variable w and c other than 3/50. It does not itself assume the field regularity and decay of W, a bound above on w, or the perturbation equation; these are separate premises of the multiplier theorem.
Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.pieceMultiplierDe.summary: Under the B.2 admissibility hypotheses and a decaying reference, a weak perturbation solving the equation modulo gradients has a divergence-free $M\in H$ satisfying (B.14), finite $\|v\|_\mu$, $\|M\|_H\le c_M(c\|v\|_w^2+c_\mu\|v\|_\mu^2)^{1/2}$, and $I^++\max(-X,0)\le\max(X,0)+I^-$ in $[0,\infty]$.

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.pieceMultiplierDe.summary: Assuming four universal assertions (the multiplier bound, smooth approximation, passage of the density bound to limits, and absorption), the formal statement concludes the weak-Hessian multiplier-density result of Proposition B.1. It proves none of the four steps or (B.21).

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.pieceRestWith.text: For a raw mode ι, start with (D−c)|Ĥι|²+(1−D)|curl Ĥι|²+(¼−Z)|curl Ĝι|²+(Z−‖D²D‖op−cw)|Ĝι|²−‖D²Z‖op|v̂ι|². Add the finite curl-piece losses coupling v,G,H to W,DW,Hᵂ across the boundary of each one-sided mode set, with the four products velocity/gradient-of-vorticity, gradient/vorticity, gradient-of-vorticity/velocity and vorticity/gradient. Add the finite velocity-piece cross-boundary losses and their η-weighted Young terms. The conversion weights D,Z are chosen by the mode's class; c specializes to 3/50. This is the modewise remainder before the whole-piece terms are absorbed in the proof of Proposition B.1. Hᵂ occurs only in the reference vorticity-gradient coupling. The definition does not assert any derivative identity or lower bound, and it is not the final five-coefficient density Iι in (B.16). The raw mode is (2ι₂−ι₁,ϰι₁) for the paper's label. No regularity, sign or integrability assumptions are part of the formula.
Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.pieceRestWith.summary: Defines the modewise remainder in the proof of Proposition B.1: quadratic terms in |Ĥι|, |curl Ĥι|, |curl Ĝι|, |Ĝι|, |v̂ι| plus the curl-piece and velocity-piece cross-boundary losses, with Hᵂ only in the reference vorticity-gradient coupling. It asserts no lower bound and is not (B.16).

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.pieceRestWith_sec.text: For a raw mode ι, start with (D−c)|Ĥι|²+(1−D)|curl Ĥι|²+(¼−Z)|curl Ĝι|²+(Z−‖D²D‖op−cw)|Ĝι|²−‖D²Z‖op|v̂ι|². Add the finite curl-piece losses coupling v,G,H to W,DW,Hᵂ across the boundary of each one-sided mode set, with the four products velocity/gradient-of-vorticity, gradient/vorticity, gradient-of-vorticity/velocity and vorticity/gradient. Add the finite velocity-piece cross-boundary losses and their η-weighted Young terms. The conversion weights D,Z are chosen by the mode's class; c specializes to 3/50. For every W, putting Hᵂ equal to its ordinary Hessian makes this expression identical to the version formed directly from W's ordinary derivatives, for all v,G,H, modes, times and points. This is an algebraic identity between the two intermediate remainders in the proof of Proposition B.1. No smoothness, summability or derivative identity for v,G,H is assumed. It does not equate a default-valued ordinary Hessian with a weak Hessian of an arbitrary nonsmooth reference.
Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.pieceRestWith_sec.summary: For every W, setting Hᵂ to its ordinary Hessian makes the weak-Hessian modewise remainder identical to the version built from the ordinary derivatives of W, for all v,G,H, modes, times and points. No smoothness, summability or derivative identity is assumed.

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.rowMultiplierIneq.text: Assume the multiplier theorem, a parameter set K containing zero through nonnegative adjoint radii, a uniformly bounded energy weight, square-integrable periodic forcing fields, and for each α∈K a C¹ periodic divergence-free reference field with the stated weak-Hessian decay. Assume admissible multiplier data for all α, with common c,c_μ and common n_λ,n_{∇λ},n_μ, and t≥0. Assume also the remaining density condition I⁻<∞ and I⁺−I⁻≥cω²|β|²−∑β_i⟨b_i,M⟩−c[F]²−t|ℓ(v)|² in its positive/negative-integral form. For every permitted weak perturbation and right-hand side, the theorem supplies M∈H and n≥0, such that ‖M‖_H≤c_M(c‖v‖_w²+c_μn²)^{1/2} and c(‖v‖_w²+ω²|β|²)+c_μn²≤⟨F,M⟩+c[F]²+t|ℓ(v)|². Here c_M²=(1+n_λ+n_{∇λ}/√w₀)²/c+n_μ/c_μ. This is the intermediate estimate in the proof of Lemma B.2; the final unsquared coercive estimate is obtained separately. For the row term, put R_F=∑_kτ_k(∫₀¹∫F·u_k)². The formal quantity is [F]=√max(R_F,0). The row fields u_k and real weights τ_k are supplied data; this statement does not assume that the rows are normalized, square integrable or mutually orthogonal, or that τ_k≥0. Under the separate certificate row conditions, the u_k are orthonormal and τ_k≥0, so [F]²=R_F; rescaling e_k=√τ_k u_k gives the paper’s convention. The ordinary integrals defining the row pairings and the constraint pairings have value zero if the corresponding integrand is not integrable. Square-integrable row fields and constraint tensors remove that possibility in the certificate application. The constraint is ℓ_i(v)=∫₀¹∫Ξ_i:∇v, with the tensor indices identified as output and differentiation direction. The admitted perturbations have Γ invariance almost everywhere. Their right-hand-side equation is understood against smooth solenoidal tests compactly supported in time and space, so equality modulo a pressure gradient suffices. Here H=L²((0,1)×ℝ³). The perturbation consists of measurable 1-periodic v, a weak gradient G, a weak Hessian H_v and g, with v(θ,·)∈L⁶ for almost every θ, zero divergence and Γ invariance almost everywhere, and G, tr H_v and g in H. The transport identity is g=S(α)^{−1}∂_θv+(v+y·∇v)/2 in distributions. The right-hand-side equation is F=g−tr H_v+(W_α·∇)v+(v·∇)W_α+∑β_i b_i modulo gradients, tested against all smooth solenoidal functions compactly supported in time and space. The proof chooses n to be the μ seminorm ‖v‖_μ. The asserted conclusion retains only n≥0 and the two displayed bounds, so it can be used as a scalar multiplier estimate without an additional identity for n.
Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.rowMultiplierIneq.summary: From the multiplier theorem and the density condition with $I^-<\infty$, each admitted solution has $M\in H$, $n\ge0$ with $\|M\|_H\le c_M(c\|v\|_w^2+c_\mu n^2)^{1/2}$ and $c(\|v\|_w^2+\omega^2|\beta|^2)+c_\mu n^2\le\langle F,M\rangle+c[F]^2+t|\ell(v)|^2$.

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.rows_nonneg.text: For any finite family of fields eₐ:ℝ×ℝ³→ℝ³, real weights τₐ and field F:ℝ×ℝ³→ℝ³, define [F]=√(∑ₐτₐ⟨F,eₐ⟩²), where the pairing is the iterated ordinary integral over space and then θ∈[0,1]. The formal statement proves [F]≥0 for every choice of these data. It assumes neither integrability nor nonnegative τₐ. A real square root is assigned zero at negative arguments; each ordinary integral is assigned zero when its own integrand is not integrable. Thus this is unconditional nonnegativity of the expression used for (7.17). It does not prove that it is a seminorm or that [F]≤c₀‖F‖𝓗 for a prescribed row bound c₀; those conclusions need further row hypotheses.
Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.rows_nonneg.summary: The row expression [F]=√(∑ₐτₐ⟨F,eₐ⟩²) is nonnegative for every choice of data, without integrability or τₐ≥0, since a real square root of a negative number is taken as zero. It is not shown to be a seminorm or bounded by c₀‖F‖𝓗.

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.stretchFormWith.text: For a reference field W, a supplied second derivative of W, a perturbation v and a supplied gradient G, this defines J=−curl v·S curl v+((v·∇)curl W)·curl v+(1/2)∑_j∇(curl W)_j·(v×∂_jv). Here S is the symmetric part of the actual first derivative of W, curl v is formed from G, and ∇curl W is formed by contracting the supplied second derivative of W. All values are functions of real θ and y∈ℝ³. Once G is the weak gradient of v and the supplied reference array is its weak second derivative, this is the paper's (B.18) almost everywhere. As a definition it imposes no regularity, sign or integrability; those enter the estimates separately.
Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.stretchFormWith.summary:
$J=-\operatorname{curl}v\cdot S\operatorname{curl}v+((v\cdot
abla)\operatorname{curl}W)\cdot\operatorname{curl}v+	frac12\sum_j
abla(\operatorname{curl}W)_j\cdot(v	imes\partial_jv)$, $S$ the symmetric part of $
abla W$, curls from supplied derivatives; with weak derivatives this is (B.18) a.e.

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.stretchFormWith_s.text: Put ω=curl G, let 𝕊=(DW+(DW)ᵀ)/2, and put L=L_{Hᵂ}, where (L eₘ)ⱼ=∑_{a,b}εⱼₐᵦHᵂ(eₘ,eₐ)ᵦ. At (θ,y) define J=−ω·𝕊ω+(Lv)·ω+½∑ⱼ,m(L eₘ)ⱼ(v×G eⱼ)ₘ. For every reference W, substituting its ordinary second spatial derivative for Hᵂ gives the earlier stretching expression, as a function of all v,G,θ,y. The formal statement imposes no regularity assumption: both expressions use the same derivative convention, including default zero where a required derivative does not exist. This is an algebraic identity between two representations of (B.18). Its unconditional validity does not establish that those derivatives agree with distributional derivatives of a nonsmooth W.
Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.stretchFormWith_s.summary: For every reference W, substituting its ordinary Hessian for Hᵂ gives the earlier stretching expression, for all v,G,θ,y, with no regularity assumption. This identity between two forms of (B.18) does not show that these derivatives agree with distributional ones.

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.vortGradMap.text: For a bilinear vector map A, let L_A be the matrix whose component j in direction m is ∑_{a,b}εⱼₐᵦ A(eₘ,eₐ)ᵦ, where ε is the alternating symbol. Thus, if A=∇²W with the derivative direction entered first, L_A=∇curl W. The formal expression defines L_A as a linear map on ℝ³ for every A. It does not assume that A is symmetric or is any field's derivative. Its operator norm is the norm used in the full vorticity-gradient bound in the weak version of Proposition B.1; componentwise Fourier amplitudes elsewhere use Frobenius norms. This is an explicit encoding of the derivative contraction in (B.18), not an additional PDE statement.
Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.vortGradMap.summary: Defines L_A, the matrix with (L_A eₘ)ⱼ=∑_{a,b}εⱼₐᵦA(eₘ,eₐ)ᵦ, for any bilinear vector map A; when A=∇²W, L_A=∇curl W. It encodes the derivative contraction in (B.18) and does not assume A is symmetric or a derivative.

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.vortGradMap_secon.text: Suppose W:ℝ×ℝ³→ℝ³ is jointly C². At every θ,y, contraction of its ordinary Hessian gives the ordinary gradient of its vorticity: L_{∇²W}(θ,y)=D(curl W(θ,·))(y), where (L_A eₘ)ⱼ=∑_{a,b}εⱼₐᵦA(eₘ,eₐ)ᵦ, eₘ are the standard basis vectors and ε is the alternating symbol. This is the classical derivative identity used in the stretching term (B.18) and its pointwise bounds. No periodicity, solenoidality, decay or equation for W is assumed. Joint C² regularity is a sufficient hypothesis in the formal statement; this theorem asserts no analogous pointwise identity for an arbitrary weak Hessian.
Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.vortGradMap_secon.summary: If W is jointly C², then L_{∇²W}(θ,y)=D(curl W(θ,·))(y) at every θ,y: contracting the Hessian gives the gradient of the vorticity, as used in (B.18). No periodicity, solenoidality, decay or equation for W is assumed.

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.vortGradSupWith.text: For a bilinear vector map A, let L_A be the matrix whose component j in direction m is ∑_{a,b}εⱼₐᵦ A(eₘ,eₐ)ᵦ, where ε is the alternating symbol. Thus, if A=∇²W with the derivative direction entered first, L_A=∇curl W. For Hᵂ(θ,y), take the real supremum of ‖L_{Hᵂ(θ,Rφy)}‖op over all real θ,φ. If Hᵂ is the reference Hessian, this is the full vorticity-gradient size used in the curl-piece loss of Proposition B.1. The formal definition does not require measurability, periodicity, boundedness or a weak derivative identity. An unbounded real supremum is assigned zero; it is then not an upper bound for the displayed norms. The surrounding admissibility hypotheses supply an actual finite dominating function.
Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.vortGradSupWith.summary: Defines the real supremum over θ,φ of ‖L_{Hᵂ(θ,Rφy)}‖op, the full vorticity-gradient size in the curl-piece loss of Proposition B.1. An unbounded supremum is taken as zero, and is then no upper bound; no measurability or boundedness is required.

Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.zero_mem_params.text: Let J⊂{1,…,k} be the selected parameter indices, let ρⱼ,ρ*,dⱼ be supplied real numbers, and put K={q∈ℝᵏ: |qⱼ|≤ρⱼ for j∈J, ∑ⱼ∉J(dⱼqⱼ)²≤ρ*²}, the parameter set (7.29). If ρⱼ≥0 for every j∈J, then q=0 belongs to K. The selected-coordinate inequalities read 0≤ρⱼ, and the remaining-coordinate inequality reads 0≤ρ*². No assumption on the signs or nonvanishing of dⱼ, or the sign of ρ*, is required for this conclusion. This proves nonemptiness under fewer hypotheses than the compactness and nondegeneracy conditions surrounding (7.29). It does not establish compactness, convexity or invertibility of any parameter frame.
Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.zero_mem_params.summary: If ρⱼ≥0 for every j∈J, then q=0 lies in the parameter set K of (7.29). No condition on dⱼ or ρ* is needed; compactness, convexity and invertibility of a parameter frame are not established.

Breakdown.ContractionInternal.exists_sma.text:
Let $Z$ be a complete normed abelian group and let $G:Z\to Z$. Suppose $b,K\ge0$, $8Kb\le1$, $\|Gz\|\le b+K\|z\|^2$ for every $z$, and $\|Gz-Gw\|\le K(\|z\|+\|w\|)\|z-w\|$ for every $z,w$. The formal statement proves that some $z\in Z$ satisfies $Gz=z$ and $\|z\|\le2b$. 

No vector space structure or differentiability of $G$ is required. The proof restricts $G$ to the closed ball of radius $2b$, where its contraction constant is at most $1/2$. In the paper this lemma is applied after composing the quadratic term with a bounded right inverse. The constants $b$ and $K$ must then be estimated in terms of the defect, the initial perturbation and that right inverse. The formal statement contains none of the specific symbols $C_{\mathcal R}$, $c_*$, $\varepsilon_0$ or the two smallness inequalities chosen in §5.2.
Breakdown.ContractionInternal.exists_sma.summary: On a complete normed abelian group, let $b,K\ge0$, $8Kb\le1$, $\|Gz\|\le b+K\|z\|^2$ and $\|Gz-Gw\|\le K(\|z\|+\|w\|)\|z-w\|$. Then $Gz=z$ for some $\|z\|\le2b$, the fixed-point estimate used in §4.5.

Breakdown.ContractionStatement.text: Let $\mathcal X,Y$ be real Banach spaces; let $A_n:Y\to Y$, $\Gamma:\mathcal X\to Y$, $E:Y\to\mathcal X$, and $J:\mathcal X\to\mathcal X$ be bounded linear maps; and let $N:Y\times Y\to Y$ be a bounded bilinear map. Fix $0<\theta\le1$. Write $\ell^\infty(Y)$ for the bounded sequences $z=(z_n)_{n\ge0}$ with their supremum norm. Suppose a bounded linear map $R:\ell^\infty(Y)\to\mathcal X\times\ell^\infty(Y)$ solves the linear problem: if $R g=(e,z)$, then $z_0-A_0z_0-\Gamma Je=g_0$ and $z_n-A_nz_n-\theta^{-1}\Gamma Ez_{n-1}=g_n$ for every $n\ge1$. Then there are $\varrho_0>0$ and a real $C_1$ such that for each $\xi\in\mathcal X$ with $\|\xi\|\le\varrho_0$ there are $e\in\mathcal X$ and a bounded sequence $z$ satisfying $\|e\|\le C_1\|\xi\|$, $z_0-A_0z_0-\Gamma(Je+\xi)=N(z_0,z_0)$, and $z_n-A_nz_n-\theta^{-1}\Gamma Ez_{n-1}=\theta^nN(z_n,z_n)$ for $n\ge1$. This is the discrete contraction step. The finite-dimensional range of the correction, the identification with continuous-time solutions, smoothness, and finite energy require further hypotheses and results. Every index and power is natural-number valued; the factor $\theta^{-1}$ is legitimate since $\theta>0$.
Breakdown.ContractionStatement.summary: Given a bounded linear $R$ solving the linear recurrence $z_0-A_0z_0-\Gamma Je=g_0$, $z_n-A_nz_n-\theta^{-1}\Gamma Ez_{n-1}=g_n$, each small $\xi$ yields $e$ with $\|e\|\le C_1\|\xi\|$ and bounded $z$ solving the quadratic version with $\theta^nN(z_n,z_n)$. This is the discrete step only.

Breakdown.DichotomyHolds.text: Let $\mathcal X$ be a real Hilbert space and let $T_0,C$ be bounded linear operators, with $C$ compact. Let $0\le b\le\alpha<\beta$ and $\|T_0\|\le b$, and write $T=T_0+C$. This assertion says that there are $\alpha<r_1<r_2<\beta$, $K>0$, and a bounded projection $P_u$ commuting with $T$, whose range is finite-dimensional, such that $\|T^n(I-P_u)\|\le Kr_1^n$ and $\|P_ux\|\le Kr_2^{-n}\|T^nP_ux\|$ for every natural number $n$ and every $x\in\mathcal X$. The restriction of $T$ maps the range of $P_u$ onto itself. Hence the complement has a controlled forward evolution and the finite-dimensional part has a controlled inverse evolution. The inequalities imply $r_2>0$, so the reciprocal in $r_2^{-n}$ is an ordinary reciprocal. The formulation uses projections and powers rather than a list of complex eigenvalues. It does not impose the existence or size of an unstable eigenvalue. Taking $b=e^{-S/4}$ and choosing $\beta<1$ is the application to the period map.
Breakdown.DichotomyHolds.summary: For $T=T_0+C$ on a real Hilbert space with $C$ compact and $\|T_0\|\le b\le\alpha<\beta$, there are $\alpha<r_1<r_2<\beta$, $K>0$ and a finite-rank projection $P_u$ commuting with $T$ with $\|T^n(I-P_u)\|\le Kr_1^n$ and $\|P_ux\|\le Kr_2^{-n}\|T^nP_ux\|$.

Breakdown.DiscreteDichotomyInternal.norm.text: Let $E$ be a real Banach space and $N:E\to E$ bounded and linear. Suppose $0<\Theta<r_2$, $A\ge0$, and $\|N^{j+1}z\|\le Ar_2^{-j-1}\|z\|$ for all natural $j$ and all $z$. For any sequence with $\|f_j\|\le R$, the formal statement proves $\|-\sum_{j\ge0}\Theta^jN^{j+1}f_j\|\le Ar_2^{-1}R(1-\Theta/r_2)^{-1}$. The proof establishes convergence by geometric comparison. The denominators are positive because $r_2>\Theta>0$. With $N$ the inverse monodromy on the projected subspace, this is the boundedness estimate for the choice of initial datum from future forcing. The paper writes the same mechanism using an unweighted decaying source sequence.
Breakdown.DiscreteDichotomyInternal.norm.summary: If $0<\Theta<r_2$, $\|N^{j+1}z\|\le Ar_2^{-j-1}\|z\|$ and $\|f_j\|\le R$, then $\|-\sum_{j\ge0}\Theta^jN^{j+1}f_j\|\le Ar_2^{-1}R(1-\Theta/r_2)^{-1}$. The paper writes the same mechanism with an unweighted decaying source.

Breakdown.DiscreteDichotomyInternal.rec_.text:
Let $E$ be a real Banach space, $B:E\to E$ bounded and linear, and let sequences $w_n,d_n$ satisfy $w_{n+1}=Bw_n+d_n$ for every natural $n$.

The formal statement proves $w_n=B^nw_0+\sum_{m=0}^{n-1}B^{n-1-m}d_m$. At $n=0$ the sum is empty and $B^0=I$. All exponents are natural numbers; the sum includes only $m<n$, so the expression $n-1-m$ agrees with ordinary nonnegative subtraction. No decay, projection, compactness or convergence hypothesis is needed because the sum is finite. Taking $B$ to be the normalized monodromy on the complementary subspace gives the forward part of the calculation in Proposition 4.3.
Breakdown.DiscreteDichotomyInternal.rec_.summary: If $w_{n+1}=Bw_n+d_n$ for all $n$, then $w_n=B^nw_0+\sum_{m=0}^{n-1}B^{n-1-m}d_m$. This is the forward part of the calculation in Proposition 4.3.

Breakdown.DiscreteDichotomyInternal.step.text:
Let $E$ be a real Banach space, let $N,M,P:E\to E$ be bounded and linear, and assume $PN=N$ and $MN=P$. Suppose $0<\Theta<r_2$, $A\ge0$, and $\|N^{j+1}z\|\le Ar_2^{-j-1}\|z\|$ for every natural $j$ and vector $z$. For a bounded sequence $f$, write $U(f)=-\sum_{j\ge0}\Theta^jN^{j+1}f_j$.

The formal statement proves $\Theta^{-1}(MU(f)+Pf_0)=U((f_{j+1})_{j\ge0})$. Geometric convergence validates the infinite sums. This is the projected, normalized recurrence for the solution determined by the future tail. It does not by itself identify the paper’s source $f_n$ with the forcing derived from the continuous linearized equation.
Breakdown.DiscreteDichotomyInternal.step.summary: If $PN=N$, $MN=P$, $0<\Theta<r_2$ and $\|N^{j+1}z\|\le Ar_2^{-j-1}\|z\|$, then $U(f)=-\sum_j\Theta^jN^{j+1}f_j$ satisfies $\Theta^{-1}(MU(f)+Pf_0)=U((f_{j+1})_j)$ for bounded $f$. It does not identify $f_n$ with the paper's forcing.

Breakdown.DiscreteDichotomyInternal.tail.text: For a bounded operator $N$ on a real normed space, a real $\Theta$, and a sequence $f_0,f_1,\ldots$, this defines $-\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\Theta^jN^{j+1}f_j$. In the dichotomy argument, $N$ is the inverse of the monodromy on the projected subspace, extended by zero on the complementary subspace. If the space is complete, $\|N^{j+1}z\|\le Ar_2^{-j-1}\|z\|$, $0<\Theta<r_2$ and $f$ is bounded, the series converges absolutely and selects the projected initial component. Natural-number powers are used. The infinite-sum operation is total and assigns zero to a nonsummable sequence, so this definition alone proves neither convergence nor the recurrence; those facts are established by the adjacent estimates.
Breakdown.DiscreteDichotomyInternal.tail.summary: Defines $-\sum_{j\ge0}\Theta^jN^{j+1}f_j$, the projected datum selected from future forcing. A nonsummable sequence gives zero, so convergence and the recurrence are proved separately.

Breakdown.DiscreteDichotomyStatement.text:
Let $E$ be a real Banach space, $M,P:E\to E$ bounded linear operators with $P^2=P$ and $PM=MP$, and let $0\le r_1<\Theta<r_2$. Suppose $\|M^n(I-P)\|\le Kr_1^n$, $\|Px\|\le Kr_2^{-n}\|M^nPx\|$ for every natural $n$ and every $x$, and $M$ maps $\operatorname{ran}P$ onto itself.

The formal statement asserts a bounded linear map $U:\ell^\infty(E)\to E$ with $PUc=Uc$, and a real $K'$, such that if $Px_0=Uc$, then the recurrence $x_{n+1}=\Theta^{-1}(Mx_n+c_n)$ obeys $\|x_n\|\le K'(\|x_0\|+\|c\|_{\ell^\infty})$ for every natural $n$. The datum’s stable component is free; its projected component is selected from the entire future source sequence.

The statement requires no finite-rank assumption. It is an estimate for a normalized sequence, not for a global physical-time curve.

This formal statement specifies an implication. Defining the implication does not prove it.
Breakdown.DiscreteDichotomyStatement.summary: Under the dichotomy bounds with $0\le r_1<\Theta<r_2$, asserts a bounded linear $U$ with $PU=U$ and $K'$ such that if $Px_0=Uc$ then $x_{n+1}=\Theta^{-1}(Mx_n+c_n)$ satisfies $\|x_n\|\le K'(\|x_0\|+\|c\|_\infty)$. No finite rank is required.

Breakdown.EnergyBoundedOn.text: For a field $U:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ and $T\in\mathbb R$, the formal condition is that some finite constant bounds $\int_{\mathbb R^3}|U(t,x)|^2\,dx$ for every $t\in[0,T]$. The integral is the extended nonnegative integral of the squared Euclidean norm. In the formula, a real bound $A$ is replaced by $\max(A,0)$; the existential condition is therefore equivalent to the existence of a finite nonnegative bound. For measurable time slices and $T\ge0$, it implies finite kinetic energy at every time in the closed interval. Measurability is not part of this definition: without it the integral is interpreted as a lower integral, and its finiteness alone is not an assertion of $L^2$ membership. In the smooth-solution applications all time slices are measurable. The condition contains no smoothness or equation, no comparison with the initial energy, and no assertion that a single bound works as $T$ varies. The fields have values at all real times, with no restriction outside the given interval; for $T<0$ the interval is empty.
Breakdown.EnergyBoundedOn.summary: Defines the condition that one finite constant bounds $\int_{\mathbb R^3}|U(t,x)|^2dx$ for every $t\in[0,T]$, using the nonnegative integral. It contains no smoothness, equation or uniformity in $T$; for $T<0$ the interval is empty.

Breakdown.EpsPiece.text: One index p∈𝓟λ of Appendix B.2 carries a set Nₚ of raw integer modes, a constant real angular rate νₚ, a spatial weight λₚ, two energy shares, a balancing length, four further balancing functions, a scale function for mode couplings, and a transport majorant. The eight auxiliary functions are the two shares, the length, the four balancing functions and the scale. Positivity, measurability, axial symmetry and the positive frequency condition on Nₚ belong to admissibility, not to these data. The mathematical roles agree with the curl pieces in (B.14)–(B.19), but these bare data permit arbitrary mode sets and arbitrary real functions, beyond the piecewise-polynomial form required by the paper.
Breakdown.EpsPiece.summary: One curl piece of Appendix B.2: a set Nₚ of raw modes, an angular rate νₚ, a weight λₚ, eight auxiliary functions and a transport majorant. Admissibility is separate; unlike the paper, arbitrary mode sets and real functions are allowed, beyond the piecewise-polynomial form.

Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.text: For a natural number $n$, the data contain arbitrary real functions and fields: a symmetry set $\Gamma$; the period $S(\alpha)$; the approximate profile, a proposed weak Hessian and a field representing its pressure gradient; approximate forcing coefficients and complete-field constraint targets; $n$ forcing fields and $n$ matrix constraint fields; a reference profile; a spatial weight with proposed lower and upper bounds; the finite pairing fields with weights; and all scalar bounds in the linear, nonlinear and residual estimates. They also contain an invertible-matrix candidate $V$, nonzero-scale candidates $d_j$, radii and selected coordinates for $\mathcal K$, adjoint fields, the matrix $Y$, and the adjoint and complementary-coordinate bounds. Parameters, times and space points range over all of $\mathbb R^n$, $\mathbb R$ and $\mathbb R^3$. The declaration provides the objects and imposes no equations, signs, regularity, invertibility or inequalities. Those are separate certificate hypotheses. In particular these data are not intrinsically a finite machine-readable encoding: a restriction to prescribed polynomial and harmonic forms is imposed only in the later cell-data construction.
Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.summary: For natural $n$, certificate data are arbitrary real functions and fields: symmetries, period, approximate profile, weak Hessian, forcing and constraint fields, weight, adjoint fields and scalar bounds. No equations, signs, regularity or inequalities are imposed; those are separate hypotheses.

Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.IsHeld.text:
Here $X$ is the divergence-free homogeneous Sobolev space on $\mathbb R^3$, represented by its $L^6$ velocity, with $\|v\|_X=\|

abla)W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}$, $\ell_i(v)=\int_0^1\int
abla v:\Xi_i$, and $ ar\ell_i(\alpha)=t_i(\alpha)-\ell_i(W_\alpha^{\mathrm a})$, where $t_i$ is the prescribed constraint value. The assertion is a condition on supplied $f$ and $ eta$; it does not assert their existence. It imposes $ eta^{m a}(\alpha)+ eta=0$ nowhere. Although the data carry a general $\omega$, this condition uses coefficient weight one. To pass from the paper’s positive coefficient weight $\omega$ to this unit-weight condition, replace $b_i$ by $b_i/\omega$, $ eta_i$ by $\omega eta_i$, $ eta_i^{m a}$ by $\omega eta_i^{m a}$, $V$ by $V/\omega$, $b_*$ by $b_*/\omega$ and $a_*$ by $a_*/\omega$. The coefficient bound then becomes $| eta_{m formal}|^2=\omega^2| eta_{m paper}|^2$, while $\sum_i eta_i b_i$ and the column pairings with $V$ are unchanged. Rescaling $ eta$ alone would change the forcing term. Its upper bound is an essential supremum on the time circle; a bound at every real time requires a continuous representative. Positivity of $S$, validity of the inverse and integrability of the nonlinear expression are justified by separate certificate results, rather than by this definition alone. The predicate is defined for arbitrary supplied data and parameters. If a selected operator has no operator satisfying its defining characterization, it is assigned the value zero; conversion of a non-$L^2$ field to $L^2$ also uses zero. The ordinary equation written above is its interpretation under the certificate hypotheses and the realization results.
Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.IsHeld.summary: A supplied $f\in\mathcal H_{\rm div}^\Gamma$, $\beta$ is a bounded correction when, with $v=\mathcal T_S^{-1}f$, the projected equation holds, $\ell(v)=\bar\ell(\alpha)$, $(E_w(v)+|\beta|^2)^{1/2}\le2\varepsilon$ and $U(v)\le M$. Weight one: $\omega\beta$, $b_i/\omega$ replace $\beta,b_i$.

Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.actuat.text: For $\alpha$ and $j$, this is the real vector with components $\langle b_l,\psi_{\alpha,j}\rangle_{\mathcal H}-V_{lj}$. Thus it equals $\langle b,\psi_{\alpha,j}\rangle_{\mathcal H}-V_j$, using the $j$th column of $V$. The vector is used in the square-root term of (7.35). It is not the unshifted vector defined in (7.31). For the selected indices and admissible parameters the forcing and adjoint fields have finite period integrals, so the pairings are genuine $L^2$ inner products.
Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.actuat.summary: Defines the vector with components $\langle b_l,\psi_{\alpha,j}\rangle_{\mathcal H}-V_{lj}$, that is $\langle b,\psi_{\alpha,j}\rangle_{\mathcal H}-V_j$, used in the square-root term of (7.35). It is not the unshifted vector of (7.31).

Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.adjoin.text: The data assign a field $\psi_{\alpha,j}:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ for every parameter $\alpha\in\mathbb R^n$ and every coordinate $j$. Only selected indices $j\in\mathcal J$ and parameters $\alpha\in\mathcal K$ are constrained by the certificate hypotheses. No continuity in $\alpha$ is imposed by this data declaration. The certificate separately requires measurability, period one and a uniform $L^2$ bound on every time slice, followed by the quadratic and linear adjoint estimates.
Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.adjoin.summary: The data assign $\psi_{\alpha,j}:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ for every $\alpha\in\mathbb R^n$ and coordinate $j$; only $j\in\mathcal J$, $\alpha\in\mathcal K$ are constrained. Measurability, period one, slice $L^2$ bounds and the adjoint estimates are separate certificate conditions.

Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.adjust.text: For a parameter $\alpha$ and coordinate $j$, this is $V_j\cdot\beta^{\mathrm a}(\alpha)-\langle F_\alpha^{\mathrm a},\psi_{\alpha,j}\rangle_{\mathcal H}-(Y(\alpha)\bar\ell(\alpha))_j$. The target $\bar\ell$ is obtained by subtracting the approximate profile’s constraint from the complete-field target. This expression omits the term $d_j\alpha_j$ and has no bound attached; (7.34) is the separate requirement that its difference from $d_j\alpha_j$ have absolute value at most $o_j$.
Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.adjust.summary: Defines $V_j\cdot\beta^{\mathrm a}(\alpha)-\langle F_\alpha^{\mathrm a},\psi_{\alpha,j}\rangle_{\mathcal H}-(Y(\alpha)\bar\ell(\alpha))_j$. It omits $d_j\alpha_j$ and carries no bound; (7.34) separately bounds its difference from $d_j\alpha_j$ by $o_j$.

Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.atProf.text: For certificate data let $\vartheta=(c_1+c_0)c_{\mathrm r}$. This transformation replaces $W^{\mathrm r}$ by $W^{\mathrm a}$, sets the profile gap and quadratic-form shift to zero, divides $c_1,c_2,c_0$ and the residual seminorm bound by $1-\vartheta$, divides the seminorm weights by $(1-\vartheta)^2$, and uses the final quadratic-form constant as the new reference constant. The other relevant data are retained. The definition itself makes sense with zero-division defaults. For valid certificates $\vartheta<1$, so denominators are positive; a separate theorem proves the transformed data remain a certificate.
Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.atProf.summary: With $\vartheta=(c_1+c_0)c_{\mathrm r}$, replaces $W^{\mathrm r}$ by $W^{\mathrm a}$, sets the gap and form shift to zero, divides $c_1,c_2,c_0$ and the residual seminorm bound by $1-\vartheta$ and the seminorm weights by $(1-\vartheta)^2$. A separate theorem shows the result is a certificate.

Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.coupli.text: The data supply a real $n\times n$ matrix $Y(\alpha)$ for every parameter $\alpha$. Its $j$th row acts on the constraint vector by $(Y(\alpha)\ell(v))_j=\sum_lY_{jl}(\alpha)\ell_l(v)$. No continuity or differentiability in $\alpha$ and no invertibility of $Y$ is required. Its role is specified by the linear adjoint estimate and offset budget, rather than by this data declaration alone.
Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.coupli.summary: The data supply a real $n\times n$ matrix $Y(\alpha)$ for every $\alpha$, acting by $(Y(\alpha)\ell(v))_j=\sum_lY_{jl}(\alpha)\ell_l(v)$. No continuity, differentiability or invertibility is required.

Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.defect.text: For each parameter $\alpha$, the residual is defined pointwise as $F_\alpha^{\mathrm a}=S(\alpha)^{-1}\partial_\theta W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}+\tfrac12W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}+\tfrac12(D_yW_\alpha^{\mathrm a})y-\operatorname{tr}H_\alpha+(D_yW_\alpha^{\mathrm a})W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}+\sum_i\beta_i^{\mathrm a}(\alpha)b_i+g_\alpha$. Here $H_\alpha$ is the supplied weak Hessian, and $g_\alpha$ is a supplied field assumed to have zero pairing with every compact solenoidal space-time test. Thus $g_\alpha$ represents the gradient term without requiring a scalar pressure in the data. The square-integrability bound is imposed on this full residual, before Leray projection. The definition gives no continuity in $\alpha$ and no symmetry of the raw residual. Division by zero is assigned zero outside the certificate hypotheses; admissible periods are positive.
Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.defect.summary: Defines the residual $F_\alpha^{\rm a}=S^{-1}\partial_\theta W+\tfrac12W+\tfrac12(D_yW)y-\operatorname{tr}H_\alpha+(D_yW)W+\sum_i\beta_i^{\rm a}b_i+g_\alpha$, with $W=W_\alpha^{\rm a}$, $S=S(\alpha)$ and $g_\alpha$ a supplied gradient term. Division by zero is taken as zero.

Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.heldRi.text: For supplied certificate data, a parameter $\alpha$ and a periodic perturbation $u$, the defined right side is the pair $(-\mathbb PF_\alpha^{\rm a}-\mathbb P((u\cdot\nabla)u),\bar\ell(\alpha))$. The first component belongs to the solenoidal periodic $L^2$ space; the second records the desired values of the finitely many constraints. Thus the quadratic input has already been evaluated at $u$. Equation (7.57) in the paper initially allows an independently chosen $g\in\mathcal H$. No equation is solved and no size bound is asserted by this definition. Fields that fail the square-integrability conditions can be assigned zero during conversion to these $L^2$ spaces; the certificate and product estimates establish the required integrability in the application.
Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.heldRi.summary: Defines the right side $(-\mathbb PF_\alpha^{\rm a}-\mathbb P((u\cdot\nabla)u),\bar\ell(\alpha))$, with the quadratic term already evaluated at $u$; (7.57) in the paper first allows an independent $g\in\mathcal H$. No equation is solved and no bound asserted.

Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.params.text: For $n$ coordinates, a selected subset $\mathcal J$, radii $\varrho_j$ and $\varrho_*$, and scales $d_j$, the set is $\{\alpha:|\alpha_j|\le\varrho_j\ (j\in\mathcal J),\ \sum_{j\notin\mathcal J}(d_j\alpha_j)^2\le\varrho_*^2\}$. This is exactly (7.29). Nonnegative radii and nonzero scales are separate certificate hypotheses. Under them the set is nonempty, compact and convex; it may have empty interior. If $n=0$, the parameter space contains one empty vector and every displayed sum is zero. The definition itself imposes no sign on its input radii.
Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.params.summary: Defines $\mathcal K=\{\alpha:|\alpha_j|\le\varrho_j\ (j\in\mathcal J),\ \sum_{j\notin\mathcal J}(d_j\alpha_j)^2\le\varrho_*^2\}$, exactly (7.29). Under nonnegative radii and nonzero scales it is nonempty, compact and convex, possibly with empty interior.

Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.period.text: The data supply an everywhere-defined real function $S:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$. For a certificate, its restriction to $\mathcal K$ is continuous and satisfies $0<S(\alpha)\le S_{\max}$. These conditions are separate hypotheses; the data declaration alone permits arbitrary values, including zero or negative values and values outside the parameter set. The time coordinate of the supplied approximate field is already $\theta=s/S(\alpha)$.
Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.period.summary: The data supply an arbitrary real function $S:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$; a certificate separately requires continuity on $\mathcal K$ and $0<S(\alpha)\le S_{\max}$ there. The time coordinate of the approximate field is already $\theta=s/S(\alpha)$.

Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.profil.text: For each parameter $\alpha\in\mathbb R^n$, the data specify a field $W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$. The parameter vector has $n$ real coordinates, indexed by a finite set of size $n$; $n=0$ is allowed. The field is defined for all parameters, times and spatial points, including parameters outside $\mathcal K$. This declaration merely supplies the function. Smoothness, divergence freedom, decay, periodicity and symmetry are imposed by distinct certificate conditions.
Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.profil.summary: For each $\alpha\in\mathbb R^n$, $n=0$ allowed, the data supply a field $W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$, also for parameters outside $\mathcal K$. Smoothness, divergence freedom, decay, periodicity and symmetry are separate certificate conditions.

Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.rows.text: For a right-hand side F, this is [F]=(∑ₐτₐ⟨F,eₐ⟩²𝓗)¹ᐟ², using the certificate's finite row family over normalized time [0,1] and all of ℝ³.
