Validity requires the eₐ to be measurable, period one, square integrable and orthonormal, with 0≤τₐ≤c₀². Thus it equals (7.17) after replacing the paper's fields by √τₐeₐ, and [F]≤c₀‖F‖𝓗. The expression itself does not assert these conditions; its real square root returns zero for nonpositive arguments.
Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.rows.summary: The forcing seminorm [F]=(∑ₐτₐ⟨F,eₐ⟩²𝓗)¹ᐟ². Under validity (orthonormal eₐ, 0≤τₐ≤c₀²) it equals (7.17) with the paper's rows √τₐeₐ and satisfies [F]≤c₀‖F‖𝓗; the square root returns zero for nonpositive arguments.

Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.target.text: For each $\alpha$ and coordinate $i$, this expression is $\bar\ell_i(\alpha)=t_i(\alpha)-\ell_i(W_\alpha^{\mathrm a})$, where $t(\alpha)$ is the supplied target for the complete field and $\ell_i(U)=\int_0^1\int\nabla U:\Xi_i$. Thus the formal data prescribe the constraint on $W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}+v$, and subtract the approximate profile’s value to obtain the target for $v$. The paper directly names the latter target $\bar\ell$. This definition asserts neither the equality $\ell(v)=\bar\ell$ nor its smallness; those occur elsewhere.
Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.target.summary: Defines $\bar\ell_i(\alpha)=t_i(\alpha)-\ell_i(W_\alpha^{\mathrm a})$, where $t$ is the target for the complete field. The paper names the target for $v$ directly as $\bar\ell$; the equality $\ell(v)=\bar\ell$ is not asserted here.

Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.transf.text: This real number is defined by $\vartheta=(c_1+c_0)c_{\mathrm r}$, where $c_1$ is the full-norm coefficient in the reference a priori estimate, $c_0$ bounds the finite pairing seminorm, and $c_{\mathrm r}$ bounds the change of convection from reference to approximate profile. The definition asserts no sign or smallness. The certificate separately imposes nonnegativity of these constants and $\vartheta<1$.
Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.transf.summary: Defines $\vartheta=(c_1+c_0)c_{\mathrm r}$ from the reference a priori coefficient, the seminorm bound and the convection-change bound. No sign or smallness is asserted; the certificate separately requires nonnegativity and $\vartheta<1$.

Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.withUn.text: For data with force weight ω, replace bᵢ by bᵢ/ω and βᵢᵃ by ωβᵢᵃ, set the force weight to one, and divide the forcing bound b*, frame matrix V and remaining-coordinate operator bound a* by ω. All other fields are retained. For ω>0 this leaves ∑βᵢᵃbᵢ and the weighted coefficient energy ω²|β|² unchanged after rescaling β. It is an auxiliary normalization of (7.14) and (7.30)–(7.37), not an additional result stated in the paper. The operation is defined even at ω=0 using division by zero equal to zero; only valid certificates, which require ω>0, give the intended equivalence.
Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.withUn.summary: Normalizes the force weight to one: bᵢ becomes bᵢ/ω, βᵢᵃ becomes ωβᵢᵃ, and b*, V and a* are divided by ω. For ω>0 this preserves ∑βᵢᵃbᵢ and ω²|β|²; at ω=0 division by zero is taken as zero. It is an auxiliary normalization absent from the paper.

Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateHypothesis.text:
The formal statement asserts that there exist an integer k≥0 and data satisfying every condition below. It corresponds to the certificate premise of Corollary 7.2 with the explicit differences listed here. No numerical certificate is supplied by this existence hypothesis.

The formal statement imposes the following conditions for an integer k≥0, a set J⊆{1,…,k}, and K={α∈ℝᵏ: |αⱼ|≤ρⱼ for j∈J, ∑ⱼ∉J(dⱼαⱼ)²≤ρ*²}. The symmetry set Γ consists of pairs (R,θ₀)∈O(3)×ℝ, with invariance v(θ+θ₀,Ry)=Rv(θ,y), pointwise for approximate profiles and almost everywhere for perturbations. Conditions involving α hold for every α∈K unless all parameters are explicitly specified. This is the certificate of §§7.2–7.3 in a specific representation, with the differences stated below. Write 𝓗=L²((0,1)×ℝ³), ℓᵢ(v)=⟨∇v,Ξᵢ⟩𝓗, ‖v‖²w=∫₀¹∫(|Δv|²+w|∇v|²), and ‖(v,β)‖²w,ω=‖v‖²w+ω²|β|².

Parameter and scalar conditions. The selected radii and ρ* are nonnegative and every dⱼ is nonzero. The weight satisfies 0<w*≤w(y)≤wmax, is measurable and Γ-invariant. The force weight ω is positive. The constants c₁,c₂,c₀,cᵣ, the frozen-form transfer bound, b*, the reference-form bound and ε are nonnegative. Writing c₃ʳ for the reference-form bound, η₃ for the frozen-form transfer bound and c₃ for the final bound, one has c₃ʳ+η₃≤c₃. M and c_L are positive. With ϑ=(c₁+c₀)cᵣ, one has ϑ<1 and c₁+c₀≤(1−ϑ)c_L. S is continuous on K with 0<S(α)≤Smax. The positive integer m is 1 or is 2 with an orthogonal half-period symmetry in Γ. βᵃ and the total-field target t are continuous on K.

Approximate and reference fields. Wᵃ is jointly C¹ in all parameters, time and space, is period one for all parameters, and on K is solenoidal and Γ-invariant. One common D bounds |Wᵃ|, |DWᵃ| and the supplied Hessian |Hᵃ| by D/(1+|y|), D/(1+|y|)² and D/(1+|y|)³, respectively; the derivative norms in these three bounds are operator norms. The gradients in 𝓗 and in the weighted energies instead have the Frobenius norm. Hᵃ is jointly measurable up to null sets and period one, and at every time is the distributional derivative of DWᵃ. The supplied pressure-gradient representative hα is jointly measurable up to null sets, period one and has zero pairing with every compactly supported solenoidal space-time test. Each bᵢ is measurable, periodic, Γ-invariant almost everywhere and ∑ᵢ‖bᵢ‖²𝓗≤b*². Each Ξᵢ is jointly measurable up to null sets with finite L² norm on [0,1]×ℝ³; its values outside that interval are unused, so its periodicity is not a condition. Wʳα is jointly C¹ in time and space and period one. The change (Wᵃ−Wʳ)·∇v+v·∇(Wᵃ−Wʳ) has 𝓗 norm at most cᵣ‖v‖w for every admissible perturbation; for each time and admissible spatial u, Q_Wᵃ(u)−Q_Wʳ(u)≥−η₃|u|²w, where Q_P(u)=∫(|Δu|²+¼|∇u|²)−∫[(P·∇)u+(u·∇)P]·Δu is the form in (7.22).

A priori estimates. The finite row family eₐ is measurable, periodic, square integrable and orthonormal, with 0≤τₐ≤c₀². Define [F]²=∑ₐτₐ⟨F,eₐ⟩². A weak perturbation is represented by v,g:ℝ×ℝ³→ℝ³, a linear-map field G and a bilinear-map field H, all jointly measurable up to null sets and pointwise period one in θ. For almost every θ, v,G,H are locally integrable in space, G=∇v and H(a,eⱼ)=∂ₐ(Geⱼ) distributionally, div v=tr G=0 almost everywhere, and v(θ)∈L⁶(ℝ³). Require G, tr H and g in 𝓗, with the Frobenius norm for G and tr H=∑ⱼH(eⱼ,eⱼ). Against every compactly supported smooth vector test on ℝ×ℝ³, g represents S⁻¹∂θv+½v+½(y·∇)v. For each (R,θ₀)∈Γ require v(θ+θ₀,Ry)=Rv(θ,y) almost everywhere in space and time. This specifies representatives and their distributional identities; it does not require the chosen v to be continuous in time. In these certificate conditions S>0. Put 𝓣ˢv=g−tr H. For a reference P, the equation F≃𝓣ˢv+(P·∇)v+(v·∇)P+∑ᵢβᵢbᵢ means that, for every compactly supported smooth solenoidal test φ, ∫F·φ=∫[(g+GP+(DP)v+∑ᵢβᵢbᵢ)·φ+G:∇φ], integrated over ℝ×ℝ³. Here F is jointly measurable up to a null set, pointwise period one and in 𝓗; F is not required to be solenoidal or Γ-invariant.

For every such perturbation, every β∈ℝᵏ and every such F with P=Wʳ, one has ‖(v,β)‖w,ω≤c₁‖F‖𝓗+[F]+c₂|ℓ(v)|. For the frozen-time estimates, a spatial test field is represented by u,Gᵤ,Hᵤ with locally integrable weak derivatives Gᵤ=∇u and Hᵤ(a,eⱼ)=∂ₐ(Gᵤeⱼ), div u=0, u∈L⁶(ℝ³), and Gᵤ,tr Hᵤ∈L²(ℝ³). It obeys u(Ry)=Ru(y) almost everywhere for each (R,0)∈Γ. Write |u|²w=∫ℝ³(|tr Hᵤ|²+w|Gᵤ|²), with the Frobenius norm for Gᵤ. All unlabelled space integrals use Lebesgue measure. At every normalized time θ and for every such spatial field, the reference form satisfies Q_Wʳ(u)≥−c₃ʳ|u|²w.

Residual and size bounds. The residual is Fᵃ=S⁻¹∂θWᵃ+½Wᵃ+½(y·∇)Wᵃ−tr Hᵃ+(Wᵃ·∇)Wᵃ+∑ᵢβᵢᵃbᵢ+hα; θ=s/S is normalized time, and tr Hᵃ=∑ⱼHᵃ[eⱼ,eⱼ] represents ΔWᵃ. Nonnegative δ,δ₀ satisfy ‖Fᵃ‖𝓗≤δ≤δmax and [Fᵃ]≤δ₀. With ℓ̄=t−ℓ(Wᵃ), c₁δ+δ₀+c₂|ℓ̄|≤(1−ϑ)ε. For c_w=(4π√w*)⁻¹ᐟ² and L=Smax/m the required inequalities are 2c_Lc_wM<1; 4ε²(1/w*+2Lc₃+2Lb*/ω+2L/c_L)≤M²; and 4(1/w*+2Lc₃)ε²+4Lε(δmax+2c_wεM+2b*ε/ω)≤M². Finally 4ε²/w*<‖∇Wᵃ‖²𝓗 ensures nontriviality.

Adjoint bounds and parameter inclusion. The real matrix V is invertible; Vⱼ denotes its jth column, so Vⱼ·x=∑ᵢVᵢⱼxᵢ. The real coefficients Y=Y(α) are supplied and may depend on α. For j∈J, ψα,ⱼ is measurable and period one, with a nonnegative uniform-in-time spatial L² bound Lⱼ; the linear and quadratic error bounds aⱼ,ãⱼ are nonnegative. For every admissible v, |⟨(v·∇)v,ψα,ⱼ⟩|≤ãⱼ‖v‖²w. Put 𝓒αv=(Wᵃα·∇)v+(v·∇)Wᵃα. For every F with the measurability, periodicity and L² conditions above satisfying F≃𝓣ˢv+𝓒αv, |⟨F,ψα,ⱼ⟩−(Yℓ(v))ⱼ|≤aⱼ‖v‖w. The offset is bounded by |Vⱼ·βᵃ−⟨Fᵃ,ψα,ⱼ⟩−(Yℓ̄)ⱼ−dⱼαⱼ|≤oⱼ, and ãⱼ(2ε)²+2ε√(aⱼ²+|⟨b,ψα,ⱼ⟩−Vⱼ|²/ω²)+oⱼ≤|dⱼ|ρⱼ. For the other coordinates a*≥0, ∑ⱼ∉J(Vⱼ·x)²≤a*²|x|² for every x, √(∑ⱼ∉J(Vⱼ·βᵃ−dⱼαⱼ)²)≤o*, and 2εa*/ω+o*≤ρ*.

Comparison. The core estimates are (7.18)–(7.37). The formal statement additionally requires global C¹ parameter dependence, a pointwise Hessian decay bound and a uniform-in-time L² bound for each adjoint field; the paper's displayed assumptions only require joint continuity of Wᵃ and its time and spatial first derivatives on K, locally integrable second derivatives, and ψα,ⱼ∈𝓗. It restricts c₂ to be nonnegative whereas §7.3 initially allows c₂∈ℝ. Its unit-normalized rows with separate weights give the same seminorm as the paper's scaled orthogonal rows. The formal choice m=1 is permitted even in the presence of a half-period symmetry, whereas (7.6) chooses m=2 then; this doubles Smax/m in the two size bounds. The statement assumes these conditions for the supplied data; it does not verify a numerical instance.
Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateHypothesis.summary: There exist $k\ge0$ and data satisfying all certificate conditions of §§7.2–7.3, the premise of Corollary 7.2, with global $C^1$ parameter dependence, Hessian decay, uniform-in-time $L^2$ adjoint bounds and $c_2\ge0$ added; $m=1$ is allowed with a half-period symmetry. No values are supplied.

Breakdown.FarField.BilinKernel.text: This defines the following assertion. For every $\tau>0$ and every $g\in X$, let $u=Vg\in L^6(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$ be its reconstructed velocity. Then the physical velocity reconstructed from $K(\tau)(g,g)$ must equal $-H_\tau*(u\otimes u)$ almost everywhere in $\mathbb R^3$. The space $X$ is the real solenoidal space of frequency classes, with $g$ representing $2\pi|\xi|\hat u$, and $H_{ijk}(\tau,x)$ is the derivative kernel $\partial_k(O_\tau)_{ij}$ in its heat-kernel representation. Thus this is the diagonal case $u=v$ of the second identity in (3.10), with coefficient $-1$. It concerns arbitrary inputs in the homogeneous Sobolev space, without smoothness, but the equality is almost everywhere and the two inputs are equal. It does not state the identity for a general $W^{1,1}$ tensor divergence. This definition specifies the condition; a separate theorem proves it from the test-field identity, decay bounds for the test convolutions and a pointwise $L^3$ bound for the kernel convolution.
Breakdown.FarField.BilinKernel.summary: Defines the condition that for every $\tau>0$ and $g\in X$ with velocity $u=Vg$, the velocity of $K(\tau)(g,g)$ equals $-H_\tau*(u\otimes u)$ almost everywhere: the diagonal case $u=v$ of (3.10). A separate theorem proves it.

Breakdown.FarField.BilinTestKernel.text: This defines an assertion about the diagonal bilinear term. For every $\tau>0$ and every smooth compactly supported divergence-free field $\varphi:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$, it requires $K(\tau)(J\varphi,J\varphi)=J(-H_\tau*(\varphi\otimes\varphi))$ in $X$. Here $Jf$ is the representation of a physical field by its gradient-weighted Fourier class, $X$ is the real solenoidal $L^2$ frequency space, and $(H_\tau*F)_i=\sum_{j,k}\int H_{ijk}(\tau,y-z)F_{jk}(z)\,dz$, with $H_{ijk}=\partial_k(O_\tau)_{ij}$ in the usual heat-kernel representation. The coefficient is $-1$ because the two equal inputs cancel the $1/2$ in (3.10). Equality is asserted in the represented homogeneous Sobolev space. For arbitrary functions, a derivative is assigned zero where it does not exist, a non-$L^2$ derivative input is replaced by the zero class, and the final frequency class is assigned zero if it is not solenoidal. This condition alone therefore does not establish regularity or decay of the convolution; that is a separate hypothesis of the extension theorem. The statement supplies no general tensor-divergence identity. This formal statement states the condition. It is not, by itself, a proof that the condition holds.
Breakdown.FarField.BilinTestKernel.summary: States the condition $K(\tau)(J\varphi,J\varphi)=J(-H_\tau*(\varphi\otimes\varphi))$ in $X$ for every $\tau>0$ and smooth compactly supported divergence-free $\varphi$. The coefficient $-1$ arises from the $1/2$ in (3.10); this definition supplies no proof that the condition holds.

Breakdown.FarField.DecayBounds.text: For supplied everywhere-defined $W:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$, $q:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$ and $C\in\mathbb R$, this condition is $\|\nabla_y^jW(s,y)\|\leq C/(1+|y|)^{j+1}$ for every $s,y$ and every natural number $j\leq2$, together with $\|D_yq(s,y)\|\leq C/(1+|y|)^3$ for every $s,y$. At order zero the first norm is the Euclidean velocity norm; at orders one and two it is the linear or multilinear operator norm. The pressure derivative norm equals the Euclidean norm of the pressure gradient. These are bounds at every time and point. No existence, differentiability, periodicity or equation is asserted by the definition itself; differentiability must be supplied when interpreting the formal derivative symbols as classical derivatives. The derivatives are assigned default values where differentiability fails. The denominator is always at least one, so division by zero is irrelevant. With a smooth solution and the physical rescaling, the order-zero inequality becomes (7.66).
Breakdown.FarField.DecayBounds.summary: The condition $\|\nabla_y^jW(s,y)\|\le C/(1+|y|)^{j+1}$ for $j\le2$ and $\|D_yq(s,y)\|\le C/(1+|y|)^3$ at every $s,y$, with operator norms for derivatives. No existence or differentiability is asserted; derivatives take default values where differentiability fails.

Breakdown.FarField.HeatVelocity.text: The formal statement specifies the following identification. Let $g$ be an element of the real Hilbert space of square-integrable complex vector fields on frequency space with $g(-\xi)=\overline{g(\xi)}$ and $\xi\cdot g(\xi)=0$ almost everywhere. This represents a velocity $u\in\dot H^1_{\mathrm{div}}(\mathbb R^3)\subset L^6$ by $g(\xi)=2\pi|\xi|\widehat u(\xi)$. For every $t>0$, reconstructing the $L^6$ velocity after multiplying $g$ by $e^{-4\pi^2t|\xi|^2}$ gives, almost everywhere in $x$, the Gaussian convolution $\int(4\pi t)^{-3/2}e^{-|x-z|^2/(4t)}u(z)\,dz$. Thus it identifies the frequency construction with (2.1) on this homogeneous Sobolev space. It is a condition stated as a proposition, rather than the proof of that condition. It concerns equality of almost-everywhere classes and positive times; it does not state the heat theory on every $L^p$ space.
Breakdown.FarField.HeatVelocity.summary: States as a condition that for $g\in X$ representing $u\in\dot H^1_{\mathrm{div}}$ and every $t>0$, the velocity of $e^{-4\pi^2t|\xi|^2}g$ equals the Gaussian convolution of $u$ almost everywhere, identifying the frequency construction with (2.1).

Breakdown.FarField.IsSmoothOrbitField.text: For supplied $W,q,S,R$, the condition requires $S>0$, joint smoothness of $W$ and $q$ on all $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3$, the similarity Navier–Stokes equation and zero divergence at every point, the relation $W(s+S,y)=R W(s,R^{-1}y)$ for all $s,y$, and at least one nonzero value of $W$. It also requires one bound uniform in $s,y$ for spatial derivatives of orders zero through three, uniform spatial tail vanishing, and a square-integrable pressure gradient on every time slice. Uniform tail vanishing means: for each $\epsilon>0$ some radius works for all times. The recurrence is imposed on the velocity; no matching recurrence or normalization of the pressure is part of the condition. Spatial derivative orders are natural numbers and their norms are operator norms. The data may carry any orthogonal $R$, including the identity. No quantitative inverse-distance decay or association with a specified weak field is included.
Breakdown.FarField.IsSmoothOrbitField.summary: For $W,q,S,R$: $S>0$, $W,q$ jointly smooth, the similarity equation and $\operatorname{div}W=0$ pointwise, $W(s+S,y)=RW(s,R^{-1}y)$, $W$ nonzero somewhere, bounded derivatives to order three, uniform tail vanishing and $\nabla q(s)\in L^2$. No inverse-distance decay is included.

Breakdown.FarField.IsVelocityOf.text: Here $X$ is the divergence-free homogeneous Sobolev space on $\mathbb R^3$, represented by its $L^6$ velocity, with $\|v\|_X=\|\nabla v\|_{L^2}$. The periodic forcing space is $\mathcal H_{\rm div}=L^2(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z;L^2_{\rm div}(\mathbb R^3))$. Its elements, and the periodic perturbations, are identified when equal almost everywhere. Given a curve $w:\mathbb R\to X$ and a pointwise vector field $W:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$, this condition says that for every $s\in\mathbb R$, the $L^6$ velocity representing $w(s)$ equals $W(s,\cdot)$ almost everywhere in space. The exceptional spatial set may depend on $s$. Time is quantified by every $s$, rather than almost every $s$. The condition contains no equation, smoothness, periodicity, bound or existence assertion. When $w(s)$ has already been identified with $\mathcal W(s/S)$ in $X$, it is exactly the representative relation needed for (7.62). The definition alone does not establish that identification.
Breakdown.FarField.IsVelocityOf.summary: For a curve $w:\mathbb R\to X$ and a field $W$, for every $s\in\mathbb R$ the $L^6$ velocity of $w(s)$ equals $W(s,\cdot)$ almost everywhere in space, the exceptional set depending on $s$. No equation, smoothness or bound is included.

Breakdown.FarField.bilinKernel_of_test_d.text: The formal statement is a conditional extension theorem. Assume, first, that for every positive $\tau$ and smooth compactly supported divergence-free $\varphi$, the identity in the homogeneous Sobolev space $K(\tau)(J\varphi,J\varphi)=J(-H_\tau*(\varphi\otimes\varphi))$ holds. Assume, second, that every such negative convolution is smooth, divergence-free and satisfies bounds $|f(y)|\le A/(1+|y|)$ and $\|Df(y)\|_{\rm op}\le A/(1+|y|)^2$ for some $A$. Assume, third, that there is a constant $C$ such that for every $\tau>0$ and every tensor field $F\in L^3$, the component convolution integrals are integrable at every $y$ and $|H_\tau*F(y)|\le C\tau^{-1}\|F\|_3$. In this third assumption the tensor norm is the maximum absolute entry, whereas the paper uses the Frobenius norm; finite-dimensional equivalence changes the constant. Then, for every $g\in X$ with physical velocity $u=Vg$, the velocity of $K(\tau)(g,g)$ equals $-H_\tau*(u\otimes u)$ almost everywhere. Here $X$ is the real solenoidal gradient-weighted Fourier space and $H_{ijk}=\partial_k(O_\tau)_{ij}$ in its heat-kernel representation. The conclusion gives the diagonal part of (3.10). For distinct inputs, bilinearity and polarization give the mixed identity after taking the finite union of the relevant exceptional null sets; this deduction is not stated by this formal statement. Arbitrary tensor divergences are outside its conclusion.
Breakdown.FarField.bilinKernel_of_test_d.summary: Assuming the test-field identity, decay bounds for the convolutions and $|H_\tau*F|\le C\tau^{-1}\|F\|_3$, the velocity of $K(\tau)(g,g)$ equals $-H_\tau*(u\otimes u)$ a.e. for every $g\in X$: the diagonal part of (3.10). The last bound uses the maximum-entry tensor norm; the paper uses Frobenius.

Breakdown.FarField.breakdownOnTorus_of_w.text:
**Hypothesis.** There are a number $P>0$, an orthogonal map $R$ of $\mathbb R^3$, a nonzero measurable velocity $W(s,y)$, and supplied weak first and second spatial derivatives $G$ and $H$, all defined on $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3$. The recurrence $W(s+P,y)=R W(s,R^{-1}y)$ holds at every $(s,y)$. At every time, $G$ is the weak gradient of $W$ and $\operatorname{tr}G=0$ almost everywhere in space; the weak second derivative identity holds for almost every time. There is a finite common bound for $\int_{\mathbb R^3}|W(s)|^6$ and $\int_{\mathbb R^3}\|G(s)\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2$, at every $s$, and $\int_0^P\int_{\mathbb R^3}\|H\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2<\infty$. The operator norm of the supplied derivatives is used here; a uniform Frobenius-norm bound follows by a fixed dimensional factor. Nonzero means that $W$ does not vanish almost everywhere in space-time. For every smooth compactly supported divergence-free test field $\varphi$, the formal statement requires integrability and vanishing of
$\displaystyle \int_{\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3}\left[-W\cdot\partial_s\varphi-W\cdot\varphi-\tfrac12 W\cdot(y\cdot\nabla)\varphi+\sum_{i=1}^3 G e_i\cdot\partial_i\varphi-\sum_{i=1}^3 W_i W\cdot\partial_i\varphi\right].$
This is the viscosity-one similarity equation modulo gradients. It contains no pressure variable. The coefficient $-1$ on $W\cdot\varphi$ is the sum of the original $1/2$ zeroth-order term and the $-3/2$ term from integration by parts in the dilation. The time and space integrations use Lebesgue measure; including the endpoints of $[0,P]$ does not change the integral. Real upper bounds in nonnegative integrals are read as their nonnegative parts, so the finite bound can be chosen nonnegative.

**Conclusion.** For every viscosity $\nu>0$ there exists a smooth divergence-free datum $u_0:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$, of period one in each spatial coordinate, for which there is no globally smooth solution $(u,p)$ on $[0,\infty)\times\mathbb R^3$ with $u(0)=u_0$, satisfying $\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u=\nu\Delta u-\nabla p$ and $\operatorname{div}u=0$ for every $t>0$, whose velocity retains those three coordinate periods at every $t\ge0$. This represents the unit torus $\mathbb R^3/\mathbb Z^3$ by periodic functions on its covering space. The pressure is a real-valued function on the covering space and is allowed to be nonperiodic; the nonexistence conclusion is quantified over that larger pressure class. The formal functions are total in time, while the solution conditions concern $t\ge0$. No finite singular time, asymptotic rate, or same-profile statement is included.

**Comparison with Corollary 7.2.** A separate certificate-to-weak-profile theorem supplies the premise when certificate data are available. This formal statement starts with a weak recurrent profile and returns a nonexistence assertion. It does not retain a certificate parameter or identify the singular behavior with the smooth profile chosen in Theorem 7.1.
Breakdown.FarField.breakdownOnTorus_of_w.summary: If a nonzero weak recurrent profile exists, then for every $\nu>0$ some smooth divergence-free $u_0$ of period one in each coordinate has no globally smooth spatially periodic solution; the pressure may be nonperiodic. No singular time, rate or same-profile statement is included.

Breakdown.FarField.farFieldDecay_holds.text:
Assume a specified smooth nonzero velocity $W$ and pressure $q$ on $\mathbb R	imes\mathbb R^3$ solve the similarity equation and are divergence-free. Assume $S>0$ and $R\in O(3)$ with $W(s+S,y)=R W(s,R^{-1}y)$, a uniform bound on spatial derivatives of orders zero through three, uniform vanishing of $W$ at spatial infinity, and $
abla q(s)\in L^2(\mathbb R^3)$ for every $s$. In addition assume the infinite-time Leray-kernel integral equation $W(s,y)=-\int_0^\infty(1+	au)^{-1}\,
abla O_	au* igl[W(s-\log(1+	au),\cdot/\sqrt{1+	au})\otimes W(s-\log(1+	au),\cdot/\sqrt{1+	au}) igr](y)\,d	au$. The formal statement supplies $C$ such that $\|
abla_y^jW(s,y)\|\leq C(1+|y|)^{-j-1}$ for the natural-number orders $j=0,1,2$, and $|
abla q(s,y)|\leq C(1+|y|)^{-3}$, for every $s,y$. Derivative norms are multilinear operator norms. The proof is an integral-equation decay argument followed by differentiation and a pressure estimate; it does not import the cited Chae–Wolf theorem. Under the physical change of variables, its velocity estimate gives $|u(t,x)|\leq C/(\sqrt{1-t}+|x|)$ for $t<1$.
Breakdown.FarField.farFieldDecay_holds.summary:
For a smooth nonzero recurrent similarity solution with bounded derivatives, tail vanishing, $
abla q\in L^2$ and the Leray-kernel integral equation, $\|
abla_y^jW\|\le C(1+|y|)^{-j-1}$, $j=0,1,2$, and $|
abla q|\le C(1+|y|)^{-3}$. It does not import the Chae–Wolf theorem.

Breakdown.FarField.heatConv.text: For $t>0$ and a field $f:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$, the formal expression is the Bochner integral $\int_{\mathbb R^3}(4\pi t)^{-3/2}\exp(-|x-z|^2/(4t))f(z)\,dz$. On an $L^p$ field, $1\le p\le\infty$, this is the positive-time Gaussian convolution in (2.1). The expression is defined for every real $t$ and every field, without an integrability hypothesis in the definition. An integral of a nonintegrable function is assigned the value zero; integrability must therefore be justified before this expression is used analytically. Division by zero is assigned the value zero, and the value of the negative real power of zero here is zero. Consequently the expression at $t=0$ is zero, even for nonzero $f$. The identity $e^{0\Delta}f=f$ belongs to the separate heat operator. No assertion about negative-time heat evolution is made.
Breakdown.FarField.heatConv.summary: Defines $\int(4\pi t)^{-3/2}e^{-|x-z|^2/(4t)}f(z)\,dz$ for every real $t$ and every field. A nonintegrable integral and division by zero are taken as zero, so the expression is zero at $t=0$; integrability must be justified before analytic use.

Breakdown.FarField.heatKernelBounds_hold.text: For $G_\tau(x)=(4\pi\tau)^{-3/2}\exp(-|x|^2/(4\tau))$ and every $\tau>0$, the formal statement provides one constant $C$ with $G_\tau(x)\leq C(|x|+\sqrt\tau)^{-3}$, $|\partial_kG_\tau(x)|\leq C(|x|+\sqrt\tau)^{-4}$ and $|\partial_i\partial_j\partial_kG_\tau(x)|\leq C(|x|+\sqrt\tau)^{-6}$ for all $x$ and all three coordinate indices. The third derivative is specified by its explicit polynomial times the Gaussian. The powers $-3/2$ and the square root are real operations on positive arguments here. The exact identity for the $L^{12/11}$ norm is not stated; its scaling follows by integrating the explicit Gaussian, or a bound of the required order follows by integrating the first majorant. The theorem gives estimates for kernels, without a conclusion about a Navier–Stokes solution.
Breakdown.FarField.heatKernelBounds_hold.summary: For $G_\tau(x)=(4\pi\tau)^{-3/2}e^{-|x|^2/(4\tau)}$ and $\tau>0$, one $C$ gives $G_\tau\le C(|x|+\sqrt\tau)^{-3}$, $|\partial_kG_\tau|\le C(|x|+\sqrt\tau)^{-4}$ and $|\partial_i\partial_j\partial_kG_\tau|\le C(|x|+\sqrt\tau)^{-6}$. The $L^{12/11}$ norm identity is not stated.

Breakdown.FarField.heatVelocity_of_heatC.text: The formal statement proves Gaussian convolution agrees almost everywhere with the $L^6$ velocity of the heat evolution for every element of $\dot H^1_{\mathrm{div}}(\mathbb R^3)$ and every $t>0$, assuming two preceding facts. First, for the Gaussian $H_t(x)=(4\pi t)^{-3/2}e^{-|x|^2/(4t)}$, one common constant bounds $H_t(x)$, each first derivative, and each third derivative by the respective powers $(|x|+\sqrt t)^{-3}$, $(|x|+\sqrt t)^{-4}$, and $(|x|+\sqrt t)^{-6}$. Second, convolution with $H_t$ sends each smooth compactly supported solenoidal field $\varphi$ to a smooth solenoidal field with velocity decay $C/(1+|x|)$ and derivative decay $C/(1+|x|)^2$, and its weighted Fourier state is the heat evolution of the weighted Fourier state of $\varphi$. The state for a velocity $u$ is $2\pi|\xi|\widehat u(\xi)$ in $L^2$, and its physical velocity is an $L^6$ almost-everywhere class. The conclusion extends the test-field identity to all such states by density and continuity. Both assumptions remain explicit in this particular theorem. It asserts no pointwise identity for an arbitrary representative and no identity at $t=0$.
Breakdown.FarField.heatVelocity_of_heatC.summary: Assuming kernel bounds for the Gaussian and the test-field identity with decay, Gaussian convolution agrees almost everywhere with the $L^6$ velocity of the heat evolution for every element of $\dot H^1_{\mathrm{div}}(\mathbb R^3)$ and every $t>0$, by density. Nothing is asserted at $t=0$.

Breakdown.FarField.kernelConv.text: For a real matrix field $F=(F_{jk})$ on $\mathbb R^3$ and real parameter $\tau$, this defines the vector field with components $\int_{\mathbb R^3}\sum_{j,k=1}^3H_{ijk}(\tau,y-z)F_{jk}(z)\,dz$. The kernel $H_{ijk}$ is the heat-kernel expression for $\partial_k(O_\tau)_{ij}$ at positive time, so the index contraction is exactly the expression denoted $\nabla O_\tau*F$ in §3.2. The finite sum is inside each component integral; when the terms are integrable it may be taken outside, as in the paper’s convolution notation. No regularity or integrability condition on $F$ is part of this definition. The real integral is assigned zero when its integrand is not integrable. The hypotheses of the subsequent convolution theorems establish ordinary integrability on the positive-time domains where an analytic conclusion is used. This definition alone does not identify the convolution with projected heat evolution of an arbitrary tensor divergence.
Breakdown.FarField.kernelConv.summary: Defines the vector field with components $\int\sum_{j,k}H_{ijk}(\tau,y-z)F_{jk}(z)\,dz$, the expression $\nabla O_\tau*F$ of §3.2. No integrability is imposed on $F$; a nonintegrable integral is taken as zero.

Breakdown.FarField.kernelConvSup_holds.text: There is a real constant $C$ such that, for every $\tau>0$, measurable tensor field $F:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ and real $A$ satisfying $\max_{j,k}|F_{jk}(x)|\le A$ for every $x$, the vector $V$ with components $V_i(y)=\sum_{j,k}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\partial_k(O_\tau)_{ij}(y-x)F_{jk}(x)\,dx$ obeys $|V(y)|_{\mathbb R^3}\le C\tau^{-1/2}A$ for every $y$. The input tensor norm is the maximum absolute entry. The output vector norm is Euclidean. A Frobenius-norm bound on $F$ implies the stated input bound. The pointwise hypothesis is explicit; no choice of representative satisfying only an essential supremum is made in this statement. The differentiated kernel has integrable scalar components, so bounded measurable input gives absolutely convergent component integrals. In §7.10 this spatial estimate controls the nonlinear integral for bounded velocities. It does not itself assert a Duhamel identity or continuity of a velocity.
Breakdown.FarField.kernelConvSup_holds.summary: For measurable $F:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ with $\max_{j,k}|F_{jk}(x)|\le A$ for every $x$, the Euclidean norm of $\sum_{j,k}\partial_k(O_\tau)_{ij}*F_{jk}$ is at most $C\tau^{-1/2}A$ everywhere, for $\tau>0$. The constant is universal.

Breakdown.FarField.kernelL1Bound_holds.text: There is a finite real constant $C$ such that, for every $i,j,k\in\{1,2,3\}$ and every $\tau>0$, $x\mapsto H_{ijk}(\tau,x)$ is Lebesgue integrable and $\int_{\mathbb R^3}|H_{ijk}(\tau,x)|\,dx\le C\tau^{-1/2}$. Here $H_{ijk}$ is the three-index kernel representing $\partial_k(O_\tau)_{ij}$, defined by the heat-kernel formula $\delta_{ij}\partial_kG_\tau+\int_\tau^\infty\partial_i\partial_j\partial_kG_\rho\,d\rho$. The constant is independent of the indices and positive time. Integrability is an explicit conclusion, so the integral is the usual finite integral and not its exceptional zero value for a nonintegrable function. This theorem supplies the integrability needed to convolve tensor divergences and the $p=1$ bound with the expected exponent. It states an inequality; it does not itself give the exact scaling equality or every $L^p$ norm in the sentence following (3.9).
Breakdown.FarField.kernelL1Bound_holds.summary: There is one constant $C$ such that for all $i,j,k$ and $\tau>0$, $H_{ijk}(\tau,\cdot)$ is integrable with $\int|H_{ijk}(\tau,x)|\,dx\le C\tau^{-1/2}$. It is an inequality; it does not give the exact scaling equality or every $L^p$ norm after (3.9).

Breakdown.FarField.kernelScaling_holds.text: For all $\mu>0$, $\tau>0$ and $x\in\mathbb R^3$, the formal statement proves $G_{\mu\tau}(\sqrt\mu x)=\mu^{-3/2}G_\tau(x)$ and $H_{ijk}(\mu\tau,\sqrt\mu x)=\mu^{-2}H_{ijk}(\tau,x)$ for every coordinate triple. Here $G$ is the standard three-dimensional heat kernel and $H_{ijk}=\delta_{ij}\partial_kG_\tau+\int_\tau^\infty\partial_i\partial_j\partial_kG_\rho\,d\rho$, representing $\partial_k(O_\tau)_{ij}$. Both are pointwise identities, and all square roots and denominators are taken at positive parameters. The theorem states the homogeneity of the heat kernel and of the first derivative kernel. The paragraph following (3.9) instead states the homogeneity of $O_\tau$ itself and then an exact $L^p$ scaling law for all $1\le p\le\infty$. The derivative-kernel identity here is the scaling ingredient for that latter law; integration and finiteness of the relevant norms are additional steps.
Breakdown.FarField.kernelScaling_holds.summary: For $\mu,\tau>0$, $G_{\mu\tau}(\sqrt\mu x)=\mu^{-3/2}G_\tau(x)$ and $H_{ijk}(\mu\tau,\sqrt\mu x)=\mu^{-2}H_{ijk}(\tau,x)$ pointwise. The paper states homogeneity of $O_\tau$ and an $L^p$ scaling law; this identity is an ingredient for the latter.

Breakdown.FarField.lerayKernel.text: For indices $i,j,k\in\{1,2,3\}$, this defines the scalar kernel $H_{ijk}(\tau,x)=\delta_{ij}\partial_kG_\tau(x)+\int_\tau^\infty\partial_i\partial_j\partial_kG_\rho(x)\,d\rho$, where $G_\rho(x)=(4\pi\rho)^{-3/2}e^{-|x|^2/(4\rho)}$ on $\rho>0$. The first derivative is inserted as $-x_kG_\tau(x)/(2\tau)$, and the third derivative is inserted as its explicit polynomial times the Gaussian. This is the usual heat-kernel expression for $\partial_k(O_\tau)_{ij}$, the kernel acting on tensor divergences in (3.10). The formal object has three indices and defines that derivative kernel directly. It contains no definition of an arbitrary spatial derivative of $O_\tau$. The expression is assigned a value for every real $\tau$ by the conventions for real powers, division and integration, including division by zero equal to zero and zero assigned to a nonintegrable integral. The estimates and analytic interpretation used here require $\tau>0$, where the denominators are nonzero and convergence of the tail integral is established in the sources.
Breakdown.FarField.lerayKernel.summary: Defines $H_{ijk}(\tau,x)=\delta_{ij}\partial_kG_\tau(x)+\int_\tau^\infty\partial_i\partial_j\partial_kG_\rho(x)\,d\rho$, the heat-kernel expression for $\partial_k(O_\tau)_{ij}$. Values at $\tau\le0$ come from conventions such as division by zero taken as zero; the analysis requires $\tau>0$.

Breakdown.FarField.lerayKernelBound_hold.text: There is one finite real constant $C$ such that, for every $i,j,k\in\{1,2,3\}$, $\tau>0$ and $x\in\mathbb R^3$, the formal statement proves $|H_{ijk}(\tau,x)|\le C/(|x|+\sqrt\tau)^4$. Here $H_{ijk}=\delta_{ij}\partial_kG_\tau+\int_\tau^\infty\partial_i\partial_j\partial_kG_\rho\,d\rho$, with the standard three-dimensional heat kernel $G_\rho$; it represents $\partial_k(O_\tau)_{ij}$. The constant is uniform in space, positive time and all three coordinate indices. The inequality is componentwise. A norm bound for the entire first derivative follows by summing finitely many components and changing the constant. The exponent $4$ is a fixed natural-number power, and $|x|+\sqrt\tau>0$ under the hypothesis. The paper's (3.9) allows every nonnegative integer derivative order $l$, with a constant depending on $l$. This theorem gives its first-derivative case only.
Breakdown.FarField.lerayKernelBound_hold.summary: One constant $C$ gives $|H_{ijk}(\tau,x)|\le C/(|x|+\sqrt\tau)^4$ for all $i,j,k$, $\tau>0$ and $x$. The paper's (3.9) covers every derivative order $l$; this is its first-derivative case only.

Breakdown.FarField.lerayKernelC1_holds.text: For every $i,j,k\in\{1,2,3\}$ and every $\tau>0$, the formal statement proves that $x\mapsto H_{ijk}(\tau,x)$ is continuously differentiable on $\mathbb R^3$. The kernel is $H_{ijk}=\delta_{ij}\partial_kG_\tau+\int_\tau^\infty\partial_i\partial_j\partial_kG_\rho\,d\rho$, representing $\partial_k(O_\tau)_{ij}$. The asserted differentiability is in the spatial variable at a fixed positive time. It has no estimate for derivatives of arbitrary order, and it does not quantify over derivatives in $\tau$. The paper states that the Oseen tensor itself is smooth; this first-order regularity theorem for its derivative kernel supplies only part of that regularity information.
Breakdown.FarField.lerayKernelC1_holds.summary: For all $i,j,k$ and $\tau>0$, $x\mapsto H_{ijk}(\tau,x)$ is continuously differentiable on $\mathbb R^3$. The paper states the Oseen tensor is smooth; this gives only first-order spatial regularity of its derivative kernel.

Breakdown.FarField.periodicLerayProfileE.text:
**Hypothesis.** There are a number $P>0$, an orthogonal map $R$ of $\mathbb R^3$, a nonzero measurable velocity $W(s,y)$, and supplied weak first and second spatial derivatives $G$ and $H$, all defined on $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3$. The recurrence $W(s+P,y)=R W(s,R^{-1}y)$ holds at every $(s,y)$. At every time, $G$ is the weak gradient of $W$ and $\operatorname{tr}G=0$ almost everywhere in space; the weak second derivative identity holds for almost every time. There is a finite common bound for $\int_{\mathbb R^3}|W(s)|^6$ and $\int_{\mathbb R^3}\|G(s)\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2$, at every $s$, and $\int_0^P\int_{\mathbb R^3}\|H\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2<\infty$. The operator norm of the supplied derivatives is used here; a uniform Frobenius-norm bound follows by a fixed dimensional factor. Nonzero means that $W$ does not vanish almost everywhere in space-time. For every smooth compactly supported divergence-free test field $\varphi$, the formal statement requires integrability and vanishing of
$\displaystyle \int_{\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3}\left[-W\cdot\partial_s\varphi-W\cdot\varphi-\tfrac12 W\cdot(y\cdot\nabla)\varphi+\sum_{i=1}^3 G e_i\cdot\partial_i\varphi-\sum_{i=1}^3 W_i W\cdot\partial_i\varphi\right].$
This is the viscosity-one similarity equation modulo gradients. It contains no pressure variable. The coefficient $-1$ on $W\cdot\varphi$ is the sum of the original $1/2$ zeroth-order term and the $-3/2$ term from integration by parts in the dilation. The time and space integrations use Lebesgue measure; including the endpoints of $[0,P]$ does not change the integral. Real upper bounds in nonnegative integrals are read as their nonnegative parts, so the finite bound can be chosen nonnegative.

**Conclusion.** There exist $P>0$, an orthogonal map $R$, a finite constant $C$, and smooth functions $W:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ and $q:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$, such that $W$ is nonzero and, at every $(s,y)$,
$\displaystyle \partial_sW+\tfrac12W+\tfrac12(y\cdot\nabla)W-\Delta W+(W\cdot\nabla)W+\nabla q=0,\qquad\operatorname{div}W=0,$
$\displaystyle W(s+P,y)=R W(s,R^{-1}y),\qquad \|\nabla^jW(s,y)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le \frac C{(1+|y|)^{j+1}}\quad(j=0,1,2),\qquad |\nabla q(s,y)|\le\frac C{(1+|y|)^3}.$
The derivative orders are the three natural numbers $0,1,2$; order zero means the velocity norm. First and second derivative norms are operator norms, with the second derivative viewed as a bilinear map. The paper uses the Frobenius norm for its first-derivative bound. Since $C$ is existential and can be enlarged, that norm change does not change existence of a decaying profile. The second-derivative and pressure-gradient bounds are additional to the two displayed bounds in (1.3). The denominator is always positive. No spatial periodicity is imposed here: this is a profile on $\mathbb R^3$. The recurrence condition is on the velocity; there is no separate recurrence requirement on the pressure.

**What is retained.** The formal statement is an implication between two existence assertions. It does not take a particular weak velocity as an argument and return an identified representative of it. In particular, its conclusion contains no certificate parameter, prescribed symmetry set, chosen correction, or comparison bound. Intermediate results in the proof retain more data, but this implication by itself does not establish the same-profile assertions in Theorem 7.1 or Proposition 7.11.
Breakdown.FarField.periodicLerayProfileE.summary: If a nonzero weak recurrent profile exists, a smooth nonzero recurrent profile and pressure exist solving the similarity equation with $\|\nabla^jW\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le C(1+|y|)^{-j-1}$, $j=0,1,2$, and $|\nabla q|\le C(1+|y|)^{-3}$. The two profiles are not identified.

Breakdown.FarField.smoothFieldOfOrbit_ho.text:
Here $X$ is the divergence-free homogeneous Sobolev space on $\mathbb R^3$, represented by its $L^6$ velocity, with $\|v\|_X=\|
abla v\|_{L^2}$. The periodic forcing space is $\mathcal H_{m div}=L^2(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z;L^2_{m div}(\mathbb R^3))$. Its elements, and the periodic perturbations, are identified when equal almost everywhere. Assume a specified continuous, nonzero curve $w:\mathbb R	o X$, a period $S>0$ and $R\in O(3)$, with $w(s+S)=ho_Rw(s)$ and the similarity-variable mild identity on every interval $[s',s]$. The formal statement constructs jointly smooth functions $W(s,y)$ and $q(s,y)$ on $\mathbb R	imes\mathbb R^3$ solving $\partial_sW+ rac12W+ rac12(y\cdot
abla)W-\Delta W+(W\cdot
abla)W+
abla q=0$ and $
abla\cdot W=0$ pointwise. It retains the supplied $S$ and $R$, proves $W(s+S,y)=R W(s,R^{-1}y)$, and identifies $W(s,\cdot)$ with the velocity of $w(s)$ almost everywhere in space for every real $s$. It also proves nonvanishing, a uniform bound on spatial derivatives of orders zero through three, uniform vanishing of $W(s,y)$ as $|y|	o\infty$, and $
abla q(s)\in L^2(\mathbb R^3)$ for every $s$. The source proves these facts through Sobolev regularization and a convergent iteration for the mild equation. The theorem does not yet supply a rate of spatial decay. Equality with the specific normalized weak field $\mathcal W(s/S)$ is an additional identification, absent from its hypotheses and conclusion.
Breakdown.FarField.smoothFieldOfOrbit_ho.summary: A continuous nonzero mild orbit $w$ with $w(s+S)=\rho_Rw(s)$ yields smooth $W,q$ solving the similarity equation, with the same $S,R$, $W(s,\cdot)$ equal to $w(s)$ a.e., bounded derivatives to order three, $W\to0$ at infinity and $\nabla q\in L^2$. No decay rate is given.

Breakdown.FarField.tensorField.text: For arbitrary fields $u,v:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$, this defines the matrix field $(u\otimes v)_{jk}(x)=u_j(x)v_k(x)$. The first index records the component of $u$ and the second the component of $v$, exactly as in the paragraph before (3.10). The coordinates are represented by three possible indices, corresponding to the paper's $1,2,3$. No measurability, smoothness, incompressibility or integrability is imposed by this definition. It defines the entries only: the identity $(u\cdot\nabla)v=\operatorname{div}(v\otimes u)$ needs differentiation and zero divergence of $u$, and is not a conclusion of this formal statement. The paper's Frobenius norm $|F|^2=\sum_{j,k}F_{jk}^2$ is also a separate convention.
Breakdown.FarField.tensorField.summary: Defines $(u\otimes v)_{jk}(x)=u_j(x)v_k(x)$ for arbitrary fields, as in the paragraph before (3.10). The identity $(u\cdot\nabla)v=\operatorname{div}(v\otimes u)$ and the Frobenius norm are separate.

Breakdown.FlowBounds.text: For the earlier multiplier, these fields supply a transport majorant for each mode class; bounds for the mean field's vorticity, vorticity gradient, largest symmetric-gradient quadratic form and full gradient; and bounds for the sum of wave velocity, gradient, curl and curl-gradient amplitudes. Two more fields bound the wave part of the symmetric gradient and of the vorticity gradient uniformly in time and angle. All are real functions of y. Merely supplying them proves no nonnegativity, measurability or inequality. They play the role of the reference-profile bounds in Appendix B.2, but use a separate mean/wave decomposition rather than the paper's per-harmonic and full-field data.
Breakdown.FlowBounds.summary: Real functions of y bounding, for the earlier multiplier, the mean field's transport, vorticity, vorticity gradient, strain and gradient, and the sums of wave amplitudes. They prove nothing by themselves and use a mean/wave split instead of the per-harmonic data of Appendix B.2.

Breakdown.FlowBounds.IsValid.text: For a real reference field W and a finite wave set, this condition first requires exact pointwise reconstruction of W(θ,y) as its real zero mode averaged from time θ plus the real parts of the listed waves, also evaluated at θ. The mean field W̄ used in the subsequent inequalities is the zero mode averaged from time zero. Identifying these two zero modes uses time periodicity and integrability; neither is imposed by this condition alone. For every class it bounds |W̄+½y−a(y)e₃×y| by its transport majorant. Separate inequalities bound the mean vorticity norm, its gradient operator norm, u·DW̄u from above for every real u by the mean strain bound times |u|², and the full operator norm |DW̄|. At every time and point, the sums of modal velocity, gradient, curl and curl-gradient Euclidean amplitudes must lie below their four supplied wave bounds. At every time, angle and point, the wave symmetric-gradient quadratic form in absolute value is bounded by its strain majorant times |u|², and the wave vorticity-gradient operator norm by its final majorant. All these inequalities concern actual derivatives; smoothness of W is required separately in the multiplier theorem. This mean/wave format differs from the per-harmonic and whole-field bounds described in Appendix B.2.
Breakdown.FlowBounds.IsValid.summary: Requires $W$ to equal its zero mode averaged from time $\theta$ plus the real parts of the listed waves, and bounds the mean $\bar W$ averaged from time zero, wave amplitudes, strain and vorticity gradient by supplied majorants; equating the two zero modes needs periodicity.

Breakdown.Freq.BilinCompact.text: For positive heat time, the operator in the second input is compact when its first input is a compact smooth solenoidal field in the dense test class. Lemma 3.2 allows every first input in X; extending to that class uses density and continuity in operator norm.

Breakdown.Freq.DilationAlgebra.text:
An element of the paper’s $X$ represents a divergence-free field on $\mathbb R^3$ in $L^6$ with square-integrable gradient. Its norm is exactly $(\int_{\mathbb R^3}\sum_{i=1}^3|\partial_i u|^2)^{1/2}$; the formal representation is a closed real subspace of a complex Fourier $L^2$ space. Let $G(t)=e^{t\Delta}$ denote the heat evolution in this space. For positive real scales $\mu,
u$, the formal statement asserts $\|D_\mu x\|=\mu^{1/4}\|x\|$, $D_1=I$, $D_{\mu
u}=D_\mu D_
u$, and $D_\mu G(\mu t)=G(t)D_\mu$ for $t\ge0$. For a smooth decaying field, the Fourier representative is $F(\xi)=2\pi|\xi|\widehat u(\xi)$, so $\|F\|_2=\|
abla u\|_2$. The formal Fourier dilation is $F(\xi)\mapsto\mu^{-1/2}F(\xi/\sqrt\mu)$. The value at $\xi=0$ is immaterial in $L^2$. In physical variables $D_\mu f(y)=\sqrt\mu f(\sqrt\mu y)$. Substituting $\mu=(1-t)^{-1}$ supplies the factor $(1-t)^{-1/4}$ for $t<1$; upper or lower bounds for the particular profile remain separate. The exponent $1/4$ is real, whereas the repeated dilations in period formulas are indexed by natural numbers. No norm identity is asserted at nonpositive scale.

This formal statement specifies the assertion; defining it does not prove it.
Breakdown.Freq.DilationAlgebra.summary:
States, for positive scales $\mu,
u$ on $X$, $\|D_\mu x\|=\mu^{1/4}\|x\|$, $D_1=I$, $D_{\mu
u}=D_\mu D_
u$ and $D_\mu G(\mu t)=G(t)D_\mu$ for $t\ge0$, with $D_\mu f(y)=\sqrt\mu f(\sqrt\mu y)$. No identity is asserted at nonpositive scale; this specifies the assertion only.

Breakdown.Freq.HeatSemigroup.text: The space $X$ is the closed real subspace of $L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^3)$ satisfying $h(-\xi)=\overline{h(\xi)}$ and $\xi\cdot h(\xi)=0$ almost everywhere. An element represents a solenoidal velocity with one homogeneous derivative in $L^2$; for a smooth decaying velocity $f$, its embedding has squared norm $\int\sum_i|\partial_i f|^2$. For $t\ge0$, $G(t)$ is multiplication in frequency by $e^{-4\pi^2t|\xi|^2}$. The formal assertion states $G(0)=I$, $G(s+t)=G(s)G(t)$ for $s,t\ge0$, $\|G(t)\|\le1$, strong continuity on $[0,\infty)$, and, for every real $t$, self-adjointness and agreement with the ambient multiplier using $\max(t,0)$. The definition uses $\max(t,0)$, so negative times give the time-zero multiplier; the semigroup conclusions are restricted as stated. For $0<\kappa<1/4$, contractivity and $(1-t)^{1/4-\kappa}\le1$ yield the weighted estimate $\|G(\cdot)\chi\|_\kappa\le\|\chi\|$ on $[0,1)$, although that weighted conclusion is not itself part of this declaration.
Breakdown.Freq.HeatSemigroup.summary: States, for multiplication by $e^{-4\pi^2t|\xi|^2}$ on $X$: $G(0)=I$, $G(s+t)=G(s)G(t)$ for $s,t\ge0$, $\|G(t)\|\le1$, strong continuity on $[0,\infty)$, and self-adjointness for all real $t$. Negative times give the time-zero multiplier; the weighted estimate is not included.

Breakdown.Freq.Internal.BilinCompact.tot.text: Fix $\tau>0$, a compact set $B\subset\mathbb R^3$ and $C\ge0$. Assume that the formal Fourier transformation agrees with the integral Fourier transform on $L^1\cap L^2$, and that bounded measurable matrix multipliers combined with invertible linear changes of the frequency variable have their asserted almost-everywhere action. The formal statement proves that the set $\{2\pi|\xi|e^{-4\pi^2\tau|\xi|^2}\hat f(\xi):f\in L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3),\ \|f\|_2\le C,\ f=0\text{ a.e. outside }B\}$ is totally bounded in $L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^3)$. Total boundedness means that finitely many norm balls of every positive radius cover this image; completeness then gives compact closure. The two assumptions identify the operators already constructed in the frequency representation. This is the compactness mechanism used in the formal proof: truncate high frequencies and use compactness for the remaining Fourier transforms. It differs from the paper's particular local $H^1(B)$ to $L^2(B)$ argument through Rellich's theorem.
Breakdown.Freq.Internal.BilinCompact.tot.summary: Assuming two identifications of the Fourier operators, for $\tau>0$, compact $B$ and $C\ge0$ the set of $2\pi|\xi|e^{-4\pi^2\tau|\xi|^2}\hat f$ with $\|f\|_2\le C$, $f=0$ outside $B$, is totally bounded in $L^2$. This replaces the paper's Rellich argument by frequency truncation.

Breakdown.Freq.Internal.Dilation.longitu.text:
For every nonzero real number $c$, every $\xi\in\mathbb R^3$ and every $z\in\mathbb C^3$, the formal statement proves $Q_{c\xi}z=Q_\xi z$, where $Q_\xi z=\xi(\xi\cdot z)/|\xi|^2$ is the longitudinal projection for $\xi
e0$. The projection is extended by $Q_0=0$, using the convention that the reciprocal of zero is zero; the identity consequently also holds at $\xi=0$. The hypothesis $c
e0$ is essential when $\xi
e0$. Since the paper's solenoidal projection is $\mathbb P_\xi=I-Q_\xi$, the same identity holds for $\mathbb P$ after subtracting from the identity. Thus this is the degree-zero homogeneity used after (3.8), expressed for the complementary projection. It is an algebraic pointwise identity with no function-space hypotheses.
Breakdown.Freq.Internal.Dilation.longitu.summary: For nonzero real $c$, $Q_{c\xi}z=Q_\xi z$, where $Q_\xi z=\xi(\xi\cdot z)/|\xi|^2$ and $Q_0=0$. Since $\mathbb P_\xi=I-Q_\xi$, this is the degree-zero homogeneity used after (3.8).

Breakdown.Freq.Internal.NiceApprox.cutof.text: Let $A:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ be smooth and let $R\in\mathbb R$ satisfy $R\ne0$. For the fixed smooth bump $b$ centred at zero, equal to one on $|x|\le1$ and zero for $|x|\ge2$, the formal statement proves that $\operatorname{curl}(b(x/R)A(x))$ is smooth, compactly supported and divergence-free. These three conditions are exactly membership in $C^\infty_{c,\mathrm{div}}(\mathbb R^3)$. No decay, integrability or divergence condition is required of the potential $A$. Taking $R=r/2$ and $\eta(x)=b(2x)$ gives the paper's cutoff formula. The theorem does not itself assert the inner agreement with $u^*$ or either estimate in (5.2). The nonzero hypothesis on $R$ is essential for the compact support conclusion; division by zero is defined to be zero in the underlying scalar arithmetic.
Breakdown.Freq.Internal.NiceApprox.cutof.summary: For smooth $A$ and $R\ne0$, $\operatorname{curl}(b(x/R)A(x))$ is smooth, compactly supported and divergence-free, with $b$ the fixed bump equal to one on $|x|\le1$ and zero for $|x|\ge2$. It does not assert agreement with $u^*$ or (5.2).

Breakdown.Freq.Internal.NiceApprox.stdBu.text: This definition fixes a smooth scalar bump $b$ on Euclidean $\mathbb R^3$, centred at zero, with inner radius $1$ and outer radius $2$. As a function it satisfies $0\le b\le1$, equals one on the closed unit ball and vanishes where $|x|\ge2$. The cutoff required in (5.1) can be chosen as $\eta(x)=b(2x)$; then $\eta(x/r)=b(2x/r)$ for $r>0$. The formal radii are $1$ and $2$, so the rescaling must be stated to identify this particular definition with the paper's radii $1/2$ and $1$. No vector field or PDE is part of this definition.
Breakdown.Freq.Internal.NiceApprox.stdBu.summary: Fixes a smooth bump $b$ on $\mathbb R^3$ with $0\le b\le1$, equal to one on the closed unit ball and zero for $|x|\ge2$. The cutoff of (5.1) is $\eta(x)=b(2x)$, matching the paper's radii $1/2$ and $1$.

Breakdown.Freq.Internal.Rotation.longitu.text: For every $R\in O(3)$, $\xi\in\mathbb R^3$ and $z\in\mathbb C^3$, the formal statement proves $Q_\xi(Rz)=R\,Q_{R^{-1}\xi}z$. Here $Q_\xi z=\xi(\xi\cdot z)/|\xi|^2$ for nonzero $\xi$ and $Q_0=0$; $R$ acts complex linearly on the vector components. Replacing $\xi$ by $R\xi$ gives $Q_{R\xi}R=RQ_\xi$. Subtracting from the identity gives the paper's relation $\mathbb P_{R\xi}R=R\mathbb P_\xi$, where $\mathbb P=I-Q$. Rotations and reflections are both included. The equality holds at the origin as well because the longitudinal projection is assigned zero there. This is a pointwise algebraic identity, independent of any smoothness or integrability of a field.
Breakdown.Freq.Internal.Rotation.longitu.summary: For $R\in O(3)$, $Q_\xi(Rz)=R\,Q_{R^{-1}\xi}z$, with $Q_0=0$. Subtracting from the identity gives the paper's $\mathbb P_{R\xi}R=R\mathbb P_\xi$; rotations and reflections are both included.

Breakdown.Freq.IsMildX.text: Here $X=\dot H^1_{\mathrm{div}}(\mathbb R^3)$ is represented by the Fourier field $2\pi|\xi|\widehat u(\xi)$ in $L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^3)$, with conjugate symmetry and $\xi\cdot\widehat u=0$. Its norm is $\|\nabla u\|_2$; the velocity is recovered as an $L^6$ equivalence class. For $u:\mathbb R\to X$ and real endpoints $a,b$, this condition means continuity on $[a,b]$ and, for every $t$ there, Bochner integrability together with $u(t)=e^{(t-a)\Delta}u(a)+\int_a^tK(t-s)(u(s),u(s))\,ds$. The formal definition uses fields represented up to equality almost everywhere. It places no condition on $u$ outside $[a,b]$. At $t=a$ the integral is zero; the value chosen for $K(0)$ is immaterial to all the integrals. This is a definition of the conclusion of Lemma 3.6, not a proof that its hypotheses imply that conclusion.
Breakdown.Freq.IsMildX.summary: For $u:\mathbb R\to X=\dot H^1_{\mathrm{div}}(\mathbb R^3)$: continuity on $[a,b]$ and, for each $t$ there, Bochner integrability and $u(t)=e^{(t-a)\Delta}u(a)+\int_a^tK(t-s)(u(s),u(s))\,ds$. Nothing is required outside $[a,b]$. This defines the conclusion of Lemma 3.6 without proving it.

Breakdown.Freq.IsWeakSolution.text:
Let $a,b$ be finite real numbers and let $v:\mathbb R	imes\mathbb R^3	o\mathbb R^3$. For each $t\in[a,b]$, assume $v(t)$ is smooth and divergence-free and, for some constant $C_t$, $|v(t,x)|\le C_t/(1+|x|)$ and $\|D_xv(t,x)\|\le C_t/(1+|x|)^2$. The derivative norm here is the operator norm. No common $C_t$ is required. The formal space $X=\dot H^1_{m div}(\mathbb R^3)$ is represented by $g(\xi)=2\pi|\xi|\widehat v(\xi)\in L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^3)$, with the Fourier transform understood distributionally when $v$ itself is not integrable. Reality is $g(-\xi)=\overline{g(\xi)}$ and incompressibility is $\xi\cdot g(\xi)=0$, both almost everywhere. Its norm is $\|g\|_{L^2}=\|
abla v\|_{L^2}$, where the latter sums the squared spatial partial derivatives. The value of a representative at the single frequency $\xi=0$ does not affect the space or norm. Assume $t\mapsto v(t)$ is continuous in this space, that every difference $v(t)-v(t')$ belongs to $L^2(\mathbb R^3)$, and that $\|v(t)-v(t_0)\|_{L^2}	o0$ as $t	o t_0$ within $[a,b]$. For each smooth compactly supported divergence-free $\psi$, assume the pairing $\int v(t)\cdot\psi$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and has derivative $-\int\sum_i\partial_i v(t)\cdot\partial_i\psi-\int((v(t)\cdot
abla)v(t))\cdot\psi$ at every $a<t<b$. The formal condition consists of precisely these assumptions. It contains no pressure variable. For smooth divergence-free slices and compactly supported test fields, integration by parts rewrites the derivative as $\int[v(t)\cdot\Delta\psi+(v(t)\otimes v(t)):
abla\psi]$, with the contraction convention of (3.14). The derivative is imposed only in $(a,b)$, while continuity of the pairing is imposed up to both endpoints. Individual slices need not be in $L^2$: the $L^2$ assumptions concern their differences. Compared with Lemma 3.6, smoothness, pointwise decay and continuity of these differences are extra assumptions; continuous differentiability at the endpoints is not required. The definition itself does not require $a<b$. When $a>b$ its interval conditions are vacuous; the weak-to-mild theorem separately assumes $a<b$.
Breakdown.Freq.IsWeakSolution.summary: Defines the weak equation for a curve of smooth divergence-free slices with decay $C_t/(1+|x|)$, continuous in $X$ with $L^2$-continuous differences, whose pairings with test fields have the stated derivative on $(a,b)$. Smoothness, decay and $L^2$ differences are extra compared with Lemma 3.6.

Breakdown.Freq.MildOfWeak.text:
Let $a<b$ be finite real numbers and let $v:\mathbb R	imes\mathbb R^3	o\mathbb R^3$. For each $t\in[a,b]$, assume $v(t)$ is smooth and divergence-free and, for some constant $C_t$, $|v(t,x)|\le C_t/(1+|x|)$ and $\|D_xv(t,x)\|\le C_t/(1+|x|)^2$. The derivative norm here is the operator norm. No common $C_t$ is required. The formal space $X=\dot H^1_{m div}(\mathbb R^3)$ is represented by $g(\xi)=2\pi|\xi|\widehat v(\xi)\in L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^3)$, with the Fourier transform understood distributionally when $v$ itself is not integrable. Reality is $g(-\xi)=\overline{g(\xi)}$ and incompressibility is $\xi\cdot g(\xi)=0$, both almost everywhere. Its norm is $\|g\|_{L^2}=\|
abla v\|_{L^2}$, where the latter sums the squared spatial partial derivatives. The value of a representative at the single frequency $\xi=0$ does not affect the space or norm. Assume $t\mapsto v(t)$ is continuous in this space, that every difference $v(t)-v(t')$ belongs to $L^2(\mathbb R^3)$, and that $\|v(t)-v(t_0)\|_{L^2}	o0$ as $t	o t_0$ within $[a,b]$. For each smooth compactly supported divergence-free $\psi$, assume the pairing $\int v(t)\cdot\psi$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and has derivative $-\int\sum_i\partial_i v(t)\cdot\partial_i\psi-\int((v(t)\cdot
abla)v(t))\cdot\psi$ at every $a<t<b$. The assertion concludes that $t\mapsto v(t)$, represented in the Fourier realization of $X$, is continuous on $[a,b]$ and satisfies $v(t)=e^{(t-a)\Delta}v(a)+\int_a^tK(t-s)(v(s),v(s))\,ds$ there, with each integral Bochner integrable in $X$. The Fourier representation has norm $\|
abla v(t)\|_{L^2}$ for the smooth decaying fields under consideration. This is a weak-to-mild implication for the stated class of fields. Lemma 3.6 makes its implication for an arbitrary continuous $X$-valued curve with continuously differentiable test pairings, without these additional spatial and $L^2$-difference assumptions.
Breakdown.Freq.MildOfWeak.summary: States that smooth solenoidal decaying curves, continuous in $X$ with $L^2$-continuous differences and satisfying the weak equation on $(a,b)$, obey Duhamel’s formula on $[a,b]$. Lemma 3.6 has weaker spatial hypotheses and stronger endpoint testing.

Breakdown.Freq.Sig.text: The formal statement defines a real subspace of $L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^3)$ by the two conditions $g(-\xi)=\overline{g(\xi)}$ and $\xi\cdot g(\xi)=0$, both understood almost everywhere. The second condition is imposed by setting the longitudinal projection of $g$ equal to zero. For $\xi\ne0$ that projection is $\xi(\xi\cdot g(\xi))/|\xi|^2$; at $\xi=0$ it is assigned zero. These are bounded operations on classes modulo equality almost everywhere. In the paper's interpretation $g=2\pi|\xi|\hat u$, so they express reality and incompressibility of the velocity. The norm is the $L^2$ norm of $g$, corresponding to the homogeneous $H^1$ norm of $u$. This defines the space and its constraints; it contains no Fourier differentiation theorem and does not itself prove the physical Plancherel identity in (3.2).
Breakdown.Freq.Sig.summary: Defines the real subspace of $L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^3)$ given by $g(-\xi)=\overline{g(\xi)}$ and $\xi\cdot g(\xi)=0$ a.e., expressing reality and incompressibility for $g=2\pi|\xi|\hat u$. It does not prove the Plancherel identity in (3.2).

Breakdown.Freq.X.text: The formal space $X$ is the closed real subspace of $L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^3)$ consisting of classes $g$ such that $g(-\xi)=\overline{g(\xi)}$ and $\xi\cdot g(\xi)=0$ almost everywhere. The first condition represents a real velocity; the second represents zero divergence. The interpretation for a physical velocity $u$ is $g(\xi)=2\pi|\xi|\hat u(\xi)$, with the Fourier convention $e^{-2\pi i x\cdot\xi}$. Thus the norm on the formal space is $\|g\|_2$, corresponding to $\|\nabla u\|_2$. Elements are classes modulo equality almost everywhere, with no smoothness imposed. The denominator in the longitudinal projection is $|\xi|^2$; its reciprocal is assigned zero at $\xi=0$, which does not affect an $L^2$ class. The paper defines $X$ as divergence-free physical fields in $L^6$ with gradient in $L^2$. Identifying that description with this Fourier space requires the reconstruction and density results. This definition by itself does not assert the paper's completion theorem for all fields.
Breakdown.Freq.X.summary: $X$ is the closed real subspace of $L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^3)$ with $g(-\xi)=\overline{g(\xi)}$ and $\xi\cdot g(\xi)=0$ a.e., representing $g=2\pi|\xi|\hat u$. The paper defines $X$ by physical $L^6$ fields; the identification needs separate reconstruction and density results.

Breakdown.Freq.bilinCompact_holds.text: For every $\tau>0$ and every $g$ in the real linear span of represented smooth compactly supported divergence-free fields, the formal statement proves that $v\mapsto K(\tau)(g,v)$ is a compact linear operator from $X$ to $X$. Here $X$ is the real solenoidal $L^2$ frequency representation, whose norm corresponds to the homogeneous $H^1$ norm of physical velocities. Each element of the indicated span is the representation of one such compact smooth field, and that span is dense in $X$. Compact means that the image of the unit ball has compact closure in the norm of $X$. Lemma 3.2 allows an arbitrary first input $g\in X$. The formal statement is restricted to the dense test class; passing to every first input also uses bounded bilinearity and closure of compact operators in the operator norm. Those two ingredients explain the paper's extension, but the universal first-input quantifier is not present in this formal statement. The source proof establishes compactness by frequency truncation of compactly supported $L^2$ forcing.
Breakdown.Freq.bilinCompact_holds.summary: For $\tau>0$ and $g$ in the span of represented test fields, $v\mapsto K(\tau)(g,v)$ is compact on $X$. Lemma 3.2 allows any $g\in X$; that extension uses bilinear bounds and closure of compact operators and is not stated here.

Breakdown.Freq.bilinCont_holds.text: Fix any two elements $u,v$ of the real solenoidal homogeneous Sobolev space $X$, represented in frequency by $2\pi|\xi|\hat u$ and $2\pi|\xi|\hat v$. The formal statement proves that $\tau\mapsto K(\tau)(u,v)$ is continuous from $(0,\infty)$ to $X$ in its Hilbert norm. At positive time the bilinear term represents $-\tfrac12e^{\tau\Delta}\mathbb P[(u\cdot\nabla)v+(v\cdot\nabla)u]$, defined in $X$ by its dual pairing. The statement fixes the two input fields, imposes no smoothness or compact support on them, and does not include $\tau=0$. The total family is assigned zero at nonpositive parameters; continuity at that endpoint is not asserted. This is continuity for the bilinear input class. Lemma 3.1 separately asserts continuity for projected heat evolution of each arbitrary $L^{3/2}$ forcing.
Breakdown.Freq.bilinCont_holds.summary: For fixed $u,v\in X$, $\tau\mapsto K(\tau)(u,v)$ is continuous from $(0,\infty)$ to $X$; continuity at $\tau=0$ is not asserted. Lemma 3.1 separately concerns arbitrary $L^{3/2}$ forcing.

Breakdown.Freq.bilinDilate_holds.text: For every $\mu>0$, $\tau>0$ and $u,v\in X$, the formal statement proves $\mu D_\mu K(\mu\tau)(u,v)=K(\tau)(D_\mu u,D_\mu v)$. The space $X$ is the real solenoidal Hilbert space representing a velocity by $2\pi|\xi|\hat u$; the positive dilation represents $D_\mu u(x)=\sqrt\mu\,u(\sqrt\mu x)$. The bilinear term is the $X$-valued symmetric projected heat evolution of the two advective products, with the coefficient $-1/2$. The equality is an equality of elements of the homogeneous Sobolev space, hence of reconstructed velocities almost everywhere. Both parameters and their product are positive, so no zero default at nonpositive parameters is used. This proves the second identity in (3.8), including the factor $\mu$ on the left, for arbitrary elements of $X$.
Breakdown.Freq.bilinDilate_holds.summary: For $\mu,\tau>0$ and $u,v\in X$, $\mu D_\mu K(\mu\tau)(u,v)=K(\tau)(D_\mu u,D_\mu v)$, with $D_\mu u(x)=\sqrt\mu\,u(\sqrt\mu x)$. This proves the second identity in (3.8) for arbitrary elements of $X$.

Breakdown.Freq.bilinForm.text:
Let $X$ be the real solenoidal frequency space, with norm corresponding to $\|
abla u\|_2$, and reconstruct each element as an $L^6$ velocity with $L^2$ coordinate derivatives. For $	au>0$ and $u,v,\psi\in X$, this defines the real number $-	frac12\int_{\mathbb R^3}[(u\cdot
abla)v+(v\cdot
abla)u]\cdot\Phi_	au\psi\,dx$. In this formula physical velocities and reconstructed derivatives are used. If $g_\psi$ is the frequency representative of $\psi$, then $\Phi_	au\psi$ is the real inverse Fourier transform of $2\pi|\xi|e^{-4\pi^2	au|\xi|^2}g_\psi$; for smooth fields it represents $-\Delta e^{	au\Delta}\psi$. The bilinear term is characterized by setting its $X$ inner product with $\psi$ equal to this number. The displayed definition has all real parameters and uses integrals assigned zero when nonintegrable. The estimates in the construction prove integrability for the positive-time inputs used in the paper. This definition states the dual form and contains no existence or norm bound for the represented bilinear operator.
Breakdown.Freq.bilinForm.summary: Defines, for $u,v,\psi\in X$, the number $-\tfrac12\int[(u\cdot\nabla)v+(v\cdot\nabla)u]\cdot\Phi_\tau\psi$, where $\Phi_\tau\psi$ represents $-\Delta e^{\tau\Delta}\psi$. The bilinear term is characterized by this dual form; no existence or bound is included.

Breakdown.Freq.bilinRotate_holds.text: For every orthogonal map $R\in O(3)$, every real $\tau$ and all $u,v\in X$, the formal statement proves $\rho_R K(\tau)(u,v)=K(\tau)(\rho_Ru,\rho_Rv)$. The space $X$ is the real solenoidal $L^2$ frequency representation of homogeneous $H^1$ velocities. Its orthogonal action sends $g(\xi)$ to $Rg(R^{-1}\xi)$, corresponding to the physical action $u(x)\mapsto Ru(R^{-1}x)$ almost everywhere. At $\tau>0$, $K$ is the symmetric projected heat evolution of the two advective products, as in (2.3). At $\tau\le0$, the family is assigned zero, and the asserted equality holds for that zero map. Rotations and reflections both occur; orientation preservation is not assumed. On the positive-time range of the paper this is the last identity of (3.8).
Breakdown.Freq.bilinRotate_holds.summary: For $R\in O(3)$, real $\tau$ and $u,v\in X$, $\rho_RK(\tau)(u,v)=K(\tau)(\rho_Ru,\rho_Rv)$, with $\rho_R$ acting by $g(\xi)\mapsto Rg(R^{-1}\xi)$. For $\tau\le0$, $K$ is zero; on $\tau>0$ this is the last identity of (3.8).

Breakdown.Freq.bilinShift_holds.text: For every $s\ge0$, $\tau>0$ and $u,v\in X$, the formal statement proves $G(s)K(\tau)(u,v)=K(s+\tau)(u,v)$. Here $X$ is the real solenoidal frequency representation with norm $\|2\pi|\xi|\hat u\|_2$, $G(s)$ is multiplication by $e^{-4\pi^2s|\xi|^2}$, and $K$ is the symmetric Navier–Stokes bilinear term defined by duality and representing $-\tfrac12 e^{\tau\Delta}\mathbb P[(u\cdot\nabla)v+(v\cdot\nabla)u]$. Both bilinear time arguments are strictly positive under the hypotheses, so their assigned zero values at nonpositive parameters do not occur. No smoothness, compact support or time dependence of the two inputs is required. This is exactly the first identity of (3.8); an identity for arbitrary forcing is a different statement.
Breakdown.Freq.bilinShift_holds.summary: For $s\ge0$, $\tau>0$ and $u,v\in X$, $G(s)K(\tau)(u,v)=K(s+\tau)(u,v)$, where $G(s)$ multiplies by $e^{-4\pi^2s|\xi|^2}$. This is exactly the first identity of (3.8).

Breakdown.Freq.bilinTestFormula_holds.text: Let $\varphi:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ be smooth, compactly supported and divergence-free, let $v\in X$, and let $\tau>0$. Reconstruct $v$ as an $L^6$ velocity and its coordinate derivatives as $L^2$ fields. The formal statement proves $K(\tau)(J\varphi,v)=-\tfrac12H_\tau[(\varphi\cdot\nabla)v+(v\cdot\nabla)\varphi]$, as an equality in $X$. Here $J\varphi$ represents $2\pi|\xi|\hat\varphi$ and $H_\tau$ sends a physical $L^2$ forcing to its projected heat evolution in the weighted frequency representation. The forcing is represented by its $L^2$ class; the construction uses the zero class for a function outside $L^2$, and the estimates for this compact smooth input establish that the actual forcing belongs to $L^2$. Thus the formula agrees with the advection expression in the proof of Lemma 3.2. It is stated for one compact smooth input and one arbitrary input in the homogeneous solenoidal $H^1$ space; it does not quantify over arbitrary tensor fields.
Breakdown.Freq.bilinTestFormula_holds.summary: For smooth compactly supported divergence-free $\varphi$, $v\in X$ and $\tau>0$, $K(\tau)(J\varphi,v)=-\tfrac12H_\tau[(\varphi\cdot\nabla)v+(v\cdot\nabla)\varphi]$ in $X$, agreeing with the advection expression in the proof of Lemma 3.2.

Breakdown.Freq.bilinX.text: For each $\tau>0$, the formal definition chooses a bounded real bilinear map $K(\tau):X\times X\to X$ satisfying $\langle K(\tau)(u,v),\psi\rangle_X=-\tfrac12\int[(u\cdot\nabla)v+(v\cdot\nabla)u]\cdot\Phi_\tau\psi$ for every $u,v,\psi\in X$. The space $X$ is represented by real solenoidal frequency classes $g=2\pi|\xi|\hat u$ in $L^2$, and physical velocities lie in $L^6$. The test field $\Phi_\tau\psi$ has frequency transform $2\pi|\xi|e^{-4\pi^2\tau|\xi|^2}g_\psi$, so for smooth fields it represents $-\Delta e^{\tau\Delta}\psi$. If $\tau\le0$, or if no bounded bilinear map with the displayed property exists, the definition assigns the zero map. The supplied existence theorem proves that such a map exists for every $\tau>0$. The value at $\tau=0$ is consequently a convention; when it occurs at the endpoint of a time integral it is a single null-time value. The positive-time estimate and symmetry are separate statements.
Breakdown.Freq.bilinX.summary: For $\tau>0$, chooses a bounded bilinear $K(\tau):X\times X\to X$ with $\langle K(\tau)(u,v),\psi\rangle_X=-\tfrac12\int[(u\cdot\nabla)v+(v\cdot\nabla)u]\cdot\Phi_\tau\psi$. For $\tau\le0$, or if no such map exists, the zero map is assigned; existence for $\tau>0$ is proved separately.

Breakdown.Freq.bilinX_symm.text: For every real $\tau$ and every $u,v\in X=\dot H^1_{\mathrm{div}}(\mathbb R^3)$, the formal theorem proves $K(\tau)(u,v)=K(\tau)(v,u)$. In the source, $u$ and $v$ are represented by the square-integrable frequency fields $2\pi|\xi|\widehat u(\xi)$ and $2\pi|\xi|\widehat v(\xi)$, with conjugate symmetry and zero component parallel to $\xi$. For positive $\tau$, the operator is specified by the symmetrized transport pairing, with coefficient $-1/2$. For $\tau\le0$ it is defined to be zero, so symmetry there is a convention without a backward-time interpretation. The equality is an equality in the Hilbert space, hence an equality of the corresponding physical velocities almost everywhere. This theorem asserts symmetry; the size estimate and identification with the projected transport expression require their own statements.
Breakdown.Freq.bilinX_symm.summary: For every real $\tau$ and $u,v\in X$, $K(\tau)(u,v)=K(\tau)(v,u)$. For $\tau\le0$ the operator is zero by definition, so symmetry there is a convention.

Breakdown.Freq.bilin_holds.text:
On the real solenoidal space $X$, whose frequency representative is $g=2\pi|\xi|\hat u$ and whose norm corresponds to $\|
abla u\|_2$, the formal statement proves that a bounded real bilinear map $K(	au):X	imes X	o X$ exists for every $	au>0$. It is characterized by $\langle K(	au)(u,v),\psiangle_X=-	frac12\int[(u\cdot
abla)v+(v\cdot
abla)u]\cdot\Phi_	au\psi$, using the reconstructed physical velocities and derivatives. Here $\Phi_	au\psi$ is the real inverse Fourier transform of $2\pi|\xi|e^{-4\pi^2	au|\xi|^2}g_\psi$. There is one constant $C\ge0$, independent of $	au,u,v$, such that $\|K(	au)(u,v)\|_X\le C	au^{-3/4}\|u\|_X\|v\|_X$. The power $-3/4$ is a real exponent and $	au>0$ excludes its singular endpoint. This is the bilinear conclusion (3.7). The theorem's inputs are two elements of $X$; it does not state the first part of Lemma 3.1 for arbitrary $L^{3/2}$ forcing.
Breakdown.Freq.bilin_holds.summary: For every $\tau>0$ a bounded bilinear $K(\tau)$ on $X$ with the dual characterization exists, and one constant $C$ gives $\|K(\tau)(u,v)\|_X\le C\tau^{-3/4}\|u\|_X\|v\|_X$. This is (3.7); it does not state Lemma 3.1 for $L^{3/2}$ forcing.

Breakdown.Freq.dilationCont_holds.text: For every fixed $g$ in the real solenoidal $L^2$ frequency space $X$, the formal statement proves that $\mu\mapsto D_\mu g$ is continuous on $(0,\infty)$ in the norm of $X$. Here $D_\mu g(\xi)=\mu^{-1/2}g(\xi/\sqrt\mu)$ for $\mu>0$, representing the physical field $\sqrt\mu\,u(\sqrt\mu x)$ when $g=2\pi|\xi|\hat u$. The quantifier fixes $g$ before asserting continuity. The paper asserts joint continuity of $(\mu,g)\mapsto D_\mu g$. This follows on adding the separately proved norm formula, since $\|D_\mu g-D_{\mu_0}g_0\|\le\mu^{1/4}\|g-g_0\|+\|D_\mu g_0-D_{\mu_0}g_0\|$. The joint assertion is therefore a consequence of two results, while this statement alone gives strong continuity. No continuity at the excluded parameter $\mu=0$ is claimed.
Breakdown.Freq.dilationCont_holds.summary: For each fixed $g\in X$, $\mu\mapsto D_\mu g$ is continuous on $(0,\infty)$, where $D_\mu g(\xi)=\mu^{-1/2}g(\xi/\sqrt\mu)$. The paper asserts joint continuity in $(\mu,g)$, which follows on adding the norm formula.

Breakdown.Freq.dilation_holds.text:
Let $X$ be the real solenoidal $L^2$ frequency space, with $g=2\pi|\xi|\hat u$ representing a velocity. For $\mu>0$, its dilation acts by $g(\xi)\mapsto\mu^{-1/2}g(\xi/\sqrt\mu)$, which represents $D_\mu u(x)=\sqrt\mu\,u(\sqrt\mu x)$. The formal statement proves $\|D_\mu g\|_X=\mu^{1/4}\|g\|_X$, $D_1=I$, $D_{\mu
u}=D_\mu D_
u$ for $\mu,
u>0$, and $D_\mu G(\mu t)=G(t)D_\mu$ for $\mu>0$ and $t\ge0$, where $G(t)$ is the heat multiplier. It also confirms the stated action on frequency classes. The exponent $1/4$ is a real exponent. Although the formal dilation family has values at all real parameters, it is assigned zero for $\mu\le0$ and none of these positive-parameter identities uses those values. These conclusions establish the three identities of (3.5) in the Fourier representation.
Breakdown.Freq.dilation_holds.summary:
For $\mu,
u>0$ and $t\ge0$: $\|D_\mu g\|_X=\mu^{1/4}\|g\|_X$, $D_1=I$, $D_{\mu
u}=D_\mu D_
u$ and $D_\mu G(\mu t)=G(t)D_\mu$. These are the three identities of (3.5) in the Fourier representation.

Breakdown.Freq.embedNormLinear_holds.text: For a smooth divergence-free field $f:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$, assume $|f(y)|\le A/(1+|y|)$ and $\|Df(y)\|_{\rm op}\le A/(1+|y|)^2$ for one finite constant $A$ and every $y$. Its representation $Jf$ is formed from the $L^2$ Fourier transforms of the derivatives by $\sum_j(-i\xi_j/|\xi|)\widehat{\partial_j f}$; this equals the expected weighted transform $2\pi|\xi|\hat f$ when Fourier differentiation is used. The formal statement proves $\|Jf\|_X^2=\int\sum_{j=1}^3|\partial_j f|^2$, and proves that $J$ respects sums, differences and real scalar multiples of fields in this decay class. The norm of $X$ is the $L^2$ norm of the represented frequency class. The multipliers involving division by $|\xi|$ are assigned zero at $\xi=0$, which is a null set. This proves the physical energy identity for the stated smooth decay class; the statement does not quantify over every physical $L^6$ field with a weak gradient in $L^2$.
Breakdown.Freq.embedNormLinear_holds.summary: For smooth divergence-free $f$ with $|f|\le A/(1+|y|)$ and $\|Df\|_{\rm op}\le A/(1+|y|)^2$, $\|Jf\|_X^2=\int\sum_j|\partial_jf|^2$, and $J$ is linear on this decay class. It does not cover every $L^6$ field with gradient in $L^2$.

Breakdown.Freq.freqTrL2.text: This is the unitary Fourier transform on $L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^3)$ with Lebesgue measure and character $e^{-2\pi i x\cdot\xi}$. Elements of $L^2$ identify functions equal almost everywhere. On integrable square-integrable fields it agrees almost everywhere with $\hat f(\xi)=\int e^{-2\pi i x\cdot\xi}f(x)\,dx$; on general square-integrable fields it is the extension by continuity in the $L^2$ norm. Thus a pointwise absolutely convergent integral is not asserted for every input. The transform is complex linear, invertible and norm preserving. Its use for the homogeneous space $X$ is through a weighted Fourier representation of derivatives, rather than an assumption that every velocity belongs to $L^2$.
Breakdown.Freq.freqTrL2.summary: The unitary Fourier transform on $L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^3)$ with character $e^{-2\pi ix\cdot\xi}$. It agrees a.e. with the integral on $L^1\cap L^2$ and extends by continuity; it is complex linear, invertible and norm preserving.

Breakdown.Freq.gradSixDecay.text: There is a finite real constant $S$ such that the following holds for every smooth divergence-free field $f:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$. Assume there is one constant $A$ for which $|f(y)|\le A/(1+|y|)$ and $\|Df(y)\|_{\rm op}\le A/(1+|y|)^2$ at every $y$. Then $f\in L^6(\mathbb R^3)$ and $\|f\|_6\le S\bigl(\int_{\mathbb R^3}\sum_{j=1}^3|\partial_j f|^2\bigr)^{1/2}$.
