The integral on the right is the sum of the squares of the three column derivatives, hence the usual $\|\nabla f\|_2$; the pointwise decay hypothesis uses the operator norm of $Df$. Lebesgue measure is used throughout. The constant $S$ is independent of $f$ and $A$. The conclusion explicitly includes finite $L^6$ norm, so its conversion to a real number does not discard an infinite norm. This proves the stated inequality on the smooth solenoidal decay class. The paper's (3.1) also covers nonsolenoidal and nonsmooth $L^6$ fields with gradient in $L^2$.
Breakdown.Freq.gradSixDecay.summary: One constant $S$ gives $f\in L^6$ and $\|f\|_6\le S\|\nabla f\|_2$ for every smooth divergence-free $f$ with $|f|\le A/(1+|y|)$ and $\|Df\|_{\rm op}\le A/(1+|y|)^2$. The paper's (3.1) also covers nonsolenoidal and nonsmooth fields.

Breakdown.Freq.heatDivFree.text: For a physical real vector field $f\in L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$, this defines an $X$-valued bounded real linear operator by Fourier transformation, multiplication by $2\pi|\xi|e^{-4\pi^2\tau|\xi|^2}$, and orthogonal projection onto the real solenoidal frequency space $X$. At $\tau>0$, its intended physical velocity is $e^{\tau\Delta}\mathbb P f$; the factor $2\pi|\xi|$ is present because elements of $X$ represent this weighted velocity transform. Here $\mathbb P_\xi=I-\xi\otimes\xi/|\xi|^2$ for $\xi\ne0$, and the reciprocal at the origin is assigned zero. The value at the origin has no effect on the $L^2$ class. The construction is defined for every real $\tau$ by choosing a bounded multiplier when one exists and zero otherwise; the analytic interpretation used here is for $\tau>0$. The input of this particular operator is $L^2$. It therefore does not, by itself, assert (3.6) for arbitrary $L^{3/2}$ forcing.
Breakdown.Freq.heatDivFree.summary: Defines a bounded linear map from $L^2$ fields to $X$ by Fourier transform, multiplication by $2\pi|\xi|e^{-4\pi^2\tau|\xi|^2}$ and projection onto $X$, representing $e^{\tau\Delta}\mathbb Pf$ for $\tau>0$. Its input is $L^2$, so it does not give (3.6) for $L^{3/2}$ forcing.

Breakdown.Freq.heatFactor.text: For a real parameter $t$ and $\xi\in\mathbb R^3$, this defines $\exp(-4\pi^2\max\{t,0\}|\xi|^2)$. On the paper's domain $t\ge0$ it is exactly the heat multiplier $e^{-4\pi^2t|\xi|^2}$ for the convention $e^{-2\pi i x\cdot\xi}$. It acts on the frequency representative $g=2\pi|\xi|\hat u$, and hence gives the same multiplier on the physical transform $\hat u$ away from the origin. For $t<0$ the definition gives the constant multiplier $1$, so these negative parameter values do not describe backward heat evolution. This is the multiplier formula; the semigroup law, norm bound and strong continuity require the accompanying theorem.
Breakdown.Freq.heatFactor.summary: Defines $\exp(-4\pi^2\max\{t,0\}|\xi|^2)$, the heat multiplier for $t\ge0$. For $t<0$ it is the constant $1$, so negative parameters do not describe backward heat flow.

Breakdown.Freq.heatX.text: The formal space $X$ consists of real solenoidal frequency classes $g\in L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^3)$, representing $2\pi|\xi|\hat u$. This defines the operator $G(t):X\to X$ obtained by multiplying $g(\xi)$ by $e^{-4\pi^2\max\{t,0\}|\xi|^2}$. The construction first forms a bounded real linear operator on $L^2$ and then restricts it to $X$; if a required bounded operator or invariance property were absent, its defining formula would choose zero. The realization results in the formalisation establish both properties for this multiplier. On $t\ge0$, $G(t)$ is the representation of $e^{t\Delta}$ on the paper's $X$. On $t<0$ its multiplier is $1$, so the total definition extends the family by the identity. The definition alone is not the statement of the semigroup and continuity properties.
Breakdown.Freq.heatX.summary: Defines $G(t):X\to X$ as multiplication by $e^{-4\pi^2\max\{t,0\}|\xi|^2}$, representing $e^{t\Delta}$ for $t\ge0$ and the identity for $t<0$. Semigroup and continuity properties are stated separately.

Breakdown.Freq.heat_holds.text: On the real Hilbert space $X$ of $L^2$ classes $g$ with $g(-\xi)=\overline{g(\xi)}$ and $\xi\cdot g(\xi)=0$ almost everywhere, let $G(t)$ be multiplication by $e^{-4\pi^2\max\{t,0\}|\xi|^2}$. The formal statement proves $G(0)=I$, $G(s+t)=G(s)G(t)$ for $s,t\ge0$, $\|G(t)\|\le1$ for $t\ge0$, and continuity of $t\mapsto G(t)g$ on $[0,\infty)$ for each $g\in X$. It also states self-adjointness, $\langle G(t)g,h\rangle=\langle g,G(t)h\rangle$, for all real $t$, and confirms the indicated Fourier multiplier. An element $g$ represents $2\pi|\xi|\hat u$, so $\|g\|_X$ corresponds to $\|\nabla u\|_2$ and $G(t)$ represents the paper's heat flow. Continuity is strong continuity for each fixed input, including the endpoint $0$; no continuity in operator norm at $0$ is asserted. Negative parameters use the identity extension and are outside the forward semigroup law.
Breakdown.Freq.heat_holds.summary: On $X$, $G(0)=I$, $G(s+t)=G(s)G(t)$ and $\|G(t)\|\le1$ for $s,t\ge0$, $t\mapsto G(t)g$ is continuous on $[0,\infty)$, and $G(t)$ is self-adjoint for all real $t$. Continuity is strong continuity, not in operator norm.

Breakdown.Freq.isClosed_sig.text: The formal statement proves that the real subspace $\{g\in L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^3):g(-\xi)=\overline{g(\xi)},\ \xi\cdot g(\xi)=0\text{ a.e.}\}$ is closed in $L^2$. Each constraint is the kernel of a bounded real linear operator, and their intersection is closed. The subspace therefore inherits a real Hilbert space structure and completeness. Its elements represent the paper's velocities through $g=2\pi|\xi|\hat u$; its norm is $\|g\|_2$. This is the closedness result for the Fourier representation. The identification with all physical divergence-free $L^6$ fields whose gradient lies in $L^2$ uses additional reconstruction results. No compact support or smoothness is required of $g$.
Breakdown.Freq.isClosed_sig.summary: The real subspace of $g\in L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^3)$ with $g(-\xi)=\overline{g(\xi)}$ and $\xi\cdot g(\xi)=0$ a.e. is closed, hence a real Hilbert space. Identification with physical $L^6$ fields needs further reconstruction results.

Breakdown.Freq.mild_holds.text:
Let $a<b$ be finite real numbers and let $v:\mathbb R	imes\mathbb R^3	o\mathbb R^3$. For each $t\in[a,b]$, assume $v(t)$ is smooth and divergence-free and, for some constant $C_t$, $|v(t,x)|\le C_t/(1+|x|)$ and $\|D_xv(t,x)\|\le C_t/(1+|x|)^2$. The derivative norm here is the operator norm. No common $C_t$ is required. The formal space $X=\dot H^1_{m div}(\mathbb R^3)$ is represented by $g(\xi)=2\pi|\xi|\widehat v(\xi)\in L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^3)$, with the Fourier transform understood distributionally when $v$ itself is not integrable. Reality is $g(-\xi)=\overline{g(\xi)}$ and incompressibility is $\xi\cdot g(\xi)=0$, both almost everywhere. Its norm is $\|g\|_{L^2}=\|
abla v\|_{L^2}$, where the latter sums the squared spatial partial derivatives. The value of a representative at the single frequency $\xi=0$ does not affect the space or norm. Assume $t\mapsto v(t)$ is continuous in this space, that every difference $v(t)-v(t')$ belongs to $L^2(\mathbb R^3)$, and that $\|v(t)-v(t_0)\|_{L^2}	o0$ as $t	o t_0$ within $[a,b]$. For each smooth compactly supported divergence-free $\psi$, assume the pairing $\int v(t)\cdot\psi$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and has derivative $-\int\sum_i\partial_i v(t)\cdot\partial_i\psi-\int((v(t)\cdot
abla)v(t))\cdot\psi$ at every $a<t<b$. The formal statement proves the closed-interval mild equation $v(t)=e^{(t-a)\Delta}v(a)+\int_a^tK(t-s)(v(s),v(s))\,ds$ in the Fourier realization of $X=\dot H^1_{m div}(\mathbb R^3)$, including Bochner integrability of the integral for every $t\in[a,b]$. The Fourier representation of each smooth decaying slice has norm $\|
abla v(t)\|_{L^2}$. This proof covers the stated spatial decay class and $L^2$-continuous differences. Its premises differ from Lemma 3.6, which starts with an arbitrary continuous $X$-valued curve and continuously differentiable test pairings up to both endpoints.
Breakdown.Freq.mild_holds.summary: For smooth divergence-free decaying curves with $L^2$-continuous differences satisfying the weak equation, the mild equation $v(t)=e^{(t-a)\Delta}v(a)+\int_a^tK(t-s)(v(s),v(s))\,ds$ holds on $[a,b]$ in $X$. Lemma 3.6 starts from an arbitrary continuous $X$-valued curve.

Breakdown.Freq.partial_holds.text: Let $X$ be the real solenoidal frequency space, with an element $g$ representing $2\pi|\xi|\hat u$. For each coordinate $j$, define the reconstructed derivative by taking the real part of the inverse Fourier transform of $(i\xi_j/|\xi|)g(\xi)$. The multiplier is assigned zero at the origin; its value there does not change the $L^2$ class. The formal statement proves two assertions. If $f$ is smooth and divergence-free with $|f(y)|\le A/(1+|y|)$ and $\|Df(y)\|_{\rm op}\le A/(1+|y|)^2$, the reconstructed derivative of $Jf$, the frequency class representing $2\pi|\xi|\hat f$, equals $\partial_j f$ almost everywhere. For every $g\in X$, the sum of the squared $L^2$ norms of the three reconstructed derivatives is at most $\|g\|_X^2$. This result provides derivative identification on the smooth decay class and a homogeneous Sobolev norm inequality on all of $X$. Its stated conclusion is an inequality, and it does not itself assert all three Fourier equalities of (3.2).
Breakdown.Freq.partial_holds.summary: The reconstructed derivative $\operatorname{Re}\mathcal F^{-1}[(i\xi_j/|\xi|)g]$ equals $\partial_jf$ a.e. for smooth divergence-free $f$ in the decay class, and for every $g\in X$ the squared $L^2$ norms of the three derivatives sum to at most $\|g\|_X^2$.

Breakdown.Freq.rotation_holds.text: For every orthogonal map $R\in O(3)$, the formal statement identifies an onto real linear isometry of $X$ with the frequency action $g(\xi)\mapsto Rg(R^{-1}\xi)$. Here $X$ consists of the real solenoidal frequency classes $g\in L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^3)$ and $R$ acts complex linearly on the three vector components. This represents $\rho_Ru(x)=Ru(R^{-1}x)$ when $g=2\pi|\xi|\hat u$. The statement proves commutation with the heat family and with the dilation family for every real value of their parameters. For $t\ge0$ and $\mu>0$, these are the operations in §3.1. The total families use the identity heat operator for $t<0$ and the zero dilation for $\mu\le0$, so the assertions at those parameters carry no backward-flow interpretation. Reflections are allowed; orientation preservation is not a hypothesis.
Breakdown.Freq.rotation_holds.summary: For each $R\in O(3)$, $g(\xi)\mapsto Rg(R^{-1}\xi)$ is an onto linear isometry of $X$, representing $u(x)\mapsto Ru(R^{-1}x)$, and it commutes with the heat and dilation families. Reflections are allowed.

Breakdown.Freq.testDense_holds.text: Let $X=\{g\in L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^3):g(-\xi)=\overline{g(\xi)},\ \xi\cdot g(\xi)=0\text{ a.e.}\}$, with its real $L^2$ Hilbert norm. For a smooth compactly supported divergence-free field $\varphi$, write $J\varphi$ for its frequency representation $2\pi|\xi|\hat\varphi$. The formal statement proves that the real linear span of these $J\varphi$ is dense in $X$. It also proves density in the graph norm of the negative Laplacian: if $g,h\in X$ satisfy $h(\xi)=4\pi^2|\xi|^2g(\xi)$ almost everywhere, then for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is such a $\varphi$ with $\|J\varphi-g\|_X<\varepsilon$ and $\|J(-\Delta\varphi)-h\|_X<\varepsilon$. A separate source statement shows that every element of the indicated span is itself represented by one compact smooth divergence-free field. Thus the first conclusion gives the density used in §3.1; the graph approximation is additional information.
Breakdown.Freq.testDense_holds.summary: The span of $J\varphi=2\pi|\xi|\hat\varphi$ over smooth compactly supported divergence-free $\varphi$ is dense in $X$, and also dense in the graph norm of $-\Delta$. The first gives the density used in §3.1; the second is additional.

Breakdown.Freq.testSpan_holds.text: Let $X$ be the real solenoidal $L^2$ frequency space representing velocities by $J\varphi=2\pi|\xi|\hat\varphi$. Let $S$ be the real linear span of the classes $J\varphi$ for all smooth compactly supported divergence-free fields $\varphi:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$. The formal statement says that every $g\in S$ equals $J\varphi$ for a single field with the same three properties. Finite linear combinations preserve smoothness, compact support and zero divergence, so taking the span has not enlarged the class of represented test fields. This assertion does not state density of $S$ in $X$; the density theorem supplies that separate conclusion.
Breakdown.Freq.testSpan_holds.summary: Every element of the real span of the classes $J\varphi$, over smooth compactly supported divergence-free $\varphi$, equals $J\varphi$ for a single such field. It does not state density of the span in $X$.

Breakdown.Freq.trilinear_holds.text: The formal theorem supplies a constant $C\in\mathbb R$ such that, for all $u,v\in X=\dot H^1_{\mathrm{div}}(\mathbb R^3)$ and all fields $w\in L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)\cap L^6(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$, meaning fields with a measurable representative and finite second and sixth integral norms, the integrand $(u\cdot\nabla)v\cdot w$ is integrable and its integral has absolute value at most $C\|u\|_X\|v\|_X\sqrt{\|w\|_{L^2}\|w\|_{L^6}}$. The state for $u$ is $2\pi|\xi|\widehat u(\xi)$; the velocity is reconstructed in $L^6$, and each derivative of $v$ is reconstructed in $L^2$ by the multiplier $i\xi_j/|\xi|$ on its state. Division at $\xi=0$ is assigned zero, a value at a set of measure zero. All products and integrals are insensitive to choices of representatives. This is the transport-pairing estimate used to construct $K$ by duality. Its conclusion is integrability and a bound for the scalar pairing, rather than an explicit assertion that the vector field $(u\cdot\nabla)v$ belongs to $L^{3/2}$ or decomposes into $L^1+L^2$.
Breakdown.Freq.trilinear_holds.summary: One constant $C$ gives, for $u,v\in X$ and $w\in L^2\cap L^6$, integrability of $(u\cdot\nabla)v\cdot w$ and $|\int(u\cdot\nabla)v\cdot w|\le C\|u\|_X\|v\|_X\sqrt{\|w\|_2\|w\|_6}$. This is the pairing estimate used to construct $K$ by duality.

Breakdown.Freq.velocity.text: For the real Hilbert space $X$ of solenoidal frequency classes $g\in L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^3)$ with conjugation symmetry, this defines a bounded real linear map $V:X\to L^6(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$. Its defining requirement is $V(J\varphi)=[\varphi]$ for every smooth compactly supported divergence-free $\varphi$, where $J\varphi$ represents $2\pi|\xi|\hat\varphi$ and brackets denote an equivalence class modulo equality almost everywhere. The definition chooses a map with this property if one exists and assigns the zero map otherwise. The existence theorem in the supplied sources proves that a suitable map exists; the exceptional zero choice is therefore not used in this setting. For arbitrary $g$, the output is an $L^6$ class, and pointwise evaluations use a representative. Equality of reconstructed fields in subsequent statements is usually almost everywhere. Boundedness yields $\|Vg\|_6\le\|V\|\|g\|_X$; this definition does not assign a numerical Sobolev constant.
Breakdown.Freq.velocity.summary: Defines a bounded real linear $V:X\to L^6(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$ with $V(J\varphi)=[\varphi]$ for every smooth compactly supported divergence-free $\varphi$, choosing zero if none exists. Existence is proved separately; no numerical Sobolev constant is assigned.

Breakdown.Freq.velocityCov_holds.text: For $g\in X$, let $Vg\in L^6(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$ be its reconstructed velocity, with $g$ representing $2\pi|\xi|\hat u$. The formal statement proves that, for every $R\in O(3)$, the velocity reconstructed from $\xi\mapsto Rg(R^{-1}\xi)$ equals $x\mapsto R(Vg)(R^{-1}x)$ almost everywhere. For every $\mu>0$, the velocity reconstructed from $\xi\mapsto\mu^{-1/2}g(\xi/\sqrt\mu)$ equals $x\mapsto\sqrt\mu\,(Vg)(\sqrt\mu x)$ almost everywhere. These identities connect the formal frequency operations with the physical formulas (3.4) for all elements of $X$, with no smoothness assumption. The equalities concern $L^6$ representatives modulo null sets, rather than prescribed values at every point. The dilation conclusion is confined to positive $\mu$.
Breakdown.Freq.velocityCov_holds.summary: For $g\in X$, the velocity of $Rg(R^{-1}\xi)$ is $R(Vg)(R^{-1}x)$ a.e. for $R\in O(3)$, and the velocity of $\mu^{-1/2}g(\xi/\sqrt\mu)$ is $\sqrt\mu(Vg)(\sqrt\mu x)$ a.e. for $\mu>0$. This connects the frequency operations with (3.4) on all of $X$.

Breakdown.Freq.velocity_holds.text: Let $X$ be the real Hilbert space of $L^2$ frequency classes $g$ satisfying $g(-\xi)=\overline{g(\xi)}$ and $\xi\cdot g(\xi)=0$ almost everywhere. The formal statement proves the existence of a bounded real linear map $V:X\to L^6(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$ with the following property: for every smooth compactly supported divergence-free field $\varphi$, $V(J\varphi)$ is the $L^6$ class of $\varphi$. Here $J\varphi$ is the frequency class representing $2\pi|\xi|\hat\varphi$. The map extends this physical interpretation from the dense class of test fields, and boundedness supplies $\|Vg\|_6\le\|V\|\|g\|_X$. The conclusion is about classes modulo equality almost everywhere, without a selected continuous representative for arbitrary $g$. The agreement explicitly stated in this theorem is on compact smooth fields; agreement on the larger smooth decay class is a separate result. This theorem gives Sobolev reconstruction for solenoidal $X$. The unrestricted physical completion statement at the beginning of §3.1 has a larger field domain.
Breakdown.Freq.velocity_holds.summary: There is a bounded real linear $V:X\to L^6(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$ with $V(J\varphi)$ the class of $\varphi$ for every smooth compactly supported divergence-free $\varphi$. This gives Sobolev reconstruction on $X$; the paper's completion statement in §3.1 has a larger field domain.

Breakdown.Freq.weak_holds.text:
Here $X=\dot H^1_{\mathrm{div}}(\mathbb R^3)$ is represented by the Fourier field $2\pi|\xi|\widehat u(\xi)$ in $L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^3)$, with conjugate symmetry and $\xi\cdot\widehat u=0$. Its norm is $\|
abla u\|_2$; the velocity is recovered as an $L^6$ equivalence class. Let $a<b$ and let $u(t,x)$ be smooth and solenoidal in space at each $t\in[a,b]$, with $|u(t,x)|\lesssim_t(1+|x|)^{-1}$ and $|
abla u(t,x)|\lesssim_t(1+|x|)^{-2}$. Assume continuity in $X$, continuous $L^2$ time differences, and the weak differential identity of (3.14) against every smooth compactly supported solenoidal field, with continuity of the pairing at the endpoints. For such a test field $\psi$ and every $t\in[a,b]$, the formal statement proves the integrated identity $(u(t),\psi)_X=(u(a),\psi)_X-\int_a^t[(u(s),-\Delta\psi)_X+\int (u(s)\cdot
abla)u(s)\cdot(-\Delta\psi)]\,ds$, including integrability. The test field is independent of time, and the outer pairing is the gradient inner product. This is a different intermediate formulation from the space-time testing identity quoted from Dubois.
Breakdown.Freq.weak_holds.summary: For smooth solenoidal $u$ with $|u|\lesssim(1+|x|)^{-1}$, $|\nabla u|\lesssim(1+|x|)^{-2}$, continuous in $X$ and satisfying the weak form of (3.14), each fixed solenoidal test $\psi$ gives $(u(t),\psi)_X=(u(a),\psi)_X-\int_a^t[(u(s),-\Delta\psi)_X+\int(u\cdot\nabla)u\cdot(-\Delta\psi)]\,ds$.

Breakdown.HarmonicBounds.text: The data give a finite set H of raw integer harmonics; four real functions for every harmonic to bound the amplitudes of Ŵ, ∇Ŵ, curl Ŵ and ∇curl Ŵ; and two spatial majorants for the full vorticity norm and the operator norm of its gradient. This is the list immediately before (B.16). The set need not yet contain zero or be closed under negation, and the proposed majorants need not yet be true. Exact harmonic reconstruction, sign and analytic requirements are supplied by the weight-admissibility and representation conditions.
Breakdown.HarmonicBounds.summary: A finite set H of raw integer harmonics, four functions per harmonic for the amplitudes of Ŵ, ∇Ŵ, curl Ŵ and ∇curl Ŵ, and two majorants for |curl W| and its gradient, as listed before (B.16). Symmetry of H and truth of the bounds are imposed separately.

Breakdown.HeatBilinear.text: Let $\mathcal X$ be a real normed space. The formal object specifies bounded linear maps $G(t):\mathcal X\to\mathcal X$ for every real $t$ and bounded bilinear maps $K(\tau):\mathcal X\times\mathcal X\to\mathcal X$ for every real $\tau$. It assumes $G(0)=I$, $G(s+t)=G(s)G(t)$ for $s,t\ge0$, and $\|G(t)\|\le1$ for $t\ge0$. For each fixed $u$, $t\mapsto G(t)u$ is continuous on $[0,\infty)$. For each fixed $u,v$, $\tau\mapsto K(\tau)(u,v)$ is continuous on $(0,\infty)$; continuity in the bilinear operator norm is not assumed. The bilinear maps are symmetric, and $G(s)K(\tau)(u,v)=K(s+\tau)(u,v)$ for $s\ge0$, $\tau>0$. One real $C_K$ must satisfy $\|K(\tau)\|\le C_K\tau^{-3/4}$ for $0<\tau\le1$. The bound at $\tau=1$ implies $C_K\ge0$. Completeness, dilation, compactness and a spatial interpretation are separate assumptions in later results. In §3.4 the space is Banach and the power estimate holds for every positive lag. Values outside the stated time ranges are defined, but the heat laws and singular estimate impose no further interpretation there.
Breakdown.HeatBilinear.summary: Assumes a contraction semigroup $G$ and symmetric bounded bilinear $K$ on a real normed space, $G(t)u$ continuous for $t\ge0$, $K(\tau)(u,v)$ continuous for $\tau>0$, $G(s)K(\tau)=K(s+\tau)$, $\|K(\tau)\|\le C_K\tau^{-3/4}$ for $0<\tau\le1$. §3.4 assumes this bound for all $\tau>0$.

Breakdown.HeatBilinear.IsMildOn.text: Let $\mathcal X$ be a real normed space. Write $G(t)$ for a strongly continuous contraction semigroup on $t\ge0$, and let $K(\tau)$ be bounded symmetric real bilinear maps on $\mathcal X$, continuous in $\tau>0$ on each pair of arguments. Assume $G(t)K(\tau)=K(t+\tau)$ for $t\ge0,\tau>0$, and $\|K(\tau)(u,v)\|\le C_K\tau^{-3/4}\|u\|\|v\|$ for $0<\tau\le1$. A curve $u:\mathbb R\to\mathcal X$ is a mild solution on $[a,b)$ when it is continuous there and, for every $t\in[a,b)$, the integrand $K(t-s)(u(s),u(s))$ is Bochner integrable from $a$ to $t$ and $u(t)=G(t-a)u(a)+\int_a^tK(t-s)(u(s),u(s))\,ds$. The real numbers $a,b$ are finite; the definition imposes no conditions outside $[a,b)$. In the Banach-space applications, explicit Bochner integrability gives the integral its usual analytic meaning. The value assigned to $K(0)$ at $s=t$ is immaterial. Completeness is not a hypothesis of this definition; the integral theorems applying it assume a Banach space, as does §3.4 of the paper. If the indicated interval is empty, its continuity and equation conditions are vacuous.
Breakdown.HeatBilinear.IsMildOn.summary: A curve $u$ is mild on $[a,b)$ if it is continuous there and, for each $t\in[a,b)$, $K(t-s)(u(s),u(s))$ is Bochner integrable on $[a,t]$ and $u(t)=G(t-a)u(a)+\int_a^tK(t-s)(u(s),u(s))\,ds$. Nothing is imposed outside $[a,b)$.

Breakdown.HeatBilinear.IsMildOnIcc.text: Let $\mathcal X$ be a real normed space. Write $G(t)$ for a strongly continuous contraction semigroup on $t\ge0$, and let $K(\tau)$ be bounded symmetric real bilinear maps on $\mathcal X$, continuous in $\tau>0$ on each pair of arguments. Assume $G(t)K(\tau)=K(t+\tau)$ for $t\ge0,\tau>0$, and $\|K(\tau)(u,v)\|\le C_K\tau^{-3/4}\|u\|\|v\|$ for $0<\tau\le1$. A curve $u:\mathbb R\to\mathcal X$ is a mild solution on $[a,b]$ when it is continuous there and, for every $t\in[a,b]$, the integrand $K(t-s)(u(s),u(s))$ is Bochner integrable from $a$ to $t$ and $u(t)=G(t-a)u(a)+\int_a^tK(t-s)(u(s),u(s))\,ds$. The real numbers $a,b$ are finite; the definition imposes no conditions outside $[a,b]$. In the Banach-space applications, explicit Bochner integrability gives the integral its usual analytic meaning. The value assigned to $K(0)$ at $s=t$ is immaterial. Completeness is not a hypothesis of this definition; the integral theorems applying it assume a Banach space, as does §3.4 of the paper. If the indicated interval is empty, its continuity and equation conditions are vacuous.
Breakdown.HeatBilinear.IsMildOnIcc.summary: A curve $u$ is mild on $[a,b]$ if it is continuous there and, for each $t\in[a,b]$, $K(t-s)(u(s),u(s))$ is Bochner integrable on $[a,t]$ and $u(t)=G(t-a)u(a)+\int_a^tK(t-s)(u(s),u(s))\,ds$. Nothing is imposed outside $[a,b]$.

Breakdown.HeatBilinear.pieceBil.text:
Let $\mathcal X$ be a real Banach space with a strongly continuous contraction semigroup $G(t)$ for $t\ge0$ and symmetric bounded bilinear operators $K(\tau)$, continuous for $\tau>0$, with $G(s)K(\tau)=K(s+\tau)$ for $s\ge0$, $\tau>0$, and $\|K(\tau)\|\le C_K\tau^{-3/4}$ for $0<\tau\le1$. In the paper $G(t)=e^{t\Delta}$.

For $T>0$ and continuous $f,g:[0,T]\to\mathcal X$, the associated bounded bilinear operator is $\mathcal B_T(f,g)(t)=\int_0^tK(t-s)(f(s),g(s))\,ds$ for $0\le t\le T$. The formal definition first selects an operator with this formula if one exists, and otherwise assigns the zero operator. The interval-operator theorem proves existence and the formula under the hypotheses just stated, so the assigned zero value is unused there. The curves are extended constantly beyond the endpoints in the written integrand; for this integral only their values inside $[0,T]$ are used. The value of $K$ at lag zero affects only an endpoint of measure zero. This is a compact-interval object; the global weighted bound of (4.19) is a different statement.
Breakdown.HeatBilinear.pieceBil.summary: For $T>0$, defines the bounded bilinear operator $\mathcal B_T(f,g)(t)=\int_0^tK(t-s)(f(s),g(s))\,ds$ on continuous curves on $[0,T]$, with an assigned zero value that is unused under the stated hypotheses. The global weighted bound of (4.19) is a different statement.

Breakdown.Held.convexCompactFixedPoint.text: For any nonnegative integer $n$, a nonempty compact convex set $K\subset\mathbb R^n$, and a function $F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n$ continuous on $K$ with $F(K)\subseteq K$, the formal statement gives $x\in K$ such that $F(x)=x$. Continuity is required only on $K$ although the function is defined on all of $\mathbb R^n$. The coordinate representation uses $n$ real entries; the proof transfers them to Euclidean space, uses the nearest-point projection and its nonexpansiveness, and applies a fixed-point theorem on a box. This declaration has no infinite-dimensional Hilbert-space variable and no weak topology. Consequently it is the finite-dimensional fixed-point step used after the nonlinear correction has been solved at each parameter, rather than the paper's stated Schauder–Tychonoff theorem on $\mathcal K\times\mathcal Z$.
Breakdown.Held.convexCompactFixedPoint.summary: For a nonempty compact convex $K\subset\mathbb R^n$ and $F$ continuous on $K$ with $F(K)\subseteq K$, some $x\in K$ has $F(x)=x$. This finite-dimensional step replaces the paper's Schauder–Tychonoff theorem on $\mathcal K\times\mathcal Z$.

Breakdown.Held.testSetZero.text:
For $n\geq0$, let $\mathcal J\subset\{1,\ldots,n\}$, let $\varrho_j\geq0$ for $j\in\mathcal J$, let $\varrho_*\geq0$, and let every $d_j
e0$. Set $\mathcal K=\{\alpha:|\alpha_j|\leq\varrho_j\ (j\in\mathcal J),\ \sum_{j
otin\mathcal J}(d_j\alpha_j)^2\leq\varrho_*^2\}$. Empty sums, including the case $n=0$, are zero. Let $V$ be an invertible real $n	imes n$ matrix and $\Phi:\mathbb R^n	o\mathbb R^n$ be continuous on $\mathcal K$. Assume for every $\alpha\in\mathcal K$ the inequalities $|V_j\cdot\Phi(\alpha)-d_j\alpha_j|\leq|d_j|\varrho_j$ for $j\in\mathcal J$ and $\sum_{j
otin\mathcal J}(V_j\cdot\Phi(\alpha)-d_j\alpha_j)^2\leq\varrho_*^2$. The formal statement proves that $\Phi$ vanishes at some point of $\mathcal K$. Its proof applies a finite-dimensional fixed-point theorem directly to $T_j(\alpha)=\alpha_j-(V_j\cdot\Phi(\alpha))/d_j$, whose image lies in $\mathcal K$ by the displayed bounds. At a fixed point, $V^T\Phi=0$, and invertibility gives $\Phi=0$. Real division is defined to be zero at denominator zero in the formal language, but every $d_j
e0$ is an explicit hypothesis here. In the certificate application $\Phi= eta^{m a}+ eta$. No nearest-point projection is needed in this direct map after the enclosure has been established.
Breakdown.Held.testSetZero.summary: For $\mathcal K$ as in (7.29), invertible $V$ and $\Phi$ continuous on $\mathcal K$ with $|V_j\cdot\Phi-d_j\alpha_j|\le|d_j|\varrho_j$ on $\mathcal J$ and the complementary sum at most $\varrho_*^2$, $\Phi$ vanishes somewhere in $\mathcal K$. Every $d_j\ne0$ is assumed.

Breakdown.Held.testSetZero_of.text: Let $\mathcal K=\{\alpha:|\alpha_j|\le\varrho_j\ (j\in\mathcal J),\sum_{j\notin\mathcal J}(d_j\alpha_j)^2\le\varrho_*^2\}$ with nonnegative radii and nonzero $d_j$, let $V$ be invertible, and let $\Phi:\mathcal K\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous. Suppose $|V_j\cdot\Phi(\alpha)-d_j\alpha_j|\le|d_j|\varrho_j$ on $\mathcal J$ and the sum of squares of those expressions on its complement is at most $\varrho_*^2$. Assuming the compact-convex fixed-point theorem, the result gives $\alpha_*\in\mathcal K$ with $\Phi(\alpha_*)=0$. The proof applies it to $\alpha_j\mapsto\alpha_j-d_j^{-1}V_j\cdot\Phi(\alpha)$, then uses invertibility of $V$. No interior point or differentiability assumption is required.
Breakdown.Held.testSetZero_of.summary: For $\mathcal K$ as in (7.29), invertible $V$ and continuous $\Phi$ satisfying the enclosure bounds, and assuming the compact-convex fixed-point theorem, there is $\alpha_*\in\mathcal K$ with $\Phi(\alpha_*)=0$. No interior point or differentiability is needed.

Breakdown.IsAxisymmetric.text: For a real scalar function f on ℝ³, the condition is f(Rφy)=f(y) for every angle φ and point y, where Rφ rotates about the third coordinate axis. This is exactly invariance under axial rotations for the weights and coefficient bounds of Appendix B.2. It is a pointwise condition, and it imposes no reflection symmetry, continuity, measurability or decay.
Breakdown.IsAxisymmetric.summary: f(Rφy)=f(y) for every angle φ and point y, with Rφ the rotation about the third axis: invariance under axial rotations, as for the weights of Appendix B.2. It is pointwise and imposes no reflection symmetry, continuity, measurability or decay.

Breakdown.IsCertificate.text:
This formal statement is a sufficient certificate in an earlier format, different from the certificate now defined in §§7.2–7.3. Its parameter set K is the coordinate box α₀−ρ≤α≤α₀+ρ in ℝᵏ, for an integer k≥0. The set Γ consists of pairs (R,θ₀)∈O(3)×ℝ; Γ-invariance means v(θ+θ₀,Ry)=Rv(θ,y), pointwise for approximate profiles and almost everywhere for perturbations. Conditions involving α hold for every α∈K unless all parameters are explicitly specified. The conditions are the following.

Every radius is nonnegative. The scalar lower weight w* is positive; w(y) is measurable, Γ-invariant, and lies between w* and a finite upper bound. The constants c₁,c_B,c₂,b*,c₃,ε are nonnegative; M and c_L are positive; c₁+c_B≤c_L. The period is continuous on K and 0<S(α)≤Smax. The integer m is 1, or 2 with an orthogonal half-period symmetry in Γ. The maps βᵃ and the target constraint are continuous on K.

Wᵃ is jointly C² in all parameters, normalized time and space, is period one for every parameter, and for α∈K is solenoidal, Γ-invariant, and satisfies |DʲWᵃ|≤C/(1+|y|)ʲ⁺¹ for j=0,1,2. These spatial derivative norms are operator norms and C is one common constant. The chosen pressure is C¹ and period one. Each forcing field bᵢ is measurable, period one, Γ-invariant almost everywhere, and ∑ᵢ‖bᵢ‖²𝓗≤b*². Each Ξᵢ is jointly measurable up to null sets and square integrable over [0,1]×ℝ³. No periodicity of Ξᵢ is required outside this interval, whose restriction suffices to define the constraint. Here 𝓗=L²((0,1)×ℝ³), ℓᵢ(v)=⟨∇v,Ξᵢ⟩𝓗 and E=∫₀¹∫(|Δv|²+w|∇v|²).

A weak perturbation is represented by v,g:ℝ×ℝ³→ℝ³, a linear-map field G and a bilinear-map field H, all jointly measurable up to null sets and pointwise period one in θ. For almost every θ, v,G,H are locally integrable in space, G=∇v and H(a,eⱼ)=∂ₐ(Geⱼ) distributionally, div v=tr G=0 almost everywhere, and v(θ)∈L⁶(ℝ³). Require G, tr H and g in 𝓗, with the Frobenius norm for G and tr H=∑ⱼH(eⱼ,eⱼ). Against every compactly supported smooth vector test on ℝ×ℝ³, g represents S⁻¹∂θv+½v+½(y·∇)v. For each (R,θ₀)∈Γ require v(θ+θ₀,Ry)=Rv(θ,y) almost everywhere in space and time. This specifies representatives and their distributional identities; it does not require the chosen v to be continuous in time. In these certificate conditions S>0. Put 𝓣ˢv=g−tr H. For a reference P, the equation F≃𝓣ˢv+(P·∇)v+(v·∇)P+∑ᵢβᵢbᵢ means that, for every compactly supported smooth solenoidal test φ, ∫F·φ=∫[(g+GP+(DP)v+∑ᵢβᵢbᵢ)·φ+G:∇φ], integrated over ℝ×ℝ³. Here F is jointly measurable up to a null set, pointwise period one and in 𝓗; F is not required to be solenoidal or Γ-invariant.

For every such perturbation, every β∈ℝᵏ and every such right-hand side F with P=Wᵃ, √(E+|β|²)≤c₁‖F‖𝓗+c_B‖F‖L²((0,1)×B_R)+c₂|ℓ(v)|. For the frozen-time estimates, a spatial test field is represented by u,Gᵤ,Hᵤ with locally integrable weak derivatives Gᵤ=∇u and Hᵤ(a,eⱼ)=∂ₐ(Gᵤeⱼ), div u=0, u∈L⁶(ℝ³), and Gᵤ,tr Hᵤ∈L²(ℝ³). It obeys u(Ry)=Ru(y) almost everywhere for each (R,0)∈Γ. Write |u|²w=∫ℝ³(|tr Hᵤ|²+w|Gᵤ|²), with the Frobenius norm for Gᵤ. All unlabelled space integrals use Lebesgue measure. The formal ball is {y∈ℝ³:|y|≤R}, with the supplied real radius R. It is empty when R<0 and is {0} when R=0; its Lebesgue L² norm equals that over the corresponding open ball. At every normalized time θ, the frozen-time form ∫(|Δu|²+¼|∇u|²)−∫[(Wᵃ·∇)u+(u·∇)Wᵃ]·Δu is bounded below by −c₃|u|²w for every admissible spatial solenoidal u and the zero-time-shift symmetries.

The residual Fᵃ=S⁻¹∂θWᵃ+½Wᵃ+½y·∇Wᵃ−ΔWᵃ+(Wᵃ·∇)Wᵃ+∑βᵢᵃbᵢ+∇q has nonnegative bounds δ,δB on its global and ball norms, with δ≤δmax. These obey c₁δ+c_BδB+c₂|target−ℓ(Wᵃ)|≤ε. With c_w=(4π√w*)⁻¹ᐟ² and L=Smax/m, the three size conditions are 2c_Lc_wM<1, 4ε²(1/w*+2Lc₃+2Lb*+2L/c_L)≤M², and 4(1/w*+2Lc₃)ε²+4Lε(δmax+2c_wεM+2b*ε)≤M².

A matrix B and a proposed inverse A obey AB=I. The coordinate bounds |βⱼᵃ(α)−(B(α−α₀))ⱼ|≤oⱼ and ∑ⱼ|Aᵢⱼ|(2ε+oⱼ)≤ρᵢ keep the parameter correction in the box. Finally 4ε²/w*<‖∇Wᵃ‖²𝓗 for every α∈K prevents a zero corrected profile. Compared with the printed certificate, there are stronger C² and Hessian-decay hypotheses, the force weight is one, and the ball norm and slope-inverse conditions replace the row and adjoint construction. The formal choice m=1 remains allowed even if Γ contains a half-period symmetry; (7.6) instead assigns m=2 in that case. Using m=1 doubles the factor Smax/m in the two corresponding size conditions. These conditions do not assert that any numerical data satisfying them have been supplied.
Breakdown.IsCertificate.summary: An earlier certificate format: coordinate-box parameters, a C² profile with Hessian decay, an a priori estimate with a ball norm, residual and size bounds, and a slope-inverse inclusion in place of rows and adjoints. Allowing m=1 with a half-period symmetry doubles Smax/m in two size conditions.

Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.text:
The formal statement imposes the following conditions for an integer k≥0, a set J⊆{1,…,k}, and K={α∈ℝᵏ: |αⱼ|≤ρⱼ for j∈J, ∑ⱼ∉J(dⱼαⱼ)²≤ρ*²}. The symmetry set Γ consists of pairs (R,θ₀)∈O(3)×ℝ, with invariance v(θ+θ₀,Ry)=Rv(θ,y), pointwise for approximate profiles and almost everywhere for perturbations. Conditions involving α hold for every α∈K unless all parameters are explicitly specified. This is the certificate of §§7.2–7.3 in a specific representation, with the differences stated below. Write 𝓗=L²((0,1)×ℝ³), ℓᵢ(v)=⟨∇v,Ξᵢ⟩𝓗, ‖v‖²w=∫₀¹∫(|Δv|²+w|∇v|²), and ‖(v,β)‖²w,ω=‖v‖²w+ω²|β|².

Parameter and scalar conditions. The selected radii and ρ* are nonnegative and every dⱼ is nonzero. The weight satisfies 0<w*≤w(y)≤wmax, is measurable and Γ-invariant. The force weight ω is positive. The constants c₁,c₂,c₀,cᵣ, the frozen-form transfer bound, b*, the reference-form bound and ε are nonnegative. Writing c₃ʳ for the reference-form bound, η₃ for the frozen-form transfer bound and c₃ for the final bound, one has c₃ʳ+η₃≤c₃. M and c_L are positive. With ϑ=(c₁+c₀)cᵣ, one has ϑ<1 and c₁+c₀≤(1−ϑ)c_L. S is continuous on K with 0<S(α)≤Smax. The positive integer m is 1 or is 2 with an orthogonal half-period symmetry in Γ. βᵃ and the total-field target t are continuous on K.

Approximate and reference fields. Wᵃ is jointly C¹ in all parameters, time and space, is period one for all parameters, and on K is solenoidal and Γ-invariant. One common D bounds |Wᵃ|, |DWᵃ| and the supplied Hessian |Hᵃ| by D/(1+|y|), D/(1+|y|)² and D/(1+|y|)³, respectively; the derivative norms in these three bounds are operator norms. The gradients in 𝓗 and in the weighted energies instead have the Frobenius norm. Hᵃ is jointly measurable up to null sets and period one, and at every time is the distributional derivative of DWᵃ. The supplied pressure-gradient representative hα is jointly measurable up to null sets, period one and has zero pairing with every compactly supported solenoidal space-time test. Each bᵢ is measurable, periodic, Γ-invariant almost everywhere and ∑ᵢ‖bᵢ‖²𝓗≤b*². Each Ξᵢ is jointly measurable up to null sets with finite L² norm on [0,1]×ℝ³; its values outside that interval are unused, so its periodicity is not a condition. Wʳα is jointly C¹ in time and space and period one. The change (Wᵃ−Wʳ)·∇v+v·∇(Wᵃ−Wʳ) has 𝓗 norm at most cᵣ‖v‖w for every admissible perturbation; for each time and admissible spatial u, Q_Wᵃ(u)−Q_Wʳ(u)≥−η₃|u|²w, where Q_P(u)=∫(|Δu|²+¼|∇u|²)−∫[(P·∇)u+(u·∇)P]·Δu is the form in (7.22).

A priori estimates. The finite row family eₐ is measurable, periodic, square integrable and orthonormal, with 0≤τₐ≤c₀². Define [F]²=∑ₐτₐ⟨F,eₐ⟩². A weak perturbation is represented by v,g:ℝ×ℝ³→ℝ³, a linear-map field G and a bilinear-map field H, all jointly measurable up to null sets and pointwise period one in θ. For almost every θ, v,G,H are locally integrable in space, G=∇v and H(a,eⱼ)=∂ₐ(Geⱼ) distributionally, div v=tr G=0 almost everywhere, and v(θ)∈L⁶(ℝ³). Comparison. The core estimates are (7.18)–(7.37). The formal statement additionally requires global C¹ parameter dependence, a pointwise Hessian decay bound and a uniform-in-time L² bound for each adjoint field; the paper's displayed assumptions only require joint continuity of Wᵃ and its time and spatial first derivatives on K, locally integrable second derivatives, and ψα,ⱼ∈𝓗. Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.summary: The certificate of §§7.2–7.3: parameter, weight and constant conditions, a C¹ profile with supplied Hessian and decay, a priori estimates, residual and size bounds, and adjoint inclusion bounds. It adds C¹ parameter dependence, Hessian decay and uniform adjoint L² bounds, and requires c₂≥0.

Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.defect_l.text: This is a hypothesis required of a certificate, extracted from the assumption that all certificate conditions hold. Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.defect_l.text: This is a hypothesis required of a certificate, extracted from the assumption that all certificate conditions hold. For every $\alpha\in\mathcal K$, the supplied bound $\delta(\alpha)$ is at most the fixed real constant $\delta_{\max}$. In combination with $\|F_\alpha^{\mathrm a}\|_{\mathcal H}\le\delta(\alpha)$, this is a uniform $\mathcal H$ bound for the full residual. Neither continuity of $\delta$ nor continuity of the residual is part of this condition.
Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.defect_l.summary: Certificate hypothesis: $\delta(\alpha)\le\delta_{\max}$ for every $\alpha\in\mathcal K$; with $\|F_\alpha^{\mathrm a}\|_{\mathcal H}\le\delta(\alpha)$ this is a uniform bound on the full residual. Continuity of $\delta$ or of the residual is not included.

For every $\alpha\in\mathcal K$, $[F_\alpha^{\mathrm a}]\le\delta_0(\alpha)$, where $[F]=(\sum_k\tau_k\langle F,e_k\rangle_{\mathcal H}^2)^{1/2}$ with orthonormal $e_k$ and nonnegative weights. Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.frame_un.text: This is a hypothesis required of a certificate, extracted from the assumption that all certificate conditions hold. The real $n\times n$ matrix $V$ is invertible in the matrix ring, equivalently it has a two-sided matrix inverse. Its columns are $V_j$, so the expression $\sum_iV_{ij}\beta_i$ is $V_j\cdot\beta$, the $j$th coordinate of $V^{\mathsf T}\beta$. In particular, if these scalar products vanish for all $j$, then $\beta=0$. For $n=0$ this is the usual invertible empty matrix convention.
Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.frame_un.summary: Certificate hypothesis: the real $n\times n$ matrix $V$ is invertible. Then $\sum_iV_{ij}\beta_i=V_j\cdot\beta$ is the $j$th coordinate of $V^{\mathsf T}\beta$, and these vanishing for all $j$ forces $\beta=0$.

Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.multipli.text: This is a hypothesis required of a certificate, extracted from the assumption that all certificate conditions hold. The scalar $\omega$ multiplying the Euclidean norm of the force coefficients is strictly positive. Thus $\|(v,\beta)\|_{w,\omega}^2=\|v\|_w^2+\omega^2|\beta|^2$, and divisions by $\omega$ in the scalar budgets and adjoint error bounds are legitimate. No value of $\omega$ is fixed by this condition; the later construction changes variables to make it one.
Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.multipli.summary: Certificate hypothesis: the weight $\omega$ on the Euclidean norm of the force coefficients is strictly positive, so $\|(v,\beta)\|_{w,\omega}^2=\|v\|_w^2+\omega^2|\beta|^2$ and divisions by $\omega$ are legitimate. No value of $\omega$ is fixed.

Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.multipli.text: This is a hypothesis required of a certificate, extracted from the assumption that all certificate conditions hold. The supplied map $\beta^{\mathrm a}:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n$ is continuous on $\mathcal K$. Its $i$th component multiplies $b_i$ in the residual expression $\mathcal T_{S(\alpha)}W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}+(W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}\cdot\nabla)W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}+\sum_i\beta_i^{\mathrm a}(\alpha)b_i$. No parameter differentiability and no sign condition on its components is assumed.
Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.multipli.summary: Certificate hypothesis: the forcing coefficients $\beta^{\mathrm a}:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n$ are continuous on $\mathcal K$; component $i$ multiplies $b_i$ in the residual. No differentiability or sign condition is assumed.

Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.nontrivi.text: This is a hypothesis required of a certificate, extracted from the assumption that all certificate conditions hold. For every $\alpha\in\mathcal K$, the formal condition is $4\varepsilon^2/w_*<\int_0^1\int|\nabla W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}|^2$, where the gradient is measured by the Frobenius sum. The right side is first an extended nonnegative integral and then converted to a real number, with infinity converted to zero. Since $w_*>0$ makes the left side nonnegative, the strict inequality itself excludes an infinite integral. Multiplication by $w_*$ gives (7.28). Combining it with $\|v\|_w\le2\varepsilon$ proves that $W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}+v$ cannot vanish almost everywhere; that conclusion is a separate result.
Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.nontrivi.summary: Certificate hypothesis: $4\varepsilon^2/w_*<\int_0^1\int|\nabla W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}|^2$ for every $\alpha\in\mathcal K$; multiplying by $w_*$ gives (7.28). An infinite integral is converted to zero, so the strict inequality excludes it.

Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.period_c.text: This is a hypothesis required of a certificate, extracted from the assumption that all certificate conditions hold. The period function $S:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ is continuous on the parameter set $\mathcal K$. The set is the product of the coordinate intervals on $\mathcal J$ and the scaled Euclidean ball on its complement. No continuity off $\mathcal K$ and no differentiability in $\alpha$ is asserted.
Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.period_c.summary: Certificate hypothesis: the period function $S$ is continuous on the parameter set $\mathcal K$. No continuity off $\mathcal K$ and no differentiability in $\alpha$ is asserted.

Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.period_l.text: This is a hypothesis required of a certificate, extracted from the assumption that all certificate conditions hold. For every $\alpha\in\mathcal K$, the period satisfies $S(\alpha)\le S_{\max}$. The number $S_{\max}$ is part of the supplied data and is independent of $\alpha$. Positivity of $S$ is a separate certificate condition. The bound is used to make the scalar estimates uniform in the parameter.
Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.period_l.summary: Certificate hypothesis: $S(\alpha)\le S_{\max}$ for every $\alpha\in\mathcal K$, with $S_{\max}$ supplied and independent of $\alpha$. It makes the scalar estimates uniform in the parameter.

Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.period_p.text: This is a hypothesis required of a certificate, extracted from the assumption that all certificate conditions hold. For every $\alpha\in\mathcal K$, the real number $S(\alpha)$ is strictly positive. This justifies the reciprocal in $\mathcal T_{S(\alpha)}$ and the rescaling $\theta=s/S(\alpha)$. The inequality concerns all admissible parameters, including boundary points. Values of $S$ outside $\mathcal K$ are unrestricted by this condition.
Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.period_p.summary: Certificate hypothesis: $S(\alpha)>0$ for every $\alpha\in\mathcal K$, including boundary points, which justifies the reciprocal in $\mathcal T_{S(\alpha)}$ and the rescaling $\theta=s/S(\alpha)$.

Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.pin_fini.text: This is a hypothesis required of a certificate, extracted from the assumption that all certificate conditions hold. For each of the $n$ supplied matrix fields $\Xi_i$, the nonnegative integral $\int_{[0,1]}\int_{\mathbb R^3}|\Xi_i|_{\rm F}^2$ is finite. Joint measurability is required separately. Unlike the paper’s statement $\Xi_i\in\mathcal H$, the formal certificate has no separate period-one hypothesis on these matrix fields. Their restriction to one period is used in the physical constraints, and their evaluation on the time circle selects the representative time in $[0,1)$. Thus the constraint data can be read through that periodization, without an asserted pointwise identity on the originally supplied time-line function.
Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.pin_fini.summary: Certificate hypothesis: each matrix field satisfies $\int_{[0,1]}\int|\Xi_i|_{\rm F}^2<\infty$. Unlike the paper's $\Xi_i\in\mathcal H$, no period-one hypothesis is imposed; the constraints use the restriction to one period.

Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.pressure.text: This is a hypothesis required of a certificate, extracted from the assumption that all certificate conditions hold. For each $\alpha\in\mathcal K$ and each smooth compactly supported solenoidal test $\varphi$, the supplied field $g_\alpha$ satisfies $\int_{\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3}g_\alpha\cdot\varphi=0$. No scalar pressure is supplied by this assertion. It expresses the gradient ambiguity in (7.10) through vanishing tests. The field is separately required to be measurable and period one. Its local integrability in the intended residual identity must be established from the other certificate bounds; the bare displayed pairing condition does not include that assertion.
Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.pressure.summary: Certificate hypothesis: for each $\alpha\in\mathcal K$ and each smooth compactly supported solenoidal test $\varphi$, $\int g_\alpha\cdot\varphi=0$. This expresses the gradient ambiguity in (7.10) without supplying a scalar pressure.

Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.profileS.text: This is a hypothesis required of a certificate, extracted from the assumption that all certificate conditions hold. For every $\alpha\in\mathcal K$, every real $\theta$ and every coordinate direction $e_j$, the supplied bilinear field $H_\alpha(\theta,y)$ is the weak spatial derivative of $y\mapsto D_yW_\alpha^{\mathrm a}(\theta,y)e_j$, with its two arguments ordered as the corresponding differentiation directions. The weak-gradient condition includes spatial local integrability of this first derivative and of the proposed derivative. This is a slice-by-slice assertion at every time, stronger in its time quantifier than the bare existence of a space-time distributional Hessian. Joint measurability and the uniform $|y|^{-3}$ bound are separate conditions.
Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.profileS.summary: Certificate hypothesis: for every $\alpha\in\mathcal K$, every time $\theta$ and each $e_j$, the supplied $H_\alpha(\theta,\cdot)$ is the weak spatial derivative of $D_yW_\alpha^{\mathrm a}e_j$. This holds slice by slice at every time, stronger than a space-time distributional Hessian.

Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.profile_.text: This is a hypothesis required of a certificate, extracted from the assumption that all certificate conditions hold. For all $\alpha\in\mathcal K$ and all $(\theta,y)$, the formal condition imposes $|W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}|\le C_{\mathrm a}/(1+|y|)$, $\|D_yW_\alpha^{\mathrm a}\|_{\rm op}\le C_{\mathrm a}/(1+|y|)^2$, and $\|H_\alpha\|_{\rm op}\le C_{\mathrm a}/(1+|y|)^3$ for a supplied weak Hessian $H_\alpha$. The derivative is a linear map and its norm here is the operator norm; the Hessian uses the iterated operator norm. The paper defines $|\nabla W|^2=\sum_j|\partial_jW|^2$, the Frobenius norm. In three dimensions $\|D W\|_{\rm op}\le|\nabla W|\le\sqrt3\|D W\|_{\rm op}$. Hence the same first-derivative constant is not preserved on conversion, and the Hessian bound is additional to (7.8). All denominators are strictly positive.
Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.profile_.summary: Certificate hypothesis: $|W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}|\le C_{\mathrm a}/(1+|y|)$, $\|D_yW_\alpha^{\mathrm a}\|_{\rm op}\le C_{\mathrm a}/(1+|y|)^2$, $\|H_\alpha\|_{\rm op}\le C_{\mathrm a}/(1+|y|)^3$. The paper uses the Frobenius norm, which costs up to $\sqrt3$; the Hessian bound is additional to (7.8).

Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.profile_.text: This is a hypothesis required of a certificate, extracted from the assumption that all certificate conditions hold. For every $\alpha\in\mathcal K$, every real $\theta$ and every $y\in\mathbb R^3$, $\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_j(W_\alpha^{\mathrm a})_j(\theta,y)=0$. The derivatives exist by the $C^1$ family assumption. Thus the approximate profile is divergence-free at every point, as required in Section 7.2.
Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.profile_.summary: Certificate hypothesis: $\sum_j\partial_j(W_\alpha^{\mathrm a})_j(\theta,y)=0$ for every $\alpha\in\mathcal K$, $\theta$ and $y$, so the approximate profile is divergence-free at every point, as Section 7.2 requires.

Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.profile_.text: This is a hypothesis required of a certificate, extracted from the assumption that all certificate conditions hold. For every $\alpha\in\mathcal K$, every $(R,\theta_0)\in\Gamma$ and every $(\theta,y)$, $W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}(\theta+\theta_0,Ry)=R W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}(\theta,y)$. Since $R$ is invertible, this is exactly (7.7) after replacing $y$ by $R^{-1}y$. Unlike the perturbation symmetry condition, this equality is required at every point.
Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.profile_.summary: Certificate hypothesis: $W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}(\theta+\theta_0,Ry)=RW_\alpha^{\mathrm a}(\theta,y)$ for every $\alpha\in\mathcal K$, $(R,\theta_0)\in\Gamma$ and every point; this is (7.7). Unlike the perturbation symmetry it holds at every point.

Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.profile_.text: This is a hypothesis required of a certificate, extracted from the assumption that all certificate conditions hold. For every $\alpha\in\mathbb R^n$ and every $(\theta,y)$, $W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}(\theta+1,y)=W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}(\theta,y)$. The formal quantifier extends over all parameters, including those outside $\mathcal K$; the paper only prescribes the family on $\mathcal K$. The equality is pointwise, rather than an equality only of equivalence classes.
Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.profile_.summary: Certificate hypothesis: $W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}(\theta+1,y)=W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}(\theta,y)$ pointwise for every $\alpha\in\mathbb R^n$, including parameters outside $\mathcal K$; the paper prescribes the family only on $\mathcal K$.

Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.profile_.text: This is a hypothesis required of a certificate, extracted from the assumption that all certificate conditions hold. The map $(\alpha,\theta,y)\mapsto W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}(\theta,y)$ is $C^1$ on all of $\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3$. In particular its time and spatial first derivatives exist and depend continuously on all variables. This also requires first derivatives in $\alpha$ and a $C^1$ extension outside $\mathcal K$. Section 7.2 asks only for joint continuity on $\mathcal K$ of the field and its time and spatial derivatives. Those are fewer requirements.
Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.profile_.summary: The approximate field is jointly $C^1$ in all real parameter, time and space variables, including outside $\mathcal K$. Section 7.2 requires joint continuity of the field and its time and spatial first derivatives on $\mathcal K$, without parameter derivatives.

Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.scale_ne.text: This is a hypothesis required of a certificate, extracted from the assumption that all certificate conditions hold. For every coordinate $j$, the supplied real number $d_j$ is nonzero. This makes the update $\alpha_j-d_j^{-1}V_j\cdot\Phi(\alpha)$ well defined with the ordinary reciprocal, and permits the inclusion bounds to be divided by $|d_j|$. No common sign or normalization is required of the scales. The condition is empty when there are no coordinates.
Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.scale_ne.summary: Certificate hypothesis: every scale $d_j$ is nonzero, so the update $\alpha_j-d_j^{-1}V_j\cdot\Phi(\alpha)$ uses the ordinary reciprocal. No common sign is required, and the condition is empty when there are no coordinates.

Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.size.text: This is a hypothesis required of a certificate, extracted from the assumption that all certificate conditions hold. For every $\alpha\in\mathcal K$, $c_1\delta(\alpha)+\delta_0(\alpha)+c_2|\bar\ell(\alpha)|\le(1-\vartheta)\varepsilon$. Here $\bar\ell_i(\alpha)=t_i(\alpha)-\int_0^1\int\nabla W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}:\Xi_i$, $\vartheta=(c_1+c_0)c_{\mathrm r}<1$, and $|\bar\ell|$ is the Euclidean norm computed as the square root of the sum of squares. This is (7.24) after translating the complete-field target into the perturbation target. It does not assert existence of a perturbation; it bounds the data supplied to the linear solve. Here $\varepsilon$ is the target perturbation radius, $\delta(\alpha)$ bounds the period-$L^2$ norm of the unprojected residual, and $\delta_0(\alpha)$ bounds its finite pairing seminorm; $c_1$ and $c_2$ are the full-forcing and constraint coefficients in the reference a priori estimate.
Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.size.summary: Certificate hypothesis: $c_1\delta(\alpha)+\delta_0(\alpha)+c_2|\bar\ell(\alpha)|\le(1-\vartheta)\varepsilon$ for every $\alpha\in\mathcal K$. This is (7.24) after translating the complete-field target into the perturbation target; it asserts no perturbation exists.

Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.small_fi.text: This is a hypothesis required of a certificate, extracted from the assumption that all certificate conditions hold. With $c_L>0$, $M>0$, $w_*>0$ and $c_w=(4\pi\sqrt{w_*})^{-1/2}$, the required inequality is $2c_Lc_wM<1$. It is exactly (7.25). In the formal construction this number becomes an upper bound for the contraction factor of the nonlinear perturbation map at a fixed parameter. The condition is strict and contains no residual size $\varepsilon$. The number $M$ is the proposed upper bound for $\operatorname*{ess\,sup}_\theta\|\nabla v(\theta)\|_2$; $c_L$ bounds the absorbed linear solution norm when the constraints vanish, and $w_*$ is the positive lower bound for the spatial energy weight.
Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.small_fi.summary: Certificate hypothesis: $2c_Lc_wM<1$ with $c_w=(4\pi\sqrt{w_*})^{-1/2}$, exactly (7.25). In the formal construction it bounds the contraction factor of the nonlinear map at a fixed parameter.

Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.small_se.text: This is a hypothesis required of a certificate, extracted from the assumption that all certificate conditions hold. For the certificate constants $\varepsilon\ge0$, $w_*,\omega,c_L,M>0$, $m\in\{1,2\}$, $S_{\max}$, $c_3$ and $b_*$, the condition is $4\varepsilon^2[w_*^{-1}+(2S_{\max}/m)(c_3+b_*/\omega+1/c_L)]\le M^2$. This is (7.26), with the same non-strict inequality. The formal proof uses it to bound differences in the nonlinear iteration. The paper explicitly says its proof below does not use (7.26). The natural number $m$ is converted to a real divisor and is positive, so zero-division defaults do not enter. The radius is $2\varepsilon$ in the norm $(\|v\|_w^2+\omega^2|\beta|^2)^{1/2}$, and $M$ bounds the essential time supremum of $\|\nabla v\|_2$. Here $w_*$ is the lower energy weight, $S_{\max}$ bounds the similarity period, $c_3$ is the frozen quadratic-form lower-bound constant, $\sum_i\|b_i\|_{\mathcal H}^2\le b_*^2$, and $\omega$ is the weight on the Euclidean force coefficients. The positive constant $c_L$ is the absorbed linear estimate constant when the constraint target is zero.
Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.small_se.summary: Certificate hypothesis: $4\varepsilon^2[w_*^{-1}+(2S_{\max}/m)(c_3+b_*/\omega+1/c_L)]\le M^2$, which is (7.26). The formal proof uses it to bound differences in the nonlinear iteration, although the paper says its proof does not use (7.26).

Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.small_th.text: This is a hypothesis required of a certificate, extracted from the assumption that all certificate conditions hold. With the certificate’s positive $w_*,\omega,M$, positive integer $m$, and $\varepsilon\ge0$, the condition is $4\varepsilon^2[w_*^{-1}+2S_{\max}c_3/m]+(4S_{\max}/m)\varepsilon[\delta_{\max}+2c_w\varepsilon M+2b_*\varepsilon/\omega]\le M^2$, where $c_w=(4\pi\sqrt{w_*})^{-1/2}$. This is (7.27) after distributing products. It provides the scalar budget for preserving the bound on $\operatorname*{ess\,sup}_\theta\|\nabla v(\theta)\|_2$ in the nonlinear solve. It is an assumed inequality, not the preservation result itself. The radius is $2\varepsilon$ in the norm $(\|v\|_w^2+\omega^2|\beta|^2)^{1/2}$, and $M$ bounds the essential time supremum of $\|\nabla v\|_2$. Here $w_*$ is the lower energy weight, $S_{\max}$ bounds the similarity period, $c_3$ is the frozen quadratic-form lower-bound constant, $\sum_i\|b_i\|_{\mathcal H}^2\le b_*^2$, and $\omega$ is the weight on the Euclidean force coefficients. The constant $\delta_{\max}$ bounds $\|F_\alpha^{\mathrm a}\|_{\mathcal H}$ uniformly in $\alpha$.
Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.small_th.summary: Certificate hypothesis: $4\varepsilon^2[w_*^{-1}+2S_{\max}c_3/m]+(4S_{\max}/m)\varepsilon[\delta_{\max}+2c_w\varepsilon M+2b_*\varepsilon/\omega]\le M^2$, which is (7.27) after distributing products. It is the scalar budget for keeping $\operatorname*{ess\,sup}_\theta\|\nabla v\|_2\le M$.

Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.stiff_in.text: This is a hypothesis required of a certificate, extracted from the assumption that all certificate conditions hold. The required scalar inequality is $2\varepsilon a_*/\omega+o_*\le\varrho_*$. Here $\varepsilon\ge0$, $a_*\ge0$, $\omega>0$ and $\varrho_*\ge0$. In conjunction with $\omega|\beta|\le2\varepsilon$, the matrix bound and the approximate offset bound in (7.36), the triangle inequality places the complementary update inside the scaled ball of radius $\varrho_*$. The formal declaration records the budget (7.37), rather than that full implication.
Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.stiff_in.summary: Certificate hypothesis, the budget (7.37): $2\varepsilon a_*/\omega+o_*\le\varrho_*$, with $\varepsilon,a_*,\varrho_*\ge0$ and $\omega>0$. The implication that the complementary update stays in the ball of radius $\varrho_*$ is not part of this statement.

Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.stiff_no.text: This is a hypothesis required of a certificate, extracted from the assumption that all certificate conditions hold. For every real coefficient vector $\beta\in\mathbb R^n$, $\sum_{j\notin\mathcal J}(V_j\cdot\beta)^2\le a_*^2|\beta|^2$. The Euclidean norms are computed as sums of coordinate squares, and the columns $V_j$ give the rows of $V^{\mathsf T}$. The separate sign condition $a_*\ge0$ permits taking square roots to obtain an operator-norm bound. If the complement of $\mathcal J$ is empty the left side is zero. This is the first inequality in (7.36).
Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.stiff_no.summary: Certificate hypothesis, the first inequality in (7.36): $\sum_{j\notin\mathcal J}(V_j\cdot\beta)^2\le a_*^2|\beta|^2$ for every $\beta\in\mathbb R^n$. With $a_*\ge0$ this is an operator-norm bound; with empty complement the left side is zero.

Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.stiff_of.text: This is a hypothesis required of a certificate, extracted from the assumption that all certificate conditions hold. For every $\alpha\in\mathcal K$, $(\sum_{j\notin\mathcal J}(V_j\cdot\beta^{\mathrm a}(\alpha)-d_j\alpha_j)^2)^{1/2}\le o_*$. This is a Euclidean norm on the complementary coordinates, including all coordinates when $\mathcal J$ is empty. With an empty complement it is zero. The condition matches the second inequality in (7.36); it does not include the perturbation coefficients $\beta$.
Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.stiff_of.summary: Certificate hypothesis, the second inequality in (7.36): $(\sum_{j\notin\mathcal J}(V_j\cdot\beta^{\mathrm a}(\alpha)-d_j\alpha_j)^2)^{1/2}\le o_*$ for every $\alpha\in\mathcal K$. It does not involve the perturbation coefficients $\beta$.

Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.transfer.text: This is a hypothesis required of a certificate, extracted from the assumption that all certificate conditions hold. The product $\vartheta=(c_1+c_0)c_{\mathrm r}$ satisfies $\vartheta<1$. With the separate nonnegativity assumptions this gives $0\le\vartheta<1$, so the positive factor $1-\vartheta$ can be used to absorb the change of linearized profile and to divide the a priori estimate. This condition is assumed, rather than derived from a size bound on the data in this section.
Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.transfer.summary: Certificate hypothesis: $\vartheta=(c_1+c_0)c_{\mathrm r}<1$, so with the nonnegativity assumptions $0\le\vartheta<1$ and $1-\vartheta$ can absorb the profile change. It is assumed, not derived from a size bound on the data.

Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.twist_me.text: This is a hypothesis required of a certificate, extracted from the assumption that all certificate conditions hold. The scalar-budget factor $m$ is a natural number satisfying either $m=1$, or $m=2$ together with the existence of an orthogonal $R$ for which $(R,1/2)\in\Gamma$. A half-period symmetry therefore allows the choice two. The formal condition also allows the choice one when that symmetry exists. In (7.6) the paper fixes the choice two whenever possible. Both values are positive; their appearance as divisors uses their corresponding real values. The symmetry implies period $1/2$ of the $\dot H^1$ norm because the spatial action is isometric.
Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.twist_me.summary: Certificate hypothesis: the factor $m$ is $1$, or $2$ when some $(R,1/2)\in\Gamma$. The formal condition allows $m=1$ even when that symmetry exists, whereas (7.6) in the paper fixes $m=2$ whenever possible.

Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.weightFn.text: This is a hypothesis required of a certificate, extracted from the assumption that all certificate conditions hold. For every $(R,\theta_0)\in\Gamma$ and every $y\in\mathbb R^3$, the spatial weight satisfies $w(Ry)=w(y)$. This is in addition to boundedness, measurability and the lower bound $w\ge w_*>0$. Section 7.3’s abstract certificate definition does not impose this symmetry on the weight. In particular it is automatic for the constant weights used later, but it is an extra restriction for a general weight.
Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.weightFn.summary: Certificate hypothesis: $w(Ry)=w(y)$ for every $(R,\theta_0)\in\Gamma$ and $y\in\mathbb R^3$. The paper's abstract certificate in Section 7.3 does not impose this symmetry; it is automatic for constant weights but extra for a general weight.

Breakdown.IsPeriodicTestField.text: The field ψ(θ,y) is jointly C∞, has period one in θ, is divergence-free in y, and vanishes outside one ball whose radius is independent of θ. These are the test fields v′ used in (B.14). Spatial compactness is uniform over time; there is no compact support in all of space-time, which would force a periodic field to vanish. The definition imposes no symmetry under Γ.
Breakdown.IsPeriodicTestField.summary: ψ(θ,y) is jointly C∞, period one in θ, divergence-free in y, and vanishes outside one ball independent of θ: the test fields v′ of (B.14). Spatial compactness is uniform in time, and no Γ symmetry is imposed.

Breakdown.IsPeriodicTestPotential.text: The real function q(θ,y) is jointly C∞, has period one in θ, and vanishes outside one fixed spatial ball for all θ. Its gradient is used to test whether a period-one multiplier is divergence-free. These scalar potentials provide the distributional meaning of the solenoidal multiplier in Appendix B.2. There is no separate mean-zero normalization, and q is a test function rather than the pressure of the solution.
Breakdown.IsPeriodicTestPotential.summary: q(θ,y) is jointly C∞, period one in θ, and vanishes outside one fixed spatial ball; its gradient tests whether a periodic multiplier is divergence-free in Appendix B.2. No mean-zero normalization is imposed.

Breakdown.IsPerturbation.text:
For a real period parameter $S$ and symmetries $\Gamma$, a perturbation is supplied by four everywhere-defined period-one fields $v,G,H,g$. They are jointly measurable up to null sets; for almost every time $G=
abla v$ and $H=
abla^2v$ in the spatial weak sense, $v$ is solenoidal and belongs to $L^6(\mathbb R^3)$, and the period integrals of $|G|_{m F}^2$, $|\operatorname{tr}H|^2$ and $|g|^2$ are finite. Against every smooth compactly supported vector test, $g=S^{-1}\partial_	heta v+	frac12v+	frac12(y\cdot
abla)v$ distributionally; the tests here need not be solenoidal. Thus $\mathcal T_Sv=g-\operatorname{tr}H$. No separate global $L^2$ condition is imposed on $\partial_	heta v$ or $(y\cdot
abla)v$. For each $(R,	heta_0)\in\Gamma$, $v(	heta+	heta_0,Ry)=Rv(	heta,y)$ almost everywhere. The domain uses explicit weak derivatives and selected periodic representatives. It does not itself assert a continuous representative in $X$. The definition permits every real $S$ with zero-division convention; applications require $S>0$.
Breakdown.IsPerturbation.summary:
A perturbation is period-one fields $v,G,H,g$: $G=
abla v$, $H=
abla^2v$ weakly, $v$ solenoidal in $L^6$, $G,\operatorname{tr}H,g$ square integrable over a period, $g=S^{-1}\partial_	heta v+	frac12v+	frac12(y\cdot
abla)v$, $\Gamma$-invariant; then $\mathcal T_Sv=g-\operatorname{tr}H$.

Breakdown.IsPerturbation.invariant.text: For a perturbation $v$ of period one with symmetry set $\Gamma$, this condition states that for each $(R,\theta_0)\in\Gamma$, $v(\theta+\theta_0,Ry)=Rv(\theta,y)$ for almost every $(\theta,y)$. Here $R$ is an orthogonal linear map of $\mathbb R^3$, and null sets may depend on the selected pair. Substitution of $R^{-1}y$ gives (7.5). With $\Gamma=\varnothing$ the condition imposes no symmetry.
Breakdown.IsPerturbation.invariant.summary: For each $(R,\theta_0)\in\Gamma$, the perturbation satisfies $v(\theta+\theta_0,Ry)=Rv(\theta,y)$ for almost every $(\theta,y)$; substituting $R^{-1}y$ gives (7.5). With $\Gamma=\varnothing$ no symmetry is imposed.

Breakdown.IsProfileField.text: The spatial vector field u:ℝ³→ℝ³ and proposed derivatives G,H must satisfy G=∇u and H=∇²u distributionally, including local integrability in each weak-gradient identity. The divergence of u is zero almost everywhere, u∈L⁶, and ∫|G|² and ∫|tr H|² are finite. For every (R,0)∈Γ, u(Ry)=Ru(y) almost everywhere. Symmetries with nonzero time shift impose no condition on this spatial field. This is the test class u∈X with Δu∈L² and the zero-time-shift symmetries in (7.22). There is no time variable and no L² condition on u itself.
Breakdown.IsProfileField.summary: A spatial field u with G=∇u and H=∇²u distributionally, div u=0, u∈L⁶, ∫|G|² and ∫|tr H|² finite, and invariance under the zero-time-shift symmetries of Γ: the test class of (7.22). There is no L² condition on u itself.

Breakdown.IsRightSide.text: Let W,v,g,F and each bᵢ be vector fields on ℝ×ℝ³, let G be a matrix field there, and let β₁,…,βₖ be real constants for a finite integer k≥0. For every smooth compactly supported solenoidal space-time test φ, the formal statement requires ∫F·φ=∫[(g+GW+DW[v]+∑ᵢβᵢbᵢ)·φ+G:∇φ], with both integrals over all ℝ×ℝ³. Here DW is the spatial derivative of W, and G:∇φ=∑ⱼ(G eⱼ)·∂ⱼφ is the Frobenius pairing. When the terms are integrable, S>0, G=∇v, and g=S⁻¹∂θv+½v+½(y·∇)v, the identity expresses F≃𝓣ˢv+(W·∇)v+(v·∇)W+∑ᵢβᵢbᵢ, the relation in (7.18), where 𝓣ˢv=g−Δv and ≃ denotes equality modulo spatial gradients. F need not be solenoidal. These derivative and integrability conditions are separate assumptions. An ordinary integral is assigned zero if its integrand is nonintegrable, so the single integral of the sum on the right cannot in general be replaced by a sum of separate integrals. The derivative of W also has a default zero value where it does not exist.
Breakdown.IsRightSide.summary: For every smooth compactly supported solenoidal test φ, ∫F·φ=∫[(g+GW+DW[v]+∑ᵢβᵢbᵢ)·φ+G:∇φ]. With the derivative identifications this expresses F≃𝓣ˢv+(W·∇)v+(v·∇)W+∑ᵢβᵢbᵢ of (7.18); a nonintegrable integral is taken as zero.

Breakdown.IsSimilarityProfile.text:
Let $W:\mathbb R	imes\mathbb R^3	o\mathbb R^3$ and $q:\mathbb R	imes\mathbb R^3	o\mathbb R$ be jointly smooth. For every $s\in\mathbb R$ and $y\in\mathbb R^3$, assume $\partial_sW+ rac12W+ rac12(y\cdot
abla)W-\Delta W+(W\cdot
abla)W+
abla q=0$ and $\operatorname{div}W=0$. Assume one real constant $C$ gives $\|D_y^jW(s,y)\|\le C(1+|y|)^{-j-1}$ for the integers $j=0,1,2$, and $|
abla_yq(s,y)|\le C(1+|y|)^{-3}$, uniformly in all $s,y$. Here $D_y^0W=W$, while for $j=1,2$ the derivative is a linear or bilinear map with its operator norm. The paper uses the square root of the sum of squared coordinate derivatives. These norms are equivalent in dimension three, with fixed factors; an unspecified bound transfers after enlarging $C$, but the same numerical constant is not asserted. This condition does not require a positive period, an orthogonal recurrence, or nonzero velocity. Those are separate assumptions in the existence statement. In particular, this condition by itself includes the zero field. All denominators are positive because $1+|y|>0$. The derivative bounds are for the three natural-number orders $0,1,2$, rather than for every real order. The pressure-gradient bound and the second-derivative bound are additional explicit assumptions compared with (1.2) and (1.3).
Breakdown.IsSimilarityProfile.summary: Smooth $W,q$ satisfying the similarity equation and $\operatorname{div}W=0$ everywhere, with $\|D_y^jW\|\le C(1+|y|)^{-j-1}$ for $j=0,1,2$ and $|\nabla q|\le C(1+|y|)^{-3}$. The second-derivative and pressure bounds are extra compared with (1.2) and (1.3); the zero field is included.

Breakdown.IsSmoothSolution.text:
Fix a real viscosity $
u$, a datum $u_0:\mathbb R^3	o\mathbb R^3$, and functions $u:\mathbb R	imes\mathbb R^3	o\mathbb R^3$ and $p:\mathbb R	imes\mathbb R^3	o\mathbb R$. This condition requires $u,p$ to be jointly smooth up to the boundary on $[0,\infty)	imes\mathbb R^3$, $u(0,x)=u_0(x)$ for every $x$, and $\partial_tu+(u\cdot
abla)u=
u\Delta u-
abla p$ and $\operatorname{div}u=0$ at every $t>0$ and $x$. The Laplacian is the sum of the three pure second spatial derivatives, and advection is the derivative of $u(t,\cdot)$ applied to $u(t,x)$. The definition alone does not assume $
u>0$, finite energy, spatial periodicity, or decay. It concerns the whole half-line, whereas the paper also defines solutions on finite intervals. The equations are expressly imposed only at positive times; smoothness and the initial value include $t=0$. The functions have values at negative times, on which no regularity or equation is required. Smoothness makes the derivative operations ordinary classical derivatives on the positive-time domain.
Breakdown.IsSmoothSolution.summary:
Requires $u,p$ jointly smooth on $[0,\infty)	imes\mathbb R^3$, $u(0)=u_0$, and $\partial_tu+(u\cdot
abla)u=
u\Delta u-
