u>0$, finite energy, periodicity or decay, and covers the whole half-line only.

Breakdown.IsSpaceTimeTestField.text: This condition says that $\varphi:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ is smooth jointly in time and space, has compact support in space-time, and satisfies $\operatorname{div}_y\varphi(\theta,y)=0$ at every point. It is the test class in (7.2). The tests are defined on the whole real time axis and are not required to be periodic. The definition specifies the class; it does not itself say that any given field has zero pairing with all its members.
Breakdown.IsSpaceTimeTestField.summary: A field $\varphi:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ is a test field when it is jointly smooth, compactly supported in space-time and satisfies $\operatorname{div}_y\varphi=0$ everywhere. It is the test class of (7.2); tests need not be periodic.

Breakdown.IsSpaceTimeTestVector.text: The field φ:ℝ×ℝ³→ℝ³ is jointly smooth and compactly supported in the full space-time product. Its divergence is unrestricted. These tests identify the vector-valued distribution S⁻¹∂θv+½v+½(y·∇)v in (7.4). Using unrestricted tests here retains all vector components; the separate solenoidal test class is used when equality is only modulo gradients.
Breakdown.IsSpaceTimeTestVector.summary: φ:ℝ×ℝ³→ℝ³ is jointly smooth and compactly supported in space-time, with unrestricted divergence. These tests identify the vector distribution S⁻¹∂θv+½v+½(y·∇)v in (7.4).

Breakdown.IsTestField.text: The formal statement defines the class $C_{c,\mathrm{div}}^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$: a field $\varphi:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ is smooth of every order, has compact support, and satisfies $\operatorname{div}\varphi(x)=0$ at every $x$. Compact support means that the closure of the set where $\varphi$ is nonzero is compact. The divergence is the sum of the three classical directional derivatives in the coordinate directions. There is no time variable, norm bound, or equation of motion in this condition. This is a definition of the admissible test fields; it does not itself assert their density in a Sobolev space.
Breakdown.IsTestField.summary: Defines $C^\infty_{c,\mathrm{div}}(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$: fields that are smooth, compactly supported and satisfy $\operatorname{div}\varphi=0$ at every point. It does not assert density in a Sobolev space.

Breakdown.IsTestFunction.text: A test function φ:ℝ³→ℝ is C∞ and has compact support. The definition contains no time variable, divergence condition, sign condition or normalization of its integral. These are the usual spatial test functions used to define distributional derivatives in §3.5 and the weak derivatives of the space X in §3.1.
Breakdown.IsTestFunction.summary: A function φ:ℝ³→ℝ that is C∞ with compact support: the usual spatial test function for distributional derivatives in §3.5 and for the weak derivatives of X in §3.1.

Breakdown.IsTimePeriodic.text: For an everywhere-defined field $F$ on $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3$, with any value space, this condition means $F(\theta+1,y)=F(\theta,y)$ for every real $\theta$ and every $y$. It imposes neither measurability nor integrability. The identity concerns the selected representative at every point, even when later normed spaces identify fields that agree almost everywhere. It is period one in the rescaled variable $\theta=s/S$.
Breakdown.IsTimePeriodic.summary: A field $F$ on $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3$ is period one when $F(\theta+1,y)=F(\theta,y)$ at every point. No measurability or integrability is imposed; the period is one in the rescaled variable $\theta=s/S$.

Breakdown.IsWeakGradient.text: For f:ℝ³→ℝ³ and a matrix-valued field G, both f and G must be locally integrable. For every scalar φ∈C∞c(ℝ³) and every coordinate direction eᵢ, the vector identity ∫φ(y)G(y)eᵢdy=−∫∂ᵢφ(y)f(y)dy must hold. Thus G(y)eᵢ represents ∂ᵢf, with the derivative direction as the argument of the matrix. This is the usual distributional gradient underlying X in §§2.1 and 3.1. Local integrability is required explicitly, so the integrals are ordinary finite integrals against compactly supported tests. Values on null sets are immaterial to these identities.
Breakdown.IsWeakGradient.summary: f and G are locally integrable and ∫φGeᵢ=−∫∂ᵢφ f for every φ∈C∞c(ℝ³) and direction eᵢ, so Geᵢ represents ∂ᵢf. This is the usual distributional gradient underlying X in §§2.1 and 3.1.

Breakdown.MildFramework.IsMildOn.text: Let $X$ be a real Hilbert space equipped with the heat operators $e^{t\Delta}$ and symmetric bounded bilinear maps $K(\tau)$ used in the construction. In the whole-space application, an element of $X$ is the frequency state $2\pi|\xi|\widehat u(\xi)$ for a solenoidal $L^6$ velocity with gradient in $L^2$, and the norm is its homogeneous $H^1$ norm. The formal condition on a map $u:\mathbb R\to X$ and real endpoints $a,b$ is continuity on $[a,b)$ and, for every $a\le t<b$, Bochner integrability of $s\mapsto K(t-s)(u(s),u(s))$ on $[a,t]$, together with $u(t)=e^{(t-a)\Delta}u(a)+\int_a^tK(t-s)(u(s),u(s))\,ds$. The integrability clause prevents a default value for an undefined integral from satisfying the equation. Although the map has values at all real times, nothing is required outside $[a,b)$. The definition itself allows $b\le a$, when the condition is vacuous; the paper assumes $a<b$. The value of $K(0)$ at the single integration endpoint has no effect on the integral. This condition defines a mild solution, without asserting pointwise smoothness or existence of a pressure.
Breakdown.MildFramework.IsMildOn.summary: A map $u:\mathbb R\to X$ is mild on $[a,b)$ if continuous there and, for $a\le t<b$, $s\mapsto K(t-s)(u(s),u(s))$ is Bochner integrable on $[a,t]$ with $u(t)=e^{(t-a)\Delta}u(a)+\int_a^t\cdots$. The condition is vacuous for $b\le a$; the paper assumes $a<b$.

Breakdown.MildFramework.IsMildOnIcc.text: Let $X$ be a real Hilbert space equipped with the heat operators $e^{t\Delta}$ and symmetric bounded bilinear maps $K(\tau)$ used in the construction. In the whole-space application, an element of $X$ is the frequency state $2\pi|\xi|\widehat u(\xi)$ for a solenoidal $L^6$ velocity with gradient in $L^2$, and the norm is its homogeneous $H^1$ norm. For a map $u:\mathbb R\to X$ and endpoints $a,b\in\mathbb R$, the formal condition requires continuity on $[a,b]$, and for every $a\le t\le b$ it requires both Bochner integrability on $[a,t]$ and the identity $u(t)=e^{(t-a)\Delta}u(a)+\int_a^tK(t-s)(u(s),u(s))\,ds$. This includes the right endpoint $b$. The map is defined at every real time but is constrained only on this interval. If $b<a$ the condition is vacuous; for $b=a$ the integral is zero and the identity follows from $e^{0\Delta}=I$. For positive interval length, the diagonal value $K(0)$ has no effect on the integral. The condition asserts the integral equation in $X$ and contains no smoothness or pressure conclusion.
Breakdown.MildFramework.IsMildOnIcc.summary: A map $u:\mathbb R\to X$ is mild on $[a,b]$ if continuous there and, for every $a\le t\le b$, the integrand is Bochner integrable on $[a,t]$ and $u(t)=e^{(t-a)\Delta}u(a)+\int_a^tK(t-s)(u(s),u(s))\,ds$. It is vacuous if $b<a$ and has no smoothness or pressure content.

Breakdown.MildFramework.IsOrbit.text: Let $\mathcal X$ be a real Hilbert space. Let $G(t)$ be bounded linear operators with $G(0)=I$, $G(s+t)=G(s)G(t)$ and $\|G(t)\|\le1$ for nonnegative times, with $t\mapsto G(t)x$ continuous there. Let $K(\tau)$ be symmetric bounded bilinear maps, continuous for positive $\tau$ on each pair of arguments, with $G(s)K(\tau)=K(s+\tau)$ for $s\ge0,\tau>0$, and $\|K(\tau)\|\le C_K\tau^{-3/4}$ for $0<\tau\le1$. Let $D_\mu$, $\mu>0$, be strongly continuous dilations with $D_1=I$, $D_\mu D_\eta=D_{\mu\eta}$, $\|D_\mu x\|=\mu^{1/4}\|x\|$, $D_\mu G(\mu t)=G(t)D_\mu$, and $\mu D_\mu K(\mu\tau)(x,y)=K(\tau)(D_\mu x,D_\mu y)$. Assume $x\mapsto K(\tau)(f,x)$ is compact for every $\tau>0$ and every $f$ in some dense subset of $\mathcal X$. In the whole-space application $\mathcal X$ is the Fourier realization of $\dot H^1_{\mathrm{div}}(\mathbb R^3)$, $G(t)=e^{t\Delta}$, and $D_\mu f(x)=\sqrt\mu f(\sqrt\mu x)$. Let $\rho$ be a surjective linear isometry, and let $w:\mathbb R\to\mathcal X$ be continuous and nonzero at some time, with $S>0$ and $w(s+S)=\rho w(s)$. Put $\mathcal S(\tau)=D_{e^{-\tau}}G(1-e^{-\tau})$ and $\mathcal K(\tau)(x,y)=D_{e^{-\tau}}K(1-e^{-\tau})(x,y)$. Assume, for every $s'\le s$, that the Bochner integral is integrable and $w(s)=\mathcal S(s-s')w(s')+\int_{s'}^s\mathcal K(s-\sigma)(w(\sigma),w(\sigma))\,d\sigma$. The period acts on the velocity by $\rho_Rf=Rf(R^{-1}\cdot)$ in the physical application. This defines the profile condition in the Hilbert space; it contains a mild equation in addition to recurrence. It assumes no smooth physical pressure and gives no pointwise decay. Values of the integrand at the endpoints have no effect on a Bochner integral. The recurrence and equation hold for every real similarity time, including negative times.
Breakdown.MildFramework.IsOrbit.summary: Defines a recurrent mild profile: continuous $w$, nonzero at some time, with $w(s+S)=\rho w(s)$ for a surjective isometry $\rho$ and $S>0$, satisfying the similarity-time mild equation for all $s'\le s$, under the heat, bilinear, dilation and compactness assumptions. No pressure or decay.

Breakdown.MildFramework.gluePieces.text: For a real Hilbert space $X$, dilations $D_\mu$, a scale $\mu$ and curves $u_n\in C([0,1-\mu];X)$, the formal function is $v(t)=D_{(\mu^n)^{-1}}u_n(\sigma)$ with $n=\lfloor\log(1-t)/\log\mu\rfloor_{\mathbb N}$ and $\sigma=(t-(1-\mu^n))/\mu^n$. On $0\le t<1$ with $0<\mu<1$, this selects $0\le\sigma<1-\mu$ and $1-t=\mu^n(1-\sigma)$. The natural-number floor truncates negative values to zero. For $\mu\le1$, each compact-interval curve is extended constantly at its endpoints before evaluation; for $\mu>1$ the interval is empty and the extension is zero. The definition is total even outside the physical range, where division by zero is assigned zero, $\log0=0$, and the real logarithm of a negative number is $\log|x|$. These assigned values do not give a continuation through $t=1$. Continuity and mildness require separate interval-matching hypotheses; no global weighted norm is defined here.
Breakdown.MildFramework.gluePieces.summary: Defines $v(t)=D_{(\mu^n)^{-1}}u_n(\sigma)$ with $n=\lfloor\log(1-t)/\log\mu\rfloor$ and $\sigma=(t-(1-\mu^n))/\mu^n$, so $1-t=\mu^n(1-\sigma)$ on $0\le t<1$ for $0<\mu<1$. Continuity and mildness need separate matching hypotheses.

Breakdown.MildFramework.profilePiece.text: For a real Hilbert space $X$ with dilations $D_\mu$, a curve $w:\mathbb R\to X$, a real $S$ and natural $k,n$, set $L=1-e^{-S/k}$. The formal object is the continuous curve on $[0,L]$ obtained by restricting $\sigma\mapsto D_{(1-\sigma)^{-1}}w(nS/k-\log(1-\sigma))$. If that restriction is not continuous, the definition assigns the zero curve. In the intended use $S>0$, $k\ge1$ and a continuous recurrent orbit are supplied, so the displayed formula and $0<L<1$ hold. This is a piece of the exact background profile. It is not the normalized perturbation $v_n$, normalized source $g_n$, initial value $\chi_n$, or forcing $f_n$ of (4.13). The index $n$ counts short intervals of length $S/k$ in similarity time. Division by zero is assigned zero; in particular $k=0$ gives $S/k=0$ and $L=0$. No positive interval is then asserted.
Breakdown.MildFramework.profilePiece.summary: With $L=1-e^{-S/k}$, the continuous curve $\sigma\mapsto D_{(1-\sigma)^{-1}}w(nS/k-\log(1-\sigma))$ on $[0,L]$, or zero if not continuous. It is a piece of the exact background profile, not the perturbation, source or forcing of (4.13).

Breakdown.MildFramework.selfSimilar.text: For a real Hilbert space $X$, a family of bounded linear dilations $D_\mu$ and any curve $w:\mathbb R\to X$, this defines $u_{s_0}(t)=D_{(1-t)^{-1}}w(s_0-\log(1-t))$. For the paper’s homogeneous $H^1$ realization, $D_\mu f(x)=\sqrt\mu f(\sqrt\mu x)$ for $\mu>0$, so $u_0=u^*$ on $[0,1)$. This definition alone asserts no continuity, mild equation, recurrence or norm estimate. It is total in real $t$. The physical interpretation requires $t<1$; at $t=1$, the reciprocal and $\log0$ are assigned zero, so the value is $D_0w(s_0)$. For $t>1$ the real logarithm means $\log|1-t|$, and the scale is negative. The dilation laws impose no condition at these nonpositive scales, so these values do not describe a physical continuation.
Breakdown.MildFramework.selfSimilar.summary: Defines $u_{s_0}(t)=D_{(1-t)^{-1}}w(s_0-\log(1-t))$, so $u_0=u^*$ on $[0,1)$ in the homogeneous $H^1$ space. It asserts no continuity, equation or bound; the physical meaning requires $t<1$.

Breakdown.MildFramework.stepOp.text:
Let $X$ be a real Hilbert space with the heat and bilinear operators of §3.4: $G(t)$ is a strongly continuous contraction semigroup, $K(\tau)$ is symmetric, continuous for $\tau>0$, obeys $G(s)K(\tau)=K(s+\tau)$ and $\|K(\tau)\|\le C_K\tau^{-3/4}$ for $0<\tau\le1$. Suppose the dilations satisfy $D_1=I$, $D_\mu D_\nu=D_{\mu\nu}$, $\|D_\mu x\|=\mu^{1/4}\|x\|$, $D_\mu G(\mu t)=G(t)D_\mu$, and $\mu D_\mu K(\mu\tau)(x,y)=K(\tau)(D_\mu x,D_\mu y)$ for positive scales, with continuous dependence on scale. Assume $K(\tau)(f,\cdot)$ is compact for a dense set of $f$ and every $\tau>0$.

For a curve $w:\mathbb R\to X$, a real $S$ and natural $k,n$, put $L=1-e^{-S/k}$ and let $u_n(\sigma)=D_{(1-\sigma)^{-1}}w(nS/k-\log(1-\sigma))$ on $[0,L]$ when this is continuous. This defines the bounded linear map $A_n v=2\mathcal B_L(u_n,v)$ on $C([0,L];X)$. In the paper it is the integral term in the equation linearized about the profile on a short rescaled interval. The definition supplies no invertibility of $I-A_n$. Formally, restriction to a compact continuous curve defaults to zero if continuity fails, and the Duhamel operator is assigned zero if no bounded bilinear operator with its integral formula exists. The profile and positive-period hypotheses used by the monodromy theorem remove those cases; $k>0$ is imposed there as well. Here $\mathcal B_L(f,g)(\sigma)=\int_0^\sigma K(\sigma-r)(f(r),g(r))\,dr$ for continuous curves on $[0,L]$, and the norm of each input or output curve is the supremum norm on that interval.
Breakdown.MildFramework.stepOp.summary: Defines the bounded linear map $A_nv=2\mathcal B_L(u_n,v)$ on $C([0,L];X)$, $L=1-e^{-S/k}$, where $u_n$ is the profile piece: the integral term of the equation linearized about the profile on a short interval. Invertibility of $I-A_n$ is not supplied.

Breakdown.MildRegular.text: This declaration defines a regularity property for an abstract Navier–Stokes realization on a real Hilbert space $\mathcal X$. The realization supplies heat and bilinear operators and a map embedding smooth decaying solenoidal fields. Separately prescribe a bounded real linear map from $\mathcal X$ to $L^6(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$, whose value is the reconstructed velocity in this property. Let $\varphi:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ be smooth, compactly supported and divergence-free, and let $T>0$. Suppose $u$ is a continuous mild curve in the stated Hilbert space $\mathcal X$ on the closed interval $[0,T]$, with initial element equal to the embedded $\varphi$. Here mild means $u(t)=G(t)u(0)+\int_0^t K(t-s)(u(s),u(s))\,ds$ for every $0\le t\le T$, with each time integral Bochner integrable; $G$ and $K$ are the heat and bilinear operators supplied by the realization. The formal conclusion supplies fields $U:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ and $P:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$, smooth up to the time boundary of $[0,T]\times\mathbb R^3$. They satisfy $U(0,x)=\varphi(x)$, $\operatorname{div}U=0$ on the closed interval, and $\partial_tU+(U\cdot\nabla)U=\Delta U-\nabla P$ for $0<t<T$. For some finite constants $A,B$, $\int|U(t,x)|^2dx\le A$ for every $t\in[0,T]$, and $|U(t,x)|\le B$, $\|D_xU(t,x)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le B$ for every such $t$ and every $x$. The last derivative bound is pointwise in space and uniform in time; it is not a bound on the spatial $L^2$ norm of the gradient. For each $t\in[0,T]$, the reconstructed $L^6$ velocity of $u(t)$ equals $U(t,\cdot)$ almost everywhere. There is no constraint on the extensions outside the time interval. For a solution on $[0,T_*)$, the property may be applied separately to every closed interval $[0,T]$ with $T<T_*$. The declaration itself does not assemble these representatives into a single one on the full half-open interval. It also does not state $\|U(t)\|_2\le\|\varphi\|_2$, and it contains no periodic version of the assertion. It defines the property, without proving it for an arbitrary realization.
Breakdown.MildRegular.summary: Defines the property: a continuous mild curve on $[0,T]$ from an embedded test field $\varphi$ has smooth $U,P$ solving Navier–Stokes for $0<t<T$, with $U(0)=\varphi$, bounded energy, pointwise bounds on $U,D_xU$, and $U(t)$ a.e. equal to its velocity. It is a definition, not a proof.

Breakdown.ModeWeights.text: The input assigns every raw integer mode (n,k) to a class; supplies a finite set of nonzero waves; and, for each class, an angular-rate function, a signed curl weight ε, a signed velocity weight μ, conversion functions D,Z, a first energy share and a positive-parameter candidate η. Common spatial data supply two further shares, two balancing lengths and a lower bound candidate ηmin; common real constants are c,cμ. None of the sign, smoothness, decay, finiteness-of-classes or inequality requirements is part of the data itself. This is the earlier multiplier format; Appendix B.2 uses finitely many pieces with sets of modes and separate weights, so it is not a transcription of those piece data.
Breakdown.ModeWeights.summary: Data for the earlier class-based multiplier: a class for each raw mode, a finite set of nonzero waves, and per class an angular rate, signed curl and velocity weights, conversion functions, a share and η, plus common shares, lengths and constants. Appendix B.2 instead uses finite pieces.

Breakdown.ModeWeights.IsAdmissible.text:
For a period S, energy weight w, class-based signed curl and velocity weights ε,μ, and reference bounds, the formal statement imposes the following conditions. There are finitely many classes, 0<c<1, 0<cμ<1, S>0, and w≥w*>0 is measurable and axisymmetric. The finite wave set excludes zero and is closed under negation. Under mode negation ε,μ change sign, while the rotation rate a, conversion weights D,Z, first share a₁ and η are unchanged. The signed weights are globally Lipschitz and axisymmetric. The rates, conversion weights, shares and balancing lengths are axisymmetric; the rotation rates, shares and balancing lengths are measurable, and the rates are bounded uniformly over classes and space.

For every mode, Ωε≥0 and Ωμ≥0 where Ω=2πn/S+ka. Uniform bounds |ε|≤E*, |∇ε|≤E′* and |y||ε|≤B hold. One constant bounds |μ|, |y|²|μ| and |y||∇μ|. For a nonnegative ratio R, |μ|≤R|Ω|. Each D,Z is C²; D≥0. Their derivatives of integer orders j=0,1,2 satisfy uniform bounds |y|ʲ|DʲD|≤B and (1+|y|)ʲ|DʲZ|≤B, respectively.

The share a₁ is nonnegative and strictly positive wherever |ε|+|∇ε|>0. The shares a₂,a₄ and lengths L,L₂ are everywhere positive. The share a₄ is bounded. If Q₁ bounds the wave vorticity-gradient operator, both Q₁L and |y|²Q₁/L are bounded. If Q₂ bounds the sum of wave curl-gradient amplitudes, both L₂Q₂E* and |y|²Q₂E*/L₂ are bounded. Each η and its lower bound ηmin are positive, with ηmin≤η. Finally D≤1−â, where â=a₁1_(|ε|+|∇ε|>0)+a₂1_(largest neighboring |ε|>0). This keeps the residual curl-gradient coefficient nonnegative.

These are assumptions on the supplied fields, not numerical verification of them. They implement an earlier sufficient multiplier construction. Appendix B.2 uses finite pieces and does not print this class-based list. The positivity conditions justify the divisions; an inactive first share may vanish only where its numerator vanishes.
Breakdown.ModeWeights.IsAdmissible.summary: Admissibility of the earlier class-based weights: finitely many classes, sign changes under mode negation, Lipschitz axisymmetric weights, Ωε≥0 and Ωμ≥0, decay bounds, positive shares and lengths, and D≤1−â. These are assumptions; Appendix B.2 does not print this list.

Breakdown.ModeWeights.IsMultiplierField.text: For a perturbation v with supplied weak gradient G and Hessian H, a real field M must be measurable, period one and square integrable over [0,1]×ℝ³. It must annihilate gradients of all smooth period-one scalar potentials of uniformly compact spatial support. For every smooth period-one solenoidal test ψ of uniformly compact spatial support, require ⟨M,ψ⟩=⟨−tr H,ψ⟩+∑_ι∫Re(iε_ι curl Ĝ_ι·overline(curl ∇ψ̂_ι)+iμ_ι v̂_ι·overline(ψ̂_ι)). Here ε_ι,μ_ι are the signed class weights; their absolute values occur in the energy estimates. All integrals cover θ∈[0,1] and all of ℝ³. With θ=s/S there is no additional factor S; the factor 1/(2π) already belongs to the angular average defining each mode. This characterizes the earlier multiplier as a solenoidal L² field when G,H really are the derivatives. It is the class-based counterpart of (B.14), whose weights are sums over finite pieces. The real series is the order-independent sum over all integer pairs, assigned zero if not summable. Ordinary real integrals also have default zero values when their integrands are nonintegrable. The multiplier construction must justify the convergent analytic interpretation.
Breakdown.ModeWeights.IsMultiplierField.summary: M is measurable, periodic and square integrable, annihilates gradients of periodic test potentials, and satisfies ⟨M,ψ⟩=⟨−tr H,ψ⟩+∑_ι∫Re(iε_ι curl Ĝ_ι·overline(curl ∇ψ̂_ι)+iμ_ι v̂_ι·overline(ψ̂_ι)): the class-based counterpart of (B.14).

Breakdown.ModeWeights.azimuthalDensity_n.text: Let q₁=(k−1)²/r² and q₂=(k−2)²/r² for real k,r; real division by zero is assigned zero. Suppose θ≥0, 0≤a≤1, A′=A+θq₂≥0, B′=B+aA′q₁≥0, and C²≤4(1−a)A′B′. If q₁x₀²≤x₁² and q₂x₁²≤x₂², then θx₂²+Ax₁²+Bx₀²−Cx₁x₀≥0. This is the scalar consequence of angular gains used in Appendix B.3. It makes no assumption r>0 or k≥2 because the two gain inequalities are explicit hypotheses; geometric application off the axis needs those conditions separately. The source's radius-zero case is an algebraic convention, not a bound with a singular denominator.
Breakdown.ModeWeights.azimuthalDensity_n.summary: Let q₁=(k−1)²/r², q₂=(k−2)²/r², A′=A+θq₂, B′=B+aA′q₁, with division by zero taken as zero. If θ≥0, 0≤a≤1, A′,B′≥0, C²≤4(1−a)A′B′, q₁x₀²≤x₁² and q₂x₁²≤x₂², then θx₂²+Ax₁²+Bx₀²−Cx₁x₀≥0, as used in Appendix B.3.

Breakdown.ModeWeights.coefA.text: Fix raw mode ι and y. Write ε=|ε_ι|, μ=|μ_ι|, Ω=2πn/S+ka, ε′=|∇ε_ι| and μ′=|∇μ_ι|; εnb and μnb are the maximum neighboring magnitudes over the finite wave set. D,Z,a,a₁,η are the class's conversion functions, rotation rate, first share and balancing number; a₂,a₄,L,L₂,ηmin are common auxiliary data. Let U bound the mean relative transport, O₀=|curl W̄|bound, Q₀=|∇curl W̄|bound, G₀=|DW̄|bound, and U₁,G₁,O₁,Q₁ bound the sums of wave velocity, gradient, curl and curl-gradient amplitudes. The coefficient is A=¼+ε|Ω|−(εU+ε′)²/(4a₁)−ε²U₁²/(4a₂)−ε(O₀/2+|a|+G₁/2+O₁/2+L₂Q₁/2). It is the coefficient before the conversion subtracts Z. All quantities are evaluated at y. Division by zero is assigned zero in the bare formulas; admissibility makes the used balancing denominators positive, except an inactive first share whose numerator vanishes. This belongs to the earlier class-based multiplier; Appendix B.2 uses finite families of pieces, so the displayed formula is an auxiliary version rather than the exact five-coefficient density (B.16).
Breakdown.ModeWeights.coefA.summary: The earlier class-based curl coefficient A=¼+ε|Ω|−(εU+ε′)²/(4a₁)−ε²U₁²/(4a₂)−ε(O₀/2+|a|+G₁/2+O₁/2+L₂Q₁/2), before Z is subtracted; division by zero is taken as zero. It is an auxiliary version, not the five-coefficient density (B.16).

Breakdown.ModeWeights.coefAA.text: Fix raw mode ι and y. Write ε=|ε_ι|, μ=|μ_ι|, Ω=2πn/S+ka, ε′=|∇ε_ι| and μ′=|∇μ_ι|; εnb and μnb are the maximum neighboring magnitudes over the finite wave set. D,Z,a,a₁,η are the class's conversion functions, rotation rate, first share and balancing number; a₂,a₄,L,L₂,ηmin are common auxiliary data. Let U bound the mean relative transport, O₀=|curl W̄|bound, Q₀=|∇curl W̄|bound, G₀=|DW̄|bound, and U₁,G₁,O₁,Q₁ bound the sums of wave velocity, gradient, curl and curl-gradient amplitudes. The coefficient is A₁=Z−√2 εO₀−|D²D|op−cw−εnb(G₁+O₁/2)−a₄1_(μnb>0), where w is the energy weight and c is the retained coercive fraction. It multiplies |∇v̂|² after conversion of curl terms. All quantities are evaluated at y. Division by zero is assigned zero in the bare formulas; admissibility makes the used balancing denominators positive, except an inactive first share whose numerator vanishes. This belongs to the earlier class-based multiplier; Appendix B.2 uses finite families of pieces, so the displayed formula is an auxiliary version rather than the exact five-coefficient density (B.16).
Breakdown.ModeWeights.coefAA.summary: The earlier gradient coefficient A₁=Z−√2 εO₀−|D²D|op−cw−εnb(G₁+O₁/2)−a₄1_(μnb>0), multiplying |∇v̂|² after conversion of curl terms. It belongs to the class-based multiplier and is not the five-coefficient density (B.16).

Breakdown.ModeWeights.coefB.text: Fix raw mode ι and y. Write ε=|ε_ι|, μ=|μ_ι|, Ω=2πn/S+ka, ε′=|∇ε_ι| and μ′=|∇μ_ι|; εnb and μnb are the maximum neighboring magnitudes over the finite wave set. D,Z,a,a₁,η are the class's conversion functions, rotation rate, first share and balancing number; a₂,a₄,L,L₂,ηmin are common auxiliary data. Let U bound the mean relative transport, O₀=|curl W̄|bound, Q₀=|∇curl W̄|bound, G₀=|DW̄|bound, and U₁,G₁,O₁,Q₁ bound the sums of wave velocity, gradient, curl and curl-gradient amplitudes. The coefficient is B=(1−cμ)μ|Ω|−μ|a|−μ²U₁²/(4a₄)−|D²Z|op−εnbQ₁/(2L₂)−P, where P=(G₀²/η+ημ²/2)1_(μ_ι is nonzero somewhere)+(G₁²/ηmin)1_(a neighboring μ is nonzero somewhere). It multiplies |v̂|². All quantities are evaluated at y. Division by zero is assigned zero in the bare formulas; admissibility makes the used balancing denominators positive, except an inactive first share whose numerator vanishes. This belongs to the earlier class-based multiplier; Appendix B.2 uses finite families of pieces, so the displayed formula is an auxiliary version rather than the exact five-coefficient density (B.16).
Breakdown.ModeWeights.coefB.summary: The earlier velocity coefficient B=(1−cμ)μ|Ω|−μ|a|−μ²U₁²/(4a₄)−|D²Z|op−εnbQ₁/(2L₂)−P, multiplying |v̂|², with P the η-balancing terms; division by zero is taken as zero. It is not the five-coefficient density (B.16).

Breakdown.ModeWeights.coefC.text: Fix raw mode ι and y. Write ε=|ε_ι|, μ=|μ_ι|, Ω=2πn/S+ka, ε′=|∇ε_ι| and μ′=|∇μ_ι|; εnb and μnb are the maximum neighboring magnitudes over the finite wave set. D,Z,a,a₁,η are the class's conversion functions, rotation rate, first share and balancing number; a₂,a₄,L,L₂,ηmin are common auxiliary data. Let U bound the mean relative transport, O₀=|curl W̄|bound, Q₀=|∇curl W̄|bound, G₀=|DW̄|bound, and U₁,G₁,O₁,Q₁ bound the sums of wave velocity, gradient, curl and curl-gradient amplitudes. The coefficient is C=√2 εQ₀+μU+μ′. It occurs as the subtracted mixed term C|∇v̂||v̂|. Its nonnegativity follows from appropriate nonnegative majorants, rather than from the arbitrary-data definition itself. All quantities are evaluated at y. Division by zero is assigned zero in the bare formulas; admissibility makes the used balancing denominators positive, except an inactive first share whose numerator vanishes. This belongs to the earlier class-based multiplier; Appendix B.2 uses finite families of pieces, so the displayed formula is an auxiliary version rather than the exact five-coefficient density (B.16).
Breakdown.ModeWeights.coefC.summary: The earlier mixed coefficient C=√2 εQ₀+μU+μ′, subtracted as C|∇v̂||v̂|; it is nonnegative given nonnegative majorants. It belongs to the class-based multiplier, not the five-coefficient density (B.16).

Breakdown.ModeWeights.densityNeg.text: For a perturbation v with proposed derivatives G,H and reference W, the pointwise value is ∑_ι max(−I_ι,0)+max(−J,0). I_ι is the earlier class-based modal quadratic form in the amplitudes of Ĥ, its curl contraction, Ĝ, its curl and v̂; J is the stretching expression (B.18). Thus the negative part is taken for each entire mode term and separately for J, before summing. The result lies in [0,∞] and may be infinite. This uses the same positive/negative-part convention stated after (B.18), but the earlier I_ι contains a mixed gradient–velocity term absent from (B.16). No cancellation or finiteness is asserted by this definition.
Breakdown.ModeWeights.densityNeg.summary: The pointwise value ∑_ι max(−I_ι,0)+max(−J,0) in [0,∞], with I_ι the earlier class-based modal form and J the stretching expression (B.18). The earlier I_ι has a mixed gradient–velocity term absent from (B.16); no finiteness is asserted.

Breakdown.ModeWeights.densityPos.text: For a perturbation v with proposed derivatives G,H and reference W, the pointwise value is ∑_ι max(I_ι,0)+max(J,0). I_ι is the earlier class-based modal quadratic form in the amplitudes of Ĥ, its curl contraction, Ĝ, its curl and v̂; J is the stretching expression (B.18). Thus the positive part is taken for each entire mode term and separately for J, before summing. The result lies in [0,∞] and may be infinite. This uses the same positive/negative-part convention stated after (B.18), but the earlier I_ι contains a mixed gradient–velocity term absent from (B.16). No cancellation or finiteness is asserted by this definition.
Breakdown.ModeWeights.densityPos.summary: The pointwise value ∑_ι max(I_ι,0)+max(J,0) in [0,∞], with I_ι the earlier class-based modal form and J the stretching expression (B.18). The earlier I_ι has a mixed gradient–velocity term absent from (B.16); no finiteness is asserted.

Breakdown.ModeWeights.diagonalDensity.text: For real coefficients θ,A,B,C and real amplitudes x₂,x₁,x₀, the scalar is θx₂²+Ax₁²+Bx₀²−Cx₁x₀. In angular positivity estimates the three amplitudes represent second derivative, first derivative and velocity sizes. This is a general algebraic reduction used for the estimates in Appendix B.3, not the full five-term density (B.16). Its coefficients and arguments are arbitrary real numbers; positivity is not part of the definition.
Breakdown.ModeWeights.diagonalDensity.summary: The scalar θx₂²+Ax₁²+Bx₀²−Cx₁x₀ for real coefficients and amplitudes, which stand for second-derivative, first-derivative and velocity sizes in Appendix B.3. It is not the full density (B.16), and no positivity is built in.

Breakdown.ModeWeights.diagonalDensity_no.text: If θ≥0, A≥0, B≥0 and C²≤4AB, then θx₂²+Ax₁²+Bx₀²−Cx₁x₀≥0 for every real x₂,x₁,x₀. The conclusion includes degenerate cases A=0 or B=0, where the hypothesis forces the relevant cross term to vanish. This is the elementary discriminant argument supporting the quadratic lower bounds in Appendix B.3. It concerns arbitrary real amplitudes, without needing a field, a derivative identity or a radius.
Breakdown.ModeWeights.diagonalDensity_no.summary: If θ≥0, A≥0, B≥0 and C²≤4AB, then θx₂²+Ax₁²+Bx₀²−Cx₁x₀≥0 for all real x₂,x₁,x₀, including the degenerate cases A=0 or B=0. This is the discriminant argument behind the quadratic lower bounds of Appendix B.3.

Breakdown.ModeWeights.dop.text: For raw mode (n,k), period S and the angular rate a of that mode’s class, define Ω=2πn/S+ka(y). The rate may depend on y. Under S>0 this is the usual rotating-frame frequency; division by zero is assigned zero outside that hypothesis. This belongs to the earlier class-based multiplier; Appendix B.2 uses finite families of pieces, so the displayed formula is an auxiliary version rather than the exact five-coefficient density (B.16).
Breakdown.ModeWeights.dop.summary: Ω=2πn/S+ka(y) for raw mode (n,k), with a the angular rate of the mode's class; division by zero is taken as zero when S=0. It belongs to the earlier class-based multiplier, not the five-coefficient density (B.16).

Breakdown.ModeWeights.eps.text: For raw mode (n,k) and point y, take the absolute value of the signed curl weight ε assigned to that mode’s class. The output is nonnegative; the original sign is retained separately in the multiplier identity. Admissibility links the signed weight to the rotating-frame frequency. This belongs to the earlier class-based multiplier; Appendix B.2 uses finite families of pieces, so the displayed formula is an auxiliary version rather than the exact five-coefficient density (B.16).
Breakdown.ModeWeights.eps.summary: |ε| for the signed curl weight of the mode's class at y; the sign is kept separately in the multiplier identity. It belongs to the earlier class-based multiplier.

Breakdown.ModeWeights.epsGrad.text: For raw mode (n,k), take the operator norm of the real derivative of its class’s signed curl weight ε(y). This is |∇ε| wherever the weight is differentiable; it is the derivative of ε, not a separately asserted derivative of |ε|. The admissible weights are Lipschitz, so the derivative exists almost everywhere; at other points a default zero derivative is used. This belongs to the earlier class-based multiplier; Appendix B.2 uses finite families of pieces, so the displayed formula is an auxiliary version rather than the exact five-coefficient density (B.16).
Breakdown.ModeWeights.epsGrad.summary: The operator norm of the derivative of the class's signed curl weight ε(y), equal to |∇ε| where ε is differentiable; a default zero derivative is used elsewhere. It belongs to the earlier class-based multiplier.

Breakdown.ModeWeights.epsNb.text: For mode ι and point y, take max{|ε_(ι+α)(y)|: α is in the finite wave set}. The maximum is zero if the wave set is empty. This bounds the weights coupled to ι by the reference waves; it is a maximum, not the sum of those weights. This belongs to the earlier class-based multiplier; Appendix B.2 uses finite families of pieces, so the displayed formula is an auxiliary version rather than the exact five-coefficient density (B.16).
Breakdown.ModeWeights.epsNb.summary: max{|ε_(ι+α)(y)|: α in the finite wave set}, zero for an empty wave set: a maximum, not a sum, of the weights coupled to ι by the reference waves. It belongs to the earlier class-based multiplier.

Breakdown.ModeWeights.frequencySeminormS.text: Sum over every raw mode ι=(n,k) the nonnegative period integral of |μ_ι(y)|·|2πn/S+ka_ι(y)|·|v̂_ι(θ,y)|². Here μ_ι is the signed class velocity weight and a_ι the class rotation rate. The result lies in [0,∞] and may be infinite. It is the class-based counterpart of ‖v‖²μ in Appendix B.2, which instead sums contributions from the finite family of pieces. No finiteness or positive period is asserted by this definition; at S=0 the reciprocal convention is zero.
Breakdown.ModeWeights.frequencySeminormS.summary: The sum over raw modes ι=(n,k) of the period integrals of |μ_ι|·|2πn/S+ka_ι|·|v̂_ι|², a value in [0,∞]. It is the class-based counterpart of ‖v‖²μ in Appendix B.2; at S=0 the reciprocal is taken as zero.

Breakdown.ModeWeights.ind.text: For any stated mathematical condition, the value is 1 when that condition holds and 0 otherwise. This is a scalar logical indicator used to activate terms in the multiplier coefficients, unlike the indicator of a spatial region. The condition determines its value; this definition does not supply a numerical method for deciding that condition. This belongs to the earlier class-based multiplier; Appendix B.2 uses finite families of pieces, so the displayed formula is an auxiliary version rather than the exact five-coefficient density (B.16).
Breakdown.ModeWeights.ind.summary: The indicator equal to 1 when a stated condition holds and 0 otherwise, used to activate terms in the earlier multiplier coefficients. It specifies a mathematical value for each condition.

Breakdown.ModeWeights.le_of_ennreal_boun.text: Let X,Y be real and D⁺,D⁻∈[0,∞], with D⁻ finite. If D⁺+max(−X,0)≤max(X,0)+D⁻ and max(Y,0)+D⁻≤D⁺+max(−Y,0), then Y≤X. The first inequality also forces D⁺ finite. This is the finite-negative-part bookkeeping used when combining (B.20) with (B.21). The finiteness assumption is essential: cancelling two infinite quantities would not prove a real inequality.
Breakdown.ModeWeights.le_of_ennreal_boun.summary: For real X,Y and D⁺,D⁻∈[0,∞] with D⁻ finite, D⁺+max(−X,0)≤max(X,0)+D⁻ and max(Y,0)+D⁻≤D⁺+max(−Y,0) imply Y≤X. This combines (B.20) with (B.21); the finiteness of D⁻ is essential.

Breakdown.ModeWeights.modeDensity.text: For a fixed raw mode ι and point y, and arbitrary real arguments x₂,x_c,x₁,x_ω,x₀, the value is (D−c)x₂²+(1−â−D)x_c²+(A−Z)x_ω²+A₁x₁²+Bx₀²−Cx₁x₀. D and Z are the class conversion weights, â the assigned energy share, c the retained fraction, and A,A₁,B,C the coefficient functions obtained from the class weights and mean/wave bounds. On a perturbation the five arguments are respectively |∇²v̂|, |∇curl v̂|, |∇v̂|, |curl v̂|, |v̂|. It is a signed quadratic expression with no positivity assertion. Unlike (B.16), this earlier class-based density retains an explicit mixed gradient–velocity term.
Breakdown.ModeWeights.modeDensity.summary: The earlier class-based modal form (D−c)x₂²+(1−â−D)x_c²+(A−Z)x_ω²+A₁x₁²+Bx₀²−Cx₁x₀, whose arguments on a perturbation are |∇²v̂|, |∇curl v̂|, |∇v̂|, |curl v̂|, |v̂|. It has no positivity assertion and, unlike (B.16), keeps a mixed gradient–velocity term.

Breakdown.ModeWeights.modeTerm.text: For v, proposed weak derivatives G,H, raw mode ι and point (θ,y), evaluate the earlier quadratic form at the Euclidean amplitudes of the modal Hessian Ĥ, its curl-gradient contraction, the modal gradient Ĝ, its curl contraction, and v̂, in that order. If G=∇v and H=∇²v these are |∇²v̂|, |∇curl v̂|, |∇v̂|, |curl v̂| and |v̂|. The form is (D−c)x₂²+(1−â−D)x_c²+(A−Z)x_ω²+A₁x₁²+Bx₀²−Cx₁x₀, with class weights and mean/wave bounds. This is the earlier mixed-term density; (B.16) uses the later five-coefficient expression without that mixed term. The definition itself imposes no derivative or integrability conditions.
Breakdown.ModeWeights.modeTerm.summary: Evaluates the earlier quadratic form at the amplitudes of Ĥ, its curl-gradient contraction, Ĝ, its curl and v̂; if G=∇v and H=∇²v these are |∇²v̂|, |∇curl v̂|, |∇v̂|, |curl v̂|, |v̂|. It keeps the mixed term absent from (B.16) and imposes no derivative or integrability conditions.

Breakdown.ModeWeights.mode_azimuthal_gai.text: For a period-one Γ-invariant weak solenoidal perturbation v with weak gradient G and Hessian H, spatial L⁶ slices, and square-integrable gradient, Laplacian and similarity transport part, let (n,k) be a raw mode with |k|≥2. Then almost everywhere in time and space, ((|k|−1)²/r²)|v̂|²≤|Ĝ|² and ((|k|−2)²/r²)|Ĝ|²≤|Ĥ|², where r is distance to the rotation axis and tensor sizes are Euclidean component norms. These are the angular gains underlying Appendix B.3. The paper's mode has k=ϰι₁. The equalities identifying G,H with derivatives are weak, so the conclusion is almost everywhere. On r=0 the quotients are defined to be zero; the axis has spatial measure zero.
Breakdown.ModeWeights.mode_azimuthal_gai.summary: For an admissible weak perturbation and raw mode (n,k) with |k|≥2, almost everywhere ((|k|−1)²/r²)|v̂|²≤|Ĝ|² and ((|k|−2)²/r²)|Ĝ|²≤|Ĥ|², with r the distance to the axis: the angular gains of Appendix B.3. On r=0 the quotients are taken as zero.

Breakdown.ModeWeights.mu.text: For raw mode (n,k) and point y, take the absolute value of the signed order-zero multiplier weight μ assigned to its class. This nonnegative magnitude enters the frequency energy. Its sign in the skew multiplier is supplied separately, and no decay or size bound follows from taking its absolute value. This belongs to the earlier class-based multiplier; Appendix B.2 uses finite families of pieces, so the displayed formula is an auxiliary version rather than the exact five-coefficient density (B.16).
Breakdown.ModeWeights.mu.summary: |μ| for the signed order-zero velocity weight of the mode's class at y, which enters the frequency energy; its sign is supplied separately. It belongs to the earlier class-based multiplier.

Breakdown.ModeWeights.muGrad.text: For raw mode (n,k), take the operator norm of the derivative of its class’s signed velocity weight μ(y). For a differentiable scalar weight this is |∇μ|. Lipschitz regularity and almost-everywhere differentiability are separate conditions; derivative defaults are used where differentiability fails. This belongs to the earlier class-based multiplier; Appendix B.2 uses finite families of pieces, so the displayed formula is an auxiliary version rather than the exact five-coefficient density (B.16).
Breakdown.ModeWeights.muGrad.summary: The operator norm of the derivative of the class's signed velocity weight μ(y), equal to |∇μ| where it is differentiable; default values are used where differentiability fails. It belongs to the earlier class-based multiplier.

Breakdown.ModeWeights.muNb.text: For mode ι and point y, take max{|μ_(ι+α)(y)|: α is in the finite wave set}. It is zero on an empty wave set. The result is a nonnegative bound on neighboring order-zero weights, without asserting that the reference field actually has just these waves. This belongs to the earlier class-based multiplier; Appendix B.2 uses finite families of pieces, so the displayed formula is an auxiliary version rather than the exact five-coefficient density (B.16).
Breakdown.ModeWeights.muNb.summary: max{|μ_(ι+α)(y)|: α in the finite wave set}, zero on an empty wave set: a nonnegative bound on neighboring order-zero weights. It belongs to the earlier class-based multiplier.

Breakdown.ModeWeights.multiplierConstant.text: Given retained fractions c,cμ, lower energy weight w*, upper bounds E* for the curl weights and E′* for their gradients, and a velocity-weight ratio R, define a=[(1+E*+E′*/√w*)²/c+R/cμ]¹ᐟ². In the admissible case c,cμ,w*>0 and R≥0, this is the constant bounding the multiplier norm by a√(c‖v‖²w+cμ‖v‖²μ). For c=3/50 it has the normalization of c_M in Proposition B.1. This earlier class-based quantity is only a formula here; no bound is proved. Zero divisors and nonpositive square-root arguments use their assigned zero values outside the admissible hypotheses.
Breakdown.ModeWeights.multiplierConstant.summary: The constant a=[(1+E*+E′*/√w*)²/c+R/cμ]¹ᐟ², which in the admissible case bounds the multiplier norm by a√(c‖v‖²w+cμ‖v‖²μ); at c=3/50 it has the normalization of c_M in Proposition B.1. Only the formula is given; zero divisors give zero.

Breakdown.ModeWeights.multiplierGap.text: For right-hand side F, multiplier M, forcing fields bᵢ and coefficients βᵢ, define X=⟨F,M⟩𝓗−cE−cμN−∑ᵢβᵢ⟨bᵢ,M⟩𝓗. Here E=∫₀¹∫(|Δv|²+w|∇v|²) when the supplied derivatives are valid, the weight is bounded, measurable and nonnegative, and the integral is finite, and N is the real conversion of the earlier frequency energy ∑_ι∫|μ_ι||Ω_ι||v̂_ι|². This is the left side of the analogue of (B.20), before bounding it by the signed density integral. Infinity is converted to zero in E and N unless finiteness is supplied; the definition alone asserts no estimate or convergence. For arbitrary data the energy is formed from max(|tr H|²+w|G|²,0); negative densities are discarded before integration.
Breakdown.ModeWeights.multiplierGap.summary: $X=\langle F,M\rangle_{\mathcal H}-cE-c_\mu N-\sum_i\beta_i\langle b_i,M\rangle_{\mathcal H}$, with $E$ the weighted derivative energy and $N$ the earlier frequency energy: the left side of the analogue of (B.20). Infinity is converted to zero in $E$ and $N$, and no estimate is asserted.

Breakdown.ModeWeights.multiplierInequali.text: Suppose the earlier box of parameters has nonnegative radii; its profile is jointly C², period one for every parameter, solenoidal on the box, and has uniform decay |DʲWᵃ|≤D/(1+|y|)ʲ⁺¹ for j=0,1,2. Assume the energy weight is bounded above, the forcing fields are measurable, periodic and square integrable, and for every parameter the class weights are admissible with common fractions c,cμ and common bounds E*,E′*,R. Assume the reference mean/wave bounds are valid. Finally, for every admissible weak perturbation solving the linearized equation modulo gradients and every associated multiplier M, assume I⁻<∞ and I⁺−I⁻≥c|β|²−∑ᵢβᵢ⟨bᵢ,M⟩−cK²‖F‖²B−t|ℓ(v)|², expressed with separate positive and negative parts; t,K≥0. Here I± are the signed density parts, E=∫₀¹∫(|Δv|²+w|∇v|²), ℓ is the gradient-constraint vector and ‖F‖B is the ball-restricted period L² norm. The conclusion is existence of M,n≥0 with ‖M‖≤a√(cE+cμn²) and c(E+|β|²)+cμn²≤⟨F,M⟩+cK²‖F‖²B+t|ℓ(v)|², where a²=(1+E*+E′*/√w*)²/c+R/cμ. This is the cancellation step of Lemma B.2 in the earlier format. The global density lower bound remains a hypothesis.
Breakdown.ModeWeights.multiplierInequali.summary: In the earlier box format with a C² profile, admissible class weights and valid mean/wave bounds, and assuming the density lower bound with I⁻<∞, there are M and n≥0 with ‖M‖≤a√(cE+cμn²) and c(E+|β|²)+cμn²≤⟨F,M⟩+cK²‖F‖²B+t|ℓ(v)|²: the cancellation of Lemma B.2.

Breakdown.ModeWeights.multiplier_density.text: Fix S>0, a bounded measurable axisymmetric weight w≥w*>0, a C² reference W that is period one, solenoidal, and satisfies |DʲW(θ,y)|≤D/(1+|y|)ʲ⁺¹ for j=0,1,2. The finitely many forcing fields are measurable, periodic and in 𝓗=L²((0,1)×ℝ³). Let v be any Γ-invariant solenoidal period-one weak perturbation with v(θ)∈L⁶ and its gradient, Laplacian and similarity transport part in 𝓗. Let β∈ℝᵏ and F∈𝓗 be period one and satisfy F≃𝓣ˢv+(W·∇)v+(v·∇)W+∑βᵢbᵢ. Assume additionally all class-based weight conditions: finite classes, 0<c,cμ<1, Lipschitz signed weights of the required decay and frequency sign, positive auxiliary denominators, bounded weight and gradient sums E*,E′*, ratio R, nonnegative remaining curl-gradient coefficient, and all pointwise mean/wave reconstruction and majorant inequalities. The conclusion supplies a measurable, periodic, solenoidal multiplier M∈𝓗 satisfying its testing identity, finite frequency energy N=‖v‖²μ, and ‖M‖𝓗≤a√(cE+cμN), where E=‖v‖²w and a²=(1+E*+E′*/√w*)²/c+R/cμ. If I⁺ and I⁻ are integrals of the separately positive and negative modal and stretching terms, and X=⟨F,M⟩−cE−cμN−∑βᵢ⟨bᵢ,M⟩, it states I⁺+max(−X,0)≤max(X,0)+I⁻ in [0,∞]. When I⁻<∞ this gives I⁺<∞ and I⁺−I⁻≤X. Without that extra finiteness, the nonnegative-integral inequality does not assert a finite signed integral. This is an earlier version of Proposition B.1, with class-based signed weights and a mixed modal term. Its retained fraction c may be any number in (0,1), its symmetry set Γ is arbitrary, and its forcing fields need satisfy neither Γ-invariance nor separation from the weighted modes. Its reference must be jointly C² with the stated Hessian decay, whereas Appendix B.1 permits C¹ fields with weak second derivatives. These are distinct changes of hypothesis from Proposition B.1.
Breakdown.ModeWeights.multiplier_density.summary: For a C² periodic solenoidal reference with Hessian decay and admissible class-based weights, a solenoidal periodic multiplier M exists with ‖M‖𝓗≤a√(cE+cμN) and I⁺+max(−X,0)≤max(X,0)+I⁻, so I⁺−I⁻≤X when I⁻<∞: an earlier version of Proposition B.1 with c∈(0,1).

Breakdown.ModeWeights.penalty.text: Fix raw mode ι and y. Write ε=|ε_ι|, μ=|μ_ι|, Ω=2πn/S+ka, ε′=|∇ε_ι| and μ′=|∇μ_ι|; εnb and μnb are the maximum neighboring magnitudes over the finite wave set. D,Z,a,a₁,η are the class's conversion functions, rotation rate, first share and balancing number; a₂,a₄,L,L₂,ηmin are common auxiliary data. Let U bound the mean relative transport, O₀=|curl W̄|bound, Q₀=|∇curl W̄|bound, G₀=|DW̄|bound, and U₁,G₁,O₁,Q₁ bound the sums of wave velocity, gradient, curl and curl-gradient amplitudes. The loss is (G₀²/η+ημ²/2)1_(μ_ι is nonzero somewhere)+(G₁²/ηmin)1_(some neighboring μ is nonzero somewhere). The indicators concern whether whole weight functions vanish identically, rather than their value at y. This distinction affects the loss even at a point where μ vanishes. All quantities are evaluated at y. Division by zero is assigned zero in the bare formulas; admissibility makes the used balancing denominators positive, except an inactive first share whose numerator vanishes. This belongs to the earlier class-based multiplier; Appendix B.2 uses finite families of pieces, so the displayed formula is an auxiliary version rather than the exact five-coefficient density (B.16).
Breakdown.ModeWeights.penalty.summary: The earlier velocity-weight loss (G₀²/η+ημ²/2)1_(μ_ι is nonzero somewhere)+(G₁²/ηmin)1_(some neighboring μ is nonzero somewhere). The indicators ask whether whole weight functions vanish identically, not their value at y. It belongs to the earlier class-based multiplier.

Breakdown.ModeWeights.secondDerivNorm.text: For f:ℝ³→ℝ, the number at y is the operator norm of the second derivative D²f(y), as a bilinear form. For C² f it is |∇²f|op, the convention explicitly specified after (B.16), not the sum of squares of Hessian entries. The expression assigns a value for every function and point and imposes no differentiability assumption. It is formed by iterating the assigned derivative; a zero assigned first derivative at a point does not by itself make the next derivative zero there. This is the same Hessian norm convention as Appendix B.2.
Breakdown.ModeWeights.secondDerivNorm.summary: The operator norm of D²f(y) as a bilinear form, for f:ℝ³→ℝ; for C² f it is |∇²f|op, the convention stated after (B.16), not the sum of squares of the entries. No differentiability is assumed.

Breakdown.ModeWeights.shareHat.text: For mode ι, write a₁ for its class’s first share, a₂ for the common second share, ε=|ε_ι|, ε′=|∇ε_ι| and εnb=max_α|ε_(ι+α)| over the finite wave set. The quantity is a₁·1_(ε+ε′>0)+a₂·1_(εnb>0). It counts the curl-gradient energy already assigned to error estimates; no sign or upper bound is asserted by this formula. This belongs to the earlier class-based multiplier; Appendix B.2 uses finite families of pieces, so the displayed formula is an auxiliary version rather than the exact five-coefficient density (B.16).
Breakdown.ModeWeights.shareHat.summary: The earlier allocated curl-gradient share a₁·1_(ε+ε′>0)+a₂·1_(εnb>0), counting the energy assigned to error estimates; no sign or upper bound is asserted. It belongs to the earlier class-based multiplier.

Breakdown.ModeWeights.stretchCharge.text: For mode ι, let x₀=|v̂_ι|, x₁=|∇v̂_ι| and xω=|curl v̂_ι|. If s₀,s₁ are the mean and wave strain bounds, q₀,q₁ the mean and wave vorticity-gradient bounds, and L(y)>0 a balancing length, the expression is (s₀+s₁)xω²+(√2+½)q₀x₀x₁+½(√2+½)q₁(Lx₁²+x₀²/L). It is the cost used to bound the negative time-angle average of the stretching term (B.18) in the earlier mean/wave argument. This definition does not assert the bound, positivity of L or validity of the majorants. At L=0 the quotient is assigned zero.
Breakdown.ModeWeights.stretchCharge.summary: The expression (s₀+s₁)xω²+(√2+½)q₀x₀x₁+½(√2+½)q₁(Lx₁²+x₀²/L), the cost bounding the negative time-angle average of the stretching term (B.18) in the earlier mean/wave argument. No bound is asserted; at L=0 the quotient is taken as zero.

Breakdown.ModeWeights.stretch_mean_bound.text: Let W be C² and divergence-free and suppose its finite mean/wave decomposition and all supplied bounds are valid. Let L(y)>0 and let v be an admissible Γ-invariant weak perturbation, with proposed gradient G and Hessian H identified distributionally. For almost every y, max(−∫₀¹∫₀²πJ(θ,Rφy)dφdθ,0)≤2π∑_ι max(C_ι(y),0). J is the stretching density (B.18), and C_ι=(s₀+s₁)|curl v̂_ι|²+(√2+½)q₀|v̂_ι||∇v̂_ι|+½(√2+½)q₁(L|∇v̂_ι|²+|v̂_ι|²/L), evaluated at time zero. Here s₀,s₁ bound mean and wave strain and q₀,q₁ their vorticity gradients. The estimate takes the positive part after integrating J and keeps the full 2π angular factor: the angular integral on the left is unnormalized. Its ordinary real integrals have default zero values in the nonintegrable case; the theorem does not separately assert integrability of |J|. The nonnegative series on the right may be infinite. It is an earlier sufficient treatment of (B.18), not a pointwise positivity result for J.
Breakdown.ModeWeights.stretch_mean_bound.summary: For C² divergence-free W with valid mean/wave bounds, L>0 and an admissible weak perturbation, for almost every y, max(−∫₀¹∫₀²πJ(θ,Rφy)dφdθ,0)≤2π∑_ι max(C_ι(y),0), with J the stretching density (B.18). This is an earlier sufficient treatment of (B.18), not pointwise positivity of J.

Breakdown.MonodromyStatement.text:
Let $X$ be a real Hilbert space with the heat and bilinear operators of §3.4: $G(t)$ is a strongly continuous contraction semigroup, $K(\tau)$ is symmetric, continuous for $\tau>0$, obeys $G(s)K(\tau)=K(s+\tau)$ and $\|K(\tau)\|\le C_K\tau^{-3/4}$ for $0<\tau\le1$. Suppose the dilations satisfy $D_1=I$, $D_\mu D_\nu=D_{\mu\nu}$, $\|D_\mu x\|=\mu^{1/4}\|x\|$, $D_\mu G(\mu t)=G(t)D_\mu$, and $\mu D_\mu K(\mu\tau)(x,y)=K(\tau)(D_\mu x,D_\mu y)$ for positive scales, with continuous dependence on scale. Assume $K(\tau)(f,\cdot)$ is compact for a dense set of $f$ and every $\tau>0$.

Let $S>0$, let $\rho$ be a surjective linear isometry commuting with $G$, $K$ and $D$, and let $w:\mathbb R\to X$ be continuous, nonzero at some time, with $w(s+S)=\rho w(s)$ and the similarity-time mild equation. Here that equation uses $\mathcal S(a)=D_{e^{-a}}G(1-e^{-a})$ and $\mathcal K(a)=D_{e^{-a}}K(1-e^{-a})$ and reads $w(s)=\mathcal S(s-s_0)w(s_0)+\int_{s_0}^{s}\mathcal K(s-r)(w(r),w(r))\,dr$ for $s_0\le s$.

Fix a positive natural $k$, set $\mu=e^{-S/k}$, $L=1-\mu$, and put $A_n=2\mathcal B_L(u_n,\cdot)$ where $u_n(\sigma)=D_{(1-\sigma)^{-1}}w(nS/k-\log(1-\sigma))$ on $[0,L]$. Assume $\|A_n\|\le1/4$ for every natural $n$. Let $S_n=D_\mu\operatorname{ev}_L(I-A_n)^{-1}\Gamma$, where $\Gamma x(\sigma)=G(\sigma)x$, and let $M=\rho^{-1}S_{k-1}\cdots S_0$.

The formal statement asserts that every $I-A_n$ is invertible with inverse norm at most $4/3$, that $S_{n+k}=\rho S_n\rho^{-1}$, that $M-\rho^{-1}(D_\mu G(L))^k$ is compact, and that $\|\rho^{-1}(D_\mu G(L))^k\|\le e^{-S/4}$. The norm and heat-scaling identities identify the free product with $\rho^{-1}D_{e^{-S}}G(1-e^{-S})$. These are the compactness and free-operator bound used in Lemma 4.4. The formal statement assumes the chosen subdivision and $\|A_n\|\le1/4$; it does not choose that subdivision or state equality with the paper's unsplit trajectory $h_\chi$.

The positive $k$ and the small-operator hypotheses make the inverses genuine, with no default-value ambiguity. Here $\mathcal B_L(f,g)(\sigma)=\int_0^\sigma K(\sigma-r)(f(r),g(r))\,dr$ for continuous curves on $[0,L]$, and the norm of each input or output curve is the supremum norm on that interval.

This formal statement specifies an implication. Defining the implication does not prove it.
Breakdown.MonodromyStatement.summary: For a recurrent profile with $\|A_n\|\le1/4$, each $I-A_n$ is invertible with inverse norm at most $4/3$, $S_{n+k}=\rho S_n\rho^{-1}$, $M-\rho^{-1}(D_\mu G(L))^k$ is compact, and $\|\rho^{-1}(D_\mu G(L))^k\|\le e^{-S/4}$, as in Lemma 4.4 for the split product. It states the assertion only.

Breakdown.MuPiece.text: One index p∈𝓟μ of Appendix B.2 carries a set Nₚ of raw integer modes, a constant real angular rate νₚ, a spatial weight μₚ, an energy-share function, one more balancing function, a balancing real number ηₚ, and a transport majorant. The weight contributes an order-zero skew term in (B.14). Nonnegativity of μₚ, positivity of the auxiliary quantities, regularity and the condition Ωₚ>0 on Nₚ are checked separately. This is the same kind of data as in the paper, with arbitrary functions allowed until their representation and admissibility are imposed.
Breakdown.MuPiece.summary: One velocity piece of Appendix B.2: a set Nₚ of raw modes, an angular rate νₚ, a weight μₚ, an energy-share function, a balancing function, a real number ηₚ and a transport majorant. Its conditions, including Ωₚ>0 on Nₚ, are checked separately; this is the same kind of data as in the paper.

Breakdown.MultiplierInequality.text:
The condition requires c>0 and cμ,t,a,K≥0. For every parameter and every admissible period-one weak perturbation v, coefficient vector β and F∈𝓗 satisfying the linearized equation modulo gradients, there must exist a measurable M∈𝓗 and n≥0 such that ‖M‖𝓗≤a√(cE+cμn²) and c(E+|β|²)+cμn²≤⟨F,M⟩𝓗+cK²‖F‖²L²((0,1)×B_R)+t|ℓ(v)|². Here E is the formal squared energy, ℓᵢ(v)=∫₀¹∫∇v:Ξᵢ, and admissibility means solenoidal, Γ-invariant, v(θ)∈L⁶ with gradient, Laplacian and similarity transport part in 𝓗. This is the algebraic form used before the Cauchy–Schwarz step of Lemma B.2, in the earlier ball-norm format and with force weight one. It does not require M to be periodic or divergence-free in this particular condition; the construction of M supplies stronger properties.

For arbitrary supplied data, put I=∫₀¹∫ℝ³ max(|tr H|²+w|G|²,0), with values in [0,∞] and the Frobenius norm for G. The formal squared energy equals I when I is finite and equals zero when I is infinite. With G=∇v, H=∇²v and a bounded measurable weight w≥w*>0, the perturbation hypotheses make this the usual energy ∫₀¹∫ℝ³(|Δv|²+w|∇v|²). The isolated condition does not impose those assumptions on w.
Breakdown.MultiplierInequality.summary: For every parameter, admissible weak perturbation, $\beta$ and $F$ solving the linearized equation, some $M\in\mathcal H$, $n\ge0$ have $\|M\|\le a\sqrt{cE+c_\mu n^2}$ and $c(E+|\beta|^2)+c_\mu n^2\le\langle F,M\rangle+cK^2\|F\|^2_{L^2(B_R)}+t|\ell(v)|^2$, before Cauchy–Schwarz in Lemma B.2.

Breakdown.Periodic.AdvectShellBounds.text:
The whole-space norm is $\|v\|_X=\|\nabla v\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^3)}$ on solenoidal velocities in $L^6(\mathbb R^3)$.

Local data are a tuple $(A_1,A_2,A_3,v)$ with $A_j\in L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$ and $v\in L^6(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$, measured by $\max\{\max_j\|A_j\|_2,\|v\|_6\}$. No compatibility condition $A_j=\partial_jv$ or divergence condition is part of this data space.

For every $\varphi\in C^\infty_{c,\mathrm{div}}(\mathbb R^3)$, every real $b$, and every local tuple $\zeta=(A_1,A_2,A_3,v)$, put $f=1_{\bar B_b}\sum_j(\varphi_jA_j+v_j\partial_j\varphi)$.

The formal statement asserts a constant $C\ge0$, independent of these inputs, such that $\|f\|_{3/2}\le C\|\varphi\|_X\|\zeta\|$, and asserts that $f$ vanishes almost everywhere outside $\bar B_b$. The estimate applies without requiring $A_j=\partial_jv$ or $\operatorname{div}v=0$. Its time dependence in (6.8) is obtained only after substituting the bound for the chosen time-dependent background.

This declaration records the assertion; its proof is a separate declaration.
Breakdown.Periodic.AdvectShellBounds.summary: States that one $C\ge0$ gives $\|f\|_{3/2}\le C\|\varphi\|_X\|\zeta\|$ for $f=1_{\bar B_b}\sum_j(\varphi_jA_j+v_j\partial_j\varphi)$, with $f$ zero outside $\bar B_b$, for every test field $\varphi$ and local tuple $\zeta$. It does not require $A_j=\partial_jv$ or $\operatorname{div}v=0$.

Breakdown.Periodic.ApproxField.Internal..text: Let $g:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ be smooth on its entire domain. Fix $a=(1/2,1/2,1/2)$ and the smooth cutoff $\chi$ equal to one on the ball of radius $1/16$ about $a$ and zero outside the ball of radius $1/8$. For $A(t,x)=\int_0^1\sigma\,g(t,a+\sigma(x-a))\times(x-a)\,d\sigma$, the formal statement proves that $\chi(x)g(t,x)+\nabla\chi(x)\times A(t,x)$ is smooth jointly in $(t,x)$. It makes no divergence or PDE assumption. Its input is globally smooth in time; the physical profile is smooth only before its terminal time, so its application there uses a local smooth extension in time, supplied in the same source file. The cutoff and centre are fixed, whereas Lemma 5.1 uses $\eta(x/r)$ and centre zero.
Breakdown.Periodic.ApproxField.Internal..summary: For $g$ smooth on $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3$, $\chi(x)g(t,x)+\nabla\chi(x)\times A(t,x)$ with the radial potential about $a=(1/2,1/2,1/2)$ is jointly smooth in $(t,x)$. The cutoff and centre are fixed, whereas Lemma 5.1 uses $\eta(x/r)$ and centre zero.

Breakdown.Periodic.ApproxResidualBound.text:
Assume that $W:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ and $q:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$ are smooth, that $\operatorname{div}W=0$, and that $\partial_sW+\tfrac12W+\tfrac12(y\cdot\nabla)W-\Delta W+(W\cdot\nabla)W+\nabla q=0$ for every $(s,y)$. A single constant $C$ bounds $\|D^jW(s,y)\|\le C(1+|y|)^{-j-1}$ for the integer orders $j=0,1,2$, and $|\nabla q(s,y)|\le C(1+|y|)^{-3}$, uniformly in $s$. The norms of $D^jW$ are multilinear operator norms; for $j=1$ the paper’s Frobenius norm is between the operator norm and $\sqrt3$ times that norm.

For $T>0$ and $t<T$, put $s=\log(T/(T-t))$ and $u_T^*(t,x)=(T-t)^{-1/2}W(s,(x-a)/\sqrt{T-t})$, where $a=(1/2,1/2,1/2)$. Choose a fixed smooth cutoff $\chi$, equal to one on $\bar B_{1/16}(a)$ and zero when $|x-a|\ge1/8$. Put $A_g(x)=\int_0^1\tau g(a+\tau(x-a))\times(x-a)\,d\tau$. The cutoff is $\bar u_T=\chi u_T^*+\nabla\chi\times A_{u_T^*}$, which equals $\operatorname{curl}(\chi A_{u_T^*})$ when $u_T^*$ is solenoidal.

Put $p^*(t,x)=(T-t)^{-1}q(s,(x-a)/\sqrt{T-t})$ and $p^{\mathrm a}(t,x)=\chi(x)[p^*(t,x)-p^*(t,a+(3/32)e_1)]$. Define $F=\partial_t\bar u_T+(\bar u_T\cdot\nabla)\bar u_T-\Delta\bar u_T+\nabla p^{\mathrm a}$.

The formal statement asserts the existence of $K\in\mathbb R$ such that $|F(t,x)|\le K(T-t)^{-1/2}$ whenever $0<T\le1$ and $0\le t<T$, and $F(t,x)\ne0$ implies $1/16\le|x-a|\le1/8$. This is the pointwise differential residual used in the formal route to small Duhamel residuals. The paper estimates the global Duhamel residual by comparing whole-space and periodic heat flows.

This declaration records the assertion; its proof is a separate declaration.
Breakdown.Periodic.ApproxResidualBound.summary: States that for a smooth profile with the decay bounds, the residual $F$ of the cutoff $\bar u_T$ with pressure $p^{\mathrm a}$ satisfies $|F|\le K(T-t)^{-1/2}$ for $0<T\le1$, $0\le t<T$, and vanishes outside $1/16\le|x-a|\le1/8$. The paper instead compares whole-space and periodic heat flows.

Breakdown.Periodic.ApproxResidualSmall.text:
Assume that $W:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ and $q:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$ are smooth, that $\operatorname{div}W=0$, and that $\partial_sW+\tfrac12W+\tfrac12(y\cdot\nabla)W-\Delta W+(W\cdot\nabla)W+\nabla q=0$ for every $(s,y)$. A single constant $C$ bounds $\|D^jW(s,y)\|\le C(1+|y|)^{-j-1}$ for the integer orders $j=0,1,2$, and $|\nabla q(s,y)|\le C(1+|y|)^{-3}$, uniformly in $s$. The norms of $D^jW$ are multilinear operator norms; for $j=1$ the paper’s Frobenius norm is between the operator norm and $\sqrt3$ times that norm.

The periodic space is the real solenoidal Fourier realization of $H^1(\mathbb R^3/\mathbb Z^3)$, with squared norm $\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^3}(1+4\pi^2|k|^2)|\widehat v(k)|^2$. Its zero Fourier coefficient is allowed to be nonzero.

For $T>0$ and $t<T$, put $s=\log(T/(T-t))$ and $u_T^*(t,x)=(T-t)^{-1/2}W(s,(x-a)/\sqrt{T-t})$, where $a=(1/2,1/2,1/2)$. Choose a fixed smooth cutoff $\chi$, equal to one on $\bar B_{1/16}(a)$ and zero when $|x-a|\ge1/8$. Put $A_g(x)=\int_0^1\tau g(a+\tau(x-a))\times(x-a)\,d\tau$. The cutoff is $\bar u_T=\chi u_T^*+\nabla\chi\times A_{u_T^*}$, which equals $\operatorname{curl}(\chi A_{u_T^*})$ when $u_T^*$ is solenoidal.

Write $\mu_n=T\lambda^n$, $t_n=T-\mu_n$, $\ell=1-\lambda$, and $a_n(s)=\mu_n^{1/4}u^{\mathrm a}(t_n+\mu_ns)$ for $0\le s\le\ell$, where $u^{\mathrm a}$ is the unit-periodic extension of the solenoidal cutoff of the centered self-similar field. The index $n$ is a nonnegative integer and the interval norm is the supremum norm.

Assume the periodic heat-bilinear estimate $\|K_{\mathbb T}(\tau)\|\le C_{\mathbb T}\tau^{-3/4}$ for $0<\tau\le1$, $0<\lambda<1$, and $\theta>\lambda^{1/4}$. On interval $n$ use $G_n(s)=e^{\mu_ns\Delta}$ and $K_n(\tau)=\mu_n^{3/4}K_{\mathbb T}(\mu_n\tau)$, and let $\mathcal B_n$ be the resulting Duhamel integral.

The formal statement asserts that there is $K\ge0$ such that, for every $0<T\le1$ and $n\ge0$, $\|a_n-G_n(\cdot)a_n(0)-\mathcal B_n(a_n,a_n)\|_{C([0,\ell];H^1)}\le\theta^nKT^{1/4}$. The assertion itself has no hypothesis $\theta<1$; that further inequality is needed when this is used as decay in $n$. This is a sequence estimate, rather than the paper’s single $C_\kappa$ estimate with an explicit large-period constant.

This declaration records the assertion; its proof is a separate declaration.
Breakdown.Periodic.ApproxResidualSmall.summary: States that, given the periodic kernel estimate, $0<\lambda<1$ and $\theta>\lambda^{1/4}$, some $K\ge0$ bounds the Duhamel residual of $a_n$ on $[0,\ell]$ by $\theta^nKT^{1/4}$ for $0<T\le1$, $n\ge0$. It has no hypothesis $\theta<1$ and replaces the paper's single $C_\kappa$ estimate.

Breakdown.Periodic.ApproxSizes.text:
Assume that $W:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ and $q:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$ are smooth, that $\operatorname{div}W=0$, and that $\partial_sW+\tfrac12W+\tfrac12(y\cdot\nabla)W-\Delta W+(W\cdot\nabla)W+\nabla q=0$ for every $(s,y)$. A single constant $C$ bounds $\|D^jW(s,y)\|\le C(1+|y|)^{-j-1}$ for the integer orders $j=0,1,2$, and $|\nabla q(s,y)|\le C(1+|y|)^{-3}$, uniformly in $s$. The norms of $D^jW$ are multilinear operator norms; for $j=1$ the paper’s Frobenius norm is between the operator norm and $\sqrt3$ times that norm.

The periodic space is the real solenoidal Fourier realization of $H^1(\mathbb R^3/\mathbb Z^3)$, with squared norm $\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^3}(1+4\pi^2|k|^2)|\widehat v(k)|^2$. Its zero Fourier coefficient is allowed to be nonzero.

For $T>0$ and $t<T$, put $s=\log(T/(T-t))$ and $u_T^*(t,x)=(T-t)^{-1/2}W(s,(x-a)/\sqrt{T-t})$, where $a=(1/2,1/2,1/2)$. Choose a fixed smooth cutoff $\chi$, equal to one on $\bar B_{1/16}(a)$ and zero when $|x-a|\ge1/8$. Put $A_g(x)=\int_0^1\tau g(a+\tau(x-a))\times(x-a)\,d\tau$. The cutoff is $\bar u_T=\chi u_T^*+\nabla\chi\times A_{u_T^*}$, which equals $\operatorname{curl}(\chi A_{u_T^*})$ when $u_T^*$ is solenoidal.

Write $\mu_n=T\lambda^n$, $t_n=T-\mu_n$, $\ell=1-\lambda$, and $a_n(s)=\mu_n^{1/4}u^{\mathrm a}(t_n+\mu_ns)$ for $0\le s\le\ell$, where $u^{\mathrm a}$ is the unit-periodic extension of the solenoidal cutoff of the centered self-similar field. The index $n$ is a nonnegative integer and the interval norm is the supremum norm.

Assume $0<\lambda<1$ and $c>0$ with $c\le\|W(s)\|_X$ for every real $s$.

The formal statement asserts the existence of $T_0>0$ and $M\in\mathbb R$ such that, for every $0<T<T_0$ and every $n\ge0$, $\|a_n\|_{C([0,\ell];H^1)}\le M$ and $c/2\le\|a_n(s)\|_{H^1}$ for every $0\le s\le\ell$. Here $\|W(s)\|_X=\|\nabla W(s)\|_2$. The curve is represented by its continuous restriction; the general construction uses zero if continuity fails, while the profile hypotheses ensure continuity here. The statement gives no equality with a whole-space homogeneous norm and no explicit factor $c_*-CL^{-1/2}$.

This declaration records the assertion; its proof is a separate declaration.
Breakdown.Periodic.ApproxSizes.summary: States that if $c\le\|W(s)\|_X$ for all $s$ and $0<\lambda<1$, there are $T_0>0$ and $M$ with $\|a_n\|_{C([0,\ell];H^1)}\le M$ and $\|a_n(s)\|_{H^1}\ge c/2$ for $0<T<T_0$ and all $n$. There is no explicit factor $c_*-CL^{-1/2}$.

Breakdown.Periodic.ApproxSizes.Internal..text: Fix $a=(1/2,1/2,1/2)$ and the smooth cutoff $\chi$ equal to one for $|x-a|\le1/16$ and zero for $|x-a|\ge1/8$. For an arbitrary function $W:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ and real $T,t$ with $t<T$, put $\ell=T-t>0$, $s=-\log(\ell/T)$ and $g(x)=\ell^{-1/2}W(s,(x-a)/\sqrt\ell)$. Form $\bar u=\chi g+\nabla\chi\times A_g$ with the radial potential about $a$, and let $f(y)=\sqrt\ell\,\bar u(a+\sqrt\ell y)$. The formal statement proves $f(y)=\chi(a+\sqrt\ell y)W(s,y)+\sqrt\ell\,\nabla\chi(a+\sqrt\ell y)\times\int_0^1\sigma W(s,\sigma y)\times y\,d\sigma$. No smoothness, equation or decay of $W$ is assumed, and the only time hypothesis is $t<T$. If $T=0$, division by zero is taken to be zero and $\log0=0$; for a negative logarithm argument the formal real logarithm is the logarithm of its absolute value. For the intended case $T>0$, every logarithm and square root has a positive argument. Nonintegrable vector integrals are assigned zero, so this purely algebraic identity is stated even for inputs for which the potential is not an ordinary integral.
Breakdown.Periodic.ApproxSizes.Internal..summary: For any $W$ and $t<T$, the cutoff in similarity coordinates is $f(y)=\chi(a+\sqrt\ell y)W(s,y)+\sqrt\ell\nabla\chi(a+\sqrt\ell y)\times\int_0^1\sigma W(s,\sigma y)\times y\,d\sigma$, $\ell=T-t$. It is purely algebraic, with no smoothness or decay assumed.

Breakdown.Periodic.ApproxSizes.Internal..text:
Let $W:\mathbb R	imes\mathbb R^3	o\mathbb R^3$ and $q:\mathbb R	imes\mathbb R^3	o\mathbb R$ be smooth and satisfy $\partial_sW+ rac12W+ rac12(y\cdot
abla)W-\Delta W+(W\cdot
abla)W+
abla q=0$ and $
abla\cdot W=0$ for every $(s,y)$. Assume, uniformly in $s,y$, $\|D_y^jW(s,y)\|_{m op}\le C(1+|y|)^{-j-1}$ for the three integer orders $j=0,1,2$, and $|
abla_yq(s,y)|\le C(1+|y|)^{-3}$. These assumptions imply $C\ge0$; recurrence and nonvanishing are not required here. The norm on a first derivative is its operator norm; the paper's pointwise matrix norm is the square root of the sum of the squared column lengths, which is at most $\sqrt3$ times this norm.
