The periodic space is the real solenoidal Fourier realization of $H^1(\mathbb R^3/\mathbb Z^3)$, with squared norm $\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^3}(1+4\pi^2|k|^2)|\widehat v(k)|^2$. Its zero Fourier coefficient is allowed to be nonzero.

For $T>0$, $0<\lambda<1$, $0<\theta<1$ and $c_0>0$, assume continuous curves $a_n,z_n,v_n$ on $[0,1-\lambda]$ satisfy $\|a_n(s)\|\ge c_0$, $\|z_n\|_\infty\le Z$, and $v_n=a_n+\theta^nz_n$.

The formal statement proves that the assembled norm is unbounded on $[0,T)$. At $t_n=T-T\lambda^n$ its value is $(T\lambda^n)^{-1/4}v_n(0)$; the correction $\theta^nz_n(0)$ tends to zero and the prefactor tends to infinity. Endpoint matching and the mild equation are not required for this norm argument. This result supplies the unboundedness used by the final formal conclusion; it does not state the paper’s all-time estimate (6.18).
Breakdown.Periodic.glueUnbounded.summary: If continuous $a_n,z_n,v_n$ satisfy $\|a_n(s)\|\ge c_0$, $\|z_n\|_\infty\le Z$ and $v_n=a_n+\theta^nz_n$ with $0<\theta<1$, the assembled norm is unbounded on $[0,T)$. Matching and the mild equation are not required; it does not state (6.18).

Breakdown.Periodic.heat.text: The formal periodic space represents real divergence-free fields of period one by sequences $a(n)\in\mathbb C^3$, $n\in\mathbb Z^3$, with $\sum_n|a(n)|^2<\infty$, $a(-n)=\overline{a(n)}$ and $n\cdot a(n)=0$. The physical Fourier coefficient is $c(n)=a(n)/(1+4\pi^2|n|^2)^{1/2}$. Its squared norm is $\|u\|^2=\sum_n(1+4\pi^2|n|^2)|c(n)|^2$, the inhomogeneous $H^1$ norm; the mean $c(0)$ may be nonzero. For any real $t$, the heat operator multiplies $c(n)$ by $\exp(-4\pi^2|n|^2\max\{t,0\})$. For $t\ge0$ this is the heat semigroup on the unit torus. For $t<0$ the definition gives the identity operator, so it does not define backward heat evolution. The zero mode is unchanged. The family acts on weighted coefficient sequences by the same multiplier, and the norm is the inhomogeneous norm stated above.
Breakdown.Periodic.heat.summary: On the period-one space, the heat operator multiplies $c(n)$ by $\exp(-4\pi^2|n|^2\max\{t,0\})$: the heat semigroup for $t\ge0$ and the identity for $t<0$. The zero mode is unchanged.

Breakdown.Periodic.heatDivFreeComparison.text:
This theorem assumes five representation identities. First, for every invertible real linear change of frequency variables $A$ and every strongly measurable uniformly bounded matrix multiplier $M(\xi)$, the selected $L^2$ operator agrees almost everywhere with $f\mapsto[\xi\mapsto M(\xi)f(A\xi)]$. Second, the $L^2$ Fourier transform of an $L^1\cap L^2$ complex vector field agrees almost everywhere with its Fourier integral. Third, the Fourier transform of a real $L^2$ vector field satisfies $\widehat f(-\xi)=\overline{\widehat f(\xi)}$. Fourth, if two solenoidal Fourier representatives satisfy $h(\xi)=2\pi|\xi|g(\xi)$ almost everywhere, the velocity reconstructed from $h$ is the real inverse Fourier transform of $g$. Fifth, the inverse $L^2$ Fourier transform of an $L^1\cap L^2$ field agrees almost everywhere with its inverse Fourier integral. The Fourier convention is $\widehat f(\xi)=\int e^{-2\pi i\xi\cdot x}f(x)\,dx$. These are hypotheses of this particular proof theorem; the main construction supplies their proofs.

The whole-space norm is $\|v\|_X=\|\nabla v\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^3)}$ on solenoidal velocities in $L^6(\mathbb R^3)$.

Local data are a tuple $(A_1,A_2,A_3,v)$ with $A_j\in L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$ and $v\in L^6(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$, measured by $\max\{\max_j\|A_j\|_2,\|v\|_6\}$. No compatibility condition $A_j=\partial_jv$ or divergence condition is part of this data space.

Let $a=(1/2,1/2,1/2)$ and let $w(x)$ reduce coordinates modulo integers to the unit cell centered at $a$. Whole-space restriction to $\bar B_b$ consists of $1_{\bar B_b}\partial_jv$ and $1_{\bar B_b}v$. At an admissible periodic scale $0<\mu\le1$, $b>0$, $\sqrt\mu\,b\le1/8$, periodic restriction consists of $1_{\bar B_b}\mu^{3/4}\partial_jz(a+\sqrt\mu\,y)$ and $1_{\bar B_b}\mu^{1/4}z(a+\sqrt\mu\,y)$, interpreted almost everywhere. It is defined to be zero if these scale conditions fail.

Given $b,b^{\prime},\varepsilon,\delta>0$, the formal statement asserts the existence of $\mu_0>0$ such that, for $0<\mu<\mu_0$, every $\tau\in[\varepsilon,\varepsilon^{-1}]$ and every $A\in L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$ supported almost everywhere in $\bar B_{b^{\prime}}$, the difference between the restricted whole-space field $e^{\tau\Delta}\mathbb PA$ and the restricted rescaled unit-torus field is at most $\delta\|A\|_{3/2}$. The latter field is $\mu^{-1/4}e^{\mu\tau\Delta}\mathbb P[A((w(x)-a)/\sqrt\mu)]$ before the periodic restriction. Compact support makes $\|A\|_{3/2}$ finite. If $\varepsilon>1$, the time interval is empty. The statement has no explicit rate in $\mu$ and no assertion for all positive times. Lemma 6.1 instead assumes a tensor $F\in W^{1,1}$ and bounds the heat flow of $\operatorname{div}F$ by $CL^{-7/2}\|F\|_1$.
Breakdown.Periodic.heatDivFreeComparison.summary: Assuming five Fourier identities, for small $\mu$, $\tau\in[\varepsilon,\varepsilon^{-1}]$ and $A\in L^2$ supported in $\bar B_{b'}$, the restricted whole-space and rescaled torus projected heat fields differ by at most $\delta\|A\|_{3/2}$. No rate; Lemma 6.1 uses $W^{1,1}$ tensors.

Breakdown.Periodic.heat_add.text: The formal periodic space represents real divergence-free fields of period one by sequences $a(n)\in\mathbb C^3$, $n\in\mathbb Z^3$, with $\sum_n|a(n)|^2<\infty$, $a(-n)=\overline{a(n)}$ and $n\cdot a(n)=0$. The physical Fourier coefficient is $c(n)=a(n)/(1+4\pi^2|n|^2)^{1/2}$. Its squared norm is $\|u\|^2=\sum_n(1+4\pi^2|n|^2)|c(n)|^2$, the inhomogeneous $H^1$ norm; the mean $c(0)$ may be nonzero. For real $s,t\ge0$, the formal statement proves $G(s+t)=G(s)G(t)$ as bounded linear operators on the periodic space. The multipliers are $\exp(-4\pi^2|n|^2t)$ on this range of times. The restriction $s,t\ge0$ matters because the definition replaces a negative time by zero. The law is on the unit-torus inhomogeneous space and contains no arbitrary period parameter.
Breakdown.Periodic.heat_add.summary: For $s,t\ge0$, $G(s+t)=G(s)G(t)$ on the period-one inhomogeneous space. The restriction $s,t\ge0$ matters because negative times are replaced by zero.

Breakdown.Periodic.heat_continuousOn.text: The formal periodic space represents real divergence-free fields of period one by sequences $a(n)\in\mathbb C^3$, $n\in\mathbb Z^3$, with $\sum_n|a(n)|^2<\infty$, $a(-n)=\overline{a(n)}$ and $n\cdot a(n)=0$. The physical Fourier coefficient is $c(n)=a(n)/(1+4\pi^2|n|^2)^{1/2}$. Its squared norm is $\|u\|^2=\sum_n(1+4\pi^2|n|^2)|c(n)|^2$, the inhomogeneous $H^1$ norm; the mean $c(0)$ may be nonzero. For every $u$ in this space, the formal statement proves continuity of $t\mapsto G(t)u$ on $[0,\infty)$ in the inhomogeneous norm, including at $t=0$. Here $G(t)$ multiplies the Fourier coefficient at $n$ by $e^{-4\pi^2|n|^2t}$ for nonnegative $t$. This is strong continuity, which fixes $u$ before taking the limit; continuity in operator norm is not asserted.
Breakdown.Periodic.heat_continuousOn.summary: For each $u$ in the period-one space, $t\mapsto G(t)u$ is continuous on $[0,\infty)$ in the inhomogeneous norm, including at $t=0$. Continuity in operator norm is not asserted.

Breakdown.Periodic.heat_zero.text: The formal periodic space represents real divergence-free fields of period one by sequences $a(n)\in\mathbb C^3$, $n\in\mathbb Z^3$, with $\sum_n|a(n)|^2<\infty$, $a(-n)=\overline{a(n)}$ and $n\cdot a(n)=0$. The physical Fourier coefficient is $c(n)=a(n)/(1+4\pi^2|n|^2)^{1/2}$. Its squared norm is $\|u\|^2=\sum_n(1+4\pi^2|n|^2)|c(n)|^2$, the inhomogeneous $H^1$ norm; the mean $c(0)$ may be nonzero. The formal statement proves $G(0)=I$ on this space, where $G(t)$ multiplies the coefficient at $n$ by $\exp(-4\pi^2|n|^2\max\{t,0\})$. At $t=0$ this multiplier is one for every integer frequency, including the zero mode. This is the identity clause of (3.11) for the fixed period-one realization.
Breakdown.Periodic.heat_zero.summary: $G(0)=I$ on the period-one space, since the multiplier is one at every frequency, including the zero mode. This is the identity clause of (3.11) at period one.

Breakdown.Periodic.homotopyCurl.text: For every $x_0\in\mathbb R^3$ and every smooth field $g:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ with $\nabla\cdot g=0$ everywhere, the formal statement proves that $A(x)=\int_0^1\sigma\,g(x_0+\sigma(x-x_0))\times(x-x_0)\,d\sigma$ is smooth and $\operatorname{curl}A(x)=g(x)$ for every $x$. No decay or compact support is assumed. The three coordinates of curl use the usual Euclidean orientation. Choosing $x_0=0$ and a fixed time slice $g=u^*(t)$ gives the identity used in (5.1). Smoothness makes the integral over $[0,1]$ and every derivative in the assertion ordinary derivatives and integrals. The statement is spatial; smooth dependence on $t$ is a separate assertion.
Breakdown.Periodic.homotopyCurl.summary: For every $x_0$ and smooth $g$ with $\nabla\cdot g=0$, $A(x)=\int_0^1\sigma g(x_0+\sigma(x-x_0))\times(x-x_0)\,d\sigma$ is smooth and $\operatorname{curl}A=g$ everywhere, with no decay or support assumed. With $x_0=0$ this is the identity used in (5.1).

Breakdown.Periodic.homotopyPotential.text: For a centre $x_0\in\mathbb R^3$ and field $g:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$, this defines $A(x)=\int_0^1 s\,g(x_0+s(x-x_0))\times(x-x_0)\,ds$. The integral is a vector-valued Bochner integral over the scalar parameter $s$. For an arbitrary field the definition assigns zero to this integral when the integrand is not integrable. For smooth $g$ the integrand is continuous on the compact interval, so this is the ordinary integral. In the paper the centre is the origin; the formal formula permits any centre. This definition alone neither assumes $\operatorname{div}g=0$ nor proves $\operatorname{curl}A=g$. The latter identity requires the separate smoothness and divergence-free hypotheses. No decay at spatial infinity is needed to define this finite radial integral for smooth $g$.
Breakdown.Periodic.homotopyPotential.summary: Defines $A(x)=\int_0^1s\,g(x_0+s(x-x_0))\times(x-x_0)\,ds$ for any centre $x_0$; the paper uses the origin. It neither assumes $\operatorname{div}g=0$ nor proves $\operatorname{curl}A=g$.

Breakdown.Periodic.kernel.text: The formal periodic space represents real divergence-free fields of period one by sequences $a(n)\in\mathbb C^3$, $n\in\mathbb Z^3$, with $\sum_n|a(n)|^2<\infty$, $a(-n)=\overline{a(n)}$ and $n\cdot a(n)=0$. The physical Fourier coefficient is $c(n)=a(n)/(1+4\pi^2|n|^2)^{1/2}$. Its squared norm is $\|u\|^2=\sum_n(1+4\pi^2|n|^2)|c(n)|^2$, the inhomogeneous $H^1$ norm; the mean $c(0)$ may be nonzero. For $\tau>0$, its unweighted coefficient at $n$ is $-\tfrac12e^{-4\pi^2\tau|n|^2}P_n(A_{u,v}(n)+A_{v,u}(n))$, where $A_{u,v}(n)=2\pi i\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z^3}(j\cdot c_u(n-j))c_v(j)$. These sums converge for the indicated weighted square-summable inputs. The projection is $P_nc=c-n(n\cdot c)/|n|^2$ for $n\ne0$ and $P_0c=c$. This is the Fourier form of the symmetrized projected transport term in (3.17) at period one, acting in the larger inhomogeneous space that permits a nonzero mean. The bilinear map is defined to be zero for $\tau\le0$; the paper defines it only for positive times. The factor $-1/2$ is included.
Breakdown.Periodic.kernel.summary: For $\tau>0$, the bilinear map with coefficient $-\tfrac12e^{-4\pi^2\tau|n|^2}P_n(A_{u,v}(n)+A_{v,u}(n))$, the Fourier form of (3.17) at period one in the inhomogeneous space with nonzero mean allowed; zero for $\tau\le0$.

Breakdown.Periodic.kernelSharpBound_hold.text: The formal periodic space represents real divergence-free fields of period one by sequences $a(n)\in\mathbb C^3$, $n\in\mathbb Z^3$, with $\sum_n|a(n)|^2<\infty$, $a(-n)=\overline{a(n)}$ and $n\cdot a(n)=0$. The physical Fourier coefficient is $c(n)=a(n)/(1+4\pi^2|n|^2)^{1/2}$. Its squared norm is $\|u\|^2=\sum_n(1+4\pi^2|n|^2)|c(n)|^2$, the inhomogeneous $H^1$ norm; the mean $c(0)$ may be nonzero. The formal statement proves that one constant $C>0$ satisfies $\|K_{\mathbb T}(\tau)(u,v)\|\le C\tau^{-3/4}\|u\|\|v\|$ for all inputs and $0<\tau\le1$. Equivalently it bounds the norm of the bounded bilinear map by $C\tau^{-3/4}$. The map has Fourier coefficients of $-\tfrac12e^{\tau\Delta}\mathbb P[(u\cdot\nabla)v+(v\cdot\nabla)u]$. The constant is independent of the two fields and of $\tau$ in this interval. Equation (3.20) instead quantifies all $\tau>0$ and all torus periods $L>0$, with homogeneous mean-zero norms. The formal statement of the bound supplies neither those additional quantifiers nor the separate linear-forcing estimate (3.19).
Breakdown.Periodic.kernelSharpBound_hold.summary: One $C>0$ gives $\|K_{\mathbb T}(\tau)(u,v)\|\le C\tau^{-3/4}\|u\|\|v\|$ for $0<\tau\le1$ in the period-one inhomogeneous $H^1$ space. (3.20) instead covers all $\tau>0$ and all periods $L$ with homogeneous mean-zero norms.

Breakdown.Periodic.kernel_symm.text: The formal periodic space represents real divergence-free fields of period one by sequences $a(n)\in\mathbb C^3$, $n\in\mathbb Z^3$, with $\sum_n|a(n)|^2<\infty$, $a(-n)=\overline{a(n)}$ and $n\cdot a(n)=0$. The physical Fourier coefficient is $c(n)=a(n)/(1+4\pi^2|n|^2)^{1/2}$. Its squared norm is $\|u\|^2=\sum_n(1+4\pi^2|n|^2)|c(n)|^2$, the inhomogeneous $H^1$ norm; the mean $c(0)$ may be nonzero. The formal statement proves $K_{\mathbb T}(\tau)(u,v)=K_{\mathbb T}(\tau)(v,u)$ for every real $\tau$ and all $u,v$ in this space. For $\tau>0$, the operator is the coefficient form of $-\tfrac12e^{\tau\Delta}\mathbb P[(u\cdot\nabla)v+(v\cdot\nabla)u]$. For $\tau\le0$ both sides are zero by definition. Symmetry concerns exchange of the two input velocities; it is not an assertion of self-adjointness.
Breakdown.Periodic.kernel_symm.summary: $K_{\mathbb T}(\tau)(u,v)=K_{\mathbb T}(\tau)(v,u)$ for every real $\tau$ and all $u,v$ in the period-one space; for $\tau\le0$ both sides are zero. It is not a self-adjointness assertion.

Breakdown.Periodic.mildUniqueness.text: The domain here is the unit torus $\mathbb R^3/\mathbb Z^3$. A real solenoidal field is represented by its Fourier coefficients, multiplied by $(1+4\pi^2|k|^2)^{1/2}$, in $\ell^2(\mathbb Z^3;\mathbb C^3)$. The resulting norm is the inhomogeneous $H^1$ norm. The zero Fourier coefficient is allowed. Assume a bound $\|K_{\mathbb T}(\tau)\|\leq C\tau^{-3/4}$ for some $C>0$ and $0<\tau\leq1$. If $u$ is a mild solution on $[a,b)$ and $v$ is a mild solution on $[a,b]$ with $u(a)=v(a)$, then $u(t)=v(t)$ for every $a\leq t<b$. Mild means norm-continuity and the Bochner integral equation with the periodic heat flow and bilinear term. The conclusion concerns equality of Fourier representatives in $H^1$; it supplies no existence or smoothing theorem.
Breakdown.Periodic.mildUniqueness.summary: On the unit torus in the inhomogeneous $H^1$ Fourier representation, assuming $\|K_{\mathbb T}(\tau)\|\le C\tau^{-3/4}$ for $0<\tau\le1$, a mild solution on $[a,b)$ and one on $[a,b]$ with equal values at $a$ agree on $[a,b)$. It gives no existence or smoothing.

Breakdown.Periodic.norm_heat_le.text: The formal periodic space represents real divergence-free fields of period one by sequences $a(n)\in\mathbb C^3$, $n\in\mathbb Z^3$, with $\sum_n|a(n)|^2<\infty$, $a(-n)=\overline{a(n)}$ and $n\cdot a(n)=0$. The physical Fourier coefficient is $c(n)=a(n)/(1+4\pi^2|n|^2)^{1/2}$. Its squared norm is $\|u\|^2=\sum_n(1+4\pi^2|n|^2)|c(n)|^2$, the inhomogeneous $H^1$ norm; the mean $c(0)$ may be nonzero. The formal statement proves $\|G(t)\|\le1$ for every real $t$. For $t\ge0$ this follows from the heat multiplier $\exp(-4\pi^2|n|^2t)$ having modulus at most one. For $t<0$ the definition sets $G(t)=I$, so the extension of the bound to negative times makes no assertion about backward heat flow. The conclusion is an operator-norm bound in the inhomogeneous space, including constants.
Breakdown.Periodic.norm_heat_le.summary: $\|G(t)\|\le1$ for every real $t$ on the period-one inhomogeneous space. For $t<0$, $G(t)=I$ by definition, so this says nothing about backward heat flow.

Breakdown.Periodic.norm_sq_eq_tsum.text: The formal periodic space represents real divergence-free fields of period one by sequences $a(n)\in\mathbb C^3$, $n\in\mathbb Z^3$, with $\sum_n|a(n)|^2<\infty$, $a(-n)=\overline{a(n)}$ and $n\cdot a(n)=0$. The physical Fourier coefficient is $c(n)=a(n)/(1+4\pi^2|n|^2)^{1/2}$. Its squared norm is $\|u\|^2=\sum_n(1+4\pi^2|n|^2)|c(n)|^2$, the inhomogeneous $H^1$ norm; the mean $c(0)$ may be nonzero. For every vector $u$ in this formal space, the formal statement proves the identity $\|u\|^2=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z^3}(1+4\pi^2|n|^2)|c(n)|^2$. Square summability of the weighted coefficients ensures convergence of the nonnegative series. The identity is exact for the inhomogeneous unit-torus norm. It contains neither the mean-zero hypothesis nor the factor $L^3$ and frequencies $n/L$ of (3.15).
Breakdown.Periodic.norm_sq_eq_tsum.summary: For every $u$ in the period-one space, $\|u\|^2=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z^3}(1+4\pi^2|n|^2)|c(n)|^2$. It has neither the mean-zero hypothesis nor the factor $L^3$ and frequencies $n/L$ of (3.15).

Breakdown.Periodic.operatorNormBounds_ho.text:
The whole-space norm is $\|v\|_X=\|\nabla v\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^3)}$ on solenoidal velocities in $L^6(\mathbb R^3)$.

The periodic space is the real solenoidal Fourier realization of $H^1(\mathbb R^3/\mathbb Z^3)$, with squared norm $\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^3}(1+4\pi^2|k|^2)|\widehat v(k)|^2$. Its zero Fourier coefficient is allowed to be nonzero.

Local data are a tuple $(A_1,A_2,A_3,v)$ with $A_j\in L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$ and $v\in L^6(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$, measured by $\max\{\max_j\|A_j\|_2,\|v\|_6\}$. No compatibility condition $A_j=\partial_jv$ or divergence condition is part of this data space.

An approximation on $[0,\ell]$ is specified, for every integer $n\ge0$, by a finite sum $A_n(s)=\sum_{j=1}^m\alpha_{n,j}(s)\varphi_{n,j}$, where each $\alpha_{n,j}$ is continuous, each $\varphi_{n,j}$ is smooth, compactly supported and solenoidal with support in $\bar B_b$, and both the weights and $\|\varphi_{n,j}\|_X$ have one uniform bound. The number $m$ is fixed.

The formal statement proves that one $C\ge0$ bounds the whole-space and periodic localized Duhamel operators by $CM$, if $\sup_n\|A_n\|_{C([0,\ell];X)}\le M$, and bounds the whole-space and scaled periodic restriction operators by $C$. For the whole-space Duhamel estimate $0<\ell\le1$; restriction alone only requires $\ell>0$. The periodic estimates assume $0<T\le1$, $0<\lambda<1$, $b>0$, $\sqrt T b\le1/8$ and $\ell=1-\lambda$. Restriction records the value with factor $\mu_n^{1/4}$ and each derivative with factor $\mu_n^{3/4}$ after $x=a+\sqrt{\mu_n}y$, where $\mu_n=T\lambda^n$ and $a=(1/2,1/2,1/2)$. The same statement bounds the previous-interval heat propagation operator by $\lambda^{1/4}/\theta$, for $\theta>0$. In the whole-space formula $\lambda=e^{-P/k}$ with $P>0$ and positive integer $k$; the periodic propagation bound allows $0<\lambda\le1$. Thus the propagation is a strict contraction when $\lambda^{1/4}<\theta$. These are supremum norms on interval sequences, rather than the paper’s continuous $C_\kappa$ norm.
Breakdown.Periodic.operatorNormBounds_ho.summary: One $C\ge0$ bounds the whole-space and periodic localized Duhamel operators by $CM$ when $\sup_n\|A_n\|\le M$, and the restriction operators by $C$; the propagation operator has norm at most $\lambda^{1/4}/\theta$. These are supremum norms on interval sequences, not the paper's $C_\kappa$ norm.

Breakdown.Periodic.r3Lambda.text:
The whole-space norm is $\|v\|_X=\|\nabla v\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^3)}$ on solenoidal velocities in $L^6(\mathbb R^3)$.

Local data are a tuple $(A_1,A_2,A_3,v)$ with $A_j\in L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$ and $v\in L^6(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$, measured by $\max\{\max_j\|A_j\|_2,\|v\|_6\}$. No compatibility condition $A_j=\partial_jv$ or divergence condition is part of this data space.

An approximation on $[0,\ell]$ is specified, for every integer $n\ge0$, by a finite sum $A_n(s)=\sum_{j=1}^m\alpha_{n,j}(s)\varphi_{n,j}$, where each $\alpha_{n,j}$ is continuous, each $\varphi_{n,j}$ is smooth, compactly supported and solenoidal with support in $\bar B_b$, and both the weights and $\|\varphi_{n,j}\|_X$ have one uniform bound. The number $m$ is fixed.

For a bounded sequence of continuous local curves $\zeta_n$, the operator acts on interval $n$ as $\sum_j\int_0^s\alpha_{n,j}(\sigma)\Lambda_{\varphi_{n,j}}(s-\sigma)\zeta_n(\sigma)\,d\sigma$, where $\Lambda_\varphi(\tau)\zeta=-e^{\tau\Delta}\mathbb P[1_{\bar B_b}\sum_i(\varphi_iA_i+v_i\partial_i\varphi)]$. The domain and range have the supremum norm over $n$ and $s$. The displayed integral interpretation is proved for $0<\ell\le1$ using the $\tau^{-3/4}$ estimate and continuity for positive lags.

The general definition selects the bounded linear map with this formula if it exists and uses zero otherwise; the analytic estimates exclude that alternative in the application. This assembles localized interactions of finite-sum approximations, rather than the paper’s one global curve $\bar u$.
Breakdown.Periodic.r3Lambda.summary: Defines on bounded sequences of local curves $\sum_j\int_0^s\alpha_{n,j}(\sigma)\Lambda_{\varphi_{n,j}}(s-\sigma)\zeta_n(\sigma)d\sigma$, with $\Lambda_\varphi(\tau)$ the projected heat flow of the localized transport term. It assembles finite-sum approximations, not one global curve $\bar u$.

Breakdown.Periodic.r3LambdaBound_holds.text:
The whole-space norm is $\|v\|_X=\|\nabla v\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^3)}$ on solenoidal velocities in $L^6(\mathbb R^3)$.

Local data are a tuple $(A_1,A_2,A_3,v)$ with $A_j\in L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$ and $v\in L^6(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$, measured by $\max\{\max_j\|A_j\|_2,\|v\|_6\}$. No compatibility condition $A_j=\partial_jv$ or divergence condition is part of this data space.

For every $\varphi\in C^\infty_{c,\mathrm{div}}(\mathbb R^3)$, real $b$, $\tau>0$ and local tuple $\zeta=(A_1,A_2,A_3,v)$, define $f_\zeta=1_{\bar B_b}\sum_j(\varphi_jA_j+v_j\partial_j\varphi)$.

The formal statement proves a constant $C\ge0$ such that $\|e^{\tau\Delta}\mathbb Pf_\zeta\|_X\le C\tau^{-3/4}\|\varphi\|_X\|\zeta\|$. The constant is independent of $b,\tau,\varphi,\zeta$, and no relation between the derivative entries and the velocity entry is assumed. This is a fixed-lag estimate; integrability and continuity of the Duhamel integral require the time-dependent inputs.
Breakdown.Periodic.r3LambdaBound_holds.summary: One constant $C\ge0$, independent of $b,\tau,\varphi,\zeta$, gives $\|e^{\tau\Delta}\mathbb Pf_\zeta\|_X\le C\tau^{-3/4}\|\varphi\|_X\|\zeta\|$ for $f_\zeta=1_{\bar B_b}\sum_j(\varphi_jA_j+v_j\partial_j\varphi)$, with no relation assumed between $A_j$ and $v$. It is a fixed-lag estimate.

Breakdown.Periodic.r3Op.text:
The whole-space norm is $\|v\|_X=\|\nabla v\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^3)}$ on solenoidal velocities in $L^6(\mathbb R^3)$.

Fix a heat semigroup $G$, a symmetric bilinear kernel $K$ with $\|K(\tau)\|\le C_K\tau^{-3/4}$ for $0<\tau\le1$, and dilations $D$ compatible with them.

The supplied whole-space operator data also impose $G(0)=I$, the semigroup law for nonnegative times, strong continuity, $\|G(t)\|\le1$ for $t\ge0$, symmetry and positive-lag continuity of $K$, and $G(s)K(\tau)=K(s+\tau)$ for $s\ge0$, $\tau>0$. The dilations obey $D_1=I$, $D_\mu D_\nu=D_{\mu\nu}$, $\|D_\mu v\|=\mu^{1/4}\|v\|$, strong continuity for $\mu>0$, $D_\mu G(\mu t)=G(t)D_\mu$, and $\mu D_\mu K(\mu\tau)(u,v)=K(\tau)(D_\mu u,D_\mu v)$. For a dense set of inputs $u$, each map $K(\tau)(u,\cdot)$ is compact when $\tau>0$. Put $\lambda=e^{-P/k}$ and $\ell=1-\lambda$, where $P$ is real and $k$ is a natural number. For a normed space $E$, bounded linear $J:E\to X$, continuous curves $f_n:[0,\ell]\to X$, and bounded interval sequences $z$, the formal definition has component $z_n-2\mathcal B(f_n,z_n)-h_n$, where $\mathcal B(f,g)(s)=\int_0^sK(s-\sigma)(f(\sigma),g(\sigma))\,d\sigma$, $h_0(s)=G(s)Je$, and $h_n(s)=\theta^{-1}G(s)D_\lambda z_{n-1}(\ell)$ for $n\ge1$. For $P>0$, $k>0$, $\theta>0$, and bounded $f_n$, this is the rescaled interval linearization.

The definition itself permits degenerate parameters, uses zero for sequence operators that have no bounded realization, and takes division by zero to be zero. Those values are excluded by the stated application hypotheses. It does not isolate the cutoff error in (6.14).
Breakdown.Periodic.r3Op.summary: Defines the whole-space interval linearization with component $z_n-2\mathcal B(f_n,z_n)-h_n$, where $h_0(s)=G(s)Je$ and $h_n(s)=\theta^{-1}G(s)D_\lambda z_{n-1}(\ell)$, $\lambda=e^{-P/k}$, $\ell=1-\lambda$. Degenerate parameters use zero conventions; it does not isolate the cutoff error in (6.14).

Breakdown.Periodic.restrictTorus.text:
The periodic space is the real solenoidal Fourier realization of $H^1(\mathbb R^3/\mathbb Z^3)$, with squared norm $\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^3}(1+4\pi^2|k|^2)|\widehat v(k)|^2$. Its zero Fourier coefficient is allowed to be nonzero.

Local data are a tuple $(A_1,A_2,A_3,v)$ with $A_j\in L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$ and $v\in L^6(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$, measured by $\max\{\max_j\|A_j\|_2,\|v\|_6\}$. No compatibility condition $A_j=\partial_jv$ or divergence condition is part of this data space.

Whole-space restriction to $\bar B_b$ consists of $1_{\bar B_b}\partial_jv$ and $1_{\bar B_b}v$. Write $a=(1/2,1/2,1/2)$ for the fixed centre of the unit cell. At an admissible periodic scale $0<\mu\le1$, $b>0$, $\sqrt\mu\,b\le1/8$, periodic restriction consists of $1_{\bar B_b}\mu^{3/4}\partial_jz(a+\sqrt\mu\,y)$ and $1_{\bar B_b}\mu^{1/4}z(a+\sqrt\mu\,y)$, interpreted almost everywhere. It is defined to be zero if these scale conditions fail.

This is a bounded linear map for every real pair $(\mu,b)$. The derivatives and velocity are recovered from Fourier series in $L^2$ and $L^6$, respectively. The derivative entries are restrictions of the derivatives of the original field; they are not asserted to be the distributional derivatives of its zero extension. It records local values and derivative values as independent coordinates, so its target is larger than the image of $H^1(B)$. On admissible scales the normalized local norms are bounded by a constant times the unit-torus $H^1$ norm, uniformly in the admissible scale. The paper instead restricts an unscaled field on a large torus and uses the sum of the gradient and velocity norms.
Breakdown.Periodic.restrictTorus.summary: A bounded linear map sending a period-one field $z$ to $1_{\bar B_b}\mu^{3/4}\partial_jz(a+\sqrt\mu y)$ and $1_{\bar B_b}\mu^{1/4}z(a+\sqrt\mu y)$, $a$ the cell centre, for $0<\mu\le1$, $\sqrt\mu b\le1/8$, and zero otherwise. The paper restricts an unscaled field on a large torus.

Breakdown.Periodic.rightInversePerturb.text:
Let $E,F$ be real Banach spaces, let $A,A^{\prime}:E\to F$, $R:F\to E$ be bounded linear maps, and assume $AR=I_F$, $\|R\|\le K$, $\|A^{\prime}-A\|K\le1/2$.

The formal statement proves the existence of a bounded linear $R^{\prime}:F\to E$ with $A^{\prime} R^{\prime}=I_F$ and $\|R^{\prime}\|\le2K$. Its proof takes $R^{\prime}=R[I+(A^{\prime}-A)R]^{-1}$. Since $\|(A^{\prime}-A)R\|\le1/2$, this inverse is given by a convergent geometric series. A total inverse that is zero on noninvertible operators is used in the definitions; the norm hypothesis ensures that it is the ordinary inverse here.
Breakdown.Periodic.rightInversePerturb.summary: If $AR=I_F$, $\|R\|\le K$ and $\|A'-A\|K\le1/2$ for bounded linear maps between real Banach spaces, then some bounded linear $R'$ has $A'R'=I_F$ and $\|R'\|\le2K$.

Breakdown.Periodic.selfSimilar.text: For a field $W:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$, the definition is $u_T^*(t,x)=(T-t)^{-1/2}W(-\log((T-t)/T),(T-t)^{-1/2}(x-a))$, with $a=(1/2,1/2,1/2)$. On the physical interval $T>0$, $t<T$, the similarity time is $\log(T/(T-t))$ and all denominators are positive. The function is defined for every real $T,t$ with division by zero equal to zero, $\log0=0$, $\log x=\log|x|$ for $x<0$, and $(T-t)^{-1/2}=0$ for $t\ge T$; consequently the defined field is zero there. Its interpretation as the self-similar flow is restricted to $T>0$, $t<T$. The paper centers the singularity at the origin; this definition centers it in the unit period cell.
Breakdown.Periodic.selfSimilar.summary: Defines $u_T^*(t,x)=(T-t)^{-1/2}W(-\log((T-t)/T),(T-t)^{-1/2}(x-a))$ with $a=(1/2,1/2,1/2)$; by the conventions it is zero for $t\ge T$. The paper centres the singularity at the origin; this definition centres it in the unit cell.

Breakdown.Periodic.selfSimilarSolves.text:
Let $W:\mathbb R	imes\mathbb R^3	o\mathbb R^3$ and $q:\mathbb R	imes\mathbb R^3	o\mathbb R$ be jointly smooth. For every $s\in\mathbb R$ and $y\in\mathbb R^3$, assume $\partial_sW+ rac12W+ rac12(y\cdot
abla)W-\Delta W+(W\cdot
abla)W+
abla q=0$ and $\operatorname{div}W=0$. Assume one real constant $C$ gives $\|D_y^jW(s,y)\|\le C(1+|y|)^{-j-1}$ for the integers $j=0,1,2$, and $|
abla_yq(s,y)|\le C(1+|y|)^{-3}$, uniformly in all $s,y$. Here $D_y^0W=W$, while for $j=1,2$ the derivative is a linear or bilinear map with its operator norm. The paper uses the square root of the sum of squared coordinate derivatives. These norms are equivalent in dimension three, with fixed factors; an unspecified bound transfers after enlarging $C$, but the same numerical constant is not asserted. For every $T>0$, put $a=(1/2,1/2,1/2)$, $s=\log(T/(T-t))$ and $y=(x-a)/\sqrt{T-t}$ for $t<T$. Define $u(t,x)=(T-t)^{-1/2}W(s,y)$ and $p(t,x)=(T-t)^{-1}q(s,y)$. The formal statement proves joint smoothness of $u,p$ on $(-\infty,T)	imes\mathbb R^3$ and, at every point of that domain, $\operatorname{div}u=0$ and $\partial_tu+(u\cdot
abla)u-\Delta u+
abla p=0$. Recurrence and nontriviality are unnecessary for this assertion. The centre differs from the origin in (1.4); translating space identifies the formulas. Values assigned by reciprocal and real powers outside $t<T$ do not enter the result. In particular, the assertion does not extend the solution through time $T$.
Breakdown.Periodic.selfSimilarSolves.summary: For a smooth profile with the decay bounds and $T>0$, $u(t,x)=(T-t)^{-1/2}W(s,y)$ and $p=(T-t)^{-1}q(s,y)$, centred at $a=(1/2,1/2,1/2)$, are smooth on $(-\infty,T)\times\mathbb R^3$ and solve Navier–Stokes there. Recurrence is not needed; no extension through $T$.

Breakdown.Periodic.seqPerturbation.text:
This theorem assumes two analytic properties for every real Banach space with a strongly continuous contraction semigroup $G$ and a symmetric positive-lag continuous bilinear kernel $K$ satisfying $G(s)K(\tau)=K(s+\tau)$ and $\|K(\tau)\|\le C_K\tau^{-3/4}$ for $0<\tau\le1$. First, on every interval $[0,\ell]$, $\ell>0$, the bounded bilinear curve operator is the Duhamel integral, has norm at most $4C_K\ell^{1/4}$ if $\ell\le1$, and the free curve operator is $x\mapsto G(\cdot)x$ with norm at most one. Second, if continuous curves $u,v$ on $[a,b]$, $a\le b$, have bounds $M,N$, their Duhamel integrals from $a$ to $t$ are integrable and continuous for every $t\in[a,b]$, and their norms are at most $4C_K(t-a)^{1/4}MN$ when $t-a\le1$. It proves the interval correction statement below from these two properties. Their proofs are supplied elsewhere in the same source package.

Let $X,E$ be real Banach spaces. For each integer $n\ge0$, let $G_n$ be a strongly continuous contraction heat semigroup and $K_n$ a continuous symmetric bilinear kernel satisfying $G_n(s)K_n(\tau)=K_n(s+\tau)$ for $s\ge0$, $\tau>0$, with $\|K_n(\tau)\|\le C_K\tau^{-3/4}$ for $0<\tau\le1$, where $C_K\ge0$ is independent of $n$. Fix $0<\ell\le1$, $0<\theta<1$, a real endpoint factor $c$, bounded linear $J:E\to X$, and continuous interval curves $a_n,r_n:[0,\ell]\to X$. Assume $\|a_n\|_\infty\le M$, $a_{n+1}(0)=c\,a_n(\ell)$, $a_n=G_n(\cdot)a_n(0)+\mathcal B_n(a_n,a_n)+r_n$, and $\|r_n\|_\infty\le\theta^n\rho$. Here $\mathcal B_n(f,g)(s)=\int_0^sK_n(s-\sigma)(f(\sigma),g(\sigma))\,d\sigma$.

Suppose a bounded linear map $R$ takes each bounded interval sequence $g$ to $(e,z)$ satisfying $z_n-2\mathcal B_n(a_n,z_n)-G_n(\cdot)Je=g_0$ for $n=0$, and $z_n-2\mathcal B_n(a_n,z_n)-(c/\theta)G_n(\cdot)z_{n-1}(\ell)=g_n$ for $n\ge1$.

For a datum displacement $\xi\in X$, assume $64\|R\|^2C_K\ell^{1/4}(\rho+\|\xi\|)\le1$.

The formal statement proves an $e$ and curves $z_n$ with $\|e\|,\sup_n\|z_n\|_\infty\le2\|R\|(\rho+\|\xi\|)$, such that, on writing $v_n=a_n+\theta^nz_n$, each $v_n$ satisfies $v_n(s)=G_n(s)v_n(0)+\mathcal B_n(v_n,v_n)(s)$ on the closed interval, with an integrable nonlinear term. Moreover $v_{n+1}(0)=c\,v_n(\ell)$ and $z_0(0)=\xi+Je$. The sequence norm and the product norm are maxima. The positive hypotheses exclude zero denominators.
Breakdown.Periodic.seqPerturbation.summary: Assuming the interval operator bounds and Duhamel integrability, if residuals are at most $\theta^n\rho$ and the linear equations have a right inverse $R$ with $64\|R\|^2C_K\ell^{1/4}(\rho+\|\xi\|)\le1$, then $v_n=a_n+\theta^nz_n$ are exact matched mild curves with $z_0(0)=\xi+Je$.

Breakdown.Periodic.shellInverseTransfer.text:
The theorem assumes the general stability of a bounded linear right inverse in real Banach spaces: if $AR=I$, $\|R\|\le K$ and $\|A^{\prime}-A\|K\le1/2$, there is a bounded linear $R^{\prime}$ with $A^{\prime}R^{\prime}=I$ and $\|R^{\prime}\|\le2K$. Under this premise it proves the inverse-transfer assertion below. The supplied source proves the stability premise separately.

Let $E,Y,Y_{\mathbb T},Z$ be real Banach spaces. Take bounded linear maps $S:Y\to Y$, $G:E\to Y$, $B:Z\to Y$, $R:Y\to Z$, and corresponding bounded linear periodic maps $S_{\mathbb T},G_{\mathbb T},B_{\mathbb T},R_{\mathbb T}$. Define $\mathcal L(e,y)=y-Sy-Ge-BRy$ and its periodic counterpart. Assume $0\le q<1$, $\|S\|,\|S_{\mathbb T}\|\le q$, and a bounded linear right inverse $F:Y\to E\times Y$ with $\mathcal LF=I$ and $\|F\|\le K$. Suppose the two operator differences $R_{\mathbb T}(I-S_{\mathbb T})^{-1}B_{\mathbb T}-R(I-S)^{-1}B$ and $R_{\mathbb T}(I-S_{\mathbb T})^{-1}G_{\mathbb T}-R(I-S)^{-1}G$ each have norm at most $\delta$, and $4\delta[1+K\|B\|(1+\|R\|)]\le1$.

The formal statement proves an exact periodic right inverse $F_{\mathbb T}$ with norm at most $(1-q)^{-1}\{1+2(\|B_{\mathbb T}\|+\|G_{\mathbb T}\|+1)[1+K\|B\|(1+\|R\|)]\|R_{\mathbb T}\|(1-q)^{-1}\}$. Product spaces use the maximum norm.

The strict contraction hypotheses make the displayed inverses ordinary bounded inverses and make $1-q$ nonzero. This transfers an inverse through local comparisons; it does not assert the paper’s formula (6.12) or its explicit defect rate.
Breakdown.Periodic.shellInverseTransfer.summary: Assuming stability of bounded right inverses, if $\|S\|,\|S_{\mathbb T}\|\le q<1$, $\mathcal L$ has a right inverse of norm at most $K$ and both localized differences are at most $\delta$ with $4\delta[1+K\|B\|(1+\|R\|)]\le1$, the periodic operator has an exact right inverse. Not (6.12).

Breakdown.Periodic.smoothPeriodicIsMild_.text: The domain here is the unit torus $\mathbb R^3/\mathbb Z^3$. A real solenoidal field is represented by its Fourier coefficients, multiplied by $(1+4\pi^2|k|^2)^{1/2}$, in $\ell^2(\mathbb Z^3;\mathbb C^3)$. The resulting norm is the inhomogeneous $H^1$ norm. The zero Fourier coefficient is allowed. Let $u,p$ be a global smooth solution of the unforced equations with viscosity one and with both velocity and pressure periodic of period one in each spatial coordinate for every $t\geq0$. For every finite $T>0$, the Fourier representative of $u$ is a mild solution on $[0,T]$: it is continuous in $H^1$ and satisfies the heat-flow integral equation with a Bochner integrable nonlinear term. The solution and pressure in the hypothesis are already smooth. The direction of this result is therefore the reverse of the periodic smoothing conclusion of Lemma 2.3.
Breakdown.Periodic.smoothPeriodicIsMild_.summary: If $u,p$ is a global smooth solution of the unforced equations with viscosity one and both velocity and pressure unit-periodic, then for every $T>0$ the Fourier representative of $u$ is a mild solution on $[0,T]$ in $H^1$ of the torus. This is the reverse of the smoothing direction in Lemma 2.3.

Breakdown.Periodic.sourceCoefFormula.text: Let $A\in L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$ vanish almost everywhere outside $\bar B_{b^{\prime}}$. Suppose $\mu>0$ and $\sqrt\mu\,b^{\prime}\le1/4$. For each integer vector $k$, the formal statement asserts that the $k$th Fourier coefficient on $[0,1]^3$ of $A((w(x)-a)/\sqrt\mu)$ is $\mu^{3/2}e^{-2\pi i k\cdot a}\widehat A(\sqrt\mu\,k)$, where $a=(1/2,1/2,1/2)$, $w$ reduces coordinates to the cell centered at $a$, and $\widehat A(\xi)=\int e^{-2\pi i\xi\cdot y}A(y)\,dy$. Compact support gives the integrability required by this formula. The factor is the volume Jacobian and the phase records translation. The paper’s factor $L^{-3}$ is the analogous Jacobian with $\mu=L^{-2}$; the statement here concerns vector forcing on the unit torus.
Breakdown.Periodic.sourceCoefFormula.summary: States that for $A\in L^2$ supported in $\bar B_{b'}$, $\mu>0$ and $\sqrt\mu b'\le1/4$, the $k$th unit-torus Fourier coefficient of $A((w(x)-a)/\sqrt\mu)$ is $\mu^{3/2}e^{-2\pi ik\cdot a}\widehat A(\sqrt\mu k)$. The paper's $L^{-3}$ is the analogous Jacobian with $\mu=L^{-2}$.

Breakdown.Periodic.stepFrame.text: The formal periodic space represents real divergence-free fields of period one by sequences $a(n)\in\mathbb C^3$, $n\in\mathbb Z^3$, with $\sum_n|a(n)|^2<\infty$, $a(-n)=\overline{a(n)}$ and $n\cdot a(n)=0$. The physical Fourier coefficient is $c(n)=a(n)/(1+4\pi^2|n|^2)^{1/2}$. Its squared norm is $\|u\|^2=\sum_n(1+4\pi^2|n|^2)|c(n)|^2$, the inhomogeneous $H^1$ norm; the mean $c(0)$ may be nonzero. Assume a constant $C>0$ satisfies $\|K_{\mathbb T}(r)\|\le Cr^{-3/4}$ for $0<r\le1$, and choose $0<\mu\le1$. The construction defines $G_\mu(t)=e^{\mu t\Delta}$ and $K_\mu(\tau)=\mu^{3/4}K_{\mathbb T}(\mu\tau)$ on the same fixed periodic space. It supplies the contraction semigroup laws for $t\ge0$, symmetry and continuity for $\tau>0$, the identity $G_\mu(t)K_\mu(\tau)=K_\mu(t+\tau)$, and $\|K_\mu(\tau)\|\le C\tau^{-3/4}$ for $0<\tau\le1$. The same $C$ works for all permitted $\mu$. The positive hypothesis on $\mu$ makes every fractional power and division in the estimates ordinary real operations. This construction rescales time and interaction amplitude in the unit-torus norm. Formula (3.21) also changes the spatial period and uses a homogeneous norm; those are different assertions.
Breakdown.Periodic.stepFrame.summary: Given $\|K_{\mathbb T}(r)\|\le Cr^{-3/4}$ for $0<r\le1$ and $0<\mu\le1$, $e^{\mu t\Delta}$ and $K_\mu(\tau)=\mu^{3/4}K_{\mathbb T}(\mu\tau)$ satisfy the semigroup, symmetry and shift laws and $\|K_\mu(\tau)\|\le C\tau^{-3/4}$ for $0<\tau\le1$, same $C$. (3.21) also changes the period.

Breakdown.Periodic.torusBlowup_of_parts.text: The construction combines approximation, right-inverse transfer, perturbation and gluing, retaining the stated analytic hypotheses.

Breakdown.Periodic.torusLambda.text:
The periodic space is the real solenoidal Fourier realization of $H^1(\mathbb R^3/\mathbb Z^3)$, with squared norm $\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^3}(1+4\pi^2|k|^2)|\widehat v(k)|^2$. Its zero Fourier coefficient is allowed to be nonzero.

Local data are a tuple $(A_1,A_2,A_3,v)$ with $A_j\in L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$ and $v\in L^6(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$, measured by $\max\{\max_j\|A_j\|_2,\|v\|_6\}$. No compatibility condition $A_j=\partial_jv$ or divergence condition is part of this data space.

An approximation on $[0,\ell]$ is specified, for every integer $n\ge0$, by a finite sum $A_n(s)=\sum_{j=1}^m\alpha_{n,j}(s)\varphi_{n,j}$, where each $\alpha_{n,j}$ is continuous, each $\varphi_{n,j}$ is smooth, compactly supported and solenoidal with support in $\bar B_b$, and both the weights and $\|\varphi_{n,j}\|_X$ have one uniform bound. The number $m$ is fixed.

Put $\mu_n=T\lambda^n$ with $0<T\le1$ and $0<\lambda<1$, and assume $b>0$, $\sqrt T b\le1/8$ and $0<\ell\le1$. The operator on a bounded sequence of local curves is $\sum_j\int_0^s\alpha_{n,j}(\sigma)\Lambda^{(\mu_n)}_{\varphi_{n,j}}(s-\sigma)\zeta_n(\sigma)\,d\sigma$ on interval $n$. Here $\Lambda^{(\mu)}_\varphi(\tau)\zeta=-\mu^{-1/4}e^{\mu\tau\Delta}\mathbb P[f_\zeta((w(x)-a)/\sqrt\mu)]$, with $a=(1/2,1/2,1/2)$, coordinate reduction $w$, and $f_\zeta=1_{\bar B_b}\sum_i(\varphi_iA_i+v_i\partial_i\varphi)$. Both sequence norms are suprema in $n$ and in interval time. The construction uses zero when the required bounded integral map does not exist; the scale hypotheses and the heat estimate establish the integral formula here. This is the interval version of the paper’s $\mathcal A_{\mathbb T}$.
Breakdown.Periodic.torusLambda.summary: Defines the periodic interval operator: on interval $n$, with $\mu_n=T\lambda^n$, it integrates the weighted rescaled torus projected heat flow of the transplanted transport term against the local curve. It is the interval version of the paper's $\mathcal A_{\mathbb T}$.

Breakdown.Periodic.torusLambdaBound_hold.text:
The periodic space is the real solenoidal Fourier realization of $H^1(\mathbb R^3/\mathbb Z^3)$, with squared norm $\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^3}(1+4\pi^2|k|^2)|\widehat v(k)|^2$. Its zero Fourier coefficient is allowed to be nonzero.

The whole-space norm is $\|v\|_X=\|\nabla v\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^3)}$ on solenoidal velocities in $L^6(\mathbb R^3)$.

Local data are a tuple $(A_1,A_2,A_3,v)$ with $A_j\in L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$ and $v\in L^6(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$, measured by $\max\{\max_j\|A_j\|_2,\|v\|_6\}$. No compatibility condition $A_j=\partial_jv$ or divergence condition is part of this data space.

Let $\varphi\in C^\infty_{c,\mathrm{div}}(\mathbb R^3)$, suppose $0<\mu\le1$, $b>0$, $\sqrt\mu b\le1/8$, and assume $\tau>0$, $\mu\tau\le1$. Put $f_\zeta=1_{\bar B_b}\sum_j(\varphi_jA_j+v_j\partial_j\varphi)$ for a local tuple $\zeta$. With $a=(1/2,1/2,1/2)$ and coordinate reduction $w$, the formal statement asserts a constant $C\ge0$ such that $\|\mu^{-1/4}e^{\mu\tau\Delta}\mathbb P[f_\zeta((w(x)-a)/\sqrt\mu)]\|_{H^1(\mathbb T^3)}\le C\tau^{-3/4}\|\varphi\|_X\|\zeta\|$. The constant is uniform in the stated parameters. The restriction $\mu\tau\le1$ concerns physical time and is part of this periodic estimate.
Breakdown.Periodic.torusLambdaBound_hold.summary: States that for a test field $\varphi$, $0<\mu\le1$, $b>0$, $\sqrt\mu b\le1/8$, $\tau>0$ and $\mu\tau\le1$, one uniform $C\ge0$ gives $\|\mu^{-1/4}e^{\mu\tau\Delta}\mathbb P[f_\zeta((w(x)-a)/\sqrt\mu)]\|_{H^1(\mathbb T^3)}\le C\tau^{-3/4}\|\varphi\|_X\|\zeta\|$.

Breakdown.Periodic.torusOp.text:
The periodic space is the real solenoidal Fourier realization of $H^1(\mathbb R^3/\mathbb Z^3)$, with squared norm $\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^3}(1+4\pi^2|k|^2)|\widehat v(k)|^2$. Its zero Fourier coefficient is allowed to be nonzero.

The definition takes as an input the periodic kernel bound: a constant $C_{\mathbb T}>0$ with $\|K_{\mathbb T}(\tau)\|\le C_{\mathbb T}\tau^{-3/4}$ for every $0<\tau\le1$. This bound is proved separately. Fix $0<T\le1$, $0<\lambda\le1$, a real $\theta$, a normed datum space $E$, a bounded linear map $J:E\to H^1_{\mathrm{div}}(\mathbb T^3)$, and a sequence $f_n$ of continuous curves on $[0,1-\lambda]$. Put $\mu_n=T\lambda^n$. On a bounded sequence $z=(z_n)$, the formal definition is $\mathcal L(e,z)=z-Sz-Ge-2\mathcal B(f,z)$. For $n=0$, $(Ge)_0(s)=e^{Ts\Delta}Je$ and $(Sz)_0=0$; for $n\ge1$, $(Sz)_n(s)=(\lambda^{1/4}/\theta)e^{\mu_ns\Delta}z_{n-1}(1-\lambda)$ and $(Ge)_n=0$. The interval bilinear term is $\mathcal B_n(f,z)(s)=\int_0^s\mu_n^{3/4}K_{\mathbb T}(\mu_n(s-\sigma))(f(\sigma),z(\sigma))\,d\sigma$. The pointwise interpretation of the last term requires the family to be bounded; the general definition uses zero for a family that fails to define a bounded sequence operator. Division by zero is set to zero, so using this as a weighted linearization requires $\theta>0$.

In the application $\lambda^{1/4}<\theta<1$ and $f_n$ is uniformly bounded. Formula (6.6) instead combines the same roles in a single physical trajectory.
Breakdown.Periodic.torusOp.summary: Defines the periodic interval linearization $\mathcal L(e,z)=z-Sz-Ge-2\mathcal B(f,z)$, with $(Ge)_0(s)=e^{Ts\Delta}Je$ and $(Sz)_n(s)=(\lambda^{1/4}/\theta)e^{\mu_ns\Delta}z_{n-1}(1-\lambda)$. Division by zero is taken as zero, so the use requires $\theta>0$; (6.6) uses one physical trajectory.

Breakdown.Periodic.transplantDilate.text:
Write $a=(1/2,1/2,1/2)$ and let $w(x)$ reduce each coordinate of $x$ modulo integers to the cell centered at $a$. For $\mu>0$, the transplanted field is $g_\mu(x)=\mu^{-1/2}g((w(x)-a)/\sqrt\mu)$.

For every $\mu>0$, $c>0$, and function $f:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$, the formal statement asserts $f_\mu=(D_cf)_{\mu c}$, where $(D_cf)(y)=c^{1/2}f(c^{1/2}y)$. No regularity, integrability or solenoidal hypothesis is needed for this pointwise identity. It explains the compatibility of the two spatial rescalings, without asserting the change of homogeneous norm or the transport of the mild equation under a change of the torus period.
Breakdown.Periodic.transplantDilate.summary: States that for $\mu,c>0$ and any $f$, $f_\mu=(D_cf)_{\mu c}$ with $(D_cf)(y)=c^{1/2}f(c^{1/2}y)$, a pointwise identity with no regularity hypothesis. It does not assert the change of norm or of the mild equation under a change of period.

Breakdown.Periodic.transplantField.text:
Write $a=(1/2,1/2,1/2)$ and let $w(x)$ reduce each coordinate of $x$ modulo integers to the cell centered at $a$. For $\mu>0$, the transplanted field is $g_\mu(x)=\mu^{-1/2}g((w(x)-a)/\sqrt\mu)$.

This is a function on all of $\mathbb R^3$, with period one in each coordinate. When $g$ is supported in $\bar B_b$ and $\sqrt\mu b\le1/8$, its periodic copies have disjoint supports. It is then the translated and rescaled version of the paper’s periodization.

The definition itself imposes neither support nor smoothness. Reciprocal and square root are defined for all real inputs; for $\mu\le0$ the square root and its reciprocal are zero, so this field is zero. Statements using the physical dilation assume $\mu>0$.
Breakdown.Periodic.transplantField.summary: Defines $g_\mu(x)=\mu^{-1/2}g((w(x)-a)/\sqrt\mu)$, a period-one function on $\mathbb R^3$; when $g$ is supported in $\bar B_b$ with $\sqrt\mu b\le1/8$ it is the translated and rescaled periodization of the paper. For $\mu\le0$ the field is zero.

Breakdown.Periodic.transplantNorm.text:
This proof assumes the following transplant regularity statement for every smooth solenoidal field $g$ supported in $\bar B_b$: if $0<\mu\le1$, $b>0$ and $\sqrt\mu b\le1/8$, its unit-periodic transplant is smooth and solenoidal, and agrees with $\mu^{-1/2}g((x-a)/\sqrt\mu)$ on $|x-a|\le1/4$, where $a=(1/2,1/2,1/2)$. The conclusion is the norm identity below. The regularity premise is separately proved in the supplied source.

Write $a=(1/2,1/2,1/2)$ and let $w(x)$ reduce each coordinate of $x$ modulo integers to the cell centered at $a$. For $\mu>0$, the transplanted field is $g_\mu(x)=\mu^{-1/2}g((w(x)-a)/\sqrt\mu)$.

The periodic space is the real solenoidal Fourier realization of $H^1(\mathbb R^3/\mathbb Z^3)$, with squared norm $\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^3}(1+4\pi^2|k|^2)|\widehat v(k)|^2$. Its zero Fourier coefficient is allowed to be nonzero.

For every smooth solenoidal $g$ supported in $\bar B_b$, with $0<\mu\le1$, $b>0$ and $\sqrt\mu b\le1/8$, the formal statement asserts $\|\mu^{1/4}g_\mu\|_{H^1(\mathbb T^3)}^2=\int_{\mathbb R^3}|\nabla g|^2+\mu\int_{\mathbb R^3}|g|^2$. The gradient square is the sum of the squares of the three directional derivatives. Compact support and smoothness make these integrals finite. This identity includes an $L^2$ term and an amplitude normalization, whereas (6.1) concerns unscaled periodization and the homogeneous norm.
Breakdown.Periodic.transplantNorm.summary: Assuming the transplant regularity statement, for smooth solenoidal $g$ supported in $\bar B_b$ with $0<\mu\le1$, $\sqrt\mu b\le1/8$, $\|\mu^{1/4}g_\mu\|_{H^1(\mathbb T^3)}^2=\int|\nabla g|^2+\mu\int|g|^2$. Unlike (6.1), it includes an $L^2$ term and amplitude normalization.

Breakdown.Periodic.transplantSmooth.text:
Write $a=(1/2,1/2,1/2)$ and let $w(x)$ reduce each coordinate of $x$ modulo integers to the cell centered at $a$. For $\mu>0$, the transplanted field is $g_\mu(x)=\mu^{-1/2}g((w(x)-a)/\sqrt\mu)$.

For every smooth solenoidal $g$ supported in $\bar B_b$, with $0<\mu\le1$, $b>0$ and $\sqrt\mu b\le1/8$, the formal statement proves that $g_\mu$ is smooth, unit-periodic and solenoidal. On $|x-a|\le1/4$ it equals $\mu^{-1/2}g((x-a)/\sqrt\mu)$. The support condition removes the discontinuities that coordinate reduction could otherwise introduce at cell boundaries. No zero-mean conclusion or norm equality is included.
Breakdown.Periodic.transplantSmooth.summary: For smooth solenoidal $g$ supported in $\bar B_b$ with $0<\mu\le1$, $b>0$ and $\sqrt\mu b\le1/8$, $g_\mu$ is smooth, unit-periodic and solenoidal, and equals $\mu^{-1/2}g((x-a)/\sqrt\mu)$ on $|x-a|\le1/4$. No zero-mean conclusion or norm equality is included.

Breakdown.Periodic.trigHs.text: The formal statement proves that there is $C>0$ such that for every finite set $F\subset\mathbb Z^3$ and every family of coefficients $c(n)\in\mathbb C^3$, the polynomial $p(x)=\sum_{n\in F}e^{2\pi in\cdot x}c(n)$ satisfies $\|p\|_{L^6([0,1]^3)}\le C(\sum_{n\in F}(1+4\pi^2|n|^2)|c(n)|^2)^{1/2}$. The constant is independent of $F$ and the coefficients. There is no reality, divergence-free or mean-zero hypothesis. Both integrals and finite sums are ordinary ones, and the fractional powers are positive real powers. This is an inhomogeneous unit-torus estimate for finite Fourier sums. Equation (3.18) concerns all mean-zero fields with the homogeneous gradient norm, uniformly for every period $L>0$; that assertion is not the conclusion written here.
Breakdown.Periodic.trigHs.summary: One $C>0$ gives $\|p\|_{L^6([0,1]^3)}\le C(\sum_{n\in F}(1+4\pi^2|n|^2)|c(n)|^2)^{1/2}$ for every finite Fourier sum $p$, with no reality, divergence or mean-zero hypothesis. (3.18) is a homogeneous estimate uniform in the period.

Breakdown.Periodic.weight.text: For $n\in\mathbb Z^3$, the weight is $w(n)=1+4\pi^2|n|^2$, where $n$ is regarded as a vector in Euclidean three-space. The formal periodic norm is $\sum_nw(n)|c(n)|^2$ under a square root. It includes the $L^2$ term and gives weight one to the zero mode. For the homogeneous norm in (3.15), the corresponding multiplier is $4\pi^2|n|^2$ at period one and the mean is required to vanish. This weight is positive for every $n$, so its square root can be inverted even at $n=0$. The definition of the weight does not prove the mean-zero norm equivalence in (3.16).
Breakdown.Periodic.weight.summary: Defines $w(n)=1+4\pi^2|n|^2$, the weight of the inhomogeneous periodic norm, giving weight one to the zero mode. The homogeneous norm in (3.15) uses $4\pi^2|n|^2$ with zero mean.

Breakdown.PeriodicInverseStatement.text:
Let $X,Y$ be real Banach spaces, $k\ge1$ a natural number, $\rho:X\to X$ a surjective linear isometry, and $A_n:Y\to Y$, $\Gamma:X\to Y$, $\operatorname{Ev}:Y\to X$, $J,P:X\to X$ bounded and linear. Assume all $I-A_n$ are invertible with a common inverse bound. Put $S_n=\operatorname{Ev}(I-A_n)^{-1}\Gamma$ and $M=\rho^{-1}S_{k-1}\cdots S_0$, and assume $S_{n+k}=\rho S_n\rho^{-1}$, $P^2=P$, $PM=MP$, and $PJ=P$. Let $\theta>0$ and $0\le r_1<\theta^k<r_2$. Require $\|M^n(I-P)\|\le Kr_1^n$, $\|Px\|\le Kr_2^{-n}\|M^nPx\|$, and surjectivity of $M$ on $\operatorname{ran}P$. Then there is a bounded linear $\mathcal R:\ell^\infty(Y)\to X\times\ell^\infty(Y)$ such that $(e,z)=\mathcal Rg$ has $e\in\operatorname{ran}P$, $z_0-A_0z_0-\Gamma Je=g_0$, and $z_n-A_nz_n-\theta^{-1}\Gamma\operatorname{Ev}z_{n-1}=g_n$ for $n\ge1$. In §4, $Y=C([0,L];X)$ with supremum norm.

The statement neither defines the global $C_\kappa$ norm nor assumes finite rank of $P$; that comes from the separate spectral application. Positive $\theta$ and invertibility exclude the assigned zero value for a nonexistent inverse.

This formal statement specifies an implication. Defining the implication does not prove it.
Breakdown.PeriodicInverseStatement.summary: States that if $S_{n+k}=\rho S_n\rho^{-1}$, $PJ=P$ and $M=\rho^{-1}S_{k-1}\cdots S_0$ has a dichotomy with $0\le r_1<\theta^k<r_2$, there is a bounded linear $\mathcal R$ solving the interval equations with $e\in\operatorname{ran}P$. It defines no $C_\kappa$ norm and assumes no finite rank of $P$.

Breakdown.PeriodicSimilarityProfileExist.text:
Let $W:\mathbb R	imes\mathbb R^3	o\mathbb R^3$ and $q:\mathbb R	imes\mathbb R^3	o\mathbb R$ be jointly smooth. For every $s\in\mathbb R$ and $y\in\mathbb R^3$, assume $\partial_sW+ rac12W+ rac12(y\cdot
abla)W-\Delta W+(W\cdot
abla)W+
abla q=0$ and $\operatorname{div}W=0$. Assume one real constant $C$ gives $\|D_y^jW(s,y)\|\le C(1+|y|)^{-j-1}$ for the integers $j=0,1,2$, and $|
abla_yq(s,y)|\le C(1+|y|)^{-3}$, uniformly in all $s,y$. Here $D_y^0W=W$, while for $j=1,2$ the derivative is a linear or bilinear map with its operator norm. The paper uses the square root of the sum of squared coordinate derivatives. These norms are equivalent in dimension three, with fixed factors; an unspecified bound transfers after enlarging $C$, but the same numerical constant is not asserted. In addition, there are $S>0$ and an orthogonal linear map $R:\mathbb R^3	o\mathbb R^3$ such that $W(s+S,y)=RW(s,R^{-1}y)$ for every $s,y$, and $W(s,y)
e0$ for at least one pair $(s,y)$. Both rotations and orientation-reversing orthogonal maps are admitted. No recurrence condition is imposed on $q$ itself. This is the assertion that some such $W,q,S,R,C$ exist. It supplies no numerical example and no chosen period or rotation. The formal statement explicitly includes second-derivative and pressure-gradient decay, beyond the two displayed inequalities in (1.3). Remark 1.2 derives the second-derivative estimate from the smooth similarity equation and the velocity bound, with a possibly larger constant, so that clause is not an independent restriction on the paper’s profiles. A corresponding implication for the stated pressure-gradient bound is not supplied by that remark. The Hessian clause therefore does not by itself make the formal premise stronger than the paper's. The denominator is always positive. The pressure is determined only to the extent imposed by its equation and gradient bound; time-dependent spatial constants are not fixed.
Breakdown.PeriodicSimilarityProfileExist.summary: Asserts existence of a nonzero smooth recurrent profile solving the similarity equation, with $S>0$, orthogonal $R$, and decay of $W$, its first two spatial derivatives and $\nabla q$. Remark 1.2 already derives the Hessian bound from the paper’s velocity bound and equation.

Breakdown.PhysicalMomentum.text:
Let $W:\mathbb R	imes\mathbb R^3	o\mathbb R^3$ and $q:\mathbb R	imes\mathbb R^3	o\mathbb R$ be smooth, solve $\partial_sW+	frac12W+	frac12(y\cdot
abla)W-\Delta W+(W\cdot
abla)W+
abla q=0$, and satisfy $\operatorname{div}W=0$. Assume, for one real $C$, $\|D_y^jW(s,y)\|\le C(1+|y|)^{-j-1}$ for the natural-number orders $j=0,1,2$ and $\|D_yq(s,y)\|\le C(1+|y|)^{-3}$, uniformly in $s,y$. The derivative norms here are operator norms; the paper’s pointwise gradient norm is the sum-of-squares norm of its coordinate derivatives.

For any real phase $s_0$ and every $t<1$, the formal statement asserts $\partial_tu=\Delta u-(u\cdot
abla)u-
abla p$ pointwise on $\mathbb R^3$, where $u=(1-t)^{-1/2}W(s_0-\log(1-t),x/\sqrt{1-t})$ and $p=(1-t)^{-1}q(s_0-\log(1-t),x/\sqrt{1-t})$. The Laplacian is the sum of the three second coordinate derivatives. The conclusion is a time-derivative identity at each fixed spatial point; incompressibility and spatial smoothness are supplied by the profile assumptions and spatial scaling. The condition $t<1$ makes every physical scaling denominator positive. This formal statement specifies an implication. Defining the implication does not prove it. The corresponding calculation uses the time and space chain rules.
Breakdown.PhysicalMomentum.summary: States that for a smooth profile with the decay bounds, any phase $s_0$ and $t<1$, $u=(1-t)^{-1/2}W(s_0-\log(1-t),x/\sqrt{1-t})$ and the matching $p$ satisfy $\partial_tu=\Delta u-(u\cdot\nabla)u-\nabla p$ pointwise. This names the assertion; its proof uses the chain rule.

Let $W:\mathbb R	imes\mathbb R^3	o\mathbb R^3$ and $q:\mathbb R	imes\mathbb R^3	o\mathbb R$ be smooth, solve $\partial_sW+	frac12W+	frac12(y\cdot
abla)W-\Delta W+(W\cdot
abla)W+
abla q=0$, and satisfy $\operatorname{div}W=0$. Assume, for one real $C$, $\|D_y^jW(s,y)\|\le C(1+|y|)^{-j-1}$ for the natural-number orders $j=0,1,2$ and $\|D_yq(s,y)\|\le C(1+|y|)^{-3}$, uniformly in $s,y$. The derivative norms here are operator norms; the paper’s pointwise gradient norm is the sum-of-squares norm of its coordinate derivatives.

For every phase $s_0$, every $t<1$ and every smooth compactly supported divergence-free test field $\psi$, the formal statement asserts $ rac d{dt}\int u(t,x)\cdot\psi(x)\,dx=-\int\sum_i\partial_i u\cdot\partial_i\psi\,dx-\int((u\cdot
abla)u)\cdot\psi\,dx$, where $u(t,x)=(1-t)^{-1/2}W(s_0-\log(1-t),x/\sqrt{1-t})$. The integrals are over $\mathbb R^3$ with Lebesgue measure. This is the pressure-free identity used before passing to a mild solution. The test field is time independent. The conclusion is a derivative identity, and does not by itself include the homogeneous $H^1$ continuity or time-integrability hypotheses needed for the subsequent mild-solution statement.
Breakdown.PhysicalWeak.summary: States that for a smooth profile with the decay bounds, $t<1$ and a time-independent test field $\psi$, $\frac d{dt}\int u\cdot\psi=-\int\sum_i\partial_iu\cdot\partial_i\psi-\int((u\cdot\nabla)u)\cdot\psi$. It omits the continuity and integrability hypotheses needed for the mild statement.

Breakdown.Piece.text: For a real normed vector space $\mathcal X$ and real $T$, the formal object is the space $C([0,T];\mathcal X)$ with the supremum norm. Its elements are functions defined on the closed interval itself, with continuity built into membership. When $\mathcal X$ is complete this is a Banach space. It has no factor $(1-t)^{1/4-\kappa}$ and is not the global space $C_\kappa([0,1);\mathcal X)$ of (4.5). In the formal proof, bounded sequences of such curves carry the weights through geometric rescaling. All applications discussed here impose $T>0$; the space is also defined for $T<0$, when the interval is empty and its continuous function space contains only the empty function.
Breakdown.Piece.summary: The space $C([0,T];\mathcal X)$ with the supremum norm, a Banach space when $\mathcal X$ is complete. It carries no weight $(1-t)^{1/4-\kappa}$ and is not the global space $C_\kappa([0,1);\mathcal X)$ of (4.5).

Breakdown.PieceOperatorStatement.text:
Let $\mathcal X$ be a real Banach space with a strongly continuous contraction semigroup $G(t)$ for $t\ge0$ and symmetric bounded bilinear operators $K(\tau)$, continuous for $\tau>0$, with $G(s)K(\tau)=K(s+\tau)$ for $s\ge0$, $\tau>0$, and $\|K(\tau)\|\le C_K\tau^{-3/4}$ for $0<\tau\le1$. In the paper $G(t)=e^{t\Delta}$.

For every $T>0$, the formal statement asserts the integral identity $\mathcal B_T(f,g)(t)=\int_0^tK(t-s)(f(s),g(s))\,ds$ for continuous curves on $[0,T]$, the free-evolution identity $\Gamma_Tx(t)=G(t)x$, and $\|\Gamma_T\|\le1$. If $T\le1$, it also gives $\|\mathcal B_T\|\le4C_KT^{1/4}$, with the ordinary supremum norm on $C([0,T];\mathcal X)$. The exponent $1/4$ is real and the interval length is positive. Because the statement identifies both operators with these integral formulas, the zero values assigned in degenerate cases play no role. It asserts no $C_\kappa$ norm on the full half-open interval $[0,1)$.

This formal statement specifies an implication. Defining the implication does not prove it.
Breakdown.PieceOperatorStatement.summary: For $T>0$, asserts the integral formula for $\mathcal B_T$, $\Gamma_Tx(t)=G(t)x$ and $\|\Gamma_T\|\le1$ on $C([0,T];\mathcal X)$, and $\|\mathcal B_T\|\le4C_KT^{1/4}$ if $T\le1$. It states the assertion only.

Breakdown.PiecePerturbationStatement.text:
Let $\mathcal X$ be a real Banach space with a strongly continuous contraction semigroup $G(t)$ for $t\ge0$ and symmetric bounded bilinear operators $K(\tau)$, continuous for $\tau>0$, with $G(s)K(\tau)=K(s+\tau)$ for $s\ge0$, $\tau>0$, and $\|K(\tau)\|\le C_K\tau^{-3/4}$ for $0<\tau\le1$. In the paper $G(t)=e^{t\Delta}$.

Write $\Gamma_Tx(t)=G(t)x$ and $\mathcal B_T(f,g)(t)=\int_0^tK(t-s)(f(s),g(s))\,ds$. Let $0<T\le1$, let $u^{\mathrm b},v\in C([0,T];\mathcal X)$, and let $x\in\mathcal X$. Assume $u^{\mathrm b}$ is a mild solution and $v=\Gamma_Tx+2\mathcal B_T(u^{\mathrm b},v)+\mathcal B_T(v,v)$.

The formal statement asserts $v(0)=x$ and that $u^{\mathrm b}+v$ is a mild solution on $[0,T]$. Integrability and continuity belong to the mild-solution conclusion. Compact-interval curves are extended constantly outside their endpoints for evaluation as real-time functions. The implication proved is from the perturbation identity to an exact mild solution. The paper states an equivalence on $[0,1)$; the formal statement gives the forward implication on each compact interval. It involves an exact background, with no residual term.

This formal statement specifies an implication. Defining the implication does not prove it.
Breakdown.PiecePerturbationStatement.summary: If $u^{\mathrm b}$ is a mild solution on $[0,T]$, $0<T\le1$, and $v=\Gamma_Tx+2\mathcal B_T(u^{\mathrm b},v)+\mathcal B_T(v,v)$, then $v(0)=x$ and $u^{\mathrm b}+v$ is a mild solution. The paper states an equivalence on $[0,1)$; this gives the forward implication on each compact interval.

Breakdown.PieceWeights.text: The data assign each raw integer mode to a class, give two spatial conversion weights D,Z per class, two finite families of curl and velocity pieces, and real retained fractions c,cμ. Each curl piece has a mode set, rotation rate, nonnegative-weight candidate and auxiliary functions; each velocity piece also has its positive-number candidate. This encodes the ingredients of (B.14)–(B.16). At this level the class set need not be finite and none of the weights is known to satisfy an inequality. Admissibility supplies those conditions. The formal c is a free parameter; the paper fixes c=3/50.
Breakdown.PieceWeights.summary: Data for the finite families of weights: a class for each raw mode, conversion weights D,Z per class, finite families of curl and velocity pieces, and fractions c,cμ, encoding the ingredients of (B.14)–(B.16). No conditions hold at this level; c is free, while the paper fixes c=3/50.

Breakdown.PieceWeights.IsAdmissible.text:
There are finitely many mode classes, 0<c,cμ<1, S>0, and w≥w*>0 is measurable and axisymmetric. A finite raw harmonic set H contains zero and is closed under negation, and W is exactly the sum of the real parts of its H modes. For each β∈H, the four supplied functions bound |Ŵβ|, |∇Ŵβ|, |curl Ŵβ| and |∇curl Ŵβ| at every time and point. Two additional functions bound full vorticity and its gradient operator norm at every time, angle and point. Each piece's transport bound dominates |W+½y−νₚe₃×y| at every time and rotated point. On each piece mode set Nₚ, Ωₚ=2πn/S+νₚk is bounded below by a positive constant, which excludes Nₚ∩(−Nₚ).

The curl and velocity weights λₚ,μₚ are nonnegative, globally Lipschitz and axisymmetric. The curl-weight sums satisfy ∑λₚ≤E* and ∑|∇λₚ|≤E′*. One constant bounds |y|λₚ; another bounds μₚ, |y|²μₚ and |y||∇μₚ| uniformly over pieces. For R≥0, (∑ₚ|sgnₚ(ι)|μₚ)²≤R∑ₚ|sgnₚ(ι)||Ωₚ(ι)|μₚ. All eight auxiliary curl functions and both auxiliary velocity functions are positive, measurable and axisymmetric; each velocity balancing number ηₚ is positive.

The conversion weights D,Z are even under mode negation, C² and axisymmetric; D≥0. For integer derivative orders j=0,1,2, |y|ʲ|DʲD| and (1+|y|)ʲ|DʲZ| are bounded uniformly over classes. The allocated curl-gradient share â obeys D≤1−â at every mode and point. These are conditions on the data, not conclusions established by merely supplying them. This gives the weight and pointwise-bound conditions behind (B.19). The derivative expressions of W are defined for every function and receive default values where differentiability fails; joint C² regularity, time periodicity, incompressibility and decay of W are separate hypotheses of the multiplier theorem. It allows arbitrary admissible spatial functions and arbitrary c∈(0,1), whereas the paper prescribes particular piecewise-polynomial representations and c=3/50. The reflection symmetries (B.17) and separation from forcing harmonics are additional conditions used later, not fields of this admissibility statement.
Breakdown.PieceWeights.IsAdmissible.summary: Admissibility of the piece data: finite classes, 0<c,cμ<1, exact harmonic reconstruction of W with valid amplitude and transport bounds, positive frequencies on each Nₚ, Lipschitz axisymmetric weights with sum bounds, and D≤1−â. These are the conditions behind (B.19), with c∈(0,1) in place of 3/50.

Breakdown.PieceWeights.IsMultiplierField.text: For a velocity v and supplied spatial derivatives G=∇v, H=∇²v, this condition says that M:ℝ×ℝ³→ℝ³ is measurable, has period 1, belongs to L²((0,1)×ℝ³), and has zero pairing with gradients of smooth periodic compactly supported scalar tests. For every smooth divergence-free vector test v′ of period 1 and uniformly compact spatial support, it requires ⟨M,v′⟩=⟨−tr H,v′⟩+∑_ξ∫Re[i∑_p sgn_p(ξ)λ_p curl hat v_ξ·overline{curl hat v′_ξ}+i∑_p sgn_p(ξ)μ_p hat v_ξ·overline{hat v′_ξ}]. All integrals run over [0,1]×ℝ³ and ξ=(j,j′) ranges over ℤ², with j indexing normalized time θ and j′ indexing azimuth φ. This is (B.14), with divergence freedom expressed by pressure orthogonality. The condition alone asserts neither existence nor a norm bound for M. The supplied derivatives acquire their mathematical meaning through the perturbation assumptions. The real series and ordinary integrals appearing in this definition are assigned zero when their respective summability or integrability condition fails. The defining pairing alone does not assert convergence of every displayed series; the analytic estimates are what justify their usual integral and series interpretation in the multiplier theorem.
Breakdown.PieceWeights.IsMultiplierField.summary: $M$ is measurable, 1-periodic, in $L^2((0,1)\times\mathbb R^3)$ and orthogonal to gradients of periodic tests, and its pairing with each smooth solenoidal periodic test $v'$ is $\langle-\operatorname{tr}H,v'\rangle$ plus the $\lambda$ curl and $\mu$ velocity mode terms, as in (B.14).

Breakdown.PieceWeights.backSum.text: Fix a finite reference harmonic set H, a set N of raw integer modes, amplitude functions aβ(y), and a mode ι. The value is ∑_{β∈H, ι−β∉N} aβ(y). It sums the supplied amplitudes whose subtraction sends ι outside N. Membership of ι itself is not required in this definition. This is a finite coupling sum in the explicit coefficients behind (B.16); the paper describes these joins but does not print their full formulas. It is defined without a sign assumption on aβ or a finiteness assumption on N; an empty H contributes zero.
Breakdown.PieceWeights.backSum.summary: The finite sum ∑_{β∈H, ι−β∉N} aβ(y) of the amplitudes whose subtraction sends ι outside N; ι∈N is not required. It is a coupling sum behind (B.16), whose full formulas the paper does not print.

Breakdown.PieceWeights.coefA.text: Fix a raw mode ι=(n,k) and a spatial point y. For a piece with mode set N define χ=1_(ι∈N or −ι∈N). For any reference amplitude family aβ and finite harmonic set H, define I(a)=∑_{β∈H,ι−β∉N}aβ if ι∈N, or ∑_{β∈H,−ι−β∉N}aβ if −ι∈N, and zero otherwise; define O(a)=1_(ι∉N)∑_{β∈H,ι+β∈N}aβ+1_(−ι∉N)∑_{β∈H,−ι+β∈N}aβ. All these amplitudes are evaluated at y. U,A,B,Q denote the supplied modal bounds for W, ∇W, curl W and ∇curl W; O*,Q* bound the full vorticity and its gradient. For each piece Ω=2πn/S+νk, u is the proposed relative-transport bound, and λ or μ is its weight. Curl pieces carry functions a₁,a₂,L,t₀,t₁,t₂,t₃,s; velocity pieces carry functions a₄,t₄ and a real number η. Admissibility makes the weights nonnegative and these auxiliary quantities positive. The scalar Aω equals ¼+∑_{curl p}χ[λ|Ω|−(λu+|∇λ|)²/(4a₁)−λ²sI(U)/(4a₂)−λ(|ν|+(1+t₀)O*/2+LQ*/2+t₁I(A)/2+t₂I(Q)/2+t₃I(B)/2)]−∑_{curl p}λO(A)/(2t₁). The final coefficient of |curl v̂|² in (B.16) is Aω−Z, where Z is the class conversion weight. The formal statement supplies the full expression. The paper specifies its role and baseline without printing these error terms, so their detailed equality cannot be checked from the paper alone. Every sum over pieces is finite. The formula is defined for arbitrary real data; admissibility supplies positive denominators. At a zero divisor the assigned quotient is zero, so the formula alone is not the analytic bound.
Breakdown.PieceWeights.coefA.summary: The curl coefficient Aω before conversion, given in full; the coefficient of |curl v̂|² in (B.16) is Aω−Z. The paper gives its role and baseline without printing these error terms, so the detailed equality cannot be checked from the paper alone. Zero divisors give zero.

Breakdown.PieceWeights.coefAA.text: Fix a raw mode ι=(n,k) and a spatial point y. For a piece with mode set N define χ=1_(ι∈N or −ι∈N). For any reference amplitude family aβ and finite harmonic set H, define I(a)=∑_{β∈H,ι−β∉N}aβ if ι∈N, or ∑_{β∈H,−ι−β∉N}aβ if −ι∈N, and zero otherwise; define O(a)=1_(ι∉N)∑_{β∈H,ι+β∈N}aβ+1_(−ι∉N)∑_{β∈H,−ι+β∈N}aβ. All these amplitudes are evaluated at y. U,A,B,Q denote the supplied modal bounds for W, ∇W, curl W and ∇curl W; O*,Q* bound the full vorticity and its gradient. For each piece Ω=2πn/S+νk, u is the proposed relative-transport bound, and λ or μ is its weight. Curl pieces carry functions a₁,a₂,L,t₀,t₁,t₂,t₃,s; velocity pieces carry functions a₄,t₄ and a real number η. Admissibility makes the weights nonnegative and these auxiliary quantities positive. The coefficient of |∇v̂|² is Z−|D²D|op−cw−∑_{curl p}λ[χO*/(2t₀)+O(B)/(2t₃)]−∑_{velocity p}[χ1_(μ+|∇μ|>0)a₄+μO(U)/(2t₄)]. Here D,Z are the conversion functions for ι's class, w is the energy weight and c is the retained fraction. This supplies the coefficient I₁,ι used in the formal version of (B.16). The paper omits its full error terms, so their detailed equality cannot be checked from the paper alone. At c=3/50 and with no pieces it reduces exactly to the baseline displayed there. The Hessian norm is an operator norm, not a Frobenius norm; positivity and smoothness requirements on these inputs are imposed separately.
Breakdown.PieceWeights.coefAA.summary: The coefficient I₁,ι of |∇v̂|² in the formal (B.16): Z−|D²D|op−cw minus the curl-piece and velocity-piece losses. The paper omits its full error terms; at c=3/50 with no pieces it reduces exactly to the printed baseline. The Hessian norm is an operator norm.

Breakdown.PieceWeights.coefB.text: Fix a raw mode ι=(n,k) and a spatial point y. For a piece with mode set N define χ=1_(ι∈N or −ι∈N). For any reference amplitude family aβ and finite harmonic set H, define I(a)=∑_{β∈H,ι−β∉N}aβ if ι∈N, or ∑_{β∈H,−ι−β∉N}aβ if −ι∈N, and zero otherwise; define O(a)=1_(ι∉N)∑_{β∈H,ι+β∈N}aβ+1_(−ι∉N)∑_{β∈H,−ι+β∈N}aβ. All these amplitudes are evaluated at y. U,A,B,Q denote the supplied modal bounds for W, ∇W, curl W and ∇curl W; O*,Q* bound the full vorticity and its gradient. For each piece Ω=2πn/S+νk, u is the proposed relative-transport bound, and λ or μ is its weight. Curl pieces carry functions a₁,a₂,L,t₀,t₁,t₂,t₃,s; velocity pieces carry functions a₄,t₄ and a real number η. Admissibility makes the weights nonnegative and these auxiliary quantities positive. Put AΣ=∑_{β∈H}Aβ. The coefficient of |v̂|² is −|D²Z|op−∑_{curl p}λ[χQ*/(2L)+O(Q)/(2t₂)]+∑_{velocity p}χ[(1−cμ)μ|Ω|−(μu+|∇μ|)²/(4a₄)−μ|ν|−t₄μI(U)/2−ημ²/2−AΣ(AΣ−I(A))/(2η)]−∑_{velocity p}AΣO(A)/(2η). Here Z is the class conversion weight and cμ the frequency-energy fraction. This supplies the coefficient I₀,ι used in the formal version of (B.16). The paper omits its full error terms, so their detailed equality cannot be checked from the paper alone. With no pieces it is −|D²Z|op as printed there. The displayed quotients use positive balancing data under admissibility; zero divisors otherwise receive the assigned zero value.
Breakdown.PieceWeights.coefB.summary: The coefficient I₀,ι of |v̂|² in the formal (B.16): −|D²Z|op minus curl-piece losses plus the velocity-piece gains and losses. The paper omits its full error terms, so they cannot be checked from it; with no pieces it is −|D²Z|op as printed.

Breakdown.PieceWeights.densityNeg.text: At (θ,y), this is ∑_ιmax(−I_ι,0)+max(−J,0), with I_ι the five-term mode density evaluated on v and its proposed derivatives G,H, and J the stretching expression formed from reference W and G. The result is a nonnegative extended real number and may be infinite. It follows exactly the separate positive/negative-part convention after (B.18), after c=3/50 and the Fourier-index translation. Taking a part after the whole sum would be a different operation because positive and negative mode contributions could cancel. Derivative identification, integrability and finiteness are separate hypotheses.
Breakdown.PieceWeights.densityNeg.summary: At (θ,y), ∑_ιmax(−I_ι,0)+max(−J,0) in [0,∞], with I_ι the five-term mode density and J the stretching expression. It follows the positive/negative-part convention after (B.18), with c=3/50 and the index translation; the parts are taken before summing.

Breakdown.PieceWeights.densityPos.text: At (θ,y), this is ∑_ιmax(I_ι,0)+max(J,0), with I_ι the five-term mode density evaluated on v and its proposed derivatives G,H, and J the stretching expression formed from reference W and G. The result is a nonnegative extended real number and may be infinite. It follows exactly the separate positive/negative-part convention after (B.18), after c=3/50 and the Fourier-index translation. Taking a part after the whole sum would be a different operation because positive and negative mode contributions could cancel. Derivative identification, integrability and finiteness are separate hypotheses.
Breakdown.PieceWeights.densityPos.summary: At (θ,y), ∑_ιmax(I_ι,0)+max(J,0) in [0,∞], with I_ι the five-term mode density and J the stretching expression. It follows the positive/negative-part convention after (B.18), with c=3/50 and the index translation; the parts are taken before summing.

Breakdown.PieceWeights.frameFreq.text: For real period S, rate ν and integer frequencies (j,j′), this defines Ω=2πj/S+νj′. With j=2ι₂−ι₁ and j′=κι₁ it is the frequency in (B.15). The value is a real scalar, independent of θ and y, and changes sign when the frequency pair is negated. The definition accepts S=0 and then takes the quotient 2πj/S to be zero. Admissible multiplier data require S>0, so this default does not enter the analytic estimate. Positive lower bounds on Ω over the selected mode sets are separate hypotheses.
Breakdown.PieceWeights.frameFreq.summary: $\Omega=2\pi j/S+\nu j'$, a real scalar that changes sign with $(j,j')$; with $j=2\iota_2-\iota_1$, $j'=\kappa\iota_1$ it is the frequency of (B.15). Division by $S=0$ is taken as zero, which does not enter since admissible data have $S>0$.

Breakdown.PieceWeights.fwdSum.text: Fix a finite reference harmonic set H, a set N of raw integer modes, amplitude functions aβ(y), and a mode ι. The value is ∑_{β∈H, ι+β∈N} aβ(y). It sums the supplied amplitudes of the reference harmonics whose addition sends ι into N. This is a finite coupling sum in the explicit coefficients behind (B.16); the paper describes these joins but does not print their full formulas. It is defined without a sign assumption on aβ or a finiteness assumption on N; an empty H contributes zero.
Breakdown.PieceWeights.fwdSum.summary: The finite sum ∑_{β∈H, ι+β∈N} aβ(y) of the amplitudes of the reference harmonics whose addition sends ι into N. It is a coupling sum behind (B.16), whose full formulas the paper does not print.

Breakdown.PieceWeights.harmonicSum.text: For the finite reference harmonic set H, this is ∑_{β∈H}Aβ(y), where Aβ is the supplied majorant for the Euclidean amplitude of ∇Ŵβ. It bounds the full gradient amplitude when the reconstruction and individual bounds of Appendix B.2 hold. The definition itself is simply a finite sum, without those inequalities; for an empty H it is zero.
Breakdown.PieceWeights.harmonicSum.summary: The finite sum ∑_{β∈H}Aβ(y) of the gradient majorants, which bounds the full gradient amplitude when the reconstruction and individual bounds of Appendix B.2 hold. It is zero for empty H.

Breakdown.PieceWeights.inPiece.text: For a raw mode ι and a set N of modes, the condition is ι∈N or −ι∈N. Thus it selects N∪(−N), the support of |sgnₚ| in the admissible case of Appendix B.2. It is a membership condition, not a numerical bound, and does not assert that N is finite or disjoint from its negative. The zero mode is excluded by a positive-frequency condition only when admissibility is assumed.
Breakdown.PieceWeights.inPiece.summary: The condition ι∈N or −ι∈N, selecting N∪(−N), the support of |sgnₚ| in the admissible case of Appendix B.2. It does not assert that N is finite or disjoint from its negative.

Breakdown.PieceWeights.inward.text: Fix a finite reference harmonic set H, a set N of raw integer modes, amplitude functions aβ(y), and a mode ι. If ι∈N, the value is ∑_{β∈H, ι−β∉N}aβ(y); otherwise if −ι∈N, it is ∑_{β∈H, −ι−β∉N}aβ(y); otherwise it is zero. The first branch has priority if the two sets overlap. This is a finite coupling sum in the explicit coefficients behind (B.16); the paper describes these joins but does not print their full formulas. It is defined without a sign assumption on aβ or a finiteness assumption on N; an empty H contributes zero.
Breakdown.PieceWeights.inward.summary: If ι∈N, ∑_{β∈H, ι−β∉N}aβ(y); otherwise if −ι∈N, ∑_{β∈H, −ι−β∉N}aβ(y); otherwise zero, with the first branch taking priority. It is a coupling sum behind (B.16), whose full formulas the paper does not print.

Breakdown.PieceWeights.modeDensity.text: For raw mode ι and point y, and arbitrary real x₂,x_c,x₁,x_ω,x₀, the formal expression is (D−c)x₂²+(1−â−D)x_c²+(Aω−Z)x_ω²+A₁x₁²+A₀x₀². D,Z are conversion weights; â is the sum of shares assigned to multiplier errors; Aω,A₁,A₀ are the explicit piece-coefficient functions of the weights and harmonic bounds. In its field application the arguments are |∇²v̂|, |∇curl v̂|, |∇v̂|, |curl v̂|, |v̂|, respectively. In this argument order the coefficients are I₂ for x₂², I′₂ for x_c², I₁ for x₁², I′₁ for x_ω², and I₀ for x₀². The paper writes the curl term before the full-gradient term in (B.16), while the five arguments list the full gradient before the curl. Their roles and displayed baseline match after setting c=3/50 and translating the raw Fourier indices; the complete piece contributions are not printed in the paper. The definition permits any real c and arbitrary real amplitudes and asserts no lower bound. Unlike the earlier class version there is no explicit mixed x₁x₀ term.
Breakdown.PieceWeights.modeDensity.summary: The five-term form (D−c)x₂²+(1−â−D)x_c²+(Aω−Z)x_ω²+A₁x₁²+A₀x₀², with arguments |∇²v̂|, |∇curl v̂|, |∇v̂|, |curl v̂|, |v̂|.
