Roles and baseline match (B.16) at c=3/50 after index translation; the full piece terms are not printed in the paper. There is no mixed x₁x₀ term.

Breakdown.PieceWeights.modeTerm.text: For a real velocity v and supplied derivative fields G,H, form their Fourier coefficients at ξ=(j,j′) by the averages in normalized time θ and axial rotation φ. Here j and j′ are the respective integer indices. The definition evaluates I_ξ=I_{2,ξ}|hat H_ξ|²+I′_{2,ξ}|∇curl hat v_ξ|²+I′_{1,ξ}|curl hat v_ξ|²+I_{1,ξ}|hat G_ξ|²+I_{0,ξ}|hat v_ξ|². The curls are formed by the alternating contractions of hat G and hat H; tensor squares are sums of squared component magnitudes. The coefficient functions are those calculated from the multiplier weights and reference-profile bounds: I₂=D−c, I′₂=1−D minus the allocated curl-gradient losses, I′₁=1/4−Z plus the λ frequency gains and their errors, I₁=Z−|∇²D|_{op}−cw minus errors, and I₀=−|∇²Z|_{op} plus the μ frequency gains and errors. Setting c=3/50 gives (B.16). The definition does not assume G,H are derivatives or assert sign or integrability of I_ξ. The paper omits the full error formulas, so only its printed terms and stated allocation of errors can be compared directly.
Breakdown.PieceWeights.modeTerm.summary: $I_\xi=I_{2,\xi}|\hat H_\xi|^2+I'_{2,\xi}|\nabla\operatorname{curl}\hat v_\xi|^2+I'_{1,\xi}|\operatorname{curl}\hat v_\xi|^2+I_{1,\xi}|\hat G_\xi|^2+I_{0,\xi}|\hat v_\xi|^2$, with coefficients from the weights; $c=3/50$ gives (B.16). The paper omits full error formulas.

Breakdown.PieceWeights.multiplierGap.text: Let F be the right-hand side, M a multiplier, bᵢ forcing fields and β their coefficients. The quantity is X=⟨F,M⟩𝓗−c‖v‖²w−cμ‖v‖²μ−∑ᵢβᵢ⟨bᵢ,M⟩𝓗, with all pairings over [0,1]×ℝ³, weighted derivative energy ‖v‖²w=∫(|Δv|²+w|∇v|²), and frequency energy ∑ₚ,ι∫|sgnₚ||Ωₚ|μₚ|v̂_ι|². It is the left side of (B.20) when c=3/50. In the formal expression the positive parts of the two displayed energy densities are integrated in [0,∞] and then converted to real numbers, with infinity converted to zero; the theorem proves or assumes the finiteness needed for the displayed analytic interpretation. No inequality is part of this definition.
Breakdown.PieceWeights.multiplierGap.summary: X=⟨F,M⟩𝓗−c‖v‖²w−cμ‖v‖²μ−∑ᵢβᵢ⟨bᵢ,M⟩𝓗, the left side of (B.20) when c=3/50. The two energies are converted to real numbers with infinity taken as zero; no inequality is part of the definition.

Breakdown.PieceWeights.multiplierInequal.text: For every parameter in the earlier nonempty box, assume a jointly C² periodic solenoidal profile with uniform j=0,1,2 decay, bounded energy weight, and measurable periodic square-integrable forcing fields. The finite-piece weights must be admissible with common c,cμ,E*,E′*,R and valid pointwise harmonic and transport bounds. Let t,K≥0. For every admissible weak perturbation and F solving its linearized equation modulo gradients, and every multiplier M satisfying its periodic testing identity, assume the negative density integral is finite and I⁺−I⁻≥c|β|²−∑βᵢ⟨bᵢ,M⟩−cK²‖F‖²B−t|ℓ(v)|². Here ℓᵢ(v)=∫₀¹∫∇v:Ξᵢ and ‖F‖B is the period L² norm inside the specified ball. Then a multiplier exists with ‖M‖≤a√(cE+cμn²) and c(E+|β|²)+cμn²≤⟨F,M⟩+cK²‖F‖²B+t|ℓ(v)|², for some n≥0, where E=∫₀¹∫(|Δv|²+w|∇v|²) and a²=(1+E*+E′*/√w*)²/c+R/cμ. This implements the cancellation in Lemma B.2, but the conclusion still uses the earlier ball seminorm and unit force weight. It assumes the lower bound corresponding to (B.21); it does not derive that bound from numerical cell data.
Breakdown.PieceWeights.multiplierInequal.summary: In the earlier box format, with a C² profile, admissible finite-piece weights and an assumed lower bound corresponding to (B.21) with finite I⁻, there are M and n≥0 with ‖M‖≤a√(cE+cμn²) and c(E+|β|²)+cμn²≤⟨F,M⟩+cK²‖F‖²B+t|ℓ(v)|²: the cancellation of Lemma B.2.

Breakdown.PieceWeights.outward.text: Fix a finite reference harmonic set H, a set N of raw integer modes, amplitude functions aβ(y), and a mode ι. The value is 1_(ι∉N)∑_{β∈H,ι+β∈N}aβ(y)+1_(−ι∉N)∑_{β∈H,−ι+β∈N}aβ(y). Both displayed contributions are added; they are not mutually exclusive branches. This is a finite coupling sum in the explicit coefficients behind (B.16); the paper describes these joins but does not print their full formulas. It is defined without a sign assumption on aβ or a finiteness assumption on N; an empty H contributes zero.
Breakdown.PieceWeights.outward.summary: 1_(ι∉N)∑_{β∈H,ι+β∈N}aβ(y)+1_(−ι∉N)∑_{β∈H,−ι+β∈N}aβ(y), with both contributions added. It is a coupling sum behind (B.16), whose full formulas the paper does not print.

Breakdown.PieceWeights.piece_multiplier_.text: Let W be jointly C², period one and solenoidal, with |DʲW(θ,y)|≤D/(1+|y|)ʲ⁺¹ for j=0,1,2. Let w be bounded above, and let the curl/velocity pieces and their finite harmonic bounds be admissible: positive period and lower weight, 0<c,cμ<1, positive-frequency mode sets, Lipschitz decaying nonnegative weights, valid pointwise transport and harmonic bounds, positive auxiliary functions, and uniform sums E*,E′* and ratio R as in (B.19). Let all forcing fields bᵢ be measurable, period one and square integrable. For any Γ-invariant solenoidal weak perturbation v with L⁶ slices and gradient, Laplacian and similarity transport part in 𝓗, any β and any period-one F∈𝓗 satisfying F≃𝓣ˢv+(W·∇)v+(v·∇)W+∑βᵢbᵢ, there exists a solenoidal periodic multiplier M∈𝓗 satisfying (B.14). The frequency energy N=‖v‖²μ is finite, and ‖M‖≤a√(cE+cμN) with E=‖v‖²w and a²=(1+E*+E′*/√w*)²/c+R/cμ. Put X=⟨F,M⟩−cE−cμN−∑βᵢ⟨bᵢ,M⟩. For the integrals I± of the separate positive and negative mode and stretching terms, the formal conclusion is I⁺+max(−X,0)≤max(X,0)+I⁻. If I⁻ is finite this yields I⁺−I⁻≤X and I⁺ finite. At c=3/50 the norm constant and, when I⁻ is finite, the signed-density inequality have the form of Proposition B.1. The hypotheses differ in both directions: the formal statement requires a jointly C² reference with the displayed Hessian decay, while it permits an arbitrary symmetry set Γ, all raw integer modes, and forcing fields without invariance or separation from the weighted modes. Appendix B.1 instead allows C¹ reference fields with weak second derivatives and prescribes its harmonic representation and symmetries. The later weak-Hessian theorem is the relevant statement for those C¹ fields.
Breakdown.PieceWeights.piece_multiplier_.summary: For C² periodic solenoidal W with Hessian decay and admissible pieces, a multiplier M satisfying (B.14) exists, N is finite, ‖M‖≤a√(cE+cμN), and I⁺−I⁻≤X when I⁻ is finite. At c=3/50 this has the form of Proposition B.1, but needs C² W while allowing arbitrary Γ and forcing.

Breakdown.PieceWeights.seminormSq.text: For v:ℝ×ℝ³→ℝ³, a real period S and finitely many μ indices p, this defines the possibly infinite nonnegative quantity ∑_p∑_{(j,j′)∈ℤ²}∫₀¹∫|sgn_p(j,j′)|·|2πj/S+ν_pj′|·μ_p(y)|hat v_{j,j′}(θ,y)|²,dy,dθ. The inner product underlying the complex vector square is the sum of squared absolute values of its three components. The integrand is replaced by its positive part in this definition; with μ_p≥0 this changes nothing. The time interval is [0,1], whose endpoints do not affect the integral. This is the paper's ‖v‖_μ² on the allowed symmetry lattice. Finiteness is a conclusion of the multiplier theorem and must be known before treating it as an ordinary real squared norm.
Breakdown.PieceWeights.seminormSq.summary: Defines the possibly infinite nonnegative quantity ∑_p∑_{(j,j′)∈ℤ²}∫₀¹∫|sgn_p(j,j′)|·|2πj/S+ν_pj′|·μ_p(y)|hat v_{j,j′}|²dy dθ, the paper's ‖v‖_μ². Finiteness comes from the multiplier theorem and must be known before treating it as a real squared norm.

Breakdown.PieceWeights.sgn.text: For a set N⊆ℤ² and frequency ξ, this defines sgn_N(ξ)=1 when ξ∈N, −1 when ξ∉N and −ξ∈N, and 0 otherwise. If N∩(−N)=∅, these cases are the three cases printed in B.2. The definition itself does not require disjointness and gives priority to membership in N if both memberships hold. In the admissible multiplier data Ω(ξ) is uniformly positive on N and Ω(−ξ)=−Ω(ξ), which excludes such an overlap. The inputs here are Fourier index pairs (j,j′) in normalized time and azimuth; paper labels are inserted through (j,j′)=(2ι₂−ι₁,κι₁).
Breakdown.PieceWeights.sgn.summary: Defines sgn_N(ξ)=1 if ξ∈N, −1 if ξ∉N and −ξ∈N, and 0 otherwise. When N∩(−N)=∅ these are the three cases of B.2; without disjointness, membership in N takes priority.

Breakdown.PieceWeights.shareHat.text: For raw mode ι and point y, sum over curl pieces p the quantity a₁,p·1_(ι∈±Nₚ)·1_(λₚ+|∇λₚ|>0)+a₂,p·1_(λₚ>0)·Oₚ(U;ι)/sₚ. Here a₁,p,a₂,p are the two shares, λₚ≥0 is the curl weight, sₚ is its positive coupling scale, and Oₚ(U;ι)=1_(ι∉Nₚ)∑_{β∈H,ι+β∈Nₚ}Uβ+1_(−ι∉Nₚ)∑_{β∈H,−ι+β∈Nₚ}Uβ, with Uβ the reference-velocity amplitude majorant. This is the energy removed from the coefficient 1−D of |∇curl v̂|² in (B.16). The paper does not display this full expression. Admissibility requires D≤1−this sum; the formula itself gives no positivity. Zero scale has assigned quotient zero outside the admissible hypotheses.
Breakdown.PieceWeights.shareHat.summary: The sum over curl pieces of a₁,p·1_(ι∈±Nₚ)·1_(λₚ+|∇λₚ|>0)+a₂,p·1_(λₚ>0)·Oₚ(U;ι)/sₚ: the energy removed from the coefficient 1−D of |∇curl v̂|² in (B.16). The paper does not display this expression; admissibility requires D≤1−this sum.

Breakdown.PieceWeights.wtGrad.text: For a real weight f(y), this is ‖Df(y)‖, equal to |∇f(y)| where f is differentiable. It is the gradient magnitude in (B.19) and in the multiplier coefficient losses. The admissible piece weights are globally Lipschitz, so derivatives exist almost everywhere; the formal derivative is assigned zero at nondifferentiable points. No differentiability, bound or axial symmetry is asserted by the definition alone.
Breakdown.PieceWeights.wtGrad.summary: ‖Df(y)‖ for a real weight f, equal to |∇f(y)| where f is differentiable and zero at nondifferentiable points: the gradient size in (B.19) and in the coefficient losses. No differentiability or bound is asserted.

Breakdown.PotentialShape.AxisCellsVanish.text: For a two-variable Hermite amplitude, this requires every coefficient whose polar basis function meets the first or last polar interval to be zero, for every radial coefficient index. Under a valid partition of $[-1,1]$ this makes the amplitude vanish in neighborhoods of $\eta=-1$ and $\eta=1$, the two directions of the cylindrical axis. It is an alternative to an explicit positive axis power for nonzero-angular auxiliary fields in (B.51). This condition is stronger than vanishing just at the endpoints.
Breakdown.PotentialShape.AxisCellsVanish.summary: Every coefficient of a two-variable Hermite amplitude whose polar basis function meets the first or last polar interval is zero. Under a valid partition of $[-1,1]$ the amplitude then vanishes near $\eta=-1$ and $\eta=1$, the axis directions; this is stronger than vanishing at the endpoints.

Breakdown.PotentialShape.CylModeData.text: This supplies a finite set of integer time-angle harmonic labels and, for each label and each of the three cylindrical components, a complex Hermite amplitude in the physical variables $(r,z)$. The amplitudes are later multiplied by $r$, by the harmonic factor (B.2) and by the corresponding cylindrical unit vector. This is the representation of the compactly supported fields $\Phi_i$ used to approximate the constraints after (B.10). The definition supplies no regularity, support or symmetry conditions; those are imposed on the amplitude partitions and coefficients.
Breakdown.PotentialShape.CylModeData.summary: A finite set of integer time-angle harmonic labels and, for each label and cylindrical component, a complex Hermite amplitude in $(r,z)$, later multiplied by $r$, the factor (B.2) and the unit vector. This represents the fields $\Phi_i$ after (B.10); no regularity, support or symmetry is imposed.

Breakdown.PotentialShape.EndVanishOrder.text: For a Hermite amplitude with $N$ radial intervals and an integer $z\ge0$, this requires all coefficients for radial derivative orders $p<z$ at the final node $N$ to vanish, for every polar index. Under a valid partition this is vanishing to order $z$ at $\sigma=1$, which adds to the decay power $(1-\sigma)^h$ of the auxiliary field. This is used to obtain (B.51). At order zero the condition is empty; the companion validity conditions require $z$ not to exceed the radial interpolation depth.
Breakdown.PotentialShape.EndVanishOrder.summary: All coefficients for radial derivative orders $p<z$ at the final node $N$ vanish, for every polar index. Under a valid partition this is vanishing to order $z$ at $\sigma=1$, adding to the decay power $(1-\sigma)^h$ used for (B.51); at order zero the condition is empty.

Breakdown.PotentialShape.IsCylModeData.text: This requires $0<R_{\mathrm{supp}}<R_{\mathrm{mesh}}$. For every selected harmonic and component, the radial Hermite partition is valid on $[0,R_{\mathrm{mesh}}]$ and the axial partition on $[-R_{\mathrm{mesh}},R_{\mathrm{mesh}}]$, both with positive interpolation depth. The support radius must be a radial breakpoint and both of its signs must be axial breakpoints. All coefficients on or beyond those boundaries must satisfy the nodal and interior vanishing conditions. These are explicit sufficient support and continuity conditions for the represented constraint potentials $\Phi_i$ after (B.10). No divergence-free condition or approximation bound for $\Xi_i-\nabla\Phi_i$ is imposed here.
Breakdown.PotentialShape.IsCylModeData.summary: Requires $0<R_{\mathrm{supp}}<R_{\mathrm{mesh}}$, valid radial and axial Hermite partitions with positive depth, the support radius and its signs as breakpoints, and vanishing coefficients on and beyond them: sufficient support conditions for $\Phi_i$ after (B.10). No error bound is imposed.

Breakdown.PotentialShape.IsJetMesh.text: For a one-dimensional Hermite partition and prescribed real endpoints $a,b$, this requires its breakpoints to be strictly increasing in their list order, its first breakpoint to be $a$ and its last to be $b$. Unlike the stronger partition condition used for smooth amplitudes, this condition imposes no positive interpolation depth. It is used for the transverse partition of a flux component in the auxiliary fields of (B.51). The paper does not specify this split between endpoint geometry and interpolation depth.
Breakdown.PotentialShape.IsJetMesh.summary: The breakpoints of a one-dimensional Hermite partition are strictly increasing, the first is $a$ and the last is $b$; no positive interpolation depth is required. It is used for the transverse partition of a flux component in (B.51); the paper does not specify this split.

Breakdown.PotentialShape.IsPinShapeEntry.text: The supplied cell mesh must be valid. Each cylindrical representation of $\Phi_i$ must have valid partitions and the stated compact support strictly inside their mesh radius. Each set of shape parameters for $\widetilde\Phi_i$ must be valid, its harmonic data must satisfy the compact-support representation conditions, and its compactified support endpoint must be a break of every relevant radial amplitude partition. These conditions provide the regularity and support of the auxiliary fields described after (B.10). They do not alone impose an error bound for $\Xi_i-\nabla\Phi_i$, an error bound for $\Phi_i-\widetilde\Phi_i$, or identification of the represented tensors with a separate certificate; those are checked elsewhere.
Breakdown.PotentialShape.IsPinShapeEntry.summary: A valid cell mesh, valid compactly supported cylindrical data for $\Phi_i$, and valid shape data for $\widetilde\Phi_i$ with matching support breaks, giving the regularity and support described after (B.10). Error bounds for $\Xi_i-\nabla\Phi_i$ and $\Phi_i-\widetilde\Phi_i$ are checked elsewhere.

Breakdown.PotentialShape.IsPotentialScal.text: For desired origin and decay orders $a,b\in\mathbb N$, this requires a Hermite amplitude with valid partitions of $[0,1]$ and $[-1,1]$ and interpolation depths at least two in both variables, giving first-order matching. There must be orders $z_0,z_1$ within the radial depth such that the amplitude vanishes to those orders at the radial endpoints and $h_0+z_0\ge a$, $h+z_1\ge b$. Thus endpoint coefficient vanishing may supply part of the required orders instead of explicit powers. These are sufficient representation conditions for the auxiliary decay and regularity in (B.51). Axis conditions are separate.
Breakdown.PotentialShape.IsPotentialScal.summary: A Hermite amplitude with valid partitions of $[0,1]$ and $[-1,1]$, depths at least two, and endpoint vanishing orders $z_0,z_1$ with $h_0+z_0\ge a$ and $h+z_1\ge b$. These are sufficient conditions for the decay and regularity in (B.51); axis conditions are separate.

Breakdown.PotentialShape.IsPotentialSeri.text: Every harmonic component of $\mathsf G$ must have first-order matching in both compactified variables, total origin order at least two and total decay order at least two. The corresponding requirements for $\mathsf U$ are origin order at least two and decay order at least one. For each nonzero-angular harmonic, each component of both vectors either has positive axis power or vanishes on the two polar endpoint cells. Each radial-flux amplitude has a valid positive-depth radial partition and an ordered polar partition with endpoints $-1,1$; each polar-flux amplitude has the converse choice of stronger partition condition. Both kinds of flux have total decay order at least two. Pressure amplitudes have continuous matching, decay order at least two, and, for nonzero-angular harmonics, positive axis power and either a positive origin power or one order of radial vanishing. For zero-angular pressure harmonics, either the origin power is positive or the radial starting value is constant in the polar variable. All endpoint vanishing orders are bounded by the available interpolation depth. These are explicit sufficient representation conditions for (B.51), whose detailed formulas the paper does not give. They do not themselves bound the numerical norms used in (B.53).
Breakdown.PotentialShape.IsPotentialSeri.summary: Matching, origin, decay and axis conditions on every harmonic of $\mathsf G$, $\mathsf U$, the flux and the pressure amplitudes, with vanishing orders within the interpolation depth. They are sufficient conditions for (B.51), whose formulas the paper omits, and bound no norm in (B.53).

Breakdown.PotentialShape.PinShapeEntry.text: This supplies a cell mesh and symmetry order; a cell-polynomial matrix representation for each constraint $\Xi_i$; a cylindrical Hermite representation for each compactly supported vector field $\Phi_i$; common mesh and support radii for those vector representations; and, for each $i$, shape parameters, harmonic amplitude data and a compactified support endpoint for a solenoidal field $\widetilde\Phi_i$. These are the objects used after (B.10) and in Lemma B.12. The definition records representations only. Their validity and the bounds for $\Xi_i-\nabla\Phi_i$ and $\Phi_i-\widetilde\Phi_i$ are separate requirements.
Breakdown.PotentialShape.PinShapeEntry.summary: A cell mesh and symmetry order, cell polynomials for each $\Xi_i$, cylindrical Hermite data for each $\Phi_i$, and shape and harmonic data for a solenoidal $\widetilde\Phi_i$, as used after (B.10) and in Lemma B.12. Validity and error bounds are separate requirements.

Breakdown.PotentialShape.PinShapeEntry.p.text: This evaluates the cylindrical Hermite data as the real fields $\Phi_i$ and the compactified solenoidal harmonic data as the real fields $\widetilde\Phi_i$, returning the two families together. They are the fields compared in the approximation terms for the constraint potentials of (B.52) and (B.53). The conversion itself proves no regularity, support or error bound. In particular the fact that $\widetilde\Phi_i$ is solenoidal depends on its valid harmonic representation, and the cylindrical representation of $\Phi_i$ does not assert that property.
Breakdown.PotentialShape.PinShapeEntry.p.summary: Evaluates the represented fields $\Phi_i$ and $\widetilde\Phi_i$ compared in the constraint approximations of (B.52) and (B.53). No support, regularity or error bound is asserted; solenoidality of $\widetilde\Phi_i$ requires valid harmonic data.

Breakdown.PotentialShape.PinShapeEntry.p.text: For a chosen index $i$, this evaluates its matrix polynomials on the supplied mesh with the given harmonic symmetry order, producing a real time-dependent linear map on $\mathbb R^3$. It is the tensor field $\Xi_i$ paired with $\nabla v$ in (B.10). The cellwise field is defined by the specified polynomial and reflection conventions and vanishes off the represented cells. Its relation to $\nabla\Phi_i$ is not part of this definition; the norm bound for their difference is an independent ingredient of Lemma B.12.
Breakdown.PotentialShape.PinShapeEntry.p.summary: Evaluates the matrix polynomials for index $i$ on the mesh with the given symmetry order, giving the tensor field $\Xi_i$ paired with $\nabla v$ in (B.10), zero off the represented cells. Its relation to $\nabla\Phi_i$ is a separate ingredient of Lemma B.12.

Breakdown.PotentialShape.PotComponent.text: The representation distinguishes the combinations $G_x+iG_y$, $G_x-iG_y$ and $G_z$ of a vector field. They are stored separately because their angular factors have frequencies shifted by $+1$, $-1$ and $0$ relative to the cylindrical harmonic. This is a component convention for the auxiliary vector and matrix fields $\mathsf G,\mathsf U,\mathsf F$ in (B.51). The paper says these fields have a harmonic and piecewise-polynomial form without writing this representation. The three labels alone impose no reality or conjugacy condition.
Breakdown.PotentialShape.PotComponent.summary: The three stored combinations $G_x+iG_y$, $G_x-iG_y$ and $G_z$, whose angular frequencies are shifted by $+1$, $-1$ and $0$: a component convention for $\mathsf G,\mathsf U,\mathsf F$ in (B.51), which the paper does not write out. No reality or conjugacy condition is imposed.

Breakdown.PotentialShape.PotComponent.ca.text: The two transverse combinations $G_x+iG_y$ and $G_x-iG_y$ are marked to carry an additional factor $\sqrt{1-\eta^2}$, while the axial component is not, with $\eta=y_3/|y|$ away from the origin. This factor vanishes on the cylindrical axis away from the origin. At the origin $\eta$ is defined as zero and the factor is one; regularity there depends on the separate radial vanishing conditions. It is part of the auxiliary-field construction underlying (B.51), which the paper does not write explicitly. The marker itself provides no regularity theorem or condition on the remaining scalar amplitude.
Breakdown.PotentialShape.PotComponent.ca.summary: The transverse combinations Gₓ±iGᵧ carry √(1−η²) and the axial component does not, in the construction behind (B.51). With η=y₃/|y| set to zero at the origin, the factor vanishes on the punctured axis and equals one at the origin.

Breakdown.PotentialShape.PotComponent.sh.text: This assigns the integers $+1$, $-1$ and $0$ to the components $G_x+iG_y$, $G_x-iG_y$ and $G_z$, respectively. These shifts account for conversion between cylindrical and Cartesian vector components. Thus a cylindrical harmonic with angular frequency $\varkappa\iota_1$ has those shifted frequencies in the three stored complex components. This is a representation detail of the auxiliary fields of (B.51), not an additional physical harmonic or a change in their temporal frequency.
Breakdown.PotentialShape.PotComponent.sh.summary: Assigns the shifts $+1$, $-1$ and $0$ to $G_x+iG_y$, $G_x-iG_y$ and $G_z$, so a harmonic with angular frequency $\varkappa\iota_1$ has those shifted frequencies in the three stored components. This is a representation detail of (B.51), not a new harmonic or temporal frequency.

Breakdown.PotentialShape.PotKeyData.text: For one harmonic this supplies three scalar amplitudes for each of two vector potentials, three radial-flux amplitudes, three polar-flux amplitudes, and one scalar pressure amplitude. The component triples represent the two transverse complex combinations and the axial component. The flux amplitudes are combined with the radial and scaled polar vectors of (B.4) to form a matrix. These data represent $\mathsf G,\mathsf U,\mathsf F,q$ in (B.51) and (B.52), whose formulas the paper leaves unspecified. No matching, decay, norm bound or differential equation is asserted here.
Breakdown.PotentialShape.PotKeyData.summary: For one harmonic: three amplitudes for each of two vector potentials, three radial-flux and three polar-flux amplitudes, and a pressure amplitude, representing $\mathsf G,\mathsf U,\mathsf F,q$ in (B.51) and (B.52), which the paper leaves unspecified. No decay, bound or equation is asserted.

Breakdown.PotentialShape.PotScalar.text: This supplies a complex piecewise-polynomial amplitude in compactified radius $\sigma$ and polar ratio $\eta$, represented by endpoint derivatives and interior coefficients, and three nonnegative integer exponents. The exponents multiply the amplitude by $\sigma^{h_0}(1-\sigma)^h(1-\eta^2)^{h'}$. They control the origin, spatial infinity and the axis, respectively. This is the representation used for the potentials and pressure in (B.51). All exponents are natural numbers; no negative or fractional powers occur in this part of the amplitude. Smooth matching, additional vanishing and required lower bounds on the exponents are separate conditions.
Breakdown.PotentialShape.PotScalar.summary: A complex piecewise-polynomial amplitude in $\sigma$ and $\eta$ with three natural-number exponents, multiplied by $\sigma^{h_0}(1-\sigma)^h(1-\eta^2)^{h'}$ to control the origin, infinity and the axis; used for the potentials and pressure in (B.51). Matching and exponent lower bounds are separate.

Breakdown.PotentialShape.PotentialSeries.text: This supplies a finite set of labels, each consisting of a time-angle harmonic $\iota\in\mathbb Z^2$ and an integer radial phase index $l$, together with the vector, flux and pressure amplitude data for each label. The amplitudes are formally supplied for all labels, but only the finite selected set enters evaluation. This is the finite harmonic representation of the auxiliary fields in (B.51). The set is not required here to be closed under conjugation or reflection; the evaluated fields are real parts of the sums, and regularity conditions are imposed separately.
Breakdown.PotentialShape.PotentialSeries.summary: A finite set of labels, each a harmonic $\iota\in\mathbb Z^2$ with a radial phase index $l$, with vector, flux and pressure amplitudes: the finite representation of the auxiliary fields in (B.51). No closure under conjugation or reflection is required; the fields are real parts of the sums.

Breakdown.PotentialShape.PotentialSeries.text: This converts one finite harmonic series and its shape parameters into four real fields: the first vector potential $\mathsf G$, the second vector potential $\mathsf U$, the matrix potential $\mathsf F$ and the scalar pressure $q$. They are precisely the types of auxiliary fields used in (B.51) and (B.52) to rearrange the adjoint error into terms paired with $\Delta v$, $\nabla v$ and $v$. This conversion asserts no bounds or derivative identities; the series-validity and norm conditions establish the properties needed in Lemma B.12.
Breakdown.PotentialShape.PotentialSeries.summary: Converts a finite harmonic series and its shape parameters into the real fields $\mathsf G$, $\mathsf U$, $\mathsf F$ and $q$ used in (B.51) and (B.52) to rearrange the adjoint error into terms paired with $\Delta v$, $\nabla v$ and $v$. No bound or derivative identity is asserted.

Breakdown.PotentialShape.StartRowConstan.text: For the radial value at the first node, this requires all active polar coefficients except zeroth-derivative nodal values to vanish, and all those nodal values to be equal. Under the Hermite representation the amplitude at $\sigma=0$ is therefore constant in $\eta$. This is the origin condition for a zero-angular pressure term that has no explicit positive power of $\sigma$. It ensures that the limiting scalar value is independent of the direction of approach. The paper's analogous pressure convention is stated in Appendix B.1; this auxiliary-field representation uses it in (B.51).
Breakdown.PotentialShape.StartRowConstan.summary: At the first radial node, all active polar coefficients other than zeroth-derivative nodal values vanish and those values are equal, so the amplitude at $\sigma=0$ is constant in $\eta$. This is the origin condition for a zero-angular pressure term without a power of $\sigma$ in (B.51).

Breakdown.PotentialShape.StartVanishOrde.text: For a two-variable Hermite amplitude and a nonnegative integer $z$, this requires every coefficient associated with radial derivative order $p<z$ at the first radial node to be zero, for every polar coefficient index. It prescribes vanishing of the amplitude to order $z$ at $\sigma=0$, when the interpolation depth supports those derivatives. At $z=0$ there are no equations. These conditions augment the explicit power $\sigma^{h_0}$ in the auxiliary representations for (B.51); the regularity predicate separately ensures $z$ is no greater than the radial interpolation depth.
Breakdown.PotentialShape.StartVanishOrde.summary: Every coefficient for radial derivative order $p<z$ at the first radial node vanishes, for every polar index, prescribing vanishing to order $z$ at $\sigma=0$ when the depth allows. At $z=0$ there are no equations; this augments the power $\sigma^{h_0}$ in (B.51).

Breakdown.PotentialShape.VanishesBeyond.text: For a Hermite amplitude and radius $R$, every nodal coefficient whose radial or axial breakpoint has absolute value at least $R$ must vanish. An interior coefficient must vanish when both endpoints of its interval have absolute value at least $R$. These requirements are imposed in both variables, including every coefficient index in the other variable. A missing breakpoint is read as the supplied value $R$, so out-of-range indices satisfy the vanishing test when $R\ge0$. With a valid mesh containing $R$ and $\pm R$ as appropriate, the resulting amplitude vanishes outside $0\le r\le R$, $|z|\le R$. This is the coefficient-level support condition for the fields $\Phi_i$ after (B.10).
Breakdown.PotentialShape.VanishesBeyond.summary: Coefficients at breakpoints of absolute value at least $R$, and interior ones on intervals with both endpoints so, vanish in both variables. With a valid mesh containing $R$ and $\pm R$, the amplitude vanishes outside $0\le r\le R$, $|z|\le R$: the support condition for $\Phi_i$ after (B.10).

Breakdown.PotentialShape.componentValue.text: For one harmonic and one of the components $G_x+iG_y$, $G_x-iG_y$, $G_z$, this evaluates the scalar amplitude with angular frequency $\varkappa\iota_1+1$, $\varkappa\iota_1-1$ or $\varkappa\iota_1$, respectively. The transverse components carry the extra polar sine factor and the axial component does not. The time frequency remains $2\iota_2-\iota_1$, and the same radial phase index is retained. This is the component representation of the auxiliary fields in (B.51). The amplitude and shape parameters are supplied data; their endpoint and axis conditions are checked separately.
Breakdown.PotentialShape.componentValue.summary: Evaluates the component $G_x+iG_y$, $G_x-iG_y$ or $G_z$ of a harmonic with angular frequency $\varkappa\iota_1+1$, $\varkappa\iota_1-1$ or $\varkappa\iota_1$, the transverse ones with the polar sine factor; the time frequency $2\iota_2-\iota_1$ is unchanged. This represents the fields of (B.51).

Breakdown.PotentialShape.coordsOfCompone.text: Given three complex numbers $g_+,g_-,g_z$, this returns $((g_++g_-)/2,(g_+-g_-)/(2i),g_z)$. It inverts the change of variables $g_+=g_x+ig_y$, $g_-=g_x-ig_y$ before a real part is taken. The denominators are nonzero, so there is no division convention affecting this formula. This reconstructs the Cartesian components of the auxiliary fields used in (B.51). Arbitrary complex inputs need not themselves represent a real vector; reality is obtained later by taking real parts of the finite harmonic sum.
Breakdown.PotentialShape.coordsOfCompone.summary: Returns $((g_++g_-)/2,(g_+-g_-)/(2i),g_z)$ from $g_+,g_-,g_z$, inverting $g_+=g_x+ig_y$, $g_-=g_x-ig_y$ before a real part is taken. This reconstructs the Cartesian components of the fields of (B.51); reality comes later from real parts of the harmonic sum.

Breakdown.PotentialShape.cylField.text: Given a natural azimuthal order κ and a finite set of integer labels ι, this defines Φ(θ,y)=∑_{ι,a}Re[E_ι(θ,φ(y))r P_{ι,a}(r,z)]e_a(φ(y)), with a∈{r,φ,z}. Here r=√(y₁²+y₂²), z=y₃, and each P is a polynomial spline formed from endpoint derivative data and interior coefficients. The coordinate domain is the physical meridian plane, without radial compactification. The factor r and the assigned value φ=0 on the axis make the formula defined everywhere. Mesh, joins and vanishing coefficient conditions are separate; this definition alone asserts no compact support, L² bound or divergence freedom of Φ.
Breakdown.PotentialShape.cylField.summary: Defines Φ(θ,y)=∑_{ι,a}Re[E_ι(θ,φ(y))r P_{ι,a}(r,z)]e_a(φ(y)) with spline polynomials P on the uncompactified meridian plane, defined everywhere through the factor r and φ=0 on the axis. It asserts no compact support, L² bound or divergence freedom.

Breakdown.PotentialShape.dofMeetsEndCell.text: For a partition with $N$ intervals, a nodal coefficient is selected if its node index is at most one or at least $N-1$; an interior coefficient is selected if its interval index is zero or at least $N-1$. Thus the selected coefficients are those that can affect the first or last interval of the polar partition. This is used to make an amplitude vanish near the axis in (B.51). The subtraction is in nonnegative integers: if $N\le1$, $N-1$ is zero and every index is selected. The condition itself does not assert a valid partition.
Breakdown.PotentialShape.dofMeetsEndCell.summary: For a partition with $N$ intervals, selects nodal coefficients with index at most one or at least $N-1$ and interior coefficients with index zero or at least $N-1$: those affecting the first or last polar interval, used for vanishing near the axis in (B.51). If $N\le1$, every index is selected.

Breakdown.PotentialShape.fluxEntry.text: For a spatial input index $i$, this evaluates the radial-and-polar flux vector of each of the three stored output components, converts those complex components to Cartesian coordinates, sums over the finite harmonics and takes the real part of output component $a$. The result is the real matrix entry $F_{ai}$, with output index first and spatial input direction second. It is the matrix potential used in the divergence term of (B.52). This convention fixes the transpose appearing when the paper writes $\operatorname{div}\mathsf F^{\mathsf T}$. Regularity of the entries is a separate requirement.
Breakdown.PotentialShape.fluxEntry.summary: The real entry $F_{ai}$ of the matrix potential, output index first and input direction second, from the flux vectors of the stored components summed over harmonics. It enters the divergence term of (B.52) and fixes the transpose in the paper's $\operatorname{div}\mathsf F^{\mathsf T}$.

Breakdown.PotentialShape.fluxMap.text: At each time and spatial point, this turns the real $3\times3$ matrix of reconstructed flux entries into the linear map $u\mapsto\mathsf F u$ on Euclidean $\mathbb R^3$. Finite-dimensional linear maps are continuous, so continuity here concerns dependence on the vector argument only. It does not assert continuity of the matrix field in time or space. This is the matrix potential in (B.51) and (B.52), with its spatial regularity supplied by the spline and endpoint conditions.
Breakdown.PotentialShape.fluxMap.summary: At each time and point, the linear map $u\mapsto\mathsf F u$ on $\mathbb R^3$ given by the reconstructed flux matrix: the matrix potential in (B.51) and (B.52). Continuity here concerns only the vector argument, not time or space.

Breakdown.PotentialShape.fluxVector.text: For one harmonic and one stored complex component, this defines a complex three-vector $A\,y/|y|+B\,\mathbf p$, where $A$ is its radial-flux scalar, $B$ its polar-flux scalar, and $\mathbf p=(\eta y_1/|y|,\eta y_2/|y|,-(1-\eta^2))$. This is the input-direction part of the matrix potential used in (B.51). Here $\eta=y_3/|y|$. Quotients at the origin are assigned zero, so $y/|y|=(0,0,0)$ and $\mathbf p=(0,0,-1)$ there; the full field's regularity is supplied by its amplitude conditions. There is no separate azimuthal-direction term in this representation.
Breakdown.PotentialShape.fluxVector.summary: The complex vector $A\,y/|y|+B\,\mathbf p$ with $\mathbf p=(\eta y_1/|y|,\eta y_2/|y|,-(1-\eta^2))$, the input-direction part of the matrix potential in (B.51). Quotients at the origin are zero, so there $y/|y|=0$ and $\mathbf p=(0,0,-1)$. There is no azimuthal term.

Breakdown.PotentialShape.polarSine.text: This defines $\sqrt{1-(y_3/|y|)^2}$. For $y\ne0$ it equals $r/|y|$, with $r=\sqrt{y_1^2+y_2^2}$, and is the sine factor used in the transverse components of the auxiliary fields of (B.51). At the origin the quotient is defined to be zero, so this expression has value one there; it is not itself a continuous polar-coordinate function at the origin. The vanishing factors and matching conditions of the full represented fields provide their required regularity. The real square root is assigned zero on negative inputs, although the displayed argument is nonnegative for actual nonzero Euclidean points.
Breakdown.PotentialShape.polarSine.summary: Defines $\sqrt{1-(y_3/|y|)^2}$, equal to $r/|y|$ for $y\ne0$, the sine factor in the transverse components of (B.51). Since the quotient is taken as zero at the origin, the value there is one, and the expression is not continuous at the origin.

Breakdown.PotentialShape.pressureValue.text: This takes the real part of the finite sum of the scalar pressure amplitudes with the unshifted angular frequencies $\varkappa\iota_1$, time frequencies $2\iota_2-\iota_1$ and their integer radial phase indices. No extra polar sine factor is inserted. It is the auxiliary scalar $q_j$ whose gradient appears in (B.52), rather than the solution pressure itself. Its regularity and decay require the pressure-amplitude conditions. The definition imposes no normalization such as zero spatial mean, since only its gradient enters the adjoint remainder.
Breakdown.PotentialShape.pressureValue.summary: The real part of the finite sum of pressure amplitudes with unshifted angular frequencies $\varkappa\iota_1$, time frequencies $2\iota_2-\iota_1$ and radial phase indices: the auxiliary scalar $q_j$ whose gradient appears in (B.52), not the solution pressure. No normalization is imposed.

Breakdown.PotentialShape.scalarValue.text: This defines the complex scalar $e^{i[2\pi(2\iota_2-\iota_1)\theta+M\phi+lf(|y|^2)]}\sigma^{h_0}(1-\sigma)^h(1-\eta^2)^{h'}s(\eta)A(\sigma,\eta)$, where $\sigma=|y|/(|y|+\mathsf L)$, $\eta=y_3/|y|$, $\phi=\arg(y_1+iy_2)$, $s$ is either $1$ or $\sqrt{1-\eta^2}$, and $A$ is the supplied complex piecewise polynomial. The exponents are nonnegative integers; $M,l$ are integers. It is the auxiliary scalar representation used for (B.51), analogous to (B.5) and (B.6). At the origin $\sigma=\eta=\phi=0$ and the optional sine factor is one. Every zero denominator is assigned quotient zero, including at points with $|y|+\mathsf L=0$; zeroth powers are one even at a zero base. These conventions define the expression everywhere, and polynomial evaluation extends the first or last piece outside its listed partition. Positive length, matching and vanishing conditions are needed for the intended smoothness and decay; they are not part of this definition.
Breakdown.PotentialShape.scalarValue.summary: $e^{i[2\pi(2\iota_2-\iota_1)\theta+M\phi+lf(|y|^2)]}\sigma^{h_0}(1-\sigma)^h(1-\eta^2)^{h'}s(\eta)A(\sigma,\eta)$, $\sigma=|y|/(|y|+\mathsf L)$, $\eta=y_3/|y|$, for (B.51) as in (B.5), (B.6). Zero denominators give zero, so $\sigma=\eta=\phi=0$ at the origin; smoothness needs separate conditions.

Breakdown.PotentialShape.vectorPotential.text: Supply a rule that assigns a triple of scalar amplitudes to each harmonic’s data. This evaluates its three shifted complex components, reconstructs Cartesian coordinates, sums over the finite harmonic set and takes the real part componentwise. The result is a real vector field on all $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3$. The two choices made in the auxiliary-field construction give $\mathsf G$ and $\mathsf U$ in (B.51). No separate divergence-free condition is asserted or required by this definition. The regularity and decay used in the integration by parts of Lemma B.12 follow only under the amplitude and shape hypotheses.
Breakdown.PotentialShape.vectorPotential.summary: For a supplied rule giving each harmonic a triple of scalar amplitudes, evaluates the components, reconstructs Cartesian coordinates, sums over harmonics and takes real parts; the two choices in the auxiliary construction give $\mathsf G$, $\mathsf U$ in (B.51). No divergence-free condition.

Breakdown.ProfilePieceStatement.text:
Let $X$ be a real Hilbert space with the heat and bilinear operators of §3.4: $G(t)$ is a strongly continuous contraction semigroup, $K(\tau)$ is symmetric, continuous for $\tau>0$, obeys $G(s)K(\tau)=K(s+\tau)$ and $\|K(\tau)\|\le C_K\tau^{-3/4}$ for $0<\tau\le1$. Suppose the dilations satisfy $D_1=I$, $D_\mu D_\nu=D_{\mu\nu}$, $\|D_\mu x\|=\mu^{1/4}\|x\|$, $D_\mu G(\mu t)=G(t)D_\mu$, and $\mu D_\mu K(\mu\tau)(x,y)=K(\tau)(D_\mu x,D_\mu y)$ for positive scales, with continuous dependence on scale. Assume $K(\tau)(f,\cdot)$ is compact for a dense set of $f$ and every $\tau>0$.

Let $S>0$, let $\rho$ be a surjective linear isometry commuting with $G$, $K$ and $D$, and let $w:\mathbb R\to X$ be continuous, nonzero at some time, with $w(s+S)=\rho w(s)$ and the similarity-time mild equation. Here that equation uses $\mathcal S(a)=D_{e^{-a}}G(1-e^{-a})$ and $\mathcal K(a)=D_{e^{-a}}K(1-e^{-a})$ and reads $w(s)=\mathcal S(s-s_0)w(s_0)+\int_{s_0}^{s}\mathcal K(s-r)(w(r),w(r))\,dr$ for $s_0\le s$.

Fix a positive natural number $k$, put $\mu=e^{-S/k}$ and $L=1-\mu$, and define $u_n(\sigma)=D_{(1-\sigma)^{-1}}w(nS/k-\log(1-\sigma))$ for $0\le\sigma\le L$. For every natural $n$, the formal statement asserts that $u_n$ is a continuous mild solution, $D_\mu u_n(L)=u_{n+1}(0)$, $u_{n+k}(\sigma)=\rho u_n(\sigma)$, and $\|u_n\|_{C([0,L];X)}\le e^{S/(4k)}M$ whenever $\|w(s)\|\le M$ for all real $s$. Thus the period is split into $k$ pieces. It gives no positive lower bound on $\|u^*(t)\|$. Curves on the compact interval are extended constantly beyond either endpoint when an everywhere-defined function is needed; the mildness assertion concerns only the interval. Positivity of $k$ prevents division by zero in $S/k$.

This formal statement specifies an implication. Defining the implication does not prove it.
Breakdown.ProfilePieceStatement.summary: For a recurrent similarity-time mild solution $w$ and positive natural $k$, the pieces $u_n$ on $[0,L]$, $L=1-e^{-S/k}$, are continuous mild solutions with $D_\mu u_n(L)=u_{n+1}(0)$, $u_{n+k}=\rho u_n$ and $\|u_n\|\le e^{S/(4k)}M$. No positive lower bound on $\|u^*(t)\|$ is given.

Breakdown.RestrictStatement.text: Let $\mathcal X$ be a real Banach space. Write $G(t)$ for a strongly continuous contraction semigroup on $t\ge0$, and let $K(\tau)$ be bounded symmetric real bilinear maps on $\mathcal X$, continuous in $\tau>0$ on each pair of arguments. Assume $G(t)K(\tau)=K(t+\tau)$ for $t\ge0,\tau>0$, and $\|K(\tau)(u,v)\|\le C_K\tau^{-3/4}\|u\|\|v\|$ for $0<\tau\le1$. The assertion is the following implication. Let $a\le m\le t$, and let $u:\mathbb R\to\mathcal X$ be continuous on $[a,t]$. Suppose the quadratic Duhamel integrals are Bochner integrable and the identities $u(r)=G(r-a)u(a)+\int_a^rK(r-s)(u(s),u(s))\,ds$ hold at $r=m$ and $r=t$. Then the integral from $m$ to $t$ is Bochner integrable and $u(t)=G(t-m)u(m)+\int_m^tK(t-s)(u(s),u(s))\,ds$. The endpoints may coincide. Only the two indicated initial-time identities are needed. Formula (3.13) allows independent continuous factors $f,h$ in the integrand; this formal statement treats the quadratic case $f=h=u$.
Breakdown.RestrictStatement.summary: States: if $u$ is continuous on $[a,t]$ and the quadratic Duhamel identity from $a$ holds at $r=m$ and $r=t$, with $a\le m\le t$, then it holds from $m$ to $t$. (3.13) allows independent factors $f,h$; this treats $f=h=u$.

Breakdown.SectionInternal.exists_preimag.text: Let $X$ be a real normed space, let $P:X\to X$ be bounded and linear with finite-dimensional range, and let $C\subset X$ be a dense linear subspace. For every $v\in\operatorname{ran}P$, the formal statement proves the existence of $c\in C$ with $Pc=v$. Neither completeness of $X$ nor the projection identity $P^2=P$ is required. Taking preimages of the vectors of a basis of $\operatorname{ran}P_{\mathrm u}$ is the finite-dimensional step used to choose the compactly supported correction space in Proposition 4.3. The statement concerns individual preimages; their linear organization and boundedness are supplied by the subsequent lifting construction.
Breakdown.SectionInternal.exists_preimag.summary: For a bounded linear $P$ with finite-dimensional range on a real normed space and a dense linear subspace $C$, every $v\in\operatorname{ran}P$ equals $Pc$ for some $c\in C$. Neither completeness nor $P^2=P$ is required.

Breakdown.SectionStatement.text: Let $\mathcal X$ be a real Banach space, $P:\mathcal X\to\mathcal X$ a bounded linear projection with finite-dimensional range, and $C'\subset\mathcal X$ a dense real linear subspace. The assertion is that there is a bounded linear map $J:\mathcal X\to\mathcal X$ with $PJ=P$ and $Jx\in C'$ for every $x\in\mathcal X$. Thus a prescribed component in the range of $P$ can be represented by a datum in $C'$. In the application $C'$ consists of smooth compactly supported divergence-free fields, and $J(\operatorname{range}P)$ is finite-dimensional because the domain of this restriction is finite-dimensional. The statement does not say that the full image of $J$ is finite-dimensional, nor does it prescribe a bound on $\|J\|$ or require eigenfunctions to be smooth or compactly supported.
Breakdown.SectionStatement.summary: For a bounded finite-rank projection $P$ and a dense subspace $C'$ of a real Banach space, asserts a bounded linear $J$ with $PJ=P$ and range in $C'$. It does not bound $\|J\|$ or say the full image of $J$ is finite-dimensional.

Breakdown.SimilarityResidual.text:
For functions $W:\mathbb R	imes\mathbb R^3	o\mathbb R^3$ and $q:\mathbb R	imes\mathbb R^3	o\mathbb R$, the value at $(s,y)$ is $\partial_sW+ rac12W+ rac12(y\cdot
abla)W-\Delta W+(W\cdot
abla)W+
abla q$. This defines a vector-valued expression. It does not assert that the expression is zero, that $W$ is divergence-free, or that $W$ is recurrent. Nor does the definition itself assume differentiability: derivative operations have assigned values where a classical derivative does not exist. In every smooth-profile application the smoothness hypotheses ensure that all terms are the ordinary derivatives appearing in (1.2). The spatial Laplacian is the sum of the pure second derivatives, and the spatial derivative of $W$ applied to $y$ is $(y\cdot
abla)W$.
Breakdown.SimilarityResidual.summary:
Defines the vector expression $\partial_sW+ rac12W+ rac12(y\cdot
abla)W-\Delta W+(W\cdot
abla)W+
abla q$. It does not assert that it vanishes, that $W$ is divergence-free or recurrent, or that $W$ is differentiable.

Breakdown.SmoothFlow.IsHsCurve.text: For a nonnegative integer $m$, a Fourier field $F(t,\xi)\in\mathbb C^3$ and real $a,b$, the condition asserts measurability of $F(t,\cdot)$ and finiteness of $\int_{\mathbb R^3}(1+|\xi|^2)^m|F(t,\xi)|^2\,d\xi$ for each $t\in[a,b]$. It also requires that this same integral for $F(t,\cdot)-F(t_0,\cdot)$ tend to zero as $t\to t_0$ within $[a,b]$. Thus it expresses strong continuity in $H^m$, with Fourier normalization $e^{-2\pi i x\cdot\xi}$ and an equivalent Sobolev weight omitting the powers of $2\pi$. The order $m$ is an integer. This definition alone contains neither the Navier–Stokes equation nor an $L^2_tH^{m+1}_x$ bound.
Breakdown.SmoothFlow.IsHsCurve.summary: For integer $m\ge0$, requires $\int(1+|\xi|^2)^m|F(t,\xi)|^2\,d\xi<\infty$ for each $t\in[a,b]$ and continuity of $F$ in this norm: strong continuity in $H^m$, with a weight omitting powers of $2\pi$. It contains no Navier–Stokes equation.

Breakdown.SmoothFlow.exists_symbolFlow_o.text: Let $T>0$ and let $F_0:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb C^3$ be measurable, conjugate symmetric and pointwise orthogonal to $\xi$, with $\int(1+|\xi|^2)^3|F_0|^2<\infty$. Suppose the bound $\int|\xi|^2|F(t,\xi)|^2\,d\xi\leq M_+$, where $M_+=\max(M,0)$ for a supplied real $M$, holds for every $H^3$-continuous solenoidal Fourier solution $F$ of the unforced integral equation with initial value $F_0$ on every partial interval $[0,s]\subset[0,T]$, at all $t\leq s$. Then such a solution exists on $[0,T]$. Its velocity gradient has squared norm $4\pi^2\int|\xi|^2|F|^2$. The hypothesis quantifies over all partial solutions and assumes $H^3$ initial data; the conclusion is continuation, without the alternative of a maximal $H^1$ solution with diverging norm stated in Tao’s corollary.
Breakdown.SmoothFlow.exists_symbolFlow_o.summary: Assume $H^3$, solenoidal, conjugate-symmetric data $F_0$ and that every $H^3$-continuous partial solution on $[0,s]\subset[0,T]$ obeys $\int|\xi|^2|F|^2\le M_+$. Then a solution exists on $[0,T]$. The alternative of a diverging maximal $H^1$ solution in Tao's corollary is not stated.

Breakdown.SmoothFlow.isHsCurve_of_flow.text: Let $F(t,\xi)$ be a Fourier solution of the unforced Navier–Stokes integral equation on $[0,s]$, continuous in the norm $\int(1+|\xi|^2)^3|F|^2$. Assume $\xi\cdot F(t,\xi)=0$ and $F(t,-\xi)=\overline{F(t,\xi)}$ at every time and frequency, and $F(0)=F_0$. If $\int(1+|\xi|^2)^m|F_0|^2<\infty$ for every nonnegative integer $m$, then $t\mapsto F(t)$ is continuous in every one of these Sobolev norms on $[0,s]$. The heat multiplier is $e^{-4\pi^2t|\xi|^2}$. This statement concerns spatial Sobolev regularity; smoothness in time and the construction of the pressure are separate results.
Breakdown.SmoothFlow.isHsCurve_of_flow.summary: If an $H^3$-continuous, solenoidal, conjugate-symmetric Fourier solution of the unforced integral equation on $[0,s]$ has data with $\int(1+|\xi|^2)^m|F_0|^2<\infty$ for every integer $m\ge0$, it is continuous in every such Sobolev norm. Time smoothness and pressure are separate.

Breakdown.SmoothFlow.isSolutionOn_physFi.text: Let $T>0$ and let $F(t,\xi)$ solve the unforced projected Fourier integral equation on $[0,T]$. Assume strong continuity in every norm $\int(1+|\xi|^2)^m|F|^2$, for nonnegative integers $m$, and pointwise solenoidality and conjugate symmetry. Let $U$ be the real inverse Fourier transform of $F$, and let $P$ be the real inverse Fourier transform of $-\xi\cdot\widehat{(U\cdot\nabla)U}/(2\pi i|\xi|^2)$. The formal statement gives smoothness of both fields on $[0,T]\times\mathbb R^3$, incompressibility on the closed interval, and the viscosity-one momentum equation for $0<t<T$. Division by zero assigns the pressure coefficient at $\xi=0$ the value zero; changing one frequency does not change the inverse Fourier integral. The hypotheses contain all spatial Sobolev orders and the integral equation, rather than smooth initial data alone.
Breakdown.SmoothFlow.isSolutionOn_physFi.summary: If $F$ solves the projected Fourier integral equation on $[0,T]$, is continuous in every Sobolev norm, solenoidal and conjugate symmetric, then $U$ and the pressure $P$ are smooth on $[0,T]\times\mathbb R^3$, $U$ is incompressible, and the viscosity-one momentum equation holds for $0<t<T$.

Breakdown.Space.text: The position variable x in (1.1), and the similarity variable y in (1.2), range over ℝ³ with the Euclidean inner product and Lebesgue measure. A vector is a list of three real coordinates, indexed 0, 1, 2; the paper usually numbers them 1, 2, 3. This change of indexing does not change the space or its norm. The dimension is fixed at three. This is the same ambient space as in §1.1.
Breakdown.Space.summary: ℝ³ with the Euclidean inner product and Lebesgue measure, the range of x in (1.1) and of y in (1.2). Coordinates are indexed 0, 1, 2 where the paper uses 1, 2, 3, which does not change the space or its norm.

Breakdown.Spectral.Complexification.isCo.text:
Let $X$ be a real inner-product space and $T:X\to X$ a bounded compact real-linear operator.

The formal statement proves that $T_{\mathbb C}(x+iy)=Tx+iTy$ is compact on the complexification, whose norm satisfies $\|x+iy\|^2=\|x\|^2+\|y\|^2$. The conclusion justifies carrying the compact difference between the monodromy and the free operator into the complex setting. It is separate from the equality of their real and complex operator norms and from every assertion about the essential spectrum.
Breakdown.Spectral.Complexification.isCo.summary: For a compact bounded real-linear operator $T$ on a real inner-product space, its complexification $T_{\mathbb C}(x+iy)=Tx+iTy$ is compact, with the norm $\|x+iy\|^2=\|x\|^2+\|y\|^2$.

Breakdown.Spectral.Complexification.norm.text:
Let $X$ be a real inner-product space and $T:X\to X$ a bounded real-linear operator. Its complexification acts on pairs written $x+iy$ by $T_{\mathbb C}(x+iy)=Tx+iTy$, with norm $\|x+iy\|^2=\|x\|^2+\|y\|^2$.

The formal statement proves $\|T_{\mathbb C}\|\le\|T\|$. The paper says that the two norms are equal. The reverse inequality follows by restricting to the isometric copy $x\mapsto x+i0$, but is not the conclusion of this formal statement. No compactness or spectral assumption is involved.
Breakdown.Spectral.Complexification.norm.summary: For a bounded real-linear $T$ on a real inner-product space, the complexification satisfies $\|T_{\mathbb C}\|\le\|T\|$. The paper says the two norms are equal; the reverse inequality is not the conclusion of this statement.

Breakdown.Spectral.exists_annulus.text:
Let $Y$ be a complex Banach space, let $T_0,C$ be bounded linear operators with $C$ compact and $\|T_0\|\le b\le\alpha<\beta$.

The formal statement proves that there exist $\alpha<r_1<r_2<\beta$ such that every complex $z$ with $r_1\le|z|\le r_2$ lies in the resolvent set of $T_0+C$. Thus it gives a whole closed annulus without spectrum, which is stronger than selecting only one circle $|z|=\Theta$. In the application $\alpha=e^{-S/4}$ and $\beta=1$, any intermediate circle in this annulus can be used for the splitting. No particular numerical values for the radii are supplied.
Breakdown.Spectral.exists_annulus.summary: If $C$ is compact and $\|T_0\|\le b\le\alpha<\beta$ on a complex Banach space, there are $\alpha<r_1<r_2<\beta$ with the closed annulus $r_1\le|z|\le r_2$ in the resolvent set of $T_0+C$. This is stronger than selecting one circle $|z|=\Theta$.

Breakdown.Spectral.finite_spectrum_outsi.text:
Let $Y$ be a complex Banach space, $T_0,C:Y\to Y$ bounded linear operators, and suppose $C$ is compact and $\|T_0\|\le b<r$.

The formal statement proves that $\{z\in\sigma(T_0+C):|z|\ge r\}$ is finite. Since an operator norm is nonnegative, the hypotheses imply $r>0$. The spectrum is the set where $zI-(T_0+C)$ fails to have a bounded inverse. This is the finiteness conclusion used to select a circle avoiding the spectrum in Lemma 4.5. The formal statement does not state equality of essential spectral radii, poles of the resolvent, or their algebraic multiplicities; those are the paper’s cited route to the same finiteness conclusion.
Breakdown.Spectral.finite_spectrum_outsi.summary: If $C$ is compact and $\|T_0\|\le b<r$ on a complex Banach space, then $\{z\in\sigma(T_0+C):|z|\ge r\}$ is finite. This is the finiteness used in Lemma 4.5; the paper reaches it through essential spectral radii, which the statement does not state.

Breakdown.Spectral.norm_backProj_le.text:
Let $T$ be a bounded operator on a complex Banach space, and let $0<r<R$ with $\|T\|<R$ and $|z|=r$ contained in the resolvent set. Define $B_n=(2\pi i)^{-1}(\int_{|z|=R}z^{-n}(zI-T)^{-1}\,dz-\int_{|z|=r}z^{-n}(zI-T)^{-1}\,dz)$.

The formal statement proves that some $K>0$ satisfies $\|B_n\|\le Kr^{-n}$ for every natural $n$. A separate contour identity gives $T^nB_n=I-Q$, where $Q$ is the interior projection; this identifies the exterior inverse powers. Choosing $r>\Theta$ yields summability after multiplication by $\Theta^n$. Both contours have positive radius, so the powers $z^{-n}$ never divide by zero on them.
Breakdown.Spectral.norm_backProj_le.summary: If $0<r<R$, $\|T\|<R$ and the circle $|z|=r$ lies in the resolvent set, the contour operators $B_n$ satisfy $\|B_n\|\le Kr^{-n}$ for some $K>0$ and every natural $n$.

Breakdown.Spectral.norm_pow_mul_specProj.text:
Let $T$ be a bounded linear operator on a complex Banach space, and let $r>0$ with every point of $|z|=r$ in the resolvent set. Put $Q=(2\pi i)^{-1}\int_{|z|=r}(zI-T)^{-1}\,dz$.

The formal statement proves the existence of $K>0$ such that $\|T^nQ\|\le Kr^n$ for every natural $n\ge0$. This is a contour-integral power estimate, stated at the contour radius. To obtain the first series of (4.11), use a radius $r<\Theta$ in the spectrum-free annulus and the equality of projections for those circles, then sum $K(r/\Theta)^n$. It gives the needed geometric bound without identifying the constant with the paper’s implicit constant.
Breakdown.Spectral.norm_pow_mul_specProj.summary: If the circle $|z|=r$, $r>0$, lies in the resolvent set of $T$ and $Q$ is the contour projection inside it, then $\|T^nQ\|\le Kr^n$ for some $K>0$ and every natural $n$. The constant is not identified with the paper's implicit constant.

Breakdown.Spectral.specProj.text: For a bounded operator $T$ on a complex normed space and real radius $r$, this defines $Q=(2\pi i)^{-1}\int_{|z|=r}(zI-T)^{-1}\,dz$, with the circle traversed counterclockwise. If the space is complete, $r>0$ and the circle lies in the resolvent set, this is the spectral projection for the spectrum inside the circle. The paper denotes the projection for the exterior spectrum by $P$; with its $\Theta=r$, the corresponding operator is $P=I-Q$. The definition alone requires neither a spectral gap nor idempotence, and its total resolvent takes the value zero when an inverse does not exist. The spectral theorems impose the resolvent-set hypothesis before interpreting the integral as a projection. The contour integral is a parametrized Bochner integral; if it is not integrable, the integral is assigned zero. Completeness and the resolvent-set hypothesis provide the ordinary spectral interpretation.
Breakdown.Spectral.specProj.summary: Defines $Q=(2\pi i)^{-1}\int_{|z|=r}(zI-T)^{-1}\,dz$, counterclockwise. On a complete space with $r>0$ and the circle in the resolvent set it is the spectral projection inside the circle; the paper's exterior projection is $P=I-Q$.

Breakdown.SteadyCert.FracCertData.text:
This declaration specifies the inputs for the separate steady fractional-dissipation construction. It has no counterpart as a certificate definition in the classical paper, whose approximate profiles depend on normalized time θ (§7.1 and Appendix B.1). Here k and N are arbitrary natural numbers: there are k parameter, forcing and constraint indices, and N test fields. The fields depend on y∈ℝ³ and parameters α∈ℝᵏ; no time variable is present.

The scalar inputs are a natural-number symmetry order; a viscosity-splitting coefficient; two coercivity coefficients; a constraint penalty; a bound for test-field weights; a multiplier scale; a spatial weight w and proposed lower and upper bounds; k parameter radii, a chosen active subset, k slopes and an ellipsoid radius; a real k×k change-of-coordinate matrix and a proposed error for it. The rotation rate is a real function of α, and each of k multiplier coefficients is another such function.

The profile is a vector field W(α,y); a bilinear-map-valued field is supplied as its proposed second derivative, and a further vector field as its proposed fractional dissipative term. There are k vector forcing fields, k matrix-valued constraint fields, k proposed smooth constraint fields and a proposed distance between the two constraint families. The N vector test fields each have a real weight. The model quadratic form takes (α,v,β) to a real number, the model equation takes (α,v,β,y) to a vector, and the model constraint takes (α,v,i) to a real number, where v is any field ℝ³→ℝ³ and β∈ℝᵏ.

The remaining real inputs are proposed losses for the potential, rows, constraints and low modes; a form scale; a splitting bound; a product constant; bounds for the residual, its row projections and the correction size. For each constraint index and α, two adjoint vector fields, k adjoint constraint coefficients, and local, spreading and quadratic error bounds are supplied. Every function is defined on its full stated domain. This data declaration imposes none of the positivity, differentiability, equation, derivative-identification or error inequalities suggested by these descriptions; those are separate certificate conditions. It therefore asserts substantially less than the existence of a valid certificate or a profile.
Breakdown.SteadyCert.FracCertData.summary: Inputs for a separate steady fractional-dissipation construction, with no counterpart in the paper, whose profiles depend on θ: a time-independent profile, Hessian, dissipative term, forcing, constraints, test fields, model forms and bounds. It imposes none of the certificate conditions.

Breakdown.StepDataStatement.text:
Let $X$ be a complete real Hilbert space. Let $G(t)$, for $t\ge0$, be a strongly continuous semigroup of contractions with $G(0)=I$. Let $K(\tau):X\times X\to X$ be symmetric and bounded bilinear, continuous in $\tau>0$ on each pair of vectors, with $\|K(\tau)\|\le C_K\tau^{-3/4}$ for $0<\tau\le1$ and $G(a)K(\tau)=K(a+\tau)$ for $a\ge0$, $\tau>0$. Let $D_\mu$ be a continuous dilation action for $\mu>0$, with $D_1=I$, $D_\mu D_\nu=D_{\mu\nu}$, $\|D_\mu x\|=\mu^{1/4}\|x\|$, $D_\mu G(\mu t)=G(t)D_\mu$ for $t\ge0$, and $\mu D_\mu K(\mu\tau)(x,y)=K(\tau)(D_\mu x,D_\mu y)$. Assume there is a dense set of $f\in X$ for which $K(\tau)(f,\cdot)$ is compact for every $\tau>0$. The families $G,K,D$ are defined on all real parameters; their analytic bounds and scaling properties hold on the ranges just stated.

Let $\rho$ be a linear isometry of $X$ onto itself commuting with $G,K,D$ for all their real parameters. Let $w:\mathbb R\to X$ be continuous, nonzero at some time, and satisfy $w(s+S)=\rho w(s)$ with $S>0$. Put $\mathcal S(a)=D_{e^{-a}}G(1-e^{-a})$ and $\widetilde K(a)=D_{e^{-a}}K(1-e^{-a})$. For every $a\le s$, assume the integral below exists and $w(s)=\mathcal S(s-a)w(a)+\int_a^s\widetilde K(s-\sigma)(w(\sigma),w(\sigma))\,d\sigma$.

For every dense linear subspace $C'\subset X$ and $t_0>0$, the assertion supplies an integer $k\ge1$ and a real $\theta$ with $\delta=1-e^{-S/k}\le t_0$ and $e^{-S/(4k)}<\theta<1$. Put $\mu=e^{-S/k}$, $Y=C([0,\delta];X)$ with its supremum norm, $u_n^*(\tau)=D_{(1-\tau)^{-1}}w(nS/k-\log(1-\tau))$, $B_\delta(f,g)(\tau)=\int_0^\tau K(\tau-\sigma)(f(\sigma),g(\sigma))\,d\sigma$, $A_n=2B_\delta(u_n^*,\cdot)$, $\Gamma x(\tau)=G(\tau)x$, and $Lv=D_\mu v(\delta)$. It asserts $\|A_n\|\le1/4$ for all nonnegative integers $n$, and supplies a finite dimensional subspace $V\subset X$, a bounded linear $J:X\to X$ with range in $C'$, and a bounded linear map $\mathcal R:\ell^\infty(\mathbb N;Y)\to X\times\ell^\infty(\mathbb N;Y)$. If $(e,z)=\mathcal Rg$, then $e\in V$, $z_0-A_0z_0-\Gamma Je=g_0$ and $z_n-A_nz_n-\theta^{-1}\Gamma Lz_{n-1}=g_n$ for $n\ge1$. This is a statement of the linear correction on successive intervals; the correction of the datum is $Je\in C'$. The smooth compactly supported space $E$ of the paper is represented by $J(V)$ when $C'$ is the corresponding dense data space. The formula uses only positive $k$, $\mu$, $\theta$ and $1-\tau$, so their reciprocals are ordinary ones. The path operators are formally assigned zero if their required continuous realizations do not exist; the analytic construction for $\delta>0$ proves those realizations before using them.

The product norm controlled by $\mathcal R$ is $\max(\|e\|,\sup_n\|z_n\|_Y)$. A bound for the actual datum correction $Je$ also uses $\|J\|$. The assertion concerns sequences of compact-interval paths, whereas Proposition 4.3 is phrased for a global weighted curve.

This formal statement specifies an implication. Defining the implication does not prove it.
Breakdown.StepDataStatement.summary: For a recurrent profile and any dense $C'$ and $t_0>0$, asserts $k\ge1$, $\theta$ with $e^{-S/(4k)}<\theta<1$, $\|A_n\|\le1/4$, a finite-dimensional $V$, $J$ into $C'$ and a bounded $\mathcal R$ solving the linear correction on successive intervals. Proposition 4.3 uses a global weighted curve.

Breakdown.Symmetry.text: A symmetry is a pair $(R,\theta_0)$, where $R$ is an invertible real linear isometry of Euclidean $\mathbb R^3$ and $\theta_0\in\mathbb R$. Thus $R\in O(3)$; orientation reversal is allowed. A collection $\Gamma$ is an arbitrary set of such pairs and may be empty. Neither closure under composition nor a group structure is required. Invariance of a field under a pair is a separate condition.
Breakdown.Symmetry.summary: A symmetry is a pair $(R,\theta_0)$ with $R\in O(3)$, orientation reversal allowed, and $\theta_0\in\mathbb R$. A collection $\Gamma$ is any set of such pairs, possibly empty, with no closure or group structure required.

Breakdown.TransferHolds.text:
Let $\mathcal X$ be a real Hilbert space. The bounded linear families $e^{t\Delta}$ and $D_\mu$ and bounded bilinear family $K(	au)$ are defined at every real parameter. Assume $e^{t\Delta}$ is a strongly continuous contraction semigroup for $t\ge0$, with $e^{0\Delta}=I$. Assume $K(	au)$ is symmetric for every real $	au$, continuous in $	au>0$ on each pair of inputs, with $e^{t\Delta}K(	au)=K(t+	au)$ for $t\ge0,	au>0$ and $\|K(	au)\|\le C_K	au^{-3/4}$ for $0<	au\le1$. For positive $\mu,
u$, assume the dilations satisfy $\|D_\mu x\|=\mu^{1/4}\|x\|$, $D_1=I$, $D_\mu D_
u=D_{\mu
u}$ and strong continuity in $\mu$. Also require $D_\mu e^{\mu t\Delta}=e^{t\Delta}D_\mu$ for $\mu>0,t\ge0$ and $\mu D_\mu K(\mu	au)(x,y)=K(	au)(D_\mu x,D_\mu y)$ for $\mu,	au>0$. For each positive $	au$, $K(	au)(f,\cdot)$ is compact for $f$ in one fixed dense subset of $\mathcal X$. Let $ho$ be a surjective linear isometry, let $S>0$, and let $w:\mathbb R	o\mathcal X$ be continuous, nonzero at some time, and satisfy $w(s+S)=ho w(s)$. Write $A(\sigma)=D_{e^{-\sigma}}e^{(1-e^{-\sigma})\Delta}$ and $B(\sigma)(x,y)=D_{e^{-\sigma}}K(1-e^{-\sigma})(x,y)$. For every $a\le b$, require the Bochner-integrable orbit equation $w(b)=A(b-a)w(a)+\int_a^bB(b-s)(w(s),w(s))\,ds$. The isometry $ho$ commutes with the heat and dilation operators and preserves $K$, meaning $ho K(	au)(x,y)=K(	au)(ho x,ho y)$. These commutation conditions hold for every real value of the relevant parameter, including values outside the forward-time and positive-dilation ranges of the preceding identities. The formal statement is the following transfer property. For every dense real linear subspace $C\subset\mathcal X$ and every $\varepsilon>0$, there is one continuous mild solution $u$ on $[0,1)$ with $u(0)\in C$ and $\|u(0)-w(0)\|<\varepsilon$. There are constants $A\in\mathbb R$ and $\kappa>0$ such that $\|D_{1-t}u(t)-w(-\log(1-t))\|\le A(1-t)^\kappa$ for every $0\le t<1$. Here mild means the heat-plus-quadratic Bochner integral equation, including integrability of each time integral. The powers have real exponent and positive base $1-t$, and all logarithms are evaluated at positive arguments. Values of $u$ outside $[0,1)$ are unconstrained. In the physical application $\mathcal X=\dot H^1_{\mathrm{div}}(\mathbb R^3)$, $D_\mu f(x)=\sqrt\mu f(\sqrt\mu x)$, $w(s)=W(s,\cdot)$, and $C$ can be the embedded compact smooth solenoidal fields. The property selects one datum in each prescribed dense class. It does not state that every nearby datum can be corrected within one fixed finite-dimensional space, does not require $\kappa<1/4$, and does not explicitly state the two-sided physical blow-up rate. This declaration defines the property; separate theorems establish it from the spectral splitting.
Breakdown.TransferHolds.summary: Defines the property that for every dense subspace $C$ and $\varepsilon>0$ there is a mild solution $u$ on $[0,1)$ with $u(0)\in C$, $\|u(0)-w(0)\|<\varepsilon$ and $\|D_{1-t}u(t)-w(-\log(1-t))\|\le A(1-t)^\kappa$. It does not require $\kappa<1/4$ or state the two-sided rate.

Breakdown.UniqueStatement.text: Let $\mathcal X$ be a real Banach space. Write $G(t)$ for a strongly continuous contraction semigroup on $t\ge0$, and let $K(\tau)$ be bounded symmetric real bilinear maps on $\mathcal X$, continuous in $\tau>0$ on each pair of arguments. Assume $G(t)K(\tau)=K(t+\tau)$ for $t\ge0,\tau>0$, and $\|K(\tau)(u,v)\|\le C_K\tau^{-3/4}\|u\|\|v\|$ for $0<\tau\le1$. This assertion says that two mild solutions $u,v:\mathbb R\to\mathcal X$ with $u(a)=v(a)$ coincide throughout $[a,b)$ if both are continuous and satisfy the quadratic Duhamel equation there, and throughout $[a,b]$ if both satisfy the closed-interval version. Each Duhamel integral is required to be Bochner integrable. The initial and final times are finite real numbers. Equality is asserted only on the indicated interval; arbitrary values assigned outside it are unrestricted. There is no smallness assumption on the common datum or on the length of the interval. The closed-interval conclusion is the uniqueness clause of Lemma 3.5, and the half-open conclusion is also included.
Breakdown.UniqueStatement.summary: States that two mild solutions with $u(a)=v(a)$ coincide on $[a,b)$, and on $[a,b]$ for the closed-interval version, with no smallness of the datum or interval. The closed-interval part is the uniqueness clause of Lemma 3.5.

Breakdown.VarConstIntegralInternal.conti.text: Let $\mathcal X$ be a real Banach space. Assume that $G(t)$, $t\geq0$, is a strongly continuous contraction semigroup, and that $K(\tau)$ is a symmetric bounded bilinear map on $\mathcal X$, continuous in $\tau>0$ on each pair of arguments. Assume $\|K(\tau)\|\leq C_K\tau^{-3/4}$ for $0<\tau\leq1$ and $G(s)K(\tau)=K(s+\tau)$ for $s\geq0$, $\tau>0$. If $\tau,w,z$ are continuous maps on a subset $E$ of any topological space, with $\tau(x)>0$ for every $x\in E$, then $x\mapsto K(\tau(x))(w(x),z(x))$ is continuous on $E$. Taking $E=(0,\infty)\times\mathcal X\times\mathcal X$ gives the joint continuity used in Lemma 3.3. No assertion at $\tau=0$ is made.
Breakdown.VarConstIntegralInternal.conti.summary: Under the semigroup and kernel hypotheses ($\|K(\tau)\|\le C_K\tau^{-3/4}$ for $0<\tau\le1$, $G(s)K(\tau)=K(s+\tau)$), $x\mapsto K(\tau(x))(w(x),z(x))$ is continuous on $E$ when $\tau,w,z$ are continuous and $\tau>0$ there, giving the joint continuity of Lemma 3.3.

Breakdown.VarConstIntegralInternal.norm_.text: Let $\mathcal X$ be a real Banach space. Assume that $G(t)$, $t\geq0$, is a strongly continuous contraction semigroup, and that $K(\tau)$ is a symmetric bounded bilinear map on $\mathcal X$, continuous in $\tau>0$ on each pair of arguments. Assume $\|K(\tau)\|\leq C_K\tau^{-3/4}$ for $0<\tau\leq1$ and $G(s)K(\tau)=K(s+\tau)$ for $s\geq0$, $\tau>0$. Let $a\leq b$ and let $u,v:\mathbb R\to\mathcal X$ satisfy $\|u(s)\|\leq M$ and $\|v(s)\|\leq N$ on $[a,b]$. Extend their restrictions by the endpoint values outside this interval. For any $t\in\mathbb R$ and $0<r\leq1$, the formal statement gives $\|K(r)(u(c(t-r)),v(c(t-r)))\|\leq C_KMN r^{-3/4}$, where $c(s)=\max(a,\min(b,s))$. For $a\leq t-r\leq b$ the endpoint extension disappears. This particular estimate has the additional restriction $r\leq1$.
Breakdown.VarConstIntegralInternal.norm_.summary: Under the semigroup and kernel hypotheses, if $\|u\|\le M$ and $\|v\|\le N$ on $[a,b]$, then $\|K(r)(u(c(t-r)),v(c(t-r)))\|\le C_KMNr^{-3/4}$ for $0<r\le1$, where $c$ clamps to $[a,b]$. The estimate holds only for $r\le1$.

Breakdown.VarConstIntegralStatement.text: Let $\mathcal X$ be a real Banach space. Write $G(t)$ for a strongly continuous contraction semigroup on $t\ge0$, and let $K(\tau)$ be bounded symmetric real bilinear maps on $\mathcal X$, continuous in $\tau>0$ on each pair of arguments. Assume $G(t)K(\tau)=K(t+\tau)$ for $t\ge0,\tau>0$, and $\|K(\tau)(u,v)\|\le C_K\tau^{-3/4}\|u\|\|v\|$ for $0<\tau\le1$. This is the assertion that, if $a\le b$, $u,v:\mathbb R\to\mathcal X$ are continuous on $[a,b]$, and $\|u(s)\|\le M$, $\|v(s)\|\le N$ there, then $K(t-s)(u(s),v(s))$ is Bochner integrable from $a$ to $t$ for every $t\in[a,b]$, and its integral is continuous in $t$ on $[a,b]$. In addition, when $t-a\le1$, its norm is at most $4C_K(t-a)^{1/4}MN$. Such finite $M,N$ exist by compactness of $[a,b]$. Integrability and continuity have no restriction on $b-a$. The interval of length zero is allowed, with integral zero. Values of the curves outside $[a,b]$ and the value of $K(0)$ do not affect the conclusion.
Breakdown.VarConstIntegralStatement.summary: States: if $u,v$ are continuous on $[a,b]$ with $\|u\|\le M$, $\|v\|\le N$, then $K(t-s)(u(s),v(s))$ is Bochner integrable on $[a,t]$, its integral is continuous in $t$, and its norm is at most $4C_K(t-a)^{1/4}MN$ when $t-a\le1$.

Breakdown.WeakPeriodicSimilarityProfileE.text:
There exist $S>0$, an orthogonal map $R$, fields $W(s,y)$, $G(s,y)$ and $H(s,y)$ each admitting a measurable representative for space-time Lebesgue measure, and a finite real $C$, with the following properties. The velocity $W$ is defined on all of $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3$, and $W(s+S,y)=RW(s,R^{-1}y)$ at every point. For every $s$, $G(s,\cdot)$ is the distributional spatial derivative of $W(s,\cdot)$; for almost every $s$, $H(s,\cdot)$ is the distributional derivative of $G(s,\cdot)$. These distributional derivative conditions include local integrability. The velocity is divergence-free almost everywhere in space at every time. One constant bounds $\int|W(s)|^6\,dy$ and $\int\|G(s)\|^2\,dy$ for every $s$, and $\int_0^S\int\|H\|^2\,dy\,ds<\infty$. The formal statement assumes the similarity weak identity tested against the scaled products of a compactly supported smooth time function and a compactly supported smooth solenoidal spatial field, together with the physical pairing and scaling identities for this Sobolev representation.
