For every such perturbation, every $\beta\in\mathbb R^n$ and every period-one $F\in L^2$ admitting a measurable representative and satisfying, against all compactly supported divergence-free space-time tests, $F=\mathcal T_Sv+(W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}\cdot\nabla)v+(v\cdot\nabla)W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}+\sum_i\beta_ib_i$ up to a gradient, assume
$\sqrt{\|v\|_w^2+|\beta|^2}\le c_1\|F\|_{L^2}+c_0\|F\|_{L^2([0,1]\times\overline B_r)}+c_2|\ell(v)|$.
Here $c_0,c_1,c_2\ge0$, $c_L>0$ and $c_1+c_0\le c_L$. For every time, parameter and spatially invariant divergence-free $u\in L^6$ with weak first and second derivatives, square-integrable gradient and Laplacian, assume
$\int(|\Delta u|^2+\frac14|\nabla u|^2)-\int[(W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}\cdot\nabla)u+(u\cdot\nabla)W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}]\cdot\Delta u\ge-c_3|u|_w^2$, with $c_3\ge0$.

Define $F_\alpha^{\mathrm a}=S(\alpha)^{-1}\partial_\theta W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}+\frac12W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}+\frac12(y\cdot\nabla)W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}-\Delta W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}+(W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}\cdot\nabla)W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}+\sum_i\beta_i^{\mathrm a}(\alpha)b_i+\nabla q_\alpha$. Nonnegative bounds $\delta,\delta_0$ satisfy $\|F_\alpha^{\mathrm a}\|_{L^2}\le\delta(\alpha)\le\delta_{\max}$ and $\|F_\alpha^{\mathrm a}\|_{L^2([0,1]\times\overline B_r)}\le\delta_0(\alpha)$, and
$c_1\delta+c_0\delta_0+c_2|\ell^{\mathrm a}(\alpha)-\ell(W_\alpha^{\mathrm a})|\le\varepsilon$, where $\varepsilon\ge0$.
There is $M>0$, and $m=1$ or $m=2$; in the second case $\Gamma$ contains some $(R,1/2)$. Put $a=w_*^{-1}+2(S_{\max}/m)c_3$. The three required inequalities are $2c_Lc_wM<1$, $4\varepsilon^2[a+2(S_{\max}/m)b_*+2(S_{\max}/m)/c_L]\le M^2$, and $4a\varepsilon^2+4(S_{\max}/m)\varepsilon[\delta_{\max}+2c_w\varepsilon M+2b_*\varepsilon]\le M^2$. Also $4\varepsilon^2/w_*<\|\nabla W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}\|_{L^2}^2$ for every parameter.

For the parameter correction there are real square matrices $A,B$ with $BA=I$ and numbers $o_j$ such that $|\beta_j^{\mathrm a}(\alpha)-(A(\alpha-\alpha^0))_j|\le o_j$ throughout the box and $\sum_j|B_{ij}|(2\varepsilon+o_j)\le r_i$ for every coordinate $i$. All norms over a period use Lebesgue measure on $[0,1]\times\mathbb R^3$, and matrix derivatives in these weighted energies use the sum of squared coordinate derivatives. The finiteness conditions and explicit nonnegative integral bounds are necessary: the formal conversion of an infinite nonnegative integral to a real number would otherwise give zero. They are included here before using the corresponding norm. The positivity of $w_*,S,c_L$ makes every displayed division legitimate.

This is the earlier certificate form with a rectangular box, unit weight on the finite-dimensional forcing coefficients, a local ball norm for part of the right-hand side, and an estimate directly about the approximate profile. It is not the full parameter-set and reference-profile formulation of the current §7.3. Under this premise the formal statement concludes the following. There exist $S>0$, an orthogonal map $R$, fields $W(s,y)$, $G(s,y)$ and $H(s,y)$ each admitting a measurable representative for space-time Lebesgue measure, and a finite real $C$, with the following properties. The velocity $W$ is defined on all of $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3$, and $W(s+S,y)=RW(s,R^{-1}y)$ at every point. For every $s$, $G(s,\cdot)$ is the distributional spatial derivative of $W(s,\cdot)$; for almost every $s$, $H(s,\cdot)$ is the distributional derivative of $G(s,\cdot)$. These distributional derivative conditions include local integrability. The velocity is divergence-free almost everywhere in space at every time. One constant bounds $\int|W(s)|^6\,dy$ and $\int\|G(s)\|^2\,dy$ for every $s$, and $\int_0^S\int\|H\|^2\,dy\,ds<\infty$. The norms of $G,H$ are operator norms; they differ by fixed dimension-dependent factors from the sums of squared coordinate derivatives used in the paper. For every smooth, compactly supported, divergence-free space-time test field $\varphi$, the integrand is integrable and
$\int_{\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3}[-W\cdot\partial_s\varphi-W\cdot\varphi-\frac12W\cdot(y\cdot\nabla)\varphi+\sum_iG(e_i)\cdot\partial_i\varphi-\sum_iW_iW\cdot\partial_i\varphi],ds\,dy=0$.
Finally $W$ is not zero almost everywhere in space-time. The expression is the pressure-free weak similarity equation: the pressure term disappears because the test fields are divergence-free. No pressure, smoothness, pointwise decay, quantitative closeness to an approximate field, or prescribed value of $R$ is part of this conclusion. Nontriviality here means nonzero on a set of positive space-time measure, rather than merely at a single point. The result is conditional on the stated estimates and inequalities. It contains no instance of a certificate, no numerical period, and no numerical error $0.017$. It does not state the smooth profile, prescribed symmetries or the estimates (7.38) in its conclusion. The relevant proof is the implementation in the supplied source package; the similarly named challenge file states the verification target and contains an unproved placeholder.
Breakdown.certificate_orbit.summary: If a rectangular parameter box carries an approximate profile with the stated linear estimates, defect bounds and three smallness inequalities, a recurrent weak profile exists. It is conditional, contains no certificate instance, period or error $0.017$, and is the earlier form, not §7.3.

Breakdown.cnormSq.text: For any finite family of complex numbers z_b, this is ∑_b|z_b|². With three components it is the Euclidean square of a complex vector; with nine or twenty-seven components it is the Frobenius square of a gradient or Hessian in (B.16). It is a component sum, not the operator norm of a multilinear map. The definition also permits an empty family, whose square norm is zero.
Breakdown.cnormSq.summary: ∑_b|z_b|² for a finite family of complex numbers: the Euclidean square for three components, and the Frobenius square of a gradient or Hessian in (B.16) for nine or twenty-seven. It is a component sum, not an operator norm; an empty family gives zero.

Breakdown.coerciveClause_of_isCertificat.text: If the earlier certificate is valid, its universal linearized estimate holds: for every parameter, admissible Γ-invariant weak perturbation v, coefficient vector β and square-integrable period-one F satisfying the linearized equation modulo gradients, √(‖v‖²w+|β|²)≤c₁‖F‖𝓗+c_B‖F‖L²((0,1)×B_R)+c₂|ℓ(v)|. Here ‖v‖²w=∫₀¹∫(|Δv|²+w|∇v|²), ℓᵢ(v)=∫₀¹∫∇v:Ξᵢ, and admissibility requires v(θ)∈L⁶ with its gradient, Laplacian and similarity transport part in 𝓗=L²((0,1)×ℝ³). This is extraction of an assumed certificate condition; the multiplier argument establishing such a condition is separate. It is the earlier ball-norm variant of (7.18).
Breakdown.coerciveClause_of_isCertificat.summary: A valid earlier certificate yields its linearized estimate √(‖v‖²w+|β|²)≤c₁‖F‖𝓗+c_B‖F‖L²((0,1)×B_R)+c₂|ℓ(v)| for every parameter, admissible perturbation, β and F. This only extracts an assumed condition; it is the earlier ball-norm variant of (7.18).

Breakdown.coerciveClause_of_multiplierIn.text:
Suppose c>0, cμ,t,a,K≥0 and every admissible linearized perturbation admits a square-integrable multiplier M and n≥0 with ‖M‖≤a√(cE+cμn²) and c(E+|β|²)+cμn²≤⟨F,M⟩+cK²‖F‖²B+t|ℓ(v)|². If a/√c≤c₁, K≤c_B and √(t/c)≤c₂, then √(E+|β|²)≤c₁‖F‖𝓗+c_B‖F‖B+c₂|ℓ(v)| for every such perturbation. Here E is the formal squared energy, ‖F‖B is the L² norm on [0,1]×{|y|≤R}, and ℓ is the vector of gradient constraints. The period-one weak perturbation is solenoidal and Γ-invariant, with v(θ)∈L⁶ and its gradient, Laplacian and similarity transport part in 𝓗. This is the Cauchy–Schwarz and scalar-estimate step of Lemma B.2 in the earlier certificate's ball-norm form. It assumes the multiplier estimate rather than proving its analytic hypotheses.

For arbitrary supplied data, put I=∫₀¹∫ℝ³ max(|tr H|²+w|G|²,0), with values in [0,∞] and the Frobenius norm for G. The formal squared energy equals I when I is finite and equals zero when I is infinite. With G=∇v, H=∇²v and a bounded measurable weight w≥w*>0, the perturbation hypotheses make this the usual energy ∫₀¹∫ℝ³(|Δv|²+w|∇v|²). The isolated condition does not impose those assumptions on w.
Breakdown.coerciveClause_of_multiplierIn.summary: If $c>0$, $c_\mu,t,a,K\ge0$, every admissible perturbation admits a multiplier with the stated estimate, and $a/\sqrt c\le c_1$, $K\le c_B$, $\sqrt{t/c}\le c_2$, then $\sqrt{E+|\beta|^2}\le c_1\|F\|_{\mathcal H}+c_B\|F\|_B+c_2|\ell(v)|$: the Cauchy–Schwarz and scalar step of Lemma B.2.

Breakdown.coercive_scalar_core.text: Let c>0 and cμ,t,a,K,E,S,N_F,N_B,h≥0, and let N_M,n,P be real numbers. Assume N_M≤a√(cE+cμn²), P≤N_FN_M, and c(E+S)+cμn²≤P+cK²N_B²+th². Then √(E+S)≤(a/√c)N_F+KN_B+√(t/c)h. No sign is assumed for N_M,n or P; their displayed inequalities are sufficient. For the earlier certificate, E is perturbation energy, S=|β|², N_F is the global forcing norm, N_B its ball norm, h=|ℓ(v)| and P=⟨F,M⟩. This is the algebra behind Lemma B.2, with a local norm in place of its directional seminorm. Since c>0, the divisions and square roots have their usual meaning.
Breakdown.coercive_scalar_core.summary: Let c>0 and cμ,t,a,K,E,S,N_F,N_B,h≥0. If N_M≤a√(cE+cμn²), P≤N_FN_M and c(E+S)+cμn²≤P+cK²N_B²+th², then √(E+S)≤(a/√c)N_F+KN_B+√(t/c)h: the scalar step of Lemma B.2 in the earlier ball-norm format.

Breakdown.compactPiece.text:
Let $\mathcal X$ be a real Banach space with a strongly continuous contraction semigroup $G(t)$ for $t\ge0$ and symmetric bounded bilinear operators $K(\tau)$, continuous for $\tau>0$, with $G(s)K(\tau)=K(s+\tau)$ for $s\ge0$, $\tau>0$, and $\|K(\tau)\|\le C_K\tau^{-3/4}$ for $0<\tau\le1$. In the paper $G(t)=e^{t\Delta}$.

Assume there is a dense set of $f\in\mathcal X$ for which $K(\tau)(f,\cdot)$ is compact for every $\tau>0$. For $0<T\le1$ and every continuous background $f:[0,T]\to\mathcal X$, the formal statement proves that $g\mapsto\int_0^TK(T-s)(f(s),g(s))\,ds$ is a compact operator from $C([0,T];\mathcal X)$ with its supremum norm to $\mathcal X$. This is the compact endpoint interaction needed in the monodromy construction. Composing it with the bounded map from initial data to the linearized trajectory gives compactness of the correction to the free endpoint map. The conclusion does not assert compactness of the entire trajectory-valued Duhamel operator.
Breakdown.compactPiece.summary: If $K(\tau)(f,\cdot)$ is compact for a dense set of $f$, then for $0<T\le1$ and continuous $f$ the map $g\mapsto\int_0^TK(T-s)(f(s),g(s))\,ds$ is compact from $C([0,T];\mathcal X)$ to $\mathcal X$. Compactness of the whole trajectory-valued Duhamel operator is not asserted.

Breakdown.contraction.text:
Let $X,Y$ be real Banach spaces; let $A_n:Y\to Y$, $\Gamma:X\to Y$, $L:Y\to X$, and $J:X\to X$ be bounded linear maps, and let $N:Y\times Y\to Y$ be bounded bilinear. Fix $0<\theta\le1$. Suppose a bounded linear map $\mathcal R:\ell^\infty(\mathbb N;Y)\to X\times\ell^\infty(\mathbb N;Y)$ has the following property: if $(e,z)=\mathcal R g$, then $z_n-A_nz_n-\Gamma Je=g_0$ for $n=0$, and $z_n-A_nz_n-\theta^{-1}\Gamma Lz_{n-1}=g_n$ for $n\ge1$. 

The formal statement asserts that there are $r_0>0$ and $C_1\in\mathbb R$ such that every $\xi\in X$ with $\|\xi\|\le r_0$ admits $e\in X$ and a bounded sequence $z_n\in Y$ with $\|e\|\le C_1\|\xi\|$, $z_0-A_0z_0-\Gamma(Je+\xi)=N(z_0,z_0)$, and $z_n-A_nz_n-\theta^{-1}\Gamma Lz_{n-1}=\theta^nN(z_n,z_n)$ for $n\ge1$. 

Here $n$ is a nonnegative integer and $\ell^\infty$ has the supremum norm. No estimate for $\|z\|_{\ell^\infty}$ appears in this conclusion, and membership of $e$ in a finite dimensional subspace is absent. To apply this to the paper, $Y$ is a space of continuous paths on one time interval, $L$ is endpoint evaluation followed by dilation, and $Je$ is the correction of the datum. The bound $\|z\|\le2b$ used in the proof occurs in the separate fixed point lemma. This theorem proves the assertion for all the stated spaces and operators. It constructs $r_0=[8(\|\mathcal R\|\|N\|+1)(\|\mathcal R\|\|\Gamma\|+1)]^{-1}$, whose denominator is strictly positive. The global weighted estimate and the translation of $e$ to a smooth compactly supported correction require the remaining construction.
Breakdown.contraction.summary: Given a bounded right inverse $\mathcal R$ for the linear interval system, there are $r_0>0$ and $C_1$ such that each $\|\xi\|\le r_0$ admits $e$ with $\|e\|\le C_1\|\xi\|$ and a bounded sequence $z_n$ solving the nonlinear system. No bound on $\|z\|_{\ell^\infty}$ is included.

Breakdown.curlGradOfSecondDeriv.text: For a complex tensor h(a,b,c) representing ∂_b∂_c v_a, the entry (i,l) is ∑ⱼ,ₘεᵢⱼₘh(m,l,j). It represents ∂_l(curl v)_i, the gradient of vorticity in (B.16), with vector component first and differentiation direction second. The formula contracts a supplied tensor; the weak-Hessian identities and almost-everywhere symmetry needed for its differential interpretation are separate hypotheses.
Breakdown.curlGradOfSecondDeriv.summary: For a complex tensor h(a,b,c) representing ∂_b∂_c v_a, the entry (i,l) is ∑ⱼ,ₘεᵢⱼₘh(m,l,j), representing ∂_l(curl v)_i, the vorticity gradient in (B.16). The weak-Hessian identities needed for this interpretation are separate hypotheses.

Breakdown.curlOfGrad.text: For a complex matrix g with entries g(a,b)=∂_b v_a, the ith component is ∑ⱼ,ₗεᵢⱼₗg(l,j), where ε is the standard alternating symbol. Thus it is curl v. This is the curl of the mode used in (B.14) and (B.16). The apparent transpose is caused by the formal component-first convention; the paper writes derivatives first. For an arbitrary matrix this is simply the stated linear contraction, without any assertion that it comes from a velocity field.
Breakdown.curlOfGrad.summary: For a complex matrix g with g(a,b)=∂_b v_a, the vector with ith component ∑ⱼ,ₗεᵢⱼₗg(l,j), which is curl v: the curl of the mode in (B.14) and (B.16). The apparent transpose comes from the component-first convention, while the paper writes derivatives first.

Breakdown.curlVec.text: For a real linear map G:ℝ³→ℝ³, the ith component is ∑ⱼ,ₗεᵢⱼₗ(G eⱼ)ₗ. If G eⱼ=∂ⱼv, this is curl v with the usual orientation of ℝ³, as in (B.18). The input is an arbitrary matrix; it is identified with a velocity gradient only by a separate derivative hypothesis. This operation does not require or assert symmetry of G.
Breakdown.curlVec.summary: For a real linear map G, the vector with ith component ∑ⱼ,ₗεᵢⱼₗ(G eⱼ)ₗ; if G eⱼ=∂ⱼv this is curl v with the usual orientation, as in (B.18). G is arbitrary, and no symmetry is required.

Breakdown.cylRadius.text: At y=(y₁,y₂,y₃), r=√(y₁²+y₂²) is the distance to the vertical axis. This is the cylindrical radius used throughout Appendix B. It is nonnegative and is zero on the axis. Formulas containing 1/r or 1/r² therefore need an off-axis hypothesis for their classical interpretation; the formal arithmetic assigns division by zero the value zero. The definition itself excludes no point.
Breakdown.cylRadius.summary: r=√(y₁²+y₂²), the distance to the vertical axis and the cylindrical radius of Appendix B; it is zero on the axis. Formulas with 1/r or 1/r² need an off-axis hypothesis, since division by zero is taken as zero.

Breakdown.defectField.text: At normalized time θ and point y, the residual is S⁻¹∂θW+½W+½(y·∇)W−ΔW+(W·∇)W+∑ᵢβᵢᵃbᵢ+∇q. Here W is an approximate profile, q a chosen scalar pressure correction, S its period in similarity time, and βᵃ the proposed force coefficients. It represents a specific right-hand side Fᵃ in (7.10). The paper allows any square-integrable representative modulo gradients; this earlier formula uses a scalar pressure q. The definition places no differentiability condition on W or q: first derivatives take the zero value where they do not exist, and the Laplacian is formed from iterated derivatives. The differential expression has its classical meaning under the regularity conditions of the earlier certificate. Neither residual smallness nor S>0 is asserted. If S=0 its reciprocal is assigned zero; certificate hypotheses rule this out.
Breakdown.defectField.summary: The residual S⁻¹∂θW+½W+½(y·∇)W−ΔW+(W·∇)W+∑ᵢβᵢᵃbᵢ+∇q, a specific Fᵃ in (7.10) formed from a scalar pressure, where the paper allows any representative modulo gradients. No smallness or S>0 is asserted; at S=0 the reciprocal is zero.

Breakdown.dichotomyHolds.text:
The following assertion is proved. Let $X$ be a real Hilbert space, let $T_0,C:X\to X$ be bounded and linear, assume $C$ is compact, and let $0\le b\le\alpha<\beta$ with $\|T_0\|\le b$. Put $M=T_0+C$.

The theorem proves that there exist $\alpha<r_1<r_2<\beta$, $K>0$ and a bounded finite-rank projection $P$ with $PM=MP$ such that, for every natural $n\ge0$, $\|M^n(I-P)\|\le Kr_1^n$ and $\|Px\|\le Kr_2^{-n}\|M^nPx\|$ for all $x$. It also asserts that $M$ maps $\operatorname{ran}P$ onto itself. The second bound implies injectivity on that range, so its restriction is invertible. For Lemma 4.5 take $b=\alpha=e^{-S/4}$ and $\beta=1$, then choose $r_1<\Theta<r_2$. These geometric bounds imply both weighted series in (4.11). Natural-number powers occur throughout; $r_2>0$ excludes division by zero. The assertion is more quantitative than summability alone.
Breakdown.dichotomyHolds.summary: For $M=T_0+C$ on a real Hilbert space with $C$ compact and $\|T_0\|\le b\le\alpha<\beta$, there are $\alpha<r_1<r_2<\beta$, $K>0$ and a commuting finite-rank projection $P$ with $\|M^n(I-P)\|\le Kr_1^n$ and $\|Px\|\le Kr_2^{-n}\|M^nPx\|$; $M$ maps $\operatorname{ran}P$ onto itself.

Breakdown.dilateField.text: For any field $u:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ and real parameter $\mu$, the definition gives $D_\mu u(x)=\sqrt\mu\,u(\sqrt\mu\,x)$. Multiplication is scalar multiplication in Euclidean three-space. On $\mu>0$ this is exactly the paper's Navier–Stokes dilation, with the same factor in velocity and position. No smoothness, incompressibility or integrability is assumed in the definition. Those properties, preservation of $X$ and the factor $\mu^{1/4}$ in the homogeneous $H^1$ norm are separate assertions. The real square root is assigned zero for $\mu\le0$, so the total definition then gives the zero field. All dilation identities in (3.5) are stated only for positive parameters, where this convention has no effect.
Breakdown.dilateField.summary: Defines $D_\mu u(x)=\sqrt\mu\,u(\sqrt\mu x)$, the paper's Navier–Stokes dilation for $\mu>0$. For $\mu\le0$ the square root is taken as zero, giving the zero field; the identities in (3.5) use only $\mu>0$.

Breakdown.divergenceAt.text: For a vector field v:ℝ³→ℝ³, the expression at x is ∑ᵢ(Dv(x)eᵢ)ᵢ. When v is differentiable at x this is div v(x), with the sign and coordinate convention in (1.1). The formal expression accepts every function v; at points where the derivative does not exist, its derivative is assigned the zero linear map. Consequently the equation given by this expression alone does not assert differentiability or distributional incompressibility. The smoothness or weak-gradient hypotheses must be supplied separately.
Breakdown.divergenceAt.summary: ∑ᵢ(Dv(x)eᵢ)ᵢ, which is div v(x) where v is differentiable, as in (1.1); a zero derivative is used elsewhere. So this expression alone asserts neither differentiability nor distributional incompressibility.

Breakdown.embeddedProfileOrbit_holds.text:
Let $W:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ and $q:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$ be smooth, solve $\partial_sW+\tfrac12W+\tfrac12(y\cdot\nabla)W-\Delta W+(W\cdot\nabla)W+\nabla q=0$, and satisfy $\operatorname{div}W=0$. Assume, for one real $C$, $\|D_y^jW(s,y)\|\le C(1+|y|)^{-j-1}$ for the natural-number orders $j=0,1,2$ and $\|D_yq(s,y)\|\le C(1+|y|)^{-3}$, uniformly in $s,y$. The derivative norms here are operator norms; the paper’s pointwise gradient norm is the sum-of-squares norm of its coordinate derivatives.

An element of the paper’s $X$ represents a divergence-free field on $\mathbb R^3$ in $L^6$ with square-integrable gradient. Its norm is exactly $(\int_{\mathbb R^3}\sum_{i=1}^3|\partial_i u|^2)^{1/2}$; the formal representation is a closed real subspace of a complex Fourier $L^2$ space. 

In this concrete space, $G(t)=e^{t\Delta}$ and $K(\tau)(f,g)=-\tfrac12e^{\tau\Delta}\mathbb P[(f\cdot\nabla)g+(g\cdot\nabla)f]$, where $\mathbb P$ is the Leray projection. The formal assertion also allows any real Hilbert model supplied with the heat, bilinear and positive-dilation identities of §3.4, a homogeneous $H^1$ norm embedding respecting subtraction, nonvanishing, rotations and dilations, and the following weak-to-mild property: a decay-field curve with continuous embedded values, pairwise $L^2$ increments continuous in $L^2$, continuous pairings with compact solenoidal test fields, and the pressure-free weak derivative identity against those tests satisfies the mild equation. The test-field images form a dense linear subspace. 

Assume in addition $S>0$, $R\in O(3)$, $W(s+S,y)=RW(s,R^{-1}y)$ and $W(s,y)\ne0$ for at least one pair $(s,y)$. For any realization preserving the homogeneous $H^1$ norm, rotations and dilations and converting the stated weak solutions into mild ones, the formal statement proves that $w(s)$, the homogeneous $H^1$ element represented by $W(s,\cdot)$, is continuous, nonzero at some time, obeys $w(s+S)=\rho_Rw(s)$, and satisfies $w(s)=\mathcal S(s-s_0)w(s_0)+\int_{s_0}^{s}\mathcal K(s-r)(w(r),w(r))\,dr$ for every $s_0\le s$, with an integrable integrand, where $\mathcal S(a)=D_{e^{-a}}G(1-e^{-a})$ and $\mathcal K(a)=D_{e^{-a}}K(1-e^{-a})$. Its time variable is $s\in\mathbb R$. Proposition 4.1 is stated for the physical-time velocity on $[0,1)$; that change of variables is a separate step. The extra second-derivative and pressure-gradient estimates remain hypotheses.
Breakdown.embeddedProfileOrbit_holds.summary: A smooth, divergence-free, decaying solution $W$ of the similarity equation with $W(s+S,y)=RW(s,R^{-1}y)$, nonzero somewhere, gives a continuous nonzero homogeneous $H^1$ curve $w$ with $w(s+S)=\rho_Rw(s)$ solving the similarity-time mild equation. The extra decay estimates stay hypotheses.

Breakdown.exists_section.text:
The following assertion is proved. Let $X$ be a real Banach space, let $P:X\to X$ be a bounded linear projection with finite-dimensional range, and let $C\subset X$ be a dense linear subspace.

The formal statement proves that there exists a bounded linear map $J:X\to X$ such that $PJ=P$ and $Jx\in C$ for every $x$. In the application $P=P_{\mathrm u}$ and $C$ consists of the elements of $\dot H^1_{\mathrm{div}}(\mathbb R^3)$ represented by smooth compactly supported divergence-free fields. The restriction of $J$ to $\operatorname{ran}P$ is injective and gives the finite-dimensional correction space $E=J(\operatorname{ran}P)\subset C$. The formal conclusion presents $J$ and its projection identity; it does not name $E$ or specify a numerical bound for $\|J\|$.
Breakdown.exists_section.summary: For a bounded linear projection $P$ with finite-dimensional range on a real Banach space and a dense linear subspace $C$, there is a bounded linear $J$ with $PJ=P$ and range in $C$. No numerical bound on $\|J\|$ is given.

Breakdown.extended_certificate_breakdown.text:
**Hypothesis.** The hypothesis is existence of certificate data in a finite parameter dimension satisfying the formal conditions corresponding to §§7.1–7.3. In mathematical terms the data consist of a dimension $n\ge0$, a parameter set $\mathcal K$ given by the coordinate intervals and the remaining weighted Euclidean ball in (7.29), periods $0<S(\alpha)\le S_{\max}$, approximate divergence-free unit-period fields $W^{\mathrm a}_\alpha$, a comparison field, finitely many forcing and constraint fields, the weight $0<w_*\le w(y)\le w^*$, and constants and adjoint fields for the residual, coercivity, smallness and parameter-enclosure inequalities. These are hypotheses for every parameter and, in the coercivity and adjoint estimates, every admissible perturbation; a numerical witness to them is not produced by this implication.

The formal input differs from the paper's definition in specific ways. The approximate field is $C^1$ jointly in all real parameter, time and space variables, including parameters outside $\mathcal K$, and is unit-periodic there. A supplied weak spatial Hessian must exist at every time and satisfy the additional uniform bound $C_{\mathrm a}(1+|y|)^{-3}$, in operator norm. The first derivative decay bound is also in operator norm; (7.8) uses the Frobenius norm, and conversion at a fixed constant costs at most $\sqrt3$. The weight is measurable, bounded above and below by positive finite constants, and invariant under the spatial isometries of the prescribed symmetries. The finite family representing the row norm is orthonormal, with nonnegative weights bounded by $c_0^2$; the paper instead uses pairwise orthogonal fields of norm at most $c_0$. Multiplying each orthonormal field by the square root of its weight gives the paper’s seminorm. The coefficient $c_2$ is explicitly nonnegative. Each adjoint field has a common spatial $L^2$ bound at every time, in addition to periodicity. The residual is a specified expression using a supplied measurable periodic vector field whose pairing with compact solenoidal tests vanishes. No scalar pressure is supplied by this hypothesis; the paper allows a residual specified only modulo gradients. The integer used in the supremum estimate may be $1$, or $2$ if a half-period symmetry is present; the paper's convention (7.6) chooses $2$ whenever such a symmetry is available. The formal statement gives the nonexistence conclusion above, for every positive viscosity, and omits the constructed solution's finite time, rate and limiting profile. The paper normalizes viscosity to one; its scaling gives the same extension to other positive viscosities.

**Hypothesis.** The hypothesis is existence of certificate data in a finite parameter dimension satisfying the formal conditions corresponding to §§7.1–7.3. In mathematical terms the data consist of a dimension $n\ge0$, a parameter set $\mathcal K$ given by the coordinate intervals and the remaining weighted Euclidean ball in (7.29), periods $0<S(\alpha)\le S_{\max}$, approximate divergence-free unit-period fields $W^{\mathrm a}_\alpha$, a comparison field, finitely many forcing and constraint fields, the weight $0<w_*\le w(y)\le w^*$, and constants and adjoint fields for the residual, coercivity, smallness and parameter-enclosure inequalities. These are hypotheses for every parameter and, in the coercivity and adjoint estimates, every admissible perturbation; a numerical witness to them is not produced by this implication.

The formal input differs from the paper's definition in specific ways. The approximate field is $C^1$ jointly in all real parameter, time and space variables, including parameters outside $\mathcal K$, and is unit-periodic there. A supplied weak spatial Hessian must exist at every time and satisfy the additional uniform bound $C_{\mathrm a}(1+|y|)^{-3}$, in operator norm. The first derivative decay bound is also in operator norm; (7.8) uses the Frobenius norm, and conversion at a fixed constant costs at most $\sqrt3$. The weight is measurable, bounded above and below by positive finite constants, and invariant under the spatial isometries of the prescribed symmetries. The finite family representing the row norm is orthonormal, with nonnegative weights bounded by $c_0^2$; the paper instead uses pairwise orthogonal fields of norm at most $c_0$. Multiplying each orthonormal field by the square root of its weight gives the paper’s seminorm. The constraint matrix fields are only assumed measurable with a finite square integral on $[0,1]$; their periodicity is not a separate formal certificate hypothesis, and the time-circle construction uses the periodic extension of their restriction to $[0,1)$. The coefficient $c_2$ is explicitly nonnegative. Each adjoint field has a common spatial $L^2$ bound at every time, in addition to periodicity. The residual is a specified expression using a supplied measurable periodic vector field whose pairing with compact solenoidal tests vanishes. No scalar pressure is supplied by this hypothesis; the paper allows a residual specified only modulo gradients. The integer used in the supremum estimate may be $1$, or $2$ if a half-period symmetry is present; the paper's convention (7.6) chooses $2$ whenever such a symmetry is available. All coefficient and residual norms, positivity conditions and inequalities (7.18)–(7.37) are assumptions in the corresponding formal certificate, subject to these encodings. The index sets may be empty, and the parameter set need not have interior. The divisions by $S(\alpha)$, $w_*$, the positive forcing weight and the nonzero coordinate scales are legitimate under the stated positivity and nonvanishing assumptions.

**Conclusion.** There are a number $P>0$, an orthogonal map $R$ of $\mathbb R^3$, a nonzero measurable velocity $W(s,y)$, and supplied weak first and second spatial derivatives $G$ and $H$, all defined on $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3$. The recurrence $W(s+P,y)=R W(s,R^{-1}y)$ holds at every $(s,y)$. At every time, $G$ is the weak gradient of $W$ and $\operatorname{tr}G=0$ almost everywhere in space; the weak second derivative identity holds for almost every time. There is a finite common bound for $\int_{\mathbb R^3}|W(s)|^6$ and $\int_{\mathbb R^3}\|G(s)\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2$, at every $s$, and $\int_0^P\int_{\mathbb R^3}\|H\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2<\infty$. The operator norm of the supplied derivatives is used here; a uniform Frobenius-norm bound follows by a fixed dimensional factor. Nonzero means that $W$ does not vanish almost everywhere in space-time. For every smooth compactly supported divergence-free test field $\varphi$, the formal statement requires integrability and vanishing of
$\displaystyle \int_{\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3}\left[-W\cdot\partial_s\varphi-W\cdot\varphi-\tfrac12 W\cdot(y\cdot\nabla)\varphi+\sum_{i=1}^3 G e_i\cdot\partial_i\varphi-\sum_{i=1}^3 W_i W\cdot\partial_i\varphi\right].$
This is the viscosity-one similarity equation modulo gradients. It contains no pressure variable. The coefficient $-1$ on $W\cdot\varphi$ is the sum of the original $1/2$ zeroth-order term and the $-3/2$ term from integration by parts in the dilation. The time and space integrations use Lebesgue measure; including the endpoints of $[0,P]$ does not change the integral. Real upper bounds in nonnegative integrals are read as their nonnegative parts, so the finite bound can be chosen nonnegative.

**Relation to Theorem 7.1.** The conclusion is existential in the entire profile and its recurrence data. It does not return a parameter $\alpha\in\mathcal K$, the equality $P=S(\alpha)$, the choice $R=I$, a correction relative to $W^{\mathrm a}_\alpha$, the three assertions of (7.38), or the full family of symmetries (7.39). The construction inside the proof uses such intermediate data, but those data are not part of this formal statement. Smoothness and decay require the separate weak-to-smooth result. This implication alone therefore has a different statement from the paper's quantitative theorem.
Breakdown.extended_certificate_orbit_pro.summary: Certificate data satisfying the §§7.1–7.3 conditions give $P>0$, orthogonal $R$ and a nonzero measurable $W$ with $W(s+P,y)=RW(s,R^{-1}y)$ solving the weak similarity equation modulo gradients. Unlike Theorem 7.1 it returns no $\alpha$, no $P=S(\alpha)$, no $R=I$ and no (7.38).
