Residual and size bounds. The residual is Fᵃ=S⁻¹∂θWᵃ+½Wᵃ+½(y·∇)Wᵃ−tr Hᵃ+(Wᵃ·∇)Wᵃ+∑ᵢβᵢᵃbᵢ+hα; θ=s/S is normalized time, and tr Hᵃ=∑ⱼHᵃ[eⱼ,eⱼ] represents ΔWᵃ. Nonnegative δ,δ₀ satisfy ‖Fᵃ‖𝓗≤δ≤δmax and [Fᵃ]≤δ₀. With ℓ̄=t−ℓ(Wᵃ), c₁δ+δ₀+c₂|ℓ̄|≤(1−ϑ)ε. For c_w=(4π√w*)⁻¹ᐟ² and L=Smax/m the required inequalities are 2c_Lc_wM<1; 4ε²(1/w*+2Lc₃+2Lb*/ω+2L/c_L)≤M²; and 4(1/w*+2Lc₃)ε²+4Lε(δmax+2c_wεM+2b*ε/ω)≤M². Finally 4ε²/w*<‖∇Wᵃ‖²𝓗 ensures nontriviality.

Adjoint bounds and parameter inclusion. The real matrix V is invertible; Vⱼ denotes its jth column, so Vⱼ·x=∑ᵢVᵢⱼxᵢ. The real coefficients Y=Y(α) are supplied and may depend on α. For j∈J, ψα,ⱼ is measurable and period one, with a nonnegative uniform-in-time spatial L² bound Lⱼ; the linear and quadratic error bounds aⱼ,ãⱼ are nonnegative. For every admissible v, |⟨(v·∇)v,ψα,ⱼ⟩|≤ãⱼ‖v‖²w. Put 𝓒αv=(Wᵃα·∇)v+(v·∇)Wᵃα. For every F with the measurability, periodicity and L² conditions above satisfying F≃𝓣ˢv+𝓒αv, |⟨F,ψα,ⱼ⟩−(Yℓ(v))ⱼ|≤aⱼ‖v‖w. The offset is bounded by |Vⱼ·βᵃ−⟨Fᵃ,ψα,ⱼ⟩−(Yℓ̄)ⱼ−dⱼαⱼ|≤oⱼ, and ãⱼ(2ε)²+2ε√(aⱼ²+|⟨b,ψα,ⱼ⟩−Vⱼ|²/ω²)+oⱼ≤|dⱼ|ρⱼ. For the other coordinates a*≥0, ∑ⱼ∉J(Vⱼ·x)²≤a*²|x|² for every x, √(∑ⱼ∉J(Vⱼ·βᵃ−dⱼαⱼ)²)≤o*, and 2εa*/ω+o*≤ρ*.

Comparison. The core estimates are (7.18)–(7.37). The formal statement additionally requires global C¹ parameter dependence, a pointwise Hessian decay bound and a uniform-in-time L² bound for each adjoint field; the paper's displayed assumptions only require joint continuity of Wᵃ and its time and spatial first derivatives on K, locally integrable second derivatives, and ψα,ⱼ∈𝓗. It restricts c₂ to be nonnegative whereas §7.3 initially allows c₂∈ℝ. Its unit-normalized rows with separate weights give the same seminorm as the paper's scaled orthogonal rows. The formal choice m=1 is permitted even in the presence of a half-period symmetry, whereas (7.6) chooses m=2 then; this doubles Smax/m in the two size bounds. The statement assumes these conditions for the supplied data; it does not verify a numerical instance.

Conclusion and change of data. Assume all formal certificate conditions, with reference Wʳ, approximate profile Wᵃ and ϑ=(c₁+c₀)cᵣ<1. Replace Wʳ by Wᵃ, set the two transfer errors to zero, divide c₁,c₂,c₀ and the directional residual bound by 1−ϑ, divide the row weights by (1−ϑ)², and use the final frozen-form bound for the new reference. The resulting data again satisfy every certificate condition. This is the transfer argument after (7.21), including the resulting changes of constants. It is a preservation statement conditional on a valid certificate; it does not establish the original numerical inequalities.
Breakdown.isExtendedCertificate_atProfil.summary: Given a valid certificate with ϑ=(c₁+c₀)cᵣ<1, replacing Wʳ by Wᵃ, zeroing the transfer errors, dividing c₁,c₂,c₀ and the directional residual bound by 1−ϑ and the row weights by (1−ϑ)² gives data satisfying every certificate condition. This is the transfer after (7.21).

Breakdown.isExtendedCertificate_withUnit.text:
Hypotheses. Assume data satisfying all the following certificate conditions.

The formal statement imposes the following conditions for an integer k≥0, a set J⊆{1,…,k}, and K={α∈ℝᵏ: |αⱼ|≤ρⱼ for j∈J, ∑ⱼ∉J(dⱼαⱼ)²≤ρ*²}. The symmetry set Γ consists of pairs (R,θ₀)∈O(3)×ℝ, with invariance v(θ+θ₀,Ry)=Rv(θ,y), pointwise for approximate profiles and almost everywhere for perturbations. Conditions involving α hold for every α∈K unless all parameters are explicitly specified. This is the certificate of §§7.2–7.3 in a specific representation, with the differences stated below. Write 𝓗=L²((0,1)×ℝ³), ℓᵢ(v)=⟨∇v,Ξᵢ⟩𝓗, ‖v‖²w=∫₀¹∫(|Δv|²+w|∇v|²), and ‖(v,β)‖²w,ω=‖v‖²w+ω²|β|².

Parameter and scalar conditions. The selected radii and ρ* are nonnegative and every dⱼ is nonzero. The weight satisfies 0<w*≤w(y)≤wmax, is measurable and Γ-invariant. The force weight ω is positive. The constants c₁,c₂,c₀,cᵣ, the frozen-form transfer bound, b*, the reference-form bound and ε are nonnegative. Writing c₃ʳ for the reference-form bound, η₃ for the frozen-form transfer bound and c₃ for the final bound, one has c₃ʳ+η₃≤c₃. M and c_L are positive. With ϑ=(c₁+c₀)cᵣ, one has ϑ<1 and c₁+c₀≤(1−ϑ)c_L. S is continuous on K with 0<S(α)≤Smax. The positive integer m is 1 or is 2 with an orthogonal half-period symmetry in Γ. βᵃ and the total-field target t are continuous on K.

Approximate and reference fields. Wᵃ is jointly C¹ in all parameters, time and space, is period one for all parameters, and on K is solenoidal and Γ-invariant. One common D bounds |Wᵃ|, |DWᵃ| and the supplied Hessian |Hᵃ| by D/(1+|y|), D/(1+|y|)² and D/(1+|y|)³, respectively; the derivative norms in these three bounds are operator norms. The gradients in 𝓗 and in the weighted energies instead have the Frobenius norm. Hᵃ is jointly measurable up to null sets and period one, and at every time is the distributional derivative of DWᵃ. The supplied pressure-gradient representative hα is jointly measurable up to null sets, period one and has zero pairing with every compactly supported solenoidal space-time test. Each bᵢ is measurable, periodic, Γ-invariant almost everywhere and ∑ᵢ‖bᵢ‖²𝓗≤b*². Each Ξᵢ is jointly measurable up to null sets with finite L² norm on [0,1]×ℝ³; its values outside that interval are unused, so its periodicity is not a condition. Wʳα is jointly C¹ in time and space and period one. The change (Wᵃ−Wʳ)·∇v+v·∇(Wᵃ−Wʳ) has 𝓗 norm at most cᵣ‖v‖w for every admissible perturbation; for each time and admissible spatial u, Q_Wᵃ(u)−Q_Wʳ(u)≥−η₃|u|²w, where Q_P(u)=∫(|Δu|²+¼|∇u|²)−∫[(P·∇)u+(u·∇)P]·Δu is the form in (7.22).

A priori estimates. The finite row family eₐ is measurable, periodic, square integrable and orthonormal, with 0≤τₐ≤c₀². Define [F]²=∑ₐτₐ⟨F,eₐ⟩². A weak perturbation is represented by v,g:ℝ×ℝ³→ℝ³, a linear-map field G and a bilinear-map field H, all jointly measurable up to null sets and pointwise period one in θ. For almost every θ, v,G,H are locally integrable in space, G=∇v and H(a,eⱼ)=∂ₐ(Geⱼ) distributionally, div v=tr G=0 almost everywhere, and v(θ)∈L⁶(ℝ³). Require G, tr H and g in 𝓗, with the Frobenius norm for G and tr H=∑ⱼH(eⱼ,eⱼ). Against every compactly supported smooth vector test on ℝ×ℝ³, g represents S⁻¹∂θv+½v+½(y·∇)v. For each (R,θ₀)∈Γ require v(θ+θ₀,Ry)=Rv(θ,y) almost everywhere in space and time. This specifies representatives and their distributional identities; it does not require the chosen v to be continuous in time. In these certificate conditions S>0. Put 𝓣ˢv=g−tr H. For a reference P, the equation F≃𝓣ˢv+(P·∇)v+(v·∇)P+∑ᵢβᵢbᵢ means that, for every compactly supported smooth solenoidal test φ, ∫F·φ=∫[(g+GP+(DP)v+∑ᵢβᵢbᵢ)·φ+G:∇φ], integrated over ℝ×ℝ³. Here F is jointly measurable up to a null set, pointwise period one and in 𝓗; F is not required to be solenoidal or Γ-invariant.

For every such perturbation, every β∈ℝᵏ and every such F with P=Wʳ, one has ‖(v,β)‖w,ω≤c₁‖F‖𝓗+[F]+c₂|ℓ(v)|. For the frozen-time estimates, a spatial test field is represented by u,Gᵤ,Hᵤ with locally integrable weak derivatives Gᵤ=∇u and Hᵤ(a,eⱼ)=∂ₐ(Gᵤeⱼ), div u=0, u∈L⁶(ℝ³), and Gᵤ,tr Hᵤ∈L²(ℝ³). It obeys u(Ry)=Ru(y) almost everywhere for each (R,0)∈Γ. Write |u|²w=∫ℝ³(|tr Hᵤ|²+w|Gᵤ|²), with the Frobenius norm for Gᵤ. All unlabelled space integrals use Lebesgue measure. At every normalized time θ and for every such spatial field, the reference form satisfies Q_Wʳ(u)≥−c₃ʳ|u|²w.

Residual and size bounds. The residual is Fᵃ=S⁻¹∂θWᵃ+½Wᵃ+½(y·∇)Wᵃ−tr Hᵃ+(Wᵃ·∇)Wᵃ+∑ᵢβᵢᵃbᵢ+hα; θ=s/S is normalized time, and tr Hᵃ=∑ⱼHᵃ[eⱼ,eⱼ] represents ΔWᵃ. Nonnegative δ,δ₀ satisfy ‖Fᵃ‖𝓗≤δ≤δmax and [Fᵃ]≤δ₀. With ℓ̄=t−ℓ(Wᵃ), c₁δ+δ₀+c₂|ℓ̄|≤(1−ϑ)ε. For c_w=(4π√w*)⁻¹ᐟ² and L=Smax/m the required inequalities are 2c_Lc_wM<1; 4ε²(1/w*+2Lc₃+2Lb*/ω+2L/c_L)≤M²; and 4(1/w*+2Lc₃)ε²+4Lε(δmax+2c_wεM+2b*ε/ω)≤M². Finally 4ε²/w*<‖∇Wᵃ‖²𝓗 ensures nontriviality.

Adjoint bounds and parameter inclusion. The real matrix V is invertible; Vⱼ denotes its jth column, so Vⱼ·x=∑ᵢVᵢⱼxᵢ. The real coefficients Y=Y(α) are supplied and may depend on α. For j∈J, ψα,ⱼ is measurable and period one, with a nonnegative uniform-in-time spatial L² bound Lⱼ; the linear and quadratic error bounds aⱼ,ãⱼ are nonnegative. For every admissible v, |⟨(v·∇)v,ψα,ⱼ⟩|≤ãⱼ‖v‖²w. Put 𝓒αv=(Wᵃα·∇)v+(v·∇)Wᵃα. For every F with the measurability, periodicity and L² conditions above satisfying F≃𝓣ˢv+𝓒αv, |⟨F,ψα,ⱼ⟩−(Yℓ(v))ⱼ|≤aⱼ‖v‖w. The offset is bounded by |Vⱼ·βᵃ−⟨Fᵃ,ψα,ⱼ⟩−(Yℓ̄)ⱼ−dⱼαⱼ|≤oⱼ, and ãⱼ(2ε)²+2ε√(aⱼ²+|⟨b,ψα,ⱼ⟩−Vⱼ|²/ω²)+oⱼ≤|dⱼ|ρⱼ. For the other coordinates a*≥0, ∑ⱼ∉J(Vⱼ·x)²≤a*²|x|² for every x, √(∑ⱼ∉J(Vⱼ·βᵃ−dⱼαⱼ)²)≤o*, and 2εa*/ω+o*≤ρ*.

Comparison. The core estimates are (7.18)–(7.37). The formal statement additionally requires global C¹ parameter dependence, a pointwise Hessian decay bound and a uniform-in-time L² bound for each adjoint field; the paper's displayed assumptions only require joint continuity of Wᵃ and its time and spatial first derivatives on K, locally integrable second derivatives, and ψα,ⱼ∈𝓗. It restricts c₂ to be nonnegative whereas §7.3 initially allows c₂∈ℝ. Its unit-normalized rows with separate weights give the same seminorm as the paper's scaled orthogonal rows. The formal choice m=1 is permitted even in the presence of a half-period symmetry, whereas (7.6) chooses m=2 then; this doubles Smax/m in the two size bounds. The statement assumes these conditions for the supplied data; it does not verify a numerical instance.

Conclusion and change of data. Assume all certificate conditions of §§7.2–7.3 in the formal representation, in particular ω>0. Divide the forcing fields bᵢ, bound b*, frame matrix V and remaining-coordinate bound a* by ω, multiply βᵃ by ω, and set the force weight to one. The theorem states that these transformed data satisfy all the same certificate conditions. The positivity hypothesis prevents division by zero; the residual force is unchanged. This is an auxiliary rescaling of the certificate, not a claim that a numerical certificate has been found and not the profile-existence conclusion of Theorem 7.1.
Breakdown.isExtendedCertificate_withUnit.summary: Given a valid certificate with ω>0, dividing bᵢ, b*, V and a* by ω, multiplying βᵃ by ω and setting the force weight to one gives data satisfying all the same conditions. This is an auxiliary rescaling, not a numerical certificate or the conclusion of Theorem 7.1.

Breakdown.isUnit_one_add_of_isCompactOpe.text: Let $E$ be a real Banach space and let $K:E\to E$ be a compact bounded linear operator. If $I+K$ is injective, the formal statement proves that there is a bounded linear operator $L:E\to E$ with $L(I+K)=(I+K)L=I$. Thus $I+K$ is bijective and has a bounded inverse. Completeness of $E$ is an explicit hypothesis, and the conclusion is for bounded linear operators, not only algebraic linear maps. No Hilbert structure, symmetry, fluid equation, finite-dimensional parameter or sign condition is assumed. In Proposition 7.8 one applies this result to $E=\mathcal H_{\rm div}^{\Gamma}\times\mathbb R^n$ and $K=\mathcal Q$, once compactness and injectivity have been established. This is the exact functional-analytic step that turns injectivity into surjectivity.
Breakdown.isUnit_one_add_of_isCompactOpe.summary: On a real Banach space, if $K$ is compact and $I+K$ is injective, then $I+K$ has a bounded two-sided inverse. In Proposition 7.8 it applies to $E=\mathcal H_{\rm div}^\Gamma\times\mathbb R^n$, $K=\mathcal Q$, turning injectivity into surjectivity.

Breakdown.iterProd.text: For operators $S_0,S_1,\ldots$, the formal object at natural index $k$ is $S_{k-1}\cdots S_1S_0$, defined recursively by the empty product $I$ at $k=0$ and by left multiplication by $S_k$ at the next index. Operator multiplication means composition, so $S_0$ acts first. The definition is valid in any monoid and carries no boundedness, invertibility or periodicity hypothesis. In §4 the operators are the bounded endpoint maps of successive short linearized intervals. The monodromy is $\rho_R^{-1}S_{k-1}\cdots S_0$; the inverse twist is not part of this ordered-product definition.
Breakdown.iterProd.summary: Defines the ordered product $S_{k-1}\cdots S_1S_0$, equal to $I$ at $k=0$, with $S_0$ acting first. The monodromy is $\rho_R^{-1}S_{k-1}\cdots S_0$; the inverse twist is not part of this definition.

Breakdown.le_add_of_sq_le.text: For real numbers P,a,Q with P≥0, a≥0 and Q≥0, the theorem proves that P²≤aP+Q² implies P≤a+Q. It has no function-space or differential-equation assumptions. In Lemma B.2 one takes P²=(3/50)‖(v,β)‖_{w,ω}²+c_μ‖v‖_μ², Q²=(3/50)[F]²+1000|ℓ(v)|² and a=c_M‖F‖_H. Their nonnegativity follows from the norm and coefficient assumptions; finiteness must already have been established before applying this real-variable statement.
Breakdown.le_add_of_sq_le.summary: For real P,a,Q≥0, P²≤aP+Q² implies P≤a+Q. In Lemma B.2 it is applied with P² the weighted energy, Q² the forcing terms and a=c_M‖F‖_H, once finiteness has been established.

Breakdown.matInner.text: For real linear maps G,K:ℝ³→ℝ³, the pairing is ∑ᵢ(G eᵢ)·(K eᵢ). In coordinates G eᵢ has components ∂ᵢvⱼ when G=∇v, so this equals the matrix contraction used for ∇v and Ξᵢ in (7.11). The order of derivative and vector indices is fixed by this convention; no transpose is silently inserted. The formula applies to arbitrary matrices.
Breakdown.matInner.summary: ∑ᵢ(G eᵢ)·(K eᵢ) for real linear maps G,K on ℝ³, the matrix contraction used for ∇v and Ξᵢ in (7.11) when G=∇v. The index order is fixed by this convention, with no transpose inserted.

Breakdown.matSq.text: For a real linear map $G:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$, this defines $\sum_{i=1}^3|Ge_i|^2$, the squared Frobenius norm. With $G=Df(x)$ it is exactly the paper's $|\nabla f(x)|^2=\sum_i|\partial_i f(x)|^2$. The definition is purely algebraic and does not assert that $G$ is a derivative or that the resulting function of $x$ is integrable. It differs from the squared operator norm used for the spatial derivative in several profile hypotheses; one has $\|G\|_{\rm op}^2\le\sum_i|Ge_i|^2\le3\|G\|_{\rm op}^2$.
Breakdown.matSq.summary: Defines $\sum_{i=1}^3|Ge_i|^2$, the squared Frobenius norm, which for $G=Df(x)$ is the paper's $|\nabla f(x)|^2$. It differs from the squared operator norm: $\|G\|_{\rm op}^2\le\sum_i|Ge_i|^2\le3\|G\|_{\rm op}^2$.

Breakdown.meanField.text: For W(θ,y), take the real part of its raw (0,0) mode at normalized time zero. Equivalently this averages R₋φW(τ,Rφy) over 0≤τ≤1 and 0≤φ≤2π with factor 1/(2π). It is the mean field used by the earlier class-based multiplier to separate the stationary axisymmetric part from finitely many waves. Appendix B.2 instead states its bounds for the whole finite harmonic expansion. No time-independence or reconstruction theorem follows without periodicity and integrability assumptions on W.
Breakdown.meanField.summary: The real part of the raw (0,0) mode of W at normalized time zero, the average of R₋φW(τ,Rφy) over τ and φ with factor 1/(2π). It is the mean field of the earlier class-based multiplier; Appendix B.2 bounds the whole harmonic expansion instead.

Breakdown.mildRegular_realization.text: The formal theorem proves the following regularity property for the concrete Fourier realization $g(\xi)=2\pi|\xi|\widehat u(\xi)$ of $X=\dot H^1_{\mathrm{div}}(\mathbb R^3)$. Let $\varphi:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ be smooth, compactly supported and divergence-free, and let $T>0$. Suppose $u$ is a continuous mild curve in the homogeneous solenoidal $H^1$ space on the closed interval $[0,T]$, with initial element equal to the embedded $\varphi$. Here mild means $u(t)=G(t)u(0)+\int_0^t K(t-s)(u(s),u(s))\,ds$ for every $0\le t\le T$, with each time integral Bochner integrable; $G$ and $K$ are the heat and bilinear operators supplied by the realization. The formal conclusion supplies fields $U:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ and $P:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$, smooth up to the time boundary of $[0,T]\times\mathbb R^3$. They satisfy $U(0,x)=\varphi(x)$, $\operatorname{div}U=0$ on the closed interval, and $\partial_tU+(U\cdot\nabla)U=\Delta U-\nabla P$ for $0<t<T$. For some finite constants $A,B$, $\int|U(t,x)|^2dx\le A$ for every $t\in[0,T]$, and $|U(t,x)|\le B$, $\|D_xU(t,x)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le B$ for every such $t$ and every $x$. The last derivative bound is pointwise in space and uniform in time; it is not a bound on the spatial $L^2$ norm of the gradient. For each $t\in[0,T]$, the reconstructed $L^6$ velocity of $u(t)$ equals $U(t,\cdot)$ almost everywhere. There is no constraint on the extensions outside the time interval. The heat and bilinear terms are the frequency construction of the Navier–Stokes mild equation. The theorem proves existence of these representatives from the stated mild solution and initial datum. It treats compact time intervals, gives an unspecified energy bound, and does not itself state energy nonincrease, a representative on the entire half-open lifespan, or the torus assertion in Lemma 2.3.
Breakdown.mildRegular_realization.summary: For the whole-space Fourier realization, a continuous mild curve on $[0,T]$ from a test field $\varphi$ has smooth $U,P$ solving Navier–Stokes on $0<t<T$, with bounded energy and pointwise bounds, and $U(t)$ equal a.e. to its velocity. It omits energy nonincrease and the torus case of Lemma 2.3.

Breakdown.mildUnique.text: Let $\mathcal X$ be a real Banach space. Assume that $G(t)$, $t\geq0$, is a strongly continuous contraction semigroup, and that $K(\tau)$ is a symmetric bounded bilinear map on $\mathcal X$, continuous in $\tau>0$ on each pair of arguments. Assume $\|K(\tau)\|\leq C_K\tau^{-3/4}$ for $0<\tau\leq1$ and $G(s)K(\tau)=K(s+\tau)$ for $s\geq0$, $\tau>0$. If two continuous curves $u,v$ each satisfy $u(t)=G(t-a)u(a)+\int_a^tK(t-s)(u(s),u(s))\,ds$, with the analogous equation for $v$, and have the same initial value at $a$, they agree at every time of their common interval. The formal statement supplies this conclusion both on $[a,b)$ and on $[a,b]$, with convergence of each integral included in the definition of a mild solution. It applies to arbitrary real Banach spaces satisfying the stated semigroup and kernel assumptions. The proof uses short intervals; it does not require the exponentially weighted norm used in the paper’s proof of Lemma 3.4.
Breakdown.mildUnique.summary: On a real Banach space with the semigroup and kernel assumptions, two continuous mild solutions with the same value at $a$ agree on $[a,b)$ and on $[a,b]$. The proof uses short intervals, not the weighted norm of the paper's proof of Lemma 3.4.

Breakdown.modeAverage.text: For raw indices (n,k)∈ℤ² and a real scalar function f(τ,φ;b), the output is (2π)⁻¹∫₀¹∫₀²πexp(−i(2πnτ+kφ))f(τ,φ;b)dφ dτ. The auxiliary argument b is retained and can index vector or tensor components. This is the scalar Fourier average used in (B.12); the paper's harmonic label ι has raw indices (2ι₂−ι₁,ϰι₁). Time is already normalized, so the only prefactor is 1/(2π). The definition supplies no integrability assumption; a nonintegrable complex integral receives the default zero value.
Breakdown.modeAverage.summary: (2π)⁻¹∫₀¹∫₀²πexp(−i(2πnτ+kφ))f(τ,φ;b)dφ dτ for raw indices (n,k), the scalar Fourier average of (B.12), with the paper's label ι giving (2ι₂−ι₁,ϰι₁). A nonintegrable integral is taken as zero.

Breakdown.modeGrad.text: For a matrix field G(θ,y), the raw mode (n,k) averages R₋φG(θ+τ,Rφy)Rφ against exp(−i(2πnτ+kφ))/(2π). Entry (a,b) has vector component a and differentiation direction b. The inner integral is over 0≤φ≤2π and the outer integral over 0≤τ≤1. Each ordinary integral has value zero when its own integrand is not integrable. If G=∇v and spatial differentiation commutes with these averages, the result represents ∇v̂ in (B.16); joint C¹ regularity on time and space is a sufficient condition locally for these compact averaging intervals. The paper writes (∇v)ⱼₖ=∂ⱼvₖ, so its displayed matrix has the reversed index order; Frobenius norms and pairings agree after this consistent reindexing. Raw indices relate to the paper by (n,k)=(2ι₂−ι₁,ϰι₁). This definition alone does not identify G as a derivative or ensure convergence of its integrals.
Breakdown.modeGrad.summary: The raw mode (n,k) averages R₋φG(θ+τ,Rφy)Rφ against exp(−i(2πnτ+kφ))/(2π). Its output-first matrix is the transpose of the paper’s convention; it gives ∇v̂ in (B.16) when G=∇v and differentiation commutes with the averages.

Breakdown.modeSecondDeriv.text: For a bilinear vector field H(θ,y), the raw mode (n,k) averages R₋φH(θ+τ,Rφy)[Rφe_b,Rφe_c] in component a against exp(−i(2πnτ+kφ))/(2π). Its entries are ordered (vector component, first derivative direction, second derivative direction). The inner integral is over 0≤φ≤2π and the outer integral over 0≤τ≤1. Each ordinary integral has value zero when its own integrand is not integrable. If H=∇²v and spatial differentiation twice commutes with these averages, the result is the Hessian of v̂ in (B.16); joint C² regularity is a sufficient local condition for these compact averaging intervals. The two input directions are both rotated. The paper's label ι means (n,k)=(2ι₂−ι₁,ϰι₁). The formula imposes no symmetry, integrability or weak-derivative identity on arbitrary H.
Breakdown.modeSecondDeriv.summary: The raw mode (n,k) averages R₋φH(θ+τ,Rφy)[Rφe_b,Rφe_c] against exp(−i(2πnτ+kφ))/(2π). It gives ∇²v̂ in (B.16) when H=∇²v and differentiation commutes with averaging; the formula itself assumes no derivative identity.

Breakdown.modeVel.text: For a real vector field v:ℝ×ℝ³→ℝ³ and integer frequency pair (j,j′), this defines the complex mode (2π)^{−1}∫₀¹∫₀^{2π}e^{−i(2πjθ′+j′φ′)}R_{−φ′}v(θ+θ′,R_{φ′}y),dφ′,dθ′. Thus vectors are rotated back before averaging. For (j,j′)=(2ι₂−ι₁,κι₁), it is precisely the mode hat v_ι of (B.12). Time is represented on all of ℝ and period 1 is a separate hypothesis. The integrals are ordinary componentwise integrals when the orbit is integrable; their everywhere-defined convention assigns zero to a failed integral. The mode transformation theorems impose the required orbit integrability.
Breakdown.modeVel.summary: Defines the complex mode (2π)^{−1}∫₀¹∫₀^{2π}e^{−i(2πjθ′+j′φ′)}R_{−φ′}v(θ+θ′,R_{φ′}y)dφ′dθ′, rotating vectors back before averaging. For (j,j′)=(2ι₂−ι₁,κι₁) it is the mode hat v_ι of (B.12). A failed integral is assigned zero.

Breakdown.monodromy.text: Let $\mathcal X$ be a real Hilbert space. Let $G(t)$ be bounded linear operators with $G(0)=I$, $G(s+t)=G(s)G(t)$ and $\|G(t)\|\le1$ for nonnegative times, with $t\mapsto G(t)x$ continuous there. Let $K(\tau)$ be symmetric bounded bilinear maps, continuous for positive $\tau$ on each pair of arguments, with $G(s)K(\tau)=K(s+\tau)$ for $s\ge0,\tau>0$, and $\|K(\tau)\|\le C_K\tau^{-3/4}$ for $0<\tau\le1$. Let $D_\mu$, $\mu>0$, be strongly continuous dilations with $D_1=I$, $D_\mu D_\eta=D_{\mu\eta}$, $\|D_\mu x\|=\mu^{1/4}\|x\|$, $D_\mu G(\mu t)=G(t)D_\mu$, and $\mu D_\mu K(\mu\tau)(x,y)=K(\tau)(D_\mu x,D_\mu y)$. Assume $x\mapsto K(\tau)(f,x)$ is compact for every $\tau>0$ and every $f$ in some dense subset of $\mathcal X$. In the whole-space application $\mathcal X$ is the Fourier realization of $\dot H^1_{\mathrm{div}}(\mathbb R^3)$, $G(t)=e^{t\Delta}$, and $D_\mu f(x)=\sqrt\mu f(\sqrt\mu x)$. Let $\rho$ be a surjective linear isometry, and let $w:\mathbb R\to\mathcal X$ be continuous and nonzero at some time, with $S>0$ and $w(s+S)=\rho w(s)$. Put $\mathcal S(\tau)=D_{e^{-\tau}}G(1-e^{-\tau})$ and $\mathcal K(\tau)(x,y)=D_{e^{-\tau}}K(1-e^{-\tau})(x,y)$. Assume, for every $s'\le s$, that the Bochner integral is integrable and $w(s)=\mathcal S(s-s')w(s')+\int_{s'}^s\mathcal K(s-\sigma)(w(\sigma),w(\sigma))\,d\sigma$. The period acts on the velocity by $\rho_Rf=Rf(R^{-1}\cdot)$ in the physical application. The families $G,K,D$ are defined for all real parameters. Assume also $\rho G(t)=G(t)\rho$, $\rho D_\mu=D_\mu\rho$, and $\rho K(\tau)(x,y)=K(\tau)(\rho x,\rho y)$ for every real $t,\mu,\tau$ and every $x,y\in\mathcal X$. The semigroup, size and dilation laws stated above concern their indicated nonnegative or positive parameter ranges. Choose a positive integer $k$, let $h=S/k$ and $\ell=1-e^{-h}$, and work in $Y=C([0,\ell];\mathcal X)$ with supremum norm. Define $u_n^*(t)=D_{(1-t)^{-1}}w(nh-\log(1-t))$, $A_nz(t)=2\int_0^tK(t-r)(u_n^*(r),z(r))\,dr$, $\Gamma x(t)=G(t)x$, and $Ez=D_{e^{-h}}z(\ell)$. Assume $\|A_n\|\le1/4$ for every natural number $n$. Then $I-A_n$ is invertible with inverse norm at most $4/3$. Set $S_n=E(I-A_n)^{-1}\Gamma$. The assertion is $S_{n+k}=\rho S_n\rho^{-1}$ for every $n$ and that $\mathcal M=\rho^{-1}S_{k-1}\cdots S_0$ differs compactly from $\mathcal M_0=\rho^{-1}(D_{e^{-h}}G(\ell))^k$, with $\|\mathcal M_0\|\le e^{-S/4}$. These are operator assertions for a sufficiently small subdivision. They are the compact-perturbation and norm-bound input to the spectral argument; the assertion does not itself enumerate eigenvalues or state their multiplicities. The operators on $Y$ are defined by their integral formulas when continuous bounded operators with those formulas exist, and by zero otherwise; the heat and bilinear hypotheses ensure the integral constructions exist on the positive interval used here. All indices and powers $k,n$ are natural numbers. The formal statement proves this assertion under precisely the hypotheses just given. The positive subdivision number $k$ and the inequalities $\|A_n\|\le1/4$ are assumptions of this theorem. A separate construction chooses such a subdivision. The paper defines $\mathcal M$ through the single interval $[0,1-e^{-S}]$ in (4.10); the formal statement uses the product over $k$ subintervals.
Breakdown.monodromy.summary: For a supplied $k\ge1$ with $\|A_n\|\le1/4$, each $I-A_n$ has inverse norm at most $4/3$, $S_{n+k}=\rho S_n\rho^{-1}$, and the period map $\mathcal M$ differs by a compact operator from the free map $\mathcal M_0$, with $\|\mathcal M_0\|\le e^{-S/4}$.

Breakdown.orbitBound.text:
Let $\mathcal X$ be a real Hilbert space. The bounded linear families $e^{t\Delta}$ and $D_\mu$ and bounded bilinear family $K(	au)$ are defined at every real parameter. Assume $e^{t\Delta}$ is a strongly continuous contraction semigroup for $t\ge0$, with $e^{0\Delta}=I$. Assume $K(	au)$ is symmetric for every real $	au$, continuous in $	au>0$ on each pair of inputs, with $e^{t\Delta}K(	au)=K(t+	au)$ for $t\ge0,	au>0$ and $\|K(	au)\|\le C_K	au^{-3/4}$ for $0<	au\le1$. For positive $\mu,
u$, assume the dilations satisfy $\|D_\mu x\|=\mu^{1/4}\|x\|$, $D_1=I$, $D_\mu D_
u=D_{\mu
u}$ and strong continuity in $\mu$. Also require $D_\mu e^{\mu t\Delta}=e^{t\Delta}D_\mu$ for $\mu>0,t\ge0$ and $\mu D_\mu K(\mu	au)(x,y)=K(	au)(D_\mu x,D_\mu y)$ for $\mu,	au>0$. For each positive $	au$, $K(	au)(f,\cdot)$ is compact for $f$ in one fixed dense subset of $\mathcal X$. Let $ho$ be a surjective linear isometry, let $S>0$, and let $w:\mathbb R	o\mathcal X$ be continuous, nonzero at some time, and satisfy $w(s+S)=ho w(s)$. Write $A(\sigma)=D_{e^{-\sigma}}e^{(1-e^{-\sigma})\Delta}$ and $B(\sigma)(x,y)=D_{e^{-\sigma}}K(1-e^{-\sigma})(x,y)$. For every $a\le b$, require the Bochner-integrable orbit equation $w(b)=A(b-a)w(a)+\int_a^bB(b-s)(w(s),w(s))\,ds$. The formal theorem concludes that there is $M\in\mathbb R$ with $\|w(s)\|\le M$ for every real $s$. In the whole-space application this norm is $\|
abla W(s,\cdot)\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^3)}$. Continuity and the recurrence up to an isometry make the norm continuous and $S$-periodic, hence bounded on all of $\mathbb R$. This upper-bound theorem does not assume that the isometry commutes with the evolution operators. It provides no estimate for a corrected trajectory and no lower bound. The ambient heat, dilation, and orbit assumptions above specify the stated domain even though the proof of this particular bound uses only continuity and recurrence.
Breakdown.orbitBound.summary: For a recurrent mild orbit, some $M$ gives $\|w(s)\|\le M$ for every real $s$; in the whole-space case this is $\|\nabla W(s)\|_{L^2}$. The proof uses only continuity and recurrence; no lower bound is given.

Breakdown.orbitNorm.text:
Let $X$ be a complete real Hilbert space. Let $G(t)$, for $t\ge0$, be a strongly continuous semigroup of contractions with $G(0)=I$. Let $K(\tau):X\times X\to X$ be symmetric and bounded bilinear, continuous in $\tau>0$ on each pair of vectors, with $\|K(\tau)\|\le C_K\tau^{-3/4}$ for $0<\tau\le1$ and $G(a)K(\tau)=K(a+\tau)$ for $a\ge0$, $\tau>0$. Let $D_\mu$ be a continuous dilation action for $\mu>0$, with $D_1=I$, $D_\mu D_\nu=D_{\mu\nu}$, $\|D_\mu x\|=\mu^{1/4}\|x\|$, $D_\mu G(\mu t)=G(t)D_\mu$ for $t\ge0$, and $\mu D_\mu K(\mu\tau)(x,y)=K(\tau)(D_\mu x,D_\mu y)$. Assume there is a dense set of $f\in X$ for which $K(\tau)(f,\cdot)$ is compact for every $\tau>0$. The families $G,K,D$ are defined on all real parameters; their analytic bounds and scaling properties hold on the ranges just stated.

Let $\rho$ be a linear isometry of $X$ onto itself commuting with $G,K,D$ for all their real parameters. Let $w:\mathbb R\to X$ be continuous, nonzero at some time, and satisfy $w(s+P)=\rho w(s)$ with $P>0$. Put $S(a)=D_{e^{-a}}G(1-e^{-a})$ and $\widetilde K(a)=D_{e^{-a}}K(1-e^{-a})$. For every $a\le s$, assume the integral below exists and $w(s)=S(s-a)w(a)+\int_a^s\widetilde K(s-\sigma)(w(\sigma),w(\sigma))\,d\sigma$.

The formal statement proves that there exists $c>0$ with $\|w(s)\|\ge c$ for every $s\in\mathbb R$. In the whole-space realization the norm is $\dot H^1$, and dilation gives $\|u^*(t)\|\ge c(1-t)^{-1/4}$ for $u^*(t)=D_{(1-t)^{-1}}w(-\log(1-t))$ and $0\le t<1$. The formal conclusion is the lower bound on the recurrent orbit; it does not include a nearby solution $u$, the upper bound in (2.5), the chosen constant $c_*/2$, or uniformity over all nearby data $w_0$. Those require the quantitative correction and a separate upper bound for the orbit.
Breakdown.orbitNorm.summary: For a recurrent mild orbit with $\rho$ commuting with $G,K,D$, some $c>0$ gives $\|w(s)\|\ge c$ for every real $s$. It omits a nearby solution, the upper bound in (2.5), the constant $c_*/2$ and uniformity over nearby data.

Breakdown.orbitPhysical.text:
Let $X$ be a complete real Hilbert space. Let $G(t)$, for $t\ge0$, be a strongly continuous semigroup of contractions with $G(0)=I$. Let $K(\tau):X\times X\to X$ be symmetric and bounded bilinear, continuous in $\tau>0$ on each pair of vectors, with $\|K(\tau)\|\le C_K\tau^{-3/4}$ for $0<\tau\le1$ and $G(a)K(\tau)=K(a+\tau)$ for $a\ge0$, $\tau>0$. Let $D_\mu$ be a continuous dilation action for $\mu>0$, with $D_1=I$, $D_\mu D_\nu=D_{\mu\nu}$, $\|D_\mu x\|=\mu^{1/4}\|x\|$, $D_\mu G(\mu t)=G(t)D_\mu$ for $t\ge0$, and $\mu D_\mu K(\mu\tau)(x,y)=K(\tau)(D_\mu x,D_\mu y)$. Assume there is a dense set of $f\in X$ for which $K(\tau)(f,\cdot)$ is compact for every $\tau>0$. The families $G,K,D$ are defined on all real parameters; their analytic bounds and scaling properties hold on the ranges just stated.

Let $w:\mathbb R\to X$ be continuous. Define $S(a)=D_{e^{-a}}G(1-e^{-a})$ and $\widetilde K(a)=D_{e^{-a}}K(1-e^{-a})$, and assume that for all $a\le s$ the integral exists and $w(s)=S(s-a)w(a)+\int_a^s\widetilde K(s-\sigma)(w(\sigma),w(\sigma))\,d\sigma$. For every phase $s_0\in\mathbb R$, the formal statement proves that $u^*(t)=D_{(1-t)^{-1}}w(s_0-\log(1-t))$ is continuous on $[0,1)$ and is a mild solution there: its bilinear integral exists and $u^*(t)=G(t)u^*(0)+\int_0^tK(t-s)(u^*(s),u^*(s))\,ds$. This makes the Duhamel defect zero in §5.2. Recurrence, nonvanishing and a positive period are unnecessary for this theorem. For the whole-space realization, $D_\mu$ is the physical dilation $f(x)\mapsto\sqrt\mu f(\sqrt\mu x)$ and $X$ represents the homogeneous $H^1$ norm. The time-dependent function is defined on all of $\mathbb R$, but its asserted solution property is only on $[0,1)$.
Breakdown.orbitPhysical.summary: If $w$ is continuous and solves the similarity-time mild equation for all $a\le s$, then for every phase $s_0$, $u^*(t)=D_{(1-t)^{-1}}w(s_0-\log(1-t))$ is continuous and a mild solution on $[0,1)$. Recurrence, nonvanishing and a positive period are not needed.

Breakdown.orbitSeq.text: For a bounded linear operator $M$ on a real normed space, a real number $\theta$, a source sequence $(c_n)_{n\ge0}$ and an initial vector $x_0$, this defines $x_{n+1}=\theta^{-1}(Mx_n+c_n)$ for natural $n\ge0$. No boundedness, decay or solvability assertion accompanies the definition. In applications $0<\theta<1$, and the bounded sequence $x_n$ represents an unweighted sequence divided by its desired geometric decay. The paper’s recurrence $\chi_{n+1}=\mathcal M\chi_n+f_n$ becomes this formula after the corresponding normalization of both $\chi_n$ and $f_n$. Division by zero is defined as zero; if $\theta=0$, the definition would set every $x_{n+1}$ to zero. The dichotomy results require $\theta>0$ and exclude that case.
Breakdown.orbitSeq.summary: Defines $x_{n+1}=\theta^{-1}(Mx_n+c_n)$ from $x_0$, the paper's recurrence $\chi_{n+1}=\mathcal M\chi_n+f_n$ after normalization by the geometric decay. Division by zero is taken as zero, so $\theta=0$ sets every $x_{n+1}$ to zero; the dichotomy results require $\theta>0$.

Breakdown.periodBallLIntegral.text: For a real radius r and density f(θ,y), this is the [0,∞]-valued integral of max(f,0) over [0,1]×{y∈ℝ³:|y|≤r}. It is the spatially localized counterpart of the period integral of §7.1, used by the earlier certificate with a local forcing norm. The current (7.17) instead uses finitely many directional pairings. If r<0 the ball is empty and the integral is zero; the definition itself does not assume r>0. For r>0 the closed and open balls have the same integral for Lebesgue-measurable densities.
Breakdown.periodBallLIntegral.summary: The [0,∞]-valued integral of max(f,0) over [0,1]×{|y|≤r}, the localized period integral behind the earlier certificate's local forcing norm; the current (7.17) uses directional pairings instead. For r<0 the ball is empty and the integral is zero.

Breakdown.periodBallNorm.text: For radius r and vector field F(θ,y), this is the square root of the integral of |F|² over [0,1]×{|y|≤r}, provided that integral is finite. It measures a local forcing term in the earlier certificate version. Its infinite-integral convention is zero, and it is also zero for r<0 because the ball is empty. This local L² norm is different from the finite family of directional pairings [F] in (7.17); those two measurements should not be identified.
Breakdown.periodBallNorm.summary: The square root of ∫|F|² over [0,1]×{|y|≤r} when finite, and zero when infinite or r<0: the local forcing norm of the earlier certificate. It is different from the directional pairings [F] in (7.17).

Breakdown.periodLIntegral.text: For a real density f(θ,y), this is ∫_[0,1]∫ℝ³ max(f(θ,y),0)dy dθ, with values in [0,∞], including infinity. The time variable is θ=s/S, so no extra factor S is present. This agrees with the integrals over one period at the start of §7.1 and in (7.14) when f is nonnegative and measurable. For a signed density it integrates only its positive part; it is not its signed integral. Closed rather than open time endpoints make no difference to Lebesgue integration.
Breakdown.periodLIntegral.summary: ∫_[0,1]∫ℝ³ max(f,0)dy dθ in [0,∞], with no factor S since θ=s/S. It agrees with the period integrals of §7.1 and (7.14) for nonnegative measurable f; for a signed density it integrates only the positive part.

Breakdown.periodNorm.text: For a vector field $F$ the expression is the square root of $\int_{[0,1]}\int_{\mathbb R^3}|F|^2$, after converting that extended nonnegative integral to a real number. Finite values are preserved; an infinite value is converted to zero. Consequently this is the $\mathcal H$ norm only under a finite-integral hypothesis. All uses as a certificate residual norm carry such a hypothesis. The vector norm is Euclidean, and the endpoints of the time interval do not affect the integral.
Breakdown.periodNorm.summary: Defines the square root of $\int_{[0,1]}\int|F|^2$; an infinite integral is converted to zero. So it is the $\mathcal H$ norm only under a finite-integral hypothesis, which every certificate use carries.

Breakdown.periodPairing.text: For two vector fields $F,G$ this expression is $\int_{[0,1]}\int_{\mathbb R^3}F(\theta,y)\cdot G(\theta,y)\,dy\,d\theta$. It is the real $\mathcal H$ inner product when both fields are square integrable over a period; Cauchy–Schwarz supplies integrability. The signed integrals are defined for all input functions, with zero used when the relevant integrability condition fails. Thus the formula must be read together with its function-space hypotheses. The interval endpoints have measure zero.
Breakdown.periodPairing.summary: Defines $\int_{[0,1]}\int_{\mathbb R^3}F\cdot G$, the real $\mathcal H$ inner product when both fields are square integrable over a period. Each of the two signed integrals is assigned zero if its own integrand is not integrable.

Breakdown.periodPairing_abs_le.text: For two jointly measurable real vector fields F and M with ∫₀¹∫ℝ³|F|²<∞ and ∫₀¹∫ℝ³|M|²<∞, one has |∫₀¹∫F·M|≤(∫₀¹∫|F|²)¹ᐟ²(∫₀¹∫|M|²)¹ᐟ². No periodicity or solenoidality is assumed. This is exactly the Cauchy–Schwarz estimate used in Lemma B.2. Finiteness ensures that the formal real-valued norm formulas represent the true L² norms rather than their default value for infinite integrals.
Breakdown.periodPairing_abs_le.summary: For jointly measurable real vector fields F,M with finite period integrals of |F|² and |M|², |∫₀¹∫F·M|≤(∫₀¹∫|F|²)¹ᐟ²(∫₀¹∫|M|²)¹ᐟ². This is the Cauchy–Schwarz estimate of Lemma B.2; no periodicity or solenoidality is assumed.

Breakdown.periodicInverse.text: The inverse acts on sequences of continuous interval functions. Its first output is an exceptional coordinate e; the compactly supported initial correction is Je.

Breakdown.physicalField.text: For any $W:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ and real phase $s_0$, the field at $t<1$ is $u(t,x)=(1-t)^{-1/2}W(s_0-\log(1-t),x/\sqrt{1-t})$. Thus it agrees with (1.4) for $T=1$ and $s_0=0$. It is a definition of the change of variables, with no smoothness, equation, or recurrence hypothesis. With a general $T>0$ the paper's field satisfies $u_T^*(t,x)=T^{-1/2}u_1^*(t/T,x/\sqrt T)$ when the phase is zero. The formal function is defined at every real time; division by zero and the square root of a nonpositive number are assigned zero, so the defined field is zero for $t\ge1$. No claim of a solution at those times follows. All uses of the change of variables in the evolution restrict to $t<1$.
Breakdown.physicalField.summary: Defines $u(t,x)=(1-t)^{-1/2}W(s_0-\log(1-t),x/\sqrt{1-t})$, agreeing with (1.4) for $T=1$, $s_0=0$. It has no hypotheses; by the conventions it is zero for $t\ge1$, with no solution claim there.

Breakdown.physicalMild_unconditional.text:
Let $W:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ and $q:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$ be smooth, solve $\partial_sW+\tfrac12W+\tfrac12(y\cdot\nabla)W-\Delta W+(W\cdot\nabla)W+\nabla q=0$, and satisfy $\operatorname{div}W=0$. Assume, for one real $C$, $\|D_y^jW(s,y)\|\le C(1+|y|)^{-j-1}$ for the natural-number orders $j=0,1,2$ and $\|D_yq(s,y)\|\le C(1+|y|)^{-3}$, uniformly in $s,y$. The derivative norms here are operator norms; the paper’s pointwise gradient norm is the sum-of-squares norm of its coordinate derivatives.

An element of the paper’s $X$ represents a divergence-free field on $\mathbb R^3$ in $L^6$ with square-integrable gradient. Its norm is exactly $(\int_{\mathbb R^3}\sum_{i=1}^3|\partial_i u|^2)^{1/2}$; the formal representation is a closed real subspace of a complex Fourier $L^2$ space. 

In this concrete space, $G(t)=e^{t\Delta}$ and $K(\tau)(f,g)=-\tfrac12e^{\tau\Delta}\mathbb P[(f\cdot\nabla)g+(g\cdot\nabla)f]$, where $\mathbb P$ is the Leray projection. The formal assertion also allows any real Hilbert model supplied with the heat, bilinear and positive-dilation identities of §3.4, a homogeneous $H^1$ norm embedding respecting subtraction, nonvanishing, rotations and dilations, and the following weak-to-mild property: a decay-field curve with continuous embedded values, pairwise $L^2$ increments continuous in $L^2$, continuous pairings with compact solenoidal test fields, and the pressure-free weak derivative identity against those tests satisfies the mild equation. The test-field images form a dense linear subspace. 

Assume the map $s\mapsto W(s,\cdot)$ is continuous in the homogeneous $H^1$ norm and use any realization preserving that norm and the equation. For every phase $s_0\in\mathbb R$ and $0<T<1$, the formal statement proves that $u(t,x)=(1-t)^{-1/2}W(s_0-\log(1-t),x/\sqrt{1-t})$, represented in $X$, is continuous on $[0,T]$ and satisfies $u(t)=G(t)u(0)+\int_0^tK(t-r)(u(r),u(r))\,dr$ there, with an integrable integrand. No recurrence or nonvanishing is assumed or concluded in this statement. Its quantification over all $T<1$ supplies mildness on every compact subinterval of $[0,1)$. The functions are formally defined at all real times, but the conclusion is restricted to $0\le t\le T<1$.
Breakdown.physicalMild_unconditional.summary: If the slices of the decaying smooth similarity profile $W$ are continuous in the homogeneous $H^1$ norm, then for every phase $s_0$ and $0<T<1$, $u(t,x)=(1-t)^{-1/2}W(s_0-\log(1-t),x/\sqrt{1-t})$ is continuous and mild on $[0,T]$. No recurrence or nonvanishing is assumed.

Breakdown.physicalPressure.text: For any scalar field $q:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$ and phase $s_0\in\mathbb R$, this defines $p(t,x)=(1-t)^{-1}q(s_0-\log(1-t),x/\sqrt{1-t})$ when $t<1$. It is the pressure accompanying the velocity transformation (1.4) at final time one. The definition asserts no equation, smoothness, periodicity, or pressure normalization. It is defined at all times by the assigned values of reciprocal, logarithm and square root; at $t=1$ the prefactor is zero, while at $t>1$ the spatial argument is zero and the prefactor is negative. Those values are outside the physical interval and do not assert a continuation. On $t<1$, every denominator and logarithm argument has the usual positive-domain meaning.
Breakdown.physicalPressure.summary: Defines $p(t,x)=(1-t)^{-1}q(s_0-\log(1-t),x/\sqrt{1-t})$ for $t<1$, the pressure accompanying (1.4) at final time one. It asserts no equation; values for $t\ge1$ are conventions, not a continuation.

Breakdown.physicalScale.text: For $t<1$, the scale is $a(t)=\sqrt{(1-t)^{-1}}=(1-t)^{-1/2}$. Multiplying $x\in\mathbb R^3$ by $a(t)$ gives the similarity position. The function is defined for every real $t$; division by zero is assigned zero, and the real square root of a nonpositive number is zero. Consequently its value is zero at and after $t=1$. These values serve only to define a function everywhere. They do not extend the physical solution through its final time. The paper's general scale is $(T-t)^{-1/2}$ for $t<T$.
Breakdown.physicalScale.summary: Defines $a(t)=(1-t)^{-1/2}$ for $t<1$; by the conventions it is zero for $t\ge1$. The paper's general scale is $(T-t)^{-1/2}$.

Breakdown.physicalTime.text: For a real phase $s_0$ and time $t<1$, this defines $s=s_0-\log(1-t)$. At $s_0=0$ it equals $\log(1/(1-t))$, the similarity time in (1.4) with $T=1$. No equation or profile hypothesis is included. The function is defined for all real $t$: the real logarithm is assigned the value zero at zero and uses the absolute value for a negative argument. These extensions carry no assertion about a solution at or after time one; all physical change-of-variable statements restrict to $t<1$, where $1-t>0$. For a general final time $T>0$, the paper instead uses $\log(T/(T-t))$.
Breakdown.physicalTime.summary: Defines $s=s_0-\log(1-t)$, which at $s_0=0$ is the similarity time $\log(1/(1-t))$ of (1.4) with $T=1$. Values for $t\ge1$ are conventions; the paper uses $\log(T/(T-t))$ for general $T$.

Breakdown.pieceOperator.text: Let $\mathcal X$ be a real Banach space. Write $G(t)$ for a strongly continuous contraction semigroup on $t\ge0$, and let $K(\tau)$ be bounded symmetric real bilinear maps on $\mathcal X$, continuous in $\tau>0$ on each pair of arguments. Assume $G(t)K(\tau)=K(t+\tau)$ for $t\ge0,\tau>0$, and $\|K(\tau)(u,v)\|\le C_K\tau^{-3/4}\|u\|\|v\|$ for $0<\tau\le1$. For $T>0$, put $Y=C([0,T];\mathcal X)$ with the supremum norm. The formal statement proves that the operators $B_T(f,h)(t)=\int_0^tK(t-s)(f(s),h(s))\,ds$ and $\Gamma_Tx(t)=G(t)x$ are bounded bilinear $B_T:Y\times Y\to Y$ and bounded linear $\Gamma_T:\mathcal X\to Y$ operators, respectively. It proves $\|\Gamma_T\|\le1$, and $\|B_T\|\le4C_KT^{1/4}$ for $0<T\le1$. Consequently the linearized integral operator $h\mapsto2B_T(f,h)$ has norm at most $8C_KT^{1/4}\|f\|_\infty$ on such intervals. That last estimate is the direct operator-norm consequence of the displayed bound. A bounded inverse on every finite interval, as in Lemma 3.4, is a further conclusion and is not stated here.
Breakdown.pieceOperator.summary: For $T>0$ and $Y=C([0,T];\mathcal X)$, the theorem identifies bounded $B_T:Y\times Y\to Y$ by Duhamel integration and $\Gamma_T:\mathcal X\to Y$ by heat evolution. Their norms satisfy $\|\Gamma_T\|\le1$ and $\|B_T\|\le4C_KT^{1/4}$ for $T\le1$; no inverse is asserted.

Breakdown.piecePerturbation.text:
The following assertion is proved. Let $\mathcal X$ be a real Banach space with a strongly continuous contraction semigroup $G(t)$ for $t\ge0$ and symmetric bounded bilinear operators $K(\tau)$, continuous for $\tau>0$, with $G(s)K(\tau)=K(s+\tau)$ for $s\ge0$, $\tau>0$, and $\|K(\tau)\|\le C_K\tau^{-3/4}$ for $0<\tau\le1$. In the paper $G(t)=e^{t\Delta}$.

Write $\Gamma_Tx(t)=G(t)x$ and $\mathcal B_T(f,g)(t)=\int_0^tK(t-s)(f(s),g(s))\,ds$. Let $0<T\le1$, let $u^{\mathrm b},v\in C([0,T];\mathcal X)$, and let $x\in\mathcal X$. Assume $u^{\mathrm b}$ is a mild solution and $v=\Gamma_Tx+2\mathcal B_T(u^{\mathrm b},v)+\mathcal B_T(v,v)$.

The formal statement proves $v(0)=x$ and that $u^{\mathrm b}+v$ is a mild solution on $[0,T]$. Integrability and continuity belong to the mild-solution conclusion. Compact-interval curves are extended constantly outside their endpoints for evaluation as real-time functions. The implication proved is from the perturbation identity to an exact mild solution. The paper states an equivalence on $[0,1)$; the formal statement gives the forward implication on each compact interval. It involves an exact background, with no residual term.
Breakdown.piecePerturbation.summary: If $u^{\mathrm b}$ is a mild solution on $[0,T]$, $0<T\le1$, and $v=\Gamma_Tx+2\mathcal B_T(u^{\mathrm b},v)+\mathcal B_T(v,v)$, then $v(0)=x$ and $u^{\mathrm b}+v$ is a mild solution. The paper states an equivalence on $[0,1)$; this proves the forward implication on each compact interval.

Breakdown.pinValue.text:
Given fields $G,\Xi:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^{3\times3}$, represented as linear maps on Euclidean three-space, the definition is
$\displaystyle \int_{[0,1]}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\sum_{j=1}^3(Ge_j)\cdot(\Xi e_j)\,dy\,d\theta.$
For a velocity $v$, the derivative map has entries $G_{ij}=\partial_jv_i$. The paper writes $(\nabla v)_{ji}=\partial_jv_i$, with derivative direction first. Thus the formal matrix is the transpose of the paper's displayed gradient matrix, and the supplied constraint matrix must likewise be the transpose of the paper's $\Xi_i$. Transposing both matrices preserves their Frobenius pairing. With this identification, $G=D_yv$ and both matrix fields square integrable on $(0,1)\times\mathbb R^3$, the scalar is precisely the constraint $\ell_i(v)=\langle\nabla v,\Xi_i\rangle_{\mathcal H}$ in (7.11). Cauchy–Schwarz gives integrability, and the endpoints of $[0,1]$ have measure zero. The definition imposes no weak-derivative identity or integrability hypothesis itself. Each signed integral is assigned zero when its integrand is not integrable; those default values have no interpretation as a constraint pairing without the stated hypotheses.
Breakdown.pinValue.summary: Defines $\int_{[0,1]}\int\sum_j(Ge_j)\cdot(\Xi e_j)$. With $G=\nabla v$, both fields square integrable and $\Xi$ the transpose of the paper's $\Xi_i$, it equals $\ell_i(v)$ of (7.11), a Frobenius pairing. Nonintegrable inputs may return zero.

Breakdown.pushForward.text: For every orthogonal linear map $R:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ and every field $u:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$, this defines $\rho_Ru(x)=R\,u(R^{-1}x)$. The input $R$ includes an inverse and preserves the Euclidean norm, so both rotations and orientation-reversing orthogonal maps are allowed. There is no smoothness or divergence condition on $u$ in this definition. It gives exactly the action in (3.4); preservation of the homogeneous solenoidal $H^1$ space and commutation with the heat flow, dilation and the bilinear term are proved separately. The values are ordinary pointwise values of a field on all of $\mathbb R^3$.
Breakdown.pushForward.summary: Defines $\rho_Ru(x)=Ru(R^{-1}x)$ for orthogonal $R$, allowing rotations and reflections; this is the action in (3.4). Preservation of the homogeneous $H^1$ space and commutation properties are proved separately.

Breakdown.relativeVelocity.text: The vector is W̄(y)+½y−a(y)(e₃×y), where W̄ is the mean time-angle mode of W and a(y) is a real angular rate. This is transport plus the similarity drift after subtracting the rotation velocity. In Appendix B.2 the transport bound applies to Wʳ(θ,y)+½y−νₚe₃×y for the full reference field and a constant rate; the earlier quantity here uses only W̄ and may have a spatially varying rate. The distinction is handled by separate bounds for the remaining waves.
Breakdown.relativeVelocity.summary: W̄(y)+½y−a(y)(e₃×y), with W̄ the mean mode and a(y) a real angular rate: transport plus drift minus rotation. Appendix B.2 bounds Wʳ+½y−νₚe₃×y for the full field with a constant rate; this earlier quantity uses only W̄ and allows a varying rate.

Breakdown.restrict.text: Let $\mathcal X$ be a real Banach space. Write $G(t)$ for a strongly continuous contraction semigroup on $t\ge0$, and let $K(\tau)$ be bounded symmetric real bilinear maps on $\mathcal X$, continuous in $\tau>0$ on each pair of arguments. Assume $G(t)K(\tau)=K(t+\tau)$ for $t\ge0,\tau>0$, and $\|K(\tau)(u,v)\|\le C_K\tau^{-3/4}\|u\|\|v\|$ for $0<\tau\le1$. The formal statement proves the following implication. Let $a\le m\le t$, and let $u:\mathbb R\to\mathcal X$ be continuous on $[a,t]$. Suppose the quadratic Duhamel integrals are Bochner integrable and the identities $u(r)=G(r-a)u(a)+\int_a^rK(r-s)(u(s),u(s))\,ds$ hold at $r=m$ and $r=t$. Then the integral from $m$ to $t$ is Bochner integrable and $u(t)=G(t-m)u(m)+\int_m^tK(t-s)(u(s),u(s))\,ds$. The endpoints may coincide. Only the two indicated initial-time identities are needed. Formula (3.13) allows independent continuous factors $f,h$ in the integrand; this formal statement treats the quadratic case $f=h=u$.
Breakdown.restrict.summary: If $u$ is continuous on $[a,t]$ and the quadratic Duhamel identity from $a$ holds at $r=m$ and $r=t$, with $a\le m\le t$, then it holds from $m$ to $t$ with Bochner integrability. (3.13) allows independent factors $f,h$; this treats $f=h=u$.

Breakdown.rowNorm.text:
For an integer $N\ge0$, arbitrary vector fields $F,e_1,\ldots,e_N$ on $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3$ and real weights $\tau_k$, put
$\displaystyle p_k=\int_{[0,1]}\int_{\mathbb R^3}F(\theta,y)\cdot e_k(\theta,y)\,dy\,d\theta,\qquad [F]=\sqrt{\sum_{k=1}^N\tau_k p_k^2}.$
The definition imposes no periodicity, measurability, integrability, orthogonality or sign condition. Each signed integral is assigned zero if its integrand is not integrable, and the real square root is assigned zero for a negative argument. For $F\in\mathcal H$ and under the certificate conditions, the $e_k$ belong to the period-one space $\mathcal H$, the $e_k$ are orthonormal, $0\le\tau_k\le c_0^2$ and $c_0\ge0$. Cauchy–Schwarz then makes every pairing finite, and the expression is a seminorm. Replacing each $e_k$ by $\sqrt{\tau_k}e_k$ gives the orthogonal fields in (7.17), whose norms are at most $c_0$, and gives the same seminorm. The bound $[F]\le c_0\|F\|_{\mathcal H}$ is proved separately. When $N=0$, the sum and the expression are zero. Without the sign and function-space hypotheses, no seminorm property is asserted.
Breakdown.rowNorm.summary: Defines $[F]=(\sum_k\tau_k\langle F,e_k\rangle_{\mathcal H}^2)^{1/2}$. The certificate uses orthonormal $e_k$ and $0\le\tau_k\le c_0^2$, while the paper puts $\sqrt{\tau_k}$ into each orthogonal field; the seminorms agree. A negative radicand gets square root zero.

Breakdown.secondDerivField.text: For W(θ,y), differentiate the map y↦DW(θ,y) once more. The result H(a,b) means the derivative in direction a of DW applied to b; its values are vectors in ℝ³. For C² W it is the usual spatial Hessian, symmetric in a,b, and its trace is ΔW. This encodes the second derivatives in Appendix B.2. The definition itself imposes neither C² regularity nor symmetry and uses assigned derivatives at points where differentiation fails.
Breakdown.secondDerivField.summary: The derivative of y↦DW(θ,y), with H(a,b) the derivative in direction a of DW applied to b. For C² W it is the usual symmetric spatial Hessian with trace ΔW; the definition imposes neither C² regularity nor symmetry.

Breakdown.secondDerivTrace.text: For a bilinear vector-valued map H on ℝ³×ℝ³, take ∑ⱼH(eⱼ,eⱼ)∈ℝ³. If H is the spatial Hessian of v, this is Δv, as in (7.14). A general H need not be a Hessian or be symmetric. The weak-derivative hypotheses in §7.1 supply that identification; the trace formula by itself supplies none of them.
Breakdown.secondDerivTrace.summary: ∑ⱼH(eⱼ,eⱼ)∈ℝ³ for a bilinear vector map H; if H is the spatial Hessian of v this is Δv, as in (7.14). H need not be a Hessian or symmetric.

Breakdown.shift.text: Let $\mathcal X$ be a real Banach space. Assume that $G(t)$, $t\geq0$, is a strongly continuous contraction semigroup, and that $K(\tau)$ is a symmetric bounded bilinear map on $\mathcal X$, continuous in $\tau>0$ on each pair of arguments. Assume $\|K(\tau)\|\leq C_K\tau^{-3/4}$ for $0<\tau\leq1$ and $G(s)K(\tau)=K(s+\tau)$ for $s\geq0$, $\tau>0$. For any $a,t,c\in\mathbb R$ and $u:\mathbb R\to\mathcal X$, the variation-of-constants identity from $a$ to $t$, including integrability of $K(t-s)(u(s),u(s))$, holds if and only if the corresponding identity for $s\mapsto u(s+c)$ holds from $a-c$ to $t-c$. Integrals use the oriented interval convention when the endpoints are reversed. For the application $a\leq t$ and $c=a$, this sets the initial time equal to zero.
Breakdown.shift.summary: Under the semigroup and kernel hypotheses, the variation-of-constants identity for $u$ from $a$ to $t$, including integrability of $K(t-s)(u(s),u(s))$, holds if and only if the identity for $s\mapsto u(s+c)$ holds from $a-c$ to $t-c$. With $c=a$ the initial time becomes zero.

Breakdown.shiftedFrequency.text: For a raw time-angular mode (n,k), similarity period S and a spatial angular rate a(y), the real number is Ω(y)=2πn/S+ka(y). With (n,k)=(2ι₂−ι₁,ϰι₁), this has the frequency in (B.15); that equation uses a spatially constant rate for each piece, whereas this earlier definition allows a(y). S need not be positive in the definition and 1/0 is assigned zero. Admissibility separately requires S>0 and the sign conditions used by the multiplier.
Breakdown.shiftedFrequency.summary: Ω(y)=2πn/S+ka(y) for raw mode (n,k); with (n,k)=(2ι₂−ι₁,ϰι₁) it is the frequency in (B.15), which uses a constant rate per piece while this earlier definition allows a(y). S need not be positive, with 1/0 taken as zero.

Integration by parts in three space dimensions changes the coefficient $	frac12\mathcal W$ and the dilation term into $-\mathcal W\cdot\varphi-	frac12\mathcal W\cdot(y\cdot

Breakdown.sigmaSimilarityIntegrand.summary: Defines −S⁻¹𝓦·∂θφ−𝓦·φ−½𝓦·(y·∇)φ+G:∇φ−∑ⱼ𝓦ⱼ𝓦·∂ⱼφ, with S⁻¹=0 at S=0. Its vanishing integrals against solenoidal tests give (7.1) modulo gradients when S>0, G=∇𝓦 weakly, 𝓦 is solenoidal and the terms are locally integrable.

Breakdown.sixthPowerGradientBound_four_t.text: For a vector field $u:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ with a locally integrable weak gradient $G=\nabla u$, assume $\int|u|^6<\infty$ and $\int|G|^2<\infty$. The formal statement proves $(\int|u|^6)^{1/3}\le(4/3)\int|G|^2$. Both sides are nonnegative; taking square roots gives $\|u\|_{L^6}\le(2/\sqrt3)\|\nabla u\|_{L^2}$. The squared pointwise gradient norm is the sum of squares of all nine entries. The coefficient field in (B.47) is measured in operator norm. No solenoidality or symmetry is assumed. Thus the constant and the inequality in (B.45) agree, and the formal statement also applies to vector fields outside $X$. The power $1/3$ is a real exponent applied to a finite nonnegative integral.
Breakdown.sixthPowerGradientBound_four_t.summary: For $u:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ with $\int|u|^6<\infty$ and weak gradient in $L^2$, $(\int|u|^6)^{1/3}\le(4/3)\int|\nabla u|^2$, so $\|u\|_{L^6}\le(2/\sqrt3)\|\nabla u\|_{L^2}$. This agrees with (B.45) and assumes no solenoidality or symmetry.

Breakdown.sliceGradientContinuous_holds.text:
Let $W:\mathbb R	imes\mathbb R^3	o\mathbb R^3$ and $q:\mathbb R	imes\mathbb R^3	o\mathbb R$ be smooth, solve $\partial_sW+	frac12W+	frac12(y\cdot
abla)W-\Delta W+(W\cdot
abla)W+
abla q=0$, and satisfy $\operatorname{div}W=0$. Assume, for one real $C$, $\|D_y^jW(s,y)\|\le C(1+|y|)^{-j-1}$ for the natural-number orders $j=0,1,2$ and $\|D_yq(s,y)\|\le C(1+|y|)^{-3}$, uniformly in $s,y$. The derivative norms here are operator norms; the paper’s pointwise gradient norm is the sum-of-squares norm of its coordinate derivatives.

The formal statement proves that for every $s_0\in\mathbb R$, $\int_{\mathbb R^3}\sum_{i=1}^3|\partial_i(W(s)-W(s_0))|^2\,dy	o0$ as $s	o s_0$. Thus the profile slices are continuous in the homogeneous $H^1$ norm whenever they are represented in the homogeneous $H^1$ space. The conclusion concerns similarity time, with no restriction to a period. It uses the summed squared coordinate derivatives, exactly the paper’s homogeneous $H^1$ norm; this differs from the operator norm used in the pointwise derivative hypothesis. The physical-time continuity in Proposition 4.1 also uses continuous dependence of the dilation on $t<1$.
Breakdown.sliceGradientContinuous_holds.summary: For the smooth decaying similarity profile, $\int_{\mathbb R^3}\sum_i|\partial_i(W(s)-W(s_0))|^2\,dy\to0$ as $s\to s_0$, for every $s_0$. So the slices are continuous in similarity time for the homogeneous $H^1$ norm $\|\nabla u\|_{L^2}$.

Breakdown.stationaryEnergy.text: For spatial weak derivatives $G=\nabla u$ and $H=\nabla^2u$, this definition is $\int_{\mathbb R^3}|\operatorname{tr}H|^2+\int_{\mathbb R^3}w|G|_{\rm F}^2$. If $u\in\dot H^1_{\mathrm{div}}\cap L^6$, $\Delta u\in L^2$, and $w$ is measurable, bounded and positive, both integrals are finite and this equals $|u|_w^2$ in (7.14). The first integral measures the Laplacian, since $\operatorname{tr}H=\Delta u$; the gradient uses the Frobenius norm. There is no time integral or force coefficient. Outside integrability hypotheses, a signed integral in the definition has the value zero.
Breakdown.stationaryEnergy.summary: Defines $\int_{\mathbb R^3}|\operatorname{tr}H|^2+\int_{\mathbb R^3}w|G|_{\rm F}^2$ for $G=\nabla u$, $H=\nabla^2u$; for $u\in\dot H^1_{\mathrm{div}}\cap L^6$ with $\Delta u\in L^2$ and a bounded positive measurable weight it equals $|u|_w^2$ in (7.14). There is no time integral.

Breakdown.stepData.text:
Assume the spectral dichotomy assertion: every bounded operator on a real Hilbert space that is a compact perturbation of an operator of norm at most $b$, for $0\le b\le\alpha<\beta$, admits a commuting finite-rank projection and geometric forward and inverse bounds at radii $\alpha<r_1<r_2<\beta$. Under that additional theorem-level premise, the following assertion is proved. Let $X$ be a real Hilbert space with the heat and bilinear operators of §3.4: $G(t)$ is a strongly continuous contraction semigroup, $K(\tau)$ is symmetric, continuous for $\tau>0$, obeys $G(s)K(\tau)=K(s+\tau)$ and $\|K(\tau)\|\le C_K\tau^{-3/4}$ for $0<\tau\le1$. Suppose the dilations satisfy $D_1=I$, $D_\mu D_\nu=D_{\mu\nu}$, $\|D_\mu x\|=\mu^{1/4}\|x\|$, $D_\mu G(\mu t)=G(t)D_\mu$, and $\mu D_\mu K(\mu\tau)(x,y)=K(\tau)(D_\mu x,D_\mu y)$ for positive scales, with continuous dependence on scale. Assume $K(\tau)(f,\cdot)$ is compact for a dense set of $f$ and every $\tau>0$.

Let $S>0$, let $\rho$ be a surjective linear isometry commuting with $G$, $K$ and $D$, and let $w:\mathbb R\to X$ be continuous, nonzero at some time, with $w(s+S)=\rho w(s)$ and the similarity-time mild equation. Here that equation uses $\mathcal S(a)=D_{e^{-a}}G(1-e^{-a})$ and $\mathcal K(a)=D_{e^{-a}}K(1-e^{-a})$ and reads $w(s)=\mathcal S(s-s_0)w(s_0)+\int_{s_0}^{s}\mathcal K(s-r)(w(r),w(r))\,dr$ for $s_0\le s$.

For any dense linear subspace $C\subset X$ and any $t_0>0$, the formal statement asserts the existence of a positive natural $k$ and $\theta$ with $L=1-e^{-S/k}\le t_0$ and $e^{-S/(4k)}<\theta<1$. Put $A_n v=2\mathcal B_L(u_n,v)$ where $u_n(\sigma)=D_{(1-\sigma)^{-1}}w(nS/k-\log(1-\sigma))$ on $[0,L]$, $\Gamma x(\sigma)=G(\sigma)x$ and $\operatorname{Ev}v=D_{e^{-S/k}}v(L)$. All $\|A_n\|\le1/4$. There are a finite-dimensional $V\subset X$, a bounded linear $J:X\to X$ with range in $C$, and a bounded linear $\mathcal R:\ell^\infty(C([0,L];X))\to X\times\ell^\infty(C([0,L];X))$ such that, writing $(e,z)=\mathcal Rg$, one has $e\in V$, $z_0-A_0z_0-\Gamma Je=g_0$, and $z_n-A_nz_n-\theta^{-1}\Gamma\operatorname{Ev}z_{n-1}=g_n$ for $n\ge1$. The norm on each curve is its supremum norm.

The physical correction space is $J(V)\subset C$, not necessarily $V$. Boundedness of $\mathcal R$ controls the product norm $\max(\|e\|,\sup_n\|z_n\|)$; controlling $Je$ also uses $\|J\|$. This is a sequence formulation, rather than the global weighted-curve statement of Proposition 4.3. Here $\mathcal B_L(f,g)(\sigma)=\int_0^\sigma K(\sigma-r)(f(r),g(r))\,dr$ for continuous curves on $[0,L]$, and the norm of each input or output curve is the supremum norm on that interval.
Breakdown.stepData.summary: Assuming the spectral dichotomy, a periodic mild orbit $w$, dense $C$ and $t_0>0$ give $k$, $\theta$ with $L\le t_0$, all $\|A_n\|\le1/4$, finite-dimensional $V$, $J$ with range in $C$, and a bounded right inverse $\mathcal R$ on interval sequences: a sequence form of Proposition 4.3.

Breakdown.stepMap.text: Let $X,Y$ be real normed spaces, $A_n:Y\to Y$, $\Gamma:X\to Y$ and $\operatorname{Ev}:Y\to X$ bounded and linear. The formal object is $S_n=\operatorname{Ev}(I-A_n)^{-1}\Gamma$. When $I-A_n$ is invertible, it maps an initial datum to the rescaled endpoint of its linearized solution. In the fluid application $Y=C([0,L];X)$, $\Gamma x(t)=G(t)x$ and $\operatorname{Ev}v=D_\mu v(L)$. The inverse in this definition is total: if the operator is not invertible as a bounded operator, its assigned inverse is zero. Consequently the definition alone does not prove that the linearized problem is solvable. The monodromy theorem assumes $\|A_n\|\le1/4$ and deduces invertibility before using this map. The separate subdivision theorem chooses short intervals for which that bound holds. A whole-period monodromy also requires multiplying the $k$ successive maps and applying $\rho^{-1}$.
Breakdown.stepMap.summary: Defines $S_n=\operatorname{Ev}(I-A_n)^{-1}\Gamma$, the map from an initial datum to the rescaled endpoint of its linearized solution. The inverse is taken as zero when $I-A_n$ is not invertible, so the definition alone gives no solvability; the monodromy theorem assumes $\|A_n\|\le1/4$.

Breakdown.stretchForm.text: At (θ,y), let ω=curl v, let 𝕊 be the symmetric part of DW, and use the ordinary second spatial derivatives of W to form ∇curl W. The scalar is J=−ω·𝕊ω+((v·∇)curl W)·ω+½∑ⱼ∇(curl W)ⱼ·(v×∂ⱼv), with ∂ⱼv represented by the supplied matrix G. This is exactly the sign and order of the three terms in (B.18) when G=∇v and W is C². The density has no fixed sign. The bare definition imposes neither regularity nor integrability; derivative default values do not replace those analytic assumptions.
Breakdown.stretchForm.summary: J=−ω·𝕊ω+((v·∇)curl W)·ω+½∑ⱼ∇(curl W)ⱼ·(v×∂ⱼv), with ω=curl v, 𝕊 the symmetric part of DW and ∂ⱼv given by G; it is exactly (B.18) when G=∇v and W is C². J has no fixed sign, and no regularity or integrability is imposed.

Breakdown.sumSecondPartialsAt.text: For v:ℝ³→ℝ³, this is the vector ∑ᵢD²v(x)[eᵢ,eᵢ]. For a twice differentiable field it equals the componentwise Laplacian Δv in (1.1), with the positive sum-of-second-derivatives convention. The index of differentiation is the natural number 2. The formula is defined for arbitrary v through derivatives assigned default values where the required derivatives fail to exist; it supplies no regularity hypothesis. It is therefore the same Laplacian only under the regularity assumptions used for solutions and smooth profiles.
Breakdown.sumSecondPartialsAt.summary: ∑ᵢD²v(x)[eᵢ,eᵢ], which equals the componentwise Laplacian Δv in (1.1) for twice differentiable v. Derivatives take default values where they fail to exist, so no regularity is supplied.

Breakdown.supBoundFactor.text: For a real number $w_*$, this definition sets $c_w=1/\sqrt{2\pi(2\sqrt{w_*})}$. Under the certificate hypothesis $w_*>0$, this is the positive number $(4\pi\sqrt{w_*})^{-1/2}$ appearing in (7.15) and (7.48). The square roots here are the nonnegative real square roots. The definition accepts every real input, and the formal convention gives $\sqrt{w_*}=0$ when $w_*\le0$ and $1/0=0$; hence $c_w=0$ in that unused range. Positivity of $w_*$ excludes this extension wherever the spatial or period estimates are applied. The definition supplies only the numerical coefficient; it proves no estimate for a velocity, a derivative or a convection term.
Breakdown.supBoundFactor.summary: Defines $c_w=1/\sqrt{2\pi(2\sqrt{w_*})}$, which for $w_*>0$ is $(4\pi\sqrt{w_*})^{-1/2}$ as in (7.15) and (7.48). For $w_*\le0$ the conventions $\sqrt{w_*}=0$ and $1/0=0$ give $c_w=0$, a range never used.

Breakdown.symPartForm.text: For a real matrix G and vector u∈ℝ³, the value is u·Gu. Since u·(G−Gᵀ)u=0, this equals u·((G+Gᵀ)/2)u. Thus, when G=∇W, it is the quadratic form of the symmetric strain in (B.18). No symmetry of G or derivative origin is assumed in the definition. A bound on this scalar for all u controls the symmetric part; it does not by itself bound the full matrix norm.
Breakdown.symPartForm.summary: u·Gu, equal to u·((G+Gᵀ)/2)u; when G=∇W it is the strain quadratic form in (B.18). No symmetry of G is assumed, and a bound for all u controls only the symmetric part.

Breakdown.transferHolds_of_dichotomy.text: This transfer proof supplies the intermediate evolution estimates while retaining the spectral dichotomy as an explicit hypothesis.

Breakdown.unitVector.text: For i=0,1,2, eᵢ is the vector in ℝ³ with coordinate i equal to one and the other coordinates zero. These are the standard orthonormal coordinate directions used to form divergence, gradient and Laplacian in (1.1). The paper's directions numbered 1,2,3 correspond respectively to the formal directions 0,1,2. No coordinate or direction is omitted.
Breakdown.unitVector.summary: For i=0,1,2, eᵢ has coordinate i equal to one and the others zero: the standard directions used for divergence, gradient and Laplacian in (1.1). The paper's directions 1,2,3 correspond to 0,1,2.

Breakdown.varConstIntegral.text:
Let $\mathcal X$ be a real Banach space with a strongly continuous contraction semigroup $G(t)$ for $t\ge0$ and symmetric bounded bilinear operators $K(\tau)$, continuous for $\tau>0$, with $G(s)K(\tau)=K(s+\tau)$ for $s\ge0$, $\tau>0$, and $\|K(\tau)\|\le C_K\tau^{-3/4}$ for $0<\tau\le1$. In the paper $G(t)=e^{t\Delta}$.

Let $a\le b$, and let $u,v:\mathbb R\to\mathcal X$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ with $\|u(s)\|\le M$ and $\|v(s)\|\le N$ there.

The formal statement proves integrability of $s\mapsto K(t-s)(u(s),v(s))$ on $[a,t]$ for each $t\in[a,b]$, continuity of its integral as a function of $t$ on $[a,b]$, and $\|\int_a^tK(t-s)(u(s),v(s))\,ds\|\le4C_K(t-a)^{1/4}MN$ whenever $t-a\le1$. The value at $s=t$ has no effect on the integral. The estimate is in the ordinary norm, using constant bounds on the two input curves. It does not include the blow-up weights or the infinite-range integral of (4.18).
Breakdown.varConstIntegral.summary: For $u,v$ continuous on $[a,b]$ with $\|u\|\le M$, $\|v\|\le N$, $K(t-s)(u(s),v(s))$ is integrable on $[a,t]$, its integral is continuous in $t$, and its norm is at most $4C_K(t-a)^{1/4}MN$ for $t-a\le1$. It omits the blow-up weights of (4.18).

Breakdown.vecNorm.text: For a vector x of k real coefficients, with k any nonnegative integer, the value is (∑ᵢxᵢ²)¹ᐟ². It is the Euclidean norm |β| and the norm |ℓ(v)| used in §7.3, not a maximum norm or an infinite sequence norm. If k=0 the sum is empty and the value is zero, consistent with the paper's allowance n=0. The square root always has nonnegative argument.
Breakdown.vecNorm.summary: (∑ᵢxᵢ²)¹ᐟ² for k real coefficients, the Euclidean norms |β| and |ℓ(v)| of §7.3. If k=0 the value is zero, consistent with the paper's allowance n=0.

Breakdown.vortGrad.text: For a bilinear vector-valued map H, the (j,m) entry is ∑ₐ,ᵦεⱼₐᵦH(eₘ,eₐ)ᵦ. If H is the Hessian of W, it equals ∂ₘ(curl W)ⱼ, the vorticity derivative in (B.18). The vector component is j and the differentiation direction is m. Without a Hessian hypothesis the declaration defines only this tensor contraction, not a derivative identity.
Breakdown.vortGrad.summary: The (j,m) entry ∑ₐ,ᵦεⱼₐᵦH(eₘ,eₐ)ᵦ for a bilinear vector map H; if H is the Hessian of W it equals ∂ₘ(curl W)ⱼ, the vorticity derivative in (B.18). Otherwise it is only this contraction.

Breakdown.weakDefectField.text: Given a period S, approximate velocity W, a supplied Hessian Hᵃ, a supplied pressure-gradient representative h, forcing fields bᵢ and coefficients βᵢᵃ, the residual is S⁻¹∂θW+½W+½(y·∇)W−tr Hᵃ+(W·∇)W+∑ᵢβᵢᵃbᵢ+h. This specifies Fᵃ in (7.10) for the C¹ piecewise-polynomial profiles of Appendix B.1. Hᵃ=∇²W distributionally and the vanishing of h against solenoidal tests are separate hypotheses. No scalar pressure is required by this formula. S is an arbitrary real argument, with 1/0 assigned zero; valid certificates require S>0.
Breakdown.weakDefectField.summary: The residual S⁻¹∂θW+½W+½(y·∇)W−tr Hᵃ+(W·∇)W+∑ᵢβᵢᵃbᵢ+h, which specifies Fᵃ in (7.10) for the C¹ profiles of Appendix B.1. Hᵃ=∇²W and the vanishing of h on solenoidal tests are separate hypotheses; at S=0, 1/0 is zero.

Breakdown.weakSimilarityIntegrand.text: For profile W, a proposed weak spatial gradient G, and solenoidal compactly supported space-time test φ, the scalar integrand is −W·∂ₛφ−W·φ−½W·(y·∇)φ+∑ᵢ(G eᵢ)·∂ᵢφ−∑ᵢWᵢ W·∂ᵢφ. If G is the distributional gradient of W, W is solenoidal, and the displayed integrand is integrable, requiring its integral to vanish for every such test is the distributional velocity equation in (1.2), tested modulo spatial gradients. Solenoidality is needed to write the nonlinear term in divergence form and remains a separate condition. The coefficient −1 of W·φ combines +½W with the −3/2 produced by integration by parts in the three-dimensional drift. The definition alone neither identifies G with ∇W nor asserts integrability; both are imposed in the weak-profile condition of §7.10.
Breakdown.weakSimilarityIntegrand.summary: The integrand $-W\cdot\partial_s\varphi-W\cdot\varphi-\tfrac12W\cdot(y\cdot\nabla)\varphi+\sum_i(Ge_i)\cdot\partial_i\varphi-\sum_iW_iW\cdot\partial_i\varphi$; with $G=\nabla W$, $W$ solenoidal and integrability, imposed elsewhere, its vanishing integral is (1.2) tested modulo gradients.

Breakdown.weightedEnergy.text: For a weight $w$, a weak gradient $G=\nabla v$ and a weak Hessian $H=\nabla^2v$, the expression is $\int_{[0,1]}\int_{\mathbb R^3}(|\operatorname{tr}H|^2+w|G|_{\rm F}^2)$, provided this density is nonnegative and the integral is finite. It is then exactly $\|v\|_w^2$ in (7.14), with $\operatorname{tr}H=\Delta v$. Formally negative densities are truncated to zero before integration and an infinite integral is converted to zero. For an admissible perturbation and bounded measurable $w\ge w_*>0$, these conventions do not alter the value. The coefficient term $\omega^2|\beta|^2$ is separate.
Breakdown.weightedEnergy.summary: Defines $\int_{[0,1]}\int(|\operatorname{tr}H|^2+w|G|_{\rm F}^2)$, equal to $\|v\|_w^2$ in (7.14) for $G=\nabla v$, $H=\nabla^2v$. Negative densities are truncated and an infinite integral is set to zero; for admissible perturbations and weights these conventions change nothing.

exists_weakly_convergent_subseq.text: Let $E$ be a real Hilbert space, let $u_k\in E$, and assume $\|u_k\|\leq C$ for all natural-number indices $k$. The formal statement gives a strictly increasing sequence of indices $k_j$ and $u\in E$ with $\|u\|\leq C$ such that $\langle u_{k_j},z\rangle\to\langle u,z\rangle$ for every $z\in E$. This last quantified identity is the meaning of weak convergence. No separability of the whole Hilbert space is assumed: the proof works inside the separable closed linear span of the sequence. Applying the result to the solenoidal forcing space gives the weak subsequence for $f_k$. The finite-dimensional subsequence for the multipliers is another compactness step.
exists_weakly_convergent_subseq.summary: In a real Hilbert space, a sequence with $\|u_k\|\le C$ has a subsequence converging weakly to some $u$ with $\|u\|\le C$. No separability of the whole space is assumed.

mem_of_weak_limit.text: Let $E$ be a real Hilbert space and $K\subset E$ be convex and closed for its norm topology. If $u_k\in K$ for every $k$ and $\langle u_k,z\rangle\to\langle u,z\rangle$ for every $z\in E$, then the formal statement concludes $u\in K$. The hypotheses need neither compactness nor a chosen bound on the sequence. In the paper's application $K$ is the closed subspace of periodic solenoidal fields invariant under $\Gamma$, so a weak limit retains the prescribed symmetries. The declaration does not itself construct a weakly convergent subsequence.
mem_of_weak_limit.summary: In a real Hilbert space, if $K$ is convex and norm-closed, $u_k\in K$ and $u_k\rightharpoonup u$, then $u\in K$. Applied to the invariant periodic solenoidal fields, a weak limit keeps the prescribed symmetries.
